FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF SALAKHOV AND ISLYAMOVA v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 28005/08)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

14 March 2013

FINAL

14/06/2013

This judgment became final pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention and may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Mark Villiger, President,
Angelika Nußberger,
Boštjan M. Zupančič,
Ganna Yudkivska,
André Potocki,
Paul Lemmens,
Aleš Pejchal, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having considered the case in private on 12 February 2013,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 28005/08, lodged against Ukraine before the Court on 8 June 2008 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Linar Irekovich Salakhov, a Ukrainian national (“the first applicant”). After the first applicant died on 2 August 2008, his mother, Ms Aliya Fazylovna Islyamova, who is likewise a Ukrainian national (“the second applicant”), stated on 1 September 2008 that she wished to continue the application on his behalf and added complaints of her own to the case.

2. Mr A. Lesovoy, a lawyer practising in Simferopol, represented the applicants. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented most recently by their Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.

3. Relying on Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, the applicants alleged that the first applicant had not had access to prompt and adequate medical treatment while detained, thereby placing his life at risk. They further maintained that the State authorities had failed to arrange his immediate admission to hospital, despite the interim measure indicated by the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. Following her son’s death, the second applicant held the authorities responsible. In addition to those complaints, she objected to his being handcuffed while in hospital and alleged that no effective domestic investigation had been conducted into his death. Finally, invoking Article 3 of the Convention, she complained of the suffering she herself had endured in connection with those events.

4. On 7 September 2009, the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice to the Government of the complaints under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention concerning the first applicant. It was further decided, pursuant to Article 29 § 1, to examine the application’s admissibility and merits jointly.

5. On 29 May 2012, acting under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, the Chamber invited the parties to provide additional written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application, specifically concerning the second applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention and the State’s observance of the interim measure indicated by the Court.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6.
The first applicant, born in 1981, died on 2 August 2008. The second applicant was born in 1955 and resides in the Crimean town of Zuya.

A. Background information

7. The first applicant tested positive for HIV on 30 September 2005.

8. On 2 February 2006, the Centre for the Prevention and Combating of Aids in Crimea (“the Aids Centre”) notified him of the result and asked him to register for medical supervision. He did not follow that recommendation (see also paragraphs 21 and 59 below).

B. Criminal proceedings against the first applicant and his medical treatment in detention

9. On 20 November 2007, the police arrested the first applicant on suspicion of stealing a mobile telephone from an acquaintance. The second applicant stated that her son told the investigator that same day that he was HIV-positive and voiced concern that detention could cause his health to worsen. She alleged that this information was disregarded. The Government, however, maintained that the first applicant had not revealed his HIV status.

10. He was taken to the Temporary Detention Facility at the Bakhchysaray Police Station (“the ITT”). Following an examination, the duty officer recorded that the first applicant had no visible injuries and had made no complaints.

11. On 23 November 2007, the Bakhchysaray District Court (“the Bakhchysaray Court”) ordered that the first applicant remain in custody pending trial.

12. An X-ray performed at the local polyclinic on 30 November 2007 disclosed no lung abnormalities.

13. On 2 December 2007, the first applicant was transferred from the ITT to Simferopol Pre-Trial Detention Centre no. 15 (“the SIZO”). There, he was examined by a therapist (general practitioner), dermatologist, dentist and psychiatrist, all of whom assessed him as being in good health. His medical records indicated that he neither complained of health problems nor disclosed any illnesses. He was recorded as being 180 cm tall and weighing 78 kg.

14. The first applicant was held in the SIZO during three periods: from 2 to 28 December 2007, from 10 January to 10 February 2008, and from 18 February to 2 June 2008. In the intervals—from 28 December 2007 to 10 January 2008, from 10 to 18 February 2008, and from 2 to 20 June 2008—he was detained in the ITT.

15. Medical examination records dated 10 January and 10 and 18 February 2008 described him as apparently healthy and noted that he had made no health-related complaints.

16. Entries in the SIZO medical register show that, on 28, 29 and 30 May 2008, the first applicant reported a blocked nose, rhinitis and a sore throat. The SIZO therapist diagnosed an “acute respiratory viral infection” and prescribed medication.

17. The case file contains no documentation covering the interval between the medical records of 18 February and 28 May 2008. The applicants nevertheless asserted that the first applicant’s condition had deteriorated sharply in early March 2008.
He was allegedly suffering from a persistent fever of 39-40ºC and severe digestive problems. The applicants stated that staff at the detention facilities repeatedly called an ambulance because of his condition, although the nature of the assistance provided remained unclear.

18. On 31 May 2008, an infectious-disease specialist also examined the first applicant at the SIZO. In a note, the specialist recorded that the first applicant had complained of fever and weight loss over the previous two months. The doctor recommended an HIV test, to which the first applicant consented, and scheduled it for 2 June 2008. The test was not performed, however, because the first applicant was transferred from the SIZO to the ITT (see paragraph 14 above).

19. Following another transfer from the SIZO to the ITT on 2 June 2008, the first applicant reported weakness, fever and back pain to the ITT medical attendant, who gave him antipyretic medication.

20. On 3 June 2008, the first applicant was taken to the Central Hospital. A therapist examined him, and ultrasound scans were performed on his liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and kidneys. He also underwent a chest X-ray, an electrocardiogram, an esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and general blood and urine tests. The therapist diagnosed an ulcer, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, haemorrhoids and chronic bronchitis, and suspected HIV infection.

21. Responding to the second applicant’s enquiry of 3 June 2008, the Chief Doctor of the Aids Centre informed her on 4 June 2008 that her son had tested positive for HIV on 30 September 2005 and had been notified of the result on 2 February 2006, but had not been registered for monitoring at the Centre.

22. The first applicant was taken back to the Central Hospital on 5 June 2008 to be examined by an infectious-disease specialist. According to the doctor’s note, he complained of abdominal pain, lesions in his mouth, a skin rash, coughing and shortness of breath. He also reported losing approximately 10 kg over the previous three months. After examining him, the doctor diagnosed pneumocystis pneumonia, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiosis (thrush), and an ulcer. The doctor further concluded that his symptoms indicated fourth-stage clinical HIV infection. Although the first applicant’s condition was assessed as “moderately severe” and treatment was considered necessary for the diagnosed conditions, the overall conclusion was that urgent hospitalisation was not required.

23. The first applicant’s mother was notified of the diagnoses. She purchased the prescribed medicines, which the ITT medical attendant then administered to her son.

24.
On 6 June 2008, counsel for the first applicant applied to the Bakhchysaray Court for his client’s release on the grounds of his critical health. He submitted that the first applicant urgently needed specialist medical care, as he had fourth-stage HIV infection accompanied by oesophageal candidosis and pneumocystis pneumonia. According to the lawyer, the first applicant’s life was at imminent risk, and his release was necessary to enable him to obtain adequate treatment. Counsel further emphasised that his client had a permanent residence, had never attempted to evade the investigation or obstruct it, and, in view of his extremely poor health, posed no threat to society.

25. The Bakhchysaray Court dismissed the application. Its ruling is not contained in the case file before the Court.

26. On 11 June 2008, the Bakhchysaray District Prosecutor’s Office directed the local police department to bring the first applicant to the Central Hospital for a further medical assessment to determine whether his condition was compatible with continued detention.

27. On 13 June 2008, the first applicant was taken to the Central Hospital and re-examined by an infectious-disease specialist. The doctor provisionally diagnosed second-stage HIV infection and concluded that immediate hospitalisation was not required. He recommended an additional assessment at the Aids Centre to determine the appropriate course of treatment. The doctor also arranged laboratory investigations, including blood and urine tests, a blood-sugar test and a chest X-ray.

28. On 16 June 2008, the applicants asked the Court to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and indicate to the Ukrainian Government that, owing to the serious deterioration in the first applicant’s health and the alleged absence of adequate medical care, he should be hospitalised and treated urgently.

29. On 17 June 2008, the President of the Fifth Section allowed the request and, pursuant to Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicated to the respondent Government that the first applicant “should be transferred immediately to a hospital or other medical institution where he [could] receive the appropriate treatment for his medical condition until further notice.” The Government were notified of that decision by fax on the same day, which was a Tuesday and a working day.

30. On 18 June 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer lodged a renewed application for his release with the Bakhchysaray Court. He again maintained that his client’s life was in danger and also relied on the Court’s above-mentioned decision to apply Rule 39 in the first applicant’s case.

31.
On 18 June 2008, in response to a further inquiry from the Bakhchysaray police as to whether the first applicant needed to be admitted to hospital, the head of the Central Hospital’s Infectious Diseases Department stated that no urgent hospitalisation was required. 32. Consequently, the Bakhchysaray Court dismissed the first applicant’s application for release, which he had lodged earlier that day. 33. Also on 18 June 2008, the second applicant complained to the Central Hospital’s Chief Doctor that, despite her requests of 4 and 5 June and her two applications of 13 June 2008, the hospital staff had allegedly failed to provide her son with adequate medical care. She maintained that his life was at risk. In her account, he had never received a comprehensive medical examination, and the doctors were reluctant to treat him both because he was HIV-positive and because he was being detained. 34. On 20 June 2008, the first applicant was brought to the Aids Centre. There, doctors made the following preliminary diagnoses: fourth-stage HIV infection; systemic candidosis affecting the oropharynx and oesophagus; persistent fever accompanied by pronounced intoxication syndrome; loss of more than 15% of body weight; and seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp. The Aids Centre’s doctors found that further examinations were necessary to clarify those diagnoses and that he required in-patient treatment. 35. Later that day, the first applicant was admitted to the Central Hospital and placed in a ward guarded by police. The second applicant alleged that her son remained handcuffed to his bed at all times. She provided the Court with two photographs taken on 25 June 2008, both of which showed his left hand secured by a handcuff to the hospital bed. A letter dated 23 October 2009 from the First Deputy Minister of Public Health to the Government Agent (see also paragraph 67 below), referring to the first applicant’s Central Hospital medical records, confirmed that he had arrived at the hospital in handcuffs on 20 June 2008. The records did not, however, indicate whether he had remained handcuffed for the entire duration of his treatment there. 36. At some time on 20 June 2008, the first applicant provided the police with an “explanatory note”. In it, he stated that, “for understandable reasons”, he had not disclosed his HIV infection to either the SIZO or the ITT authorities. After his mother informed them that he might have that condition, he had been medically examined at the Central Hospital on 5 and 13 June 2008 and prescribed certain medicines, which were subsequently administered to him in the ITT by the medical attendant. He further declared that he had no complaints concerning the ITT staff. The second applicant, however, asserted that her son had been forced to write the note. 37.
On 24 June 2008, the first applicant prepared a further note stating that he had begun to feel ill while in detention, although the date on which this had occurred is illegible in the available copy. He explained that, owing to a persistent fever and pain in his kidneys, liver and intestines, he had asked to be examined by a therapist. Instead, a medical attendant had been sent to see him and had done no more than provide antipyretic medication. When his condition failed to improve, the attendant began giving him injections of ceftriaxone, an antibiotic, at some point between 22 and 25 May 2008. Nevertheless, his fever and back pain continued. Consequently, he was admitted to the SIZO hospital on 29 May 2008, but his treatment remained unchanged. After being transferred to the ITT, he began taking other medicines purchased by his mother on 4 June 2008.

38. Also on 24 June 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer submitted another request for his client’s release, citing the severity of his condition and the prosecutor’s lack of opposition to release.

39. That same day, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor asked the judge hearing the first applicant’s criminal case to advance the hearing scheduled for 3 July 2008. He referred to the first applicant’s “critical condition” and the need for treatment at Simferopol Hospital no. 7, a facility specialising in Aids treatment (“Hospital no. 7”). The prosecutor stressed that the above-mentioned release request required prompt examination.

40. On an unspecified date, possibly 4 July 2008 (see paragraph 47 below), the Bakhchysaray Court refused the request for the first applicant’s release.

41. On 26 June 2008, the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital replied to the second applicant’s complaint that her son had allegedly not received the medical care he required. He stated that the medical records available were inadequate to assess how the illness had progressed over time. According to him, the requests made to the Hospital for medical assistance had been contextual in nature, and the necessary care had been duly provided.

42. Later that day, the first applicant was transferred from the Central Hospital to Hospital no. 7.

43. An extract from his records at Hospital no. 7 listed the diagnoses made by the Aids Centre on 20 June 2008 (see paragraph 34 above), together with pneumocystis pneumonia, second-degree anaemia, severe immunosuppression, with a CD4 count[1] of 48 cells/mm3, and encephalitis of uncertain origin. Toxic hepatitis, hepatolienal syndrome, superficial gastritis and duodenogastric reflux were additionally recorded as concurrent conditions.

44. In a letter dated 23 October 2009 to the Government Agent (see also paragraph 67 below), the First Deputy Minister of Public Health also referred to information supplied by the management of Hospital no.
7, the first applicant was handcuffed while receiving treatment at Hospital no. 7 between 26 June and 18 July 2008. The above-mentioned letter also indicated, however, that no information was available as to whether he had remained handcuffed throughout that period.

45. On 2 July 2008, the Governor of the ITT considered the second applicant’s complaint that her son had allegedly not been provided with the necessary medical care. He decided not to institute a criminal investigation, observing that the first applicant had concealed his HIV-positive status from the administration and that, in any event, he had received adequate medical treatment while detained in the ITT.

46. That same day, the Chief Doctor of Hospital no. 7 informed the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police Department in writing that the first applicant required prolonged medical treatment and freedom of movement, and that any disruption of his treatment would cause his health to deteriorate sharply.

47. On 4 July 2008, the Bakhchysaray Court convicted the first applicant of fraud, rather than robbery as charged by the prosecution (see paragraph 9 above), and imposed a fine of 850 Ukrainian hryvnias, then equivalent to 115 euros. The judgment specified that he was to remain in detention until it became final.

48. Hospital no. 7 began administering antiretroviral therapy to the first applicant on 10 July 2008. According to information contained in the Public Health Ministry’s letter of 23 October 2009 to the Government Agent, the first applicant had apparently refused the prescribed medication on one occasion.

49. Also on 10 July 2008, the second applicant asked the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police Department to permit her to visit and care for her son in hospital because of his critical condition. She further complained to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor that the first applicant was being kept continuously handcuffed and requested that the measure be ended.

50. In a reply dated 15 July 2008, the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police informed the second applicant that her son would soon be released in any event, once the judgment of 4 July 2008 had become final.

51. On 18 July 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer likewise requested that the handcuffs be removed. He stated that it was already evident that his client was dying, yet he continued to be guarded by two police officers in a hospital ward with barred windows and remained handcuffed to his bed. In the lawyer’s view, those security arrangements were both unjustified and inhuman. He also reported that, according to the second applicant, some of the officers guarding her son had mockingly suggested installing a cable in the ward and handcuffing him to it, so that his movements would be “practically unrestrained”.

C. The first applicant’s medical treatment following his release from detention and his death

52.
On 18 July 2008, apparently because the judgment of 4 July had become final, the police discontinued the security measures concerning the first applicant, and the second applicant brought him home. In a note to the administration of Hospital no. 7, she stated that she was taking her son home “for family reasons”.

53. The next day, following a deterioration in his condition, the first applicant was readmitted to Hospital no. 7.

54. On 1 August 2008, the second applicant once more took him home after submitting to the hospital administration a note similar to the one she had written on 18 July 2008.

55. The first applicant died on 2 August 2008.

D. Inquiry into the first applicant’s death

56. After her son’s death, the second applicant lodged a complaint with the prosecution authorities, alleging that he had not received timely and adequate medical care while in detention and that this failure had caused his death.

57. On 20 January 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor notified her that the ITT governor’s decision of 2 July 2008 (see paragraph 45 above) had been set aside and that the inquiry into the medical assistance afforded to the first applicant had been reopened.

58. On 17 February 2009, the Ministry of Public Health established a commission to examine the matter.

59. The commission delivered its official investigation report on 20 March 2009. It found that the doctors at the Central Hospital were not responsible for the first applicant’s death. The report observed that, as early as 2 February 2006, the Aids Centre had informed the first applicant that he was HIV-positive and had explained the need for medical supervision, but that he had not undergone any medical examinations or monitoring. Consequently, antiretroviral treatment had not been initiated promptly, which complicated the course of the disease. The commission’s general conclusions were:

“1. Responsibility for providing medical care to persons in custody rests with police medical personnel.

2. Central Hospital specialists do not examine or provide medical consultations to detainees unless requested to do so by staff of the [detention facilities].

3. At the Central Hospital, the [first applicant] received examinations, specialist consultations, laboratory testing and treatment in full compliance with the approved standards.

4. The decline in [his] health and the ensuing complications resulted from his delay in seeking medical care after testing HIV-positive, together with the severity of the principal illness, which caused irreversible processes in [his] body.”

60. On 23 March 2009, the second applicant submitted a further complaint to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor. In particular, she challenged as unjustified the infectious-disease specialist’s conclusion of 13 June 2008 that her son had not required urgent hospitalisation at that time (see paragraph 27 above).

61.
On 31 March 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor declined to bring criminal proceedings against either the police or the Central Hospital staff, concluding that the second applicant’s allegations were unfounded.

62. On 3 April 2009, that decision was set aside by the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor on the ground that additional inquiries were necessary. These were to include interviews with the second applicant, members of the ITT staff and the doctors involved at the Central Hospital.

63. The prosecutor interviewed the second applicant on 4 May 2009. She stated that her son’s health had begun to worsen dramatically in March 2008 and that he had not been given timely and appropriate medical care. In her account, the detention-facility authorities had done no more than summon an ambulance several times. She requested that all medical records concerning her son—from the ITT, the SIZO, the Central Hospital and Hospital no. 7—be obtained and examined in order to assess his medical needs and the measures actually taken in response to them from November 2007 onwards.

64. On 25 May 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor again refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police or Central Hospital personnel, finding that their conduct disclosed no corpus delicti. In reaching that conclusion, he relied in particular on the findings of the commission of the Ministry of Public Health (see paragraph 59 above), together with statements made by police officers and doctors.

65. The Bakhchysaray Court upheld that decision on 18 August 2009. It observed that the first applicant had not personally made any complaints against the police or medical personnel. The court also considered that the authorities appeared to have provided him with adequate medical care as soon as they became aware that he was HIV-positive.

66. On 13 October 2009, the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea (“the Crimea Court of Appeal”) allowed the second applicant’s appeal and quashed the ruling of 18 August 2009. It faulted the investigation, notably because it had failed to examine the first applicant’s health or determine what medical assistance, if any, he had received while in detention between 20 November 2007 and early June 2008. The appellate court further observed that the contested ruling had been issued by the first-instance court in the second applicant’s absence, with no evidence that she had been properly informed of the hearing. The matter was therefore remitted to the Bakhchysaray Court.

67. On 23 October 2009, responding to an inquiry from the Government Agent made after the Court had communicated the application to the Government (see also paragraphs 35, 44 and 48 above), the First Deputy Minister of Public Health sent the Agent a letter setting out the following conclusions:

“1.
The decline in the [first applicant’s] health and the complications affecting the progression of [his] illness were attributable to the following factors: [the first applicant’s] delay in seeking specialised medical care from [the Aids Centre], which he had not approached since 2005; the severity of his underlying illness (Aids); and interruptions in his antiretroviral therapy, including [his] refusals to take the prescribed medication.

2. The [first] applicant’s death was unrelated either to the medical care he received or to the conditions in the healthcare facilities where he was kept. It resulted from the severity of the underlying illness, which caused irreversible changes in [his] body.”

68. On 17 December 2009, the Bakhchysaray Court set aside the decision of 25 May 2009 (see paragraph 64 above) and returned the case to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor for further investigation.

69. On 19 August 2010, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor commissioned a forensic medical examination to address the following issues:

(1) Whether, on 3 June 2008, the Central Hospital’s therapist correctly diagnosed the first applicant (see paragraph 20 above for details);

(2) Whether the diagnoses made by the infectious-disease specialist on 5 June 2008, and his conclusion that the first applicant did not need urgent hospitalisation, were correct (see paragraph 22 above for details);

(3) Whether, in view of the diagnoses made on 5 June 2008, the first applicant genuinely had no need for urgent hospitalisation and could instead be held in the ITT or the SIZO;

(4) Whether the treatment prescribed to the first applicant by the Central Hospital’s doctors was appropriate;

(5) Whether the Central Hospital’s doctors acted properly by waiting until 13 June 2008, rather than conducting them on 3 or 5 June 2008, to order laboratory investigations for the first applicant, including blood and urine analyses, a blood-sugar test, and a chest X-ray;

(6) Whether the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital’s Infectious Diseases Department correctly evaluated the severity of the first applicant’s condition and reached accurate conclusions when, on 18 June 2008, following a renewed request from the Bakhchysaray police concerning the need for hospitalisation, she issued a note stating that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary;

(7) Whether the staff of Hospital no. 7 acted lawfully in discharging the first applicant on 18 July 2008, given that his mother’s request for his discharge did not indicate that she had been informed of the potentially adverse consequences;

(8) Whether the medical staff’s actions complied with the applicable legislation and whether any causal connection existed between the conduct of the police and medical personnel and the first applicant’s death.

70. On 26 November 2010, the Crimea Republic Bureau for Forensic Medical Examinations finalised its expert report.

71.
72. In view of the lack of medical records concerning the first applicant’s examination on 3 June 2008, the experts considered it “extremely difficult” to answer question (1). Regarding questions (2) and (3), they concluded that the diagnoses made by the infectious disease specialist on 5 June 2008 were not based on a comprehensive examination and did not adequately reflect the severity of the first applicant’s condition, particularly his fever and haemodynamic parameters. They further found that the doctor’s conclusion that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary was inconsistent with those diagnoses. In particular, the diagnosis of pneumocystis pneumonia would, by itself, have justified immediate hospitalisation for in-patient treatment. The experts considered the prescribed antibacterial and antifungal medication appropriate; this appears to have been the answer to unspecified question (4).

73. In response to question (5), the experts determined that the doctors’ decision of 13 June 2008 to conduct additional laboratory examinations was consistent with the relevant medical standards. They observed that such tests had already been performed on 4 June 2008—although the case-file documents indicate that the correct date was 3 June 2008 (see paragraph 20 above)—but required further verification.

74. Answering question (6), the expert commission stated that, when examined on 18 June 2008, the first applicant required urgent hospitalisation and in-patient medical care.

75. With respect to questions (7) and (8), the experts explained that they lacked competence to assess the doctors’ conduct from a legal standpoint. They also concluded that, without an autopsy report, it was impossible to identify the cause of the first applicant’s death or determine whether a causal connection existed between the timing of his admission for specialised treatment and his death.

76. On 27 December 2010, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor opened a criminal investigation into the Central Hospital doctors’ alleged failure to discharge their professional duties. The decision relied primarily on the expert commission’s conclusions of 26 November 2010 and stated, in particular:

“The prosecutor’s investigation has collected sufficient evidence of inadequate compliance by the medical officials with their professional duties due to negligence. The delayed hospitalisation and, accordingly, the delayed provision of medical assistance to [the first applicant] contributed considerably to the deterioration of his health, which amounted to a grave consequence for him.”

The case file contains no information about any subsequent developments in that investigation or its eventual outcome.

77.
On 29 April 2011, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor declined to open criminal proceedings against ITT or SIZO staff concerning the medical care afforded to the first applicant. Having examined medical records dated 20 November and 2 December 2007, 10 January, 10 and 18 February, and 28 May 2008, together with subsequent medical documents, the prosecutor found no criminal conduct on the part of the detention-facility administrations.

78. On 9 August 2011, the Bakhchysaray Court dismissed the second applicant’s related complaint and upheld the prosecutor’s decision.

79. On 22 September 2011, the Crimea Court of Appeal set aside the first-instance ruling and returned the case for reconsideration.

80. On 16 November 2011, the Bakhchysaray Court once again dismissed the second applicant’s complaint.

81. On 13 March 2012, however, apparently following a further complaint by the second applicant, the Bakhchysaray Court reversed its position. It annulled the prosecutor’s decision of 29 April 2011 and remitted the case for further investigation. The court observed that the investigation had addressed the conduct of ITT staff only indirectly and had not examined the actions of the SIZO administration or medical personnel at all. Furthermore, the SIZO employees responsible for dealing with the first applicant’s complaints had not even been identified. The court also noted that the case file contained no information indicating whether records had been kept of the first applicant’s health-related complaints or establishing that he had made no such complaints while in detention.

82. The Court has received no information about any subsequent developments.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

83. Under the Rules on Medical and Sanitary Care in Detention Centres and Penitentiaries, adopted by Decree no. 3/6 of the State Department for the Enforcement of Sentences on 18 January 2000, persons infected with HIV must receive medical assistance on the same terms as all other individuals (paragraph 4.3.4). The Rules further recommend that accessible, informative and supportive counselling be provided both before and after HIV testing (annex 28 to paragraph 4.3.4).

84. The pertinent provisions of Decree no. 186/607, issued on 15 November 2005 by the Ministry of Health and the State Department for the Enforcement of Sentences concerning antiretroviral treatment for persons with HIV/AIDS held in prisons and pre-trial detention centres, are summarised in Yakovenko v. Ukraine (no. 15825/06, §§ 49-52, 25 October 2007).

85. Article 18 of the Pre-trial Detention Act 1993 regulates the application of security measures, including handcuffing.
Prison staff may resort to force and special equipment—including hand-to-hand combat techniques, handcuffs, and truncheons—to overcome physical resistance, violence, outrage (безчинства), or refusal to comply with lawful instructions issued by detention-facility authorities, provided that less coercive means of attaining the legitimate aim have failed. The specific security measure chosen, together with the timing and method of its application, must reflect the circumstances of the individual case and the detainee’s personality.

86. Under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code, medical negligence resulting in serious consequences for a patient is punishable by disqualification from holding specified posts or engaging in specified activities for up to five years, correctional labour for a maximum of two years, or restriction or deprivation of liberty for the same period.

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

87. The pertinent passages of the third General Report [CPT/Inf (93) 12] issued by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”) provide:

“a. Access to a doctor

...

35. At a minimum, prison health-care services must offer regular outpatient consultations and emergency care; they may also frequently include a hospital-style unit equipped with beds. Prison doctors must furthermore have access to specialist services.

Where appropriate, health-care personnel should oversee outpatient treatment. In many instances, adequate follow-up care cannot depend solely on the prisoner taking the initiative.

36. Direct assistance from a fully equipped hospital service, whether in a civilian or prison hospital, must be available.

...

37. If a prisoner requires hospitalisation or examination by a hospital specialist, transportation must be arranged as promptly as, and in the manner, required by the prisoner’s medical condition.”

“b. Equivalence of care

38. Prison health-care services must be capable of delivering medical treatment, nursing care, suitable diets, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and any other necessary specialist facility under conditions comparable to those available to patients in the wider community. Staffing levels for medical, nursing, and technical personnel, as well as the premises, facilities, and equipment provided, must be organised accordingly.

The pharmacy and the dispensing of medication must be properly supervised. Medicines must always be prepared by qualified personnel, such as a pharmacist or nurse.

39. An individual medical record must be created for every patient. It should include diagnostic information, a continuous account of the patient’s progress, and details of any special examinations performed.”
If a patient is transferred, his or her medical record should be sent to the physicians at the receiving institution. Health-care staff should also maintain daily logs recording any noteworthy incidents involving patients. These records serve both to give a comprehensive picture of the prison’s health-care situation and to draw attention to particular problems as they emerge.

40. For a health-care service to function effectively, doctors and nurses must be able to meet on a regular basis and work together as a team led by the senior physician responsible for the service.”

88. The World Health Organization (“WHO”) guidelines concerning antiretroviral treatment for HIV infection in adults and adolescents are reproduced in Kozhokar v. Russia, no. 33099/08, §§ 77-79, 16 December 2010.
heavy:
FIFTH SECTION

SALAKHOV AND ISLYAMOVA v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 28005/08)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

14 March 2013

FINAL

14/06/2013

This judgment became final pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention and may undergo editorial revision.

In Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine,

the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), convening as a Chamber consisting of:

Mark Villiger, President,
Angelika Nußberger,
Boštjan M. Zupančič,
Ganna Yudkivska,
André Potocki,
Paul Lemmens,
Aleš Pejchal, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

after deliberating in private on 12 February 2013,

issues the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 28005/08, brought against Ukraine before the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”). The application was lodged on 8 June 2008 by Mr Linar Irekovich Salakhov (“the first applicant”), a Ukrainian national. After the first applicant died on 2 August 2008, his mother, Ms Aliya Fazylovna Islyamova (“the second applicant”), who is also a Ukrainian national, stated on 1 September 2008 that she wished to continue the application on his behalf and added her own complaints to the case.

2. Mr A. Lesovoy, a lawyer practising in Simferopol, represented the applicants. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented most recently by their Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.

3. Relying on Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, the applicants alleged that the first applicant had not had access to prompt and adequate medical treatment while detained, thereby placing his life at risk. They further maintained that the State authorities had failed to arrange his immediate admission to hospital, despite the measure indicated by the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. After the first applicant’s death, his mother held the authorities responsible. In addition to those complaints, she objected to her son having been handcuffed while in hospital and alleged that no effective domestic investigation into his death had taken place. Finally, under Article 3 of the Convention, the second applicant complained of the suffering she herself had endured in connection with the above matters.

4. On 7 September 2009, the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice to the Government of the complaints under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention concerning the first applicant. It was also decided, pursuant to Article 29 § 1, to examine the application’s admissibility and merits simultaneously.

5. On 29 May 2012, acting under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, the Chamber decided to invite the parties to provide additional written observations on the application’s admissibility and merits, specifically regarding the second applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention and the State’s compliance with the interim measure indicated by the Court.

THE FACTS

I. THE PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6.
The first applicant, born in 1981, died on 2 August 2008. The second applicant was born in 1955 and resides in Zuya, Crimea.

A. Background

7. The first applicant received a positive HIV test result on 30 September 2005.

8. On 2 February 2006, the Crimean Centre for the Prevention and Combating of Aids (“the Aids Centre”) notified him of the result and asked him to register for medical supervision. He did not comply with that recommendation (see also paragraphs 21 and 59 below).

B. Criminal case against the first applicant and medical care during his detention

9. Police arrested the first applicant on 20 November 2007 on suspicion of stealing a mobile telephone from an acquaintance. The second applicant stated that, on the day of the arrest, her son told the investigator that he was HIV-positive and voiced concern that detention could cause his health to worsen. That information was allegedly disregarded. The Government maintained that the first applicant had not revealed his HIV status.

10. He was detained at the Temporary Detention Facility of the Bakhchysaray Police Station (“the ITT”). After examining him, the duty officer recorded that there were no visible injuries and that he had made no complaints.

11. On 23 November 2007, the Bakhchysaray District Court (“the Bakhchysaray Court”) ordered that the first applicant remain in custody pending trial.

12. An X-ray performed at the local polyclinic on 30 November 2007 showed no lung abnormalities.

13. On 2 December 2007, the first applicant was transferred from the ITT to Simferopol Pre-Trial Detention Centre no. 15 (“the SIZO”). There, he was examined by a therapist (general practitioner), dermatologist, dentist, and psychiatrist, each of whom considered him to be in good health. His medical records indicate that he neither complained about his health nor disclosed any illnesses. His height was documented as 180 cm and his weight as 78 kg.

14. The first applicant was held in the SIZO during three periods: from 2 to 28 December 2007, from 10 January to 10 February 2008, and from 18 February to 2 June 2008. In the intervals—28 December 2007 to 10 January 2008, 10 to 18 February 2008, and 2 to 20 June 2008—he was detained in the ITT.

15. Records of medical examinations conducted on 10 January and on 10 and 18 February 2008 describe him as apparently healthy and note that he made no health-related complaints.

16. Entries in the SIZO medical register for 28, 29, and 30 May 2008 state that the first applicant complained of a blocked nose, rhinitis, and a sore throat. The SIZO therapist diagnosed an “acute respiratory viral infection” and prescribed medicine.

17. The case file contains no documentation covering the interval between the records dated 18 February and 28 May 2008. Nevertheless, the applicants alleged that the first applicant’s condition had deteriorated sharply in early March 2008.
He was allegedly suffering from a persistent temperature of 39-40ºC and severe digestive problems. The applicants stated that the detention-facility authorities repeatedly called an ambulance because of his condition, although the nature of those interventions remained unclear.

18. On 31 May 2008, an infectious-disease specialist at the SIZO also examined the first applicant and issued a note. It recorded that, during the previous two months, he had experienced fevers and weight loss. The doctor recommended an HIV test, to which the first applicant consented, and scheduled it for 2 June 2008. The test was not performed, however, because the first applicant was transferred from the SIZO to the ITT (see paragraph 14 above).

19. On 2 June 2008, after another transfer from the SIZO to the ITT, the first applicant told the ITT medical attendant that he felt weak and was experiencing fever and back pain. The attendant gave him antipyretic medication.

20. On 3 June 2008, the first applicant was brought to the Central Hospital. A therapist examined him, and ultrasound examinations were conducted of his liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and kidneys. He also underwent a chest X-ray, an electrocardiogram, an esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and general blood and urine tests. The therapist diagnosed an ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, haemorrhoids and chronic bronchitis, and suspected that he was infected with HIV.

21. On 4 June 2008, responding to the second applicant’s enquiry of 3 June 2008, the Chief Doctor of the Aids Centre informed her that her son had tested positive for HIV on 30 September 2005 and had been notified of that result on 2 February 2006, but had not been registered for monitoring at the Centre.

22. On 5 June 2008, the first applicant was taken back to the Central Hospital, where an infectious-disease specialist examined him. According to the doctor’s note, he reported stomach pain, lesions in his mouth, a skin rash, coughing and shortness of breath. He further stated that he had lost approximately 10 kg over the previous three months. Following the examination, the doctor diagnosed pneumocystis pneumonia, oropharynx-esophagus candidiosis (thrush) and an ulcer. The doctor also determined that the symptoms indicated fourth-stage clinical HIV infection. Although he described the first applicant’s condition as “moderately severe” and recorded that treatment was needed for those illnesses, the overall conclusion was that immediate hospitalisation was unnecessary.

23. The first applicant’s mother was notified of the diagnoses. She purchased the prescribed medicines, which the ITT medical attendant then administered to her son.

24.
On 6 June 2008, counsel for the first applicant applied to the Bakhchysaray Court for his client’s release because of his critical medical condition. He submitted that the first applicant urgently needed specialised treatment, as he had fourth-clinical-stage HIV infection accompanied by oesophageal candidosis and pneumocystis pneumonia. According to the lawyer, the first applicant’s life was at immediate risk, and release was necessary to enable him to obtain appropriate medical care. He further emphasised that his client had a permanent residence, had never attempted to evade the investigation or obstruct it, and, in view of his extremely poor health, posed no threat to society.

25. The Bakhchysaray Court dismissed that application. Its ruling is not contained in the case file available to the Court.

26. On 11 June 2008, the Bakhchysaray District Prosecutor’s Office directed the local police department to bring the first applicant to the Central Hospital for a further medical assessment in order to determine whether his health was compatible with continued detention.

27. On 13 June 2008, the first applicant was brought to the Central Hospital and re-examined by an infectious-disease specialist. The doctor provisionally diagnosed HIV infection at the second clinical stage and concluded that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary. The doctor recommended an additional assessment at the Aids Centre to determine the treatment required. Arrangements were also made for laboratory investigations, including blood and urine analyses, a sugar test, and a chest X-ray.

28. On 16 June 2008, the applicants asked the Court, pursuant to Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, to indicate to the Ukrainian Government that the first applicant should urgently be hospitalised and treated because his health had seriously deteriorated and he had allegedly not received adequate medical care.

29. On 17 June 2008, the President of the Fifth Section granted the request and, under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicated to the respondent Government that the first applicant “should be transferred immediately to a hospital or other medical institution where he [could] receive the appropriate treatment for his medical condition until further notice.” The Government were informed of that decision by fax on the same day, which was a Tuesday and a working day.

30. On 18 June 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer submitted a further application to the Bakhchysaray Court seeking his client’s release. He again maintained that the first applicant’s life was in danger and also relied on the Court’s above-mentioned decision to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court in the first applicant’s case.

31.
On 18 June 2008, after the Bakhchysaray police made a further enquiry as to whether the first applicant needed to be admitted to hospital, the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital’s Infectious Diseases Department replied that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary. 32. Consequently, the Bakhchysaray Court dismissed the first applicant’s application for release, which he had lodged earlier that day. 33. Also on 18 June 2008, the second applicant submitted a complaint to the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital, alleging that hospital staff had failed to provide her son with adequate medical care despite her requests of 4 and 5 June and two further requests made on 13 June 2008. She maintained that his life was at risk. She also stated that her son had never received a comprehensive medical examination and believed that the doctors were reluctant to treat him because, first, he was HIV-positive and, second, he was being held in detention. 34. On 20 June 2008, the first applicant was brought to the Aids Centre. There, doctors made the following preliminary diagnoses: fourth-clinical-stage HIV infection; systemic candidosis affecting the oropharynx and oesophagus; persistent fever accompanied by pronounced intoxication syndrome; body-weight loss exceeding 15%; and seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp. The Aids Centre doctors determined that further examination was necessary to clarify those diagnoses and that he required in-patient treatment. 35. Later that same day, the first applicant was transferred to the Central Hospital and accommodated in a ward guarded by the police. The second applicant alleged that her son remained handcuffed to his bed at all times. She provided the Court with two photographs of him taken on 25 June 2008, both showing his left hand secured by a handcuff to the hospital bed. A letter dated 23 October 2009 from the First Deputy Minister of Public Health to the Government Agent (see also paragraph 67 below), referring to the first applicant’s Central Hospital medical records, confirmed that he had arrived there in handcuffs on 20 June 2008. The records did not, however, indicate whether he had continued to be handcuffed for the entire duration of his treatment at that hospital. 36. At an unspecified time on 20 June 2008, the first applicant prepared an “explanatory note” for the police. In it, he stated that, “for understandable reasons”, he had not told either the SIZO or the ITT administration that he was infected with HIV. After his mother informed them that he might have that diagnosis, he had been medically examined at the Central Hospital on 5 and 13 June 2008 and prescribed certain medicines, which were subsequently administered to him in the ITT by the medical attendant. He further declared that he had no complaints concerning the ITT staff. The second applicant, however, maintained that her son had been forced to write that note. 37.
On 24 June 2008, the first applicant prepared a further note stating that he had begun feeling ill while in detention, although the date when this occurred is illegible in the available copy. He wrote that, because he had a persistent fever and pain in his kidneys, liver and intestines, he had asked to be examined by a therapist. Instead, a medical attendant had been sent to see him and had only provided antipyretic medication. Since his condition had not improved, the attendant had started giving him ceftriaxone injections (an antibiotic) at some time between 22 and 25 May 2008. Nevertheless, his fever and back pain had continued. Consequently, on 29 May 2008 he had been admitted to the SIZO hospital, where his treatment had remained unchanged. After being transferred to the ITT, he had begun taking other medicines purchased by his mother on 4 June 2008.

38. Also on 24 June 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer again applied for his client’s release, citing both the severity of his condition and the prosecutor’s lack of objection to the release.

39. That same day, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor asked the judge handling the first applicant’s criminal case to advance the hearing set for 3 July 2008 because of the first applicant’s “critical condition” and his need to receive treatment at Simferopol Hospital no. 7, a facility specialising in Aids treatment (“Hospital no. 7”). The prosecutor emphasised that the above-mentioned application for release had to be considered without delay.

40. On an undetermined date, possibly 4 July 2008 (see paragraph 47 below), the Bakhchysaray Court refused the above-mentioned application for the first applicant’s release.

41. On 26 June 2008, the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital replied to the second applicant’s complaint alleging that her son had not received the medical care he required. He stated that the medical documentation available was inadequate to assess how the illness had progressed over time. According to him, the requests made to the Hospital for medical assistance had been contextual in nature, and the necessary assistance had been properly provided.

42. Later that day, the first applicant was moved from the Central Hospital to Hospital no. 7.

43. An extract from his Hospital no. 7 medical record listed the diagnoses made by the Aids Centre on 20 June 2008 (see paragraph 34 above), together with pneumocystis pneumonia, second-degree anaemia, severe immunosuppression, with a CD4 count[1] of 48 cells/mm3, and encephalitis of uncertain origin. Toxic hepatitis, hepatolienal syndrome, superficial gastritis and duodenogastric reflux were additionally recorded as concurrent conditions.

44. A letter dated 23 October 2009 from the First Deputy Minister of Public Health to the Government Agent (see also paragraph 67 below), which also cited information supplied by the management of Hospital no.
The first applicant was handcuffed while receiving treatment at Hospital no. 7 between 26 June and 18 July 2008. However, the above-mentioned letter stated that no information was available as to whether he had been kept in handcuffs continuously.

45. On 2 July 2008, the ITT Governor considered the second applicant’s complaint that her son had allegedly not been provided with the necessary medical care and decided not to open a criminal investigation. He observed that the first applicant had concealed his HIV-positive status from the administration and that, in any event, he had received adequate medical treatment while detained in the ITT.

46. Also on 2 July 2008, the Chief Doctor of Hospital no. 7 informed the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police Department in writing that the first applicant needed prolonged medical treatment and freedom of movement, and that any disruption of his treatment would cause his health to deteriorate sharply.

47. On 4 July 2008, the Bakhchysaray Court convicted the first applicant of fraud, rather than robbery as charged by the prosecution (see paragraph 9 above), and imposed a fine of 850 Ukrainian hryvnias, equivalent at the time to 115 euros. The judgment specified that the first applicant was to remain in detention until it became final.

48. On 10 July 2008, Hospital no. 7 began administering antiretroviral therapy to the first applicant. According to information contained in the Public Health Ministry’s letter of 23 October 2009 to the Government Agent, the first applicant had apparently refused to take the prescribed medication on one occasion.

49. On that same date, 10 July 2008, the second applicant asked the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police Department for permission to visit and care for her son in the hospital because of his critical condition. She also complained to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor that the first applicant was being kept continuously handcuffed and requested that this practice be stopped.

50. On 15 July 2008, the Chief of the Bakhchysaray Police informed the second applicant that her son would, in any event, be released shortly after the judgment of 4 July 2008 became final.

51. On 18 July 2008, the first applicant’s lawyer likewise requested that the handcuffing cease. He stated that it was already evident that his client was close to death, yet he remained under the guard of two police officers in a hospital ward with barred windows and was handcuffed to his bed. The lawyer argued that these security measures were both unjustified and inhuman. He further alleged that, as the second applicant had learned, some of the police officers guarding her son had mockingly suggested installing a cable in the ward and handcuffing him to it, so that his movements would be “practically unrestrained”.

C. The first applicant’s medical care following his release from detention and his death

52.
On 18 July 2008, apparently because the judgment of 4 July had become final, the police discontinued the security measures concerning the first applicant, and the second applicant brought him home. She submitted a note to the administration of Hospital no. 7 explaining that she was taking her son home “for family reasons”.

53. The next day, following a deterioration in his condition, the first applicant was readmitted to Hospital no. 7.

54. On 1 August 2008, the second applicant once more took him home after providing the hospital administration with a note similar to the one she had written on 18 July 2008.

55. The first applicant died on 2 August 2008.

D. Inquiry into the first applicant’s death

56. After her son’s death, the second applicant lodged a complaint with the prosecution authorities, alleging that, while in detention, he had been denied timely and adequate medical care and that this had caused his death.

57. On 20 January 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor notified her that the ITT governor’s decision of 2 July 2008 (see paragraph 45 above) had been overturned and that the investigation into the medical assistance given to the first applicant had been reopened.

58. On 17 February 2009, the Ministry of Public Health established a commission to examine the matter.

59. In its official investigation report of 20 March 2009, the commission found that the doctors at the Central Hospital were not responsible for the first applicant’s death. It observed that the Aids Centre had informed him of his HIV-positive status and explained the need for medical supervision as early as 2 February 2006, but that he had not sought medical examinations or monitoring. Consequently, antiretroviral treatment had not been initiated in a timely manner, which complicated the course of the disease. The commission summarised its conclusions as follows:

“1. Responsibility for providing medical care to persons in custody lies with police medical personnel.

2. Central Hospital specialists do not examine or provide medical consultations to detainees unless requested to do so by the staff of the [detention facilities].

3. At the Central Hospital, the [first applicant] received examinations, consultations with specialists, laboratory testing and treatment in full compliance with the approved standards.

4. The decline in [his] health and the ensuing complications resulted from his delay in seeking medical care after testing HIV-positive, together with the seriousness of the underlying disease, which caused irreversible processes in [his] body.”

60. On 23 March 2009, the second applicant submitted a further complaint to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor. In particular, she challenged as allegedly unjustified the infectious-disease specialist’s conclusion of 13 June 2008 that her son had not needed urgent hospitalisation at that point (see paragraph 27 above).

61.
On 31 March 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor concluded that the second applicant’s complaint was unfounded and declined to bring criminal proceedings against either the police or the Central Hospital staff.

62. On 3 April 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor set aside the decision of 31 March 2009, holding that further inquiries were necessary. Those inquiries were to include interviews with the second applicant, the ITT personnel and the relevant doctors from the Central Hospital.

63. The prosecutor questioned the second applicant on 4 May 2009. She stated that her son’s health had begun to worsen severely in March 2008 and that he had not been provided with timely and appropriate medical care. In her account, the detention-facility authorities had done no more than summon an ambulance several times. She requested that all medical records relating to her son—from the ITT, the SIZO, the Central Hospital and Hospital no. 7—be obtained and reviewed in order to assess both his medical needs and the measures actually taken in response to them from November 2007 onward.

64. On 25 May 2009, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor again declined to institute criminal proceedings against the police or the Central Hospital personnel, finding that their conduct disclosed no corpus delicti. In reaching that conclusion, he relied particularly on the findings of the Ministry of Public Health’s commission (see paragraph 59 above), together with statements from police officers and doctors.

65. The Bakhchysaray Court upheld that decision on 18 August 2009. It observed that the first applicant had not personally made any complaints about the police or the medical personnel. It also considered that, once the authorities had learned of his HIV status, they had provided him with adequate medical care.

66. On 13 October 2009, the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea (“the Crimea Court of Appeal”) granted the second applicant’s appeal and quashed the ruling of 18 August 2009. It faulted the investigation, in particular, for failing to examine the first applicant’s health and any medical assistance he may have received while detained between 20 November 2007 and early June 2008. The appellate court further noted that the first-instance court had issued the contested ruling without the second applicant being present and in the absence of any evidence that she had been properly informed of the hearing. The case was therefore returned to the Bakhchysaray Court.

67. On 23 October 2009, responding to an inquiry from the Government Agent after the Court had communicated the application to the Government (see also paragraphs 35, 44 and 48 above), the First Deputy Minister of Public Health sent the Government Agent a letter containing the following conclusions:

“1.
The decline in the [first applicant’s] health and the complications affecting the progression of [his] illness resulted from the following factors: [the first applicant’s] delay, since 2005, in seeking specialised medical care from [the Aids Centre]; the severity of his principal illness (Aids); and interruptions in his antiretroviral therapy, including refusals [on his part] to take the prescribed medication.

2. The [first] applicant’s death was unrelated either to the medical treatment he received or to the conditions in the medical institutions in which he was held. Rather, it resulted from the severity of his principal illness, which caused irreversible changes in [his] body.”

68. On 17 December 2009, the Bakhchysaray Court set aside the decision of 25 May 2009 (see paragraph 64 above) and returned the case to the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor for further investigation.

69. On 19 August 2010, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor commissioned a forensic medical examination to address the following issues:

(1) Whether, on 3 June 2008, the Central Hospital’s therapist had correctly diagnosed the first applicant (see paragraph 20 above for details).

(2) Whether the diagnoses made by the infectious-disease specialist on 5 June 2008 (see paragraph 22 above for details) were correct, including his conclusion that the first applicant did not need urgent hospitalisation.

(3) In view of the diagnoses made on 5 June 2008, whether the first applicant truly had no need for urgent hospitalisation and could be held in the ITT or the SIZO.

(4) Whether the treatment prescribed to the first applicant by the Central Hospital’s doctors was appropriate.

(5) Whether the Central Hospital’s doctors acted correctly by waiting until 13 June, rather than 3 or 5 June 2008, to order laboratory examinations for the first applicant, namely blood and urine analyses, a sugar test and a chest X-ray.

(6) Whether, on 18 June 2008, the Chief Doctor of the Central Hospital’s Infectious Diseases Department properly assessed the severity of the first applicant’s condition and reached correct conclusions when, after a renewed inquiry from the Bakhchysaray police concerning the need for hospitalisation, she issued a note stating that he did not require urgent hospitalisation.

(7) Whether the medical staff of Hospital no. 7 acted lawfully in discharging the first applicant on 18 July 2008, given that his mother’s discharge request contained no indication that she had been advised of the possible adverse consequences.

(8) Whether the medical staff’s conduct complied with the applicable legislation, and whether there was any causal connection between the actions of the police and medical personnel and the first applicant’s death.

70. The Crimea Republic Bureau for Forensic Medical Examinations finalised its expert report on 26 November 2010.

71.
72. In the absence of medical records concerning the first applicant’s examination on 3 June 2008, the experts considered it “extremely difficult” to respond to question (1). Regarding questions (2) and (3), they determined that the diagnoses made by the infectious-disease specialist on 5 June 2008 had not followed a comprehensive examination of the first applicant and had failed to reflect the severity of his condition, particularly his fever and haemodynamic indicators. They further found that the doctor’s conclusion that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary on 5 June 2008 was inconsistent with the diagnoses established. In particular, the first applicant had been diagnosed with pneumocystis pneumonia, which in itself required urgent admission to hospital for in-patient treatment. The experts considered the prescribed antibacterial and antifungal medicines appropriate; this was apparently the answer to question (4), although that question was not identified.

73. Answering question (5), the experts concluded that the doctors’ decision of 13 June 2008 to conduct additional laboratory examinations conformed to the relevant medical standards. They observed that those tests had already been performed on 4 June 2008, although the case-file documents indicate that the correct date was 3 June 2008 (see paragraph 20 above), but that further verification had been necessary.

74. In response to question (6), the expert commission stated that, when examined on 18 June 2008, the first applicant had needed urgent hospitalisation and in-patient medical care.

75. With respect to questions (7) and (8), the experts explained that assessing the doctors’ conduct from a legal standpoint fell outside their competence. Since no autopsy report was available, the commission was unable either to identify the cause of the first applicant’s death or to determine whether his death was causally connected to the timing of his hospitalisation for specialised treatment.

76. On 27 December 2010, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor opened a criminal investigation into the Central Hospital doctors’ failure to fulfil their professional duties. The decision relied primarily on the expert commission’s conclusions of 26 November 2010. It stated, in particular, that the prosecutor’s inquiry had obtained sufficient evidence that the medical officials had negligently and inadequately performed their professional obligations. It further found that the delay in hospitalising the first applicant—and, consequently, in providing him with medical assistance—had contributed substantially to the worsening of his health, constituting a grave consequence for him. The case file contains no information about any subsequent steps in that investigation or its outcome.

77.
On 29 April 2011, the Bakhchysaray Prosecutor decided not to initiate criminal proceedings against employees of either the ITT or the SIZO concerning the medical care afforded to the first applicant. Having examined the medical records dated 20 November and 2 December 2007, 10 January, 10 and 18 February and 28 May 2008, together with subsequent medical documents, the prosecutor found no indication of criminal conduct by the administrations of the detention facilities.

78. On 9 August 2011, the Bakhchysaray Court dismissed the second applicant’s related complaint and upheld the prosecutor’s decision.

79. On 22 September 2011, the Crimea Court of Appeal set aside the first-instance court’s ruling and returned the case for renewed examination.

80. On 16 November 2011, the Bakhchysaray Court once more dismissed the second applicant’s complaint.

81. On 13 March 2012, however, apparently following another complaint by the second applicant, the Bakhchysaray Court revised its position. It annulled the prosecutor’s decision of 29 April 2011 and sent the case back for further investigation. The court observed that the investigation had addressed the conduct of the ITT staff only indirectly and had not examined the actions of the SIZO administration or its medical personnel at all. Furthermore, the SIZO employees responsible for dealing with the first applicant’s complaints had not even been identified. The Bakhchysaray Court also noted that the case file contained no information as to whether records had been kept of the first applicant’s health-related complaints, nor any material demonstrating that he had made no such complaints while in detention.

82. The Court has received no information about any subsequent developments.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

83. Under the Rules on Medical and Sanitary Care in Detention Centres and Penitentiaries, adopted by Decree no. 3/6 of the State Department for the Enforcement of Sentences on 18 January 2000, persons infected with HIV must receive medical assistance on the same terms as all other persons (paragraph 4.3.4). The Rules further recommend that accessible, informative and supportive counselling be provided both before and after HIV testing (annex 28 to paragraph 4.3.4).

84. The pertinent provisions of Decree No. 186/607, issued jointly on 15 November 2005 by the Ministry of Health and the State Department for the Enforcement of Sentences and concerning antiretroviral treatment for persons with HIV/Aids held in prisons and pre-trial detention centres, are summarised in Yakovenko v. Ukraine (no. 15825/06, §§ 49-52, 25 October 2007).

85. The rules applicable to security measures, including handcuffing, are laid down in Article 18 of the Pre-trial Detention Act (1993).
Prison officers may employ force and special means, such as unarmed combat techniques, handcuffs and truncheons, in order to overcome physical resistance, violence, disorder (безчинства) or refusal to comply with lawful instructions issued by the detention facility’s authorities, provided that other methods of attaining the legitimate aim have been unsuccessful. The specific security measure selected, together with the timing and manner of its application, must be determined in light of the circumstances of the individual case and the detainee’s personality.

86. Under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code, medical negligence resulting in grave consequences for a patient is punishable by disqualification from occupying certain positions or carrying out certain activities for up to five years, correctional work for up to two years, or restriction or deprivation of liberty for the same period.

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

87. The pertinent passages of the third General Report [CPT/Inf (93) 12] issued by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”) provide:

“a. Access to a doctor

...

35. At a minimum, prison health-care services must be capable of offering regular outpatient consultations and emergency care; in addition, there may frequently be a hospital-type unit equipped with beds. ... Prison doctors must also have access to specialist services. ...

Where appropriate, outpatient treatment must be monitored by health-care personnel; in many instances, it is inadequate for follow-up care to depend on the prisoner taking the initiative.

36. Direct access to a fully equipped hospital service, whether in a civilian hospital or a prison hospital, must be ensured. ...

37. If prisoners require hospitalisation or examination by a hospital specialist, they must be transported as promptly and in such a manner as their medical condition requires.”

“b. Equivalence of care

38. Prison health-care services must be able to deliver medical treatment and nursing care, together with suitable diets, physiotherapy, rehabilitation and any other necessary specialised facility, under conditions comparable to those available to patients in the community. Staffing by medical, nursing and technical personnel, as well as the premises, installations and equipment provided, must be arranged accordingly.

The pharmacy and the distribution of medication must be properly supervised. In addition, medicines must always be prepared by qualified personnel, such as a pharmacist or nurse.

39. An individual medical record must be created for every patient. It must include diagnostic information, a continuous account of the patient’s progress and details of any special examinations undergone.”
If a patient is transferred, their medical file should be sent to the doctors at the receiving institution. Health-care teams should also maintain daily registers documenting any notable incidents involving patients. These records provide a general overview of the state of health care in the prison while also drawing attention to particular problems that may emerge.

41. In January 2008, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Ministry of Health of Ukraine concerning his detention conditions.

42. In a letter dated 12 March 2008, the Kyiv Department of Execution of Sentences advised the applicant that he had shared a cell measuring 52.06 square metres with eighteen other detainees. The bedding was in acceptable condition, insulation had been fitted to the windows, and cell no. 10 had been renovated.

43. A general practitioner examined the applicant on 17 March 2008 and found his health to be satisfactory.

44. On 21 May 2008, the applicant underwent examinations by a cardiologist and an ophthalmologist, neither of whom identified any pathological condition. On 28 May 2008, a urologist examined him at Kyiv City Hospital no. 3 and concluded that no specialist treatment was necessary.

D. Other developments

50. The applicant filed many complaints disputing the decision to open criminal proceedings against him and seeking the institution of criminal proceedings against various authorities; none succeeded.

In a letter dated 16 April 2012, the applicant informed the Court that police officers and prosecutors had approached him and asked him to testify as a witness in the criminal proceedings against Kr. and D. He further claimed that police officers had threatened to bring fresh criminal proceedings against him unless he withdrew his application before the Court.

II. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

52.
From 9 to 21 September 2009, a delegation from the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman and Degrading Treatment and Punishment (“the CPT”) visited Ukraine and inspected the Kyiv SIZO.53. The pertinent sections of the CPT’s report stated:

“100. ... Although the establishment had an official capacity of 2,950 places, it held 3,440 inmates on 8 September 2009 ...

101. Most cells accommodating male prisoners were severely overcrowded. For instance, one cell of approximately 50 m² housed 52 prisoners despite having only 40 beds, while another, measuring 33 m², held 32 prisoners and contained 20 beds. ...

The sheer number of people meant that ventilation was virtually absent, leaving the cells extremely hot and airless. Hygiene standards were likewise very poor: the delegation observed cockroaches in some cells, while prisoners reported mice and rats. Sanitary facilities inside the cells—generally a partitioned toilet and a sink—were dilapidated and plainly inadequate for the number of prisoners accommodated in the larger cells.

The harmful effects of these appalling physical conditions were aggravated by the prolonged periods that some prisoners had spent in the SIZO .... In the CPT’s assessment, the combined adverse factors affecting many prisoners at the Kyiv SIZO—overcrowding, dreadful material and hygienic conditions, and the near-total absence of activity programmes—could readily be regarded as inhuman and degrading treatment.

...

106. In view of the foregoing observations, the CPT recommends that the Kyiv SIZO:

...

- make vigorous efforts to reduce overcrowding and allocate prisoners more evenly across the available accommodation, with the aim of providing at least 4 m² of living space to each prisoner;
- give priority to measures ensuring that prisoner accommodation has access to natural light and adequate ventilation;
- undertake efforts to renovate prisoner accommodation and maintain satisfactory hygiene standards;
- guarantee prisoners sufficient supplies of basic personal-hygiene items and products for cleaning their cells ...”
