31. On 6 June 2006 the Sevastopol Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) affirmed the Leninskyy Court’s ruling of 29 March 2006 (see paragraphs 26-27 above). It stated that the lawfulness of the applicant’s administrative detention between 6 and 9 January 2006 fell outside the scope of its review, while considering his ensuing detention lawful. Regarding the applicant’s unsuccessful application to summon the witnesses to his arrest on 6 January 2006, the appellate court observed that the relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided no basis for such a request.

32. On 19 September 2006 the applicant applied to the Leninskyy Court for release subject to an undertaking not to abscond. He argued that there was no reason to believe that, if released, he would flee or obstruct the investigation. He supplied his address and explained that, prior to his arrest, he had worked at a construction site. He also maintained that his previous convictions should not serve as justification for his pre-trial detention in the pending criminal proceedings.

33. That same day, the Leninskyy Court dismissed the application. It concluded, in view of all the circumstances, that the applicant could not be relied upon either to cooperate with the investigation or to refrain from committing further offences.

34. The tenure of the Leninskyy Court judge handling the applicant’s case ended on 10 December 2006.

35. On 25 April 2007 the case was assigned to Judge R., who had previously tried B. (see paragraphs 13-15 above).

36. On 12 October 2007 Judge R. applied to withdraw from the case, giving the following reasons:

“Since I examined the criminal case against [B.] and have already stated my view concerning the incident involving both [the applicant] and [B.], I withdraw from the case.”

37. On 22 October 2007 the President of the Leninskyy Court refused Judge R.’s self-recusal application, finding that Article 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure disclosed no grounds for it (see paragraph 56 below).

38. As regards the incident involving K., on 14 November 2007 the Leninskyy Court, composed of a single judge, Judge R., convicted the applicant of robbery committed pursuant to a conspiracy with B. It sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. Relying on the judgment delivered against B. on 7 February 2006, the court used the evidence B. had given at that trial (see paragraphs 13-14 above), which was read aloud during the hearing. The applicant submitted that he and B.
had only been looking at K.’s vehicle and had not intended to break into it, and that he had struck K. with a bottle in self-defence. Judge R. rejected those claims as false.

39. Regarding the incident involving N., the Leninskyy Court characterised the applicant’s conduct as attempted petty theft, which constituted an administrative (minor) offence rather than a criminal one. It therefore acquitted the applicant on that count because his actions lacked the corpus delicti of a criminal offence.

40. Finally, the Leninskyy Court ruled that the applicant’s prison term was to run from 9 January 2006. It also ordered that, as a preventive measure, he remain in detention until the verdict became final.

41. During the trial, the applicant requested that B. be called and questioned as a witness, but that application was unsuccessful. The Government maintained that the request had been submitted at an improper stage of the proceedings and had not subsequently been renewed.

42. The applicant lodged an appeal. In particular, he argued that it was impermissible to rely on statements made by B. during a trial in which the applicant had not taken part. Invoking Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention, he stressed that B. had not been summoned to his trial and that, as a result, he had been unable either to challenge B.’s account or to have him examined as a key witness. In that context, the applicant also observed that Judge R., who had considered both his case and B.’s, had effectively acknowledged holding a preconceived view of the case’s circumstances and had sought to withdraw from it.

43. The applicant additionally complained that his conduct had been incorrectly classified as robbery committed by a group pursuant to a conspiracy. He argued that both he and B. had been surprised to find K. inside the car and could not possibly have planned to attack him. He also identified a number of inconsistencies and alterations in B.’s statements. In particular, he said that he had not seen B. on the day in question, although they had previously served sentences in the same prison. Nevertheless, the applicant denied that the idea of stealing property from vehicles had originated with him or that he had agreed to teach B. how to do so, especially since B. had already been convicted of several counts of car theft.

44. On 28 July 2009, after a hearing attended by the applicant’s lawyer but not by the applicant himself, the Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of 14 November 2007 without carrying out its own judicial examination of the witness testimony or the other evidence in the case. At the same time, it directed the first-instance court to clarify the date from which the prison sentence was to run. Although it acknowledged that the Leninskyy Court had relied on the statements made by B.
The Court of Appeal observed that the statements he had given in separate proceedings were consistent with the remaining evidence and, consequently, found no basis for doubting their reliability.

45. Relying on the ruling referred to above, on 16 September 2009 the applicant applied to the Leninskyy Court for correction of the calculation of his prison sentence so that it would be deemed to have commenced on 6 January 2006. On 20 October 2009 the court dismissed that application as unsubstantiated.

46. Acting on the applicant’s behalf, his mother lodged an appeal on points of law on 30 December 2009 against the judgment of 14 November 2007 and the Court of Appeal’s ruling of 28 July 2009. Invoking, in particular, Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, she argued that the applicant had had no opportunity to contest B.’s testimony, which had been given in other proceedings and relied upon to convict him.

47. On 14 January 2010, in written proceedings conducted without notifying or involving the parties, a Supreme Court judge refused the applicant’s mother leave to appeal on points of law.

48. In response to the applicant’s lawyer’s enquiry about the progress of the case, the Supreme Court stated in a letter dated 28 December 2010 that the above ruling had been dispatched to the applicant’s mother on 14 January 2010.

49. The applicant maintained that his mother had never received the Supreme Court’s letter enclosing the ruling. He also produced a document issued by the local authorities indicating that the town contained another street bearing the same name as the street on which his mother resided.

50. According to the applicant, neither he, his lawyer, nor his mother, who acted as his lay representative, became aware of the Supreme Court’s ruling of 14 January 2010 until December 2010.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

51. Article 29 of the Constitution of Ukraine, concerning the right to liberty and personal security, is reproduced in Nechiporuk and Yonkalo v. Ukraine (no. 42310/04, § 121, 21 April 2011).

52. Article 187 § 1 of the Criminal Code provides that robbery is punishable by imprisonment for a period of three to seven years. Under paragraph 2, robbery committed by a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy carries a sentence of seven to ten years’ imprisonment together with confiscation of property.

53. Article 178 of the Code on Administrative Offences provides, among other penalties, for administrative detention of up to fifteen days for intoxication in a public place. Under Article 287, in the version applicable at the relevant time, a court decision imposing a penalty for an administrative offence was final and could not be appealed.

54. The domestic provisions governing the imposition and forms of preventive measures, the time-limits applicable to pre-trial detention, and the grounds and procedure for detention by an investigating authority are set out in Molodorych v. Ukraine (no.
2161/02, §§ 56-58, 28 October 2010).

55. Article 23-2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure stipulates that, where a court identifies a breach of the law and/or citizens’ rights during a pre-trial inquiry or investigation, or while reviewing a case heard by a lower court, it must adopt a separate ruling. In that ruling, the court brings the established facts to the attention of the relevant authorities and instructs them to take specified steps to rectify the situation.

56. Pursuant to Article 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge may not take part in a trial where:

“(1) he or she is the victim, civil claimant or civil defendant, is related to any such person, or is a relative of the investigator, inquiry officer, prosecutor or accused;

(2) he or she previously participated in the proceedings as a witness, expert, specialist, interpreter, inquiry officer, investigator, prosecutor, defence counsel, or representative of the victim, civil claimant or civil defendant;

(2-1) in the course of the pre-trial investigation, he or she ordered a search, seizure or inspection; imposed, varied or terminated a preventive measure; extended a period of detention on remand; reviewed an appeal against an arrest warrant; or considered an appeal against the discontinuance of criminal proceedings;

(2-2) during the pre-trial investigation, he or she considered the question of [removing defence counsel from the proceedings];

(3) he or she, or any of his or her relatives, has an interest in the outcome of the proceedings;

(4) other circumstances exist that cast doubt on the judge’s impartiality ...”

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL INSTRUMENTS

57. The international instruments relevant to judicial impartiality are set out in Harabin v. Slovakia (no. 58688/11, §§ 104-110, 20 November 2012).

According to the applicant, between 13 and 25 January 2000 he was kept in police detention facilities, where he was severely beaten many times by the police, who forced him to confess to theft and robbery. Furthermore, the applicant’s cellmates in the SIZO had not been questioned and the case file lacked information as to when and how the applicant’s injuries had been inflicted. It was also noted that information about the applicant’s state of health upon his arrival at the SIZO was unavailable, as the relevant documentation had been destroyed after the expiry of the time-limit for its storage. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAWA. Constitution of Ukraine50. Article 63 of the Constitution read as follows:“A person shall not bear responsibility for refusing to testify or to explain anything about himself or herself, members of his or her family or close relatives in the degree determined by law.A suspect, an accused or a defendant has the right to a defence...”B. Other relevant domestic law51. Other relevant domestic law is summarised in the cases of Yaremenko v. Ukraine (no. 32092/02, §§ 45 to 49, 12 June 2008) and Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).III. INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTS Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine carried out by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) from 10 to 26 September 2000.52. According to the applicant, the following part of the report concerned him.“19.... A man, who was arrested by the Organised Crime Department of the Militia in the town of Makeyevka, Donetsk Region, on 13 January 2000, alleged that he was beaten upon arrest in the presence of his wife and child. He further alleged that, in the course of his interrogation, he was beaten with fists and clubs, trussed up with belts around his feet, legs and neck, had a plastic bag and a gas mask (the latter filled with ammonia) put over his head. He was allegedly attached to a table and had wires put on his penis and right wrist; electric shocks were applied several times. Upon arrival at SIZO No. 5, the feldsher failed to record any injuries. Further, the prisoner’s complaint of ill-treatment was apparently not taken up by the prosecutor. However, further to a court order, he was examined by doctors from the Forensic Medicine Expertise Bureau in Donetsk between 12 July and 2 August 2000 (i.e. six months after the alleged ill-treatment took place). The following injuries were recorded: "on the neck there was a 2 by 1 cm pink-purple mark; on the back a 15 by 10 cm light brown mark consistent with injuries of the skin; traces of four injuries of the skin on the shoulder; whitish-reddish marks on the back of the hip which could be old injuries of the skin; 2.5 by 2 cm traces of injuries on the gluteus; on the radial-dorsal side of the right wrist was a 1 by 0.5 cm brown pigmented linear mark; on the dorsal left side of the penis a whitish scar was visible". The expertise concluded that the injuries dated from roughly six months previously, and were consistent with the allegations made by the man. Upon examination by a medical member of the delegation, the mark on the wrist and the scar on the penis, consistent with an allegation of electrical shocks, were found to be still visible.”

1. The case originated in an application (no. 17416/03) against Ukraine lodged with the Court on 26 February 2003 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov (“the applicant”).

2. The applicant, who was granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A.P. Bushchenko, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr N. Kulchytskyy of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been subjected to ill-treatment by the police and that his right to prepare a defence had been infringed.

4. On 31 August 2009, the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1965 and resides in Makiyivka.

A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant

6. On 13 January 2000, the applicant was arrested by officers from the Makiyivka Police Department and taken to a police station, where he remained in police custody until 25 January 2000. According to the applicant, he had no access to a lawyer during that period and was compelled to confess to various offences. He claimed that, during questioning, the police officers had severely beaten him on numerous occasions, suffocated him and applied electric shocks to his genitals. According to the Government, the applicant was informed of his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination, and he signed a waiver of his right to legal representation. He was questioned about the theft of a car and confessed. He also admitted involvement in a robbery.

7. On 14 January 2000, the applicant was taken by ambulance to a hospital. Medical reports issued that day confirmed abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region sustained during the alleged beating by the police (see paragraph 37 below).

8. On 15 January 2000, the investigator initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant concerning theft from a garage, theft of non-ferrous metals and attempted robbery.

9. On 16 January 2000, the applicant was charged with theft of the car.
According to the Government, the applicant had his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination explained to him, after which he signed a waiver of his right to legal representation. The applicant was questioned about the car theft and denied his guilt. He explained that he had been unaware that the other person involved was actually stealing the car and claimed that he had previously confessed under police duress.

10. On that date, the applicant took part in an on-site reconstruction of events. An expert and two attesting witnesses also participated in that investigative action.

11. The Government maintained that on 17 January 2000 the applicant again had his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination explained to him, after which he signed a waiver of his right to legal representation. The applicant was subsequently questioned and confessed to theft from a garage, theft of non-ferrous metals, and robbery. He again took part in an on-site reconstruction of events together with two attesting witnesses.

12. On 18 January 2000 the applicant was also charged with the theft from a garage, the theft of non-ferrous metals, and the robbery.

13. According to the Government’s version of events, on 19 January 2000 the applicant once again had his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination explained to him. He waived his right to legal representation. The applicant was then questioned and pleaded guilty to the charges brought on 18 January 2000. He also took part in an on-site reconstruction of events together with two attesting witnesses. On the same date, further criminal proceedings concerning theft of property were instituted against him.

14. On 25 January 2000 the applicant was transferred to the SIZO (see paragraph 38 below).

15. On 29 February 2000 the investigator conducted a confrontation between the applicant and his co-accused, D. The applicant denied his guilt, whereas D. testified that the applicant had instigated all the crimes. The applicant refused to sign the report of that investigative action. After being formally charged on all counts, the applicant refused to testify.

16. On 2 March 2000 the applicant requested representation by lawyer M. He was questioned in the presence of his lawyer and denied his guilt. In particular, he stated that the thefts had been committed by acquaintances and that he had not been aware of them. He further stated that, although he had bought some goods from one of those acquaintances, he had not known that they were stolen. As regards the robbery, he denied robbing the victim and claimed that he had happened to be in the victim’s yard by coincidence. The applicant also maintained that he had previously confessed under duress. He then examined the case-file materials in the presence of his lawyer, M.

17. On 13 March 2000 the applicant’s mother appointed lawyer I.
to represent the applicant in court.

18. The trial in the applicant’s case began on 17 March 2000. During the court hearings, the applicant alleged that his confession had been obtained under duress, in particular that he had been beaten and ill-treated by police officers who forced him to confess. He requested the examination of witnesses who could corroborate his allegations of ill-treatment. In particular, on 2 June 2000 the applicant asked the court to summon and question Ms U.G. and Ms U.A., who had allegedly heard him screaming while he was being ill-treated at the police station. The motion was granted, and the witnesses were questioned. They testified that they had heard the applicant screaming and had seen him after the beatings. Furthermore, on 8 June 2000 the applicant requested that the court summon and question the doctor who had been working in the ambulance when he was taken to hospital on 14 January 2000 (“the ambulance doctor”; see paragraph 37 below). That request was rejected. The court ordered a forensic medical examination of the applicant on the ground that no such examination had been carried out during the pre-trial investigation.

19. In August 2000 the applicant was not brought to court because he was suffering from renal colic. The trial judge asked the head of the medical unit of the SIZO where the applicant was detained to examine him and inform the court whether he was fit to participate in court hearings.

20. Between 10 and 26 September 2000, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) visited Ukrainian detention facilities, including the SIZO where the applicant was being held. According to the applicant, he met with the CPT experts, and the meeting was reflected in their report (see paragraph 52 below).

21. In September 2000 the SIZO administration informed the court that the applicant’s state of health was satisfactory, that he had received outpatient treatment, and that he was able to attend court and participate in the hearings.

22. However, in October 2000 the head of the SIZO medical unit informed the court, without providing any details, that the applicant’s state of health was very poor, that he had been advised to remain in bed, and that he was therefore unable to attend court or participate in the hearings.

23. On 31 August 2001 the trial court asked the SIZO officials about the applicant’s state of health and his ability to participate in the proceedings. Documents submitted by the SIZO medical unit stated that the applicant could take part in court hearings and recommended that he be brought to court on a stretcher. The trial judge therefore instructed the SIZO administration to arrange for the applicant to be transported to court on a stretcher so that the examination of his criminal case could be concluded.

24.
According to the Government, in October 2001 the applicant requested that the court arrange his transportation so that the examination of his case could resume.

25. On 9 November 2001, lawyer N. took over the applicant’s defence from lawyer I., who had died.

26. On 5 December 2001, the judge asked the chief doctor of the ambulance station to arrange for the applicant to be transported to court by ambulance and under a doctor’s supervision. According to the SIZO medical unit, the applicant was able to attend court and participate in hearings, but it was recommended that he be brought to court on a stretcher. Medical records indicated that the applicant suffered from severe neurological pain in the lower spine and could neither walk nor sit.

27. On 21 December 2001, the applicant was transported to court by ambulance and brought into the courtroom on a stretcher. A doctor remained present throughout the hearing, and the applicant was represented by lawyer N. According to the applicant, he felt unwell during the hearing and lost consciousness several times. According to the Government, his state of health was satisfactory. They maintained that, on that date, the court completed its examination of the case file, concluded the judicial investigation of the matter, and proceeded to hear the parties’ final pleadings, including those of the applicant himself. According to the hearing transcript, the applicant participated in the final pleadings and indicated that he agreed to the termination of the judicial investigation. At the end of the hearing, he was given an opportunity to make a closing statement. After he failed to do so, he was examined by the doctor, who confirmed that his blood pressure was normal, although the applicant stated that he felt unwell. The doctor concluded that the applicant’s condition was satisfactory and that he was able to speak. When given another opportunity to make a closing statement, the applicant did not respond. The Government further noted that the court had not examined any witnesses at that hearing and that neither the applicant nor his lawyer had requested an adjournment on the ground that his health prevented him from participating.

28. On the same day, the court ordered that arrangements be made to transport the applicant to court by ambulance on 25 December 2001.

29. On 25 December 2001, the Gornyatskiy Local Court of Makiyivka found the applicant and several other individuals guilty of theft and robbery. The court established that, on 14 May 1999, the applicant, M., and another person had stolen a car from S. It further found that, on 30 October 1999, the applicant and his co-defendants M., St., and Mo. had stolen scrap metal from G.’s garage; and that, on 17 and 20 December 1999, the applicant, M., and Mo. had stolen scrap metal and other property belonging to R. and N.
Finally, on 22 December 1999, the applicant and D. had attempted to rob Mr and Mrs P. The court observed that the applicant had pleaded not guilty. It found that, in addition to the applicant’s previous confessions, the testimony of his co-defendants, the victims, some of whom were eyewitnesses, and other witnesses in the case, together with the material evidence, including some of the stolen goods found in the homes of the applicant’s mother and his cohabitant, constituted sufficient evidence to find the applicant guilty. It also dismissed the applicant’s complaint of ill-treatment, referring to the investigation materials and medical findings and noting that the testimony of Ms U.G. and Ms U.A. that they had heard the applicant screaming at the police station could not be accepted, as it was unsupported by other material in the case and in view of the nature of their relationship with the applicant [the applicant’s cohabitant and her mother]. The applicant was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

30. On 27 December 2001, the applicant was served with a copy of the judgment.

31. On 2 and 7 January 2002, the applicant lodged appeals against the judgment of 25 December 2001.

32. On 23 January 2002, the first-instance court declined to examine the applicant’s appeals because he had failed to comply with procedural formalities. It noted, in particular, that the applicant had not identified the judgment being appealed against or specified and substantiated his claims that the judgment was unlawful. He was given seven days to bring his appeals into compliance with the procedural requirements.

33. On 7 February 2002, the applicant lodged another appeal, which the first-instance court also declined to consider on 22 February 2002 because the new statement of appeal merely supplemented the original appeals rather than constituting a corrected version. In view of the applicant’s poor health, he was granted a further extension of time to resubmit his appeals in accordance with the procedural formalities. The applicant filed five additional supplementary statements of appeal, but without success.

34. On 13 May 2002, the applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. He complained that he had been tortured, denied access to a lawyer, and that the investigators had falsified documents in the case file. He further complained that his cellmates had not been questioned as witnesses to his ill-treatment and that the judgment had been delivered in his absence because his lawyer had persuaded him to waive his right to attend the final hearing in his case. For the same reason, he had been denied the opportunity to present arguments before the court and make closing submissions.

35.
On 29 October 2002, a panel of three judges of the Supreme Court considered the applicant’s cassation appeal and concluded that the first-instance court’s judgment was well-founded. It also found that there had been no procedural violations and that the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment had been duly examined and dismissed as unsubstantiated.

B. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment and the investigation into it

36. According to the applicant, between 13 and 25 January 2000 he was held in police detention facilities, where he was repeatedly and severely beaten by police officers, who forced him to confess to theft and robbery. During his arrest, the police used teargas. He was then tied up, kicked, punched, and beaten with a stick. He was taken to the police station, where officers placed a plastic bag and then a gas mask over his head, causing him to suffocate. He was also continuously beaten. Police officers then attached electric wires to his penis and right hand and administered electric shocks.

37. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was called for the applicant, who was weak and suffering from pain in the lumbar area and below his rib cage. The ambulance doctor examined him, and the applicant explained that he had fallen down the stairs on 13 January and had been arrested by the police later that day. He was taken to hospital for a more detailed examination. Medical reports issued by the hospital doctors on the same date recorded abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region.

38. The applicant was transferred to the SIZO on 25 January 2000. According to him, the doctor on duty noticed signs of his injuries but did not record them after speaking with a police officer. Only some of the injuries were documented, and the police warned him to tell the doctor that they had been self-inflicted. The applicant claimed that he had never been permitted to remain alone with the doctor examining him.

39. On 14 March 2000, the applicant wrote to a human rights NGO complaining of ill-treatment by the police.

40. On 25 May 2000, the Makiyivka Town Prosecutor’s Office questioned the doctors and police officers concerned and declined to institute criminal proceedings in connection with the alleged ill-treatment, finding that it could not be established beyond reasonable doubt that the applicant had been ill-treated by the police. The refusal also stated that, according to the police, the applicant had feigned illness because he intended to escape and wanted to be taken to hospital to facilitate his escape. According to the ambulance doctor who examined the applicant on 14 January 2000, he had complained of pain in various parts of his body and had explained that he had fallen on 13 January 2000 before being arrested by the police. The doctor recorded abdominal trauma and numerous bruises, mainly in the lumbar area.
He further recommended that the applicant consult a surgeon and a urologist.

41. On 8 June 2000, the trial court ordered a forensic medical examination of the applicant with a view to considering his allegations of ill-treatment. The examination was conducted between 12 July and 2 August 2000. According to its findings, no injuries to the face or scalp were detected. On the front of the neck there was a pinkish-purple mark measuring 2 x 1 cm (according to the applicant, it was a birthmark). On the right wrist there was a pale brown mark measuring 1 x 0.5 cm. On the front surface of both forearms there were scars, four on the left and nine on the right, measuring between 3 x 0.2 cm and 8 x 0.2 cm. The applicant complained of pain in the lumbar region on both sides and in the coccyx. The examination revealed an area of pale brown skin in that region measuring 15 x 10 cm. It further revealed several scars: a round scar 2.3 cm in diameter on the back of the right thigh, several scars measuring 2.2 x 0.2 cm on the left buttock, and a scar measuring 1 x 0.6 cm on the right knee. At a distance of 1 to 1.5 cm from the head of the penis, there was a dotted line of whitish skin measuring 0.1 x 2 cm. No other injuries or marks were found. The expert concluded that the brown marks on the applicant’s wrist and in the lumbar and coccyx regions could be signs of healing bruises that might have been inflicted on 13 January 2000 in the circumstances described by the applicant. As for the scars, the expert concluded that they were several years old, but the exact time of their formation could not be established.

42. On 2 August 2000, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office quashed the decision of 25 May 2000 and ordered further investigation, noting that the examination of the applicant’s complaint had been incomplete.

43. In August 2000, the prosecutor questioned the police officers, doctors, the applicant’s prison cellmates, and a number of other people. In particular, the ambulance doctor who had seen the applicant on 14 January 2000 was questioned again. Some of the applicant’s cellmates confirmed that he had told them he had been ill-treated by the police but had provided no details; others testified that the applicant had not spoken about being beaten by the police.

44. On 7 September 2000, the Makiyivka Prosecutor’s Office refused to institute criminal proceedings for lack of evidence of a crime. The decision noted that there was no proof that the applicant had been ill-treated and that the evidence given by his cellmates concerning the alleged ill-treatment was contradictory and could not provide a sufficient basis for concluding that the applicant had been ill-treated.

45. In November 2000, at the request of the applicant’s lawyer, the court ordered a forensic medical examination of the applicant.
From 22 November 2000 to 18 May 2001, the applicant underwent a series of medical examinations. The experts observed that the applicant had numerous scars, some of which were over ten years old. They also recorded brown pigmentation on his right wrist and penis, which the applicant claimed were marks from the electric shocks administered to him on 13 January 2000. The experts further concluded that there was no connection between the applicant’s injuries in January 2000 and his subsequent health problems.

46. In August 2003, the applicant was served with a copy of the decision of 7 September 2000 and challenged it before the courts.

47. On 6 November 2003, the Tsentralno-Miskyy District Court of Makiyivka quashed the decision of 7 September 2000 and remitted the case for further investigation. The court noted that the file contained neither a statement by the applicant concerning the circumstances of the alleged ill-treatment nor information about his state of health upon arrival at the SIZO and the prison where he was detained. Moreover, the applicant’s cellmates in the SIZO had not been questioned, and the case file contained no information as to when or how the applicant’s injuries had been inflicted. Finally, the higher prosecutor’s instructions had not been fully complied with.

48. On 20 May 2005, the applicant’s cellmates were questioned again by the prosecutor.

49. On 15 June 2005, the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings for lack of corpus delicti. The police officers denied having ill-treated the applicant. The applicant’s cellmates gave conflicting statements as to whether he had complained of ill-treatment and whether he had sustained any injuries at the relevant time. It was also noted that information about the applicant’s state of health upon arrival at the SIZO was unavailable because the relevant records had been destroyed after the expiry of the retention period. Furthermore, no records had been kept identifying those who had shared cells with the applicant in the SIZO, and those individuals could therefore not be identified. The prosecutor concluded that there was no evidence that the applicant had been ill-treated or had sustained any injuries at that time. The applicant did not challenge that decision.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

A. Constitution of Ukraine

50. Article 63 of the Constitution provided as follows:

“A person shall not bear responsibility for refusing to testify or to explain anything about himself or herself, members of his or her family or close relatives to the degree determined by law.

A suspect, an accused or a defendant has the right to a defence...”

B. Other relevant domestic law

51. Other relevant domestic law is summarised in the cases of Yaremenko v. Ukraine (no. 32092/02, §§ 45-49, 12 June 2008) and Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).

III.
INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTS

Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine conducted by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) from 10 to 26 September 2000.

52. According to the applicant, the following section of the report related to him.

“19. ... A man arrested by the Organised Crime Department of the Militia in the town of Makeyevka, Donetsk Region, on 13 January 2000 alleged that he had been beaten upon arrest in the presence of his wife and child. He further alleged that, during his interrogation, he was beaten with fists and clubs, trussed up with belts around his feet, legs and neck, and had a plastic bag and a gas mask (the latter filled with ammonia) placed over his head. He was allegedly fastened to a table and had wires attached to his penis and right wrist; electric shocks were administered several times. Upon his arrival at SIZO No. 5, the feldsher failed to record any injuries. Furthermore, the prisoner’s complaint of ill-treatment was apparently not pursued by the prosecutor. However, following a court order, he was examined by doctors from the Forensic Medicine Expertise Bureau in Donetsk between 12 July and 2 August 2000 (i.e. six months after the alleged ill-treatment occurred). The following injuries were recorded: ‘on the neck there was a 2 by 1 cm pink-purple mark; on the back a 15 by 10 cm light brown mark consistent with injuries of the skin; traces of four injuries of the skin on the shoulder; whitish-reddish marks on the back of the hip which could be old injuries of the skin; 2.5 by 2 cm traces of injuries on the gluteus; on the radial-dorsal side of the right wrist was a 1 by 0.5 cm brown pigmented linear mark; on the dorsal left side of the penis a whitish scar was visible’. The expertise concluded that the injuries dated from approximately six months earlier and were consistent with the man’s allegations. During an examination by a medical member of the delegation, the mark on the wrist and the scar on the penis, consistent with an allegation of electric shocks, were found to remain visible.”

In view of the applicant’s poor health, the court granted him an additional period in which to resubmit his appeals in compliance with the procedural formalities. He subsequently filed five more supplementary statements of appeal, but none was successful.

34. On 13 May 2002, the applicant lodged a cassation appeal before the Supreme Court. He alleged that he had been tortured, denied access to legal counsel, and that investigators had falsified documents in the case file. He further complained that his cellmates had not been questioned as witnesses to the alleged ill-treatment. In addition, he maintained that the judgment had been delivered in his absence because his lawyer had persuaded him to waive his right to attend the final hearing in the case. As a result, he had also been unable to present arguments to the court or make closing submissions.

35.
On 29 October 2002, a three-judge panel of the Supreme Court considered the applicant’s cassation appeal and found the first-instance judgment to be well-founded. The panel further concluded that no procedural breaches had occurred and that the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment had been properly investigated and dismissed as unsubstantiated.

B. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment and the investigation thereof

36. The applicant alleged that, from 13 to 25 January 2000, he was held in police detention facilities and repeatedly subjected to severe beatings by officers seeking to force him to confess to theft and robbery. During his arrest, the police used tear gas, tied him up, and kicked, punched and struck him with a stick. After taking him to the police station, officers allegedly covered his head first with a plastic bag and then with a gas mask, causing him to suffocate, while continuing to beat him. They subsequently attached electric wires to his penis and right hand and subjected him to electric shocks.

37. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was summoned because the applicant was weak and experiencing pain in the lumbar region and beneath his rib cage. During the examination, he told the ambulance doctor that he had fallen down the stairs on 13 January and had been arrested by the police later that day. He was then taken to hospital for a more thorough examination. Medical reports prepared by hospital doctors that same day noted abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar area.

38. On 25 January 2000, the applicant was transferred to the SIZO. He maintained that the doctor on duty observed signs of injury but, following a conversation with a police officer, failed to document them. Only certain injuries were recorded, and the police allegedly instructed the applicant to tell the doctor that he had inflicted them on himself. He further asserted that he was never permitted to remain alone with the examining doctor.

39. On 14 March 2000, the applicant sent a letter to a human-rights NGO alleging that he had been ill-treated by the police.

40. After questioning the relevant doctors and police officers, the Makiyivka Town Prosecutor’s Office decided on 25 May 2000 not to institute criminal proceedings in respect of the alleged ill-treatment. It found that police mistreatment of the applicant could not be established beyond reasonable doubt. The decision also cited the police assertion that the applicant had feigned illness because he intended to escape and wanted to be transferred to hospital to facilitate that plan. The ambulance doctor who examined him on 14 January 2000 stated that the applicant had complained of pain in various parts of his body and had said that he had fallen on 13 January, before being arrested by the police. The doctor documented abdominal trauma and numerous bruises, predominantly in the lumbar region.
He also advised the applicant to consult a surgeon and a urologist.

41. On 8 June 2000, in order to examine the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment, the trial court directed that he undergo a forensic medical examination. The examination took place from 12 July to 2 August 2000. It found no injuries to his face or scalp. A pinkish-purple mark measuring 2 × 1 cm was observed on the front of his neck; the applicant stated that it was a birthmark. A pale-brown mark measuring 1 × 0.5 cm was present on his right wrist. The front surfaces of his forearms bore scars—four on the left and nine on the right—ranging in size from 3 × 0.2 cm to 8 × 0.2 cm. The applicant reported pain on both sides of the lumbar region and in the coccyx. In that area, the examination identified a 15 × 10 cm patch of pale-brown skin. It also disclosed several scars: a round scar, 2.3 cm in diameter, on the back of the right thigh; several scars measuring 2.2 × 0.2 cm on the left buttock; and a 1 × 0.6 cm scar on the right knee. A dotted line of whitish skin measuring 0.1 × 2 cm was found between 1 and 1.5 cm from the head of the penis. No further injuries or marks were identified. The expert considered that the brown marks on the applicant’s wrist and in the lumbar and coccygeal region might have been healing bruises sustained on 13 January 2000 in the circumstances recounted by him. Regarding the scars, the expert determined that they were several years old, although their precise date of formation could not be established.

42. On 2 August 2000, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office set aside the decision of 25 May 2000 and directed that additional inquiries be carried out, finding that the applicant’s complaint had not been examined fully.

43. During August 2000, the prosecutor questioned the police officers, medical personnel, the applicant’s prison cellmates, and several other individuals. The ambulance doctor who had examined the applicant on 14 January 2000 was questioned again. Some cellmates stated that the applicant had told them that the police had ill-treated him, though he had provided no details. Others testified that he had never mentioned being beaten by the police.

44. On 7 September 2000, the Makiyivka Prosecutor’s Office declined to open criminal proceedings because there was insufficient evidence that an offence had been committed. Its decision stated that the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment had not been substantiated. It further observed that the cellmates’ accounts were inconsistent and therefore could not provide an adequate basis for finding that the applicant had been ill-treated.

45. In November 2000, acting on a request from the applicant’s lawyer, the court ordered a further forensic medical examination of the applicant.
Between 22 November 2000 and 18 May 2001, the applicant was examined by medical specialists on several occasions. They documented numerous scars, including some that were over ten years old. Brown areas of pigmentation were also observed on his right wrist and penis; according to the applicant, these marks resulted from electric shocks administered to him on 13 January 2000. The experts additionally found no causal connection between the injuries sustained by the applicant in January 2000 and his later health problems.

46. In August 2003, the applicant received a copy of the decision dated 7 September 2000 and lodged a court challenge against it.

47. On 6 November 2003, the Tsentralno-Miskyy District Court of Makiyivka set aside the decision of 7 September 2000 and returned the case for further investigation. It observed that the case file contained neither a statement from the applicant describing the alleged ill-treatment nor information about his health when he arrived at the SIZO and the prison where he was held. The applicant’s SIZO cellmates had also not been interviewed, and the file included no details establishing when or how his injuries had been caused. In addition, the higher prosecutor’s instructions had not been fully implemented.

48. On 20 May 2005, the prosecutor questioned the applicant’s cellmates once more.

49. On 15 June 2005, the prosecutor declined to institute criminal proceedings because no corpus delicti had been established. The police officers denied subjecting the applicant to any ill-treatment. His cellmates provided inconsistent accounts concerning whether he had complained of ill-treatment and whether he had shown any injuries at the relevant time. It was further recorded that information about his health upon admission to the SIZO was no longer available because the relevant documents had been destroyed after the applicable retention period had expired. Moreover, no records had been maintained identifying the persons who had shared cells with the applicant in the SIZO, making it impossible to determine who they were. The prosecutor ultimately found no evidence that the applicant had been ill-treated or had sustained any injuries during the period in question. The applicant did not contest that decision.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

A. Constitution of Ukraine

50. Article 63 of the Constitution provided:

“A person shall not be held responsible for refusing to testify or provide explanations concerning himself or herself, members of his or her family, or close relatives, to the extent prescribed by law.

A suspect, an accused person or a defendant is entitled to a defence...”

B. Other relevant domestic law

51. The remaining pertinent provisions of domestic law are summarised in Yaremenko v. Ukraine (no. 32092/02, §§ 45-49, 12 June 2008) and Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).

III.
INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTS

Report to the Government of Ukraine on the visit conducted by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) between 10 and 26 September 2000.

52. The applicant maintained that the following section of the report related to him:

“19. ... On 13 January 2000, a man was arrested by the Organised Crime Department of the Militia in Makeyevka, Donetsk Region. He alleged that, during the arrest, he was beaten in front of his wife and child. He further claimed that, while being questioned, officers struck him with their fists and clubs, bound his feet, legs and neck with belts, and placed both a plastic bag and a gas mask over his head, with the gas mask filled with ammonia. According to his account, he was fastened to a table, wires were attached to his penis and right wrist, and electric shocks were administered repeatedly.

When he arrived at SIZO No. 5, the feldsher did not document any injuries. In addition, the prosecutor apparently took no action in response to the prisoner’s complaint of ill-treatment. Following a court order, however, doctors from the Forensic Medicine Expertise Bureau in Donetsk examined him between 12 July and 2 August 2000, approximately six months after the alleged abuse.

The examination documented the following injuries: ‘a pink-purple mark measuring 2 by 1 cm on the neck; a light-brown mark measuring 15 by 10 cm on the back, consistent with skin injuries; evidence of four skin injuries on the shoulder; whitish-reddish marks on the back of the hip, possibly representing old skin injuries; traces of injuries measuring 2.5 by 2 cm on the gluteus; a brown-pigmented linear mark measuring 1 by 0.5 cm on the radial-dorsal aspect of the right wrist; and a visible whitish scar on the dorsal left side of the penis.’

The forensic experts concluded that the injuries had been sustained about six months earlier and were compatible with the man’s allegations. A medical member of the delegation subsequently examined him and confirmed that the wrist mark and penile scar remained visible and were consistent with his claim that electric shocks had been applied.”

FIFTH SECTION

TARASOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 17416/03)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

31 October 2013

31/01/2014

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment is final. It may undergo editorial revision.

In Tarasov v. Ukraine, the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of the Fifth Section and composed of:

Mark Villiger, President,  
Ann Power-Forde,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
André Potocki,  
Paul Lemmens,  
Helena Jäderblom,  
Aleš Pejchal, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

having held private deliberations on 8 October 2013,

adopts on that same date the following judgment:

PROCEDURAL HISTORY

1. These proceedings arose from application no. 17416/03, which Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov (“the applicant”), a Ukrainian national, submitted against Ukraine to the Court on 26 February 2003 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. The applicant received legal aid and was represented by Mr A.P. Bushchenko, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent from the Ministry of Justice, most recently Mr N. Kulchytskyy.

3. In particular, the applicant complained that the police had subjected him to ill-treatment and that his right to conduct his defence had been breached.

4. On 31 August 2009, the President of the Fifth Section decided to notify the Government of the application.

THE FACTS

I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

5. Born in 1965, the applicant resides in Makiyivka.

A. Criminal case against the applicant

6. Officers of the Makiyivka Police Department arrested the applicant on 13 January 2000 and brought him to a police station. He remained in police custody there until 25 January 2000. The applicant stated that throughout this period he was denied access to a lawyer and compelled to admit to several offences. He further alleged that, while being questioned, police officers repeatedly beat him severely, caused him to suffocate and administered electric shocks to his genitals. The Government maintained that the applicant had been informed of his procedural rights, including the right to legal assistance and the privilege against self-incrimination, and that he had signed a waiver of legal representation. He was questioned in connection with the theft of a car and confessed to that offence. He also admitted participating in a robbery.

7. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance took the applicant to hospital. Medical records drawn up that day documented abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar area sustained during the alleged police beating (see paragraph 37 below).

8. On 15 January 2000, the investigator opened criminal proceedings against the applicant concerning theft from a garage, theft of non-ferrous metals and attempted robbery.

9. On 16 January 2000, the applicant was formally charged with the car theft.
The Government submitted that, after the applicant had been informed of his procedural rights to legal assistance and protection against self-incrimination, he signed a waiver of his right to legal representation. When questioned about the car theft, he denied responsibility, stating that he had not known that the other person involved was in fact stealing the vehicle and alleging that his earlier confession had been obtained through police coercion.

10. That same day, the applicant took part in an on-site reconstruction of the events, attended by an expert and two attesting witnesses.

11. According to the Government, on 17 January 2000 the applicant was again advised of his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination, after which he signed another waiver of his right to legal assistance. During the ensuing questioning, he admitted to a theft from a garage, the theft of non-ferrous metals, and a robbery. He subsequently participated in another on-site reconstruction of events in the presence of two attesting witnesses.

12. On 18 January 2000, further charges were brought against the applicant in relation to the garage theft, the theft of non-ferrous metals, and the robbery.

13. The Government maintained that, on 19 January 2000, the applicant was once more informed of his procedural rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination. After waiving his right to legal assistance, he was questioned and pleaded guilty to the charges brought on 18 January 2000. He also took part in an on-site reconstruction of the events with two attesting witnesses. Later that same day, additional criminal proceedings concerning the theft of property were opened against him.

14. On 25 January 2000, the applicant was moved to the SIZO (see paragraph 38 below).

15. On 29 February 2000, the investigator arranged a confrontation between the applicant and his co-accused, D. The applicant maintained his innocence, whereas D. stated that the applicant had initiated all the offences. The applicant declined to sign the record of that investigative measure. After being formally charged on every count, he refused to give evidence.

16. On 2 March 2000, the applicant requested representation by lawyer M. Questioned in his lawyer’s presence, he denied all guilt. More specifically, he claimed that the thefts had been carried out by acquaintances without his knowledge and that, although he had purchased certain goods from one of them, he had not known they were stolen. Concerning the robbery, he denied robbing the victim and said that his presence in the victim’s yard had been purely coincidental. He further alleged that his previous confessions had been made under duress. Accompanied by lawyer M., the applicant then examined the materials in the case file.

17. On 13 March 2000, the applicant’s mother retained lawyer I.
to act on the applicant’s behalf before the court.

18. Proceedings in the applicant’s case commenced on 17 March 2000. At the hearings, he alleged that his confession had been obtained under coercion, stating in particular that police officers had beaten and otherwise ill-treated him to force him to confess. He requested that the court hear witnesses capable of corroborating those allegations. Specifically, on 2 June 2000 he applied for Ms U.G. and Ms U.A. to be summoned and examined, claiming that they had heard him scream while he was being ill-treated at the police station. The court granted the application. Both witnesses were questioned and stated that they had heard the applicant screaming and had seen him following the beatings. On 8 June 2000 the applicant also asked the court to summon and examine the doctor who had been serving in the ambulance that transported him to hospital on 14 January 2000 (“the ambulance doctor”; see paragraph 37 below). That application was refused. As no forensic medical assessment had been carried out during the pre-trial investigation, the court ordered that the applicant undergo such an examination.

19. In August 2000 the applicant was not taken to court because he was experiencing renal colic. The trial judge requested that the head of the medical unit at the SIZO where the applicant was being held examine him and advise the court whether his health allowed him to attend the hearings.

20. From 10 to 26 September 2000, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) inspected detention facilities in Ukraine, including the SIZO in which the applicant was detained. The applicant stated that he met with the CPT experts and that this was recorded in their Report (see paragraph 52 below).

21. In September 2000 the SIZO authorities notified the court that the applicant’s health was satisfactory, that he had undergone some outpatient treatment, and that he was able to appear in court and participate in the hearings.

22. In October 2000, however, the head of the SIZO medical unit advised the court, without providing further particulars, that the applicant was in very poor health, had been instructed to remain in bed, and was consequently unable to attend court or participate in the hearings.

23. On 31 August 2001 the trial court asked SIZO officials for information concerning the applicant’s health and whether he was capable of taking part in the proceedings. Records provided by the SIZO medical unit indicated that he could participate in the hearings and recommended that he be transported to court on a stretcher. The trial judge accordingly instructed the SIZO authorities to arrange for him to be brought to court on a stretcher so that consideration of his criminal case could be completed.

24.
According to the Government, the applicant requested in October 2001 that the court arrange for him to be transported there so that the examination of his case could continue.

25. Following the death of lawyer I., lawyer N. took over the applicant’s defence on 9 November 2001.

26. On 5 December 2001, the judge requested that the chief doctor of the ambulance station organise the applicant’s transport to court by ambulance under medical supervision. The SIZO medical unit considered the applicant fit to attend court and participate in hearings, but recommended that he be transported on a stretcher. Medical records indicated that he was suffering from severe neurological pain in the lower spine and was unable to walk or sit.

27. The applicant was taken to court by ambulance on 21 December 2001 and carried into the courtroom on a stretcher. A doctor remained present for the entire hearing, and lawyer N. represented him. The applicant stated that he felt unwell during the proceedings and lost consciousness several times. The Government, by contrast, maintained that his condition was satisfactory. They asserted that, on that date, the court finished reviewing the case file, concluded the judicial investigation, and proceeded to the parties’ final pleadings, including submissions made by the applicant personally. The hearing transcript records that the applicant participated in the final pleadings and agreed that the judicial investigation should be closed. At the conclusion of the hearing, he was invited to deliver a closing statement. After he failed to do so, the doctor examined him and confirmed that his blood pressure was normal, although the applicant said that he felt unwell. The doctor found his condition satisfactory and concluded that he was able to speak. When given a further opportunity to make a closing statement, the applicant did not respond. The Government further observed that no witnesses were examined at that hearing and that neither the applicant nor his lawyer sought an adjournment on the ground that his health prevented him from participating.

28. That same day, the court ordered that the applicant be transported to court by ambulance on 25 December 2001.

29. On 25 December 2001, the Gornyatskiy Local Court of Makiyivka convicted the applicant and several others of theft and robbery. It found that, on 14 May 1999, the applicant, M., and another individual had stolen a car from S. The court also established that, on 30 October 1999, the applicant and his co-defendants M., St., and Mo. had stolen scrap metal from G.’s garage, and that, on 17 and 20 December 1999, the applicant, M., and Mo. had stolen scrap metal and other property belonging to R. and N.
Lastly, on 22 December 1999, the applicant and D. attempted to rob Mr and Mrs P. The court observed that the applicant had entered a plea of not guilty. Nevertheless, it found the evidence sufficient to establish his guilt. In addition to his earlier confessions, that evidence included statements from his co-defendants, the victims—some of whom had witnessed the events—and other witnesses, together with physical evidence, notably some of the stolen property discovered in the homes of the applicant’s mother and cohabitant. The court also dismissed his allegation of ill-treatment. It relied on the investigation records and medical findings and declined to accept the statements of Ms U.G. and Ms U.A. that they had heard him screaming at the police station, because those accounts were unsupported by the other case materials and because of the witnesses’ relationship to the applicant [they were his cohabitant and her mother]. The applicant received a sentence of five years’ imprisonment.

30. A copy of the judgment was served on the applicant on 27 December 2001.

31. On 2 and 7 January 2002, he appealed against the judgment of 25 December 2001.

32. On 23 January 2002, the first-instance court declined to examine those appeals because they did not comply with the applicable procedural formalities. In particular, it stated that the applicant had neither identified the judgment being challenged nor specified and substantiated his contention that it was unlawful. He was allowed seven days to correct the appeals so that they met the procedural requirements.

33. The applicant filed a further appeal on 7 February 2002. On 22 February 2002, the first-instance court likewise refused to consider it, finding that the new appeal merely supplemented the original ones instead of constituting a corrected version. In view of the applicant’s poor health, he was granted an additional extension within which to resubmit appeals complying with the procedural formalities. He subsequently filed five more supplementary statements of appeal, without success.

34. On 13 May 2002, the applicant submitted a cassation appeal to the Supreme Court. He alleged that he had been tortured, denied access to a lawyer, and that investigators had falsified documents in the case file. He further complained that his cellmates had not been examined as witnesses regarding his ill-treatment. He also maintained that the judgment had been delivered in his absence after his lawyer persuaded him to waive his right to attend the final hearing in the case. For that same reason, he had been unable to present arguments to the court or make closing submissions.

35.
On 29 October 2002, a three-judge panel of the Supreme Court considered the applicant’s cassation appeal and found the first-instance court’s judgment to be well-founded. The panel further determined that no procedural breaches had occurred and that the applicant’s claims of ill-treatment had been properly investigated and dismissed as unsupported.

B. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment and the related investigation

36. The applicant stated that, from 13 to 25 January 2000, he was held in police detention facilities and repeatedly subjected to severe beatings by officers seeking to force him to confess to theft and robbery. He alleged that the police used teargas during his arrest, after which they tied him up and kicked, punched, and struck him with a stick. At the police station, officers allegedly put first a plastic bag and then a gasmask over his head, making him suffocate, while continuing to beat him. They subsequently attached electric wires to his penis and right hand and subjected him to electric shocks.

37. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was summoned because the applicant was weak and experiencing pain in his lumbar region and beneath his rib cage. During the examination, he told the ambulance doctor that he had fallen down the stairs on 13 January and had later been arrested by the police that same day. He was then transported to a hospital for a more thorough examination. Medical reports prepared by hospital doctors on 14 January documented abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar area.

38. On 25 January 2000, the applicant was moved to the SIZO. He alleged that the doctor on duty noticed evidence of his injuries but, following a conversation with a police officer, failed to document them. Only certain injuries were recorded, and the police instructed him to tell the doctor that he had inflicted those injuries on himself. The applicant maintained that he was never permitted to be alone with the examining doctor.

39. On 14 March 2000, the applicant sent a letter to a human-rights NGO in which he complained that the police had ill-treated him.

40. After questioning the relevant doctors and police officers, the Makiyivka Town Prosecutor’s Office decided on 25 May 2000 not to open criminal proceedings into the alleged ill-treatment, on the ground that it could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt that the police had mistreated the applicant. The refusal also stated that, according to the police, the applicant had feigned illness because he intended to escape and wanted to be transferred to a hospital to make that escape easier. The ambulance doctor who examined him on 14 January 2000 reported that the applicant had complained of pain in several areas of his body and had said that, before his arrest by the police, he had fallen down on 13 January 2000. The doctor documented abdominal trauma and multiple bruises, located chiefly in the lumbar region.
He also advised the applicant to consult a surgeon and a urologist.

41. On 8 June 2000, in order to investigate the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment, the trial court directed that he undergo a forensic medical examination. The examination took place from 12 July to 2 August 2000. It found no injuries to either the applicant’s face or scalp. A pinkish-purple mark measuring 2 x 1 cm was observed on the front of his neck; the applicant stated that it was a birthmark. A pale brown mark measuring 1 x 0.5 cm was present on his right wrist. The front surfaces of his forearms bore scars—4 on the left and 9 on the right—ranging in size from 3 x 0.2 cm to 8 x 0.2 cm. Several additional scars were recorded: a circular scar 2.3 cm in diameter on the back of the right thigh, several scars measuring 2.2 x 0.2 cm on the left buttock, and a scar measuring 1 x 0.6 cm on the right knee. A dotted line of whitish skin, measuring 0.1 x 2 cm, was found between 1 and 1.5 cm from the head of the penis. No further injuries or marks were identified. The expert considered that the brown marks on the applicant’s wrist and in the lumbar and coccygeal area might represent healing bruises that could have been sustained on 13 January 2000 in the circumstances described by him. The expert further determined that the scars were several years old, although their precise date of formation could not be established.

42. On 2 August 2000, finding that the applicant’s complaint had not been fully examined, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office set aside the decision of 25 May 2000 and instructed that additional investigative steps be taken.

43. During August 2000, the prosecutor questioned police officers, doctors, the applicant’s prison cellmates, and several other individuals. The ambulance doctor who had examined the applicant on 14 January 2000 was questioned again. Some cellmates stated that the applicant had told them the police had ill-treated him, although he had provided no details. Others testified that he had never said that the police had beaten him.

44. On 7 September 2000, the Makiyivka Prosecutor’s Office declined to open criminal proceedings because there was insufficient evidence that a crime had occurred. Its decision stated that the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment had not been proven and that the conflicting testimony of his cellmates could not provide an adequate basis for finding that he had been ill-treated.

45. In November 2000, acting on a request from the applicant’s lawyer, the court ordered that the applicant undergo a forensic medical examination.
Between 22 November 2000 and 18 May 2001, the applicant was examined medically on several occasions. The experts identified numerous scars, including some dating back more than ten years. They also observed brown areas of pigmentation on his right wrist and penis, which, according to the applicant, resulted from electric shocks administered to him on 13 January 2000. The experts additionally found no causal connection between the injuries sustained by the applicant in January 2000 and his later health problems.

46. In August 2003, the applicant received a copy of the decision dated 7 September 2000 and contested it before the courts.

47. On 6 November 2003, the Tsentralno-Miskyy District Court of Makiyivka set aside the decision of 7 September 2000 and returned the case for further investigation. It observed that the case file contained neither the applicant’s account of the circumstances surrounding the alleged ill-treatment nor information concerning his health when he arrived at the SIZO and at the prison where he was held. The applicant’s SIZO cellmates had also not been interviewed, and the file included no details indicating when or how his injuries had been caused. In addition, the higher prosecutor’s directions had not been implemented in full.

48. On 20 May 2005, the prosecutor questioned the applicant’s cellmates once more.

49. On 15 June 2005, the prosecutor declined to open criminal proceedings because of the absence of corpus delicti. The police officers denied having subjected the applicant to any ill-treatment. His cellmates provided inconsistent accounts regarding whether, at the relevant time, he had complained about ill-treatment or displayed any injuries. The decision further stated that no information was available about the applicant’s health upon admission to the SIZO, since the pertinent records had been destroyed once their prescribed retention period had expired. Moreover, no records had been maintained identifying the persons who had shared SIZO cells with the applicant, making it impossible to establish their identities. The prosecutor therefore determined that there was no evidence that the applicant had been ill-treated or injured at that time. The applicant did not appeal against that decision.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

A. Constitution of Ukraine

50. Article 63 of the Constitution provided that no one could be held responsible for refusing to testify or provide explanations concerning himself or herself, family members, or close relatives, to the extent specified by law. It also guaranteed a suspect, an accused person, or a defendant the right to a defence.

B. Other relevant domestic law

51. The remaining pertinent provisions of domestic law are summarised in Yaremenko v. Ukraine (no. 32092/02, §§ 45 to 49, 12 June 2008) and Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).

III.
INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTS

Report addressed to the Government of Ukraine concerning the visit to Ukraine by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT), conducted from 10 to 26 September 2000.

52. The applicant stated that the following section of the report referred to him:
