Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Mark Villiger, President, Ann Power-Forde, André Potocki, Paul Lemmens, Helena Jäderblom, Aleš Pejchal, judges, Stanislav Shevchuk, ad hoc judge,and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 15 October 2013,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 20602/05) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Sergeyevich Gerashchenko (“the applicant”), on 19 July 2006 (see paragraphs 71-74 below).2. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.3. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been ill-treated by the police, that a search of his home had been unlawful and arbitrary, that his pre-trial detention had been unlawful and unreasonably long and that it had lacked the requisite judicial review. He also complained that he had incriminated himself under duress and without legal assistance.4. On 16 December 2009 the complaints regarding the applicant’s pre-trial detention and the police search at his home were communicated to the Government. The Court also raised ex officio and communicated the issue of Ukraine’s compliance with Articles 8 and 34 of the Convention on account of possible monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence with the Court.5. On 15 March 2012 the President of the Section decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, that the parties should be invited to submit further written observations on the admissibility and merits of the applicant’s complaints about his ill-treatment by the police and the violations of his right to legal assistance and the privilege against self-incrimination.6. Mrs G. Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, was unable to sit in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). The President of the Chamber decided to appoint Mr S. Shevchuk to sit as an ad hoc judge (Rule 29 § 1(b)).THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE7. The applicant was born in 1958 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Odessa following his conviction in criminal proceedings subsequent and unrelated to those examined in the present case.A. Background to the case8. On 4 December 2003 the applicant was convicted of possession of illegal drugs and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. However, the sentence was suspended and he was put on probation. It was his third conviction for a drug-related offence.9. On 12 May 2004 the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department instituted criminal proceedings against an individual, Mr B., on suspicion of possession of illegal drugs. In the course of the investigation Mr B. stated that he had bought the drugs from the applicant.10. On 18 May 2004 the investigator applied to the Odessa Suvorivskyy District Court (hereafter – “the Suvorivskyy Court”), seeking authorisation of a search of the applicant’s home with a view to verifying Mr B.’s statement.11. On 19 May 2004 the Suvorivskyy Court authorised the police search, having agreed that it was required for the criminal investigation to progress.B. Events of 2 July 200412. According to the authorities, on 2 July 2004 an undercover police agent bought 1.9 millilitres of liquid opium from the applicant, having paid him 30 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) in banknotes previously marked with a luminous substance. The undercover operation was followed by a search, in the course of which the police seized the aforementioned banknotes from the applicant and equipment used for drug production that was found in his house. They also discovered a condom filled with liquid opium in his pocket.13. According to the applicant, on 2 July 2004 while he was repairing his car in the yard, a group of policemen in plain clothes broke into his property without identifying themselves or giving reasons for their intrusion and started beating him. One of the officers grabbed the applicant’s hair and pulled him into the house, where the beating continued. The applicant was then handcuffed, after which the police planted the liquid opium and the pre-marked banknotes on him. The applicant further alleged that the house search had been conducted in a chaotic and violent manner. While it was going on, he had been lying on the floor, handcuffed, in one of the rooms. From time to time, a number of officers had approached him, sworn at him and beaten him.14. The applicant’s parents and wife, as well as his acquaintance Mr Zh., who happened to be in the house at the time, witnessed the search.15. The applicant gave a written explanation to the police in which he stated that he was a drug addict and produced liquid opium for his own use. While admitting that the police had found some liquid opium and poppy straw, as well as some money in his trousers, the applicant denied selling drugs.16. According to the search report, signed by the police officers involved, two attesting witnesses and the applicant, the search lasted from 4 to 7.30 p.m.17. The undercover agent reported in writing to his superior on the same date that he had received the pre-marked banknotes at 5 p.m. and that he had bought the liquid opium from the applicant at about 6 p.m.18. After the search was completed, the police arrested the applicant and took him to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station “for further inquiries”.C. Pre-trial investigation and related facts19. On 3 July 2004 the applicant was examined by a neurosurgeon in the city hospital (see also paragraph 30 below). The medical certificate issued by the doctor read as follows:“No fainting, nausea or vomiting reported. No symptoms of neurological injury. The skull and the cervical vertebrae are without injury. No acute neurosurgical injuries have been discovered. There is no need for neurosurgical treatment at the time of examination.”20. There is no further information in the case file as to the circumstances of this examination of the applicant.21. On 5 July 2004 a criminal case was initiated against the applicant on suspicion of the production and distribution of illegal drugs, and he was arrested as a criminal suspect.22. On 7 July 2004 another criminal case was launched against him on suspicion of possession of drugs for his own consumption.23. On the same date the above criminal cases were joined.24. According to the Government, the applicant was informed of his right to have a lawyer on several occasions, but waived that right. The case file does not contain copies of those waivers.25. As it transpires from the applicant’s medical file, a copy of which was provided to the Court by the Government, on 7 July 2004 an ambulance was called for the applicant following his complaints of pain in the lower right side of the back. The applicant explained that he had been beaten up during his arrest on 2 July 2004. He was taken to the Odessa Regional Hospital, where he was examined by an urologist and X-rayed. The diagnosis was a contusion of the right kidney, with no impairment of the kidney’s functions. It was also recommended that the applicant undergo an ultrasound examination.26. On the same date the doctor in charge passed this information to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department, where the officer on duty registered it in the logbook.27. On 8 July 2004 the investigator applied to the Suvorivskyy Court for the applicant’s remand in custody as a preventive measure pending trial.28. On the same date the Suvorivskyy Court ruled that further information about the applicant was required in order for it to decide on whether to order the preventive measure. As a result, it extended his arrest to ten days (calculated from 5 July 2004). As transpires from the court’s ruling, the applicant was legally represented at that stage.29. On 14 July 2004 formal charges of possession, production and distribution of illegal drugs were brought against the applicant.30. On the same date the applicant was questioned as an accused. The investigator referred to the applicant’s allegation of having been beaten up by the police and asked whether he had sought medical assistance. As per the minutes of the questioning session, the applicant replied as follows:“Yes. After I had been taken to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station, they wanted to send me to a detention facility. As I had visible bodily injuries, I was taken to the [city hospital]. A neurosurgeon examined me and my head was X-rayed. While in the hospital, I was confused and I forgot to tell the doctor that I also had pain in the lower part of [my] back. On the following day I was taken to the detention facility. At the request of the convoy officers, I did not say anything about my injuries upon my arrival there. Today I still have blood in [my] urine and my kidneys hurt.”31. On 15 July 2004 a lawyer (apparently hired by the applicant’s relatives) was admitted to represent the applicant in the proceedings.32. On the same date the Suvorivskyy Court remanded the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial, for an initial period of two months (until 5 September 2004). The court noted the seriousness of the charges against the applicant and his extensive criminal record. It considered that he might flee and/or reoffend if at liberty.33. On 3 September 2004 the Suvorivskyy Court extended the term of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to three months (until 5 October 2004) upon the investigator’s application. It explained this decision by the necessity to conduct the following measures: the applicant’s examination with a view to establishing whether he was a drug addict; completion of the investigation; providing the applicant with the opportunity to study the case file; and approval of the indictment.34. On 9 September 2004 the applicant was examined by an addiction psychiatrist, who concluded that he was an opium addict in partial recovery.35. On 21 September 2004 the applicant asked the investigator to allow him to undergo a forensic medical examination, referring to the contusion of his right kidney which he claimed to have sustained as a result of his beating by the police on 2 July 2004. He noted that he had repeatedly asked to be examined.36. On 30 September 2004 the investigator rejected the above request referring to findings made by the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office on an unspecified date, according to which the applicant had been slandering the police officers with a view to evading criminal liability.37. On 5 October 2004 the applicant was indicted. As noted in the indictment, the investigator had conducted confrontations between the applicant and the police officers involved in his arrest, during which no claims of ill-treatment had been made. The indictment also referred to statements made by the applicant’s acquaintance, Mr Zh., who had been at the applicant’s home at the time of the search (see paragraph 14 above). According to Mr Zh., the police officers’ behaviour on 2 July 2004 had been proper and he had not witnessed any violence towards the applicant or any of his family members.D. Trial38. On 28 October 2004 the Suvorivskyy Court held a preparatory hearing, during which it decided to extend the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure pending the pronouncement of the verdict.39. By a judgment of 14 March 2005, the Suvorivskyy Court found the applicant guilty of the illegal possession, production and distribution of drugs and sentenced him to five years and two months’ imprisonment (which included the unserved part of the sentence imposed pursuant to his conviction on 4 December 2003 – see paragraph 8 above). It also ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The court based its findings mainly on the evidence obtained through the undercover operation and the searches of the applicant’s house and person carried out on 2 July 2004. It heard the police officers involved, the attesting witnesses, and three of the applicant’s neighbours. During the trial, Mr Zh. withdrew his statements given in the course of the pre-trial investigation (see paragraphs 14 and 37 above), claiming that they had been extracted from him under duress and submitting that he was not aware of any drug production or distribution by the applicant. He also maintained that he had witnessed the applicant being beaten by the police on 2 July 2004. The court dismissed this submission as untrue. It also considered the statement of the applicant’s father that he had seen a police officer planting drugs on the applicant to be untrue.40. On the same date the Suvorivskyy Court issued a separate ruling by which it held that the monitoring of the applicant’s conduct by the local police department during his probation had been inadequate.41. On 20 December 2005 the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) quashed the aforementioned judgment on the applicant’s appeal and remitted the case back to the first-instance court for fresh examination. It referred, in particular, to a number of factual discrepancies which had to be reconciled. Thus, according to the search report, the search of the applicant’s house had lasted from 4 p.m. till 7.30 p.m. on 2 July 2004. At the same time, it was indicated in the report of the undercover agent that he had received the pre-marked banknotes for the operation at about 5 p.m. and had bought liquid opium from the applicant at about 6 p.m. In other words, it appeared that the search had started about two hours before the undercover drug purchase took place. There were also discrepancies in the statements of the attesting witnesses, one of whom had submitted that the applicant had been searched in the house, while the other had noted that his body search had taken place outside, near the police car. The appellate court also noted that the applicant’s allegations of the fabrication of evidence and his beating had not been thoroughly investigated.42. Furthermore, the Court of Appeal criticised the trial court for its failure to “assess the fact that the search had been conducted on the basis of a search warrant of 19 May 2004, which had been issued at the investigator’s request concerning a different criminal case initiated a long time before the criminal investigation [against the applicant] was launched”.43. On 3 April 2006 the applicant applied to the Suvorivskyy Court for his release subject to an undertaking not to abscond.44. On 19 April 2006 the court rejected this application, having noted that the applicant was suspected of a crime punishable with more than three years’ imprisonment and that he already had three drug-related convictions to his name.45. On 6 November 2006 the applicant again applied to be released.46. On 15 November 2006 the Suvorivskyy Court replied to him by letter, stating as follows:“Your request for a change of the preventive measure of 6 November 2006 has been examined. Please be informed that you previously submitted a similar request, which was rejected by a ruling of [this court] on 19 April 2006.Given the fact that similar requests on your part have been responded to, the present request ... will be archived (“списати в наряд суду”)”.47. On 6 June 2007 the Suvorivskyy Court issued a new judgment in which it made the same findings as before. As noted therein, the two witnesses had testified that the applicant had been subjected to a body search outside the house. As to the report of the undercover agent, it was not a valid procedural document and therefore could not be relied on. The judgment was silent as to why the search of the applicant’s house had been conducted on the basis of a search warrant issued two months earlier and relating to a different criminal case.48. The Suvorivskyy Court also held as follows in the operative part of its judgment:“To maintain [the applicant’s] detention as a preventive measure pending the entry into force of the verdict.To calculate the sentence from 2 July 2004, that is from the date of [the applicant’s] actual arrest.”49. The applicant and the lawyer acting on his behalf appealed against the judgment of 6 June 2007. The lawyer submitted, in particular, that the applicant’s allegation of his beating by the police on 2 July 2004 had not been duly addressed.50. On 4 December 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld the applicant’s conviction. It noted that the applicant had chosen “the tactics of denial of the events and manipulating the established facts” by challenging the lawfulness of the police officers’ actions during his arrest. Similarly to the first-instance court, the appellate court did not address the issue of the time and context of the search warrant, on the basis of which the applicant’s house had been searched on 2 July 2004.51. On 22 March, 28 May, 11 June and 9 July 2008 the applicant lodged cassation appeals with the Supreme Court. All of them were returned to him for his failure to comply with procedural formalities, such as putting a date under his cassation appeal, signing it, or attaching a duly certified copy of the judicial decisions challenged. On three occasions the applicant was invited to rectify the indicated shortcomings. As he failed to comply, on 7 August 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal without examination on the merits.E. The applicant’s correspondence with the Court52. On 13 May 2005 the applicant wrote his first letter to the Court, in which he enquired about the procedure of introduction of an application before the Court.53. On 15 July 2005 he further wrote to the Court that he considered his case yet premature, but that he planned to introduce in the future complaints under Article 5 § 3 and Article 6 § 3 (c) and (d) of the Convention.54. On 3 August 2005 the Registry of the Court warned the applicant that his file would be destroyed if he did not submit an application form within a year.55. On 19 July 2006 the applicant submitted a completed application form, which he subsequently supplemented on a number of occasions.56. The applicant’s letters to the Court sent from the pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) on 13 May and 15 July 2005, 19 July 2006, and 7 May, 18 July and 30 November 2007, bore the SIZO stamp on their first page with a handwritten date. The first page of his letters sent to the Court from prison on 4 June 2008 and 20 January 2009 bore the stamp of the prison.57. On 22 January, 27 July and 12 September 2007 the Registry of the Court asked the applicant to submit copies of a number of documents.58. In his subsequent correspondence the applicant confirmed receipt of the Registry’s letters of 22 January and 27 July, but never referred to that of 12 September 2007 and did not comply with the request contained therein.59. According to the information provided by the Government, there was no incoming correspondence for the applicant registered in the SIZO between 10 August and 10 November 2007.60. On 20 January 2009 the applicant informed the Registry that he had sent a letter to the Court on 21 October 2008, indicating the number it had been assigned by the prison administration. He also noted that the administration charged money for sending correspondence to the Court, which he could not afford. The applicant therefore stated that he had had to send his letter of 20 January 2009 through his mother. However, that letter arrived at the Court directly from the prison, accompanied by its cover letter and with the prison stamp on the first page.61. The Court did not receive the applicant’s letter of 21 October 2008. According to the Government, it was dispatched by the prison administration on the same day as it was submitted by the applicant for postage.F. Other relevant facts62. On 4 August 2009 the applicant was released on parole.63. On an unspecified date (apparently after the case had been communicated to the Government and the Government had tried to collect the relevant information), the SIZO issued an information note stating that the logbook of detainees’ complaints for 2004 and 2005 had been destroyed on 29 January 2009.64. On 14 November 2011 the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office issued an information note stating that the materials of the investigation into the applicant’s allegation of ill-treatment (2005) had been destroyed on 20 January 2010 after the expiry of the five-year storage period envisaged by the recordkeeping guidelines approved by the General Prosecutor’s Office on 28 December 2002.II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICEA. Search of home and other property65. Article 30 of the Constitution (1996) guarantees the inviolability of everyone’s home. It prohibits entry into the home or other property of a person, and the examination or search thereof, other than pursuant to a reasoned court decision.66. Article 311 of the Civil Code (2003) reiterates the above constitutional principles.67. Article 177 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (1960) requires that for a search of a house or other property to be conducted, there must be sufficient grounds to believe that the items to be searched for might be found there and a reasoned court decision authorising the search. Such a decision by a court cannot be appealed against. Article 183 of the Code requires the investigating officer in charge of the search to serve the search warrant on the person(s) occupying the relevant premises. If the items searched for are not given to the investigating officer voluntarily, the latter must conduct the search forcibly.68. The relevant provisions of the Law “On Search and Seizure Activities” (1992) are summarised in the Volokhy v. Ukraine judgment (no. 23543/02, § 27, 2 November 2006).B. Pre-trial detention69. Article 29 of the Constitution is cited in the judgment on the case of Svershov v. Ukraine (no. 35231/02, § 39, 27 November 2008).70. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) are to be found in the judgments in the following cases: Nevmerzhitsky v. Ukraine, no. 54825/00, §§ 53-54, ECHR 2005‑II (extracts); Kucheruk v. Ukraine, no. 2570/04, §§ 67-69, 6 September 2007; and Sergey Volosyuk v. Ukraine, no. 1291/03, §§ 24-25, 12 March 2009.

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 20602/05) against Ukraine submitted to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Sergeyevich Gerashchenko (“the applicant”), on 19 July 2006 (see paragraphs 71-74 below).

He further complained that he had incriminated himself under duress and without legal assistance.

4. On 16 December 2009, the complaints concerning the applicant’s pre-trial detention and the police search of his home were communicated to the Government. The Court also raised of its own motion and communicated the question of Ukraine’s compliance with Articles 8 and 34 of the Convention in view of the possible monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence with the Court.

5. On 15 March 2012, the President of the Section decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit additional written observations on the admissibility and merits of the applicant’s complaints concerning his ill-treatment by the police and the violations of his right to legal assistance and privilege against self-incrimination.

6. Mrs G. Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, was unable to take part in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). The President of the Chamber therefore appointed Mr S. Shevchuk to sit as an ad hoc judge (Rule 29 § 1 (b)).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

7. The applicant was born in 1958 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Odessa following his conviction in subsequent criminal proceedings unrelated to those considered in the present case.

A. Background to the case

8. On 4 December 2003, the applicant was convicted of possessing illegal drugs and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. The sentence was suspended, however, and he was placed on probation. This was his third conviction for a drug-related offence.

9.
On 12 May 2004 the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department opened criminal proceedings against an individual, Mr B., on suspicion of possessing illegal drugs. During the investigation, Mr B. stated that he had purchased the drugs from the applicant.

10. On 18 May 2004 the investigator applied to the Odessa Suvorivskyy District Court (hereafter – “the Suvorivskyy Court”), requesting authorisation to search the applicant’s home in order to verify Mr B.’s statement.

11. On 19 May 2004 the Suvorivskyy Court authorised the police search, agreeing that it was necessary for the criminal investigation to proceed.

B. Events of 2 July 2004

12. According to the authorities, on 2 July 2004 an undercover police agent purchased 1.9 millilitres of liquid opium from the applicant, paying him 30 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) in banknotes that had previously been marked with a luminous substance. The undercover operation was followed by a search, during which the police seized the aforementioned banknotes from the applicant and equipment used to produce drugs found in his house. They also found a condom containing liquid opium in his pocket.

13. According to the applicant, on 2 July 2004, while he was repairing his car in the yard, a group of plain-clothes police officers entered his property without identifying themselves or explaining their intrusion and began beating him. One officer grabbed the applicant by the hair and dragged him into the house, where the beating continued. The applicant was then handcuffed, after which the police planted the liquid opium and pre-marked banknotes on him. He further alleged that the house search had been carried out in a chaotic and violent manner. While it was under way, he lay handcuffed on the floor in one of the rooms. From time to time, several officers approached him, swore at him and beat him.

14. The applicant’s parents and wife, together with his acquaintance Mr Zh., who happened to be in the house at the time, witnessed the search.

15. The applicant provided a written explanation to the police stating that he was a drug addict and produced liquid opium for his personal use. Although he admitted that the police had found some liquid opium and poppy straw, as well as money in his trousers, he denied selling drugs.

16. According to the search report, which was signed by the police officers involved, two attesting witnesses and the applicant, the search lasted from 4 to 7.30 p.m.

17. On the same date, the undercover agent reported in writing to his superior that he had received the pre-marked banknotes at 5 p.m. and had purchased the liquid opium from the applicant at about 6 p.m.

18. Once the search had been completed, the police arrested the applicant and took him to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station “for further inquiries”.

C. Pre-trial investigation and related facts

19.
On 3 July 2004 the applicant was examined by a neurosurgeon at the city hospital (see also paragraph 30 below). The medical certificate issued by the doctor stated as follows:

“No fainting, nausea or vomiting reported. No symptoms of neurological injury. The skull and cervical vertebrae are without injury. No acute neurosurgical injuries have been found. There is no need for neurosurgical treatment at the time of examination.”

20. The case file contains no further information about the circumstances of the applicant’s examination.

21. On 5 July 2004 a criminal case was opened against the applicant on suspicion of producing and distributing illegal drugs, and he was arrested as a criminal suspect.

22. On 7 July 2004 another criminal case was brought against him on suspicion of possessing drugs for his own consumption.

23. On the same date the above criminal cases were joined.

24. According to the Government, the applicant was informed on several occasions of his right to a lawyer, but waived that right. The case file contains no copies of those waivers.

25. As can be seen from the applicant’s medical file, a copy of which was submitted to the Court by the Government, on 7 July 2004 an ambulance was called after the applicant complained of pain in the lower right side of his back. The applicant stated that he had been beaten during his arrest on 2 July 2004. He was taken to Odessa Regional Hospital, where he was examined by a urologist and X-rayed. He was diagnosed with a contusion of the right kidney, without impairment of kidney function. It was also recommended that he undergo an ultrasound examination.

26. On the same date the doctor in charge conveyed this information to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department, where the duty officer recorded it in the logbook.

27. On 8 July 2004 the investigator applied to the Suvorivskyy Court for the applicant to be remanded in custody as a preventive measure pending trial.

28. On the same date the Suvorivskyy Court held that further information about the applicant was needed before it could decide whether to order the preventive measure. It therefore extended his arrest to ten days (calculated from 5 July 2004). As appears from the court’s ruling, the applicant was legally represented at that stage.

29. On 14 July 2004 the applicant was formally charged with possession, production and distribution of illegal drugs.

30. On the same date the applicant was questioned as an accused. The investigator referred to his allegation that he had been beaten by the police and asked whether he had sought medical assistance. According to the minutes of the questioning session, the applicant replied as follows:

“Yes. After I had been taken to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station, they wanted to send me to a detention facility. Since I had visible bodily injuries, I was taken to the [city hospital].”
A neurosurgeon examined me, and my head was X-rayed. While in the hospital, I was confused and forgot to tell the doctor that I also had pain in the lower part of [my] back. The next day, I was taken to the detention facility. At the request of the convoy officers, I said nothing about my injuries upon arrival there. Today, I still have blood in [my] urine and my kidneys hurt.”

31. On 15 July 2004, a lawyer (apparently retained by the applicant’s relatives) was admitted to represent the applicant in the proceedings.

32. On the same date, the Suvorivskyy Court remanded the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial, initially for two months (until 5 September 2004). The court noted the seriousness of the charges against the applicant and his extensive criminal record. It considered that, if at liberty, he might flee and/or reoffend.

33. On 3 September 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention to three months (until 5 October 2004) at the investigator’s request. It justified this decision by the need to take the following measures: examining the applicant to establish whether he was a drug addict; completing the investigation; giving the applicant an opportunity to study the case file; and approving the indictment.

34. On 9 September 2004, the applicant was examined by an addiction psychiatrist, who concluded that he was an opium addict in partial recovery.

35. On 21 September 2004, the applicant asked the investigator to allow him to undergo a forensic medical examination, referring to the contusion of his right kidney which he claimed to have sustained as a result of being beaten by the police on 2 July 2004. He noted that he had repeatedly requested an examination.

36. On 30 September 2004, the investigator rejected that request, referring to findings made by the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office on an unspecified date, according to which the applicant had been making false accusations against the police officers in order to evade criminal liability.

37. On 5 October 2004, the applicant was indicted. As stated in the indictment, the investigator had conducted confrontations between the applicant and the police officers involved in his arrest, during which no allegations of ill-treatment had been raised. The indictment also referred to statements by the applicant’s acquaintance, Mr Zh., who had been at the applicant’s home during the search (see paragraph 14 above). According to Mr Zh., the police officers had behaved properly on 2 July 2004, and he had not witnessed any violence against the applicant or any members of his family.

D. Trial

38. On 28 October 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court held a preparatory hearing, at which it decided to extend the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure pending delivery of the verdict.

39.
By a judgment of 14 March 2005, the Suvorivskyy Court found the applicant guilty of the unlawful possession, production and distribution of drugs and sentenced him to five years and two months’ imprisonment (including the unserved part of the sentence imposed following his conviction on 4 December 2003 – see paragraph 8 above). It also ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The court based its conclusions mainly on the evidence obtained through the undercover operation and the searches of the applicant’s house and person conducted on 2 July 2004. It heard the police officers involved, the attesting witnesses and three of the applicant’s neighbours. During the trial, Mr Zh. retracted the statements he had made in the course of the pre-trial investigation (see paragraphs 14 and 37 above), claiming that they had been obtained from him under duress and stating that he was unaware of any drug production or distribution by the applicant. He further maintained that he had witnessed the applicant being beaten by the police on 2 July 2004. The court rejected this submission as untrue. It likewise considered untrue the statement by the applicant’s father that he had seen a police officer planting drugs on the applicant.

40. On the same day, the Suvorivskyy Court issued a separate ruling in which it held that the monitoring of the applicant’s conduct by the local police department during his probation had been inadequate.

41. On 20 December 2005, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) quashed the above judgment following the applicant’s appeal and remitted the case to the first-instance court for fresh examination. It referred, in particular, to several factual discrepancies that needed to be reconciled. According to the search report, the search of the applicant’s house had lasted from 4 p.m. until 7.30 p.m. on 2 July 2004. At the same time, the undercover agent’s report indicated that he had received the pre-marked banknotes for the operation at about 5 p.m. and had purchased liquid opium from the applicant at about 6 p.m. In other words, it appeared that the search had begun about two hours before the undercover drug purchase took place. There were also inconsistencies in the statements of the attesting witnesses, one of whom had stated that the applicant had been searched inside the house, while the other had indicated that the body search had taken place outside, near the police car. The appellate court further noted that the applicant’s allegations concerning the fabrication of evidence and his beating had not been thoroughly investigated.

42. Furthermore, the Court of Appeal criticised the trial court for failing to “assess the fact that the search had been conducted on the basis of a search warrant of 19 May 2004, which had been issued at the investigator’s request concerning a different criminal case initiated long before the criminal investigation [against the applicant] was launched”.
On 3 April 2006 the applicant applied to the Suvorivskyy Court for release subject to an undertaking not to abscond.

44. On 19 April 2006 the court rejected the application, noting that the applicant was suspected of an offence punishable by more than three years’ imprisonment and that he already had three drug-related convictions.

45. On 6 November 2006 the applicant again applied for release.

46. On 15 November 2006 the Suvorivskyy Court replied by letter, stating as follows:

“Your request of 6 November 2006 for a change of preventive measure has been examined. Please be informed that you previously submitted a similar request, which was rejected by a ruling of [this court] on 19 April 2006.

Given that similar requests on your part have already been answered, the present request ... will be archived (‘списати в наряд суду’).”

47. On 6 June 2007 the Suvorivskyy Court delivered a new judgment in which it reached the same findings as before. As noted in the judgment, the two witnesses had testified that the applicant had been subjected to a body search outside the house. As for the undercover agent’s report, it was not a valid procedural document and therefore could not be relied upon. The judgment did not explain why the search of the applicant’s house had been carried out on the basis of a warrant issued two months earlier in connection with a different criminal case.

48. In the operative part of its judgment, the Suvorivskyy Court also held as follows:

“To maintain [the applicant’s] detention as a preventive measure pending the entry into force of the verdict.

To calculate the sentence from 2 July 2004, that is, from the date of [the applicant’s] actual arrest.”

49. The applicant and the lawyer representing him appealed against the judgment of 6 June 2007. The lawyer submitted, in particular, that the applicant’s allegation that he had been beaten by the police on 2 July 2004 had not been properly addressed.

50. On 4 December 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld the applicant’s conviction. It observed that the applicant had chosen “the tactics of denying the events and manipulating the established facts” by challenging the lawfulness of the police officers’ actions during his arrest. Like the first-instance court, the appellate court did not address the timing and context of the search warrant on the basis of which the applicant’s house had been searched on 2 July 2004.

51. On 22 March, 28 May, 11 June and 9 July 2008 the applicant lodged cassation appeals with the Supreme Court. They were all returned to him for failure to comply with procedural formalities, such as dating or signing his cassation appeal or attaching duly certified copies of the judicial decisions being challenged. On three occasions, the applicant was invited to remedy the identified shortcomings. As he failed to do so, on 7 August 2008 the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal without examining its merits.

E.
The applicant’s correspondence with the Court

52. On 13 May 2005 the applicant sent his first letter to the Court, enquiring about the procedure for lodging an application with it.

53. On 15 July 2005 he further informed the Court that he considered his case premature, but planned to lodge complaints in the future under Article 5 § 3 and Article 6 § 3 (c) and (d) of the Convention.

54. On 3 August 2005 the Court Registry warned the applicant that his file would be destroyed unless he submitted an application form within one year.

55. On 19 July 2006 the applicant submitted a completed application form, which he later supplemented on several occasions.

56. The applicant’s letters to the Court sent from the pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) on 13 May and 15 July 2005, 19 July 2006, and 7 May, 18 July and 30 November 2007 bore the SIZO stamp on the first page, together with a handwritten date. The first page of his letters sent to the Court from prison on 4 June 2008 and 20 January 2009 bore the prison stamp.

57. On 22 January, 27 July and 12 September 2007 the Court Registry asked the applicant to provide copies of several documents.

58. In his subsequent correspondence, the applicant confirmed receipt of the Registry’s letters of 22 January and 27 July, but never mentioned the letter of 12 September 2007 and did not comply with the request it contained.

59. According to the information supplied by the Government, no incoming correspondence for the applicant was registered at the SIZO between 10 August and 10 November 2007.

60. On 20 January 2009 the applicant informed the Registry that he had sent a letter to the Court on 21 October 2008, specifying the number assigned to it by the prison administration. He also stated that the administration charged a fee for sending correspondence to the Court, which he could not afford. The applicant therefore explained that he had had to send his letter of 20 January 2009 through his mother. However, that letter reached the Court directly from the prison, accompanied by a cover letter and bearing the prison stamp on its first page.

61. The Court did not receive the applicant’s letter of 21 October 2008. According to the Government, it was dispatched by the prison administration on the same day that the applicant submitted it for postage.

F. Other relevant facts

62. On 4 August 2009 the applicant was released on parole.

63. On an unspecified date (apparently after the case had been communicated to the Government and the Government had sought to collect the relevant information), the SIZO issued an information note stating that the logbook of detainees’ complaints for 2004 and 2005 had been destroyed on 29 January 2009.
On 14 November 2011, the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office issued an information note indicating that the materials from the investigation into the applicant’s allegation of ill-treatment (2005) had been destroyed on 20 January 2010, following the expiry of the five-year retention period prescribed by the recordkeeping guidelines approved by the General Prosecutor’s Office on 28 December 2002.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Search of home and other property

65. Article 30 of the Constitution (1996) guarantees the inviolability of every person’s home. It prohibits entry into a person’s home or other property, and its examination or search, except pursuant to a reasoned court decision.

66. Article 311 of the Civil Code (2003) restates the above constitutional principles.

67. Article 177 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (1960) provides that, for a search of a house or other property to be conducted, there must be sufficient grounds to believe that the items sought might be found there, as well as a reasoned court decision authorising the search. Such a court decision is not subject to appeal. Article 183 of the Code requires the investigating officer conducting the search to serve the search warrant on the person or persons occupying the premises concerned. If the items sought are not voluntarily handed over to the investigating officer, the latter must carry out the search forcibly.

68. The relevant provisions of the Law “On Search and Seizure Activities” (1992) are summarised in the judgment in Volokhy v. Ukraine (no. 23543/02, § 27, 2 November 2006).

B. Pre-trial detention

69. Article 29 of the Constitution is cited in the judgment in Svershov v. Ukraine (no. 35231/02, § 39, 27 November 2008).

70. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) are set out in the judgments in the following cases: Nevmerzhitsky v. Ukraine, no. 54825/00, §§ 53-54, ECHR 2005-II (extracts); Kucheruk v. Ukraine, no. 2570/04, §§ 67-69, 6 September 2007; and Sergey Volosyuk v. Ukraine, no. 1291/03, §§ 24-25, 12 March 2009.

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 20602/05, brought against Ukraine before the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”). The application was lodged on 19 July 2006 by Mr Anatoliy Sergeyevich Gerashchenko, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”) (see paragraphs 71-74 below).

2. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.

3. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the police had subjected him to ill-treatment; that the search of his home had been arbitrary and unlawful; and that his pre-trial detention had been illegal, excessively lengthy, and not subject to the required judicial scrutiny. He further complained that, under duress and without the assistance of a lawyer, he had incriminated himself.

4. On 16 December 2009, notice of the complaints concerning the applicant’s pre-trial detention and the police search of his home was given to the Government. Acting of its own motion, the Court also raised and communicated the question of whether Ukraine had complied with Articles 8 and 34 of the Convention in view of the possible monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence with the Court.

5. On 15 March 2012, pursuant to Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, the President of the Section decided to invite the parties to provide additional written observations on the admissibility and merits of the applicant’s complaints concerning his alleged ill-treatment by the police, the infringement of his right to legal assistance, and the violation of his privilege against self-incrimination.

6. Mrs G. Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, could not take part in the case under Rule 28 of the Rules of Court. In accordance with Rule 29 § 1 (b), the President of the Chamber appointed Mr S. Shevchuk to sit as an ad hoc judge.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

7. Born in 1958, the applicant is currently serving a prison sentence in Odessa. That sentence followed his conviction in criminal proceedings instituted after, and unrelated to, the proceedings at issue in the present case.

A. Background to the case

8. On 4 December 2003, the applicant was found guilty of possessing illegal drugs and received a three-year prison sentence. The sentence was suspended, however, and he was placed on probation. This was his third conviction for a drug-related offence.

9.
On 12 May 2004, the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department opened criminal proceedings against Mr B. on suspicion of unlawfully possessing drugs. During the investigation, Mr B. claimed that he had purchased the drugs from the applicant.

10. On 18 May 2004, the investigator requested authorisation from the Odessa Suvorivskyy District Court (“the Suvorivskyy Court”) to search the applicant’s home in order to verify Mr B.’s statement.

11. On 19 May 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court approved the search, finding that it was necessary to advance the criminal investigation.

B. Events of 2 July 2004

12. The authorities maintained that, on 2 July 2004, an undercover police agent purchased 1.9 millilitres of liquid opium from the applicant for 30 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), using banknotes that had previously been treated with a luminous substance. The police subsequently searched the applicant and his home, seizing the marked banknotes from him and finding equipment used to produce drugs in the house. They also found a condom containing liquid opium in his pocket.

13. The applicant gave a different account. He alleged that, while he was repairing his car in the yard on 2 July 2004, several plain-clothes police officers forced their way onto his property without identifying themselves or explaining their presence and began beating him. One officer seized him by the hair and dragged him into the house, where the assault continued. After handcuffing him, the officers allegedly planted the liquid opium and marked banknotes on his person. He further claimed that the search of the house was carried out violently and chaotically. Throughout the search, he lay handcuffed on the floor of one of the rooms, while various officers periodically approached him, insulted him and beat him.

14. The search was witnessed by the applicant’s parents, his wife and an acquaintance, Mr Zh., who happened to be inside the house at the time.

15. In a written statement to the police, the applicant acknowledged that he was addicted to drugs and made liquid opium for his personal consumption. Although he accepted that the officers had discovered some liquid opium, poppy straw and money in his trousers, he denied dealing in drugs.

16. The search record, which was signed by the participating police officers, two attesting witnesses and the applicant, stated that the search had taken place between 4 p.m. and 7.30 p.m.

17. In a written report submitted to his superior that same day, the undercover agent stated that he had received the pre-marked banknotes at 5 p.m. and had purchased the liquid opium from the applicant at approximately 6 p.m.

18. Once the search had ended, the police arrested the applicant and transported him to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station “for further inquiries”.

C. Pre-trial investigation and related facts

19.
On 3 July 2004, a neurosurgeon examined the applicant at the city hospital (see also paragraph 30 below). The resulting medical certificate stated:

“No fainting, nausea or vomiting reported. No symptoms of neurological injury. The skull and the cervical vertebrae are without injury. No acute neurosurgical injuries have been discovered. There is no need for neurosurgical treatment at the time of examination.”

20. The case file contains no additional information about the circumstances in which that examination took place.

21. On 5 July 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant on suspicion of producing and distributing illegal drugs, and he was arrested as a criminal suspect.

22. A further criminal case was opened against him on 7 July 2004 on suspicion of possessing drugs for his personal use.

23. The two sets of criminal proceedings were joined that same day.

24. The Government submitted that the applicant had been advised on several occasions of his right to legal assistance but had waived it. No copies of those waivers appear in the case file.

25. The applicant’s medical records, a copy of which the Government submitted to the Court, indicate that an ambulance was called for him on 7 July 2004 after he complained of pain in the lower-right part of his back. He stated that he had been beaten during his arrest on 2 July 2004. He was transported to Odessa Regional Hospital, where he underwent an X-ray examination and was seen by a urologist. He was diagnosed with a contusion of the right kidney, without any impairment of renal function. An ultrasound examination was also recommended.

26. That same day, the attending doctor communicated this information to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department, where the duty officer entered it in the logbook.

27. On 8 July 2004, the investigator asked the Suvorivskyy Court to remand the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial.

28. Also on 8 July 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court found that it needed further information concerning the applicant before deciding whether to impose the requested preventive measure. It therefore extended his arrest to ten days, calculated from 5 July 2004. The ruling indicates that the applicant had legal representation at that stage.

29. On 14 July 2004, the applicant was formally charged with possessing, producing and distributing illegal drugs.

30. He was questioned as an accused on the same day. Referring to the applicant’s allegation that the police had beaten him, the investigator asked whether he had sought medical attention. According to the record of the questioning, the applicant answered:

“Yes. After I had been taken to Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station, they wanted to send me to a detention facility. As I had visible bodily injuries, I was taken to the [city hospital].”
“A neurosurgeon examined me, and X-rays were taken of my head. While I was in hospital, I was disoriented and failed to tell the doctor that I was also experiencing pain in my lower back. The next day, I was transferred to the detention facility. At the convoy officers’ request, I did not mention my injuries when I arrived. I continue to have blood in my urine, and my kidneys still hurt.”

31. On 15 July 2004, a lawyer, apparently retained by the applicant’s relatives, was authorised to represent him in the proceedings.

32. That same day, the Suvorivskyy Court ordered the applicant’s remand in custody as a preventive measure pending trial. The initial detention period was set at two months, expiring on 5 September 2004. In reaching its decision, the court relied on the gravity of the charges and the applicant’s extensive criminal record, finding that, if released, he might abscond and/or commit further offences.

33. On 3 September 2004, acting on the investigator’s application, the Suvorivskyy Court extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention to three months, until 5 October 2004. It stated that additional time was required to determine whether the applicant was a drug addict, complete the investigation, allow him to examine the case file, and approve the indictment.

34. An addiction psychiatrist examined the applicant on 9 September 2004 and concluded that he was an opium addict in partial recovery.

35. On 21 September 2004, the applicant requested permission from the investigator to undergo a forensic medical examination. He referred to a contusion of his right kidney, which he alleged had resulted from his beating by police officers on 2 July 2004, and stated that he had repeatedly sought such an examination.

36. The investigator refused that request on 30 September 2004. The refusal relied on findings made by the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office on an unspecified date, according to which the applicant had falsely accused the police officers in an attempt to avoid criminal responsibility.

37. The applicant was indicted on 5 October 2004. The indictment stated that the investigator had arranged confrontations between the applicant and the police officers involved in his arrest, during which the applicant had made no allegations of ill-treatment. It also cited evidence from the applicant’s acquaintance, Mr Zh., who had been present at the applicant’s home during the search (see paragraph 14 above). Mr Zh. stated that the officers had behaved properly on 2 July 2004 and that he had not seen them use violence against either the applicant or any member of his family.

D. Trial

38. At a preparatory hearing on 28 October 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court decided that the applicant should remain in detention as a preventive measure until the verdict was delivered.
In a judgment delivered on 14 March 2005, the Suvorivskyy Court convicted the applicant of unlawfully possessing, producing and distributing drugs. It sentenced him to five years and two months’ imprisonment, including the unserved portion of the sentence resulting from his conviction of 4 December 2003 (see paragraph 8 above), and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The conviction rested primarily on evidence secured during the undercover operation and the searches of the applicant’s home and person on 2 July 2004. The court heard testimony from the police officers concerned, the attesting witnesses and three of the applicant’s neighbours. At trial, Mr Zh. retracted the statements he had made during the pre-trial investigation (see paragraphs 14 and 37 above), asserting that they had been obtained under duress. He stated that he had no knowledge of the applicant producing or distributing drugs and further claimed to have seen police officers beat the applicant on 2 July 2004. The court rejected that account as false. It likewise disbelieved the applicant’s father, who testified that he had witnessed a police officer planting drugs on the applicant.

40. On the same day, the Suvorivskyy Court issued a separate ruling finding that the local police department had inadequately supervised the applicant’s conduct while he was on probation.

41. On 20 December 2005, following an appeal by the applicant, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) set aside the judgment and returned the case to the first-instance court for a fresh examination. It identified, in particular, several factual inconsistencies requiring clarification. The search record stated that the applicant’s home had been searched between 4 p.m. and 7.30 p.m. on 2 July 2004. By contrast, the undercover agent’s report indicated that he had received the pre-marked banknotes at approximately 5 p.m. and purchased liquid opium from the applicant at around 6 p.m. The documents therefore suggested that the search had begun roughly two hours before the undercover drug purchase. The attesting witnesses’ accounts were also inconsistent: one stated that the applicant had been searched inside the house, whereas the other said that the body search had occurred outside, near the police vehicle. The Court of Appeal additionally observed that the applicant’s claims that evidence had been fabricated and that he had been beaten had not been investigated thoroughly.

42. The Court of Appeal further faulted the trial court for failing to “assess the fact that the search had been conducted on the basis of a search warrant of 19 May 2004, which had been issued at the investigator’s request concerning a different criminal case initiated a long time before the criminal investigation [against the applicant] was launched”.

43.
On 3 April 2006, the applicant requested that the Suvorivskyy Court release him on an undertaking not to abscond.44. The court refused that request on 19 April 2006, observing that he was suspected of an offence carrying a sentence of more than three years’ imprisonment and had three previous drug-related convictions.45. He submitted a further application for release on 6 November 2006.46. In a letter dated 15 November 2006, the Suvorivskyy Court informed him:

“Your request of 6 November 2006 for the preventive measure to be changed has been considered. You are informed that you had previously made a similar request, which [this court] rejected by its ruling of 19 April 2006.

Since replies have already been given to similar requests submitted by you, the present request ... will be archived (‘списати в наряд суду’).”47.

On 6 June 2007, the Suvorivskyy Court delivered a fresh judgment reiterating its earlier findings. It recorded that the two witnesses had stated that the applicant had been searched outside the house. The court also found that the undercover agent’s report did not constitute a valid procedural document and could therefore not be relied upon. It provided no explanation, however, as to why the applicant’s home had been searched under a warrant issued two months previously in connection with another criminal case.48. The operative part of the judgment further stated:

“[The applicant’s] detention shall remain the preventive measure until the verdict enters into force.

The sentence shall be calculated from 2 July 2004, the date of [the applicant’s] actual arrest.”49.

Both the applicant and his lawyer appealed against the judgment of 6 June 2007. Among other arguments, counsel maintained that the applicant’s allegation that the police had beaten him on 2 July 2004 had not been properly examined.50. On 4 December 2007, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. It considered that, by disputing the legality of the police officers’ conduct during his arrest, the applicant had adopted “the tactics of denial of the events and manipulating the established facts”. Like the first-instance court, it did not consider the timing or context of the warrant used to search the applicant’s home on 2 July 2004.51.

The applicant filed cassation appeals with the Supreme Court on 22 March, 28 May, 11 June and 9 July 2008. Each was returned because he had not complied with procedural requirements, including dating and signing the appeal and enclosing duly certified copies of the contested judicial decisions. He was given three opportunities to remedy the identified deficiencies. After he failed to do so, the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 7 August 2008 without examining its merits.

E.
The applicant’s correspondence with the Court

52. The applicant first contacted the Court by letter on 13 May 2005, seeking information about the procedure for lodging an application.

53. In a further letter dated 15 July 2005, he stated that he regarded his case as premature at that stage, but intended eventually to raise complaints under Article 5 § 3 and Article 6 § 3 (c) and (d) of the Convention.

54. On 3 August 2005, the Court’s Registry notified the applicant that his file would be destroyed unless he submitted an application form within one year.

55. The applicant filed a completed application form on 19 July 2006 and supplemented it several times thereafter.

56. The first pages of the letters he sent to the Court from the pre-trial detention centre (“the SIZO”) on 13 May and 15 July 2005, 19 July 2006, and 7 May, 18 July and 30 November 2007 carried the SIZO’s stamp and a handwritten date. The letters dispatched from prison on 4 June 2008 and 20 January 2009 likewise bore the prison’s stamp on their first page.

57. The Registry requested copies of various documents from the applicant on 22 January, 27 July and 12 September 2007.

58. In later correspondence, the applicant acknowledged receiving the Registry’s letters of 22 January and 27 July. He never mentioned the letter of 12 September 2007, however, and did not provide the documents requested in it.

59. The information supplied by the Government indicated that no incoming correspondence addressed to the applicant was recorded at the SIZO between 10 August and 10 November 2007.

60. On 20 January 2009, the applicant informed the Registry that he had sent the Court a letter on 21 October 2008 and gave the registration number assigned to it by the prison administration. He further stated that the administration required payment for sending correspondence to the Court and that he lacked the means to pay. For that reason, he said, he had been obliged to forward his letter of 20 January 2009 through his mother. Nevertheless, the letter reached the Court directly from the prison, together with a covering letter, and its first page carried the prison’s stamp.

61. The Court never received the applicant’s letter of 21 October 2008. According to the Government, the prison administration dispatched it on the same day that the applicant submitted it for posting.

F. Other relevant facts

62. The applicant was released on parole on 4 August 2009.

63. On an unspecified date—apparently after the application had been communicated to the Government and the Government had attempted to obtain the relevant information—the SIZO issued an information note stating that the logbook containing detainees’ complaints for 2004 and 2005 had been destroyed on 29 January 2009.
On 14 November 2011, the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office issued an information note indicating that the materials from the investigation into the applicant’s 2005 ill-treatment allegation had been destroyed on 20 January 2010. Their destruction followed the expiry of the five-year retention period prescribed by the recordkeeping guidelines approved by the General Prosecutor’s Office on 28 December 2002.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Searches of homes and other property

65. Article 30 of the Constitution (1996) guarantees the inviolability of every person’s home. Unless authorised by a reasoned judicial decision, entry into a person’s home or other property, as well as its inspection or search, is prohibited.

66. Article 311 of the Civil Code (2003) restates those constitutional safeguards.

67. Under Article 177 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (1960), a house or other property may be searched only where there are sufficient grounds for believing that the objects sought may be located there and where the search has been authorised by a reasoned court decision. Such a judicial decision is not subject to appeal. Article 183 requires the investigating officer conducting the search to serve the search warrant on the person or persons occupying the premises concerned. If the objects sought are not surrendered voluntarily, the investigating officer must carry out the search by force.

68. The pertinent provisions of the Law “On Search and Seizure Activities” (1992) are summarised in Volokhy v. Ukraine (no. 23543/02, § 27, 2 November 2006).

B. Pre-trial detention

69. Article 29 of the Constitution is reproduced in Svershov v. Ukraine (no. 35231/02, § 39, 27 November 2008).

70. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”) are set out in the following judgments: Nevmerzhitsky v. Ukraine, no. 54825/00, §§ 53-54, ECHR 2005-II (extracts); Kucheruk v. Ukraine, no. 2570/04, §§ 67-69, 6 September 2007; and Sergey Volosyuk v. Ukraine, no. 1291/03, §§ 24-25, 12 March 2009.
