Throughout the search, he lay handcuffed on the floor of one of the rooms, and various officers periodically approached him, insulted him with swear words, and beat him.

14. The search was witnessed by the applicant’s parents, his wife, and an acquaintance, Mr Zh., who happened to be inside the house at the time.

15. In a written explanation submitted to the police, the applicant stated that he was addicted to drugs and made liquid opium for his personal consumption. He acknowledged that the police had discovered some liquid opium, poppy straw, and money in his trousers, but denied that he sold drugs.

16. The search record, which was signed by the participating police officers, two attesting witnesses, and the applicant, indicated that the search took place between 4 p.m. and 7.30 p.m.

17. In a written report submitted to his superior that same day, the undercover officer stated that he had been given the pre-marked banknotes at 5 p.m. and had purchased the liquid opium from the applicant at approximately 6 p.m.

18. Once the search had ended, the police arrested the applicant and brought him to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station “for further inquiries”.

C. The pre-trial investigation and related circumstances

19.
On 3 July 2004, a neurosurgeon examined the applicant at the city hospital (see also paragraph 30 below). The doctor issued a medical certificate stating:

“The applicant reported no loss of consciousness, nausea or vomiting. There were no indications of neurological trauma. Neither the skull nor the cervical vertebrae showed any injury. No acute neurosurgical damage was identified, and, at the time of the examination, neurosurgical treatment was not required.”

20. The case file contains no additional details about the circumstances in which that examination took place.

21. On 5 July 2004, criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant on suspicion of manufacturing and distributing illegal drugs, and he was taken into custody as a criminal suspect.

22. A separate criminal case was instituted against him on 7 July 2004 on suspicion of possessing drugs for his personal use.

23. Those two sets of criminal proceedings were consolidated that same day.

24. The Government submitted that the applicant had been advised several times of his right to legal assistance but had waived it. However, the case file includes no copies of any such waivers.

25. The applicant’s medical records, a copy of which the Government supplied to the Court, indicate that an ambulance was summoned on 7 July 2004 after he complained of pain in the lower-right area of his back. He stated that he had been beaten during his arrest on 2 July 2004. He was transported to Odessa Regional Hospital, where an urologist examined him and an X-ray was taken. He was diagnosed with a bruised right kidney, although its functions were unaffected. An ultrasound examination was also recommended.

26. On that same date, the attending doctor communicated this information to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Department, where the duty officer entered it in the official logbook.

27. On 8 July 2004, the investigator asked the Suvorivskyy Court to remand the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial.

28. Also on 8 July 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court found that it needed further information concerning the applicant before deciding whether to impose the requested preventive measure. It therefore extended his arrest to ten days, calculated from 5 July 2004. The ruling shows that the applicant had legal representation at that stage.

29. On 14 July 2004, the applicant was formally charged with possessing, manufacturing and distributing illegal drugs.

30. The applicant was questioned as an accused person that same day. Referring to his allegation that police officers had beaten him, the investigator asked whether he had obtained medical assistance. According to the record of the interview, the applicant answered:

“Yes. After I was brought to the Khadzhybeyivskyy Police Station, they intended to transfer me to a detention facility. Because my bodily injuries were visible, I was instead taken to the [city hospital].”
“A neurosurgeon examined me, and an X-ray was taken of my head. Because I was disoriented while in hospital, I neglected to tell the doctor that I was also experiencing pain in the lower part of [my] back. The next day, I was transferred to the detention facility. When I arrived, the convoy officers asked me not to mention my injuries, and I complied. Even today, there is still blood in [my] urine, and I have pain in my kidneys.”

31. On 15 July 2004, a lawyer, apparently retained by the applicant’s relatives, was authorised to represent him in the proceedings.

32. That same day, the Suvorivskyy Court ordered the applicant’s remand in custody as a preventive measure while awaiting trial. The initial detention period was set at two months, expiring on 5 September 2004. In reaching its decision, the court referred to the gravity of the charges and the applicant’s extensive criminal record, finding that, if released, he might abscond and/or commit further offences.

33. Acting on an application from the investigator, the Suvorivskyy Court prolonged the applicant’s pre-trial detention on 3 September 2004 to a total of three months, until 5 October 2004. The court stated that additional time was required to determine whether the applicant was a drug addict, complete the investigation, give him an opportunity to review the case file, and approve the indictment.

34. An addiction psychiatrist assessed the applicant on 9 September 2004 and concluded that he was an opium addict in partial recovery.

35. On 21 September 2004, the applicant requested permission from the investigator to undergo a forensic medical examination. He referred to a contusion of his right kidney, which he alleged had resulted from being beaten by the police on 2 July 2004, and stated that he had repeatedly sought such an examination.

36. The investigator refused that request on 30 September 2004, relying on findings issued by the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office on an unspecified date. According to those findings, the applicant had made false accusations against the police officers in an attempt to avoid criminal liability.

37. The applicant was indicted on 5 October 2004. The indictment stated that the investigator had arranged confrontations between the applicant and the police officers who had participated in his arrest, and that no allegations of ill-treatment had been raised during those confrontations. It also cited evidence from the applicant’s acquaintance, Mr Zh., who had been present in the applicant’s home when the search took place (see paragraph 14 above). Mr Zh. stated that the officers had behaved properly on 2 July 2004 and that he had seen no violence against either the applicant or any member of his family.

D. Trial

38. At a preparatory hearing on 28 October 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court decided that the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure should continue until the verdict was delivered.

39.
In a judgment delivered on 14 March 2005, the Suvorivskyy Court convicted the applicant of unlawfully possessing, producing and distributing drugs. It imposed a prison term of five years and two months, incorporating the unserved portion of the sentence resulting from his conviction of 4 December 2003 (see paragraph 8 above), and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The conviction rested chiefly on evidence gathered during the undercover operation and during the searches of the applicant’s home and person on 2 July 2004. The court heard testimony from the police officers who had participated, the attesting witnesses and three of the applicant’s neighbours. At trial, Mr Zh. retracted the statements he had made during the pre-trial investigation (see paragraphs 14 and 37 above), asserting that they had been obtained under duress. He stated that he knew nothing about the applicant producing or distributing drugs and that he had seen police officers beat the applicant on 2 July 2004. The court rejected that account as false. It likewise found untruthful the applicant’s father’s statement that he had witnessed a police officer planting drugs on the applicant.

40. Also on 14 March 2005, the Suvorivskyy Court issued a separate ruling finding that the local police department had inadequately supervised the applicant’s conduct while he was on probation.

41. Following an appeal by the applicant, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) set aside that judgment on 20 December 2005 and returned the case to the first-instance court for a new examination. It identified, in particular, several factual inconsistencies requiring clarification. The search record stated that the search of the applicant’s home had taken place between 4 p.m. and 7.30 p.m. on 2 July 2004. However, the undercover agent’s report indicated that he had received the pre-marked banknotes for the operation at approximately 5 p.m. and purchased liquid opium from the applicant at around 6 p.m. This suggested that the search had begun roughly two hours before the undercover drug purchase. The attesting witnesses’ accounts also conflicted: one stated that the applicant had been searched inside the house, whereas the other said that the body search had occurred outside, near the police vehicle. The Court of Appeal further observed that the applicant’s claims that evidence had been fabricated and that he had been beaten had not been investigated thoroughly.

42. In addition, the Court of Appeal faulted the trial court for failing to “assess the fact that the search had been conducted on the basis of a search warrant of 19 May 2004, which had been issued at the investigator’s request concerning a different criminal case initiated a long time before the criminal investigation [against the applicant] was launched”.

43.
44. On 3 April 2006, the applicant asked the Suvorivskyy Court to release him subject to an undertaking not to abscond.

45. The court dismissed that request on 19 April 2006, observing that the applicant was suspected of an offence punishable by more than three years’ imprisonment and had already been convicted three times of drug-related offences.

46. On 6 November 2006, the applicant submitted another application for release.

47. In a letter dated 15 November 2006, the Suvorivskyy Court responded:

“Your request of 6 November 2006 for a change of preventive measure has been considered. Please note that you previously lodged a similar request, which was refused by a ruling of [this court] dated 19 April 2006.

Since responses have already been given to similar requests made by you, the present request ... will be archived (‘списати в наряд суду’).”

48. On 6 June 2007, the Suvorivskyy Court delivered a fresh judgment reiterating its earlier findings. It recorded that the two witnesses had stated that the applicant had been body-searched outside the house. The undercover agent’s report was found not to constitute a valid procedural document and could therefore not be relied upon. The judgment offered no explanation as to why the applicant’s home had been searched under a warrant issued two months previously in connection with a different criminal case.

49. In the operative part of its judgment, the Suvorivskyy Court further ordered:

“To continue [the applicant’s] detention as a preventive measure until the verdict enters into force.

To calculate the sentence from 2 July 2004, namely the date of [the applicant’s] actual arrest.”

50. Both the applicant and the lawyer representing him appealed against the judgment of 6 June 2007. The lawyer argued, in particular, that the applicant’s allegation that the police had beaten him on 2 July 2004 had not been properly examined.

51. On 4 December 2007, the Court of Appeal affirmed the applicant’s conviction. It stated that, by contesting the legality of the police officers’ conduct during his arrest, the applicant had adopted “the tactics of denial of the events and manipulating the established facts”. Like the first-instance court, it did not consider the timing or context of the search warrant used to search the applicant’s home on 2 July 2004.

The applicant filed cassation appeals with the Supreme Court on 22 March, 28 May, 11 June and 9 July 2008. Each was returned because he had not complied with procedural requirements, including dating and signing the cassation appeal and enclosing duly certified copies of the contested judicial decisions. He was given three opportunities to remedy the identified defects. After he failed to do so, the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 7 August 2008 without examining its merits.

E.
The applicant’s communications with the Court

52. The applicant first contacted the Court by letter on 13 May 2005, seeking information about the procedure for lodging an application.

53. In a further letter dated 15 July 2005, he stated that he regarded his case as premature at that stage, while indicating his intention to raise future complaints under Article 5 § 3 and Article 6 § 3 (c) and (d) of the Convention.

54. On 3 August 2005 the Court’s Registry notified the applicant that his file would be destroyed unless he submitted an application form within one year.

55. The applicant lodged a duly completed application form on 19 July 2006 and supplemented it several times thereafter.

56. The first pages of the applicant’s letters sent to the Court from the pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) on 13 May and 15 July 2005, 19 July 2006, and 7 May, 18 July and 30 November 2007 carried the SIZO stamp and a handwritten date. The prison stamp likewise appeared on the first page of the letters he sent from prison on 4 June 2008 and 20 January 2009.

57. The Court’s Registry requested copies of various documents from the applicant on 22 January, 27 July and 12 September 2007.

58. In later correspondence, the applicant acknowledged receiving the Registry’s letters of 22 January and 27 July. He never mentioned the letter of 12 September 2007, however, and did not comply with the request it contained.

59. The information supplied by the Government indicated that no incoming correspondence addressed to the applicant had been recorded at the SIZO from 10 August to 10 November 2007.

60. On 20 January 2009 the applicant advised the Registry that he had sent the Court a letter on 21 October 2008 and provided the reference number assigned to it by the prison administration. He further stated that the administration required payment for sending correspondence to the Court and that he could not afford the charge. For that reason, he claimed that he had been compelled to send his letter of 20 January 2009 through his mother. Nevertheless, the letter reached the Court directly from the prison, together with a covering letter; its first page bore the prison stamp.

61. The Court never received the applicant’s letter dated 21 October 2008. The Government stated that the prison administration had dispatched it on the same day that the applicant submitted it for posting.

F. Other relevant circumstances

62. The applicant was released on parole on 4 August 2009.

63. On an unspecified date—apparently after the case had been communicated to the Government and the Government had attempted to obtain the relevant information—the SIZO issued an information note recording that the logbook containing detainees’ complaints for 2004 and 2005 had been destroyed on 29 January 2009.

64.
According to an information note issued by the Suvorivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office on 14 November 2011, the investigation materials concerning the applicant’s 2005 allegation of ill-treatment had been destroyed on 20 January 2010. Their destruction followed the expiration of the five-year retention period prescribed by the recordkeeping guidelines adopted by the General Prosecutor’s Office on 28 December 2002.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Searches of homes and other property

65. The inviolability of every person’s home is protected by Article 30 of the Constitution (1996). Unless authorised by a reasoned judicial decision, entry into, examination of, or a search of an individual’s home or other property is prohibited.

66. The same constitutional safeguards are restated in Article 311 of the Civil Code (2003).

67. Under Article 177 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (1960), a house or other property may be searched only where there are sufficient reasons to believe that the sought items could be located there and where the search has been authorised by a reasoned court decision. No appeal lies against such a judicial decision. Article 183 of the Code provides that the investigating officer responsible for the search must present the search warrant to the person or persons occupying the premises concerned. Where the sought items are not surrendered voluntarily, the investigating officer is required to carry out the search by force.

68. A summary of the pertinent provisions of the Law “On Search and Seizure Activities” (1992) appears in Volokhy v. Ukraine (no. 23543/02, § 27, 2 November 2006).

B. Detention before trial

69. Article 29 of the Constitution is reproduced in the judgment in Svershov v. Ukraine (no. 35231/02, § 39, 27 November 2008).

70. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) are set out in the following judgments: Nevmerzhitsky v. Ukraine, no. 54825/00, §§ 53-54, ECHR 2005-II (extracts); Kucheruk v. Ukraine, no. 2570/04, §§ 67-69, 6 September 2007; and Sergey Volosyuk v. Ukraine, no. 1291/03, §§ 24-25, 12 March 2009.

original: FIFTH SECTION       CASE OF TEMCHENKO v. UKRAINE (Application no. 30579/10)        JUDGMENT   STRASBOURG 16 July 2015  FINAL 16/10/2015 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision. In the case of Temchenko v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Angelika Nußberger, President, Boštjan M. Zupančič, Ganna Yudkivska, Vincent A. De Gaetano, André Potocki, Helena Jäderblom, Aleš Pejchal, judges,and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 23 June 2015,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 30579/10) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko (“the applicant”), on 21 May 2010.2. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Mukanova and Mr M. Tarahkalo, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr N. Kulchytskyy, of the Ministry of Justice.3. On 8 December 2011 the application was communicated to the Government.THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE4. The applicant was born in 1942 and lives in Kryvyy Rig. Before his arrest he was rector of a State-owned university.5. On 23 September 2009 the applicant was medically examined. An endocrinologist noted that he had type-2 diabetes and prescribed insulin injections. The endocrinologist advised that commencement and adjustment of the insulin treatment should take place on an in-patient basis in a local hospital.A. The applicant’s detention and the criminal proceedings against him1. The applicant’s arrest and the criminal proceedings6. On 29 September 2009 an investigator from the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office arrested the applicant on suspicion of having received bribes in his capacity as university rector. He was detained in the temporary detention facility of Kryvyy Rig (“the ITT”).7. On 2 October 2009 the Dzerzhynskyy District Court of Kryvyy Rig (“the District Court”) ordered the applicant’s detention for three months, stating, without referring to any concrete facts, that he might abscond, hinder the investigation or continue his criminal activities. The court also noted that there was evidence in support of the prosecutors’ suspicion that the applicant had received bribes.8. On 5 October 2009 the applicant was transported to the Kryvyy Rig remand centre (“the SIZO”).9. On 7 October 2009 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) upheld the above decision. The court noted, without providing further details, that the case file contained evidence that the applicant had attempted to hinder the investigation, and medical documents indicating that he was physically fit for detention. No further information about the said evidence and documents was made available to the Court.10. On 18 November 2009 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention to 29 January 2010, relying on the same grounds as in its previous decision.11. On 25 November 2009 the Court of Appeal upheld that decision. Referring to unspecified medical documents, it again noted that the applicant was physically fit for detention.12. On 29 January 2010 the investigation in the applicant’s case was completed and the case was referred to the District Court for trial.13. In a preliminary hearing on 9 March 2010, the District Court ruled that the preventive measure in respect of the applicant had to be maintained as there were no reasons to change it. The court did not fix the length of the applicant’s detention.14. In a judgment of 23 May 2011, the District Court sentenced the applicant to five years and two months’ imprisonment for bribery. On 5 October 2011 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal modified that judgment and sentenced the applicant to five years’ suspended imprisonment with a probationary period of three years. On the same date the applicant was released from the SIZO. The judgment became final.15. In the course of the criminal proceedings the applicant took part in fifty court hearings and in a number of investigative actions.2. The applicant’s requests for release16. In a written request for release, the applicant stated that his state of health was incompatible with detention and that, as he no longer held the post of rector, he could not hinder the investigation. On 31 May 2010 he submitted his request to the SIZO administration asking them to send it to the District Court for examination. On 2 June 2010 the SIZO administration duly forwarded the request. On 7 June 2010 the District Court rejected the request, holding that if he were freed, the applicant could influence witnesses. It continued:“... In so far as the applicant’s health is concerned, it appears from the medical certificates provided by the SIZO and municipal hospital no. 8 that the applicant is being provided with medical treatment. Therefore, the court finds no reason to change the applicant’s preventive measure.”17. The court did not refer to any concrete facts supporting its finding that the applicant could influence witnesses. Nor did it examine the adequacy of the medical treatment provided to him. No details of the “medical certificates” to which the District Court referred were made available to the Court.18. On an unspecified date, the applicant wrote another request for release against an undertaking not to abscond. He argued that during his detention his state of health had deteriorated as a result of the inadequate medical treatment provided to him in the SIZO. He also argued that the conditions of his transportation to court hearings had been inappropriate given his state of health. In particular, due to the insufficient ventilation in the van transporting him, his blood pressure had risen and he had had difficulty breathing. It remains unknown when this request was submitted to the District Court.19. On 17 June 2010 the District Court examined and rejected the applicant’s request, stating:“... the applicant could influence witnesses and thus hinder the investigation ... Where necessary the applicant has received medical aid in the SIZO.”20. On 6 August 2010, 21 and 22 February 2011, the applicant submitted further requests for release, either against an undertaking not to abscond or on bail. Relying on the findings of forensic medical examinations carried out on 12 November 2010 and 28 January 2011 (see paragraphs 62-66 below), he argued that the treatment provided to him during his detention had not been adequate and that he needed in-patient treatment in a specialist medical institution. That kind of treatment could not be provided to him in the SIZO.21. On 28 March 2011 the District Court rejected those requests. The court based its decision on the findings of the forensic examination of 28 January 2011, noting that the applicant’s diseases were of a chronic nature and could last for a long time. The court also stated: “If necessary the applicant can be transported to court hearings in an ambulance accompanied by a doctor”.... “From the medical certificates issued by the SIZO and the certificate issued by hospital no. 9 on 25 March 2011, it follows that when necessary the applicant receives medical aid in the SIZO and in municipal hospitals. The applicant may influence witnesses”.No details of the “medical certificates” to which the District Court referred were made available to the Court.22. On 7 April 2011 the applicant submitted another request for release, advancing the same arguments as in his requests of 6 August 2010, 21 and 22 February 2011.23. On 28 April 2011 the District Court rejected the applicant’s request, essentially relying on the same grounds as in its decision of 28 March 2011.3. The applicant’s detention from 29 January to 9 March 201024. On 9 March and 7 June 2010 the District Court examined the applicant’s complaint that his detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010 had been unlawful and rejected it as unsubstantiated. The court found that, although that period of detention had not been covered by any court decision, the detention had been justified because the applicant had been awaiting committal for trial.B. Medical assistance provided to the applicant in detention25. On 5 October 2009 the doctor who had examined the applicant upon his arrival at the SIZO decided, in view of the applicant’s abnormally high blood pressure, to place him in the cardiology department of a municipal hospital. On the same date the applicant was taken to municipal hospital no. 3, which had cardiology and endocrinology departments.26. The applicant was diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, stenocardia, hypertensive diseases (stage II), chronic cholecystitis (remission stage) and pancreatitis (remission stage), type-2 subcompensated diabetes of medium severity, kidney cyst, prostate adenoma, and chronic pielonefritis (remission stage).27. The applicant was discharged from the hospital on 27 October 2009. He was recommended constant monitoring by a doctor and prescribed various medications, including an oral medication to lower his sugar level (Gliclazide).28. On the same date the applicant was returned to the SIZO medical unit, which was tasked with providing primary medical aid to SIZO detainees and did not have the equipment and staff to provide specialist medical treatment and assistance. The unit’s medical staff included two nurses, two feldshers (paramedics), a doctor, a psychologist and a gynaecologist.29. On 11 February and 9 March 2010 the SIZO medical unit informed the applicant’s lawyer that, according to the results of medical tests, the applicant’s diabetes and kidney pathology warranted in-patient examination in a specialist medical institution. However, no further steps were undertaken in this respect.30. On 24 March 2010 an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 studied the results of the applicant’s sugar-level tests and recommended that he start insulin injections on 9 April 2010.31. On 1 and 6 April 2010 the applicant was transported to municipal hospitals nos. 3 and 8 respectively, where he was examined by surgeons. On the latter date the applicant was diagnosed with chronic pancreatitis. After the examinations, which lasted for several hours, the applicant returned to the SIZO.32. On 9 April 2010 an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 confirmed the insulin prescription and recommended regular sugar-level tests. From that date onwards the applicant received insulin injections and did not raise any objection in that respect. He bought the insulin in the SIZO pharmacy, while the insulin syringes were sent to him by his relatives.33. In a letter of 15 April 2010 addressed to the applicant’s lawyer, the SIZO medical unit stated that the applicant’s condition during his detention was of medium severity and unstable.34. On 13 May 2010 the applicant complained to the SIZO medical staff of a sudden deterioration in his health. The medical staff noted that his pancreatitis had worsened and that there had been a significant rise in his sugar level. They called an ambulance to take him to hospital no. 8, which, however, did not have specialist endocrinology or cardiology departments. The applicant was placed in the intensive-care department, underwent a number of medical tests and was examined by an urologist, a neuropathologist, a cardiologist and an endocrinologist. He received treatment in connection with his diabetes and pancreatitis. The doctors established that his state of health had deteriorated since October 2009 and his general condition was serious.35. On 21 May 2010 the applicant was discharged from the hospital and transported back to the SIZO medical unit.36. In the applicant’s discharge note the hospital doctors recommended that he be monitored by an endocrinologist and that his sugar level be regularly measured. His diabetes treatment was modified and he was prescribed a special diet – so-called “fractional nutrition”.37. On three occasions between 27 May and 8 June 2010 a SIZO doctor raised the dose of insulin administered to the applicant. According to the Government, the dosage was raised on the advice of an endocrinologist. The applicant disagreed.38. On 2 June 2010 the SIZO medical unit informed the applicant’s lawyer that it did not have sufficient equipment and staff to provide the applicant with adequate insulin treatment, which could only be administered on an in-patient basis in a specialist medical institution.39. On the same date the head of the SIZO medical unit informed the judge dealing with the applicant’s criminal case that it was impossible to provide the applicant with adequate medical treatment in the SIZO. He noted that the applicant’s condition warranted comprehensive in-patient treatment in an outside medical institution and asked the judge to consider changing the applicant’s preventive measure. He also noted that further modification of the insulin dosage in the SIZO “without the endocrinologist’s supervision might lead to undesired results”. The judge did not react to that information.40. On 16 June and 2 July 2010 the applicant requested that the Court, under the Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, oblige Ukraine to transfer him to a specialist hospital, where he could receive adequate medical care. He alleged that as a consequence of that request, the SIZO medical staff stopped registering his complaints and providing him with any medical assistance. The Government contested the applicant’s allegation. On 30 July 2010 the Court refused the applicant’s request.41. On 13 July 2010 an endocrinologist examined the applicant in the SIZO, confirmed his previous diagnosis and adjusted his treatment.42. On 20 July 2010 the applicant was examined by an urologist and an oculist in hospital no. 8. He underwent a kidney ultrasonic examination and was diagnosed with retinal angiopathy. On the same date he returned to the SIZO.43. On 28 January 2011 the applicant was examined in the SIZO medical unit by an endocrinologist, a cardiologist and a urologist from municipal hospitals.44. On 30 January 2011 the SIZO administration requested hospital no. 8 to assess whether the applicant needed in-patient treatment. The hospital did not reply, and the SIZO administration did not follow up on the request.45. From 1 March 2011 onwards the SIZO medical unit had no doctors among its staff.46. On 16 March 2011, following a new request submitted by the applicant under Rule 39, the Court decided that the Government should “ensure that the applicant received treatment in the specialised institutions referred to in the report of 28 January 2011” (see paragraphs 63-66 below). On 17 March 2011 the Court informed the Government of its decision.47. On 18 March 2011 the applicant was taken by ambulance to hospital no. 8, where he remained until 19 March 2011. The Government submitted that the applicant’s hospitalisation had been based on the Court’s decision of 16 March 2011. The applicant challenged that statement and submitted that he had been hospitalised solely because of a sudden deterioration in his health, which the SIZO staff had been unable to deal with.48. On 19 March 2011 the applicant was transferred to the cardiology department of hospital no. 9, which had an endocrinologist on its staff.49. During his stay at the hospitals, the applicant was advised to undergo a coronography (heart examination) as soon as possible.50. On 26 March 2011 the applicant was discharged, the hospital doctors having noted an improvement in his state of health. He returned to the SIZO medical unit.51. The SIZO administration proposed that the applicant undergo the coronography at any of the hospitals in Kryvyy Rig and receive treatment for diabetes in the endocrinology department of hospital no. 3 in Kryvyy Rig. The applicant refused, maintaining that he did not trust the Kryvyy Rig doctors. He would only agree to be taken to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv.52. On 8 April 2011 the applicant was examined in the SIZO by an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 and his treatment for diabetes was modified.53. On 15 April 2011 the governor of the SIZO informed the judge dealing with the criminal case against the applicant that the latter’s condition was of medium severity and unstable. He asked the judge to consider changing the applicant’s preventive measure, in particular, in view of his age and state of health. The judge did not react to that request.54. On 19 April 2011 the SIZO administration asked the judge to allow the applicant to be moved to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. On 6 June 2011 the judge granted the request.55. In the meantime, on 21 April 2011, the applicant was urgently taken to the endocrinology department of hospital no. 8 because of a sudden deterioration in his health. He remained in the hospital until 27 April 2011 and received treatment for diabetes.56. On 10 July 2011 the applicant was transported to Kyiv by train.57. Between 11 and 22 July 2011 the doctors of the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv examined the applicant and prescribed non-urgent heart surgery. In addition to the diseases previously noted by other doctors, the applicant was diagnosed with poliposis of the stomach and sigmoid colon, stomach polipantruma, repeated Q-wave infarction of the posterior wall of the left ventricular valve of the heart, atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, mitral valve regurgitation, tricuspid valve regurgitation, atrioventricular valve regurgitation and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular insufficiency.58. On 30 July 2011 the applicant returned to the Kryvyy Rig SIZO medical unit.59. While the applicant remained in detention, his wife and lawyer submitted several requests to the authorities seeking his move to a specialist hospital instead of the SIZO. The SIZO administration replied that the applicant was receiving adequate treatment in the SIZO and occasionally in municipal hospitals, and that his health condition did not require specialist in-patient treatment in an outside medical institution.60. The applicant lodged a number of complaints with the prosecutors stating that he had not been provided with adequate medical assistance in detention. The prosecutors rejected his complaints as unsubstantiated. The applicant did not challenge the prosecutors’ decisions before the courts.61. According to the applicant, he was handcuffed to his bed at all times during his stays in municipal hospitals. He did not raise any complaint in this connection before the national authorities and did not provide any evidence in that regard. The Government denied that the applicant had been handcuffed.C. Forensic medical examinations of the applicant62. On 12 November 2010, following a request from the applicant’s lawyer and having studied the applicant’s medical records provided by the latter, a committee of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations based in Kyiv drew up a report on the applicant’s state of health. It found that as a result of the inadequate medical treatment provided to him during his pre-trial detention, his condition had deteriorated. It stated, in particular, that the applicant’s hypertension had been exacerbated and the type-2 diabetes had reached the stage of decompensation. The experts noted that the gravity of the applicant’s condition warranted in-patient treatment in specialist endocrinology and cardiology hospitals, such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. The experts also expressed the opinion that the applicant risked developing a brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection if he was not provided with appropriate treatment. It was recommended that he be transported in an ambulance accompanied by a doctor.63. On 23 November 2010 the District Court, following a prosecutor’s request, ordered a committee of medical experts from the Dnipropetrovsk Bureau for Forensic Examinations to assess whether the applicant was physically fit for transportation and participation in court hearings.64. The medical experts decided that, in view of the instability of the applicant’s condition, it was not necessary to examine him in person. They assessed the applicant’s condition on the basis of his medical file provided by the SIZO. In their report of 28 January 2011 the experts concluded that the applicant’s condition was grave, highly unstable and unpredictable, he was prone to sudden deterioration in his health, which could be fatal if it occurred during transportation in a vehicle without appropriate medical equipment. The applicant’s transportation was thus found to be “undesirable”. However, if it was strictly necessary for the court to contact the applicant, the experts recommended transporting him in a special cardiac ambulance accompanied by a doctor.65. The experts found that the applicant’s condition had deteriorated while in detention as a result of the inadequate and incomprehensive medical treatment provided to him during that period. If not provided with appropriate in-patient treatment at a specialist medical institution – the experts referred to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute as an example of such an institution – the applicant risked developing potentially fatal complications, such as cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage or aortic dissection.66. The report of 28 January 2011 contains the statement that “... the applicant’s diseases are of a chronic nature, and may last for a lengthy period of time”.67. On 8 June 2011, following a request from the applicant’s wife, a committee of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations studied the applicant’s medical records and found that since 12 November 2010 his health had deteriorated and that his condition warranted comprehensive in-patient treatment in a specialist hospital, in particular the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute. Without such treatment the applicant risked developing life-threatening conditions such as a brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection. The experts mentioned that, in view of the instability of the applicant’s condition, his transportation would be potentially fatal. The applicant’s short-term hospitalisations had not constituted appropriate in-patient treatment in the applicant’s case because they had been aimed only at stabilising sudden deteriorations in his condition and had not formed part of a comprehensive treatment.68. The results of the above forensic examinations were submitted to the District Court.D. Provision of the medical records to the applicant, his wife and lawyer69. The applicant claimed that on 29 June 2010 his wife had asked the SIZO administration to send her his medical records. The SIZO administration had not responded to her request. The Government stated that the SIZO administration had not received such a request. A copy of the request which the applicant submitted to the Court bears no evidence that it was received by the SIZO.70. On 4 and 11 August and 22 November 2010, 10 and 31 March 2011 respectively, the applicant’s wife submitted further requests to the SIZO administration asking them to send her the applicant’s medical records. The SIZO sent her the records on 18 August and 29 November 2010, 29 March and 6 April 2011, respectively.71. On 31 March 2011, following a request from the applicant’s lawyer, hospital no. 9 provided the lawyer with a copy of the applicant’s medical records. According to the applicant, all the medical records provided to his wife and lawyer were incomplete and contained false information.E. Conditions of the applicant’s detention in the SIZO and his transportation1. Conditions of detention in the SIZO72. According to the applicant, the window in his cell in the SIZO “had no glass in it”, which resulted in “dampness and air temperature fluctuations”. The food provided by the SIZO was of poor quality. The applicant did not provide further details in that regard.73. The special diet (“fractional nutrition”) prescribed to the applicant was not available in the SIZO and was provided to him by his relatives two or three times a week.74. On 26 August 2011 the Government examined the two cells in which the applicant had been held in the SIZO. They submitted that the windows in the cells were double glazed and measured 110 by 130 cm. The temperature in the cells was 20C and the humidity was 56%. The Government acknowledged that the SIZO had not provided the “fractional nutrition” to the applicant. According to them, he had received it from his relatives and had been able to follow the prescribed diet.2. Conditions of transportation75. From 29 September to 5 October 2009 and from 9 March 2010 to 1 February 2011 – on twenty-six occasions in total – the applicant was transported in a van used for the transportation of healthy detainees. Between 5 October 2009 and 9 March 2010 he was once transported in a police car.76. Between 18 April 2011 and 22 September 2011 the applicant was transported in an ambulance accompanied by a doctor (nineteen times in total). The exact duration of the trips remains unknown; the applicant stated that sometimes his transportation had lasted for up to three hours.77. The above-mentioned van had metal walls and one small window. According to the applicant, it was not sufficiently ventilated and had no heating system, so it was too cold in winter and too hot in summer. It does not appear from the applicant’s submissions that he was transported with other inmates. The Government argued that the van had had sufficient ventilation and the conditions of the applicant’s transportation had been adequate.78. The applicant submitted that the train carriage in which he had been transported to Kyiv had not been fit for transportation of a person in his condition. The Government maintained that the conditions in the train carriage were adequate. The parties did not provide any further details in this regard.79. On 5 July 2011 the prosecutor rejected the applicant’s complaint concerning the inappropriate conditions of his transportation in the train. The applicant did not challenge that decision before the courts.II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE80. The relevant provisions of the Civil Code and the Law “on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies of Inquiry, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts” (“the Compensation Act”) are summarised in Ratushna v. Ukraine, no. 17318/06, §§ 43-44, 2 December 2010, with further references.

CASE OF TEMCHENKO v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 30579/10)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

16 July 2015

FINAL

16/10/2015

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Temchenko v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Angelika Nußberger, President,
Boštjan M. Zupančič,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Vincent A. De Gaetano,
André Potocki,
Helena Jäderblom,
Aleš Pejchal, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 23 June 2015,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 30579/10) against Ukraine filed with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko (“the applicant”), on 21 May 2010.

2. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Mukanova and Mr M. Tarahkalo, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr N. Kulchytskyy, from the Ministry of Justice.

3. On 8 December 2011 the application was notified to the Government.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

4. The applicant was born in 1942 and resides in Kryvyy Rig. Prior to his arrest, he was rector of a State-owned university.

5. On 23 September 2009 the applicant underwent a medical examination. An endocrinologist found that he had type-2 diabetes and prescribed insulin injections. The endocrinologist recommended that the insulin treatment be commenced and adjusted on an in-patient basis at a local hospital.

A. The applicant’s detention and the criminal proceedings against him

1. The applicant’s arrest and the criminal proceedings

6. On 29 September 2009 an investigator from the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office arrested the applicant on suspicion of receiving bribes in his capacity as university rector. He was held in the temporary detention facility of Kryvyy Rig (“the ITT”).

7. On 2 October 2009 the Dzerzhynskyy District Court of Kryvyy Rig (“the District Court”) ordered that the applicant be detained for three months, stating, without citing any specific facts, that he might abscond, obstruct the investigation, or continue his criminal activities. The court further noted that there was evidence supporting the prosecutors’ suspicion that the applicant had received bribes.

8. On 5 October 2009 the applicant was transferred to the Kryvyy Rig remand centre (“the SIZO”).

9. On 7 October 2009 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) upheld that decision. Without giving further details, the court noted that the case file contained evidence that the applicant had attempted to obstruct the investigation, as well as medical documents indicating that he was physically fit for detention.
No further information concerning the evidence and documents in question was made available to the Court.

10. On 18 November 2009 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 29 January 2010, relying on the same grounds as in its earlier decision.

11. On 25 November 2009 the Court of Appeal upheld that decision. Referring to unspecified medical records, it again observed that the applicant was physically fit for detention.

12. On 29 January 2010 the investigation into the applicant’s case was completed, and the case was referred to the District Court for trial.

13. At a preliminary hearing on 9 March 2010, the District Court ruled that the preventive measure in respect of the applicant should be maintained, as there were no grounds for changing it. The court did not specify the duration of the applicant’s detention.

14. By a judgment of 23 May 2011, the District Court sentenced the applicant to five years and two months’ imprisonment for bribery. On 5 October 2011 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal amended that judgment and sentenced the applicant to five years’ suspended imprisonment, with a probationary period of three years. The applicant was released from the SIZO on the same date. The judgment became final.

15. During the criminal proceedings, the applicant participated in fifty court hearings and a number of investigative measures.

2. The applicant’s applications for release

16. In a written application for release, the applicant stated that his state of health was incompatible with detention and that, since he no longer held the position of rector, he could not obstruct the investigation. On 31 May 2010 he submitted the application to the SIZO administration, asking that it be forwarded to the District Court for consideration. On 2 June 2010 the SIZO administration duly forwarded it. On 7 June 2010 the District Court dismissed the application, finding that, if released, the applicant could influence witnesses. It continued:

“... As regards the applicant’s health, it appears from the medical certificates provided by the SIZO and municipal hospital no. 8 that the applicant is receiving medical treatment. The court therefore finds no grounds for changing the preventive measure applied to the applicant.”

17. The court did not cite any specific facts in support of its finding that the applicant could influence witnesses. Nor did it assess the adequacy of the medical treatment provided to him. No details of the “medical certificates” referred to by the District Court were made available to the Court.

18. On an unspecified date, the applicant submitted another application for release subject to an undertaking not to abscond. He contended that his health had deteriorated during his detention because of the inadequate medical treatment provided in the SIZO. He further argued that the conditions in which he was transported to court hearings had been unsuitable in view of his state of health.
In particular, owing to insufficient ventilation in the van transporting him, his blood pressure had risen and he had experienced difficulty breathing. It remains unclear when this request was submitted to the District Court.

19. On 17 June 2010 the District Court examined and rejected the applicant’s request, stating:

“... the applicant could influence witnesses and thus obstruct the investigation ... Where necessary, the applicant has received medical aid in the SIZO.”

20. On 6 August 2010 and 21 and 22 February 2011, the applicant submitted further requests for release, either against an undertaking not to abscond or on bail. Relying on the findings of forensic medical examinations conducted on 12 November 2010 and 28 January 2011 (see paragraphs 62-66 below), he argued that the treatment provided to him during his detention had been inadequate and that he required in-patient treatment in a specialist medical institution. Such treatment could not be provided to him in the SIZO.

21. On 28 March 2011 the District Court rejected those requests. The court based its decision on the findings of the forensic examination of 28 January 2011, noting that the applicant’s illnesses were chronic and could persist for a long time. The court also stated:

“If necessary, the applicant can be transported to court hearings in an ambulance accompanied by a doctor” ... “It follows from the medical certificates issued by the SIZO and the certificate issued by hospital no. 9 on 25 March 2011 that, when necessary, the applicant receives medical aid in the SIZO and in municipal hospitals. The applicant may influence witnesses.”

No details of the “medical certificates” referred to by the District Court were made available to the Court.

22. On 7 April 2011 the applicant submitted another request for release, putting forward the same arguments as in his requests of 6 August 2010 and 21 and 22 February 2011.

23. On 28 April 2011 the District Court rejected the applicant’s request, relying essentially on the same grounds as in its decision of 28 March 2011.

3. The applicant’s detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010

24. On 9 March and 7 June 2010 the District Court examined the applicant’s complaint that his detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010 had been unlawful and dismissed it as unsubstantiated. The court found that, although that period of detention had not been authorised by any court decision, the detention had been justified because the applicant had been awaiting committal for trial.

B. Medical assistance provided to the applicant in detention

25. On 5 October 2009 the doctor who examined the applicant upon his arrival at the SIZO decided, in view of his abnormally high blood pressure, to place him in the cardiology department of a municipal hospital. On the same day, the applicant was taken to municipal hospital no. 3, which had cardiology and endocrinology departments.

26.
The applicant was diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, stenocardia, stage II hypertension, chronic cholecystitis and pancreatitis (both in remission), type 2 subcompensated diabetes of medium severity, a kidney cyst, prostate adenoma, and chronic pyelonephritis (in remission).

27. The applicant was discharged from the hospital on 27 October 2009. He was advised to remain under constant medical supervision and was prescribed various medications, including an oral medicine to lower his blood sugar level (Gliclazide).

28. On the same date, the applicant was returned to the SIZO medical unit, which was responsible for providing primary medical care to SIZO detainees and lacked the equipment and personnel needed to provide specialist medical treatment and assistance. The unit’s medical staff consisted of two nurses, two feldshers (paramedics), a doctor, a psychologist, and a gynaecologist.

29. On 11 February and 9 March 2010, the SIZO medical unit informed the applicant’s lawyer that, according to the medical test results, the applicant’s diabetes and kidney condition warranted in-patient examination at a specialist medical institution. However, no further action was taken in this regard.

30. On 24 March 2010, an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 reviewed the results of the applicant’s blood-sugar tests and recommended that he begin insulin injections on 9 April 2010.

31. On 1 and 6 April 2010, the applicant was taken to municipal hospitals nos. 3 and 8 respectively, where he was examined by surgeons. On the latter date, he was diagnosed with chronic pancreatitis. Following the examinations, which lasted several hours, the applicant was returned to the SIZO.

32. On 9 April 2010, an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 confirmed the insulin prescription and recommended regular blood-sugar tests. From that date onward, the applicant received insulin injections and raised no objection in that regard. He purchased the insulin from the SIZO pharmacy, while his relatives sent him the insulin syringes.

33. In a letter dated 15 April 2010 and addressed to the applicant’s lawyer, the SIZO medical unit stated that the applicant’s condition during his detention was unstable and of medium severity.

34. On 13 May 2010, the applicant complained to the SIZO medical staff of a sudden deterioration in his health. The medical staff observed that his pancreatitis had worsened and that his blood-sugar level had risen significantly. They called an ambulance to take him to hospital no. 8, which, however, had no specialist endocrinology or cardiology departments. The applicant was admitted to the intensive-care department, underwent several medical tests, and was examined by a urologist, a neuropathologist, a cardiologist, and an endocrinologist. He received treatment for his diabetes and pancreatitis. The doctors found that his health had deteriorated since October 2009 and that his general condition was serious.

35.
On 21 May 2010 the applicant was discharged from hospital and taken back to the SIZO medical unit.

36. In the applicant’s discharge note, the hospital doctors recommended that he be monitored by an endocrinologist and that his blood sugar level be measured regularly. His diabetes treatment was modified, and he was prescribed a special diet known as “fractional nutrition”.

37. On three occasions between 27 May and 8 June 2010, a SIZO doctor increased the applicant’s insulin dosage. According to the Government, the dosage was increased on the advice of an endocrinologist. The applicant disputed this.

38. On 2 June 2010 the SIZO medical unit informed the applicant’s lawyer that it lacked sufficient equipment and staff to provide the applicant with adequate insulin treatment, which could only be administered on an in-patient basis in a specialist medical institution.

39. On the same date, the head of the SIZO medical unit informed the judge handling the applicant’s criminal case that it was impossible to provide him with adequate medical treatment in the SIZO. He stated that the applicant’s condition required comprehensive in-patient treatment in an outside medical institution and asked the judge to consider changing the applicant’s preventive measure. He also noted that any further adjustment of the insulin dosage in the SIZO “without the endocrinologist’s supervision might lead to undesired results”. The judge did not respond to that information.

40. On 16 June and 2 July 2010 the applicant requested that the Court, under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, require Ukraine to transfer him to a specialist hospital where he could receive adequate medical care. He alleged that, as a consequence of that request, the SIZO medical staff stopped recording his complaints and providing him with any medical assistance. The Government disputed the applicant’s allegation. On 30 July 2010 the Court rejected the applicant’s request.

41. On 13 July 2010 an endocrinologist examined the applicant in the SIZO, confirmed his earlier diagnosis and adjusted his treatment.

42. On 20 July 2010 the applicant was examined by a urologist and an oculist at hospital no. 8. He underwent an ultrasound examination of his kidneys and was diagnosed with retinal angiopathy. He returned to the SIZO on the same date.

43. On 28 January 2011 the applicant was examined in the SIZO medical unit by an endocrinologist, a cardiologist and a urologist from municipal hospitals.

44. On 30 January 2011 the SIZO administration asked hospital no. 8 to assess whether the applicant required in-patient treatment. The hospital did not respond, and the SIZO administration did not follow up on the request.

45. From 1 March 2011 onwards, the SIZO medical unit had no doctors on its staff.
On 16 March 2011, following a fresh request submitted by the applicant under Rule 39, the Court decided that the Government should “ensure that the applicant received treatment in the specialised institutions referred to in the report of 28 January 2011” (see paragraphs 63-66 below). On 17 March 2011, the Court notified the Government of its decision.

47. On 18 March 2011, the applicant was taken by ambulance to hospital no. 8, where he remained until 19 March 2011. The Government stated that the applicant’s hospitalisation had been based on the Court’s decision of 16 March 2011. The applicant disputed that assertion and submitted that he had been hospitalised solely because of a sudden deterioration in his health, which the SIZO staff had been unable to manage.

48. On 19 March 2011, the applicant was transferred to the cardiology department of hospital no. 9, which had an endocrinologist on staff.

49. During his stay in the hospitals, the applicant was advised to undergo a coronography (heart examination) as soon as possible.

50. On 26 March 2011, the applicant was discharged after the hospital doctors noted an improvement in his health. He returned to the SIZO medical unit.

51. The SIZO administration proposed that the applicant undergo the coronography at any hospital in Kryvyy Rig and receive diabetes treatment in the endocrinology department of hospital no. 3 in Kryvyy Rig. The applicant refused, stating that he did not trust the doctors in Kryvyy Rig. He would agree only to being taken to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv.

52. On 8 April 2011, the applicant was examined at the SIZO by an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3, and his diabetes treatment was adjusted.

53. On 15 April 2011, the governor of the SIZO informed the judge handling the criminal case against the applicant that the latter’s condition was unstable and of medium severity. He asked the judge to consider changing the applicant’s preventive measure, particularly in view of his age and health. The judge did not respond to that request.

54. On 19 April 2011, the SIZO administration asked the judge to permit the applicant’s transfer to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. On 6 June 2011, the judge granted the request.

55. In the meantime, on 21 April 2011, the applicant was urgently taken to the endocrinology department of hospital no. 8 following a sudden deterioration in his health. He remained there until 27 April 2011 and received treatment for diabetes.

56. On 10 July 2011, the applicant was transported to Kyiv by train.

57. Between 11 and 22 July 2011, doctors at the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv examined the applicant and prescribed non-urgent heart surgery.
In addition to the diseases previously identified by other doctors, the applicant was diagnosed with poliposis of the stomach and sigmoid colon, stomach polipantruma, repeated Q-wave infarction of the posterior wall of the left ventricular valve of the heart, atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, mitral valve regurgitation, tricuspid valve regurgitation, atrioventricular valve regurgitation, and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular insufficiency.

58. On 30 July 2011, the applicant returned to the Kryvyy Rig SIZO medical unit.

59. While the applicant remained in detention, his wife and lawyer made several requests to the authorities for his transfer to a specialist hospital instead of the SIZO. The SIZO administration responded that the applicant was receiving adequate treatment in the SIZO and, on occasion, in municipal hospitals, and that his condition did not require specialist in-patient treatment at an outside medical institution.

60. The applicant filed a number of complaints with the prosecutors, stating that he had not received adequate medical assistance in detention. The prosecutors dismissed his complaints as unsubstantiated. The applicant did not challenge their decisions before the courts.

61. According to the applicant, he was handcuffed to his bed throughout his stays in municipal hospitals. He did not lodge any complaint in this regard with the national authorities and provided no supporting evidence. The Government denied that the applicant had been handcuffed.

C. Forensic medical examinations of the applicant

62. On 12 November 2010, at the request of the applicant’s lawyer and after reviewing the applicant’s medical records provided by the lawyer, a committee of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations in Kyiv prepared a report on the applicant’s state of health. It concluded that his condition had deteriorated as a result of the inadequate medical treatment provided during his pre-trial detention. In particular, it stated that the applicant’s hypertension had worsened and his type-2 diabetes had reached the stage of decompensation. The experts noted that the severity of the applicant’s condition warranted in-patient treatment in specialist endocrinology and cardiology hospitals, such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. They also expressed the view that the applicant risked developing a brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection unless he received appropriate treatment. It was recommended that he be transported by ambulance and accompanied by a doctor.

63. On 23 November 2010, following a request by the prosecutor, the District Court ordered a committee of medical experts from the Dnipropetrovsk Bureau for Forensic Examinations to determine whether the applicant was physically fit for transportation and participation in court hearings.

64.
The medical experts decided that, given the instability of the applicant’s condition, it was unnecessary to examine him in person. They assessed his condition on the basis of the medical file provided by the SIZO. In their report of 28 January 2011, the experts concluded that the applicant’s condition was grave, highly unstable and unpredictable, and that he was prone to sudden deterioration in his health, which could be fatal if it occurred during transportation in a vehicle without appropriate medical equipment. The applicant’s transportation was therefore deemed “undesirable”. However, if it was strictly necessary for the court to contact him, the experts recommended that he be transported in a special cardiac ambulance accompanied by a doctor.

65. The experts found that the applicant’s condition had deteriorated while in detention as a result of the inadequate and incomplete medical treatment provided to him during that period. Unless he received appropriate in-patient treatment at a specialist medical institution – the experts cited the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute as an example – the applicant risked developing potentially fatal complications, such as cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage or aortic dissection.

66. The report of 28 January 2011 stated that “... the applicant’s diseases are chronic in nature and may persist for a lengthy period of time”.

67. On 8 June 2011, following a request by the applicant’s wife, a committee of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations reviewed the applicant’s medical records and found that his health had deteriorated since 12 November 2010 and that his condition required comprehensive in-patient treatment in a specialist hospital, particularly the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute. Without such treatment, the applicant risked developing life-threatening conditions such as a brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection. The experts noted that, given the instability of his condition, transporting him would be potentially fatal. The applicant’s short-term hospitalisations had not amounted to appropriate in-patient treatment in his case because they had been intended only to stabilise sudden deteriorations in his condition and had not formed part of comprehensive treatment.

68. The results of the above forensic examinations were submitted to the District Court.

D. Provision of the medical records to the applicant, his wife and lawyer

69. The applicant claimed that on 29 June 2010 his wife had asked the SIZO administration to send her his medical records. The SIZO administration had not replied to her request. The Government stated that the SIZO administration had not received any such request. The copy of the request submitted by the applicant to the Court bears no indication that it was received by the SIZO.

70.
On 4 and 11 August and 22 November 2010, and on 10 and 31 March 2011 respectively, the applicant’s wife submitted further requests to the SIZO administration, asking it to send her the applicant’s medical records. The SIZO sent her the records on 18 August and 29 November 2010, and on 29 March and 6 April 2011, respectively.

71. On 31 March 2011, following a request by the applicant’s lawyer, hospital no. 9 provided the lawyer with a copy of the applicant’s medical records. According to the applicant, all the medical records supplied to his wife and lawyer were incomplete and contained false information.

E. Conditions of the applicant’s detention in the SIZO and his transportation

1. Conditions of detention in the SIZO

72. According to the applicant, the window in his cell in the SIZO “had no glass in it”, resulting in “dampness and air temperature fluctuations”. The food supplied by the SIZO was of poor quality. The applicant provided no further details in that respect.

73. The special diet (“fractional nutrition”) prescribed for the applicant was unavailable in the SIZO and was brought to him by his relatives two or three times a week.

74. On 26 August 2011, the Government inspected the two cells in which the applicant had been held in the SIZO. They stated that the windows in the cells were double-glazed and measured 110 by 130 cm. The temperature in the cells was 20°C and the humidity was 56%. The Government acknowledged that the SIZO had not provided the applicant with “fractional nutrition”. According to them, he had received it from his relatives and had therefore been able to follow the prescribed diet.

2. Conditions of transportation

75. From 29 September to 5 October 2009 and from 9 March 2010 to 1 February 2011—on twenty-six occasions in total—the applicant was transported in a van used to transport healthy detainees. Between 5 October 2009 and 9 March 2010, he was transported once in a police car.

76. Between 18 April and 22 September 2011, the applicant was transported in an ambulance accompanied by a doctor (nineteen times in total). The exact duration of the journeys remains unknown; the applicant stated that his transportation had sometimes lasted up to three hours.

77. The above-mentioned van had metal walls and one small window. According to the applicant, it was insufficiently ventilated and had no heating system, making it too cold in winter and too hot in summer. It does not appear from the applicant’s submissions that he was transported with other inmates. The Government contended that the van had sufficient ventilation and that the conditions of the applicant’s transportation had been adequate.

78. The applicant submitted that the train carriage in which he had been transported to Kyiv had not been suitable for transporting a person in his condition. The Government maintained that the conditions in the train carriage had been adequate. The parties provided no further details in that regard.

79.
On 5 July 2011, the prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s complaint regarding the inappropriate conditions of his transportation by train. The applicant did not challenge that decision before the courts.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

80. The relevant provisions of the Civil Code and the Law “on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies of Inquiry, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts” (“the Compensation Act”) are summarised in Ratushna v. Ukraine, no. 17318/06, §§ 43-44, 2 December 2010, with further references.

In the case of Temchenko v. Ukraine,
