Having deliberated in private on 23 June 2015,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 30579/10, brought against Ukraine before the Court on 21 May 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”).

2. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Mukanova and Mr M. Tarahkalo, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent from the Ministry of Justice, Mr N. Kulchytskyy.

3. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 December 2011.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

4. Born in 1942, the applicant resides in Kryvyy Rig. Prior to his arrest, he served as rector of a State-owned university.

5. During a medical examination on 23 September 2009, an endocrinologist diagnosed the applicant with type 2 diabetes and prescribed insulin injections. The specialist recommended that insulin therapy be initiated and adjusted while the applicant was an inpatient at a local hospital.

A. The applicant’s detention and the criminal proceedings against him

1. The applicant’s arrest and the criminal proceedings

6. On 29 September 2009, an investigator attached to the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office arrested the applicant on suspicion of accepting bribes while acting in his capacity as university rector. He was placed in the Kryvyy Rig temporary detention facility (“the ITT”).

7. On 2 October 2009, the Dzerzhynskyy District Court of Kryvyy Rig (“the District Court”) ordered that the applicant be detained for three months. Without identifying any specific facts, it stated that he might flee, obstruct the investigation, or continue engaging in criminal activity. The court further observed that evidence existed to substantiate the prosecution’s suspicion that the applicant had accepted bribes.

8. The applicant was transferred to the Kryvyy Rig remand centre (“the SIZO”) on 5 October 2009.

9. On 7 October 2009, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) upheld that ruling. Without elaborating, it stated that the case file contained evidence that the applicant had tried to impede the investigation, as well as medical records showing that he was physically fit to remain in detention.
No additional information concerning that evidence or those documents was submitted to the Court.

10. On 18 November 2009, the District Court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 29 January 2010 on the same grounds as those cited in its earlier decision.

11. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 25 November 2009. Referring once more to unidentified medical records, it stated that the applicant was physically capable of remaining in detention.

12. The investigation into the applicant’s case was completed on 29 January 2010, after which the case was sent to the District Court for trial.

13. At a preliminary hearing held on 9 March 2010, the District Court found no grounds for changing the preventive measure and ordered that it remain in place. It did not specify how long the applicant’s detention was to continue.

14. By a judgment of 23 May 2011, the District Court convicted the applicant of bribery and sentenced him to five years and two months’ imprisonment. On 5 October 2011, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal amended the judgment, imposing a suspended five-year prison sentence with a three-year probationary period. The applicant was released from the SIZO that same day, and the judgment became final.

15. Throughout the criminal proceedings, the applicant attended fifty court hearings and participated in several investigative measures.

2. The applicant’s applications for release

16. In a written application for release, the applicant maintained that his health was incompatible with continued detention. He further submitted that, since he was no longer rector, he was unable to obstruct the investigation. On 31 May 2010, he gave the application to the SIZO administration with a request that it be forwarded to the District Court for consideration. The administration transmitted it on 2 June 2010. On 7 June 2010, the District Court dismissed the application, finding that the applicant might influence witnesses if released. It continued:

“... As regards the applicant’s health, the medical certificates issued by the SIZO and municipal hospital no. 8 indicate that he is receiving medical treatment. Accordingly, the court sees no grounds for altering the preventive measure applied to him.”

17. The court identified no specific facts substantiating its conclusion that the applicant might exert influence on witnesses. It also failed to assess whether the medical treatment he received was adequate. The Court was not provided with any particulars of the “medical certificates” mentioned by the District Court.

18. On an unspecified date, the applicant submitted a further application seeking release subject to an undertaking not to abscond. He asserted that his health had worsened while in detention because the medical care available in the SIZO was inadequate. He also contended that, in view of his condition, the arrangements for transporting him to court hearings were unsuitable.
In particular, inadequate ventilation in the van transporting him had caused his blood pressure to rise and left him struggling to breathe. It is not known when this request was lodged with the District Court.

19. On 17 June 2010, the District Court considered and dismissed the applicant’s request, stating:

“... the applicant could influence witnesses and thereby obstruct the investigation ... The applicant has received medical assistance in the SIZO whenever necessary.”

20. The applicant made additional requests for release on 6 August 2010 and 21 and 22 February 2011, seeking either bail or release subject to an undertaking not to abscond. Referring to the conclusions of forensic medical examinations conducted on 12 November 2010 and 28 January 2011 (see paragraphs 62-66 below), he maintained that the medical care he had received in detention was inadequate and that he required in-patient treatment at a specialised medical facility, which the SIZO was unable to provide.

21. On 28 March 2011, the District Court dismissed those requests. Relying on the conclusions of the forensic examination of 28 January 2011, it observed that the applicant’s illnesses were chronic and could persist for a considerable period. The court further stated:

“If necessary, the applicant can be taken to court hearings by ambulance and accompanied by a doctor” ... “The medical certificates issued by the SIZO and the certificate issued by hospital no. 9 on 25 March 2011 show that the applicant receives medical assistance in the SIZO and in municipal hospitals whenever required. The applicant may influence witnesses.”

The Court was not provided with any details concerning the “medical certificates” cited by the District Court.

22. On 7 April 2011, the applicant again applied for release, relying on the same arguments raised in his requests of 6 August 2010 and 21 and 22 February 2011.

23. On 28 April 2011, the District Court dismissed that application, relying essentially on the same reasons given in its decision of 28 March 2011.

3. The applicant’s detention between 29 January and 9 March 2010

24. On 9 March and 7 June 2010, the District Court considered and rejected as unfounded the applicant’s complaint that his detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010 had been unlawful. It held that, despite the absence of any judicial decision authorising his detention during that period, it had been justified because he was awaiting committal for trial.

B. Medical care provided to the applicant while in detention

25. On 5 October 2009, following the applicant’s arrival at the SIZO, the examining doctor decided that his abnormally high blood pressure warranted admission to the cardiology department of a municipal hospital. Later that day, the applicant was transferred to municipal hospital no. 3, which had both cardiology and endocrinology departments.

26.
The applicant was found to be suffering from ischemic heart disease, stenocardia, stage II hypertension, chronic cholecystitis and pancreatitis—both in remission—medium-severity, subcompensated type 2 diabetes, a kidney cyst, prostate adenoma, and chronic pyelonephritis in remission.

27. On 27 October 2009, he was discharged from hospital with instructions to remain under continuous medical supervision. He was also prescribed various medicines, including Gliclazide, an oral blood-sugar-lowering drug.

28. That same day, the applicant was transferred back to the SIZO medical unit. The unit was responsible for providing detainees with primary medical care but lacked the personnel and equipment required for specialist treatment and assistance. Its staff consisted of two nurses, two feldshers (paramedics), one doctor, one psychologist, and one gynaecologist.

29. On 11 February and again on 9 March 2010, the SIZO medical unit advised the applicant’s lawyer that medical test results indicated that his diabetes and kidney condition required an in-patient assessment at a specialist medical facility. Nevertheless, no further action was taken.

30. On 24 March 2010, an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 reviewed the applicant’s blood-sugar test results and recommended that insulin injections begin on 9 April 2010.

31. The applicant was taken to municipal hospital no. 3 on 1 April 2010 and to municipal hospital no. 8 on 6 April 2010, where surgeons examined him. During the latter visit, he was diagnosed with chronic pancreatitis. Each examination lasted several hours, after which he was returned to the SIZO.

32. On 9 April 2010, an endocrinologist at hospital no. 3 confirmed that insulin should be prescribed and advised that the applicant’s blood-sugar level be tested regularly. From that date, the applicant received insulin injections and raised no objections to the treatment. He purchased the insulin from the SIZO pharmacy, while his relatives supplied the syringes.

33. In a letter sent to the applicant’s lawyer on 15 April 2010, the SIZO medical unit described his condition during detention as unstable and of medium severity.

34. On 13 May 2010, the applicant informed the SIZO medical staff that his health had suddenly deteriorated. They recorded an aggravation of his pancreatitis and a substantial increase in his blood-sugar level. An ambulance was called, and he was transferred to hospital no. 8, despite that facility having no specialist cardiology or endocrinology departments. He was admitted to intensive care, underwent several medical tests, and was examined by a urologist, neuropathologist, cardiologist, and endocrinologist. Treatment was provided for his diabetes and pancreatitis. The doctors concluded that his health had worsened since October 2009 and assessed his overall condition as serious.
On 21 May 2010, the applicant left the hospital and was taken back to the SIZO medical unit.

36. The hospital’s discharge report advised regular monitoring of the applicant’s blood-sugar levels and follow-up by an endocrinologist. His diabetes regimen was altered, and he was prescribed a special diet known as “fractional nutrition”.

37. Between 27 May and 8 June 2010, a SIZO doctor increased the applicant’s insulin dose on three occasions. The Government maintained that those adjustments had been made on an endocrinologist’s recommendation, which the applicant disputed.

38. On 2 June 2010, the SIZO medical unit notified the applicant’s lawyer that it lacked the staff and equipment necessary to administer adequate insulin therapy. It stated that such treatment could be provided only on an in-patient basis in a specialist medical facility.

39. That same day, the head of the SIZO medical unit advised the judge hearing the applicant’s criminal case that adequate treatment could not be provided in the detention facility. He stated that the applicant’s state of health required comprehensive in-patient care at an outside medical institution and asked the judge to consider altering the preventive measure imposed on him. He further warned that any additional adjustment of the insulin dosage in the SIZO “without the endocrinologist’s supervision might lead to undesired results”. The judge took no action in response.

40. On 16 June and again on 2 July 2010, the applicant asked the Court to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and direct Ukraine to transfer him to a specialist hospital capable of providing appropriate medical care. He claimed that, following those requests, the SIZO medical personnel ceased recording his complaints and stopped giving him any medical assistance. The Government denied that allegation. On 30 July 2010, the Court rejected his request.

41. An endocrinologist examined the applicant at the SIZO on 13 July 2010, upheld the earlier diagnosis and modified his treatment.

42. On 20 July 2010, the applicant was seen by a urologist and an ophthalmologist at hospital no. 8. He also underwent an ultrasound examination of his kidneys and was diagnosed with retinal angiopathy. He was returned to the SIZO later that day.

43. On 28 January 2011, doctors from municipal hospitals—an endocrinologist, a cardiologist and a urologist—examined the applicant in the SIZO medical unit.

44. On 30 January 2011, the SIZO administration asked hospital no. 8 to determine whether the applicant required in-patient care. The hospital did not respond, and the SIZO administration made no further inquiry.

45. As of 1 March 2011, there were no doctors employed in the SIZO medical unit.
On 16 March 2011, after the applicant lodged a further request under Rule 39, the Court directed the Government to “ensure that the applicant received treatment in the specialised institutions referred to in the report of 28 January 2011” (see paragraphs 63-66 below). The Government was notified of that decision on 17 March 2011.

47. On 18 March 2011, the applicant was transported by ambulance to hospital no. 8, where he stayed until 19 March. According to the Government, his admission followed from the Court’s decision of 16 March 2011. The applicant disputed this, asserting that he had been hospitalised only because his health had suddenly worsened beyond the SIZO staff’s ability to manage.

48. On 19 March 2011, he was moved to the cardiology department of hospital no. 9, which employed an endocrinologist.

49. While in hospital, the applicant was advised to undergo a coronography (a heart examination) as soon as possible.

50. The applicant was discharged on 26 March 2011 after the hospital doctors observed an improvement in his condition, and he was returned to the SIZO medical unit.

51. The SIZO administration offered to arrange the coronography at any hospital in Kryvyy Rig and diabetes treatment in the endocrinology department of Kryvyy Rig hospital no. 3. The applicant declined, stating that he did not trust the doctors in Kryvyy Rig and would consent only to transfer to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv.

52. On 8 April 2011, an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 examined the applicant at the SIZO and adjusted his diabetes treatment.

53. On 15 April 2011, the SIZO governor advised the judge hearing the criminal proceedings against the applicant that his condition was unstable and of medium severity. Having regard, in particular, to the applicant’s age and health, the governor asked the judge to consider altering the preventive measure. The judge did not respond.

54. On 19 April 2011, the SIZO administration sought judicial authorisation to transfer the applicant to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. The judge approved the request on 6 June 2011.

55. Meanwhile, following an abrupt decline in his health, the applicant was urgently admitted on 21 April 2011 to the endocrinology department of hospital no. 8. He remained there until 27 April and was treated for diabetes.

56. On 10 July 2011, the applicant travelled by train to Kyiv.

57. From 11 to 22 July 2011, doctors at the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv examined him and recommended heart surgery on a non-urgent basis.
Beyond the illnesses previously identified by other physicians, the applicant was diagnosed with poliposis of the stomach and sigmoid colon, stomach polipantruma, a repeated Q-wave infarction of the posterior wall of the left ventricular valve of the heart, coronary artery atherosclerosis, mitral valve regurgitation, tricuspid valve regurgitation, atrioventricular valve regurgitation, and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular insufficiency.

58. The applicant returned to the medical unit of the Kryvyy Rig SIZO on 30 July 2011.

59. Throughout his detention, the applicant’s wife and lawyer repeatedly asked the authorities to transfer him from the SIZO to a specialist hospital. In response, the SIZO administration maintained that he was receiving appropriate treatment within the detention facility and, when necessary, at municipal hospitals. It further stated that his condition did not call for specialist in-patient care at an external medical institution.

60. The applicant filed several complaints with the prosecutors, alleging that he had not received adequate medical care in detention. The prosecutors dismissed those complaints as unfounded, and the applicant did not seek judicial review of their decisions.

61. The applicant alleged that, whenever he was treated in municipal hospitals, he remained handcuffed to his bed at all times. He neither complained about this to the domestic authorities nor submitted any supporting evidence. The Government disputed his allegation and stated that he had not been handcuffed.

C. Forensic medical examinations of the applicant

62. At the request of the applicant’s lawyer, a panel of medical experts from the Kyiv-based Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations reviewed the medical records supplied by the lawyer and, on 12 November 2010, issued a report concerning the applicant’s health. The panel concluded that his condition had worsened because of inadequate medical treatment during pre-trial detention. In particular, it found that his hypertension had become more severe and that his type-2 diabetes had progressed to the decompensation stage. Given the seriousness of his condition, the experts considered that he required in-patient care in specialist endocrinology and cardiology institutions, such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. They also warned that, without suitable treatment, he was at risk of a brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection. The panel recommended that he be transported by ambulance under a doctor’s supervision.

63. On 23 November 2010, acting on a prosecutor’s application, the District Court instructed a panel of medical experts from the Dnipropetrovsk Bureau for Forensic Examinations to determine whether the applicant was physically capable of being transported and attending court hearings.

64.
Given the instability of the applicant’s condition, the medical experts considered an in-person examination unnecessary and instead evaluated his health using the medical file supplied by the SIZO. In their report dated 28 January 2011, they described his condition as serious, highly unstable and unpredictable. He was susceptible to abrupt deterioration, which could prove fatal if it occurred while he was being transported in a vehicle lacking suitable medical equipment. They therefore deemed his transportation “undesirable”. Nevertheless, if direct contact with the applicant was strictly necessary for the court, they advised that he be conveyed in a specially equipped cardiac ambulance under a doctor’s supervision.

65. The experts determined that the applicant’s health had worsened in detention because the medical care he received during that time had been inadequate and insufficiently comprehensive. Unless he underwent appropriate in-patient treatment at a specialist medical facility—such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute—he faced potentially fatal complications, including cardiac arrest, cerebral haemorrhage or aortic dissection.

66. The report of 28 January 2011 stated that “... the applicant’s diseases are of a chronic nature, and may last for a lengthy period of time”.

67. At the request of the applicant’s wife, a panel of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations reviewed his medical records on 8 June 2011. It concluded that his health had declined since 12 November 2010 and that his condition required comprehensive in-patient care in a specialist hospital, particularly the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute. Without such treatment, he was at risk of life-threatening complications, including cerebral haemorrhage and aortic dissection. Because his condition was unstable, the experts also warned that transporting him could be fatal. They found that his brief hospital admissions had not amounted to suitable in-patient care, as they had served only to stabilise acute deteriorations rather than forming part of a comprehensive course of treatment.

68. The findings of the above forensic examinations were submitted to the District Court.

D. Disclosure of the medical records to the applicant, his wife and his lawyer

69. According to the applicant, his wife asked the SIZO administration on 29 June 2010 to send her his medical records, but received no reply. The Government maintained that the administration had never received the request. The copy furnished by the applicant to the Court contains no indication that it was received by the SIZO.

70.
On 4 and 11 August and 22 November 2010, and on 10 and 31 March 2011, the applicant’s wife lodged additional requests with the SIZO administration for copies of his medical records. The SIZO forwarded the records to her on 18 August and 29 November 2010 and on 29 March and 6 April 2011, respectively.

71. In response to a request by the applicant’s lawyer, hospital no. 9 supplied the lawyer with a copy of the applicant’s medical records on 31 March 2011. The applicant maintained that all the records sent to his wife and lawyer were incomplete and included false information.

E. The applicant’s conditions of detention in the SIZO and transportation arrangements

1. Conditions in the SIZO

72. The applicant alleged that his SIZO cell had a window “with no glass in it”, causing “dampness and air temperature fluctuations”. He also stated that the food served at the SIZO was of poor quality, without providing any additional details.

73. The SIZO did not offer the special diet prescribed for the applicant, known as “fractional nutrition”. Instead, his relatives brought it to him two or three times per week.

74. On 26 August 2011, the Government inspected both SIZO cells in which the applicant had been detained. They reported that the cells had double-glazed windows measuring 110 by 130 cm, a temperature of 20°C and humidity of 56%. Although the Government accepted that the SIZO itself had not supplied the applicant’s “fractional nutrition”, they stated that his relatives had provided it, enabling him to comply with the prescribed diet.

2. Transportation conditions

75. On a total of twenty-six occasions, between 29 September and 5 October 2009 and again from 9 March 2010 until 1 February 2011, the applicant was conveyed in a van intended for transporting healthy detainees. During the period from 5 October 2009 to 9 March 2010, he was transported once in a police car.

76. From 18 April to 22 September 2011, the applicant travelled by ambulance under a doctor’s supervision on nineteen occasions. The precise length of those journeys is unknown, although he stated that some had lasted as long as three hours.

77. The van referred to above had metal walls and a single small window. The applicant asserted that it lacked adequate ventilation and had no heating, making it excessively cold during winter and excessively hot in summer. His submissions do not indicate that other inmates travelled with him. The Government, however, contended that the van was sufficiently ventilated and that his transportation conditions were appropriate.

78. According to the applicant, the railway carriage used to take him to Kyiv was unsuitable for transporting someone in his medical condition. The Government disputed that claim, maintaining that the conditions in the carriage were adequate. Neither party supplied any further information on the matter.

79.
On 5 July 2011, the prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s complaint about the inadequate conditions in which he had been transported by train. The applicant did not seek judicial review of that decision.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

80. The pertinent provisions of the Civil Code and the Law “on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies of Inquiry, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts” (“the Compensation Act”) are summarised, together with further references, in Ratushna v. Ukraine, no. 17318/06, §§ 43-44, 2 December 2010.

51. The SIZO administration offered to arrange the applicant’s coronography at any hospital in Kryvyy Rig and proposed that his diabetes be treated in the endocrinology department of hospital no. 3 in Kryvyy Rig. He declined, stating that he did not trust the doctors in Kryvyy Rig and would consent only to transfer to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv.

52. On 8 April 2011, an endocrinologist from hospital no. 3 examined the applicant at the SIZO and adjusted his diabetes treatment.

53. On 15 April 2011, the SIZO governor notified the judge handling the criminal proceedings against the applicant that his condition was unstable and of medium severity. Taking particular account of the applicant’s age and health, the governor asked the judge to consider altering the preventive measure. The judge did not respond.

54. On 19 April 2011, the SIZO administration sought the judge’s permission to transfer the applicant to the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. The judge approved the request on 6 June 2011.

55. Meanwhile, following a sudden decline in his health on 21 April 2011, the applicant was urgently transferred to the endocrinology department of hospital no. 8. He remained there until 27 April 2011, receiving treatment for diabetes.

56. On 10 July 2011, the applicant travelled by train to Kyiv.

57. From 11 to 22 July 2011, doctors at the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv examined him and prescribed heart surgery that was not considered urgent.
Beyond the illnesses previously identified by other physicians, the applicant was also diagnosed with gastric and sigmoid-colon poliposis, stomach polipantruma, a repeated Q-wave infarction of the posterior wall of the heart’s left ventricular valve, coronary-artery atherosclerosis, mitral-valve regurgitation, tricuspid-valve regurgitation, atrioventricular-valve regurgitation, and atherosclerotic cerebrovascular insufficiency.

58. The applicant was returned to the medical unit of the Kryvyy Rig SIZO on 30 July 2011.

59. During his detention, the applicant’s wife and lawyer made several applications to the authorities requesting that he be transferred from the SIZO to a specialist hospital. The SIZO administration responded that he was being given appropriate treatment both at the SIZO and, from time to time, in municipal hospitals, and that his state of health did not necessitate specialist in-patient care at an external medical institution.

60. The applicant filed several complaints with the prosecutors, alleging that he had not received adequate medical care while in detention. The prosecutors dismissed those complaints as unfounded. He did not contest their decisions in court.

61. The applicant alleged that, whenever he was treated in municipal hospitals, he remained handcuffed to his bed at all times. He neither complained about this to the domestic authorities nor submitted any supporting evidence. The Government disputed his allegation that he had been handcuffed.

C. Forensic medical assessments of the applicant

62. At the request of the applicant’s lawyer, a panel of medical specialists from the Kyiv-based Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations examined the medical records supplied by the lawyer and issued a report on the applicant’s health on 12 November 2010. The panel concluded that his health had worsened because he had received inadequate medical treatment during his pre-trial detention. More specifically, it found that his hypertension had become more severe and that his type-2 diabetes had progressed to the decompensation stage. In the experts’ view, the seriousness of his condition required in-patient care in specialist endocrinology and cardiology facilities, including an institution such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute in Kyiv. They further considered that, without suitable treatment, he was at risk of suffering a brain haemorrhage or an aortic dissection. They recommended transporting him by ambulance with a doctor in attendance.

63. On 23 November 2010, acting on an application by a prosecutor, the District Court instructed a panel of medical experts from the Dnipropetrovsk Bureau for Forensic Examinations to determine whether the applicant was physically capable of being transported and attending court hearings.

64.
Given the instability of the applicant’s condition, the medical experts considered an in-person examination unnecessary and instead evaluated his health using the medical file supplied by the SIZO. In their report dated 28 January 2011, they determined that his condition was serious, extremely unstable and unpredictable. He was susceptible to sudden health deterioration, which could prove fatal if it occurred while he was being transported in a vehicle lacking suitable medical equipment. They therefore deemed his transportation “undesirable”. Nevertheless, if contact between the court and the applicant was strictly necessary, they advised that he be transported in a specialised cardiac ambulance with a doctor accompanying him.

65. The experts concluded that the applicant’s health had worsened during his detention because the medical treatment provided during that time had been inadequate and insufficiently comprehensive. Unless he received suitable in-patient care at a specialist medical facility—such as the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute, which they cited as an example—he faced a risk of potentially fatal complications, including cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage or aortic dissection.

66. The report of 28 January 2011 stated that “... the applicant’s illnesses are chronic and may persist for a considerable period of time”.

67. On 8 June 2011, at the request of the applicant’s wife, a panel of medical experts from the Central Bureau for Forensic Examinations reviewed his medical records. It found that his health had declined since 12 November 2010 and that his condition required comprehensive in-patient care in a specialist hospital, particularly the Strazhesko Cardiology Institute. In the absence of such treatment, he was at risk of developing life-threatening conditions, including brain haemorrhage and aortic dissection. The experts also noted that transporting him could be fatal because his condition was unstable. His brief periods of hospitalisation did not amount to appropriate in-patient treatment, as they had served only to stabilise acute deteriorations and had not been part of a comprehensive course of care.

68. The findings of the forensic examinations described above were submitted to the District Court.

D. Disclosure of the medical records to the applicant, his wife and his lawyer

69. According to the applicant, on 29 June 2010 his wife requested that the SIZO administration provide her with his medical records, but it did not reply. The Government maintained that the SIZO administration had never received the request. The copy submitted by the applicant to the Court contains no indication that the SIZO received it.

70.
The applicant’s wife made additional requests to the SIZO administration for copies of his medical records on 4 and 11 August and 22 November 2010, and on 10 and 31 March 2011. The SIZO forwarded the records to her on 18 August and 29 November 2010, and on 29 March and 6 April 2011, respectively.

71. In response to a request by the applicant’s lawyer, hospital no. 9 supplied the lawyer with a copy of the applicant’s medical records on 31 March 2011. The applicant alleged that all records given to his wife and lawyer were incomplete and included false information.

E. The applicant’s detention conditions in the SIZO and the circumstances of his transportation

1. Detention conditions in the SIZO

72. The applicant stated that his SIZO cell window “had no glass in it”, causing “dampness and air temperature fluctuations”. He also claimed that the food served at the SIZO was of poor quality, but gave no additional details.

73. The SIZO did not provide the special diet prescribed for the applicant, known as “fractional nutrition”. Instead, his relatives brought it to him two or three times per week.

74. On 26 August 2011, the Government inspected both SIZO cells in which the applicant had been detained. They reported that each cell had double-glazed windows measuring 110 by 130 cm, a temperature of 20°C, and humidity of 56%. The Government accepted that the SIZO itself had not supplied the applicant with “fractional nutrition”, but stated that his relatives had provided it and that he had therefore been able to comply with the prescribed diet.

2. Transportation conditions

75. On twenty-six occasions in total, from 29 September to 5 October 2009 and from 9 March 2010 to 1 February 2011, the applicant was transported in a van intended for healthy detainees. During the period between 5 October 2009 and 9 March 2010, he was transported once in a police car.

76. Between 18 April and 22 September 2011, the applicant was transported nineteen times in an ambulance, accompanied by a doctor. The precise length of those journeys is unknown, although the applicant said that some lasted as long as three hours.

77. The van referred to above had metal walls and a single small window. The applicant alleged that it lacked adequate ventilation and had no heating system, making it excessively cold during winter and excessively hot during summer. His submissions do not indicate that other inmates travelled with him. The Government contended that the van was adequately ventilated and that the transportation conditions were satisfactory.

78. According to the applicant, the railway carriage used to take him to Kyiv was unsuitable for transporting someone in his condition. The Government asserted that the conditions in the carriage were adequate. Neither party supplied any further particulars on this point.

79.
On 5 July 2011, the prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s complaint about the unsuitable conditions in which he had been transported by train. The applicant did not seek judicial review of that decision.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

80. The pertinent provisions of the Civil Code and the Law “on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies of Inquiry, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts” (“the Compensation Act”) are outlined, with further references, in Ratushna v. Ukraine, no. 17318/06, §§ 43-44, 2 December 2010.

Davydchuk of the Ministry of Justice.3. The applicant alleged that he had been beaten by the police whilst being apprehended and that there had been no effective investigation into this fact. He also stated that the conditions of his detention in Odesa SIZO were inhuman and degrading. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE5. The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Odesa.A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant6. On 22 January 2004, on the basis of a pre-investigation inquiry, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant and two other persons in connection with a robbery committed the night before.7. On the same day, the investigator arrested the applicant and drew up an arrest report, the relevant parts of which read as follows:“On 22 January 2004 at 1.40 p.m., investigator Ya., in accordance with Article 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine detained Kleutin Denis Vasyliyovych ... on suspicion of commission of the crime provided for by Article 186 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. ...”8. On 23 January 2004 the investigator applied to the Prymorsky District Court of Odesa (“the District Court”) with a request to place the applicant in pre-trial detention. He noted that the applicant had been suspected in having committed a serious crime and, if released, might abscond in order to avoid the investigation and prevent the establishment of the truth in the case.9. On 24 January 2004, in the presence of the prosecutor and in the absence of the applicant, the District Court remanded the applicant in custody without setting its maximum duration. The court’s order referred to the investigator’s statements as to the gravity of charges, the applicant’s previous convictions, and the risk of his committing another crime, absconding, impairing the establishment of truth and obstructing the course of justice. The applicant did not appeal against this decision.10. On 18 March 2004, in the presence of the prosecutor and in the absence of the applicant, the District Court allowed the investigator’s request and extended the applicant’s detention for one month in view of the need to carry out certain investigative steps to complete the investigation. The court found that the arguments of the investigator in this respect were reasonable.11. On 8 April 2004 the investigation was completed and the criminal case was sent for trial.12. On 5 May 2004, in the committal hearings, the District Court made no ruling in respect of the applicant’s further detention. It noted that no applications had been lodged by the parties to the proceedings and found “no violations of the requirements of Article 237 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Ukraine (“the CCP”) in the course of the preliminary investigation of the case”.13. On 18 June 2004 the District Court remitted the criminal case for additional investigation, without addressing the issue of applicant’s extended detention.14. On 18 April 2005 the District Court again remitted the criminal case for additional investigation. It made no ruling in respect of the applicant’s extended detention.15. On 13 August 2005 the additional investigation was completed and the case was sent to the District Court for trial.16. On 18 August 2005 the applicant requested that the District Court change the preventive measure to an obligation not to abscond.17. On 15 September 2005, in the committal hearings, the District Court maintained the applicant’s detention without giving any reason or setting any time-limits.18. On 7 November 2005, in June, July and on 16 October 2006 and again on 6 March 2007, the applicant applied to the District Court in writing to change the preventive measure into a non-custodial one. In his request of July 2006, he argued, inter alia, that he did not represent a danger to society, had a registered place of residence and was about to start a new job at the time when he was arrested. In reply to the applicant’s request of 7 November 2005, the court informed the applicant that all petitions should be “lodged and examined at a hearing”.19. On 8 June 2007 the applicant was found guilty of premeditated robbery as part of a group and of involving of minors in a crime and was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.20. On 15 November 2007 the Odesa Regional Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant.21. On 2 June 2008 the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected the applicant’s request for leave to appeal on points of law.22. On 22 January 2009 the applicant finished serving his sentence and was released.B. Alleged ill-treatment of the applicant by the police on 22 January 2004 and investigation thereof23. On 22 January 2004, the applicant was apprehended at his apartment and taken to the police station where he was subsequently arrested. The parties provided different accounts of the events.24. According to the applicant, he had been beaten by the police at the apprehension. He raised this complaint before the Court for the first time on 11 November 2005, having stated, inter alia, that on 9 August 2004 he had requested that the prosecutor’s office institute criminal proceedings against three police officers who had threatened him with firearms and fractured two of his ribs when trying to make him admit guilt for a crime. On 5 June 2008 the applicant submitted that on 22 January 2004, K. ‒ who was the brother of the applicant’s alleged accomplice in the said crime ‒ and his colleagues had unlawfully broken into his apartment and had severely beaten him while trying to make him confess. In his comments on the Government’s observations, the applicant stated that on 22 January 2004 three police officers, including K., had come to his place of residence, had threatened him and hit him on his head and body with their firearms, fracturing two of his ribs. Thereafter, he had been forced to go to the police station. In view of the beating he had been given, he had been unable to resist and had had to go with the officers.25. The Government submitted that no pressure or physical force had been used on the applicant whilst being apprehended and that the latter had voluntarily agreed to go with the officers to the police station.26. The documents submitted by the Government suggest that during the trial in his criminal case, the applicant repeated his complaint of ill‑treatment. Thus, according to the District Court’s ruling of 29 March 2005, the applicant submitted that on 22 January 2004, K. and three other police officers had come to his apartment and had asked him to go with them to the police station. They were armed and used physical coercion, hitting him on his head several times with their firearms. His sister had also been present in the apartment. The ruling further suggests that, when questioned as a witness, K. had stated that on 22 January 2004 whilst on duty as a security service officer, he had witnessed his brother being apprehended by the police. A police officer had approached K. and asked him to assist in the apprehension of the applicant, with whom K. was acquainted. The police officer, K. and his two subordinates then went to the applicant’s address. With the exception of one security service officer who had remained in the car, they had all gone to the applicant’s apartment. When the applicant opened the door, they had checked his documents, had apprehended him and had escorted him to the police station. K. submitted that the applicant’s sister had also been present in the apartment.27. By the aforementioned ruling of 29 March 2005, the District Court ordered the prosecutor’s office to identify, by 11 April 2005, the persons who had apprehended the applicant and to question them and the applicant’s sister in relation to the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment. The ruling also instructed the prosecutor’s office to identify other individuals who could give evidence concerning the applicant’s complaint and to question them in this respect. On 18 April 2005 the District Court noted the prosecutor’s failure to comply with the above ruling and sent the case for additional investigation.29. On 21 July 2005 the applicant’s sister was questioned and testified that on 22 January 2004 at about 10 a.m. she had opened the door to K. and two other individuals, who had identified themselves as police officers. Thereafter, she had woken the applicant, and the police officers had asked him to proceed to the police station, having informed him that two other individuals had committed a crime and he needed to present himself with a view to further inquiry. The applicant had got dressed and had gone with the police officers. The applicant’s sister further submitted she had not witnessed any ill-treatment as she had not been present in the applicant’s room. She stated, however, that she had heard raised voices during the conversation between the applicant and the police officers.30. On 23 November 2005 the applicant lodged a complaint about his ill-treatment with the prosecutor’s office. He claimed that K. and his three colleagues had come to his apartment. They had been armed and had tried to force him to assume K.’s brother’s guilt for the crime. When the applicant refused, K. and one of his colleagues, who identified himself as K.’s cousin, started beating him and fractured two of his ribs. As they were demanding that the applicant go to the police station, the applicant’s sister ‒ who had been sleeping in another room – had come in. The applicant further submitted that the police officers had left the apartment after he had stated, in his sister’s presence, that those officers had no authority to take him to the police station. An hour later they had come back, accompanied by the police officer who afterwards questioned the applicant at the police station. The officer submitted that it had been necessary to question the applicant as there was evidence about his possible involvement in a crime. They had arrived at the applicant’s apartment around lunch time. The police officer stated that he had not been armed that day and K. would only have had a pneumatic weapon, if he had one at all. After entering the apartment, the officer had identified himself and had informed the applicant that there had been testimony against him. He therefore asked the applicant to go with him to the police station and the latter agreed. The conversation had taken place in the applicant’s room but the police officer did not remember if K. had also entered the room. He further alleged that no recourse to physical force had been needed as the applicant had not resisted and had complied with his request voluntarily. He finally stated that a girl had also been present in the apartment.33. In his reply to the Government’s observations, the applicant specified that the cells had not afforded enough living space, that the sanitary conditions had been poor, and that he had been detained in those conditions for the most of the day, with no outdoor activity allowed.37. According to the Government, the conditions in those cells had been adequate and they were equipped with the requisite furnishings and facilities and a partitioned toilet. The provisions concerning the obligation to institute criminal proceedings and investigate a crime can be found in the judgment of 27 November 2008 in the case of Spinov v. Ukraine (no. 34331/03, § 33).40. Under Article 23-2, if the court discovers a violation of law and/or of citizens’ rights in the course of a pre-trial enquiry or investigation, or during an examination of a case in a lower-level court, it issues a separate ruling by which it draws the attention of the respective authorities to the established facts and directs them to take certain measures to remedy the situation. Failure to take the requisite measures constitutes an administrative offence.41. Under Article 236-1, complaints against the decision of an investigator or prosecutor to refuse to initiate criminal proceedings may be filed with the local court by a person whose interests it concerns at the place of the respective authority or official.42. The provisions concerning the application of preventive measures and their types, the time-limits for pre-trial detention, and the grounds for and procedure of detention by an enquiry body (the investigator in the instant case), can be found in the Molodorych v. Ukraine judgment, no. 2161/02, §§ 56-58, 28 October 2010.43. Article 237 obliged the judge of a trial court dealing with the case to consider in the preparatory hearing, inter alia, whether there were grounds for changing, lifting or applying a preventive measure.III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIAL44. The relevant extracts from the Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine carried out by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”) from 9 to 21 October 2005 read as follows:“... The CPT also recommends that the Ukrainian authorities review as soon as possible the norms fixed by legislation for living space per prisoner, ensuring that these are at least 4 m² in all the establishments under the authority of the Department for the Enforcement of Sentences. ...”

B. Alleged police ill-treatment of the applicant on 22 January 2004 and the ensuing investigation

On 22 January 2004, the applicant was apprehended in his apartment, taken to a police station and subsequently placed under arrest. The parties’ versions of those events differed.

The applicant alleged that the police had beaten him during his apprehension. He first raised that complaint before the Court on 11 November 2005, stating, among other things, that on 9 August 2004 he had asked the prosecutor’s office to open criminal proceedings against three police officers. According to him, they had threatened him with firearms and fractured two of his ribs in an attempt to force him to admit to a crime. The Court was not provided with a copy of that complaint. On 5 June 2008, the applicant claimed that on 22 January 2004 K. — the brother of the applicant’s alleged accomplice in the crime in question — and K.’s colleagues had unlawfully entered his apartment and severely beaten him in an effort to obtain a confession. In his comments responding to the Government’s observations, the applicant stated that three police officers, one of whom was K., had arrived at his residence on 22 January 2004, threatened him, and struck him on the head and body with their firearms, breaking two of his ribs. He had then been compelled to accompany them to the police station. Because of the beating, he had been incapable of resisting and had had no choice but to go with the officers.

The Government maintained that the applicant had neither been subjected to pressure nor had physical force used against him during his apprehension. They further asserted that he had voluntarily agreed to accompany the officers to the police station.

The materials supplied by the Government indicate that the applicant reiterated his ill-treatment allegation during the trial in his criminal case. In particular, the District Court’s ruling of 29 March 2005 records that the applicant claimed that, on 22 January 2004, K. and three other police officers had arrived at his apartment and requested that he accompany them to the police station. The officers were armed and resorted to physical coercion, striking him on the head several times with their firearms. His sister was also in the apartment at the time. The ruling additionally indicates that, when examined as a witness, K. stated that on 22 January 2004, while on duty as a security service officer, he had seen the police apprehend his brother. A police officer had then approached K.
and requested his help in apprehending the applicant, whom K. knew. The police officer then went with K. and K.’s two subordinates to the applicant’s address. All of them entered the applicant’s apartment except for one security service officer, who stayed in the car. After the applicant opened the door, they inspected his documents, apprehended him and escorted him to the police station. According to K., the applicant’s sister was also in the apartment.

27. In the above-mentioned ruling of 29 March 2005, the District Court directed the prosecutor’s office, by 11 April 2005, to establish the identities of those who had apprehended the applicant and to question them, as well as the applicant’s sister, about his allegations of ill-treatment. It further ordered the prosecutor’s office to identify and question any other persons capable of providing evidence regarding the applicant’s complaint. Finally, the prosecutor was instructed to adopt a procedural decision based on the outcome of the inquiry.

28. On 18 April 2005, having observed that the prosecutor had not complied with that ruling, the District Court remitted the case for further investigation.

29. The applicant’s sister was questioned on 21 July 2005. She stated that, at approximately 10 a.m. on 22 January 2004, she had answered the door to K. and two other people who introduced themselves as police officers. She had then awakened the applicant. The officers told him that two other individuals had committed a crime and asked him to accompany them to the police station for further inquiries. After getting dressed, the applicant left with the officers. His sister said that she had not seen any ill-treatment because she had not been in the applicant’s room, although she had heard raised voices while he and the officers were speaking.

30. On 23 November 2005, the applicant complained to the prosecutor’s office that he had been ill-treated. He alleged that K. and three of K.’s colleagues had arrived at his apartment carrying weapons and had attempted to compel him to accept responsibility for a crime committed by K.’s brother. Following his refusal, K. and one colleague, who introduced himself as K.’s cousin, began beating him and broke two of his ribs. While they were insisting that he accompany them to the police station, the applicant’s sister, who had been asleep in another room, entered. The applicant stated that, after he said in his sister’s presence that the officers lacked authority to take him to the police station, they left the apartment. They returned an hour later together with the police officer who subsequently questioned the applicant at the police station. Finally, the applicant alleged that K.
had compelled his sister to give untruthful testimony.

31. On 17 May 2007, the District Court issued a further separate order requiring the investigating authorities to examine the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment by 29 May 2007. In doing so, it observed that its order of 18 April 2005 had not been implemented.

32. On 4 June 2007, the prosecutor interviewed the police officer identified as having apprehended the applicant. The officer explained that the applicant had needed to be questioned because evidence suggested his possible involvement in a crime. K., who knew both the applicant and his home address, had happened to be near the police station at the time and offered to show the police where the applicant lived. They reached the applicant’s apartment at around lunchtime. The officer said that he had not been carrying a weapon that day and that K., if armed at all, would only have possessed a pneumatic weapon. Upon entering the apartment, the officer introduced himself and told the applicant that testimony had been given against him. He then asked the applicant to accompany him to the police station, and the applicant consented. Their discussion occurred in the applicant’s room, although the officer could not recall whether K. had also gone into that room. He additionally maintained that using physical force had been unnecessary because the applicant had offered no resistance and had voluntarily complied with the request. Lastly, he stated that a girl had also been inside the apartment.

33. Later that same day, relying on the police officer’s statements described above, the prosecutor declined to open criminal proceedings against him, concluding that no physical force had been used on the applicant and that the applicant had voluntarily agreed to accompany the officer to the police station. The applicant did not challenge that decision, which the District Court cited in its judgment of 8 June 2007.

34. The material submitted to the Court shows that the applicant was admitted to Odesa SIZO on 26 January 2004. The authorities stated that, upon admission, he was medically examined—including by X-ray—was considered healthy, and made no complaint of any injury. His medical records included an X-ray taken at the city hospital on 25 January 2004. According to the applicant, Odesa SIZO medical personnel relied on that X-ray to conclude that he “lacked part of his third left rib” (see paragraph 50 below).

35. The case-file material indicates that, in 2006, the applicant’s lawyer contacted the SIZO authorities and the city hospital to seek information about any injuries the applicant might have sustained as a result of the alleged ill-treatment. The SIZO administration supplied the lawyer with documentation concerning the applicant’s health when he entered the SIZO and the medical care he received while in detention.
The radiograph dated 25 January 2004 was listed among the documents in the applicant’s file when he was admitted to the SIZO. The city hospital stated in its response that the applicant had received no in-patient treatment in January 2004.

C. The applicant’s conditions of detention in the SIZO

36. The applicant was detained in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 until 23 November 2007. Initially, without identifying the cells in which he had been placed or the length of time spent in each, he alleged that the detention conditions had been intolerable. In response to the Government’s observations, he clarified that the cells had provided insufficient personal space and had been in poor sanitary condition. He further stated that he had spent most of each day in those conditions and had not been permitted any outdoor activity.

37. The Government provided the following information concerning the cells in which the applicant had been held:

- cell no. 209: 7.07 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 219: 6.83 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 223: 6.99 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 255: 7.58 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 257: 7.39 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 255: 7.85 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 285: 7.44 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 119: 33.42 sq. m, designed for 12 detainees;
- cell no. 129: 77.45 sq. m, designed for 42 detainees;
- cell no. 131: 35.22 sq. m, designed for 14 detainees;
- cell no. 326: 6.73 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees;
- cell no. 357: 7.31 sq. m, designed for 4 detainees.

38. In the Government’s submission, the conditions in all of those cells were satisfactory. The cells contained the necessary furniture and amenities, including a toilet separated by a partition. Their windows and ventilation systems provided natural light and fresh-air circulation, while running water and connection to the mains drainage system were also available.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

The 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, in the version applicable at the relevant time

39. The legal provisions governing the duty to open criminal proceedings and investigate an offence are set out in Spinov v. Ukraine, no. 34331/03, § 33, judgment of 27 November 2008.

40. Through that ruling, the court brings the established circumstances to the attention of the competent authorities and instructs them to adopt specific measures to correct the situation. A failure to implement the required measures amounts to an administrative offence.

41.

42. III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIAL
