UKRAINE (Application no. 30760/06)      JUDGMENT STRASBOURG 23 June 2016     FINAL 30/01/2017  This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of Kulyk v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Angelika Nußberger, President, Erik Møse, Faris Vehabović, Yonko Grozev, Síofra O’Leary, Mārtiņš Mits, judges, Sergiy Goncharenko, ad hoc judge,and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 31 May 2016,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 30760/06) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”), by Mr Anatoliy Vasilyevich Kulyk (“the applicant”), on 17 July 2006.2. The applicant was represented by Mr D. Groysman, a lawyer who was practising in Vinnytsya, Ukraine. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented most recently by their Acting Agent, Ms O. Davydchuk of the Ministry of Justice.3. The applicant alleged that he had been ill-treated by police officers, that there had been no effective investigation following his complaints, and that there had been an interference with his right of individual application to the Court.4. On 17 January 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. Mrs Ganna Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, was unable to sit in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). Accordingly, the President of the Fifth Section decided to appoint Mr Sergiy Goncharenko to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 4 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1).THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE5. The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in the town of Shargorod, Ukraine.A. Events of 30-31 December 20021. The applicant’s version6. According to the applicant, at around 1.30 p.m. on 30 December 2002, while working in the backyard of his home, he saw three young men on the premises of the nearby Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory (“the factory”). Since there had previously been thefts at the factory premises, during which scrap metal had been thrown over the fence into the applicant’s yard, the latter decided to enter the factory yard to chase after the young men. However, having climbed over the fence and realising the young men were no longer there, the applicant went to look inside the building, entering “through an opening in the wall”. The factory premises were empty but the applicant claimed to have heard adult voices. He did not want to meet anybody and so he crawled out through the same opening and quickly returned home.7. Five to ten minutes later a police officer, L., arrived at the applicant’s house. According to the applicant, he had a gun in his hand, swore at the applicant, grabbed him by his collar and hit him on the head with the gun handle. The applicant fell to the ground and the police officer started kicking him. The applicant’s mother-in-law appeared and asked the police officer not to beat the applicant, whereupon he grabbed the applicant by the sleeve and took him to the police station. The applicant was accused of stealing aluminium sheets from the factory.8. The applicant also submitted that, at the police station, L., in the presence of two other police officers, had kicked him in the kidneys, at which point the applicant fell to the ground. After he got up, one of the police officers gave him some water. L. then took the applicant into one of the offices, where he and another police officer, P., beat the applicant about the head and kicked him on various parts of his body for 15-20 minutes. Another police officer, G., arrived and L. and P. continued to beat the applicant, wanting him to confess to theft. After a while the applicant was placed in a cell.9. That night the applicant complained of a headache and general sickness. He was told by the duty police officer that a doctor would come. After some time a man wearing a white coat arrived, emptied two ampules labelled “Analgin” and “Dimedrol” (diphenylhydamine) into a plastic water bottle and gave it to the applicant.10. On the morning of 31 December 2002 the applicant was taken to court, where he was fined in administrative proceedings for disobeying a police officer’s order to stop. According to the applicant, he had wanted to show the judge his injuries but the latter refused, advising the applicant to go to a hospital and file a complaint.11. The applicant was brought back to the police station, where he signed a paper stating that nobody had ill-treated him and that his personal belongings had been returned to him. The material in the case-file includes a note, allegedly signed by the applicant and dated 31 December 2002, stating that he had no complaints about the police officers and that no physical force had been used against him.12. On the same day a decision not to institute criminal proceedings against the applicant for stealing aluminium was adopted. It was noted that the applicant had not had any intention of stealing the aluminium sheets and that he had entered the factory premises out of curiosity.13. The applicant came home and told his family what had happened. The applicant’s sister-in-law, who is a nurse, gave him an injection but the applicant did not feel any better. He was suffering from headache, nausea and fever which he claimed continued for eight months.2. The Government’s version14. The Government did not provide a detailed description of the events of 30-31 December 2002 but it appears from their observations that they agreed with the findings of the national investigation authorities (see paragraphs 48-50 below).B. Applicant’s stay in hospital15. On 2 January 2003 the applicant was examined at a hospital and was hospitalised the next day. The applicant stayed in hospital until 11 February 2003. According to the applicant’s medical records, upon arrival at the hospital, his condition was of “medium seriousness”. He had bruises mostly on the left side of his body and some scratches on his back. On his left thigh there was a large bruise measuring 12 by 6 centimetres. The applicant was suffering from headache and nausea. He told the doctors that he had been beaten by police officer L.16. In a medical certificate dated 11 February 2003, issued by the hospital, the applicant was diagnosed with multitrauma, closed brain injury, brain contusion of medium severity causing numerous neurological problems, two broken ribs, post-traumatic pneumonia and injuries to his kidneys, face and body.C. Investigation into the events of 30 December 200217. On 10 February 2003 the applicant requested the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor that criminal proceedings be instituted against the police officers. In support of his complaint the applicant outlined his version of the events which took place on 30-31 December 2002 (see paragraphs 6‑13 above).18. On 18 February and 3 March 2003 several factory employees (F., S., Lo. – the wife of police officer L. –, V. and A.) testified before the investigation authorities that a noise had been heard in one of the factory buildings. V. had asked a police officer, L., to check the origin of this noise. All of the above persons had approached the building and had seen footprints in the snow leading to a conveyor belt opening in the wall. Two of them had stayed outside while the others, accompanied by L., had entered the building and had seen aluminium sheets from the ceiling piled on the floor and a man trying to escape through the conveyor belt opening. V., who had stayed outside, had tried to catch the man, but the latter had broken free. When jumping from the conveyor belt, the man had slipped and fallen onto the asphalt and had then run away. The police officer had chased after the man. The latter had climbed over the 2.5 metre high fence but had lost his balance and fallen onto the other side. The witnesses had heard a thud and a shriek.19. L. gave similar testimony. He added that the applicant had also fallen when jumping over the fence of his house. L. had found the applicant in a coal bunker in the backyard of the applicant’s house and said that he had taken him to a police station.20. On 3 March 2003 the applicant’s mother-in-law, M., testified that L. had arrived at her house and had said that he was looking for a criminal. Later she had heard a noise behind the barn and had seen L. aiming a blow with the handle of his gun at the applicant, who was lying on the ground. M. had begged L. not to beat the applicant. After that L. had taken the applicant to a police station.21. On the same day the Vinnytsya Regional Police Department (Управління МВС України у Вінницькій області) approved the results of an internal investigation in response to the applicant’s complaint. The investigation found that on 30 December 2002 around 2 p.m. the factory employees had asked L. to check the origin of a suspicious noise that had been coming out of one of the factory’s abandoned halls. L., accompanied by five factory employees, checked the hall and found aluminium sheets, which had been torn from the ceiling and piled up on the floor. He also saw the applicant, who tried to escape. While running away, the applicant fell twice – once when climbing through a conveyor belt opening in the wall and a second time when climbing over the fence. He fell for a third time when jumping over the fence of his house. In the yard of his house the applicant hid in a coal bunker, where he was found and taken to a police station. The police officers testified that they had not ill-treated the applicant. The applicant’s mother-in-law testified that a police officer L. had aimed a blow at the applicant as he was lying on the ground but she had not seen the applicant being beaten. Although summoned by a prosecutor, the applicant did not appear for questioning and neighbours ‒ who did not want their names to be cited ‒ described him as an alcoholic inclined to involvement in scandalous conduct, theft and fraud. The internal police investigation concluded that since the submissions of the applicant, the police officers and the witnesses were contradictory, the case-file of material should be sent to a prosecutor’s office.22. On 7 March 2003 the deputy prosecutor of the Shargorodskiy District (заступник прокурора Шаргородського району) refused to institute criminal proceedings following the applicant’s complaint. The deputy prosecutor noted that the applicant had stated that he had not intended to steal aluminium but had entered the factory premises out of curiosity and had run away out of fear of being accused of theft, that L. and P. had denied using physical force on the applicant and that the factory employees said that they had not seen L. beat the applicant. It was also noted that the applicant had not appeared for the forensic medical examination. The deputy prosecutor concluded that the applicant had sustained his injuries when trying to run away from L.23. On 10 April 2003 this decision was quashed by a higher prosecutor since it had not been established how the applicant’s injuries had been inflicted.24. According to a forensic medical conclusion of 12 May 2003, the applicant had sustained the following injuries: closed concussion, two broken ribs on the left and one on the right, post-traumatic pneumonia and a kidney injury. He had numerous bruises: on the chest (20x15 cm), left shoulder (3x3 cm and 4x3 cm), left hip (12x6 cm), under the right knee (2x2 cm), left shoulder blade (5x4 cm) and scratches on the back. Those injuries were of medium severity and had been inflicted by a blunt, hard object possibly on 30 December 2002.25. Between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004 the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Шаргородського району) twice refused to institute criminal proceedings in response to the complaint from the applicant. Those decisions were quashed by higher prosecutors for reasons similar to those mentioned in the decision of 10 April 2003 and the case was referred for additional investigation.26. Between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004 the following investigative steps were taken:        on 30 August 2004 the applicant’s mother-in-law testified that she had seen L. kicking the applicant whilst he was lying on the ground;        on 30 August-1 September 2004 the applicant, his wife and the factory employees were questioned;        on 30 August 2004 a forensic expert concluded that the applicant had sustained bodily injuries of medium seriousness and that those injuries could have been inflicted by blunt objects or by several falls from different heights;        on 6-8 September 2004 police officers P. and L. were questioned;        on 27 September 2004 the factory premises were examined;        according to a forensic medical report dated 6 October 2004, the applicant could have sustained his injuries between 30 December 2002 and 2 January 2003 by being beaten or by falling from a height.27. On 27 October 2004 the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Вінницької області) instituted criminal proceedings on suspicion of abuse of power.28. On 30 November 2004 the applicant was questioned and he reiterated his version of events (see paragraphs 6-10 above), submitting, in particular, that in the police station ‒ in the presence of two police officers ‒ L. had struck him on the chest; P. had hit him several times on the head; P. and L. had kicked him on various parts of his body and P. had struck him on the chest and on the abdomen and had then beaten him in the presence of a police officer.29. On 10 January 2005 the forensic medical commission confirmed the previous expert conclusions and added that the applicant had been able to move after the injuries had been inflicted.30. Between February and June 2005 the applicant, his family members, factory employees and police officers were again questioned and a reconstruction of events was staged in the police station. The applicant’s mother-in-law testified that she had seen L. kicking the applicant as he lay on the ground. She also stated that L. had hit the applicant on the head with his gun handle. The factory employees F. and A. testified that they had seen the applicant running away and falling over on his way to the fence and again when climbing over the fence. Face-to-face confrontations between the applicant and police officers P., L. and G., and between the applicant and the factory employees were conducted.31. On 19 April 2005 the police officers P. and L. were charged with abuse of power accompanied by violence.32. By a letter of 5 May 2005 the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office informed the applicant that investigating officers K. and T. had been disciplined for delaying the investigation.33. On 18 May 2005 P. and L. were questioned as witnesses.34. On 26 May 2005 the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office asked the Head of the Internal Security Department of the Vinnytsya Region, which is part of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Ukraine (начальник УВБ у Вінницькій області ДВБ ГУБОЗ МВС України), to identify and question witnesses who had seen or talked to the applicant at the time of the events in question. On an unspecified date the police stated that it had not been possible to find any witnesses. Similar requests were also submitted on 16 May 2006 and 11 January 2007. The answers to those requests were also negative.35. On 2 June 2005 the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit (Шаргородське територіальне медичне об’єднання), in reply to a request from Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, submitted that on 30 and 31 December 2002 the applicant had not received any medical assistance from an ambulance team.36. On the same day, judge Tr. was questioned. He submitted that when he had seen the applicant in court on 31 December 2002 the applicant had had no injuries to his head or hands, nor had he complained about any health problems. The applicant also did not complain that he had been beaten.37. On 10 June 2005 the investigating officer from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office terminated the proceedings against the police officers for absence of corpus delicti. On 16 August 2005 this decision was upheld by the Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya. On 22 September 2005 the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal quashed these decisions and remitted the case for a fresh investigation. The court found that the investigating officer had failed to check whether an ambulance had been called for the applicant when he had been at the police station, and had failed to question the witnesses to the applicant’s arrest. It was also unclear whether the applicant’s injuries could have occurred as a result of his falls.38. On 28 October 2005 the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit again submitted that on 30 and 31 December 2002 the applicant had not received any medical assistance from an ambulance team while at the police station.39. In November 2005 L., A. and S. were again questioned.40. On 22 December 2005 the forensic experts concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have occurred as a result of several falls.41. On 28 December 2005 the investigating officer of the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office again terminated the proceedings for absence of corpus delicti.42. On 20 February 2006 the Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya quashed that decision because witnesses to the applicant’s arrest had not been sought and the hospital doctors had not been questioned. The applicant’s family members and some factory employees were to be additionally questioned and the evidential material from the administrative case-file against the applicant was to be included in the file. The case was remitted for further investigation.43. On 13 April 2006 the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal rejected the prosecutor’s appeal against the decision of 20 February 2006.44. Between 13 April 2006 and 19 October 2008 the proceedings were terminated three times for absence of corpus delicti and re-opened, in particular, in the light of the failure to obtain the applicant’s medical file from the hospital or to conduct a reconstruction of events with the participation of L., witnesses and a forensic medical expert in order to establish where the applicant had fallen and the circumstances in which the applicant had suffered his injuries.45. By letters of 7 July 2006 and 7 February 2007 the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office informed the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, inter alia, that the applicant’s mother-in-law, wife and sister-in-law had refused to testify, that a factory guard who had been on duty on 30 December 2002 had moved to Russia, and that “it had been impossible to question doctors at Shargorod Hospital since there was no information about any medical assistance that might have been provided to the applicant”.46. On 14 October 2008 a reconstruction of events at the factory had been conducted with the participation of L. and a forensic medical expert. The expert had also been asked additional questions on the same day.47. On 19 October 2008 an investigating officer of the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office terminated the criminal proceedings against the police officers for absence of evidence of a crime.48. It was found that on 30 December 2002 at around 1 p.m. employees of the Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory had asked a police officer L., who had been present at that time on the factory premises, to check the origin of noises coming from inside one of the locked factory buildings. L. together with V., F., A., Lo. and S. went to the premises in question. Inside the building, L. and the factory employees found aluminium sheets torn from the ceiling and piled up against a wall. They also saw the applicant, who ran away after tripping up several times. The applicant was later apprehended at his home and taken to a police station.49. After being questioned on 30 August and 30 November 2004 (see paragraphs 26 and 28 above), the applicant admitted that whilst running away he had heard people shouting behind him but had not paid any attention to them. The applicant also submitted that he had climbed over the fence having stepped on a manure pile on another side. However, the applicant’s neighbours testified that the manure pile was located 1.5 metres away from the wall. The prosecutor also referred to the testimonies given by the police officer L., factory workers, other police officers and a judge Tr. during the investigation. Numerous forensic medical experts concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have been caused by having fallen onto hard objects several times. The forensic medical expert who participated in the reconstruction of events testified that the applicant’s injuries had most probably been caused as a result of his having fallen down several times, bearing in mind the frozen ground, the height of the conveyor belt and the fence, and the body’s acceleration when running.50. In view of the above the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office concluded that there was no evidence of any crime and, since the events in question had taken place six years earlier, that there was no possibility of finding such evidence.D. Search of the office of the applicant’s representative51. On 22 September 2010 the Leninskyy District Court authorised a search of premises at K. Street 54/1. This search was the result of criminal proceedings instituted the previous day following the placement of pornographic material on an Internet page which allegedly belonged to the applicant’s representative.52. On 15 October 2010 Ya., who was using the premises at K. Street 54/3, allowed the police to inspect those premises after receiving authorisation from the owner. She confirmed that the items of property in the room at that address belonged to the applicant’s representative.53. On the same day the police officers inspected the premises at K. Street 54/3 and seized, inter alia, three computers. According to the applicant’s representative, the office of a human rights organisation was located at that address, which was where he worked.54. The applicant’s representative complained about the seizure to a prosecutor indicating that one of the seized computers contained part of confidential correspondence with the Court in the present case.55. On 5 November 2010, in response to complaints by the applicant’s representative about alleged breaches of the law in the course of the search and seizure, the Vinnytsya City Prosecutor’s Office issued a decision refusing to institute criminal proceedings. According to the applicant’s representative, he appealed against that decision but to no avail.56. According to reports in the media, in August 2013 the applicant’s representative was acquitted.II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND INTERNATIONAL MATERIALSA. Joint Decree of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine No. 307/105 of 10 May 199357. The Decree provides that the heads of medical facilities must immediately inform the internal affairs authorities about any request for medical assistance in respect of injuries (firearms, knife or sustained by other means) that have allegedly resulted from a crime.B. Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine carried out by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment from 9 to 21 October 201358. Angelika Nußberger, President,

Faris Vehabović,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

PROCEDURE

1. The case arose from an application (no. 30760/06) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Anatoliy Vasilyevich Kulyk (“the applicant”) on 17 July 2006.

2. The applicant was represented by Mr D. Groysman, a lawyer practising in Vinnytsya, Ukraine. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were most recently represented by their Acting Agent, Ms O. Davydchuk of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant alleged that he had been subjected to ill-treatment by police officers, that no effective investigation had been conducted into his complaints, and that his right of individual application to the Court had been interfered with.

4. On 17 January 2011, the application was communicated to the Government. Mrs Ganna Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, was unable to take part in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). The President of the Fifth Section therefore decided to appoint Mr Sergiy Goncharenko to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 4 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1963 and resides in the town of Shargorod, Ukraine.

A. Events of 30-31 December 2002

1. The applicant’s account

6. According to the applicant, at approximately 1.30 p.m. on 30 December 2002, while working in the backyard of his home, he noticed three young men on the premises of the nearby Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory (“the factory”). As thefts had previously occurred on the factory premises, during which scrap metal had been thrown over the fence into the applicant’s yard, he decided to enter the factory yard and pursue the young men. However, after climbing over the fence and realising that they were no longer there, the applicant went to look inside the building, entering “through an opening in the wall”. The factory premises were empty, but the applicant claimed that he heard adult voices. Wishing to avoid meeting anyone, he crawled back out through the same opening and quickly returned home.

7. Five to ten minutes later, a police officer, L., arrived at the applicant’s home.
According to the applicant, the police officer had a gun in his hand, swore at him, grabbed him by the collar and struck him on the head with the gun handle. The applicant fell to the ground, and the officer began kicking him. The applicant’s mother-in-law appeared and asked the officer not to beat him, whereupon the officer grabbed the applicant by the sleeve and took him to the police station. The applicant was accused of stealing aluminium sheets from the factory.

8. The applicant further submitted that, at the police station, L., in the presence of two other police officers, kicked him in the kidneys, causing him to fall to the ground. After he got up, one of the officers gave him some water. L. then took the applicant into one of the offices, where he and another police officer, P., beat him about the head and kicked him on various parts of his body for 15-20 minutes. Another police officer, G., arrived, and L. and P. continued beating the applicant in an attempt to make him confess to theft. After a while, the applicant was placed in a cell.

9. That night, the applicant complained of a headache and feeling generally unwell. The duty police officer told him that a doctor would come. Some time later, a man wearing a white coat arrived, emptied two ampoules labelled “Analgin” and “Dimedrol” (diphenylhydamine) into a plastic water bottle, and gave it to the applicant.

10. On the morning of 31 December 2002, the applicant was taken to court, where he was fined in administrative proceedings for failing to obey a police officer’s order to stop. According to the applicant, he wanted to show the judge his injuries, but the judge refused and advised him to go to a hospital and lodge a complaint.

11. The applicant was taken back to the police station, where he signed a document stating that no one had ill-treated him and that his personal belongings had been returned. The case file contains a note, allegedly signed by the applicant and dated 31 December 2002, stating that he had no complaints against the police officers and that no physical force had been used against him.

12. On the same day, a decision was adopted not to institute criminal proceedings against the applicant for stealing aluminium. It was noted that he had not intended to steal the aluminium sheets and had entered the factory premises out of curiosity.

13. The applicant returned home and told his family what had happened. His sister-in-law, who is a nurse, gave him an injection, but he did not feel any better. He suffered from headaches, nausea and fever, which he claimed persisted for eight months.

2. The Government’s version

14. The Government did not provide a detailed account of the events of 30-31 December 2002, but it appears from their observations that they agreed with the findings of the national investigating authorities (see paragraphs 48-50 below).

B. The applicant’s stay in hospital

15.
On 2 January 2003 the applicant was examined at a hospital and admitted the following day. He remained in hospital until 11 February 2003. According to his medical records, his condition upon arrival was of “medium seriousness”. He had bruises mainly on the left side of his body and several scratches on his back. There was a large bruise on his left thigh measuring 12 by 6 centimetres. The applicant was suffering from headaches and nausea. He told the doctors that he had been beaten by police officer L. In a medical certificate dated 11 February 2003 and issued by the hospital, the applicant was diagnosed with multiple trauma, a closed brain injury, a brain contusion of medium severity causing numerous neurological problems, two broken ribs, post-traumatic pneumonia, and injuries to his kidneys, face and body.

C. Investigation into the events of 30 December 2002

17. On 10 February 2003 the applicant requested that the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor institute criminal proceedings against the police officers. In support of his complaint, the applicant set out his account of the events of 30-31 December 2002 (see paragraphs 6-13 above).

18. On 18 February and 3 March 2003 several factory employees (F., S., Lo. – the wife of police officer L. –, V. and A.) testified before the investigating authorities that a noise had been heard in one of the factory buildings. V. had asked police officer L. to investigate the source of the noise. All of those persons had approached the building and seen footprints in the snow leading to a conveyor-belt opening in the wall. Two of them had remained outside, while the others, accompanied by L., had entered the building and seen aluminium sheets from the ceiling piled on the floor and a man attempting to escape through the conveyor-belt opening. V., who had remained outside, had tried to catch the man, but the latter had broken free. While jumping from the conveyor belt, the man had slipped and fallen onto the asphalt before running away. The police officer had chased him. The man had climbed over the 2.5-metre-high fence but had lost his balance and fallen on the other side. The witnesses had heard a thud and a shriek.

19. L. gave a similar account. He added that the applicant had also fallen while jumping over the fence of his house. L. had found the applicant in a coal bunker in the backyard of the applicant’s house and stated that he had taken him to a police station.

20. On 3 March 2003 the applicant’s mother-in-law, M., testified that L. had arrived at her house and said that he was looking for a criminal. Later, she had heard a noise behind the barn and seen L. preparing to strike the applicant, who was lying on the ground, with the handle of his gun. M. had begged L. not to beat the applicant. L. had then taken the applicant to a police station.

21.
On the same day, the Vinnytsya Regional Police Department (Управління МВС України у Вінницькій області) approved the findings of an internal investigation conducted in response to the applicant’s complaint. The investigation established that at around 2 p.m. on 30 December 2002, factory employees had asked L. to investigate the source of a suspicious noise coming from one of the factory’s abandoned halls. Accompanied by five factory employees, L. inspected the hall and found aluminium sheets that had been torn from the ceiling and piled on the floor. He also saw the applicant, who attempted to escape. While fleeing, the applicant fell twice – first while climbing through a conveyor-belt opening in the wall and again while climbing over the fence. He fell a third time when jumping over the fence of his house. In the yard, the applicant hid in a coal bunker, where he was found and taken to a police station. The police officers testified that they had not ill-treated him. The applicant’s mother-in-law testified that police officer L. had aimed a blow at the applicant while he was lying on the ground, but that she had not seen him being beaten. Although summoned by a prosecutor, the applicant failed to appear for questioning, and neighbours – who did not want their names disclosed – described him as an alcoholic prone to scandalous conduct, theft and fraud. The internal police investigation concluded that, since the statements of the applicant, the police officers and the witnesses were contradictory, the case-file materials should be forwarded to a prosecutor’s office.

22. On 7 March 2003, the deputy prosecutor of the Shargorodskiy District (заступник прокурора Шаргородського району) refused to institute criminal proceedings in response to the applicant’s complaint. The deputy prosecutor noted that the applicant had stated that he had not intended to steal aluminium, but had entered the factory premises out of curiosity and fled because he feared being accused of theft; that L. and P. had denied using physical force against the applicant; and that the factory employees had said they had not seen L. beat him. It was also noted that the applicant had failed to attend the forensic medical examination. The deputy prosecutor concluded that the applicant had sustained his injuries while trying to escape from L.

23. On 10 April 2003, that decision was quashed by a higher prosecutor because it had not been established how the applicant’s injuries had been caused.

24. According to a forensic medical conclusion dated 12 May 2003, the applicant had sustained the following injuries: a closed concussion, two broken ribs on the left and one on the right, post-traumatic pneumonia, and a kidney injury. He also had numerous bruises: on the chest (20 x 15 cm), left shoulder (3 x 3 cm and 4 x 3 cm), left hip (12 x 6 cm), under the right knee (2 x 2 cm), and left shoulder blade (5 x 4 cm), as well as scratches on his back.
Those injuries were of moderate severity and had possibly been inflicted by a hard, blunt object on 30 December 2002.

25. Between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004, the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Шаргородського району) twice refused to institute criminal proceedings in response to the applicant’s complaint. Those decisions were quashed by higher prosecutors for reasons similar to those set out in the decision of 10 April 2003, and the case was referred for further investigation.

26. Between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004, the following investigative measures were taken:
– on 30 August 2004, the applicant’s mother-in-law testified that she had seen L. kicking the applicant while he was lying on the ground;
– between 30 August and 1 September 2004, the applicant, his wife and the factory employees were questioned;
– on 30 August 2004, a forensic expert concluded that the applicant had sustained bodily injuries of moderate severity and that those injuries could have been caused by blunt objects or by several falls from different heights;
– between 6 and 8 September 2004, police officers P. and L. were questioned;
– on 27 September 2004, the factory premises were examined;
– according to a forensic medical report dated 6 October 2004, the applicant could have sustained his injuries between 30 December 2002 and 2 January 2003 as a result of being beaten or falling from a height.

27. On 27 October 2004, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Вінницької області) instituted criminal proceedings on suspicion of abuse of power.

28. On 30 November 2004, the applicant was questioned and reiterated his account of events (see paragraphs 6-10 above), stating, in particular, that at the police station – in the presence of two police officers – L. had struck him in the chest; P. had hit him several times on the head; P. and L. had kicked him on various parts of his body; and P. had struck him in the chest and abdomen before beating him in the presence of a police officer.

29. On 10 January 2005, the forensic medical commission confirmed the previous expert findings and added that the applicant had been able to move after the injuries had been inflicted.

30. Between February and June 2005, the applicant, his family members, factory employees and police officers were questioned again, and a reconstruction of events was carried out at the police station. The applicant’s mother-in-law testified that she had seen L. kicking the applicant while he lay on the ground. She further stated that L. had hit the applicant on the head with the handle of his gun. The factory employees F. and A. testified that they had seen the applicant running away and falling on his way to the fence, and again while climbing over it. Face-to-face confrontations were conducted between the applicant and police officers P., L. and G., and between the applicant and the factory employees.

31. On 19 April 2005, police officers P. and L.
were charged with abuse of power involving violence.

32. By letter of 5 May 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office informed the applicant that investigating officers K. and T. had been disciplined for delays in the investigation.

33. On 18 May 2005, P. and L. were questioned as witnesses.

34. On 26 May 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office asked the Head of the Internal Security Department of the Vinnytsya Region, which forms part of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine (начальник УВБ у Вінницькій області ДВБ ГУБОЗ МВС України), to identify and question witnesses who had seen or spoken to the applicant at the time of the events in question. On an unspecified date, the police stated that no witnesses could be found. Similar requests were made on 16 May 2006 and 11 January 2007. The responses to those requests were likewise negative.

35. On 2 June 2005, the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit (Шаргородське територіальне медичне об’єднання), replying to a request from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, stated that the applicant had not received any medical assistance from an ambulance team on 30 or 31 December 2002.

36. On the same day, Judge Tr. was questioned. He stated that when he had seen the applicant in court on 31 December 2002, the applicant had shown no injuries to his head or hands and had not complained of any health problems. Nor had the applicant alleged that he had been beaten.

37. On 10 June 2005, an investigating officer from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the proceedings against the police officers for lack of corpus delicti. On 16 August 2005, that decision was upheld by the Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya. On 22 September 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal quashed both decisions and remitted the case for a fresh investigation. The court found that the investigating officer had failed to establish whether an ambulance had been called for the applicant while he was at the police station and had not questioned witnesses to his arrest. It also remained unclear whether the applicant’s injuries could have resulted from his falls.

38. On 28 October 2005, the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit again stated that the applicant had not received any medical assistance from an ambulance team while at the police station on 30 or 31 December 2002.

39. In November 2005, L., A. and S. were questioned again.

40. On 22 December 2005, the forensic experts concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have resulted from several falls.

41. On 28 December 2005, the investigating officer from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office again discontinued the proceedings for lack of corpus delicti.

42. On 20 February 2006, the Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya quashed that decision because witnesses to the applicant’s arrest had not been sought and the hospital doctors had not been questioned.
The applicant’s family members and certain factory employees were to be questioned further, and the evidential material from the administrative case file against the applicant was to be added to the file. The case was remitted for further investigation.

43. On 13 April 2006 the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal against the decision of 20 February 2006.

44. Between 13 April 2006 and 19 October 2008 the proceedings were terminated three times for lack of corpus delicti and subsequently reopened, in particular because of the failure to obtain the applicant’s medical file from the hospital or to reconstruct the events with the participation of L., witnesses and a forensic medical expert in order to determine where the applicant had fallen and the circumstances in which he had sustained his injuries.

45. By letters dated 7 July 2006 and 7 February 2007, the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office informed the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, inter alia, that the applicant’s mother-in-law, wife and sister-in-law had refused to testify, that a factory guard who had been on duty on 30 December 2002 had moved to Russia, and that “it had been impossible to question doctors at Shargorod Hospital since there was no information about any medical assistance that might have been provided to the applicant”.

46. On 14 October 2008 a reconstruction of the events at the factory was conducted with the participation of L. and a forensic medical expert. The expert was also asked additional questions that same day.

47. On 19 October 2008 an investigating officer of the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of evidence of a crime.

48. It was established that on 30 December 2002, at approximately 1 p.m., employees of the Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory had asked police officer L., who was present on the factory premises at the time, to investigate noises coming from inside one of the locked factory buildings. L., together with V., F., A., Lo. and S., went to the premises in question. Inside the building, L. and the factory employees found aluminium sheets that had been torn from the ceiling and piled against a wall. They also saw the applicant, who fled after tripping several times. The applicant was later apprehended at his home and taken to a police station.

49. When questioned on 30 August and 30 November 2004 (see paragraphs 26 and 28 above), the applicant admitted that, while running away, he had heard people shouting behind him but had paid no attention to them. The applicant further submitted that he had climbed over the fence after stepping on a manure pile on the other side. However, the applicant’s neighbours testified that the manure pile was located 1.5 metres from the wall. The prosecutor also referred to the testimony given by police officer L., factory workers, other police officers and Judge Tr.
during the investigation. Several forensic medical experts concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have been caused by falling onto hard objects several times. The forensic medical expert who took part in the reconstruction of events testified that the applicant’s injuries had most likely resulted from his falling down several times, having regard to the frozen ground, the height of the conveyor belt and the fence, and the body’s acceleration while running.

50. In light of the above, the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office concluded that there was no evidence that any crime had been committed and, since the events in question had occurred six years earlier, that there was no possibility of obtaining such evidence.

D. Search of the office of the applicant’s representative

51. On 22 September 2010 the Leninskyy District Court authorised a search of the premises at K. Street 54/1. The search arose from criminal proceedings instituted the previous day following the posting of pornographic material on an Internet page which allegedly belonged to the applicant’s representative.

52. On 15 October 2010 Ya., who was using the premises at K. Street 54/3, permitted the police to inspect them after obtaining authorisation from the owner. She confirmed that the property in the room at that address belonged to the applicant’s representative.

53. On the same day, police officers inspected the premises at K. Street 54/3 and seized, among other things, three computers. According to the applicant’s representative, the office of a human rights organisation where he worked was located at that address.

54. The applicant’s representative complained to a prosecutor about the seizure, stating that one of the seized computers contained part of his confidential correspondence with the Court in the present case.

55. On 5 November 2010, in response to complaints by the applicant’s representative concerning alleged violations of the law during the search and seizure, the Vinnytsya City Prosecutor’s Office issued a decision declining to institute criminal proceedings. According to the applicant’s representative, he appealed against that decision, but without success.

56. According to media reports, the applicant’s representative was acquitted in August 2013.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

A. Joint Decree of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine No. 307/105 of 10 May 1993

57. The Decree stipulates that the heads of medical facilities must immediately notify the internal affairs authorities of any request for medical assistance concerning injuries (caused by firearms, knives or other means) that allegedly resulted from a crime.

B. Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine conducted by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment from 9 to 21 October 2013

58.
The relevant parts of the report provide as follows: “24. In the report on its 2009 visit, the CPT urged the Ukrainian authorities to establish an independent agency specialising in the investigation of complaints against public officials that is demonstrably separate from Internal Affairs structures and the Prosecution Service. A ‘State Bureau of Investigation’ (SBI) should be established by November 2017 at the latest. The SBI should focus on particularly serious crimes, as well as criminal offences committed by public officials. However, pending the adoption of legislation establishing it, the structure and terms of reference of this future body have remained under discussion. In this context, and given the urgency of the matter, the CPT recommended in the report on its 2012 visit that a two-step approach be adopted: as a first step, to establish without delay a national specialised team responsible for carrying out investigations throughout the country into cases involving alleged ill-treatment by public officials, and to provide it with its own support staff for the operational conduct of such investigations; as a second step, to examine the feasibility, in the medium term, of completely separating this team from the Prosecution Service so as to create a genuinely independent specialised agency for investigations of this kind.”

He fell a third time as he jumped over the fence surrounding his home. Once in his yard, he concealed himself in a coal bunker, where he was found and subsequently taken to a police station. The applicant’s mother-in-law stated that she had seen police officer L. attempt to strike the applicant while he was lying on the ground, but had not witnessed him being beaten. The applicant failed to attend questioning despite being summoned by a prosecutor. Neighbours who requested anonymity described him as an alcoholic prone to scandalous behaviour, theft and fraud. In view of the conflicting accounts given by the applicant, the police officers and the witnesses, the internal inquiry concluded that the case-file materials should be forwarded to a prosecutor’s office.

22. On 7 March 2003, the deputy prosecutor of the Shargorodskiy District (заступник прокурора Шаргородського району) declined to institute criminal proceedings in connection with the applicant’s complaint. The deputy prosecutor observed that the applicant had claimed he had entered the factory premises merely out of curiosity, without intending to steal aluminium, and had fled because he feared being accused of theft. The decision further noted that L. and P. had denied using physical force against him and that the factory employees had stated that they had not seen L. assault him. It was also recorded that the applicant had failed to attend a forensic medical examination. The deputy prosecutor concluded that the applicant’s injuries had been sustained while he was attempting to escape from L.

23. A higher-ranking prosecutor quashed that decision on 10 April 2003 because the manner in which the applicant’s injuries had been caused had not been established.

24. A forensic medical report dated 12 May 2003 recorded that the applicant had suffered a closed concussion, fractures of two ribs on the left side and one rib on the right, post-traumatic pneumonia, and a kidney injury. It also documented numerous bruises: one measuring 20 by 15 cm on the chest; two measuring 3 by 3 cm and 4 by 3 cm on the left shoulder; one measuring 12 by 6 cm on the left hip; one measuring 2 by 2 cm below the right knee; and one measuring 5 by 4 cm on the left shoulder blade. Scratches were also present on his back.
The injuries were classified as being of medium severity and may have been caused by a hard, blunt object on 30 December 2002.

25. Between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004, the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Шаргородського району) twice declined to open criminal proceedings following the applicant’s complaint. Higher-ranking prosecutors subsequently set aside both decisions on grounds similar to those stated in the decision of 10 April 2003 and ordered further investigation.

26. The following investigative measures were carried out between 15 June 2003 and 27 October 2004:

– On 30 August 2004, the applicant’s mother-in-law stated that she had witnessed L. kicking the applicant while he was lying on the ground.

– Between 30 August and 1 September 2004, investigators questioned the applicant, his wife and employees of the factory.

– On 30 August 2004, a forensic expert determined that the applicant had suffered injuries of medium severity, which could have resulted either from blows with blunt objects or from several falls from different heights.

– Police officers P. and L. were interviewed between 6 and 8 September 2004.

– The factory premises were inspected on 27 September 2004.

– A forensic medical report issued on 6 October 2004 found that the applicant’s injuries could have been sustained between 30 December 2002 and 2 January 2003, either through a beating or a fall from a height.

27. On 27 October 2004, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office (прокуратура Вінницької області) opened criminal proceedings on suspicion of abuse of power.

28. When questioned on 30 November 2004, the applicant repeated his account of the events (see paragraphs 6-10 above). In particular, he alleged that, at the police station and in the presence of two police officers, L. had struck him in the chest; P. had hit him several times on the head; P. and L. had kicked various parts of his body; and P. had struck him in the chest and abdomen before beating him in the presence of another police officer.

29. On 10 January 2005, the forensic medical commission upheld the earlier expert findings and further concluded that the applicant had remained capable of moving after sustaining the injuries.

30. From February to June 2005, the applicant, members of his family, factory workers and police officers were questioned again, and the events were reconstructed at the police station. The applicant’s mother-in-law reiterated that she had seen L. kicking the applicant while he was on the ground and added that L. had struck him on the head with the handle of his gun. Factory employees F. and A. stated that they had observed the applicant running away and falling while approaching the fence, and then falling again as he climbed over it. Investigators also arranged face-to-face confrontations between the applicant and police officers P., L. and G., as well as between the applicant and the factory employees.

31. On 19 April 2005, police officers P. and L.
were accused of abuse of authority involving violence.

32. In a letter dated 5 May 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office notified the applicant that investigating officers K. and T. had been subjected to disciplinary measures for delays in the investigation.

33. P. and L. were interviewed as witnesses on 18 May 2005.

34. On 26 May 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office requested that the Head of the Internal Security Department of the Vinnytsya Region, a division of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Ukraine (начальник УВБ у Вінницькій області ДВБ ГУБОЗ МВС України), identify and interview anyone who had seen or spoken with the applicant at the relevant time. On an unspecified date, the police reported that no such witnesses could be located. Comparable requests were made on 16 May 2006 and 11 January 2007, but those efforts likewise produced no witnesses.

35. Responding to a request by the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit (Шаргородське територіальне медичне об’єднання) stated on 2 June 2005 that no ambulance team had provided the applicant with medical assistance on 30 or 31 December 2002.

36. Judge Tr. was questioned that same day. He stated that, when the applicant had appeared before him in court on 31 December 2002, there had been no visible injuries to the applicant’s head or hands and the applicant had raised no health concerns. Nor had the applicant alleged that he had been beaten.

37. On 10 June 2005, an investigator from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the criminal proceedings against the police officers on the ground that their conduct disclosed no corpus delicti. The Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya upheld that decision on 16 August 2005. However, on 22 September 2005, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal set both decisions aside and returned the case for a new investigation. It held that the investigator had neither established whether an ambulance had been called for the applicant while he was at the police station nor interviewed those who had witnessed his arrest. The question of whether the applicant’s injuries could have resulted from falls also remained unresolved.

38. On 28 October 2005, the Shargorod Territorial Medical Unit once more confirmed that the applicant had not been attended by an ambulance team at the police station on either 30 or 31 December 2002.

39. L., A. and S. were interviewed again in November 2005.

40. On 22 December 2005, forensic experts determined that the applicant’s injuries might have been caused by several falls.

41. On 28 December 2005, the investigator from the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office once again closed the proceedings for lack of corpus delicti.

42. The Leninskyy District Court of Vinnytsya overturned that decision on 20 February 2006, finding that no effort had been made to locate witnesses to the applicant’s arrest and that the hospital doctors had not been interviewed.
The case was returned for further investigation, with instructions to question the applicant’s relatives and certain factory employees and to add to the case file the evidence from the administrative proceedings against him.

43. On 13 April 2006 the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal against the decision of 20 February 2006.

44. Between 13 April 2006 and 19 October 2008 the proceedings were discontinued three times for lack of corpus delicti and subsequently reopened. The reasons included the authorities’ failure to obtain the applicant’s hospital records and to reconstruct the events with the participation of L., witnesses and a forensic medical expert, in order to determine where the applicant had fallen and how he had sustained his injuries.

45. In letters dated 7 July 2006 and 7 February 2007, the Shargorodskyy District Prosecutor’s Office informed the Vinnytsya Regional Prosecutor’s Office, among other things, that the applicant’s mother-in-law, wife and sister-in-law had declined to give evidence; that the factory guard on duty on 30 December 2002 had relocated to Russia; and that “it had been impossible to question doctors at Shargorod Hospital since there was no information about any medical assistance that might have been provided to the applicant”.

46. A reconstruction of the events at the factory took place on 14 October 2008 in the presence of L. and a forensic medical expert. That same day, the expert was asked further questions.

47. On 19 October 2008 an investigator from the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the criminal proceedings against the police officers on the ground that there was no evidence that a crime had been committed.

48. The investigation established that at approximately 1 p.m. on 30 December 2002, employees of the Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory asked police officer L., who was then on the factory premises, to investigate noises coming from one of the factory’s locked buildings. Accompanied by V., F., A., Lo. and S., L. went to the building concerned. There, they discovered aluminium sheets that had been torn from the ceiling and stacked against a wall. They also encountered the applicant, who fled, stumbling several times as he ran. He was later arrested at his home and taken to a police station.

49. When questioned on 30 August and 30 November 2004 (see paragraphs 26 and 28 above), the applicant acknowledged that, while fleeing, he had heard people shouting behind him but had ignored them. He further stated that he had scaled the fence by stepping onto a manure pile on the other side. His neighbours, however, testified that the pile stood 1.5 metres from the wall. The prosecutor also relied on statements from police officer L., factory employees, other police officers and Judge Tr.
during the investigation. Several forensic medical experts found that the applicant’s injuries could have resulted from repeated falls onto hard objects. The forensic medical expert involved in the reconstruction of the events stated that the injuries had most likely been sustained when the applicant fell several times, taking into account the frozen ground, the height of the conveyor belt and fence, and the acceleration of the body while running.

50. On the basis of those considerations, the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office determined that there was no evidence that a crime had been committed and that, as the events concerned had occurred six years previously, it was no longer possible to obtain such evidence.

D. Search of the office used by the applicant’s representative

51. On 22 September 2010, the Leninskyy District Court authorised a search of the premises at 54/1 K. Street. The search arose from criminal proceedings opened the previous day after pornographic material had been posted on an Internet page allegedly belonging to the applicant’s representative.

52. On 15 October 2010, Ya., who was using the premises at 54/3 K. Street, permitted the police to inspect them after obtaining the owner’s authorisation. She confirmed that the property in the room at that address belonged to the applicant’s representative.

53. Later that day, police officers searched the premises at 54/3 K. Street and seized, among other items, three computers. The applicant’s representative stated that the address housed the office of a human rights organisation where he worked.

54. The applicant’s representative lodged a complaint with a prosecutor concerning the seizure, explaining that one of the confiscated computers contained part of his confidential correspondence with the Court relating to the present case.

55. On 5 November 2010, following complaints from the applicant’s representative alleging violations of the law during the search and seizure, the Vinnytsya City Prosecutor’s Office decided not to institute criminal proceedings. The applicant’s representative stated that he appealed against that decision, but without success.

56. Media reports indicated that the applicant’s representative was acquitted in August 2013.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

A. Joint Decree No. 307/105 of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine, dated 10 May 1993

57. Under the Decree, heads of medical institutions are required to notify the internal affairs authorities immediately whenever medical assistance is sought for injuries—whether caused by firearms, knives or other means—that are alleged to have resulted from a criminal offence.

B. Report to the Ukrainian Government on the visit to Ukraine conducted by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment from 9 to 21 October 2013

58.
The relevant sections of the report state:

“24. Following its 2009 visit, the CPT called on the Ukrainian authorities to create an independent body specialising in the investigation of complaints against public officials and clearly separate from both the Internal Affairs structures and the Prosecution Service. A ‘State Bureau of Investigation’ (SBI) was to be established by November 2017 at the latest, with responsibility for particularly serious crimes and criminal offences committed by public officials. However, because the necessary founding legislation had yet to be adopted, the future body’s structure and mandate remained under discussion.

Given the urgency of the issue, the CPT proposed a two-stage approach in its report on the 2012 visit. First, a national specialised team should be established without delay to investigate, across the country, allegations of ill-treatment by public officials, supported by its own staff responsible for the operational conduct of those investigations. Second, in the medium term, the authorities should assess whether that team could be fully separated from the Prosecution Service, thereby creating a genuinely independent specialised agency dedicated to investigating such cases.”

3. The applicant complained that police officers had subjected him to ill-treatment, that his allegations had not been effectively investigated, and that his right to lodge an individual application with the Court had been interfered with.

4. The application was notified to the Government on 17 January 2011. Mrs Ganna Yudkivska, the judge elected in respect of Ukraine, could not take part in the case under Rule 28 of the Rules of Court. The President of the Fifth Section therefore appointed Mr Sergiy Goncharenko to sit as an ad hoc judge, in accordance with Article 26 § 4 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1.

THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1963, the applicant resides in Shargorod, Ukraine.

A. The events of 30 and 31 December 2002

1. The applicant’s account

6. The applicant stated that, at approximately 1.30 p.m. on 30 December 2002, he was working in the backyard of his home when he noticed three young men on the grounds of the nearby Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory (“the factory”). Theft had previously occurred at the factory, with scrap metal being thrown over its fence into the applicant’s yard. He therefore decided to climb into the factory yard and pursue the young men. After scaling the fence, however, he realised that they were no longer there. He then went to inspect the inside of the building, gaining entry “through an opening in the wall”. Although the factory premises appeared empty, he claimed that he could hear adult voices. Wishing to avoid meeting anyone, he crawled back through the same opening and quickly returned to his home.

7. Between five and ten minutes later, a police officer, L., came to the applicant’s house.
The applicant stated that the police officer was holding a gun, insulted him, seized him by the collar and struck his head with the gun’s handle. When the applicant fell, the officer began kicking him. The applicant’s mother-in-law then arrived and pleaded with the officer to stop beating him. The officer subsequently took hold of the applicant’s sleeve and escorted him to the police station. The applicant was suspected of stealing aluminium sheets from the factory.

8. The applicant further alleged that, once at the police station, L. kicked him in the kidney area in front of two other officers, causing him to collapse. After he stood up, one of the officers gave him water. L. then brought him into an office, where L. and another officer, P., struck him on the head and kicked different parts of his body for 15-20 minutes. When a further officer, G., arrived, L. and P. continued assaulting the applicant in an attempt to make him confess to theft. Some time later, he was put in a cell.

9. During the night, the applicant complained that he had a headache and felt generally unwell. The officer on duty told him that a doctor would attend. After a while, a man dressed in a white coat came, poured the contents of two ampules marked “Analgin” and “Dimedrol” (diphenylhydamine) into a plastic bottle of water, and handed it to the applicant.

10. On the morning of 31 December 2002, the applicant was taken before a court and, in administrative proceedings, fined for failing to comply with a police officer’s instruction to stop. He maintained that he had tried to show the judge his injuries, but the judge declined to examine them and advised him to attend a hospital and lodge a complaint.

11. After being returned to the police station, the applicant signed a document declaring that he had not been subjected to ill-treatment and that all his personal possessions had been given back. 12. Also on that date, a decision was issued declining to open criminal proceedings against the applicant in connection with the alleged theft of aluminium. The decision recorded that he had not intended to steal the aluminium sheets and had entered the factory grounds merely out of curiosity.

13. Upon returning home, the applicant recounted the events to his family. His sister-in-law, a nurse, administered an injection, but his condition did not improve. He experienced headaches, nausea and fever, symptoms which, according to him, persisted for eight months.

2. The Government’s account

14. Although the Government gave no detailed account of what occurred on 30-31 December 2002, their observations appear to indicate that they accepted the conclusions reached by the domestic investigative authorities (see paragraphs 48-50 below).

16. A medical certificate issued by the hospital on 11 February 2003 diagnosed the applicant with multitrauma; a closed brain injury; a brain contusion of medium severity resulting in numerous neurological problems; two fractured ribs; post-traumatic pneumonia; and injuries to his kidneys, face and body.

Inside, they saw aluminium ceiling sheets stacked on the floor and a man attempting to flee through the conveyor belt opening. The man climbed over a fence 2.5 metres high, lost his balance and fell on the opposite side. The witnesses heard a thud followed by a shriek.

19. L.’s testimony was broadly the same. He further stated that the applicant had fallen while jumping over the fence at his own house. According to L., he discovered the applicant in a coal bunker in the backyard of the applicant’s home and then took him to a police station.

20. On 3 March 2003, M., the applicant’s mother-in-law, testified that L. had come to her house and said he was searching for a criminal. The forensic medical expert involved in reconstructing the events stated that the injuries were most likely sustained when the applicant fell repeatedly, taking into account the frozen ground, the height of the conveyor belt and the fence, and the acceleration of his body while running.

50. On that basis, the Tomashpilskyy District Prosecutor’s Office determined that there was no evidence that a crime had been committed and that, because the events concerned had occurred six years previously, it was no longer possible to obtain such evidence.

D. The search of the applicant’s representative’s office

51. On 22 September 2010, the Leninskyy District Court granted permission to search premises at 54/1 K. Street. The search arose from criminal proceedings opened the preceding day after pornographic material had been posted on an Internet page allegedly owned by the applicant’s representative.

52. On 15 October 2010, after obtaining the owner’s authorisation, Ya., who was occupying the premises at 54/3 K. Street, permitted the police to inspect them. She confirmed that the property located in the room at that address belonged to the applicant’s representative.

53. Later that same day, police officers searched the premises at 54/3 K. Street and confiscated, among other items, three computers. The applicant’s representative stated that a human rights organisation had its office at that address and that he worked there.

54. The applicant’s representative lodged a complaint with a prosecutor concerning the seizure, explaining that one of the confiscated computers held part of his confidential correspondence with the Court relating to the present case.

55. On 5 November 2010, following complaints by the applicant’s representative alleging violations of the law during the search and seizure, the Vinnytsya City Prosecutor’s Office decided not to institute criminal proceedings. The applicant’s representative stated that he challenged that decision, but without success.

56. Media reports indicated that the applicant’s representative was acquitted in August 2013.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW AND INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

A. Joint Decree No. 307/105 of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine, dated 10 May 1993

57. Under the Decree, the heads of medical institutions are required to notify the internal affairs authorities immediately whenever medical assistance is sought for injuries—whether caused by firearms, knives or other means—that are alleged to have arisen from a crime.

B. Report addressed to the Ukrainian Government concerning the visit to Ukraine conducted by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment between 9 and 21 October 2013

58.
24. Following its 2009 visit, the CPT called on the Ukrainian authorities to create an independent body specialising in complaints against public officials, with a clearly demonstrated separation from both the Internal Affairs structures and the Prosecution Service. A “State Bureau of Investigation” (SBI) was to be established no later than November 2017. Its mandate should cover particularly serious crimes and criminal offences committed by public officials. However, because the legislation required to establish the SBI had not yet been adopted, the future body’s structure and terms of reference remained under discussion.

Given the urgency of the issue, the CPT proposed a two-stage approach in its report on the 2012 visit. First, a specialised national team should be established without delay to investigate, throughout the country, allegations of ill-treatment by public officials, supported by its own personnel responsible for the operational conduct of those investigations. Second, consideration should be given, over the medium term, to whether that team could be fully separated from the Prosecution Service and transformed into a genuinely independent specialised agency responsible for investigating such cases.
