SECOND SECTION






CASE OF MIHHAILOV v. ESTONIA

(Application no. 64418/10)








JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

30 August 2016

FINAL

30/11/2016

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Mihhailov v. Estonia,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

 Işıl Karakaş, President,
 Julia Laffranque,
 Paul Lemmens,
 Valeriu Griţco,
 Ksenija Turković,
 Jon Fridrik Kjølbro,
 Georges Ravarani, judges,

and Stanley Naismith, Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 28 June 2016,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 64418/10) against the Republic of Estonia, lodged with the Court on 28 October 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a stateless person, Mr Aleksandr Mihhailov (“the applicant”).

2. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Gamazin, a lawyer practising in Narva. The Estonian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Kuurberg, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

3. The applicant alleged that the police had used unjustified violence against him during his arrest and subsequent detention at the police station.

4. On 13 February 2014, the complaint concerning police violence was communicated to the Government, and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1976 and resides in Narva, Estonia.

A. The applicant’s arrest
6. On 29 April 2009, shortly before 6 p.m., the police emergency call centre received a report concerning two young men at the junction of Kreenholmi and Kerese streets in Narva, Estonia. The caller stated that one of the men was carrying a knife and that the other was clearly drunk and had difficulty walking. He believed the men posed a danger to passers-by. At 5.55 p.m., Officers S.B. and E.V., who were on patrol, were instructed to respond to the call. At approximately 6 p.m., they found the men – the applicant and M.Z. – at a public playground.

7. The applicant’s account of his encounter with the police, as set out in his application and the documents submitted to the Court, is as follows. At around 6 p.m. on 29 April 2009, he and M.Z. were waiting for an acquaintance, Y.B., at a playground. Both the applicant and M.Z. were intoxicated. Two police officers approached him. He did not act aggressively or swear at them. The applicant spoke to the officers. He could not recall exactly what they discussed, except that it concerned a knife and that he said he did not have one. He also remembered that one of the officers was named Andrei (who later turned out to be S.B.). S.B. then punched him in the jaw, causing him to fall to the ground, with his face landing in a hole in the pavement. He briefly lost consciousness, and when he tried to get up, he received another blow to his back, near the base of his neck. One of the officers placed a knee on his neck and pressed him to the ground. He was handcuffed, after which the officers began punching and kicking him across his body and head. He lost consciousness following the beating and regained it only at the police station.

8. According to the Government, the criminal investigation conducted by the domestic authorities established that the applicant’s arrest had occurred as follows. The police officers who found the applicant and M.Z. at the playground had received information about two men, one of whom might have been carrying a knife, while the other was reportedly intoxicated and having difficulty walking. At the playground, the applicant behaved aggressively and used obscene language. Officer E.V. attempted to speak to him, but the applicant acted erratically and began waving his hands and shouting at the officers. Officer E.V. decided to force him to the ground and hold him there until a police patrol vehicle arrived. With the assistance of Officers S.J. and N.S., who had arrived by car, he handcuffed the applicant. While being restrained on the ground, the applicant tried to get up, kicked out and continued shouting obscenities at the officers. The officers did not use excessive force against him and did not beat him. The applicant continued resisting while being placed in a police van, which was the last vehicle to arrive and was carrying Officers S.T. and J.S.
Some force therefore had to be used to place the applicant in the van. During that process, the applicant struck his left temple against the van door. He also remained aggressive while being transported. The officers in the front seats of the van heard what sounded like one object being pounded against another in the back compartment. B. The applicant’s detention at the police station and admission to hospital
9. The applicant’s account of the events during his detention, as set out in his application and the documents submitted to the Court, is as follows. When he woke up in a room next to the detention cells at the police station, he saw in front of him the two police officers who had been present at the playground. He was lying on the floor with his hands cuffed. When he tried to stand up, S.B. kneed him near his left ear. When the applicant attempted to sit on a chair, he was knocked off his feet and ordered to sit on the floor. After E.V. left the room, S.B., who was wearing black leather gloves, began systematically punching and kicking the applicant. The applicant stood up and fell over several times. At one point, he was taken to the toilet, where the sink tap was turned on and his head was held under the water. He was then taken back to the detention room. While passing the detention cells, he asked those inside whether they would confirm anything they had seen or heard. In the detention room, the applicant sat on the chair, and S.B. punched him several more times. When E.V. returned, the applicant was knocked off the chair and beaten again all over his body. S.B. continued to beat him after E.V. left the room. The applicant lost consciousness for a while, and when he came to, there was blood on his face; he was eventually placed on the chair. His handcuffs were removed, and he was allowed to go to the toilet, where he washed himself. He returned to the detention room and was then placed in a cell to sober up. After some time, an ambulance arrived, and he was taken to hospital accompanied by different police officers. There was blood on his clothes, but he threw away the T-shirt, while his mother washed his trousers.

10. According to the Government, the facts established during the subsequent criminal investigation were as follows. The applicant, who remained handcuffed, continued to behave aggressively at the police station. He ran up to detainees in other cells, shouting that the police were beating him. As he failed to obey orders to calm down and remain still, physical force had to be used to make him sit down or to place him on the floor. When he began to calm down, he was seated on a chair with his hands still cuffed. He suddenly lost his balance and fell face down from the chair. The police officers lifted him and placed him back on the chair. Shortly afterwards, the applicant again fell to the floor. For his own safety, the officers left him sitting on the floor. The police removed the applicant’s handcuffs as soon as he had calmed down. He was then taken to a cell to sober up. A test showed that he was moderately intoxicated by alcohol.

11. At 7.45 p.m., Officers S.B. and J.S. prepared a report stating that the applicant had been taken from 10 Kreenholmi Street to recover from alcoholic intoxication.
The report stated that the applicant had been in a state of alcoholic intoxication, had difficulty walking, had fallen over and had been aggressive. It also noted that the applicant’s face had been dirty and that he had abrasions on his head.

12. At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009, Officer P.S. called an ambulance to the police station at the applicant’s request. According to ambulance registration card no. 1419, the applicant complained of pain in the left side of his head and the right wrist, as well as nausea, vomiting and loss of hearing in the left ear. The examination found that he had haematomas on the left side of the cranium and a swollen right wrist and was in a state of alcoholic intoxication. He was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and fractures of the right hand and wrist. The applicant was taken to hospital.

13. Later at the hospital, according to patient registration card no. 4460, dated 30 April 2009, the applicant complained of loss of consciousness and vomiting. The examination found that he had haematomas and oedema in the area of the left ear and eye. He was diagnosed with concussion and alcoholic intoxication.

14. At 2.15 a.m. on 30 April 2009, other police officers, not those who had allegedly beaten the applicant at the police station, took a statement from him at the hospital. At 2.40 a.m., those officers drafted a misdemeanour report stating that the applicant had been drunk in a public place, Kreenholmi Street, and had been brawling, shouting and using obscene language, conduct which amounted to a breach of the peace and a disturbance to others.

15. At 6.26 a.m. on 30 April 2009, the applicant underwent a computer tomography scan. The results showed “temporal extracranial swelling on the left side, no haemorrhage, no intracranial pathology or haemorrhage, ventricular system symmetric, no midline shift, cranial bones intact and paranasal sinuses, middle ear spaces aerated”. He was then discharged from hospital.

16. On 1 May 2009, while close to home, the applicant called an ambulance. Ambulance registration card no. 1454 indicates that he complained of severe headaches, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and pain in the neck. The examination found that he had a haematoma around the left ear, oedema in the area of the left eye, and was in a state of alcoholic intoxication. He was diagnosed with concussion and taken to hospital. At the hospital, he was examined by a traumatology doctor, who found a paraorbital haematoma and swelling around the left eye, bruises on the neck and upper limbs, the smell of alcohol on his breath, dysarthria, and an unsteady gait. He was diagnosed with concussion and alcoholic intoxication. The applicant did not wish to remain in hospital.

C. The investigation into the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment
17. On 30 April 2009 the applicant complained to the police about his ill-treatment. He alleged that police officers had beaten him during his arrest and that he had also been beaten later, while detained at the police station. The police officer on duty refused to handle the complaint and said that it had to be submitted to a prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor likewise refused to deal with it, stating that it had to be lodged with the police. When the applicant returned to the police station, a police investigator allowed him to file the complaint.

18. On 5 May 2009 the applicant sent a letter to the prosecutor’s office concerning the same circumstances. That same day, the police decided to open a criminal investigation on the basis of his complaint. According to the Government, the following day, 6 May, the police investigator requested the applicant’s medical records from the hospital.

19. On 13 May 2009 the applicant gave a statement to the police investigator, setting out his account of events (see paragraphs 7 and 9 above).

20. On the same day, the investigator took a statement from A.P., who had been held in the police station’s sobering-up cell until 9 p.m. on 29 April 2009. He stated that he had looked through the eyehole in his cell door and seen a young man, with his hands cuffed behind his back, being taken into the room opposite the sobering-up cells. Officer S.B., whose name he had seen on his nametag, knocked the young man off his feet. The young man tried to stand up, but the officer prevented him and ordered him to remain on the floor. Each time he attempted to get up, he was knocked off his feet again. Both men used foul language. A.P. also heard someone being slapped on the body and saw the police officer swing his hands towards the detainee. From those gestures, he understood that the young man was being struck. The young man was then taken into a neighbouring room. Afterwards, A.P. heard him shouting and begging for the beating to stop. According to A.P., there was clearly some kind of fight between the young man and the officers. The man was subsequently placed in a cell, where he continued shouting and asked for a doctor, but after a while he fell silent.

21. On 15 May 2009 the applicant’s legal representative sent a letter to the police requesting, among other measures, that the two police officers who had arrested the applicant, taken him to the police department and used force against him at the police station be presented to the applicant for identification. He also requested that the applicant be taken to the police station so that his statements could be compared with the actual layout of the premises and he could describe on the spot what had happened.
He further requested that the applicant’s mother be questioned about the applicant’s state of health when he had left home on 29 April and when he returned on 30 April; that the ambulance doctor and nurse be questioned as witnesses; and that a forensic medical examination of the applicant’s injuries be conducted.

22. On 15 May 2009, the police investigator took a statement from M.S., who had been held in the police station’s sobering-up cell on 29 April 2009. He said that, while he had heard somebody in the neighbouring room shout for help at one point and the police officers shout back at him, he had not seen any police officers beating anybody when he had occasionally looked through the eyehole.

23. On 15 May 2009, the police investigator also took a statement from Police Officer S.J., who had arrived at the scene of the applicant’s arrest in a police car with Officer N.S. While still in the car, they had seen Officer E.V. talking to the applicant, after which a scuffle had broken out between the applicant and the officer. S.J. and N.S. ran from the car, but by the time they reached the scene, the applicant had already been placed on the ground. He was aggressive and shouted obscenities at E.V. Officer S.J. kept him on the ground by using his knee to restrict his movement. Together with N.S., he helped E.V. handcuff the applicant’s hands behind his back, as the applicant was still physically resisting. The applicant tried to get up, continued to use indecent language and did not obey orders. The officers therefore kept him on the ground until the police van arrived to take him to the police station. No other force was used against him. S.J. added that, at some point, an elderly man had approached them and tried to give them some money which allegedly belonged to the applicant. He was told that it was not necessary to hand over the money at that time. S.J. further stated that, at the time of the events in question, Officer S.B. had been nearby talking to another young man who had a knife.

24. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator took a statement from R.L., who had been detained in the police station’s sobering-up cell on 29 April 2009. He told the investigator that he had heard through the door officers dragging somebody into the room facing the cells. He had heard the officers provoke that person into using rude language, shout at him while themselves using foul language, and then begin beating him. R.L. did not remember exactly how the officers had hit the person, but thought that punches and kicks had been involved. The person had tried to stand up, but had not been allowed to do so, as he had been knocked off his feet. He had then been taken to another room.

25. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator took a statement from M.Z. Regarding the arrest, he explained that before the events which occurred at around 6 p.m.
On 29 April 2009, he had had several beers with the applicant. They had just sat down at the playground behind some buildings when three police officers arrived in a police car. One officer came over to speak to him, while the other two approached the applicant and pushed him over. One of the policemen placed his leg on the applicant’s neck, while the other tried to stand on the applicant’s legs. M.Z. was taken to the place where the applicant had been beaten. The applicant was lying face down on the asphalt, with his face in some sand where there was a hole in the asphalt. After a while, a police van arrived with two officers. The applicant’s hands were placed behind his back and he was handcuffed, lifted to his feet, and moved towards the van. During that process, one of the police officers slapped the applicant on the head. He was placed in the van and taken to the police station.

26. Regarding the events at the police station, M.Z. stated that the applicant had been taken to a room where the cells were located. M.Z. himself had been left in the corridor situated immediately beyond the detention section. Through the open doors, he could see the applicant being placed on the floor directly in front of the doors, where two policemen began to beat him. They struck the applicant with their elbows and kicked him in the back of the head and elsewhere. No other police officers entered the room. The doors were open, as was the door to the duty room, but no one came out of that room. After some time, one of the officers who had been beating the applicant approached M.Z. and took him to an office to make a statement. He gave a statement against the applicant because he was afraid, having seen the police officer beat his friend.

27. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator also took a statement from P.S., a police officer who had been on duty at the police station at the time of the applicant’s detention. He explained that, when he arrived for work at 8 p.m. on 29 April 2009, Officer E.V. had told him that the person placed in a temporary detention cell, namely the applicant, might ask for an ambulance to be called and should be checked periodically. During the night, the applicant went to the toilet by himself, complained of pain, but declined an offer to call an ambulance. Later that night, when he was about to be released, he requested an ambulance, and P.S. called one for him. P.S. overheard the applicant tell the doctor and nurse that he had been beaten by police officers. When P.S. asked who had beaten him, the applicant replied that it was the officers who had taken him to the police station. When P.S. asked where the beating had occurred, he replied that it had happened in the street during his arrest. The ambulance then took him to the hospital.

28. On 27 May 2009, the police investigator took a statement from K.I., who had been on duty at the police station’s command centre at the time of the events in question.
He stated that, as he passed the detention room on his way out, he saw the applicant sitting on the floor with his hands cuffed. He was using offensive language, acting aggressively, and was intoxicated. K.I. stated that the applicant had not been beaten in his presence. The applicant had neither complained of being beaten nor requested an ambulance. 29. On 2 June 2009, the police investigator took a statement from one of the suspects, Police Officer S.B. According to S.B., when he and Officer E.V. arrived on foot at the playground between the buildings at 10 Kreenholmi Street and 18 Kerese Street, the applicant was very drunk and arguing with another man over some money. As S.B. had gone on to speak to M.Z., he had not seen what occurred between the applicant and Officer E.V. or how E.V. had forced the applicant to the ground. M.Z. did not have a knife on him but was wearing a large sheath on his belt. S.B. had no contact with the applicant. However, he saw that the applicant remained aggressive after E.V. had put him on the ground, while Officers S.J. and N.S. helped E.V. handcuff him and keep him on the ground. He also witnessed Officers S.T. and J.S. helping to place the applicant in the police van. The applicant was not kicked or punched. On the way to the police station, thumps and bangs could be heard from the rear compartment of the police van. 30. S.B. further stated that, at the police station, officers had placed the applicant in the room facing the detention cells. The room’s door remained open. He was alone there with the applicant for about 40 minutes but did not beat him. The applicant refused to obey orders to calm down and remain on the floor. S.B. was therefore unable to remove his handcuffs and had to use force to make him stay on the floor and calm down. At one point, E.V. assisted him. When the applicant had calmed down somewhat, he was taken to another room for his statement and seated on a chair, with his hands still cuffed behind his back. While sitting on the chair in the detention room, the applicant suddenly fell face down from it. Together with E.V., who had entered the interrogation room at that moment, S.B. put the applicant back on the chair, but he fell off once more and was again helped back onto it. After the paperwork was completed, the applicant was taken to a cell to sober up. He had no bodily injuries apart from some old scratches on his head and did not request medical assistance. 31. On 3 June 2009, the police investigator took statements from four children who had witnessed the applicant’s arrest (A.N., D.K., D.B., and E.G.). Three of them (A.N., D.K., and D.B.) had seen the applicant while he was drunk and arguing with an elderly man over some money. According to A.N.’s statement,
and D.K., two police officers arrived and first spoke with the applicant and the older man. A.N., D.K., and D.B. said that one of the officers had then moved further away to deal with the applicant’s companion, who was carrying a knife sheath. According to A.N., the applicant began shouting obscenities at the police officer who had remained with him. A.N., D.K., and D.B. stated that, following an exchange with the applicant, the police officer forced him to the ground. A.N. and D.K. said that the officer pushed the applicant over. D.K. added that the applicant was placed on the ground with his right cheek facing down. Two other officers, who had arrived by car, helped the first police officer handcuff the applicant’s hands behind his back. All of the children, including E.G., who had arrived after the applicant was put on the ground, confirmed that the officers forcibly kept him there. According to A.N. and E.G., this was done by standing on his legs, while D.K. and D.B. said that one officer knelt on the applicant’s neck to keep his head down while the other stood on his legs, near his heels. All the children said that the officers had neither punched nor kicked the applicant. The applicant had tried to get up from the ground, had continued to swear, and had said that the officers were hurting him. All of the children confirmed that the applicant resisted being taken to the police van. The police used force to place the applicant in the van, and he hit his head (the left side, according to D.B. and E.G.) against the van door.

32. On 4 June 2009, the police investigator took statements from the ambulance nurse, L.G., and the ambulance doctor, V.K. They had received a call concerning a man with head trauma at the police station. The applicant, who was drunk, said that police officers had beaten him at the station. There was no blood on his clothes, and he did not vomit. However, given the nature of his injuries, the doctor decided to take him to the hospital for further examination.

33. On 8 June 2009, the other suspect, Police Officer E.V., gave a statement. He explained that he had received an order to respond to a report that a man in a state of heavy alcoholic intoxication, possibly carrying a knife, was walking along Kreenholmi Street. He had immediately gone with his partner, Officer S.B., to where the man was believed to be. Upon reaching the building at 10 Kreenholmi Street, he saw that the applicant was behaving inappropriately, waving his hands and staggering. When he approached the men, M.Z. led the applicant by the hand behind the building at 10 Kreenholmi Street. The police officers followed and found the applicant sitting on a kerbstone with M.Z. and an elderly man who was standing beside him. When E.V. and S.B. approached, the applicant stood up and staggered towards them. M.Z. walked in a different direction. When the applicant reached the officers, E.V. politely asked him to stop.
As the applicant did not respond and walked past him, E.V. stopped him by taking hold of his elbow and spoke to him again. The applicant reacted quite violently and began arguing and waving his hands around. E.V. therefore used the radio to call for assistance to have the applicant removed so that he could sober up. Meanwhile, the elderly man had approached and told the applicant to calm down because he was dealing with police officers. The applicant replied that he did not care and began throwing money on the ground, telling the man to keep it. The man picked up the money, said he did not need it, and put it back in the applicant’s pockets. By then, S.B. had gone after M.Z. E.V. tried to calm the applicant down, but he continued walking back and forth, waving his hands and uttering obscenities. E.V. decided to handcuff the applicant because there were many children nearby. The applicant was also clearly behaving aggressively and might have injured other people, particularly given the possible presence of a knife. As the applicant would not allow E.V. to handcuff him, E.V. forced him to the ground but did not hit him. Officers N.S. and S.J. arrived and assisted in handcuffing the applicant before taking him to the police car, which was 10 metres away. The applicant did not have a knife. E.V. had no further contact with the applicant at the playground. While in the police van on the way back to the station, the applicant continued behaving aggressively, and E.V. heard what sounded like the applicant hitting himself against something.

34. E.V. further stated that, at the police station, the applicant shouted that the police were beating him while S.B. tried to calm him down and conduct a search. E.V. left the room to interview M.Z. as a witness to the applicant’s breach of the peace. When E.V. returned, he saw that the applicant had fallen face down from his chair, and he helped S.B. lift him back onto it. The applicant fell to the ground a second time and was then left on the floor. According to E.V., the applicant deliberately tried to injure himself so that he could later accuse the police. When he began behaving calmly, the handcuffs were removed. The applicant walked unaided to the sobering-up cell. He had no injuries requiring immediate medical attention. He had haematomas on his face, but these could have been sustained during transportation or when he fell from the chair. The applicant’s clothes were dirty but had no bloodstains. E.V. informed the applicant that an ambulance would be called if he had any health complaints.

35. On the same day, 8 June 2009, the investigator took a statement from Officer N.S., who had arrived at the scene of the applicant’s arrest in a police car with Officer S.J. When N.S. arrived, Officer E.V. was already holding the applicant down on the ground. When he and S.J. reached them, they saw the applicant behaving aggressively and using foul language.
N.S. helped E.V. handcuff the applicant’s hands behind his back. The applicant was then lifted to his feet and taken to the police car, but he refused to comply with orders to keep still and calm down and began kicking the vehicle. The officers therefore removed him from the car and placed him on the ground. N.S. held his hands and feet, while another officer knelt on the applicant to keep his head down. The applicant continually resisted the officers, used foul language and behaved aggressively. He was restrained to prevent him from injuring himself and others. The officers did not beat him. The applicant continued resisting the police officers while being placed in the police van and remained aggressive inside it. N.S. added that, at one point, an elderly man approached them and offered to hand over some money that allegedly belonged to the applicant. He was, however, told that it was not necessary to hand over the money at that time.

36. On the same day, 8 June 2009, the police investigator took statements from Officers S.T. and J.S., who had arrived at the scene of the applicant’s arrest in the police van. When J.S. got out of the van, he saw Officers S.J. and N.S. holding the applicant down on the ground. The applicant was aggressive, shouting and swearing, and trying to break free. N.S. and S.J. took the applicant to the police van, and J.S. opened the door for them. He did not see the applicant strike anything, but during transport sounds could be heard from the rear compartment that sounded like something being hit. S.T. stated that he had not left the van. He did not hear the applicant banging against anything while he was being placed inside. At the police station, he and J.S. carried the applicant to the detention room and left him in front of the cells. He saw no blood on the applicant or his clothes, nor did he notice any visible injuries.

37. That same day, 8 June 2009, the police investigator ordered a forensic medical assessment of the injuries based on the available documentary evidence (the ambulance cards, patient registration card, and statements from the applicant, the suspects in the case, and two other police officers acting as witnesses).

38. On 9 June 2009, the police investigator took a statement from D.R., a police officer who had been on duty at the police station on 29 April 2009. He stated that he had arrived for work at 8 p.m. At about 2 a.m., he began working on the applicant’s documents. The applicant told D.R. that he had a severe headache and that his hands hurt because of the handcuffs. He asked for an ambulance. He also stated that his head injury had been caused by other police officers. There was no blood on his clothes, and he did not vomit. When the applicant was taken to hospital, D.R. accompanied him.

39. On 15 June 2009, the applicant’s legal representative filed a complaint against the police with the prosecutor’s office.
He stated that the police had not carried out the investigative measures he had requested on 15 May 2009 (including presenting the police officers for identification; arranging a formal confrontation between the applicant and M.Z., who had allegedly witnessed him committing a breach of the peace; comparing the applicant’s statements with the circumstances at the scene of the alleged offence; conducting a forensic medical examination of the applicant’s injuries; and interviewing the children whom the applicant’s representative had identified and about whom he had informed the police investigator on 27 May 2009). He asked the prosecutor to take steps to secure the collection of evidence. The prosecutor dismissed the complaint on 1 July 2009, stating that the applicant had not challenged any acts or orders of an investigative authority.

40. On 17 June 2009 the police investigator showed the applicant photographs to identify possible suspects. According to the record of the meeting, the applicant was shown four lists containing an unspecified number of photographs of police officers with similar appearances. The applicant identified S.B. as the police officer who had beaten him at the police station. He could not remember whether that officer had also beaten him during his arrest. The applicant was uncertain about his identification of E.V. from the photographs. However, he added that he would be able to identify the other officer by his features and height if he saw him in person.

41. On 6 July 2009 the police investigator took a statement from V.Z., the person who had called the police on 29 April 2009 regarding the applicant’s alleged breach of the peace. He explained that, from his car at the intersection of Kreenholmi and Kerese Street, he had seen two young men crossing the street. One of them was carrying a knife. Another young man, who was very drunk and having difficulty walking, was walking in front of him. He had called the police after seeing the young men and the knife because he considered them clearly dangerous and was concerned for the safety of passers-by.

42. On 13 August 2009 the forensic medical expert issued his opinion on the applicant’s injuries. He concluded that the injuries found on the applicant on 30 April and 1 May had been caused by blows from a blunt object or objects. The precise cause of those injuries could not be determined because their description in the documents was insufficiently detailed. Nonetheless, the expert concluded that they had been inflicted shortly before the applicant saw a doctor, possibly on 29 April 2009. He also noted that, in the absence of detailed descriptions of the injuries to the upper limbs, it was not possible to determine whether those injuries had been sustained in self-defence. None of the documents contained any information about the ethanol level in the applicant’s blood, stating only that the applicant had been in a state of alcoholic intoxication.

43.
On 2 September 2009 the forensic expert gave an oral statement to the police investigator concerning his written opinion. In response to a question as to whether the applicant had had a haematoma around the left eye on both 30 April and 1 May, the expert stated that the documents of 30 April contained no information to that effect. He explained that it could not be ruled out that the haematoma had been inflicted on 29 April, but that it might also have been inflicted on 30 April or 1 May. In reply to a question about the cause of the injuries, he further stated that, since the documents had not contained detailed descriptions of the injuries, it was not possible to determine the exact nature of the object that had caused the traumas.

44. On 14 September 2009 the police investigator showed M.Z. photographs of officers for identification. According to the record of the meeting, M.Z. was shown four lists containing an unspecified number of photographs of police officers who were similar in appearance. M.Z. identified one of the police officers (E.V.) as the officer who, together with another officer (S.B.), had beaten the applicant at the police station and had used force against him at the playground. He was not certain about his identification of S.B. in the photographs, but pointed to another officer who, in his words, looked very similar to S.B. He also stated that no beating had taken place at the playground, but that the applicant’s hands had simply been twisted behind his back and he had been forced to the ground.

45. On 8 January 2010 the applicant complained to the prosecutor that, despite repeated requests, he had still not been informed of any decision to conduct a forensic medical examination. He added that he had still not been examined by an expert, although he had complained of headaches and loss of vision following the beating. He requested a copy of any expert report if an examination had been carried out without his knowledge. He also complained that he had not had a formal confrontation with M.Z. and the suspects in order to resolve any contradictions in their statements. The prosecutor dismissed the complaint on 14 January 2010, reiterating that the applicant had not challenged any acts or orders of an investigative authority.

46. On 20 January 2010 the police investigator decided to discontinue the investigation, finding that there was no evidence that the police officers had committed the criminal offence of abuse of authority. Their use of force had not breached the Police Act; it had been lawful, justified and not excessive. The police investigator’s decision was approved by the prosecutor on 15 February 2010.

47. As regards the applicant’s arrest, the police investigator considered the applicant’s allegations that he had been beaten to be entirely unfounded.
She concluded, in substance, that the use of force against the applicant during his arrest had been justified by the applicant’s breach of the peace while in a state of alcoholic intoxication; his refusal to comply with the officers’ lawful orders; and his attempt to leave the scene without their consent. The physical force used to bring the applicant to the ground, handcuff him and keep him there had not been excessive. 48. The decision considered it established that the applicant’s arrest had taken place as follows. While at the playground near 18 Kerese Street, the applicant had behaved inappropriately, waved his hands around, used foul language and staggered considerably. He had not responded to the orders given by the police officers. Police Officer E.V. had decided to handcuff the applicant, given that children were standing nearby, that the applicant was clearly in an aggressive state of mind, that he might have injured others and that there was a certain context to the call (the suspicion that he was carrying a knife). At that moment, Officers N.S. and S.J. had arrived and helped apply the handcuffs. The applicant had not complied with the officers’ orders to remain still and calm down, but had begun kicking the police vehicle. N.S. and S.J. had held the applicant on the ground to restrain him. The applicant had continued to resist, use foul language and act aggressively. Because of his aggressive behaviour, E.V. had been forced to call for a police van to take the applicant to the police station. The applicant had resisted being placed in the police van and had continued to act aggressively and use foul language during transport. Sounds from the transport compartment suggested that the applicant had struck himself against something. 49. In reaching the conclusion that the applicant had not been beaten and that only lawful force had been used, the police investigator relied specifically on the statements of the children, Police Officers N.S., S.J., J.S. and S.T., the suspected police officers, S.B. and E.V., and on the statements of M.Z., who had said during the presentation of the identification photographs that there had been no beating at the playground, that the applicant’s hands had merely been forced behind his back and that he had been forced to the ground. 50. As regards the events at the police department, the police investigator dismissed M.Z.’s statements as unreliable because he could not have seen what was happening to the applicant in the detention room. Although the door to that room had been open, M.Z. had been standing farther away. As for the people detained at the police station, the investigator concluded that their statements had not directly confirmed that the applicant had been beaten. The statements of the detainees A.P.
and R.L., who had stated that the applicant had been beaten, were dismissed because they contradicted the statements of the third detainee – M.S. – and other evidence. Four other police officers involved in the applicant’s arrest and transportation, as well as one police officer who had been present at the police station during his detention, had also stated that the applicant had not been beaten.

51. As regards the applicant’s injuries, the police investigator cited observations in the report drawn up when the applicant was taken to sober up, as well as the ambulance and patient registration cards. Concerning the haematoma around the left eye, first documented at the hospital on 1 May 2009, the investigator referred to the forensic expert’s opinion that it could have been caused on 29 April, 30 April or 1 May 2009 and that, on the basis of the documents, it was impossible to establish its cause. Based on that information, the investigator concluded that the applicant’s allegation that the haematoma around his left eye had been caused during his beating at the police department was unfounded and untrue. Turning to the applicant’s allegations that he had vomited and that there had been blood on his clothing, the investigator considered them disproven by the statements of the police officers, as well as those of the ambulance doctor and nurse, who had not seen any blood on the applicant’s clothes or witnessed him vomiting.

52. The police investigator ultimately found that, while at the police station, the applicant had been aggressive, continued to use foul language and disregarded orders to keep still. The force used against him by S.B. and E.V. had been justified and lawful and had not been excessive.

53. On 15 March 2010 the applicant appealed against the decision to discontinue the criminal investigation. He submitted, among other things, that the investigation had not been objective; that witness statements had been selectively cited and distorted; that some witnesses (such as Y.B., who had witnessed the applicant’s arrest, and A.D., who had been detained at the police station at the same time as the applicant) had not been questioned; that he himself had not undergone a forensic medical examination; and that formal confrontations had not been arranged to resolve contradictions in the statements in the case.

54. On 23 March 2010 the State Prosecutor’s Office rejected the applicant’s appeal against the decision to discontinue the investigation on the grounds that it had been lodged out of time. The decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings had stated that the applicant was required to lodge an appeal with the State Prosecutor’s Office within ten days of receiving the relevant decision. The decision had been sent to the applicant’s address by ordinary mail on 26 February 2010. Estonian Post had indicated that a standard letter was delivered to an addressee on the next working day of the post office.
The letter should therefore have reached the applicant on 1 March 2010, meaning that the final day for lodging an appeal was 11 March 2010. The applicant lodged his appeal on 15 March 2010. He stated that he had received the letter only on 5 March 2010, after returning home from his job in another city. Although the applicant had not requested restoration of the time-limit for his appeal, the State Prosecutor’s Office stated that, in any event, there were no grounds for such a procedure. It considered that the applicant had a duty to exercise diligence regarding his mail because he knew that proceedings were pending in which decisions concerning his situation might be made. The applicant had had several options available to avoid exceeding the time-limit.

55. On 30 April 2010 the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the State Prosecutor’s Office’s decision. The court agreed with the applicant’s counsel that the time-limit for an appeal began to run from the date of actual receipt of the decision, rather than from the date on which it should have been received according to calculations based on mail-delivery deadlines. Nevertheless, it considered that the decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings had reached the applicant’s mailbox on 1 March 2010, without explaining the evidence on which that conclusion was based. The court also stated that there was no need to express an opinion regarding restoration of the time-limit for the appeal, because the applicant had not believed that he had missed the deadline and had not sought its restoration.

D. Applicant’s acquittal of misdemeanour charges
56. On 25 May 2009, the East Police Prefecture found the applicant guilty of the misdemeanour of breaching the peace at Kreenholmi Street and ordered him to pay a fine. The applicant appealed against that decision to the Viru County Court.

57. On 17 November 2010, following a public hearing on 4 November, the Viru County Court acquitted the applicant of the charges. It considered that there was no evidence proving that his conduct had constituted a misdemeanour.

58. The court set aside, as unlawfully obtained evidence, the statements made by the applicant on 30 April 2009 at 2.15 a.m. in the hospital, which had been included in the misdemeanour report drawn up that same night at 2.40 a.m. It noted that the evidence had been collected more than eight hours after the offence had allegedly been committed and after the applicant had, in the meantime, been taken to sober up at 7.45 p.m.

59. The court considered that witness M.Z. had given credible testimony at the hearing on 4 November 2010 when he stated that the police had improperly influenced him to give evidence against the applicant by allowing him to hear the applicant being beaten. The court found that statement corroborated by the fact that the applicant had been taken to the hospital and questioned there.

60. The court concluded that the evidence in the misdemeanour proceedings had been obtained unlawfully, infringing the applicant’s honour and dignity and endangering his health. That conclusion was based on the statements of the applicant and M.Z., information from the hospital, and the place and time at which the misdemeanour report had been drafted.

61. The court further stated that there had been a material breach of the provisions governing misdemeanour proceedings because the applicant had been arrested at 5.40 p.m. and taken immediately to the police station, but had not been taken to sober up until 7.45 p.m. Moreover, his statement had not been taken at the hospital until 2.15 a.m., and the misdemeanour report had not been drawn up there until 2.40 a.m.

62. The East Police Prefecture did not appeal against that judgment.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
63. Section 13(1)(1) of the Police Act (Politseiseadus), as applicable at the material time, provided that the police were entitled to require individuals and officials to maintain public order and cease any violations thereof, as well as to apply coercive measures prescribed by law against offenders.

64. Section 14(2) of the Police Act, as applicable at the material time, stipulated that before applying coercive measures, the police had to warn the person against whom they intended to use such measures. It further provided that a warning could be dispensed with only where it was impossible to issue one owing to an urgent need to terminate an offence.

65. Section 14(2)(1) of the Police Act, as applicable at the material time, stipulated that a police officer could use physical force if no other administrative coercive measure could secure the performance of an obligation imposed by a valid administrative act for the purpose of establishing or countering a threat or eliminating an offence.

66. Article 291 of the Penal Code (Karistusseadustik), entitled “Abuse of authority”, as applicable at the material time, provided that the unlawful use of a weapon, special equipment or physical force by an official in the performance of his or her official duties was punishable by a fine or one to five years’ imprisonment.

67. Article 77 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Kriminaalmenetluse seadustik) provides that persons may be confronted where a contradiction in their statements cannot otherwise be resolved. During the confrontation, the relationship between the persons concerned is ascertained, and they are asked a series of questions concerning the contradictory facts. Previous statements made by a person confronted may be disclosed, and other evidence may be presented. With the permission of an official of the investigative body, the persons confronted may put questions to each other through that official concerning the contradictions in their statements.

68. Article 81 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that a photograph, film, or audio or video recording of a person, thing or other object may, where necessary, be used for identification purposes.

69. Article 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states that a report of a criminal offence may be submitted orally or in writing to an investigative authority or a Prosecutor’s Office. Under the same article, a report made on the premises of an investigative authority or Prosecutor’s Office must be recorded in writing, while a report of a criminal offence communicated by telephone must be recorded in writing or by means of an audio recording.

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 64418/10, which Mr Aleksandr Mihhailov (“the applicant”), a stateless person, lodged against the Republic of Estonia on 28 October 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. Mr A. Gamazin, a lawyer practising in Narva, represented the applicant. The Estonian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Kuurberg of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

3. The applicant claimed that the police had subjected him to unjustified violence both when arresting him and later while he was detained at the police station.

4. On 13 February 2014, the complaint relating to police violence was communicated to the Government; the rest of the application was declared inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1976, the applicant resides in Narva, Estonia.

A. The arrest of the applicant
6. On 29 April 2009, shortly before 6 p.m., the police emergency call centre was notified of two young men at the intersection of Kreenholmi and Kerese streets in Narva, Estonia. The caller stated that one man had a knife, while the other was visibly intoxicated and struggling to walk, and expressed the view that they posed a danger to pedestrians. At 5.55 p.m., patrol officers S.B. and E.V. were instructed to attend the scene. At approximately 6 p.m., they located the two men—the applicant and M.Z.—at a public playground.

7. The applicant’s account of the encounter, as set out in his application and the documents provided to the Court, was as follows. At about 6 p.m. on 29 April 2009, he and M.Z., both of whom were drunk, were waiting at a playground for an acquaintance, Y.B. Two police officers approached the applicant. He maintained that he neither acted aggressively nor swore at them. He spoke to the officers but could not recall the discussion in detail, other than that it concerned a knife and that he told them he did not have one. He also remembered that one officer was called Andrei, who was later identified as S.B. According to the applicant, S.B. then struck him in the jaw, causing him to fall and land face-first in a hole in the pavement. He briefly lost consciousness. When he tried to stand up, he was struck again, this time on his back near the base of his neck. One officer placed a knee on his neck and pinned him to the ground. After handcuffing him, the officers allegedly punched and kicked him repeatedly across his body and head. He lost consciousness following the beating and did not regain it until he was at the police station.

8. The Government submitted that the domestic criminal investigation had established a different sequence of events. Before finding the applicant and M.Z. at the playground, the officers had been informed that one of the two men might be carrying a knife and that the other was reportedly intoxicated and having difficulty walking. Once approached, the applicant behaved aggressively and used obscene language. Although Officer E.V. attempted to speak with him, the applicant acted erratically, waving his arms and shouting at the officers. E.V. therefore decided to restrain him on the ground until a police patrol vehicle arrived. With assistance from Officers S.J. and N.S., who arrived by car, E.V. handcuffed the applicant. While being held on the ground, the applicant tried to rise, kicked out, and continued directing obscenities at the officers. The Government maintained that the officers neither beat him nor used excessive force. The applicant also continued resisting as he was placed in a police van, which arrived last and was occupied by Officers S.T. and J.S.
The officers therefore had to use some force to place the applicant in the van. During this process, he struck his left temple against the van door. He continued to behave aggressively while being transported. From the rear compartment, the officers seated in the front of the van heard a noise resembling one object being pounded against another.

B. The applicant’s detention at the police station and admission to hospital
9. The applicant’s version of what occurred while he was in detention, as set out in his application and the documents lodged with the Court, may be summarised as follows. On regaining consciousness in a room adjoining the police-station cells, he found himself lying handcuffed on the floor, with the two officers who had been at the playground standing before him. When he tried to get up, S.B. struck him with a knee near his left ear. He then attempted to sit on a chair, but was knocked down and told to remain on the floor. Once E.V. had left, S.B., wearing black leather gloves, began repeatedly punching and kicking him. The applicant got to his feet and fell over several times. At one stage, he was taken to the toilet, where the tap was turned on and his head was held under the running water, after which he was brought back to the detention room. As he passed the cells, he asked the detainees whether they would corroborate anything they had witnessed or heard. Back in the room, he sat on the chair, whereupon S.B. punched him several more times. When E.V. returned, the applicant was knocked from the chair and beaten all over his body. After E.V. departed again, S.B. continued the assault. The applicant briefly lost consciousness; when he came to, his face was covered in blood, and he was eventually placed on the chair. His handcuffs were removed, and he was permitted to use the toilet, where he washed himself. He then returned to the detention room before being transferred to a cell to sober up. Some time later, an ambulance arrived and took him to hospital, accompanied by other police officers. His clothing was bloodstained; he discarded the T-shirt, while his mother washed the trousers.

10. The Government submitted that the facts established during the ensuing criminal investigation presented a different account. At the police station, the applicant remained handcuffed and continued acting aggressively. He approached detainees in other cells and shouted that the police were beating him. Because he ignored instructions to calm down and remain still, the officers had to use physical force to seat him or place him on the floor. Once he began settling down, he was seated on a chair with his hands still cuffed. He abruptly lost his balance and fell face down from the chair. The officers helped him up and reseated him, but shortly afterwards he fell to the floor once more. For his own safety, they then left him sitting on the floor. As soon as he had calmed down, the officers removed the handcuffs and transferred him to a cell to sober up. Testing indicated that he was moderately intoxicated by alcohol.

11. At 7.45 p.m., Officers S.B. and J.S. prepared a report stating that the applicant had been brought from 10 Kreenholmi Street to recover from alcohol intoxication.
The report indicated that the applicant was intoxicated, had difficulty walking, had fallen, and had behaved aggressively. It further noted that his face was dirty and that he had abrasions on his head.

12. At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009, at the applicant’s request, Officer P.S. summoned an ambulance to the police station. Ambulance registration card no. 1419 recorded that the applicant reported pain on the left side of his head and in his right wrist, together with nausea, vomiting, and loss of hearing in his left ear. An examination revealed haematomas on the left side of his cranium, swelling of the right wrist, and alcoholic intoxication. He was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and fractures of the right hand and wrist, and was transported to hospital.

13. According to patient registration card no. 4460 of 30 April 2009, the applicant subsequently complained at the hospital of vomiting and loss of consciousness. The examination disclosed haematomas and oedema around his left ear and eye. He was diagnosed with concussion and alcoholic intoxication.

14. At 2.15 a.m. on 30 April 2009, police officers other than those alleged to have assaulted the applicant at the police station took his statement at the hospital. At 2.40 a.m., those officers prepared a misdemeanour report stating that the applicant had been intoxicated in a public place, namely Kreenholmi Street, where he had been brawling, shouting, and using obscene language. According to the report, this conduct breached the peace and disturbed others.

15. A computer tomography scan was carried out at 6.26 a.m. on 30 April 2009. The results recorded “temporal extracranial swelling on the left side, no haemorrhage, no intracranial pathology or haemorrhage, ventricular system symmetric, no midline shift, cranial bones intact and paranasal sinuses, middle ear spaces aerated”. The applicant was then discharged from hospital.

16. On 1 May 2009, while near his home, the applicant called an ambulance. Ambulance registration card no. 1454 noted his complaints of severe headaches, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and neck pain. Upon examination, he was found to have a haematoma around the left ear and oedema near the left eye, and to be intoxicated. After being diagnosed with concussion, he was taken to hospital. There, a traumatologist observed a paraorbital haematoma and swelling around the left eye, bruising on the neck and upper limbs, alcohol on the applicant’s breath, dysarthria, and a staggering gait. The diagnoses were concussion and alcoholic intoxication. The applicant declined to remain in hospital.

C. Investigation of the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment
17. On 30 April 2009, the applicant reported to the police that he had been ill-treated. He claimed that police officers had beaten him during his arrest and again later while he was detained at the police station. The officer on duty declined to handle the complaint, directing him instead to the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor likewise refused to deal with it and referred him back to the police. Upon returning to the police station, the applicant was permitted by a police investigator to lodge his complaint.

18. On 5 May 2009, the applicant wrote to the prosecutor’s office concerning the same events. That day, the police decided to initiate a criminal investigation on the basis of his complaint. The Government stated that, on the following day, 6 May, the police investigator requested the applicant’s medical records from the hospital.

19. On 13 May 2009, the applicant gave the police investigator a statement setting out his version of the events (see paragraphs 7 and 9 above).

20. Also on 13 May 2009, the investigator obtained a statement from A.P., who had remained in the police station’s sobering-up cell until 9 p.m. on 29 April 2009. A.P. said that, looking through the eyehole in his cell door, he had seen a young man whose hands were cuffed behind his back being brought into the room opposite the sobering-up cells. An officer whom he identified as S.B. from his nametag knocked the young man to the ground. When the man tried to rise, the officer prevented him from doing so and ordered him to remain on the floor. Every further attempt to get up resulted in him being knocked down again. Both the officer and the young man used foul language. A.P. also heard the sound of someone being slapped on the body and observed the officer swinging his hands towards the detainee. From those movements, he concluded that the young man was being struck. The detainee was subsequently taken into an adjoining room, after which A.P. heard him shouting and pleading for the beating to stop. In A.P.’s view, some form of fight had undoubtedly occurred between the young man and the officers. The man was later placed in a cell, where he continued shouting and asked for a doctor, although he eventually became quiet.

On 15 May 2009, the applicant’s legal representative wrote to the police seeking, among other steps, an identification procedure in which the applicant would be shown the two officers who had arrested him, transported him to the police department and used force against him at the station. The representative also requested that the applicant be brought to the police station so that his account could be checked against the premises’ actual layout and he could describe on site what had occurred.
He also asked for the applicant’s mother to be questioned about her son’s health when he left home on 29 April and when he returned on 30 April. In addition, he requested that the ambulance doctor and nurse be interviewed as witnesses and that a forensic medical examination of the applicant’s injuries be carried out.

However, when he occasionally looked through the eyehole, he did not see any officers beating anyone.

On 29 April 2009, he and the applicant had consumed several beers. They had just sat down in a playground behind some buildings when a police car carrying three officers arrived. One officer approached him, while the other two went over to the applicant and knocked him down. One policeman placed his leg on the applicant’s neck, and the other tried to stand on his legs. M.Z. was then taken to the spot where the applicant had been assaulted. The applicant was lying face down on the asphalt, with his face in sand that had collected in a hole in the pavement. Upon their arrival, the applicant was heavily intoxicated and arguing with another man about money. He nevertheless observed that, after E.V. had forced him to the ground, the applicant remained aggressive. Officers S.J. and N.S. assisted E.V. in handcuffing the applicant and holding him down. S.B. also witnessed Officers S.T. and J.S. helping to place the applicant in the police van. According to him, the applicant was neither punched nor kicked. During the journey to the police station, banging and thumping noises came from the van’s rear compartment.

E.V. entered the interrogation room at that moment and helped S.B. return the applicant to the chair. The applicant then fell off a second time and was again assisted back onto it. and D.K., two police officers arrived and initially spoke to the applicant and the older man. A.N., D.K. and D.B. stated that one officer then moved farther away to deal with the applicant’s companion, who had a knife sheath. A.N. reported that the applicant began shouting obscenities at the officer who remained with him. Every child said that the officers neither punched nor kicked him. The applicant tried to rise, continued swearing and complained that the officers were hurting him. The children also unanimously confirmed that he resisted as he was being escorted to the police van. The officers used force to place him inside, during which he struck his head against the van door; according to D.B. and E.G., it was the left side of his head.

32. On 4 June 2009, the police investigator obtained statements from L.G., an ambulance nurse, and V.K., an ambulance doctor.
