33. On 8 June 2009, Police Officer E.V., the other suspect, provided a statement. He said that he had been instructed to respond to a report of a man who was heavily intoxicated, might be carrying a knife and was walking along Kreenholmi Street. E.V. and his partner, Officer S.B., immediately proceeded to the location where the man was thought to be. Upon arriving at the building at 10 Kreenholmi Street, E.V. observed the applicant behaving abnormally: he was waving his arms and staggering. As the officers approached the men, M.Z. took the applicant by the hand and led him behind the building. Following them, the officers found the applicant seated on a kerbstone beside M.Z. and an elderly man who was standing nearby. When E.V. and S.B. came closer, the applicant rose and staggered towards them, while M.Z. walked away in another direction. Once the applicant reached the officers, E.V. politely asked him to stop.
When the applicant ignored him and continued walking, E.V. took hold of his elbow to stop him and addressed him once more. The applicant responded in a highly agitated manner, arguing and gesticulating. E.V. consequently radioed for assistance so that the applicant could be taken away to sober up. In the meantime, the elderly man approached and urged the applicant to calm down, pointing out that he was dealing with police officers. The applicant said that he did not care, threw money onto the ground and told the man to keep it. The man picked up the money, stated that he did not need it and returned it to the applicant’s pockets. By then, S.B. had followed M.Z.

Although E.V. tried to settle the applicant, he continued pacing back and forth, waving his arms and shouting obscenities. Since many children were nearby, E.V. decided to place him in handcuffs. The applicant was plainly aggressive and posed a risk of injuring others, especially in view of the possibility that he was carrying a knife. When the applicant resisted being handcuffed, E.V. forced him to the ground but did not strike him. Officers N.S. and S.J. then arrived, assisted in applying the handcuffs and escorted the applicant to a police vehicle approximately 10 metres away. No knife was found on him. E.V. had no further interaction with the applicant at the playground. During the journey to the police station in the police van, the applicant remained aggressive, and E.V. heard noises suggesting that he was hitting himself against something.

34. E.V. also stated that, at the police station, the applicant yelled that the police were beating him while S.B. attempted to calm him and carry out a search. E.V. left the room to question M.Z. as a witness to the applicant’s breach of the peace. On returning, he saw that the applicant had fallen face down from his chair and helped S.B. place him back on it. After the applicant fell to the floor a second time, he was left there. In E.V.’s view, the applicant was deliberately attempting to harm himself so that he could subsequently accuse the police. Once he became calm, the handcuffs were removed. He then walked without assistance to the sobering-up cell. He had no injuries requiring urgent medical treatment. Although there were haematomas on his face, E.V. considered that they could have been sustained either during transportation or when the applicant fell from the chair. His clothing was dirty but bore no bloodstains. E.V. advised him that an ambulance would be called if he had any health-related complaints.

35. Later on 8 June 2009, the investigator obtained a statement from Officer N.S., who had travelled with Officer S.J. by police car to the location where the applicant was arrested. By the time N.S. arrived, E.V. was already restraining the applicant on the ground. As N.S. and S.J. approached, they observed that the applicant was acting aggressively and using offensive language.
N.S. assisted E.V. in handcuffing the applicant with his hands behind his back. After being raised to his feet, the applicant was escorted to the police car. However, he refused instructions to remain still and calm and began kicking the vehicle. The officers consequently took him out of the car and placed him on the ground. N.S. restrained his hands and feet, while another officer knelt on him to hold his head down. Throughout the incident, the applicant resisted the officers, used offensive language and acted aggressively. He was restrained to stop him from injuring himself or anyone else. The officers did not strike him. The applicant continued resisting as he was placed in the police van and remained aggressive inside it. N.S. further stated that, at one stage, an elderly man approached the officers and offered them money that allegedly belonged to the applicant. The man was told, however, that there was no need to hand over the money at that time.

36. Later on 8 June 2009, the police investigator obtained statements from Officers S.T. and J.S., who had arrived at the scene of the applicant’s arrest in the police van. After stepping out of the van, J.S. saw Officers S.J. and N.S. holding the applicant on the ground. The applicant was behaving aggressively, shouting, swearing and trying to free himself. N.S. and S.J. escorted him to the van, whose door J.S. opened for them. J.S. did not observe the applicant strike anything while being placed inside. During the journey, however, noises resembling something being hit could be heard from the rear compartment. S.T. stated that he had remained inside the van. He heard no sound of the applicant striking anything as the applicant was being put into it. Once at the police station, S.T. and J.S. carried the applicant to the detention area and left him in front of the cells. S.T. saw no blood on either the applicant or his clothing and noticed no visible injuries.

37. On 8 June 2009, the police investigator also commissioned a forensic medical assessment of the applicant’s injuries based on the documentary material then available, namely the ambulance cards, the patient registration card, and statements given by the applicant, the suspects in the case and two other police officers acting as witnesses.

38. On 9 June 2009, the police investigator interviewed D.R., a police officer who had been on duty at the police station on 29 April 2009. D.R. said that he had begun his shift at 8 p.m. and had started processing the applicant’s documents at approximately 2 a.m. The applicant complained of a severe headache and pain in his hands caused by the handcuffs and asked for an ambulance. He also claimed that other police officers had caused his head injury. There was no blood on his clothing, and he did not vomit. D.R. accompanied the applicant when he was taken to hospital.

39. On 15 June 2009, the applicant’s legal representative filed a complaint concerning the police with the prosecutor’s office.
He submitted that the police had failed to carry out the investigative steps he had requested on 15 May 2009. Those measures included arranging for him to identify the police officers in person; conducting a formal confrontation between him and M.Z., who had allegedly seen him breach the peace; comparing his account with the circumstances at the scene of the alleged offence; obtaining a forensic medical assessment of his injuries; and interviewing the children identified by his representative, whose details had been provided to the police investigator on 27 May 2009. He asked the prosecutor to ensure that the necessary evidence was collected. On 1 July 2009 the prosecutor dismissed the complaint, explaining that the applicant had not contested any measure or order issued by an investigative authority.

40. On 17 June 2009 the police investigator presented the applicant with photographs for the purpose of identifying possible suspects. The record indicates that he was shown four sets containing an unspecified number of photographs of police officers with similar appearances. He identified S.B. as the officer who had assaulted him at the police station, although he could not recall whether S.B. had also struck him during the arrest. He was uncertain whether E.V. was the person depicted in one of the photographs. However, he stated that, if he saw the other officer in person, he would be able to recognise him by his facial features and height.

41. On 6 July 2009 the investigator interviewed V.Z., who had telephoned the police on 29 April 2009 to report the applicant’s alleged breach of the peace. V.Z. stated that, while sitting in his car at the intersection of Kreenholmi and Kerese Street, he had observed two young men crossing the road, one of whom was carrying a knife. A third young man, who appeared heavily intoxicated and was struggling to walk, was moving ahead of them. Concerned for the safety of passers-by and believing that the young men and the knife presented an obvious danger, he had called the police.

42. The forensic medical expert issued his opinion concerning the applicant’s injuries on 13 August 2009. He found that the injuries documented on 30 April and 1 May had resulted from blows delivered with one or more blunt objects. Their precise cause could not be determined because the descriptions contained in the records lacked sufficient detail. Nonetheless, the expert considered that the injuries had been sustained shortly before the applicant sought medical attention, possibly on 29 April 2009. He further observed that the absence of detailed descriptions of the injuries to the applicant’s upper limbs made it impossible to determine whether they had been sustained while acting in self-defence. None of the records provided information about the level of ethanol in the applicant’s blood; they merely stated that he had been under the influence of alcohol.

43.
On 2 September 2009, the forensic expert provided the police investigator with an oral statement concerning his written opinion. Asked whether the applicant had had a haematoma around his left eye on both 30 April and 1 May, he replied that the documents dated 30 April contained no such information. He explained that the haematoma might have been caused on 29 April, but could equally have been inflicted on 30 April or 1 May. As to the cause of the injuries, the expert stated that the records lacked sufficiently detailed descriptions to determine precisely what kind of object had caused the trauma.

44. On 14 September 2009, the police investigator showed M.Z. photographs of police officers for identification purposes. The record of the meeting indicates that M.Z. was presented with four lists containing an unspecified number of photographs of officers of similar appearance. He identified E.V. as one of the officers who, together with S.B., had beaten the applicant at the police station and used force against him at the playground. Although M.Z. could not identify S.B. with certainty from the photographs, he selected another officer whom he described as looking very similar to S.B. M.Z. further clarified that no beating had occurred at the playground; rather, the applicant’s arms had been twisted behind his back and he had been forced to the ground.

45. On 8 January 2010, the applicant complained to the prosecutor that, despite making repeated requests, he had still not been notified of any decision ordering a forensic medical examination. He stated that no expert had examined him, notwithstanding his complaints of headaches and loss of vision following the beating. He asked to receive a copy of any expert report that might have been prepared without his knowledge. The applicant also objected that no formal confrontation had been arranged between him, M.Z. and the suspects to resolve inconsistencies in their accounts. On 14 January 2010, the prosecutor dismissed the complaint, reiterating that the applicant had not challenged any act or order issued by an investigative authority.

46. On 20 January 2010, the police investigator terminated the investigation, finding no evidence that the officers had committed the criminal offence of abuse of authority. The investigator concluded that the force used had not breached the Police Act and had been lawful, justified and proportionate. The prosecutor approved that decision on 15 February 2010.

47. With regard to the applicant’s arrest, the police investigator considered his allegations of having been beaten to be entirely unfounded.
She found, in essence, that the force used during the applicant’s arrest was justified because, while intoxicated, he had breached the peace, disobeyed the officers’ lawful instructions, and attempted to leave the scene without their permission. The force employed to bring him to the ground, handcuff him, and keep him there was not considered excessive.

48. The decision treated the following account of the arrest as established. At the playground near 18 Kerese Street, the applicant had behaved inappropriately: he had waved his arms, used foul language, and staggered considerably. He had failed to respond to the police officers’ instructions. Officer E.V. had decided to handcuff him because children were nearby, the applicant was plainly in an aggressive state of mind and might injure others, and the call had arisen in a particular context, namely a suspicion that he was carrying a knife. Officers N.S. and S.J. had arrived at that point and assisted in applying the handcuffs. Instead of obeying the officers’ directions to remain still and calm down, the applicant had begun kicking the police vehicle. N.S. and S.J. had restrained him by holding him on the ground. He had continued to resist, swear, and act aggressively. His conduct had compelled E.V. to request a police van to take him to the police station. The applicant had resisted being placed in the van and had remained aggressive and continued using foul language during the journey. Noises coming from the transport compartment suggested that he had struck himself against something.

49. In determining that the applicant had not been beaten and that the officers had used only lawful force, the police investigator relied specifically on statements from the children; Police Officers N.S., S.J., J.S., and S.T.; the suspected officers S.B. and E.V.; and M.Z. During the presentation of the identification photographs, M.Z. had stated that no beating had occurred at the playground and that the applicant’s hands had merely been forced behind his back before he was brought to the ground.

50. As regards what occurred at the police department, the investigator dismissed M.Z.’s account as unreliable because he could not have observed what was happening to the applicant in the detention room. Although the room’s door had been open, M.Z. had been standing some distance away. Concerning those detained at the police station, the investigator found that their accounts did not directly substantiate the allegation that the applicant had been beaten. The statements of detainees A.P.
The accounts given by R.L. and another person, who had claimed that the applicant had been beaten, were rejected because they conflicted with the testimony of the third detainee, M.S., and with other evidence. Four police officers who had participated in the applicant’s arrest and transportation, together with an officer who had been at the police station while the applicant was detained there, likewise stated that no beating had occurred.

51. In addressing the applicant’s injuries, the police investigator relied on the observations recorded when the applicant was taken to sober up, as well as on the ambulance and patient registration records. The haematoma around the applicant’s left eye was first noted at the hospital on 1 May 2009. The investigator cited the forensic expert’s opinion that it could have been sustained on 29 April, 30 April or 1 May 2009, and that the available documents did not make it possible to determine its cause. On that basis, the investigator found the applicant’s claim that the haematoma had resulted from a beating at the police department to be false and unfounded. The applicant’s assertions that he had vomited and that his clothing had been stained with blood were also considered refuted by the statements of the police officers, the ambulance doctor and the nurse, none of whom had observed him vomiting or seen blood on his clothes.

52. The police investigator ultimately determined that, while at the police station, the applicant had behaved aggressively, continued using foul language and disobeyed instructions to remain still. The force employed by S.B. and E.V. was therefore deemed lawful, justified and not excessive.

53. On 15 March 2010, the applicant appealed against the decision to terminate the criminal investigation. He argued, among other things, that the investigation had lacked objectivity and that witness statements had been quoted selectively and misrepresented. He further complained that certain witnesses had not been interviewed, including Y.B., who had witnessed his arrest, and A.D., who had been held at the police station at the same time. He also pointed out that he had not undergone a forensic medical examination and that no formal confrontations had been organised to resolve inconsistencies between the statements obtained in the case.

54. On 23 March 2010, the State Prosecutor’s Office dismissed the appeal against the discontinuation decision on the ground that it had been submitted out of time. The decision terminating the criminal proceedings had specified that any appeal had to be filed with the State Prosecutor’s Office within ten days after receipt of that decision. It had been dispatched to the applicant’s address by ordinary post on 26 February 2010. According to information from Estonian Post, a standard letter was sent to the recipient on the post office’s next working day.
Accordingly, the letter should have been delivered to the applicant on 1 March 2010, making 11 March 2010 the deadline for lodging an appeal. He filed his appeal on 15 March 2010. The applicant maintained that he had not received the letter until 5 March 2010, when he returned home from working in another city. Although he had not applied for restoration of the appeal time-limit, the State Prosecutor’s Office observed that, in any event, there were no grounds for granting such a request. In its view, the applicant was required to exercise due diligence in monitoring his mail, since he was aware of pending proceedings in which decisions affecting his situation could be taken. It further considered that several means had been available to him to avoid missing the deadline.

55. On 30 April 2010, the Tartu Court of Appeal affirmed the State Prosecutor’s Office’s decision. It agreed with the applicant’s counsel that the period for appealing began on the date the decision was actually received, rather than on the date it was presumed to have arrived on the basis of standard postal delivery times. Nevertheless, the court found that the decision terminating the criminal proceedings had been placed in the applicant’s mailbox on 1 March 2010, without identifying the evidence supporting that finding. It also held that there was no need to rule on restoration of the appeal deadline, as the applicant did not consider that he had missed it and had not requested its restoration.

D. The applicant’s acquittal on misdemeanour charges
56. On 25 May 2009, the East Police Prefecture convicted the applicant of the misdemeanour of breaching the peace in Kreenholmi Street and imposed a fine. The applicant challenged that decision before the Viru County Court.

57. Following a public hearing on 4 November 2010, the Viru County Court acquitted the applicant on 17 November 2010, finding no evidence that his conduct had amounted to a misdemeanour.

58. The court excluded as unlawfully obtained evidence the statements made by the applicant in hospital at 2.15 a.m. on 30 April 2009 and recorded in the misdemeanour report drawn up there later that night, at 2.40 a.m. It observed that the evidence had been obtained more than eight hours after the alleged offence and after the applicant had, in the interim, been taken to sober up at 7.45 p.m.

59. The court regarded as credible the testimony given by M.Z. at the hearing on 4 November 2010. M.Z. stated that the police had improperly pressured him into giving evidence against the applicant by allowing him to hear the applicant being beaten. In the court’s view, this account was supported by the fact that the applicant had been taken to hospital and questioned there.

60. On the basis of the statements made by the applicant and M.Z., the hospital records, and the time and place at which the misdemeanour report had been prepared, the court found that the evidence in the proceedings had been gathered unlawfully, violating the applicant’s honour and dignity and placing his health at risk.

61. The court also found a material breach of the rules governing misdemeanour proceedings. Although the applicant had been arrested at 5.40 p.m. and taken directly to the police station, he was not taken to sober up until 7.45 p.m. Moreover, his statement was obtained only at 2.15 a.m. in the hospital, where the misdemeanour report was not drawn up until 2.40 a.m.

62. The East Police Prefecture did not appeal against the judgment.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
63. Under section 13(1)(1) of the Police Act (Politseiseadus), in the version applicable at the relevant time, the police were empowered to require individuals and officials to preserve public order and bring any breaches of it to an end, and to use against offenders the coercive measures laid down by law.

64. Section 14(2) of the Police Act, as applicable at the relevant time, required the police to warn a person before subjecting him or her to coercive measures. Such a warning could be omitted only where it was impossible to give one because an offence had to be terminated urgently.

65. Pursuant to section 14(2)(1) of the Police Act, in force at the relevant time, a police officer was entitled to employ physical force where no other administrative coercive measure could ensure compliance with an obligation imposed by a valid administrative act for the purpose of identifying or averting a threat or putting an end to an offence.

66. Article 291 of the Penal Code (Karistusseadustik), headed “Abuse of authority”, provided at the relevant time that an official who unlawfully used a weapon, special equipment or physical force while carrying out his or her official duties was liable to a fine or imprisonment for a term of one to five years.

67. Article 77 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Kriminaalmenetluse seadustik) permits a confrontation where contradictions between statements cannot be resolved by other means. In the course of the confrontation, the relationship between the persons involved is established, after which they are questioned in turn about the conflicting facts. Earlier statements made by a person participating in the confrontation may be disclosed, and additional evidence may be presented. With the authorisation of an official from the investigative body, the persons confronted may, through that official, put questions to one another concerning the inconsistencies in their statements.

68. Article 81 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows, where necessary, a photograph, film, or audio or video recording of a person, item or other object to be used for identification.

69. According to Article 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a criminal offence may be reported orally or in writing to an investigative authority or a Prosecutor’s Office. The same provision requires a report made on the premises of either an investigative authority or a Prosecutor’s Office to be reduced to writing, while a report communicated by telephone must be documented either in writing or by means of an audio recording.

CASE OF MIHHAILOV v. ESTONIA

(Application no. 64418/10)

In Mihhailov v. Estonia,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Işıl Karakaş, President,
Julia Laffranque,
Paul Lemmens,
Valeriu Griţco,

Georges Ravarani, judges,

and Stanley Naismith, Section Registrar,

After deliberating in private on 28 June 2016,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 64418/10, brought against the Republic of Estonia before the Court on 28 October 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Aleksandr Mihhailov (“the applicant”), a stateless person.

2. Mr A. Gamazin, a lawyer practising in Narva, represented the applicant. The Estonian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Kuurberg of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

3. The applicant claimed that the police had subjected him to unjustified violence both when arresting him and during his subsequent detention at the police station.

4. On 13 February 2014, notice of the complaint relating to police violence was given to the Government, while the rest of the application was found inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1976, the applicant resides in Narva, Estonia.

A. Arrest of the applicant
6. Shortly before 6 p.m. on 29 April 2009, the police emergency call centre was informed of two young men at the intersection of Kreenholmi and Kerese streets in Narva, Estonia. According to the caller, one of them had a knife, while the other appeared clearly intoxicated and was struggling to walk. The caller believed that they posed a danger to people passing by. At 5.55 p.m., patrol Officers S.B. and E.V. were directed to attend the scene. At approximately 6 p.m., they located the two men—the applicant and M.Z.—at a public playground.

7. The applicant’s account of his encounter with the police, as set out in his application and the materials he submitted to the Court, was as follows. At about 6 p.m. on 29 April 2009, he and M.Z., both of whom were drunk, were waiting at a playground for an acquaintance, Y.B. Two police officers approached the applicant. He neither acted aggressively nor swore at them. He spoke to the officers but could not remember the precise content of their conversation, other than that it concerned a knife and that he told them he did not have one. He also remembered that one officer was called Andrei, who was later identified as S.B. S.B. then punched him in the jaw, causing him to fall and strike his face in a hole in the pavement. He briefly lost consciousness. When he tried to stand up, he was struck again on the back, near the base of his neck. One officer placed a knee on his neck and pressed him against the ground. After he had been handcuffed, the officers began kicking and punching him across his head and body. He lost consciousness following the assault and did not regain it until he was at the police station.

8. The Government stated that the domestic criminal investigation had established a different sequence of events surrounding the applicant’s arrest. Before finding the applicant and M.Z. at the playground, the officers had received a report concerning two men, one of whom might have had a knife, while the other was said to be intoxicated and having trouble walking. At the playground, the applicant acted aggressively and used obscene language. Officer E.V. attempted to speak with him, but the applicant behaved erratically, waving his arms and shouting at the officers. E.V. therefore decided to restrain him on the ground and keep him there until a police patrol vehicle arrived. With assistance from Officers S.J. and N.S., who arrived by car, E.V. handcuffed the applicant. While restrained on the ground, the applicant tried to rise, kicked out, and continued directing obscenities at the officers. The officers neither beat him nor applied excessive force. The applicant continued resisting as he was placed in a police van, the final vehicle to arrive, which was occupied by Officers S.T. and J.S.
The officers therefore had to use a degree of force to place the applicant inside the van. While this was being done, his left temple struck the van door. He continued to behave aggressively while being transported. From the front seats, the officers heard noises from the rear compartment that sounded as though one object was being repeatedly struck against another.

B. The applicant’s detention at the police station and subsequent admission to hospital
9. The version of events during his detention given by the applicant, as set out in his application and the material filed with the Court, may be summarised as follows. On regaining consciousness in a room adjoining the police station’s detention cells, he found himself lying handcuffed on the floor, with the two officers who had been at the playground standing before him. When he tried to get up, S.B. struck him with a knee near his left ear. He then attempted to sit on a chair, but was knocked down and instructed to remain seated on the floor. Once E.V. had left, S.B., wearing black leather gloves, began repeatedly punching and kicking him. The applicant got to his feet and fell over several times. At one stage, he was brought to the toilet, where the sink tap was opened and his head was held under the running water, after which he was returned to the detention room. As he passed the cells, he asked the detainees whether they would corroborate anything they had heard or witnessed. Back in the room, he sat on the chair, and S.B. again punched him several times. When E.V. came back, the applicant was knocked from the chair and beaten all over his body. After E.V. departed, S.B. carried on assaulting him. The applicant briefly lost consciousness; when he regained awareness, his face was bloody, and he was ultimately placed on the chair. The handcuffs were taken off, and he was permitted to use the toilet, where he washed. After returning to the detention room, he was put in a cell to sober up. Some time later, an ambulance arrived and transported him to hospital, accompanied by other police officers. His clothing was stained with blood; he discarded the T-shirt, while his mother washed the trousers.

10. The Government submitted that the facts established during the ensuing criminal investigation presented a different sequence of events. At the police station, the applicant remained handcuffed and continued acting aggressively. He approached detainees in other cells, yelling that police officers were beating him. Because he ignored instructions to stay still and calm down, officers had to apply physical force to seat him or put him on the floor. As he started settling down, he was seated on a chair with his hands still cuffed. He abruptly lost his balance and fell face first from the chair. The officers picked him up and returned him to the seat. Soon afterwards, he fell to the floor once more. For his own protection, the officers then left him seated on the floor. His handcuffs were removed as soon as he had calmed down, following which he was placed in a cell to sober up. Testing indicated that he was moderately intoxicated by alcohol.

11. At 7.45 p.m., Officers S.B. and J.S. prepared a report stating that the applicant had been brought from 10 Kreenholmi Street to recover from alcohol intoxication.
The report recorded that the applicant was intoxicated by alcohol, had difficulty walking, had fallen, and had behaved aggressively. It further noted that his face was dirty and that there were abrasions on his head.

12. At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009, at the applicant’s request, Officer P.S. summoned an ambulance to the police station. Ambulance registration card no. 1419 indicated that the applicant reported pain on the left side of his head and in his right wrist, together with nausea, vomiting, and loss of hearing in his left ear. Examination revealed haematomas on the left side of his cranium, swelling of the right wrist, and alcoholic intoxication. He was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and fractures of the right hand and wrist, and was transported to hospital.

13. Subsequently, at the hospital, patient registration card no. 4460, dated 30 April 2009, recorded that the applicant complained of vomiting and loss of consciousness. The examination identified haematomas and oedema around his left ear and eye. He was diagnosed with concussion and alcoholic intoxication.

14. At 2.15 a.m. on 30 April 2009, police officers other than those alleged to have assaulted the applicant at the police station took his statement in the hospital. At 2.40 a.m., those officers prepared a misdemeanour report stating that, while drunk in the public area of Kreenholmi Street, he had engaged in brawling, shouted, and used obscene language, thereby breaching the peace and disturbing others.

15. At 6.26 a.m. on 30 April 2009, the applicant underwent a computer tomography scan. Its findings were: “temporal extracranial swelling on the left side, no haemorrhage, no intracranial pathology or haemorrhage, ventricular system symmetric, no midline shift, cranial bones intact and paranasal sinuses, middle ear spaces aerated”. He was discharged from hospital afterwards.

16. On 1 May 2009, while near his home, the applicant called an ambulance. According to ambulance registration card no. 1454, he complained of intense headaches, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and neck pain. Examination showed a haematoma surrounding the left ear, oedema around the left eye, and alcoholic intoxication. He was diagnosed with concussion and transported to hospital. There, a traumatology doctor examined him and observed a paraorbital haematoma and swelling around the left eye, bruising on the neck and upper limbs, alcohol odour from his mouth, dysarthria, and a staggering gait. The diagnoses were concussion and alcoholic intoxication. The applicant declined to remain in hospital.

C. Investigation of the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment
17. On 30 April 2009, the applicant reported to the police that he had been ill-treated. He claimed that police officers had beaten him during his arrest and had assaulted him again while he was detained at the police station. The officer on duty declined to handle the complaint, directing him instead to the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor likewise refused to process it and told him to submit it to the police. After returning to the police station, the applicant was permitted by a police investigator to lodge his complaint.

18. On 5 May 2009, the applicant also wrote to the prosecutor’s office concerning the same events. That day, the police decided to initiate a criminal investigation into his allegations. The Government stated that, on the following day, 6 May, the police investigator requested the applicant’s medical records from the hospital.

19. On 13 May 2009, the applicant was interviewed by the police investigator and presented his version of the events (see paragraphs 7 and 9 above).

20. Also on 13 May 2009, the investigator obtained a statement from A.P., who had remained in the police station’s sobering-up cell until 9 p.m. on 29 April 2009. A.P. said that, through the peephole in his cell door, he had observed a young man whose hands were handcuffed behind his back being brought into the room opposite the sobering-up cells. An officer identified by the name S.B. on his badge knocked the young man to the ground. Whenever the man tried to rise, the officer prevented him, instructed him to remain on the floor, and knocked him down again. Both the officer and the young man used offensive language. A.P. also heard slaps landing on someone’s body and saw the officer moving his hands toward the detainee in a swinging motion, leading him to understand that the young man was being struck. The detainee was subsequently moved into an adjoining room. A.P. then heard him screaming and pleading for the beating to end. In A.P.’s view, some form of physical altercation had unquestionably occurred between the young man and the officers. The man was later placed in a cell, where he continued shouting and asked for a doctor, although he eventually became silent.

21. On 15 May 2009, the applicant’s lawyer wrote to the police seeking several investigative steps. Among other things, he requested that the applicant be given an opportunity to identify the two officers who had arrested him, transported him to the police department, and used force against him at the station. He further asked that the applicant be brought back to the police station so that his account could be assessed against the actual arrangement of the premises and he could describe at the scene what had occurred.
He also asked investigators to question the applicant’s mother about his health when he left home on 29 April and when he came back on 30 April, to interview the ambulance doctor and nurse as witnesses, and to arrange a forensic medical assessment of the applicant’s injuries.

22. On 15 May 2009, the police investigator obtained a statement from M.S., who had been confined in the police station’s sobering-up cell on 29 April 2009. M.S. stated that he had heard someone in the adjoining room shout for help at one point and police officers shout back. However, whenever he occasionally looked through the eyehole, he did not see any officers beating anyone.

23. The police investigator also interviewed Police Officer S.J. on 15 May 2009. S.J. and Officer N.S. had travelled in a police car to the location where the applicant was arrested. Before leaving the vehicle, they saw Officer E.V. speaking with the applicant, after which a struggle broke out between them. S.J. and N.S. rushed from the car, but the applicant had already been put on the ground by the time they arrived. He behaved aggressively and directed obscene language at E.V. S.J. used his knee to limit the applicant’s movements and keep him down. Because the applicant continued to resist physically, S.J. and N.S. assisted E.V. in handcuffing his hands behind his back. The applicant tried to rise, persisted in using indecent language and refused to follow instructions. Consequently, the officers held him on the ground until a police van arrived to take him to the police station. They applied no additional force. S.J. also reported that an elderly man approached the officers at some stage and tried to give them money said to belong to the applicant. The man was informed that there was no need to hand over the money at that moment. According to S.J., Officer S.B. had meanwhile been nearby, speaking to another young man who possessed a knife.

24. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator interviewed R.L., who had been detained in the police station’s sobering-up cell on 29 April 2009. R.L. said that, through the door, he heard officers drag someone into the room opposite the cells. He then heard the officers goad the person into speaking rudely, yell at him while themselves using offensive language, and begin beating him. Although R.L. could not recall precisely how the blows had been delivered, he believed that the officers had punched and kicked the person. The person tried to get to his feet, but the officers prevented him from doing so by knocking him down. He was subsequently moved to a different room.

25. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator obtained a statement from M.Z. Regarding the arrest, M.Z. explained that, before the events occurring at approximately 6 p.m.
On 29 April 2009, he and the applicant had consumed several beers. They had just sat down in a playground behind some buildings when a police car carrying three officers arrived. One officer approached him, while the other two went over to the applicant and knocked him down. One policeman pressed his leg against the applicant’s neck, and the other tried to stand on his legs. M.Z. was then brought to the place where the applicant had been assaulted. The applicant was lying face down on the asphalt, with his face in sand that had collected in a hole in the surface. Some time later, a police van arrived with two officers. The applicant’s arms were placed behind his back, he was handcuffed, raised to his feet, and taken towards the van. During this process, one of the officers struck him on the head with an open hand. The applicant was placed inside the van and transported to the police station.

26. As to what occurred at the station, M.Z. stated that the applicant had been taken into the area containing the cells. M.Z. was left in the corridor immediately beyond the detention section. Through the open doors, he saw the applicant being forced onto the floor directly in front of the doorway, after which two policemen began assaulting him. They struck him with their elbows and kicked him in the back of the head and other parts of his body. No other officers entered the room. Both those doors and the door to the duty room remained open, yet nobody emerged from the duty room. After a while, one of the policemen involved in beating the applicant approached M.Z. and escorted him to an office to give a statement. M.Z. made a statement against the applicant because he was frightened, having witnessed that officer assault his friend.

27. On 18 May 2009, the police investigator also obtained a statement from P.S., an officer who had been on duty at the station while the applicant was detained. P.S. said that, upon reporting for work at 8 p.m. on 29 April 2009, Officer E.V. informed him that the individual placed in a temporary detention cell—namely, the applicant—might ask for an ambulance and should be monitored periodically. During the night, the applicant walked unaided to the toilet, reported being in pain, but refused an offer to summon an ambulance. Later that night, when he was due to be released, he asked for an ambulance, which P.S. called. P.S. heard the applicant tell the doctor and nurse that police officers had assaulted him. Asked by P.S. which officers were responsible, the applicant said they were those who had brought him to the station. When P.S. asked where the assault had occurred, the applicant answered that it had taken place in the street during his arrest. The ambulance subsequently transported him to hospital.

28. On 27 May 2009, the police investigator obtained a statement from K.I., who had been serving in the police station’s command centre when the events at issue occurred.
As he was leaving and passed the detention room, he saw the applicant sitting on its floor in handcuffs. The applicant was intoxicated, acting aggressively and using offensive language. K.I. stated that no one had beaten the applicant in his presence and that the applicant had neither alleged that he had been beaten nor asked for an ambulance.

29. On 2 June 2009, the police investigator obtained a statement from Police Officer S.B., one of the suspects. S.B. explained that he and Officer E.V. had walked to the playground between the buildings at 10 Kreenholmi Street and 18 Kerese Street. On their arrival, the applicant was heavily intoxicated and arguing with another man about money. S.B. then moved farther away to speak with M.Z. and consequently did not witness what occurred between the applicant and Officer E.V., including how E.V. forced the applicant to the ground. Although M.Z. had no knife, he was wearing a large sheath on his belt. S.B. had no contact with the applicant. He nevertheless observed that the applicant remained aggressive after E.V. had brought him to the ground, while Officers S.J. and N.S. assisted E.V. in handcuffing him and holding him there. S.B. also witnessed Officers S.T. and J.S. helping to put the applicant into the police van. No one kicked or punched the applicant. During the journey to the police station, thumping and banging could be heard from the van’s rear compartment.

30. S.B. further stated that, upon arrival at the police station, the officers placed the applicant in the room opposite the detention cells and left the door open. S.B. remained alone there with the applicant for approximately 40 minutes but did not beat him. Because the applicant refused instructions to calm down and remain on the floor, S.B. was unable to remove his handcuffs and had to use force to keep him on the floor and settle him down. E.V. assisted him at one point. After the applicant had calmed somewhat, he was moved to another room so that his statement could be taken. He was seated on a chair, with his hands still cuffed behind his back. While seated in the detention room, the applicant abruptly fell face first from the chair. E.V. entered the interrogation room at that moment and, together with S.B., lifted the applicant back onto the chair. The applicant fell off once more and was again helped back onto it. Once the paperwork was completed, he was placed in a cell to sober up. Apart from several old scratches on his head, he had no bodily injuries and did not ask for medical assistance.

31. On 3 June 2009, the police investigator took statements from four children who had witnessed the applicant’s arrest: A.N., D.K., D.B. and E.G. Three of them—A.N., D.K. and D.B.—had seen the intoxicated applicant arguing with an elderly man about money. According to A.N.’s statement
According to D.K. and the other witness, two police officers arrived and initially spoke to the applicant and the older man. A.N., D.K. and D.B. reported that one officer then moved farther away to deal with the applicant’s companion, who had a knife sheath. A.N. stated that the applicant began shouting obscenities at the officer who remained with him. A.N., D.K. and D.B. said that, after an exchange between them, the officer forced the applicant to the ground. A.N. and D.K. described the officer as pushing him over, and D.K. added that the applicant was placed face down with his right cheek against the ground. Two additional officers arrived by car and helped the first officer handcuff the applicant’s hands behind his back.

Every child witness, including E.G., who arrived after the applicant had been taken to the ground, confirmed that the officers forcibly kept him there. A.N. and E.G. said that the officers stood on his legs. D.K. and D.B., by contrast, stated that one officer knelt on the applicant’s neck to hold his head down while another stood on his legs near his heels. All the children agreed that the officers neither kicked nor punched him. The applicant tried to rise, continued swearing and said that the officers were hurting him. They also unanimously confirmed that he resisted when the officers attempted to walk him to the police van. The police used force to place him inside, during which he struck his head against the van door; according to D.B. and E.G., it was the left side of his head.

32. On 4 June 2009, the police investigator obtained statements from ambulance nurse L.G. and ambulance doctor V.K. They had been called to the police station regarding a man with head trauma. The applicant, who was intoxicated, told them that police officers had beaten him at the station. There was no blood on his clothing, and he did not vomit. Nevertheless, because of the nature of his injuries, the doctor decided that he should be taken to hospital for further examination.

33. On 8 June 2009, Police Officer E.V., the other suspect, made a statement. He said that he had been instructed to respond to a report that a man who was heavily intoxicated and might be carrying a knife was walking along Kreenholmi Street. He and his partner, Officer S.B., immediately went to the location where the man was thought to be. Upon arriving at the building at 10 Kreenholmi Street, E.V. saw the applicant behaving inappropriately, waving his arms and staggering. As the officers approached the men, M.Z. took the applicant by the hand and led him behind the building at 10 Kreenholmi Street. The officers followed and found the applicant seated on a kerbstone beside M.Z., with an elderly man standing nearby. When E.V. and S.B. came closer, the applicant stood and staggered towards them, while M.Z. walked off in another direction. Once the applicant reached the officers, E.V. politely asked him to stop.
When the applicant ignored E.V. and continued walking past, E.V. took hold of his elbow to stop him and addressed him once more. The applicant responded very violently, arguing and gesticulating. E.V. consequently radioed for assistance so that the applicant could be removed and allowed to sober up. In the meantime, the elderly man came over and urged the applicant to calm down, pointing out that he was dealing with police officers. The applicant said that he did not care, threw money onto the ground and told the man to keep it. The man picked up the money, stated that he did not need it, and returned it to the applicant’s pockets. By then, S.B. had followed M.Z. Although E.V. tried to settle the applicant, he continued pacing back and forth, waving his hands and uttering obscenities. Because many children were present, E.V. decided to place him in handcuffs. The applicant was plainly aggressive and could have injured others, especially in view of the possible presence of a knife. When the applicant resisted being handcuffed, E.V. forced him to the ground but did not strike him. Officers N.S. and S.J. then arrived, assisted in handcuffing the applicant, and took him to the police car located 10 metres away. No knife was found on the applicant. E.V. had no further contact with him at the playground. During the journey to the station in the police van, the applicant remained aggressive, and E.V. heard noises that sounded as though the applicant was hitting himself against something.

34. E.V. also stated that, at the police station, the applicant shouted that the police were beating him while S.B. attempted to calm him and carry out a search. E.V. left the room to question M.Z. as a witness concerning the applicant’s breach of the peace. On returning, E.V. saw that the applicant had fallen face down from his chair, and he helped S.B. lift him back onto it. After the applicant fell to the floor a second time, he was left there. In E.V.’s view, the applicant was deliberately trying to injure himself so that he could later make accusations against the police. Once he became calm, his handcuffs were removed. He then walked without assistance to the sobering-up cell. He had no injuries requiring immediate medical treatment. Although there were haematomas on his face, they could have been sustained during transportation or when he fell from the chair. His clothing was dirty but bore no bloodstains. E.V. told the applicant that an ambulance would be summoned if he had any health-related complaints.

35. Later that same day, 8 June 2009, the investigator obtained a statement from Officer N.S., who, together with Officer S.J., had arrived by police car at the place where the applicant was arrested. By the time N.S. reached the scene, Officer E.V. was already restraining the applicant on the ground. As N.S. and S.J. approached, they observed that the applicant was acting aggressively and using foul language.
N.S. assisted E.V. in handcuffing the applicant with his hands behind his back. After being helped to his feet, the applicant was taken to the police car. However, he disobeyed instructions to remain still and calm and began kicking the vehicle. The officers consequently took him out of the car and placed him on the ground. N.S. restrained his hands and feet, while another officer knelt on him to hold his head down. Throughout the incident, the applicant resisted the officers, acted aggressively and used offensive language. He was restrained on the ground to stop him from injuring either himself or others. The officers did not strike him. The applicant continued resisting as he was placed in the police van and remained aggressive inside it. N.S. further stated that, at one point, an elderly man approached the officers and offered them money that allegedly belonged to the applicant. The man was told, however, that there was no need to hand over the money at that time.

36. Later that same day, 8 June 2009, the police investigator obtained statements from Officers S.T. and J.S., who had arrived at the location of the applicant’s arrest in the police van. Upon leaving the van, J.S. observed Officers S.J. and N.S. restraining the applicant on the ground. The applicant was behaving aggressively, shouting, swearing and trying to free himself. N.S. and S.J. brought him to the police van, whose door J.S. opened for them. J.S. did not see the applicant strike or collide with anything, although during the journey noises resembling something being hit came from the rear compartment. S.T. said that he had remained inside the van. He heard no sounds of the applicant banging against anything while the applicant was being placed in it. Once at the police station, S.T. and J.S. carried the applicant to the detention room and left him in front of the cells. S.T. observed neither blood on the applicant or his clothing nor any visible injuries.

37. Also on 8 June 2009, the police investigator commissioned a forensic medical examination of the injuries based on the documentary material then available, namely the ambulance cards, the patient registration card, and statements from the applicant, the suspects in the case and two other police officers acting as witnesses.

38. On 9 June 2009, the police investigator interviewed D.R., a police officer who had been on duty at the police station on 29 April 2009. D.R. stated that he had reported for work at 8 p.m. and had begun processing the applicant’s documents at approximately 2 a.m. The applicant complained of a severe headache and pain in his hands caused by the handcuffs, and asked for an ambulance. He also alleged that other police officers had caused his head injury. There was no blood on his clothing, and he did not vomit. D.R. accompanied the applicant when he was taken to hospital.

39. On 15 June 2009, the applicant’s legal representative submitted a complaint concerning the police to the prosecutor’s office.
He maintained that the police had failed to carry out the investigative steps he had sought on 15 May 2009. Those steps included arranging for the police officers to be presented for identification; conducting a formal confrontation between him and M.Z., who had allegedly seen him breach the peace; comparing his account with the conditions at the location of the alleged offence; obtaining a forensic medical assessment of his injuries; and interviewing the children identified by his representative, whose details had been provided to the police investigator on 27 May 2009. He asked the prosecutor to ensure that evidence was gathered. On 1 July 2009, the prosecutor dismissed the complaint on the ground that the applicant had not contested any act or order issued by an investigative authority.

40. On 17 June 2009, the police investigator presented the applicant with photographs for the purpose of identifying possible suspects. The meeting record indicates that he was shown four sets containing an unspecified number of photographs of police officers with similar appearances. He recognised S.B. as the officer who had assaulted him at the police station, although he could not recall whether S.B. had also struck him during the arrest. He was not certain that the person shown in the photographs was E.V. Nonetheless, he said that, if he saw the other officer in person, he could identify him by his physical features and height.

41. On 6 July 2009, the police investigator obtained a statement from V.Z., who had contacted the police on 29 April 2009 regarding the applicant’s alleged disturbance of the peace. V.Z. said that, while sitting in his car at the junction of Kreenholmi and Kerese Street, he had observed two young men crossing the road, one of whom was carrying a knife. Another young man, who appeared heavily intoxicated and was struggling to walk, was moving ahead of him. After noticing the young men and the knife, V.Z. called the police because he regarded them as plainly dangerous and feared for the safety of people passing by.

42. On 13 August 2009, the forensic medical expert issued an opinion concerning the applicant’s injuries. The expert determined that the injuries documented on 30 April and 1 May had resulted from blows delivered with one or more blunt objects. Their precise cause could not be determined because the records did not describe them in sufficient detail. Even so, the expert found that the injuries had been sustained shortly before the applicant consulted a doctor, possibly on 29 April 2009. The expert further observed that, owing to the absence of detailed descriptions of the injuries to the upper limbs, it was impossible to determine whether they had been sustained while acting in self-defence. Although none of the documents contained information about the level of ethanol in the applicant’s blood, they stated generally that he had been intoxicated by alcohol.

43.
On 2 September 2009, the forensic expert orally clarified his written opinion for the police investigator. Asked whether the applicant had had a haematoma around his left eye on both 30 April and 1 May, he said that the documents dated 30 April contained no such information. He explained that the haematoma might have been caused on 29 April, although it could equally have been inflicted on 30 April or 1 May. As to the cause of the injuries, the expert stated that the absence of detailed descriptions in the documents made it impossible to determine precisely what kind of object had caused the traumas.

44. On 14 September 2009, the police investigator showed M.Z. photographs of officers for identification purposes. The record of that meeting indicated that M.Z. had been presented with four lists containing an unspecified number of photographs of police officers with similar appearances. He identified E.V. as one of the officers who, together with S.B., had beaten the applicant at the police station and used force against him at the playground. Although M.Z. could not confidently identify S.B. from the photographs, he selected another officer who, in his words, closely resembled S.B. M.Z. further stated that the applicant had not been beaten at the playground; rather, his arms had merely been twisted behind his back and he had been forced onto the ground.

45. On 8 January 2010, the applicant lodged a complaint with the prosecutor, stating that despite repeated requests, he had still not been notified of any decision ordering a forensic medical examination. He added that no expert had yet examined him, notwithstanding his complaints of headaches and loss of vision following the beating. He asked to receive a copy of any expert report that might have been prepared without his knowledge. He also complained that no formal confrontation had been arranged between him, M.Z. and the suspects to resolve inconsistencies in their statements. On 14 January 2010, the prosecutor dismissed the complaint, reiterating that the applicant had not contested any act or order issued by an investigative authority.

46. On 20 January 2010, the police investigator terminated the investigation after finding no evidence that the police officers had committed the criminal offence of abuse of authority. The investigator concluded that their use of force had complied with the Police Act and had been lawful, warranted and proportionate. The prosecutor approved that decision on 15 February 2010.

47. With respect to the applicant’s arrest, the police investigator considered his allegations that he had been beaten to be entirely unfounded.
In essence, she found that the force used against the applicant during his arrest had been warranted because, while intoxicated by alcohol, he had disturbed the peace, disobeyed lawful police instructions, and attempted to leave without the officers’ permission. The physical force employed to bring him to the ground, handcuff him, and hold him there had not been disproportionate.

48. According to the factual findings in the decision, the arrest had unfolded as follows. At the playground near 18 Kerese Street, the applicant had behaved improperly: he had waved his arms, used offensive language, and staggered considerably. He had failed to respond to the police officers’ commands. Officer E.V. had decided to handcuff him because children were nearby, the applicant was plainly in an aggressive state of mind and might have harmed others, and the call had involved a particular concern—namely, a suspicion that he was carrying a knife. Officers N.S. and S.J. had then arrived and assisted in applying the handcuffs. Instead of obeying instructions to remain still and calm down, the applicant had begun kicking the police vehicle. N.S. and S.J. had restrained him by holding him on the ground. He had continued resisting, swearing, and acting aggressively. His conduct had compelled E.V. to request a police van to take him to the police station. The applicant had resisted being placed in the van and, during the journey, had continued behaving aggressively and using foul language. Noises coming from the transport compartment suggested that he had struck himself against something.

49. In finding that the applicant had not been beaten and that the officers had used only lawful force, the police investigator relied specifically on statements from the children; Police Officers N.S., S.J., J.S., and S.T.; the police officers under suspicion, S.B. and E.V.; and M.Z. When shown the identification photographs, M.Z. had stated that no beating had occurred at the playground: the applicant’s arms had merely been forced behind his back, and he had been brought to the ground.

50. As regards what had occurred at the police department, the police investigator considered M.Z.’s account unreliable because he could not have observed what was happening to the applicant in the detention room. Although the room’s door had been open, M.Z. had been standing farther away. Concerning those detained at the police station, the investigator found that their statements did not directly establish that the applicant had been beaten. The statements made by detainees A.P.
The statements of R.L. and another person, both of whom had claimed that the applicant had been beaten, were rejected because they conflicted with the account given by the third detainee, M.S., and with other evidence. Four additional police officers who had participated in the applicant’s arrest and transportation, together with an officer who had been at the police station while the applicant was detained there, likewise stated that he had not been beaten.

51. In addressing the applicant’s injuries, the police investigator relied on the observations recorded when the applicant was taken to sober up, as well as on the ambulance and patient registration cards. The haematoma around his left eye had first been documented at the hospital on 1 May 2009. The investigator referred to the forensic expert’s conclusion that it might have been sustained on 29 April, 30 April or 1 May 2009 and that the available documents did not make it possible to determine how it had been caused. On that basis, the investigator concluded that the applicant’s claim that the haematoma had resulted from his being beaten at the police department was false and without foundation. The investigator also considered the applicant’s assertions that he had vomited and that his clothes had been stained with blood to have been refuted by the accounts of the police officers, the ambulance doctor and the nurse, none of whom had observed either blood on his clothing or any vomiting.

52. The police investigator ultimately found that, while at the police station, the applicant had behaved aggressively, continued using offensive language and disregarded instructions to remain still. The force employed by S.B. and E.V. had therefore been lawful and justified and had not been disproportionate.

53. On 15 March 2010, the applicant appealed against the decision terminating the criminal investigation. Among other arguments, he alleged that the investigation had lacked objectivity; that witness statements had been quoted selectively and misrepresented; that certain witnesses had not been interviewed, including Y.B., who had witnessed the applicant’s arrest, and A.D., who had been detained at the police station at the same time; that he had not undergone a forensic medical examination; and that no formal confrontations had been organised to resolve inconsistencies between the statements obtained in the case.

54. On 23 March 2010, the State Prosecutor’s Office dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decision to end the investigation because it had been submitted after the applicable deadline. The decision discontinuing the criminal proceedings had informed the applicant that any appeal to the State Prosecutor’s Office had to be filed within ten days after he received that decision. It had been dispatched to his address by ordinary post on 26 February 2010. According to information provided by Estonian Post, an ordinary letter was delivered to its addressee on the post office’s next working day.
The letter was therefore deemed to have arrived on 1 March 2010, making 11 March 2010 the last day on which the applicant could appeal. He lodged his appeal on 15 March 2010. According to the applicant, he received the letter only on 5 March 2010, after returning home from work in another city. Although he had not applied for restoration of the appeal time-limit, the State Prosecutor’s Office maintained that, in any case, there were no grounds for doing so. In its view, the applicant was required to exercise due diligence in monitoring his mail, since he knew that proceedings were pending in which decisions affecting his situation could be taken. It further considered that he had had several means of preventing the time-limit from expiring.

55. On 30 April 2010, the Tartu Court of Appeal affirmed the State Prosecutor’s Office’s decision. It accepted the argument of the applicant’s counsel that the appeal period began on the date when the decision was actually received, rather than on the date when it should have arrived according to calculated postal delivery times. Nonetheless, the court found that the decision discontinuing the criminal proceedings had been delivered to the applicant’s mailbox on 1 March 2010, without identifying the evidence on which that finding was based. It also held that there was no reason to address restoration of the appeal deadline, as the applicant did not consider that he had missed it and had not requested its restoration.

D. The applicant’s acquittal on misdemeanour charges
56. On 25 May 2009, the East Police Prefecture convicted the applicant of the misdemeanour of breaching the peace on Kreenholmi Street and imposed a fine. The applicant challenged that decision before the Viru County Court.

57. Following a public hearing held on 4 November, the Viru County Court acquitted the applicant on 17 November 2010. It found that no evidence established that his conduct amounted to a misdemeanour.

58. The court excluded, as unlawfully obtained evidence, the statements made by the applicant in hospital at 2.15 a.m. on 30 April 2009 and recorded in the misdemeanour report drawn up there that night at 2.40 a.m. It observed that this evidence had been obtained more than eight hours after the alleged offence and after the applicant had, in the meantime, been taken to sober up at 7.45 p.m.

59. The court found credible the testimony given by M.Z. at the hearing on 4 November 2010. M.Z. had stated that the police had improperly pressured him into giving evidence against the applicant by allowing him to hear the applicant being beaten. In the court’s view, this account was supported by the fact that the applicant had been taken to hospital and questioned there.

60. On the basis of the applicant’s and M.Z.’s statements, the hospital information, and the location and timing of the preparation of the misdemeanour report, the court concluded that the evidence in the misdemeanour proceedings had been obtained unlawfully, violating the applicant’s honour and dignity and placing his health at risk.

61. The court also held that the rules governing misdemeanour proceedings had been materially breached: although the applicant had been arrested at 5.40 p.m. and immediately taken to the police station, he was not taken to sober up until 7.45 p.m.; moreover, his statement was not obtained in hospital until 2.15 a.m., and the misdemeanour report was not drawn up there until 2.40 a.m.

62. The East Police Prefecture did not appeal the judgment.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
63. Under section 13(1)(1) of the Police Act (Politseiseadus), in the version applicable at the material time, the police were entitled to require individuals and officials to preserve public order and put an end to any breaches of it, and to use the coercive measures provided for by law against offenders.

64. Section 14(2) of the Police Act, as applicable at the material time, required the police to warn a person before using coercive measures against him or her. Such a warning could be omitted only where the urgent need to stop an offence made it impossible to give one.

65. Pursuant to section 14(2)(1) of the Police Act, in force at the material time, a police officer was permitted to use physical force where no other administrative coercive measure could ensure compliance with an obligation imposed by a valid administrative act for the purpose of identifying or countering a threat or bringing an offence to an end.

66. Article 291 of the Penal Code (Karistusseadustik), which was entitled “Abuse of authority” and was applicable at the material time, stipulated that an official’s unlawful use of a weapon, special equipment or physical force while carrying out official duties was punishable by a fine or imprisonment for a term of one to five years.

67. Article 77 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Kriminaalmenetluse seadustik) allows persons to be confronted where contradictions in their statements cannot be resolved by other means. In the course of the confrontation, the relationship between those persons is established, and they are questioned in turn about the conflicting facts. Earlier statements made by a confronted person may be revealed, and other evidence may be presented. If authorised by an official of the investigative body, the persons involved may, through that official, ask each other questions relating to the inconsistencies in their statements.

68. Article 81 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits, where necessary, the use of a photograph, film, or audio or video recording of a person, item or other object for identification purposes.

69. According to Article 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a criminal-offence report may be lodged orally or in writing with either an investigative authority or a Prosecutor’s Office. The same article requires a report submitted at the premises of an investigative authority or Prosecutor’s Office to be documented in writing, while a report communicated by telephone must be preserved either in written form or as an audio recording.

70. Article 207, entitled “Appeal to the Public Prosecutor’s Office against a refusal to commence or a decision to discontinue criminal proceedings”, in the version in force at the material time, stipulated that a
