Having examined the applicant’s request for a hearing, the Chamber decided, under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, that no hearing was required in the case.THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE7. The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Cherkasy.A. The applicant’s conviction and requests for review of his sentence8. On 23 August 2001 the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal found the applicant guilty of murder, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms, and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 12 February 2002 the Supreme Court upheld that judgment.9. Subsequently, the applicant applied to the courts for a review of his sentence. Although initially the courts refused the requested review, in 2009 the Supreme Court changed the applicant’s sentence to fifteen years’ imprisonment, considering that life imprisonment had been imposed on him not in compliance with the law.B. The applicant’s detention10. During the investigations and trial the applicant was held in the Cherkasy Temporary Investigative Isolation Unit (“the SIZO”) No. 30. He remained there until 22 September 2004, when he was transferred to Kyiv SIZO no. 13.11. On 15 October 2004 the applicant was placed in Sokalska Correctional Colony no. 47 in the Lviv Region (“Sokalska Prison”). In November 2007 he was transferred to the Zamkova Correctional Colony no. 58, in the Khmelnytsk Region (“Zamkova Prison”).12. In May 2012 the applicant suffered an ischemic stroke and was taken to a hospital within the Shepetivska Correctional Colony No. 98, in which he underwent treatment as regards the stroke and generally hypertension. On 23 October 2012 the applicant was released from prison. In particular, it was noted that given his health condition he could no longer serve his sentence and he no longer posed danger to the society.C. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment on 15 October 200413. According to the applicant, on the day he arrived at Sokalska Prison (15 October 2004) he was beaten by several guards. As a result, he allegedly suffered an eye injury and several bruises and scratches on his body. Subsequently, the applicant was placed in a cell in which he was visited by a group of officers, including the prison governor and medical officer, with a view to completing the formalities related to the applicant’s transfer to that prison. The applicant claimed to have complained to those officers that he had been beaten up, but to no avail. Allegedly, his injuries were not noted and he received no medical assistance. In October 2005 the applicant was diagnosed with left-eye mydriasis of traumatic origin, which allegedly developed because of the eye injury he had received on 15 October 2004.14. The applicant stated that on 19 October 2004 he had asked the prison authorities to send a complaint about his alleged beating to a prosecutor. The administration of the prison refused to send that complaint or other similar complaints which the applicant continued submitting after that date.15. On 28 June 2006, during an official visit to the prison by a prosecutor in charge of supervising the prison authorities’ compliance with the law, the applicant handed his complaint of beating to that prosecutor.16. By a decision of 18 August 2006, the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation into the applicant’s complaint, finding that there was no evidence of the alleged beating. The prosecutor based his decision on the information available from the applicant’s medical file and the written statements obtained from the prison staff, including the medical officer who had examined the applicant upon his arrival at the prison, and also from some of the prisoners who had been transferred to the prison on the same day as the applicant. Those prisoners, except for one of them, L., stated that the prison staff had not beaten or otherwise ill-treated them. L. stated that he had been punched on the limbs and back, but that he had not seen other prisoners being beaten.17. On 26 October 2006 the applicant challenged the prosecutor’s decision before the courts, stating that it had not been based on the facts. In support of his appeal, the applicant submitted a statement, allegedly written by L. in June 2005, that the applicant had had bruises on his limbs on 16 October 2004.18. The courts at two levels of jurisdiction upheld the prosecutor’s findings, relying, in the main, on the material contained in the prosecutor’s file concerning the applicant’s complaint that he had been beaten.19. The applicant stated that the courts had refused his requests to be heard in person and for the prisoners who had been detained with him in Sokalska Prison to be questioned. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.20. On 17 December 2007 the Supreme Court refused to consider the applicant’s cassation appeal, because he had failed to submit certified copies of the lower courts’ decisions. On 30 January 2008 the applicant sent the required copies to the Supreme Court, asking it to review his case in cassation. The applicant did not provide any further information concerning that set of proceedings.D. Conditions of the applicant’s detention and medical assistance in Sokalska Prison1. Size of the cells, sanitation and hygiene, quality of food and water and application of restraints(a)  Submissions by the applicant21. During his detention in Sokalska Prison between October 2004 and November 2007 the applicant stayed in cells of twelve square metres, together with three other inmates. According to him, as the cells contained sanitary facilities, four bunks, a table and two benches, the applicant and his cellmates had very limited living space, which, given the fact that they spent twenty-three hours a day in the cell and were not allowed to take physical exercise, was humiliating and intolerable. The cells were unventilated, always damp, and not sufficiently heated in winter. For several weeks in 2004 and 2005 the applicant was held in the same cells in which inmates suffering from the open form of tuberculosis were also detained.22. Every time he left his cell the applicant was handcuffed and was followed by several prison officers with a guard dog. While the applicant was escorted to a medical unit or a meeting place, allegedly a felt-lined bag was put over his head, which prevented him from seeing and limited his air supply. When the applicant was taken out of his cell to the exercise area he was allegedly obliged to walk with his hands handcuffed behind his back and raised above his head, causing him physical and mental suffering. The exercise area measured about twenty-two square metres; it was damp and lacked direct sunlight.23. According to the applicant, the food and water provided to him and other prisoners were unsatisfactory and hazardous to their health. The prison authorities did not ensure adequate sanitary conditions and he was not offered a chance to work and earn money to enable him to purchase medicine, sanitary supplies or additional food.24. In 2005-06 the applicant allegedly tried to complain to prosecutors about the conditions of his detention. However, the prison authorities refused to send, or delayed sending, about twenty letters addressed by the applicant to prosecutors. Although some of his letters reached the prosecutors, his complaints about the conditions of his detention contained in those letters were not examined.(b)  Submissions by the Government25. According to the Government, a part of the applicant’s submissions concerning the conditions of his detention, specifically his allegations that he had been detained in cells with poor sanitary and hygiene conditions together with inmates suffering from the open form of tuberculosis, that he had been escorted to a medical unit or a meeting place with a felt-lined bag over his head, and that while handcuffed he had been obliged to walk with his hands raised above his head, were untrue and not supported by any evidence.26. The Government stated that the open-air exercise area measured twenty-four square metres and was equipped with a canopy protecting inmates from rain and snow. It was not dark or damp. There was also equipment enabling inmates to do physical exercises.27. They further submitted that the applicant had had no opportunity to work, as at the time no facilities for work were available in the maximum security sector of Sokalska Prison. The food and water was regularly checked and was of adequate quality.28. The Government contended that the applicant had made no complaint to the domestic authorities concerning the material conditions of his detention.2. Medical assistance(a)  Submissions by the applicant29. According to the applicant, his principal health problem was hypertension and in 2005 he had had four heart attacks. Allegedly, he had not received adequate medical treatment in that regard and had not been allowed to keep medication he needed.30. In August 2005 the applicant complained of inadequate medical assistance to a prosecutor in charge of supervising the prison authorities’ compliance with the law. The prosecutor conducted an inquiry into the applicant’s complaints of inadequate medical assistance. The prosecutor found that the medical assistance provided to the applicant by the administration of the prison had been adequate; the applicant was informed of this by a letter of 3 November 2005. The prosecutor’s finding was based on the information contained in the applicant’s medical file, according to which the applicant had received treatment for hypertension in October and December 2004, in January and February 2005, and between April and July 2005, which included the administration of inosine, nitroglycerinum and other medication. It was noted that the applicant had also been given the medication his relatives had sent him. The treatment prescribed by the prison doctors was later endorsed by a cardiologist from a civilian hospital, who examined the applicant in August 2005.31. The applicant disagreed with the prosecutor’s findings and complained to the Sokal Town Court. By a ruling of 20 February 2006, the court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint, holding that the matter fell outside the court’s jurisdiction. On 14 August 2006 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld that ruling. On 8 July 2008 the Higher Administrative Court quashed those decisions, finding that the matter had to be examined in the framework of the administrative proceedings. The case was remitted to the Lviv Administrative Court for fresh examination. By a ruling of 16 October 2008, that court returned the case, refusing to examine it as the applicant had failed to submit a formal claim with documents in support. The applicant did not pursue the matter further.(b)  Submissions by the Government32. According to the information submitted by the Government, throughout the period of his detention in the SIZO and in Sokalska Prison the applicant had been examined by various doctors, including doctors from civilian medical institutions, and had been provided with treatment for different medical issues he had at the time, including hypertension.E. Restrictions on family visits and telephone calls1. Submissions by the applicant33. According to the applicant, during his post-conviction detention he maintained contact with his wife, two minor children whose ages were not specified, his mother, and four other relatives. Generally, he was entitled to family visits no more than once every six months and for no longer than four hours per visit.34. During his stay in the Cherkasy SIZO allegedly only three adults and one child or two adults and two children could be present at any one time at such meetings. In Sokalska Prison no more than two adults and one child could be present at any one time. His family members, who lived in the Cherkasy Region, had experienced difficulties travelling to see him in Sokalska Prison, which is in the Lviv Region (about 700 km away).35. In that prison, only one room was made available for family visits, on a specified day (Sunday), which, because of the high demand for such visits, usually resulted in the duration of the visits being substantially reduced. In particular, the applicant’s meetings with his family on 28 November 2004, 29 May 2005 and 28 November 2006 lasted no longer than two hours, whereas on 27 November 2005 and 28 May 2006 they lasted no longer than three hours.36. The family visits took place in the presence of a guard with a guard dog; the applicant was placed in a cage and separated from the others by a glass partition. The applicant and his visitors had to use a telephone during such meetings and their conversations were constantly monitored by a prison guard.37. Despite numerous requests by the applicant, the administration of the Cherkasy SIZO and Sokalska Prison did not allow him to have any intimate contact with his wife. The refusal was based on the ground that prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment did not have a statutory right to long family meetings.38. Between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005 the applicant allegedly was not allowed to make any telephone calls to his family. On the latter date he was allowed to make a telephone call to his wife, the duration of which was limited to five minutes. Subsequently, the applicant was only allowed to receive telephone calls once every three months upon his written request.39. The applicant complained to the Sokalska Prison authorities about the above-mentioned restrictions on family visits and telephone calls. In reply, they provided the applicant with extracts of the provisions of the Code on the Execution of Sentences of 2003 governing the conditions of detention of persons sentenced to life imprisonment.2. Submissions by the Government40. The Government challenged the trustworthiness of part of the applicant’s submissions concerning restrictions on family visits and telephone calls, specifically his allegations that family visits had lasted less than two hours, that he had not been allowed to make telephone calls between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005, that other restrictions had been imposed on his right to make telephone calls after 2 November 2005, that only three adults and one minor child or two adults and two minor children had been allowed to visit him at any one time in the Cherkasy SIZO, that only two adults and two minor children had been allowed to visit him at any one time in Sokalska Prison, and that those visits had taken place in the presence of a guard with a guard dog. The Government further stated that the applicant had not raised those complaints before the domestic authorities.F. Alleged events during the applicant’s detention in Zamkova Prison in 201241. In a letter dated 19 May 2012 the applicant stated that the Court’s letter, sent to him in January 2012, had been opened and read by the administration of Zamkova Prison no. 58, where he had been serving a prison sentence, and that he had been persecuted by the administration of the Prison for communicating with the Court. In particular, the applicant was placed in solitary confinement for the period from 28 January to 15 May 2012; on an unspecified date all the documents in his possession and his pen were taken from him; and he was not given the opportunity to contact his relatives for two months, the exact calendar period not being specified. The applicant also stated that before those events he had been subjected to disciplinary sanctions when he had received letters from the Court in detention, but provided no details in this regard.42. The Government in their turn contended that no letter to the applicant had been opened, that there had been no interference with his communication with the outside world, and that the applicant’s allegations of persecution for complaining to the Court were wholly unfounded. According to them, the applicant was disciplined on several occasions for breaches of prison regulations, which included, inter alia, not respecting the prison daily schedule and insulting the prison guards.G. The applicant’s previous application to the Court43. On 4 July 2002 the applicant lodged an application with the Court, complaining, inter alia, under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been tortured by the police and under Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention that he had been unfairly convicted and that his sentence had not been based on the law in force at the material time.44. In order to substantiate his complaints before the Court, the applicant tried to obtain from the domestic courts copies of various documents from his criminal case file. By letters dated 19 April and 10 May 2002 and 26 March 2003 his requests for copies of documents were refused by the President and Vice-President of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal as having no basis in law.45. In 2002-03 the applicant’s mother and wife, who were given leave to represent him during his trial (see paragraph 8 above) and after the trial by a ruling of 6 March 2003 issued by a judge of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, visited that court on several occasions with a view to obtaining copies of the documents from the applicant’s criminal case file. According to the applicant, they were not allowed to consult the file or to take any documents from it. On an unspecified date their copy of the ruling of 6 March 2003 was allegedly taken and not returned by that judge.46. By letters dated 19 August 2003 and 25 February 2004, the Court asked the applicant to submit documentary evidence in respect of his complaints under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. In particular, he was invited to submit copies of his written complaints to the national authorities concerning his alleged ill-treatment, a copy of the prosecutor’s decision concerning those complaints, a copy of his cassation appeal against the judgment of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal of 23 August 2001, and copies of his written applications to have a witness on his behalf examined by that court.47. Further to the Court’s letters, the applicant submitted several requests to the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, asking for copies of the requested documents. The applicant’s requests were refused, but he was informed that, at the request of the Court, the entire criminal case file would be sent to it.48. On an unspecified date the applicant’s mother hired a lawyer to represent the applicant before the authorities. The lawyer obtained copies of the documents indicated in the Court’s letters, and they were subsequently submitted to the Court. However, the applicant stated that the lawyer had not obtained copies of all the necessary documents, and that the applicant’s mother’s further attempts to obtain copies of additional documents had been unsuccessful.49. Meanwhile, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Prydniprovskyy District Court against the judges of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, challenging their refusal to provide him with copies of documents from his case file or to allow his relatives to represent him before the domestic authorities.50. On 10 June 2004 the court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, holding that the matter did not fall to be considered by the courts. On 16 November 2004 the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal confirmed the ruling of the first-instance court.51. On 16 June 2006 the Higher Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal as lodged out of time. According to the applicant, he missed the deadline because the Sokalska Prison authorities had failed to dispatch his correspondence on time. The applicant lodged a new cassation appeal with the Higher Administrative Court, together with a request for an extension of the time-limit. The outcome of that appeal is unknown.52. On 27 March 2007 the Court declared the applicant’s previous application inadmissible.II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAWA. Correctional Labour Code of 1970 (repealed on 1 January 2004), as worded at the material time53. Article 30 provided that prisoners sentenced to imprisonment, who were temporarily in an investigative isolation unit (SIZO), were subject to the rules governing detention at the type of penal institution in which they were to be placed pursuant to their sentence. They were allowed to have only short meetings with relatives and other persons.54. Under Article 39, prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were entitled to have a four-hour meeting with relatives or other persons in the presence of a prison guard once every six months. Provided it was technically possible, once every three months they were allowed a fifteen‑minute telephone call under the supervision of the prison authorities and against a charge for its cost.B. Execution of Sentences Code of 2003 (in force on 1 January 2004), as worded at the material time55. Article 150 provided that prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were to serve their sentences in correctional colonies of the highest level of security.56. Pursuant to Article 151, they were, as a rule, placed in two-person cells. In certain circumstances they could be placed in solitary confinement. They were allowed to have one hour’s exercise daily. Prior to the amendments to the Code on 21 January 2010 (which came into effect on 16 February 2010), life prisoners were entitled to short visits (up to four hours) from their relatives and other persons once every six months. With those amendments, life prisoners became entitled to such visits once every three months.57. Prisoners were also entitled to have four fifteen-minute telephone conversations a year under the supervision of the prison authorities, the costs of which were to be borne by prisoners (Article 110).C. Internal Regulations of Penal Institutions, approved by Order No. 275 of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences on 25 December 2003 (repealed on 23 January 2015), as worded at the material time58. The rules governing the detention of prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment subjected them to special restrictions as regards physical conditions, activities and opportunities for human contact, which included permanent separation from the rest of the prison population, limited visit entitlements, prohibition of communication with other prisoners, and being escorted by three officers with a guard dog and handcuffed with their arms behind their back whenever they were taken out of their cell (Sections 23‑25).59. Pursuant to Section 26, the admission of newly arriving prisoners was carried out by a commission composed of the prison staff, including medical officers, and headed by the prison governor. Upon their arrival at the prison, prisoners had to undergo a medical examination.60. Under Section 47, prisoners were entitled to meetings with no more than three adults at one time; these could also be accompanied by the prisoner’s minor children.61. Pursuant to Section 94, prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were to receive medical assistance, as a rule, in their cells in the presence of at least three guards. Prisoners were to be transferred to a medical institution of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences, or to a civilian medical institution, if they needed urgent medical assistance.62. Annex 9 to the Regulations provided that prisoners were not allowed to keep in their possession any medication or medical items.63. Annex 17 provided for two options of equipping a room for short meetings. According to the first option, the meeting room was to be equipped with tables along the room separated by free space of 120 centimetres in width. There were to be no more than ten chairs for visitors; stools for the prisoners were to be fixed to the floor.64. According to the second option, a meeting room was to be equipped with booths 80 centimetres in width and 100 centimetres in length. One or two booths were to be of 140 centimetres in width to accommodate two visitors or visitors with children coming to see the same prisoner. The visitors’ booths and the prisoners’ booths were to be separated by glass partitions. Booths were to be equipped with a loudspeaker and a telephone handset. Booths for life prisoners had to be additionally equipped with metal bars and doors with mechanical locks. The supervising officer’s table was to be equipped with a device for listening to the conversations in the booths.III. Relevant Council of Europe documents65. The Council of Europe material pertaining to family visits to prisoners was quoted in Trosin v. Ukraine (no. 39758/05, §§ 30‑31, 23 February 2012).

FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF GUK v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 16995/05)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

8 December 2016

This judgment is final, but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Guk v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

André Potocki, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Síofra O’Leary, judges,

and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 15 November 2016,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 16995/05) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Viktor Mykhaylovych Guk (“the applicant”), on 21 April 2005.

2. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant initially complained that the authorities had impeded his access to the criminal case file and had refused to provide him with copies of documents he needed to substantiate his previous application to the Court. He also complained of a lack of access to a court in this connection. Subsequently, the applicant complained mainly under Article 3 of the Convention of ill-treatment by prison guards, the conditions of his detention, and inadequate medical assistance; under Article 8, of restrictions on family visits and telephone calls; and under Article 13, of the absence of an effective domestic remedy for his complaints under Article 3. He further complained of interference with the effective exercise of his right of application in the present case, as guaranteed by Article 34.

4. On 29 March 2010, the application was communicated to the Government.

5. On 14 June 2012, the President of the Section invited the parties to submit additional observations concerning factual developments occurring after communication of the case. The applicant and the Government each submitted further observations and comments.

6. Having considered the applicant’s request for a hearing, the Chamber decided, pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, that a hearing was unnecessary.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

7. The applicant was born in 1966 and resides in Cherkasy.

A. The applicant’s conviction and requests for review of his sentence

8. On 23 August 2001, the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 12 February 2002, the Supreme Court upheld that judgment.

9. The applicant subsequently applied to the courts for review of his sentence.
Although the courts initially refused the requested review, in 2009 the Supreme Court reduced the applicant’s sentence to fifteen years’ imprisonment, finding that the life sentence had not been imposed in accordance with the law.

B. The applicant’s detention

10. During the investigation and trial, the applicant was held in Cherkasy Temporary Investigative Isolation Unit (“the SIZO”) No. 30. He remained there until 22 September 2004, when he was transferred to Kyiv SIZO No. 13.

11. On 15 October 2004, the applicant was placed in Sokalska Correctional Colony No. 47 in the Lviv Region (“Sokalska Prison”). In November 2007, he was transferred to Zamkova Correctional Colony No. 58 in the Khmelnytsk Region (“Zamkova Prison”).

12. In May 2012, the applicant suffered an ischemic stroke and was taken to a hospital within Shepetivska Correctional Colony No. 98, where he received treatment for the stroke and hypertension generally. On 23 October 2012, the applicant was released from prison. In particular, it was noted that, given his state of health, he could no longer serve his sentence and no longer posed a danger to society.

C. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment on 15 October 2004

13. According to the applicant, on the day of his arrival at Sokalska Prison (15 October 2004), he was beaten by several guards. As a result, he allegedly sustained an eye injury and several bruises and scratches on his body. The applicant was subsequently placed in a cell, where he was visited by a group of officers, including the prison governor and a medical officer, to complete the formalities relating to his transfer to the prison. The applicant claimed that he complained to those officers that he had been beaten, but to no avail. Allegedly, his injuries were not recorded, and he received no medical assistance. In October 2005, the applicant was diagnosed with left-eye mydriasis of traumatic origin, which had allegedly developed as a result of the eye injury he had sustained on 15 October 2004.

14. The applicant stated that on 19 October 2004, he had asked the prison authorities to forward a complaint about his alleged beating to a prosecutor. The prison administration refused to send that complaint or other similar complaints that the applicant continued to submit after that date.

15. On 28 June 2006, during an official visit to the prison by a prosecutor responsible for supervising the prison authorities’ compliance with the law, the applicant handed that prosecutor his complaint concerning the beating.

16. By a decision of 18 August 2006, the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation into the applicant’s complaint, finding that there was no evidence of the alleged beating.
The prosecutor based his decision on the information in the applicant’s medical file and the written statements obtained from prison staff, including the medical officer who had examined the applicant upon his arrival at the prison, as well as from some of the prisoners transferred there on the same day as the applicant. With the exception of one prisoner, L., those prisoners stated that prison staff had not beaten or otherwise ill-treated them. L. stated that he had been punched on the limbs and back, but had not seen other prisoners being beaten.

17. On 26 October 2006 the applicant challenged the prosecutor’s decision before the courts, arguing that it had not been based on the facts. In support of his appeal, he submitted a statement, allegedly written by L. in June 2005, indicating that the applicant had bruises on his limbs on 16 October 2004.

18. The courts at two levels of jurisdiction upheld the prosecutor’s findings, relying mainly on the material in the prosecutor’s file concerning the applicant’s complaint that he had been beaten.

19. The applicant stated that the courts had refused his requests to be heard in person and to question the prisoners who had been detained with him in Sokalska Prison. He lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.

20. On 17 December 2007 the Supreme Court refused to consider the applicant’s cassation appeal because he had failed to provide certified copies of the lower courts’ decisions. On 30 January 2008 the applicant sent the required copies to the Supreme Court and asked it to review his case in cassation. He provided no further information concerning those proceedings.

D. Conditions of the applicant’s detention and medical assistance in Sokalska Prison

1. Size of the cells, sanitation and hygiene, quality of food and water, and use of restraints

(a) Submissions by the applicant

21. During his detention in Sokalska Prison between October 2004 and November 2007, the applicant stayed in twelve-square-metre cells with three other inmates. According to him, since the cells contained sanitary facilities, four bunks, a table and two benches, he and his cellmates had very limited living space. Given that they spent twenty-three hours a day in the cell and were not allowed to exercise, those conditions were humiliating and intolerable. The cells were unventilated, constantly damp and insufficiently heated in winter. For several weeks in 2004 and 2005, the applicant was held in cells with inmates suffering from the open form of tuberculosis.

22. Whenever he left his cell, the applicant was handcuffed and accompanied by several prison officers with a guard dog. While he was being escorted to a medical unit or meeting place, a felt-lined bag was allegedly placed over his head, preventing him from seeing and restricting his air supply.
When the applicant was taken from his cell to the exercise area, he was allegedly required to walk with his hands cuffed behind his back and raised above his head, causing him physical and mental suffering. The exercise area measured approximately twenty-two square metres; it was damp and had no direct sunlight.

23. According to the applicant, the food and water supplied to him and other prisoners were unsatisfactory and harmful to their health. The prison authorities failed to maintain adequate sanitary conditions, and he was not given an opportunity to work and earn money to purchase medicine, sanitary supplies, or additional food.

24. In 2005-06, the applicant allegedly attempted to complain to prosecutors about his detention conditions. However, the prison authorities refused to send, or delayed sending, approximately twenty letters he had addressed to prosecutors. Although some letters reached the prosecutors, the complaints concerning his detention conditions contained in them were not examined.

(b) Submissions by the Government

25. According to the Government, some of the applicant’s submissions regarding his detention conditions were untrue and unsupported by evidence. These included his allegations that he had been held in cells with poor sanitary and hygiene conditions alongside inmates suffering from the open form of tuberculosis; that he had been escorted to a medical unit or meeting place with a felt-lined bag over his head; and that, while handcuffed, he had been forced to walk with his hands raised above his head.

26. The Government stated that the open-air exercise area measured twenty-four square metres and had a canopy protecting inmates from rain and snow. It was neither dark nor damp. Equipment was also available for inmates to exercise.

27. They further submitted that the applicant had had no opportunity to work because, at the relevant time, no work facilities were available in the maximum-security sector of Sokalska Prison. The food and water were regularly inspected and were of adequate quality.

28. The Government maintained that the applicant had not complained to the domestic authorities about the material conditions of his detention.

2. Medical assistance

(a) Submissions by the applicant

29. According to the applicant, his main health problem was hypertension, and in 2005 he had suffered four heart attacks. He alleged that he had not received adequate medical treatment for that condition and had not been permitted to keep the medication he required.

30. In August 2005, the applicant complained about inadequate medical assistance to a prosecutor responsible for supervising the prison authorities’ compliance with the law. The prosecutor conducted an inquiry into those complaints.
The prosecutor found that the medical assistance provided to the applicant by the prison administration had been adequate; the applicant was notified of this by a letter dated 3 November 2005. The prosecutor’s finding was based on information in the applicant’s medical file, according to which he had received treatment for hypertension in October and December 2004, in January and February 2005, and from April to July 2005, including the administration of inosine, nitroglycerinum and other medication. It was also noted that the applicant had been given medication sent by his relatives. The treatment prescribed by the prison doctors was subsequently endorsed by a cardiologist from a civilian hospital, who examined the applicant in August 2005.

31. The applicant disagreed with the prosecutor’s findings and lodged a complaint with the Sokal Town Court. By a ruling of 20 February 2006, the court declined to consider the applicant’s complaint, holding that the matter fell outside its jurisdiction. On 14 August 2006 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld that ruling. On 8 July 2008 the Higher Administrative Court quashed those decisions, finding that the matter had to be considered within the framework of administrative proceedings. The case was remitted to the Lviv Administrative Court for fresh consideration. By a ruling of 16 October 2008, that court returned the case, declining to examine it because the applicant had failed to submit a formal claim with supporting documents. The applicant did not pursue the matter further.

(b) Submissions by the Government

32. According to the information provided by the Government, throughout his detention in the SIZO and Sokalska Prison, the applicant had been examined by various doctors, including doctors from civilian medical institutions, and had received treatment for the different medical issues he had at the time, including hypertension.

E. Restrictions on family visits and telephone calls

1. Submissions by the applicant

33. According to the applicant, during his post-conviction detention he remained in contact with his wife, two minor children whose ages were not specified, his mother, and four other relatives. As a rule, he was entitled to family visits no more than once every six months and for no longer than four hours per visit.

34. During his stay in the Cherkasy SIZO, allegedly only three adults and one child, or two adults and two children, could attend such meetings at any one time. In Sokalska Prison, no more than two adults and one child could be present at any one time. His family members, who lived in the Cherkasy Region, had encountered difficulties travelling to visit him in Sokalska Prison, which is located in the Lviv Region, about 700 km away.

35.
In that prison, only one room was available for family visits on a specified day (Sunday), which, owing to the high demand for such visits, usually resulted in their duration being substantially reduced. In particular, the applicant’s meetings with his family on 28 November 2004, 29 May 2005 and 28 November 2006 lasted no more than two hours, while those on 27 November 2005 and 28 May 2006 lasted no more than three hours.

36. The family visits took place in the presence of a guard accompanied by a guard dog; the applicant was placed in a cage and separated from the others by a glass partition. The applicant and his visitors had to communicate by telephone during such meetings, and their conversations were constantly monitored by a prison guard.

37. Despite the applicant’s numerous requests, the administrations of the Cherkasy SIZO and Sokalska Prison did not permit him to have any intimate contact with his wife. The refusal was based on the fact that prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment had no statutory right to long family visits.

38. Between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005, the applicant was allegedly not permitted to make any telephone calls to his family. On the latter date, he was allowed to call his wife, but the call was limited to five minutes. Subsequently, the applicant was only permitted to receive telephone calls once every three months upon written request.

39. The applicant complained to the Sokalska Prison authorities about the above restrictions on family visits and telephone calls. In response, they provided him with extracts from the provisions of the Code on the Execution of Sentences of 2003 governing the detention conditions of persons sentenced to life imprisonment.

2. Submissions by the Government

40. The Government disputed the reliability of part of the applicant’s submissions concerning restrictions on family visits and telephone calls, specifically his allegations that family visits had lasted less than two hours; that he had not been allowed to make telephone calls between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005; that further restrictions had been imposed on his right to make telephone calls after 2 November 2005; that only three adults and one minor child, or two adults and two minor children, had been allowed to visit him at any one time in the Cherkasy SIZO; that only two adults and two minor children had been allowed to visit him at any one time in Sokalska Prison; and that those visits had taken place in the presence of a guard accompanied by a guard dog. The Government further submitted that the applicant had not raised those complaints before the domestic authorities.

F. Alleged events during the applicant’s detention in Zamkova Prison in 2012

41. In a letter dated 19 May 2012, the applicant stated that the Court’s letter, sent to him in January 2012, had been opened and read by the administration of Zamkova Prison no.
58, where he was serving a prison sentence, and that he had been persecuted by the prison administration for communicating with the Court. In particular, the applicant was held in solitary confinement from 28 January to 15 May 2012; on an unspecified date, all the documents in his possession and his pen were confiscated; and he was denied the opportunity to contact his relatives for two months, the precise calendar period not being specified. The applicant further stated that, before those events, he had been subjected to disciplinary sanctions when he received letters from the Court while in detention, but provided no details in that regard.

42. The Government, for their part, maintained that no letter to the applicant had been opened, that there had been no interference with his communication with the outside world, and that his allegations of persecution for complaining to the Court were entirely unfounded. According to them, the applicant had been disciplined on several occasions for breaches of prison regulations, including, inter alia, failure to respect the prison’s daily schedule and insulting prison guards.

G. The applicant’s earlier application to the Court

43. On 4 July 2002, the applicant lodged an application with the Court, complaining, inter alia, under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been tortured by the police and, under Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention, that he had been unfairly convicted and that his sentence had not been based on the law in force at the relevant time.

44. To substantiate his complaints before the Court, the applicant sought to obtain from the domestic courts copies of various documents from his criminal case file. By letters dated 19 April and 10 May 2002 and 26 March 2003, his requests for copies of documents were refused by the President and Vice-President of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal as lacking any basis in law.

45. In 2002-03, the applicant’s mother and wife, who had been granted leave to represent him during his trial (see paragraph 8 above) and after the trial by a ruling of 6 March 2003 issued by a judge of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, visited that court on several occasions to obtain copies of documents from the applicant’s criminal case file. According to the applicant, they were not permitted to consult the file or take any documents from it. On an unspecified date, their copy of the ruling of 6 March 2003 was allegedly taken by that judge and not returned.

46. By letters dated 19 August 2003 and 25 February 2004, the Court requested that the applicant submit documentary evidence concerning his complaints under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.
In particular, he was asked to submit copies of his written complaints to the national authorities regarding his alleged ill-treatment, a copy of the prosecutor’s decision on those complaints, a copy of his cassation appeal against the judgment of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal of 23 August 2001, and copies of his written requests to have a witness on his behalf examined by that court.

47. Following the Court’s letters, the applicant submitted several requests to the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal for copies of the documents concerned. His requests were refused, but he was informed that, at the Court’s request, the entire criminal case file would be forwarded to it.

48. On an unspecified date, the applicant’s mother hired a lawyer to represent him before the authorities. The lawyer obtained copies of the documents referred to in the Court’s letters, which were subsequently submitted to the Court. However, the applicant stated that the lawyer had not obtained copies of all the necessary documents and that his mother’s further attempts to secure copies of additional documents had been unsuccessful.

49. Meanwhile, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Prydniprovskyy District Court against the judges of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, contesting their refusal to provide him with copies of documents from his case file or to permit his relatives to represent him before the domestic authorities.

50. On 10 June 2004, the court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, finding that the matter was not one for consideration by the courts. On 16 November 2004, the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal upheld the ruling of the first-instance court.

51. On 16 June 2006, the Higher Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal as having been lodged out of time. According to the applicant, he had missed the deadline because the Sokalska Prison authorities had failed to dispatch his correspondence promptly. The applicant lodged a fresh cassation appeal with the Higher Administrative Court, accompanied by a request for an extension of the time-limit. The outcome of that appeal is unknown.

52. On 27 March 2007, the Court declared the applicant’s previous application inadmissible.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

A. Correctional Labour Code of 1970 (repealed on 1 January 2004), as worded at the material time

53. Article 30 provided that prisoners sentenced to imprisonment who were temporarily held in an investigative isolation unit (SIZO) were subject to the rules governing detention in the type of penal institution in which they were to be placed pursuant to their sentence. They were permitted to have only short meetings with relatives and other persons.

54. Under Article 39, prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were entitled to a four-hour meeting with relatives or other persons, in the presence of a prison guard, once every six months.
Provided that it was technically feasible, once every three months they were permitted a fifteen-minute telephone call under the supervision of the prison authorities and at their own expense.

B. Execution of Sentences Code of 2003 (in force on 1 January 2004), as worded at the material time

55. Article 150 stipulated that prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were to serve their sentences in correctional colonies with the highest level of security.

56. Under Article 151, they were generally placed in two-person cells. In certain circumstances, they could be held in solitary confinement. They were entitled to one hour of exercise per day. Before the amendments to the Code of 21 January 2010 (which entered into force on 16 February 2010), life prisoners were entitled to short visits (lasting up to four hours) from relatives and other persons once every six months. Following those amendments, life prisoners became entitled to such visits once every three months.

57. Prisoners were also entitled to four fifteen-minute telephone conversations per year under the supervision of the prison authorities, with the costs to be borne by the prisoners (Article 110).

C. Internal Regulations of Penal Institutions, approved by Order No. 275 of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences on 25 December 2003 (repealed on 23 January 2015), as worded at the material time

58. The rules governing the detention of prisoners serving life sentences imposed special restrictions concerning physical conditions, activities and opportunities for human contact. These included permanent separation from the rest of the prison population, limited visiting rights, a prohibition on communicating with other prisoners, and escort by three officers with a guard dog, while handcuffed with their arms behind their backs, whenever they were taken out of their cells (Sections 23-25).

59. Under Section 26, newly arriving prisoners were admitted by a commission made up of prison staff, including medical officers, and headed by the prison governor. Upon arrival at the prison, prisoners were required to undergo a medical examination.

60. Pursuant to Section 47, prisoners were entitled to meetings with no more than three adults at a time, who could also be accompanied by the prisoner’s minor children.

61. Under Section 94, prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment were, as a rule, to receive medical assistance in their cells in the presence of at least three guards. Prisoners were to be transferred to a medical institution of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences or to a civilian medical institution if they required urgent medical assistance.

62. Annex 9 to the Regulations stated that prisoners were not permitted to keep any medication or medical items in their possession.

63. Annex 17 set out two options for equipping a room for short meetings.
According to the first option, the meeting room was to be furnished with tables placed along the room and separated by free space 120 centimetres wide. There were to be no more than ten chairs for visitors, while stools for prisoners were to be fixed to the floor.64. Under the second option, the meeting room was to contain booths 80 centimetres wide and 100 centimetres long. One or two booths were to be 140 centimetres wide to accommodate two visitors or visitors with children coming to see the same prisoner. The visitors’ and prisoners’ booths were to be separated by glass partitions. The booths were to be fitted with a loudspeaker and a telephone handset. Booths for life prisoners were also required to have metal bars and doors with mechanical locks. The supervising officer’s table was to be fitted with a device for listening to conversations in the booths.III. Relevant Council of Europe documents65. The Council of Europe material concerning family visits to prisoners was cited in Trosin v. Ukraine (no. 39758/05, §§ 30‑31, 23 February 2012).

In the case of Guk v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee comprising:

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case arose from an application (no. 16995/05) lodged against Ukraine on 21 April 2005 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Viktor Mykhaylovych Guk, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”).

2. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant first alleged that the authorities had impeded his access to the criminal case file and had declined to give him copies of documents that he needed to support an earlier application to the Court. In that connection, he also complained that he had been denied access to a court. Later, his principal complaints concerned, under Article 3 of the Convention, ill-treatment by prison guards, the conditions in which he was detained, and insufficient medical care; under Article 8, limitations on family visits and telephone calls; and, under Article 13, the absence of an effective domestic remedy in respect of his Article 3 complaints. He further maintained that the effective exercise of his right of individual application in the present case, as protected by Article 34, had been hindered.

4. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 March 2010.

5. On 14 June 2012, the President of the Section invited both parties to provide additional observations concerning factual developments that had occurred following communication of the case. Both the applicant and the Government submitted further observations and comments.

6. After considering the applicant’s request for a hearing, the Chamber concluded, pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, that a hearing was unnecessary.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

7. The applicant, who was born in 1966, resides in Cherkasy.

A. The applicant’s conviction and applications for review of his sentence

8. On 23 August 2001, the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of murder, attempted murder, and unlawful possession of firearms, sentencing him to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 12 February 2002.

9. Thereafter, the applicant asked the courts to review his sentence.
Although the courts initially declined to review the case, in 2009 the Supreme Court reduced the applicant’s sentence to fifteen years’ imprisonment after finding that the life sentence had not been imposed in accordance with the law.

B. The applicant’s detention

10. Throughout the investigation and trial, the applicant was detained in Cherkasy Temporary Investigative Isolation Unit no. 30 (“the SIZO”). He remained there until 22 September 2004, when he was transferred to Kyiv SIZO no. 13.

11. On 15 October 2004, the applicant was transferred to Sokalska Correctional Colony no. 47 in the Lviv Region (“Sokalska Prison”). In November 2007, he was moved to Zamkova Correctional Colony no. 58 in the Khmelnytsk Region (“Zamkova Prison”).

12. In May 2012, the applicant suffered an ischemic stroke and was admitted to the hospital at Shepetivska Correctional Colony no. 98, where he received treatment for the stroke and hypertension generally. He was released from prison on 23 October 2012. It was noted, in particular, that his state of health prevented him from continuing to serve his sentence and that he no longer posed a danger to society.

C. The applicant’s alleged ill-treatment on 15 October 2004

13. The applicant alleged that several guards beat him on 15 October 2004, the day of his arrival at Sokalska Prison. He claimed that the assault caused an eye injury, as well as several bruises and scratches on his body. He was subsequently placed in a cell, where a group of officials—including the prison governor and a medical officer—visited him to complete the formalities associated with his transfer to the prison. According to the applicant, he informed those officials that he had been beaten, but they took no action. His injuries were allegedly neither recorded nor treated. In October 2005, he was diagnosed with traumatic mydriasis of the left eye, which he maintained had developed as a result of the eye injury sustained on 15 October 2004.

14. The applicant stated that on 19 October 2004 he had asked the prison authorities to forward a complaint concerning the alleged beating to a prosecutor. The prison administration refused to send that complaint and continued to withhold similar complaints that he submitted thereafter.

15. On 28 June 2006, while a prosecutor responsible for overseeing the prison authorities’ compliance with the law was making an official visit to the prison, the applicant personally handed the prosecutor his complaint about the beating.

16. By a decision dated 18 August 2006, the prosecutor declined to institute a criminal investigation into the applicant’s allegations, concluding that no evidence supported the claim that he had been beaten.
The prosecutor reached his decision on the basis of the material in the applicant’s medical records and written statements taken from prison personnel, including the medical officer who had examined the applicant when he arrived at the prison. He also considered statements from several prisoners who had been transferred there on the same day as the applicant. With the exception of L., those prisoners denied having been beaten or otherwise subjected to ill-treatment by prison staff. L. reported that he had been punched on his limbs and back, but said that he had not witnessed any other prisoners being beaten.

17. On 26 October 2006 the applicant appealed against the prosecutor’s decision before the courts, arguing that it was not supported by the facts. In support of his challenge, he produced a statement purportedly written by L. in June 2005, according to which the applicant had bruises on his limbs on 16 October 2004.

18. Courts at two levels of jurisdiction endorsed the prosecutor’s conclusions, relying principally on the documents in the prosecutor’s case file relating to the applicant’s allegation that he had been beaten.

19. According to the applicant, the courts rejected his requests to appear and be heard in person and to have the prisoners detained with him in Sokalska Prison questioned. He subsequently filed a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.

20. On 17 December 2007 the Supreme Court declined to examine the cassation appeal because the applicant had not provided certified copies of the lower courts’ decisions. He forwarded the required copies to the Supreme Court on 30 January 2008 and requested cassation review of his case. No further information was submitted by the applicant regarding those proceedings.

D. Conditions of the applicant’s detention and medical assistance in Sokalska Prison

1. Cell size, sanitation and hygiene, food and water quality, and use of restraints

(a) Submissions by the applicant

21. While detained in Sokalska Prison from October 2004 until November 2007, the applicant shared twelve-square-metre cells with three other inmates. He maintained that the sanitary facilities, four bunks, a table and two benches occupied much of the available area, leaving him and his cellmates with very little personal space. In his view, these conditions were humiliating and intolerable, particularly because they remained in the cell for twenty-three hours each day and were not permitted to exercise. The cells had no ventilation, were constantly damp and were inadequately heated during winter. For several weeks in both 2004 and 2005, he was also confined in cells with prisoners suffering from active tuberculosis.

22. The applicant was handcuffed whenever he was taken out of his cell and was accompanied by several prison officers and a guard dog. He further alleged that, while being escorted to the medical unit or a meeting area, a felt-lined bag was placed over his head, obstructing his vision and restricting his air supply.
Whenever the applicant was removed from his cell for outdoor exercise, he was allegedly forced to walk with his hands cuffed behind his back and lifted above his head, which caused him physical and psychological suffering. The exercise yard, measuring approximately twenty-two square metres, was damp and received no direct sunlight.

23. The applicant maintained that the food and water supplied to him and the other prisoners were of inadequate quality and posed a risk to their health. He further alleged that the prison administration failed to maintain proper sanitary conditions and gave him no opportunity to work and earn money with which to buy medication, hygiene products or extra food.

24. In 2005 and 2006, the applicant allegedly attempted to complain to prosecutors about his detention conditions. However, the prison authorities either refused to dispatch or delayed the dispatch of approximately twenty letters he had addressed to prosecutors. Although some correspondence eventually reached them, the complaints about his conditions of detention raised in those letters were not investigated.

(b) Submissions by the Government

25. The Government argued that some of the applicant’s allegations regarding his detention conditions were false and unsupported by evidence. In particular, they disputed his claims that he had been held in cells with poor sanitary and hygienic conditions alongside prisoners suffering from the open form of tuberculosis; that he had been taken to the medical unit or meeting area with a felt-lined bag covering his head; and that he had been forced, while handcuffed, to walk with his hands elevated above his head.

26. According to the Government, the outdoor exercise yard covered twenty-four square metres and had a canopy shielding prisoners from rain and snow. They denied that the area was dark or damp and stated that it contained equipment for physical exercise.

27. The Government further submitted that the applicant had been unable to work because, at the relevant time, the maximum-security section of Sokalska Prison had no work facilities. They also stated that the food and water were regularly inspected and were of satisfactory quality.

28. The Government maintained that the applicant had not lodged any complaint with the domestic authorities about the material conditions in which he was detained.

2. Medical assistance

(a) Submissions by the applicant

29. The applicant stated that hypertension was his main health condition and that he had suffered four heart attacks in 2005. He alleged that he had not received appropriate medical care for those problems and had not been permitted to retain the medication he required.

30. In August 2005, the applicant complained about insufficient medical care to the prosecutor responsible for overseeing the prison authorities’ compliance with the law. That prosecutor opened an inquiry into the allegations of inadequate medical assistance.
The prosecutor concluded that the prison administration had provided the applicant with adequate medical care and notified him of that conclusion by letter dated 3 November 2005. The assessment relied on the applicant’s medical records, which showed that he had been treated for hypertension in October and December 2004, January and February 2005, and from April to July 2005. His treatment included inosine, nitroglycerinum, and other medicines, as well as medication sent by his relatives. In August 2005, after examining the applicant, a cardiologist from a civilian hospital endorsed the treatment prescribed by the prison doctors.

31. Disputing the prosecutor’s conclusions, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Sokal Town Court. On 20 February 2006, that court declined to consider the complaint on the ground that it lacked jurisdiction over the matter. The Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 14 August 2006. On 8 July 2008, however, the Higher Administrative Court set aside both decisions, holding that the matter should be considered in administrative proceedings, and remitted the case to the Lviv Administrative Court for fresh examination. By a ruling of 16 October 2008, the latter court returned the case without examining it because the applicant had not submitted a formal claim accompanied by supporting documents. He took no further steps in the matter.

(b) Submissions by the Government

32. The Government stated that, throughout the applicant’s detention in the SIZO and Sokalska Prison, he had been examined by various physicians, including doctors from civilian medical institutions, and had received treatment for the health problems affecting him at the relevant times, including hypertension.

E. Restrictions on family visits and telephone calls

1. Submissions by the applicant

33. The applicant stated that, while detained following his conviction, he remained in contact with his wife, his two minor children, whose ages were not specified, his mother, and four other relatives. As a general rule, he was permitted family visits no more frequently than once every six months, with each visit lasting no longer than four hours.

34. He alleged that, during his detention in the Cherkasy SIZO, such visits could be attended at any one time by either three adults and one child or two adults and two children. At Sokalska Prison, attendance was limited to two adults and one child at a time. His relatives, who lived in the Cherkasy Region, encountered difficulties travelling to Sokalska Prison in the Lviv Region, approximately 700 kilometres away.

35.
At that prison, a single room was designated for family visits, which were held on a specified day—Sunday. Owing to the high demand, visits were generally shortened considerably. More specifically, the applicant’s meetings with his family on 28 November 2004, 29 May 2005 and 28 November 2006 lasted no more than two hours, while those on 27 November 2005 and 28 May 2006 did not exceed three hours.

36. During family visits, a guard accompanied by a guard dog was present. The applicant was confined in a cage and separated from his visitors by a glass screen. He and his visitors communicated by telephone, and a prison guard continuously monitored their conversations.

37. Although the applicant made repeated requests, the administrations of Cherkasy SIZO and Sokalska Prison refused to permit intimate contact with his wife. They based their refusal on the absence of any statutory entitlement to extended family visits for prisoners serving life sentences.

38. The applicant alleged that he had been prohibited from telephoning his family between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005. On 2 November 2005, he was allowed to call his wife, but the conversation was restricted to five minutes. Thereafter, he was permitted only to receive telephone calls once every three months, subject to submitting a written request.

39. The applicant complained to the Sokalska Prison authorities about the restrictions described above concerning family visits and telephone communications. In response, the authorities supplied him with extracts from the relevant provisions of the 2003 Code on the Execution of Sentences regulating the detention conditions applicable to persons sentenced to life imprisonment.

2. Submissions by the Government

40. The Government disputed the reliability of several of the applicant’s assertions regarding limitations on family visits and telephone calls. In particular, they contested his claims that family visits had lasted under two hours; that he had been prevented from making telephone calls from 15 October 2004 until 2 November 2005; that further restrictions on his telephone rights had been imposed after 2 November 2005; that, at Cherkasy SIZO, no more than three adults and one minor child, or two adults and two minor children, could visit him at the same time; that, at Sokalska Prison, visits had been limited to two adults and two minor children at any one time; and that a guard accompanied by a guard dog had attended those visits. The Government also submitted that the applicant had not brought those complaints before the national authorities.

F. Alleged events during the applicant’s detention in Zamkova Prison in 2012

41. In a letter of 19 May 2012, the applicant asserted that correspondence sent to him by the Court in January 2012 had been opened and read by the administration of Zamkova Prison no.
58, in which he was serving a prison sentence, and alleged that the prison administration had persecuted him for corresponding with the Court. More specifically, he was held in solitary confinement from 28 January until 15 May 2012; on an unspecified date, all documents in his possession, together with his pen, were confiscated; and, for an unspecified period of two months, he was prevented from contacting his relatives. He further claimed that, prior to those incidents, disciplinary penalties had been imposed on him whenever he received letters from the Court while in detention, although he provided no further particulars.

42. The Government, for their part, maintained that none of the applicant’s letters had been opened, that his contacts with the outside world had not been obstructed, and that his allegations of persecution for applying to the Court were entirely without foundation. They submitted that he had been disciplined on several occasions for violating prison rules, including, among other things, failing to comply with the daily prison schedule and insulting prison officers.

G. The applicant’s earlier application to the Court

43. On 4 July 2002, the applicant submitted an application to the Court. He complained, among other matters, under Article 3 of the Convention that the police had tortured him, and under Articles 6 and 7 that his conviction had been unfair and that the sentence imposed on him had not been founded on the law applicable at the relevant time.

44. Seeking to support those complaints before the Court, the applicant attempted to obtain copies of various documents from his criminal case file from the domestic courts. His requests were rejected as lacking any legal basis by the President and Vice-President of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal in letters of 19 April and 10 May 2002 and 26 March 2003.

45. During 2002 and 2003, the applicant’s mother and wife visited that court on several occasions in an effort to secure copies of documents from his criminal case file. They had been authorised to represent him during the trial (see paragraph 8 above) and, following the trial, by a ruling delivered on 6 March 2003 by a judge of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal. According to the applicant, they were denied access to the file and were not permitted to remove any documents from it. He also alleged that, on an unspecified date, the same judge took their copy of the ruling of 6 March 2003 and did not return it.

46. In letters dated 19 August 2003 and 25 February 2004, the Court requested that the applicant provide documentary evidence supporting his complaints under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.
In particular, he was asked to provide copies of the written complaints he had submitted to the national authorities about his alleged ill-treatment; the prosecutor’s decision on those complaints; his cassation appeal against the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal’s judgment of 23 August 2001; and his written requests for that court to examine a witness on his behalf.

47. Following the Court’s letters, the applicant repeatedly asked the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal to supply copies of the relevant documents. Although those requests were refused, he was informed that the complete criminal case file would be forwarded to the Court if the Court requested it.

48. On an unspecified date, the applicant’s mother retained a lawyer to represent him before the authorities. The lawyer obtained copies of the documents identified in the Court’s letters, which were subsequently submitted to the Court. The applicant maintained, however, that the lawyer had not secured copies of all the documents required and that his mother’s subsequent efforts to obtain further documents had proved unsuccessful.

49. In the meantime, the applicant brought a complaint before the Prydniprovskyy District Court against the judges of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal. He contested their refusal either to give him copies of documents from his case file or to permit his relatives to represent him before the domestic authorities.

50. On 10 June 2004, the court rejected the complaint on the ground that the matter was not one for judicial determination. The Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 16 November 2004.

51. On 16 June 2006, the Higher Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal because it had been filed outside the prescribed time-limit. The applicant alleged that he had missed the deadline because the Sokalska Prison authorities had not dispatched his correspondence promptly. He then filed a fresh cassation appeal with the Higher Administrative Court and requested an extension of the time-limit. The result of that appeal is not known.

52. On 27 March 2007, the Court declared the applicant’s earlier application inadmissible.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

A. Correctional Labour Code of 1970 (repealed on 1 January 2004), in the version applicable at the relevant time

53. Article 30 stipulated that sentenced prisoners temporarily held in an investigative isolation unit (SIZO) were governed by the detention rules applicable to the category of penal institution in which they were to serve their sentence. Such prisoners could receive only short visits from relatives and other persons.

54. Pursuant to Article 39, prisoners serving life sentences were permitted one four-hour visit from relatives or other persons every six months, under the supervision of a prison guard.
Where technically feasible, they were permitted, once every three months, to make a fifteen-minute telephone call supervised by the prison authorities, with the cost borne by them.

B. Execution of Sentences Code of 2003 (in force from 1 January 2004), as applicable at the material time

55. Under Article 150, persons serving life sentences were required to be detained in correctional colonies with the highest security level.

56. Article 151 stipulated that, as a general rule, such prisoners were to be accommodated in two-person cells, although solitary confinement was possible in certain circumstances. They were entitled to one hour of daily exercise. Before the Code was amended on 21 January 2010, with effect from 16 February 2010, life prisoners could receive short visits, lasting no more than four hours, from relatives and other persons once every six months. Following those amendments, such visits were permitted once every three months.

57. Article 110 further entitled prisoners to four fifteen-minute telephone calls per year. The calls were monitored by the prison authorities and paid for by the prisoners.

C. Internal Regulations of Penal Institutions, adopted by Order No. 275 of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences on 25 December 2003 (repealed on 23 January 2015), as applicable at the material time

58. The provisions regulating the detention of life prisoners imposed particular limitations on their physical conditions, activities and opportunities for interpersonal contact. These included continuous segregation from the rest of the prison population, restricted visiting rights, a ban on communicating with other inmates and, whenever prisoners left their cells, escort by three officers with a guard dog while they were handcuffed behind their backs (Sections 23-25).

59. In accordance with Section 26, newly arrived prisoners were admitted by a commission chaired by the prison governor and comprising prison personnel, including medical officers. Prisoners were also required to undergo a medical examination upon arrival.

60. Section 47 allowed prisoners to meet with a maximum of three adults at any one time, who could also be accompanied by the prisoner’s minor children.

61. Under Section 94, medical care for life prisoners was, as a rule, to be provided in their cells and in the presence of at least three guards. Where urgent treatment was required, prisoners were to be transferred either to a medical facility operated by the State Department for the Execution of Sentences or to a civilian medical institution.

62. Annex 9 to the Regulations prohibited prisoners from possessing any medicines or medical items.

63. Annex 17 set out two possible arrangements for equipping rooms used for short visits.
Under the first arrangement, tables were to be placed along the meeting room, with 120-centimetre-wide gaps between them. Visitors were to have no more than ten chairs, while the prisoners’ stools were to be secured to the floor.64. The second arrangement envisaged a meeting room fitted with booths measuring 80 centimetres in width and 100 centimetres in length. One or two booths were to be 140 centimetres wide so that two visitors, or visitors accompanied by children, could meet the same prisoner. Glass partitions were to separate the visitors’ booths from those occupied by prisoners. Each booth was to contain a loudspeaker and a telephone handset. Booths intended for life prisoners also had to have metal bars and doors fitted with mechanical locks. The supervising officer’s desk was to include equipment enabling conversations in the booths to be monitored.

III. Relevant Council of Europe documents

65. Council of Europe materials concerning prisoners’ family visits were cited in Trosin v. Ukraine (no. 39758/05, §§ 30-31, 23 February 2012).
