34. He alleged that, during his detention in the Cherkasy SIZO, such visits could be attended at any one time by either three adults and one child or two adults and two children. In Sokalska Prison, no more than two adults and one child could attend simultaneously. His relatives lived in the Cherkasy Region and had difficulty travelling to Sokalska Prison in the Lviv Region, approximately 700 km away, to visit him.

35.
Only one room in the prison was designated for family visits, which were held on Sundays. Owing to the large number of requests for such visits, their length was generally reduced considerably. More specifically, the applicant’s family meetings on 28 November 2004, 29 May 2005 and 28 November 2006 lasted no more than two hours, while those on 27 November 2005 and 28 May 2006 lasted no more than three hours.

36. During family visits, a guard accompanied by a guard dog was present. The applicant remained inside a cage, separated from his visitors by a glass screen. He and his visitors communicated by telephone, and a prison guard continuously monitored their conversations.

37. Although the applicant made numerous requests, the administrations of the Cherkasy SIZO and Sokalska Prison refused to permit intimate contact with his wife. They explained that prisoners serving life sentences had no statutory entitlement to long family visits.

38. The applicant alleged that, from 15 October 2004 until 2 November 2005, he was prohibited from making any telephone calls to his family. On 2 November 2005, he was permitted to call his wife, but the conversation was restricted to five minutes. Thereafter, he was allowed only to receive telephone calls once every three months and only after submitting a written request.

39. The applicant complained to the Sokalska Prison authorities about the restrictions described above concerning family visits and telephone calls. In response, they supplied him with extracts from the provisions of the 2003 Code on the Execution of Sentences regulating the detention conditions applicable to persons serving life sentences.

2. The Government’s submissions

40. The Government disputed the reliability of some of the applicant’s claims about limitations on family visits and telephone calls. In particular, they contested his assertions that family visits had lasted less than two hours; that he had been unable to make any telephone calls between 15 October 2004 and 2 November 2005; that further restrictions had applied to his right to make telephone calls after 2 November 2005; that, in the Cherkasy SIZO, no more than three adults and one minor child, or two adults and two minor children, could visit him at the same time; that, in Sokalska Prison, visits were limited to two adults and two minor children at any one time; and that a guard accompanied by a guard dog had been present during those visits. The Government also maintained that the applicant had not brought those complaints before the domestic authorities.

F. Events allegedly occurring during the applicant’s detention in Zamkova Prison in 2012

41. In a letter of 19 May 2012, the applicant asserted that the Court’s letter sent to him in January 2012 had been opened and read by the administration of Zamkova Prison no.
58, in which he was serving a prison term, and alleged that the Prison administration had persecuted him for corresponding with the Court. More specifically, he was held in solitary confinement between 28 January and 15 May 2012; on an unidentified date, all documents in his possession, together with his pen, were confiscated; and for two months—without specification of the precise dates—he was denied any opportunity to communicate with his relatives. He further claimed that, before those incidents, disciplinary measures had been imposed on him whenever he received correspondence from the Court while in detention, although he supplied no further particulars.

42. The Government, for their part, maintained that none of the applicant’s letters had been opened, that his contacts with the outside world had not been obstructed, and that his claims of persecution for applying to the Court were entirely baseless. They stated that he had been subjected to disciplinary penalties on several occasions for violating prison rules, including, among other things, failing to comply with the prison’s daily timetable and insulting prison officers.

G. The applicant’s earlier application to the Court

43. On 4 July 2002, the applicant submitted an application to the Court. He complained, among other matters, under Article 3 of the Convention that the police had tortured him, and under Articles 6 and 7 that his conviction had been unfair and that his sentence had not been founded on the law applicable at the relevant time.

44. To support his complaints before the Court, the applicant sought copies of various materials from his criminal case file from the domestic courts. His requests were rejected by the President and Vice-President of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, in letters of 19 April and 10 May 2002 and 26 March 2003, on the ground that they had no legal basis.

45. During 2002-03, the applicant’s mother and wife visited that court several times in an attempt to obtain copies of documents from his criminal case file. They had been authorised to represent him during the trial (see paragraph 8 above) and, following the trial, by a decision of 6 March 2003 made by a judge of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal. The applicant alleged that they were neither permitted to inspect the file nor allowed to remove any documents from it. He also claimed that, on an unspecified date, the same judge took their copy of the ruling of 6 March 2003 and failed to return it.

46. In letters dated 19 August 2003 and 25 February 2004, the Court requested that the applicant provide documentary material supporting his complaints under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.
More specifically, he was asked to provide copies of: his written complaints to the national authorities about the alleged ill-treatment; the prosecutor’s decision on those complaints; his cassation appeal against the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal’s judgment of 23 August 2001; and his written requests for that court to examine a witness on his behalf.

47. Following the Court’s letters, the applicant made several requests to the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal for copies of the relevant documents. Those requests were denied, although he was told that the complete criminal case file would be forwarded to the Court if the Court requested it.

48. At an unspecified time, the applicant’s mother retained a lawyer to represent him before the authorities. The lawyer secured copies of the documents identified in the Court’s letters, which were later submitted to the Court. The applicant maintained, however, that the lawyer had not obtained all the required documents and that his mother’s subsequent efforts to acquire copies of further documents had failed.

49. In the meantime, the applicant brought a complaint before the Prydniprovskyy District Court against the judges of the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal, contesting their refusal either to give him copies of documents contained in his case file or to permit his relatives to represent him before the domestic authorities.

50. On 10 June 2004, the court rejected the complaint on the ground that the issue was not one for determination by the courts. The Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance ruling on 16 November 2004.

51. On 16 June 2006, the Higher Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal because it had been filed outside the prescribed period. The applicant asserted that he had missed the deadline because the Sokalska Prison authorities had not sent his correspondence promptly. He then submitted another cassation appeal to the Higher Administrative Court, accompanied by an application to extend the time-limit. The result of that appeal is not known.

52. On 27 March 2007, the Court ruled that the applicant’s earlier application was inadmissible.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW

A. The 1970 Correctional Labour Code (repealed with effect from 1 January 2004), in the version applicable at the relevant time

53. Article 30 stipulated that convicted prisoners serving terms of imprisonment who were temporarily held in an investigative isolation unit (SIZO) were governed by the detention rules applicable to the category of penal institution to which they were to be assigned under their sentence. Such prisoners could receive only short visits from relatives and other persons.

54. Pursuant to Article 39, inmates serving life sentences had the right, once every six months, to a four-hour visit with relatives or other persons, conducted in the presence of a prison officer.
Where technically feasible, they could make one fifteen-minute telephone call every three months, supervised by the prison authorities and at their own expense.

B. Execution of Sentences Code 2003 (effective from 1 January 2004), in the version applicable at the relevant time

55. Under Article 150, persons serving life sentences were required to be held in correctional colonies operating at the highest security level.

56. Article 151 stipulated that, as a general rule, life prisoners were to be accommodated in cells for two inmates, although solitary confinement was permitted in certain circumstances. They were entitled to one hour of daily exercise. Before the Code was amended on 21 January 2010, with the amendments taking effect on 16 February 2010, life prisoners could receive short visits lasting up to four hours from relatives and other individuals once every six months. Following those amendments, such visits were allowed once every three months.

57. Article 110 also granted prisoners four telephone calls per year, each lasting fifteen minutes. The calls were monitored by the prison authorities, and prisoners had to pay the associated costs.

C. Internal Regulations of Penal Institutions, adopted by Order No. 275 of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences on 25 December 2003 and repealed on 23 January 2015, in the version applicable at the relevant time

58. The provisions regulating the detention of life prisoners imposed particular limitations concerning material conditions, activities and possibilities for contact with others. These included continuous segregation from the general prison population, restricted visiting rights and a ban on communicating with other inmates. Whenever prisoners were removed from their cells, they were escorted by three officers accompanied by a guard dog and were handcuffed with their hands behind their backs (Sections 23-25).

59. Section 26 required newly arrived prisoners to be admitted by a commission consisting of prison personnel, including medical officers, under the chairmanship of the prison governor. Prisoners were also required to undergo a medical examination upon arrival.

60. According to Section 47, a prisoner could meet with no more than three adults at the same time; the prisoner’s minor children could accompany those adults.

61. Section 94 provided that medical care for life prisoners was generally to be administered inside their cells and in the presence of at least three guards. Where urgent medical treatment was necessary, prisoners were to be transferred either to a medical facility of the State Department for the Execution of Sentences or to a civilian medical institution.

62. Annex 9 prohibited prisoners from retaining any medicines or medical items in their possession.

63. Annex 17 set out two possible arrangements for furnishing a room intended for short visits.
Under the first arrangement, tables were to be placed along the meeting room, with 120 centimetres of open space between them. A maximum of ten chairs was to be provided for visitors, while the prisoners were to sit on stools secured to the floor.64.

The second arrangement required the meeting room to contain booths measuring 80 centimetres in width and 100 centimetres in length. One or two wider booths, each 140 centimetres across, were to be available for two visitors, or for visitors accompanied by children, meeting the same prisoner. Glass partitions were to divide the visitors’ booths from those used by prisoners. Every booth was to have a loudspeaker and telephone handset. Those intended for life prisoners also had to be fitted with metal bars and mechanically locking doors. The supervising officer’s desk was to include equipment enabling conversations in the booths to be monitored.

III. Pertinent Council of Europe materials

65. Council of Europe documents concerning prisoners’ family visits were cited in Trosin v. Ukraine (no. 39758/05, §§ 30-31, 23 February 2012).

On 14 August 2012 the applicant asked the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine to order the return of M. from Ukraine to the USA in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (“the Hague Convention” – see paragraph 37 below).15. On 24 September 2012 the Minnesota District Court dissolved the marriage between the applicant and S. The court reserved the issue of M.’s custody, finding that it did not have jurisdiction over that issue pursuant to Minnesota Statutes §518D.201.16. On 19 March 2013 the Chernihiv Regional Department of the State Migration Service of Ukraine issued a certificate declaring M.’s citizenship of Ukraine pursuant to section 7 § 1 of the Citizenship Act 2001.17. On 10 April 2013 the Chernihiv Regional Chief Department of Justice, acting in the applicant’s interests, lodged a claim with the Desnyansky District Court of Chernihiv (“the Desnyansky District Court”), asserting that M. had been wrongfully retained in Ukraine and must be returned to the USA in accordance with the Hague Convention.18. The applicant submitted that he had expected S. and M. to return from Ukraine to the USA on 16 August 2011; however, S. changed her plans and decided to stay on with M. in Ukraine after that date. During the hearings the applicant stated that he was prepared to cover travel expenses for both the child and the mother if the latter were to be ordered to accompany the child to the USA.19. S. objected and submitted that it was the applicant who had asked her to stay in Ukraine with the child beyond 16 August 2011. In that regard S. stated that on 9 August 2011 the applicant had sent her four parcels from Minneapolis containing all her and M.’s personal belongings, including toys and clothes. The applicant also sent her M.’s vaccination certificate for his admission to a child-care centre in Ukraine. In July 2012, despite the divorce action initiated by the applicant in the USA, S. agreed to spend a holiday with him and their son in Ukraine, trying to restore good relations. She further submitted that the applicant had arrived in Ukraine in 2013 and stayed for a considerable period of time but had not attempted to meet up with the child. S. therefore alleged that there was no factual child abduction or unlawful retention which would necessitate a return order under the Hague Convention.20. On 19 June 2013 the Desnyansky District Court found that M. had arrived in Ukraine with both parents’ agreement, but that later the mother had retained the child in Ukraine without the father’s consent. The court found that such retention was wrongful within the meaning of the Hague Convention and that the child should be returned to the country of his habitual residence, the USA. No exceptions under the Hague Convention applied. Given the applicant’s verbal assurances, the court considered that there were no objective obstacles to the mother’s accompanying the child to the USA and resolving the custody dispute before the courts of that country. In the operative part of the decision, the court ordered that M. should be returned to the USA ‒ to the father’s home address in Minneapolis ‒ specifying that the child should be accompanied on the journey by both parents.21. On 2 July 2013 the Desnyansky District Court issued an additional decision stating that if the child were not returned voluntarily, S. would be ordered to transfer the child to the applicant at his home address in Minneapolis.22. S. appealed against those decisions, maintaining that there was no abduction or unlawful retention of the child and that, in any event, there were grounds to apply the exception provided by Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) as regarded the risk of psychological harm to the child and his being placed in an intolerable situation.23. In that regard the Court of Appeal stated that M. was completely settled in his new environment, as he had been living in Ukraine since June 2011. M. had always lived with the mother and there were close ties between them. There was no realistic possibility for the mother to accompany M. to the USA and stay near him in that country. In addition, the Court of Appeal noted that the applicant had not provided any information regarding his actual place of residence in the USA, his current living conditions, or his level of income.25. On 20 November 2013 the Higher Specialised Court of Ukraine for Civil and Criminal Matters (“the Cassation Court”) quashed the decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above) and upheld the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above), noting that they were well substantiated and had been adopted in compliance with the requirements of the Hague Convention. It found the submissions concerning the risk of exposing M. to psychological harm unconvincing.26. On 28 April 2014 the Cassation Court declared the request admissible and referred the case to the Supreme Court.29. Having examined the domestic judicial practice, the Supreme Court found that Articles 3, 12 and 13 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) had been applied divergently. It set out the principles which had to be followed when interpreting and applying those provisions. As regards the present case, the Supreme Court found that the domestic courts had failed to apply the provisions properly. In particular, there had been no clear stance on the question of whether or not the removal or retention of the child had been wrongful, and ‒ if that were the case ‒ at what moment it started to be wrongful, nor as to whether or not the father had consented to or subsequently acquiesced as regards the child’s retention, nor whether facts existed demonstrating that the child was settled in his current environment. On 30 July 2014 the Cassation Court quashed the Court of Appeal’s decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above), on the grounds that the Court of Appeal had breached procedural rules and had failed to establish all the relevant facts. The case was remitted to the Court of Appeal.31. On 5 September 2014 the Court of Appeal found that there was no dispute regarding removal of the child because the father had only complained about the wrongful retention of the child in Ukraine. The Court of Appeal then considered the applicant’s updated submissions, in which he no longer argued that the retention of the child had been wrongful as from 16 August 2011 but rather as from 20 June 2012, which was the date when he had first expressed his disagreement with the child’s retention in Ukraine. It was also established that in August 2011 the applicant had sent parcels to Ukraine containing the child’s belongings.32. It also considered that M.’s return to the USA without his mother – who no longer had legal basis for entering and living in the USA – would not be in the best interests of the child. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW35. Section 7 § 1 of the Law of Ukraine on Ukrainian citizenship of 18 January 2001 (“the Citizenship Act 2001”) provides that a person shall qualify for Ukrainian citizenship if at the time of his or her birth one or both parents had Ukrainian citizenship.36. By Resolution no. 952 of 10 July 2006 the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine approved the regulations on execution of the Hague Convention on the territory of Ukraine. The regulations provide that the functions of the Ukrainian Central Authority are performed by the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine and by its territorial departments. The regulations lay down, in particular, the procedure for dealing with the applications for assistance in securing the return of children from Ukraine to foreign countries. According to the regulations, it is for the Ministry of Justice to institute court proceedings in order to ensure the return of the child; the Ministry of Justice should notify, if appropriate, the foreign Central Authority and/or the applicant about the necessity of providing additional information in support of such applications (paragraph 9).III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL LAW37. The relevant provisions of the Hague Convention (entered into force in respect of Ukraine on 1 September 2006), state as follows:Article 3“The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where -(a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention; and(b) at the time of removal or retention those rights were actually exercised, either jointly or alone, or would have been so exercised but for the removal or retention.The rights of custody mentioned in sub-paragraph (a) above, may arise in particular by operation of law or by reason of a judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement having legal effect under the law of that State.”Article 4“The Convention shall apply to any child who was habitually resident in a Contracting State immediately before any breach of custody or access rights. The Convention shall cease to apply when the child attains the age of 16 years.”Article 5“For the purposes of this Convention -(a) “rights of custody” shall include rights relating to the care of the person of the child and, in particular, the right to determine the child’s place of residence;(b) “rights of access” shall include the right to take a child for a limited period of time to a place other than the child’s habitual residence....”Article 11“The judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States shall act expeditiously in proceedings for the return of children.If the judicial or administrative authority concerned has not reached a decision within six weeks from the date of commencement of the proceedings, the applicant or the Central Authority of the requested State, on its own initiative or if asked by the Central Authority of the requesting State, shall have the right to request a statement of the reasons for the delay.”Article 12“Where a child has been wrongfully removed or retained in terms of Article 3 and, at the date of the commencement of the proceedings before the judicial or administrative authority of the Contracting State where the child is, a period of less than one year has elapsed from the date of the wrongful removal or retention, the authority concerned shall order the return of the child forthwith.The judicial or administrative authority, even where the proceedings have been commenced after the expiration of the period of one year referred to in the preceding paragraph, shall also order the return of the child, unless it is demonstrated that the child is now settled in its new environment.Where the judicial or administrative authority in the requested State has reason to believe that the child has been taken to another State, it may stay the proceedings or dismiss the application for the return of the child.”Article 13“Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding Article, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested State is not bound to order the return of the child if the person, institution or other body which opposes its return establishes that -(a)   the person, institution or other body having the care of the person of the child was not actually exercising the custody rights at the time of removal or retention, or had consented to or subsequently acquiesced in the removal or retention; or(b) there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.The judicial or administrative authority may also refuse to order the return of the child if it finds that the child objects to being returned and has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of its views.In considering the circumstances referred to in this Article, the judicial and administrative authorities shall take into account the information relating to the social background of the child provided by the Central Authority or other competent authority of the child’s habitual residence....”Article 16“After receiving notice of a wrongful removal or retention of a child in the sense of Article 3, the judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been removed or in which it has been retained shall not decide on the merits of rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be returned under this Convention or unless an application under this Convention is not lodged within a reasonable time following receipt of the notice....”Article 19“A decision under this Convention concerning the return of the child shall not be taken to be a determination on the merits of any custody issue.”Article 20“The return of the child under the provisions of Article 12 may be refused if this would not be permitted by the fundamental principles of the requested State relating to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms....”

She further submitted that the applicant had travelled to Ukraine in 2013 and stayed for a considerable period but had made no attempt to meet the child. S. therefore alleged that there had been no actual child abduction or unlawful retention requiring a return order under the Hague Convention.20. On 19 June 2013, the Desnyansky District Court found that M. had arrived in Ukraine with both parents’ agreement, but that the mother had subsequently retained the child there without the father’s consent. The court held that such retention was wrongful within the meaning of the Hague Convention and that the child should be returned to his country of habitual residence, the USA. It found that none of the exceptions under the Hague Convention applied. In view of the applicant’s verbal assurances, the court considered that there were no objective obstacles preventing the mother from accompanying the child to the USA and resolving the custody dispute before the courts of that country. In the operative part of its decision, the court ordered that M. be returned to the USA—to the father’s home address in Minneapolis—and specified that the child should be accompanied on the journey by both parents.21.
On 2 July 2013 the Desnyansky District Court issued an additional decision stating that, if the child was not returned voluntarily, S. would be ordered to transfer the child to the applicant at his home address in Minneapolis.

22. S. appealed against those decisions, arguing that there had been no abduction or unlawful retention of the child and that, in any event, there were grounds to apply the exception under Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below), given the risk of psychological harm to the child and of his being placed in an intolerable situation.

23. On 13 August 2013 the Municipal Centre of Social Services for Family, Children and Youth of Chernihiv issued a certificate setting out its psychiatrist’s opinion that M. was “well settled in Ukraine and, having regard to the strong bond between the child and the mother and the need to avoid causing the child psychological trauma, it would be inappropriate to remove the child to the other place of residence”.

24. On 14 August 2013 the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) quashed the decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and dismissed the applicant’s claim as unfounded. The court found that there was a grave risk that M.’s return to the USA would expose him to psychological harm or otherwise place him in an intolerable situation, within the meaning of Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention. In that connection, the Court of Appeal stated that M. was fully settled in his new environment, having lived in Ukraine since June 2011. M. had always lived with his mother, and there were close ties between them. There was no realistic possibility that the mother could accompany M. to the USA and remain near him there. The Court of Appeal also noted that the applicant had not provided any information about his actual place of residence in the USA, his current living conditions, or his income level.

25. On 20 November 2013 the Higher Specialised Court of Ukraine for Civil and Criminal Matters (“the Cassation Court”) quashed the decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above) and upheld the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above), finding that they were well substantiated and had been adopted in accordance with the requirements of the Hague Convention. It considered the submissions concerning the risk of psychological harm to M. unconvincing.

26. On 26 November 2013 the Desnyanskyy District Court issued a writ of execution in respect of its decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013. On the same day, S.’s lawyer contacted the USA Embassy in Kyiv and enquired about applying for a USA visa in the particular circumstances.

27. On 27 November 2013 the Desnyanskyy District Department of the State Bailiffs Service instituted enforcement proceedings, which resulted in fines being imposed on S. for failing to comply with the return order.

28.
In February 2014, S. requested that the Supreme Court review the case on the grounds that the Hague Convention had been applied divergently in the cassation proceedings, leading to inconsistent judicial practice. On 28 April 2014, the Cassation Court declared the request admissible and referred the case to the Supreme Court.

29. On 18 June 2014, the Supreme Court examined S.’s request for review of the Cassation Court’s decision of 20 November 2013 (see paragraph 25 above) on the basis of divergent application of the law by the cassation courts. Having reviewed the domestic judicial practice, the Supreme Court found that Articles 3, 12 and 13 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) had been applied inconsistently. It set out the principles to be followed when interpreting and applying those provisions. With regard to the present case, the Supreme Court found that the domestic courts had failed to apply the provisions correctly. In particular, they had taken no clear position on whether the removal or retention of the child had been wrongful and, if so, when it had become wrongful; whether the father had consented to or subsequently acquiesced in the child’s retention; or whether there were facts demonstrating that the child was settled in his current environment. The Supreme Court quashed the decision of 20 November 2013 and remitted the case to the Cassation Court for fresh consideration.

30. On 30 July 2014, the Cassation Court quashed the Court of Appeal’s decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above), finding that the Court of Appeal had breached procedural rules and failed to establish all the relevant facts. The case was remitted to the Court of Appeal.

31. On 5 September 2014, the Court of Appeal found that there was no dispute concerning the child’s removal, as the father had complained only about the child’s wrongful retention in Ukraine. It then considered the applicant’s updated submissions, in which he no longer claimed that the child’s retention had been wrongful from 16 August 2011, but instead from 20 June 2012, the date on which he had first expressed his disagreement with the child’s retention in Ukraine. It was also established that, in August 2011, the applicant had sent parcels to Ukraine containing the child’s belongings.

32. Regarding the period beginning on 20 June 2012, the Court of Appeal considered that the applicant had continued to consent to the child’s retention in Ukraine, as he had raised no express objection on that point before submitting the request under the Hague Convention. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant’s divorce claim had been delivered to S.’s representative on 20 June 2012.
In that claim, the applicant also sought to obtain sole custody of the child; however, this did not mean that he objected to the child’s continued stay in Ukraine. Moreover, in July 2012, the applicant had spent a holiday with S. and M. in Ukraine, and in August 2012, following his return to the USA, he had sent M.’s vaccination certificate to facilitate M.’s admission to a child-care centre in Ukraine. The Court of Appeal concluded that, in those circumstances, the applicant enjoyed custody rights in respect of M. and had failed to show that those rights had been violated. For those reasons, the child’s retention during that period could not be regarded as wrongful within the meaning of the Hague Convention.

33. The Court of Appeal further stated that, even assuming that the child had been wrongfully retained, the return request could be refused under Articles 12, 13 and 20 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below). It examined the evidence concerning the child’s place of residence in Ukraine and the social and medical care provided to him there, and found that M. had all the conditions necessary for his proper development. On the basis of the evidence submitted, and having regard to the overall period during which the child had lived in Ukraine, the Court of Appeal found that M. was fully settled in his current environment. It also considered that M.’s return to the USA without his mother – who no longer had a legal basis for entering and residing in the USA – would not be in the child’s best interests. The Court of Appeal therefore quashed the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and dismissed the applicant’s claim as unfounded.

34. On 4 December 2014, the Cassation Court dismissed the appeals on points of law lodged by the applicant and the Ministry of Justice and upheld the decision of 5 September 2014 (see paragraphs 31–33 above).

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

35. Section 7 § 1 of the Law of Ukraine on Ukrainian Citizenship of 18 January 2001 (“the Citizenship Act 2001”) provides that a person qualifies for Ukrainian citizenship if, at the time of his or her birth, either or both parents held Ukrainian citizenship.

36. By Resolution no. 952 of 10 July 2006, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine approved the regulations governing the implementation of the Hague Convention in Ukraine. The regulations provide that the functions of the Ukrainian Central Authority are carried out by the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine and its territorial departments. In particular, the regulations set out the procedure for handling applications for assistance in securing the return of children from Ukraine to foreign countries.
Under the regulations, it is for the Ministry of Justice to institute court proceedings to ensure the child’s return; where appropriate, the Ministry of Justice should notify the foreign Central Authority and/or the applicant of the need to provide additional information in support of such applications (paragraph 9).

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL LAW

37. The relevant provisions of the Hague Convention (which entered into force in respect of Ukraine on 1 September 2006) read as follows:

Article 3

“The removal or retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where –

(a) it breaches rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention; and

(b) at the time of removal or retention, those rights were actually exercised, either jointly or alone, or would have been so exercised but for the removal or retention.

The rights of custody referred to in sub-paragraph (a) above may arise, in particular, by operation of law, by reason of a judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement having legal effect under the law of that State.”

Article 4

“The Convention shall apply to any child who was habitually resident in a Contracting State immediately before a breach of custody or access rights. The Convention shall cease to apply when the child reaches the age of 16 years.”

Article 5

“For the purposes of this Convention –

(a) ‘rights of custody’ shall include rights concerning the care of the child and, in particular, the right to determine the child’s place of residence;

(b) ‘rights of access’
shall encompass the right to take a child, for a limited period, to a place other than the child’s habitual residence....”

Article 11

“The judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States shall proceed expeditiously in proceedings for the return of children.

If the judicial or administrative authority concerned has not made a decision within six weeks from the commencement of the proceedings, the applicant or the Central Authority of the requested State, acting on its own initiative or at the request of the Central Authority of the requesting State, shall have the right to seek a statement explaining the reasons for the delay.”

Article 12

“Where a child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of Article 3 and, on the date proceedings commence before the judicial or administrative authority of the Contracting State where the child is located, less than one year has passed since the wrongful removal or retention, the authority concerned shall order the immediate return of the child.

The judicial or administrative authority, even where proceedings have begun after the expiration of the one-year period referred to in the preceding paragraph, shall likewise order the return of the child, unless it is established that the child is now settled in its new environment.

Where the judicial or administrative authority in the requested State has reason to believe that the child has been taken to another State, it may suspend the proceedings or dismiss the application for the child’s return.”

Article 13

“Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding Article, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested State is not required to order the return of the child if the person, institution or other body opposing the return establishes that—

(a) the person, institution or other body responsible for the care of the child was not actually exercising custody rights at the time of the removal or retention, or had consented to or later acquiesced in the removal or retention; or

(b) there is a grave risk that the child’s return would expose him or her to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.

The judicial or administrative authority may also decline to order the child’s return if it finds that the child objects to returning and has reached an age and level of maturity at which it is appropriate to consider the child’s views.

In assessing the circumstances referred to in this Article, the judicial and administrative authorities shall consider the information concerning the child’s social background provided by the Central Authority or another competent authority of the child’s habitual residence....”

Article 16

“Upon receiving notice of the wrongful removal or retention of a child within the meaning of Article 3, the judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been removed or in which it
where the child has been retained shall not determine the merits of custody rights until it has been established that the child is not to be returned under this Convention, or unless an application under this Convention is not filed within a reasonable time after receipt of the notice....”

Article 19

“A decision under this Convention regarding the return of the child shall not be regarded as a determination on the merits of any custody issue.”

Article 20

“The return of the child under Article 12 may be refused if it would not be permitted under the fundamental principles of the requested State concerning the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms....”

(Application no. 21267/14)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

3 October 2017

FINAL

03/01/2018

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment has become final. It remains subject to possible editorial revision.

In the case of Vilenchik v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Vincent A. De Gaetano, President,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
Paulo Pinto de Albuquerque,  
Faris Vehabović,  
Carlo Ranzoni,  
Georges Ravarani,  
Marko Bošnjak, judges,

and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar,

Having considered the case in private on 5 September 2017,

Gives the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 21267/14, which Mr Andrew Vilenchik (“the applicant”), a national of the United States of America (“the USA”), lodged against Ukraine on 10 March 2014 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. Mr J. Kanetkar, a lawyer practising in Englewood Cliffs, USA, represented the applicant. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant complained that the Ukrainian authorities had not secured his son’s return to the USA.

4. Notice of the application was given to the Government on 14 October 2015.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1978, the applicant resides in Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA.

6. On 24 July 2009, he married S., a Ukrainian national, in Minneapolis.

7. Their son, M., was born in Minneapolis on 28 August 2009. The family made their home there, and M. was issued with a US passport.

8. S. acquired permanent resident status in the USA on 10 May 2010.

9. In June 2011, the family travelled to Ukraine for a holiday and to visit S.’s relatives.

10. The applicant returned to the USA by himself on 13 July 2011, while M. remained in Ukraine with S.

11. S.’s US permanent resident card expired in May 2012.

12. In June 2012, the applicant brought proceedings before the Minnesota 4th Judicial District Family Court (“the Minnesota District Court”), requesting the dissolution of the marriage and sole custody of M. Although S. consented to the dissolution of the marriage, she maintained that, under section 518D.201 of the Minnesota Statutes, the Minnesota District Court lacked jurisdiction to determine M.’s custody because he had lived in Ukraine for more than six consecutive months.

13. In July 2012, the applicant spent a holiday in Ukraine with S. and M.

14. On 14 August 2012, relying on the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (“the Hague Convention”; see paragraph 37 below), the applicant asked the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine to order M.’s return from Ukraine to the USA.

15.
On 24 September 2012, the Minnesota District Court terminated the marriage of the applicant and S. It deferred the question of custody of M., concluding that it lacked jurisdiction to determine that matter under Minnesota Statutes § 518D.201.16.

On 19 March 2013, pursuant to section 7 § 1 of the Citizenship Act 2001, the Chernihiv Regional Department of the State Migration Service of Ukraine issued a certificate confirming that M. was a Ukrainian citizen.17.

Acting on behalf of the applicant, the Chernihiv Regional Chief Department of Justice brought proceedings before the Desnyansky District Court of Chernihiv (“the Desnyansky District Court”) on 10 April 2013. It alleged that M. had been unlawfully retained in Ukraine and sought the child’s return to the USA under the Hague Convention.18.

The applicant maintained that S. and M. had been due to return from Ukraine to the USA on 16 August 2011, but that S. had subsequently altered her plans and decided to remain in Ukraine with M. after that date. At the hearings, he stated that, if S. were ordered to accompany the child to the USA, he was willing to pay the travel costs of both mother and child.19.

S. contested the claim, arguing that the applicant himself had asked her to remain in Ukraine with M. beyond 16 August 2011. She stated that, on 9 August 2011, he had sent four parcels from Minneapolis containing all of her and M.’s personal possessions, including clothing and toys. He had also forwarded M.’s vaccination certificate so that the child could be enrolled in a Ukrainian child-care centre. According to S., although the applicant had already instituted divorce proceedings in the USA, she agreed in July 2012 to spend a holiday with him and their son in Ukraine in an effort to repair their relationship. She further asserted that the applicant had come to Ukraine in 2013 and remained there for a substantial period without trying to see the child. On that basis, S. contended that no child abduction or unlawful retention had in fact occurred and that there were therefore no grounds for ordering M.’s return under the Hague Convention.20.

In a decision of 19 June 2013, the Desnyansky District Court held that M. had initially travelled to Ukraine with the consent of both parents, but that the mother had later kept him there without the father’s agreement. It found that this amounted to wrongful retention for the purposes of the Hague Convention and ordered the child’s return to the USA, his country of habitual residence. The court determined that none of the exceptions provided for by the Convention was applicable. Relying on the applicant’s oral assurances, it also concluded that no objective impediment prevented the mother from accompanying M. to the USA and having the custody dispute decided by the courts there. In the operative part of its judgment, the court directed that M. be returned to the applicant’s home address in Minneapolis, USA, and specified that both parents were to accompany the child on the journey.21.
22. In a supplementary decision delivered on 2 July 2013, the Desnyansky District Court held that, unless the child was returned voluntarily, S. would be required to hand him over to the applicant at the latter’s home address in Minneapolis.

23. S. challenged those decisions on appeal. She argued that the child had neither been abducted nor unlawfully retained and that, in any event, the exception under Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) was applicable because his return would create a risk of psychological harm and place him in an intolerable situation. On 13 August 2013, the Municipal Centre of Social Services for Family, Children and Youth of Chernihiv issued a certificate recording its psychiatrist’s view that M. was “well settled in Ukraine and, having regard to the strong bond between the child and the mother and the need to avoid causing the child psychological trauma, it would be inappropriate to remove the child to the other place of residence”.

24. On 14 August 2013, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) set aside the decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and rejected the applicant’s claim as unsubstantiated. It found that returning M. to the USA would entail a grave risk of exposing him to psychological harm or otherwise placing him in an intolerable situation within the meaning of Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention. The Court of Appeal observed that M., who had lived in Ukraine since June 2011, had become fully settled in his new surroundings. He had always resided with his mother, with whom he shared a close bond. There was no realistic prospect that she could accompany him to the USA and remain near him there. The court further noted that the applicant had submitted no information about his actual residence in the USA, his current living conditions, or his income.

25. On 20 November 2013, the Higher Specialised Court of Ukraine for Civil and Criminal Matters (“the Cassation Court”) overturned the judgment of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above) and reinstated the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above). It held that those decisions were properly reasoned and had been adopted in accordance with the Hague Convention. The Cassation Court was not persuaded by the arguments that M. would be at risk of psychological harm.

26. The Desnyanskyy District Court issued a writ of execution for its decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 on 26 November 2013. That same day, S.’s lawyer contacted the United States Embassy in Kyiv to ask about applying for a United States visa in the particular circumstances.

27. On 27 November 2013, the Desnyanskyy District Department of the State Bailiffs Service opened enforcement proceedings. Those proceedings led to fines being imposed on S. for failing to comply with the return order.
In February 2014, S. applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the case, arguing that the Hague Convention had been interpreted differently in the cassation proceedings, thereby creating inconsistent judicial practice. On 28 April 2014, the Cassation Court ruled the application admissible and transferred the case to the Supreme Court.

29. On 18 June 2014, the Supreme Court examined S.’s application for review of the Cassation Court’s decision of 20 November 2013 (see paragraph 25 above), which was based on the divergent application of the law by the cassation courts. After reviewing the domestic case-law, it concluded that Articles 3, 12 and 13 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) had not been applied consistently and identified the principles to be observed in interpreting and applying those provisions. Turning to the present case, the Supreme Court held that the domestic courts had applied them incorrectly. In particular, they had not clearly determined whether the child’s removal or retention had been wrongful or, if so, when it had become wrongful. Nor had they established whether the father had consented to, or subsequently acquiesced in, the child’s retention, or whether there were facts showing that the child had become settled in his current environment. The Supreme Court therefore quashed the decision of 20 November 2013 and sent the case back to the Cassation Court for reconsideration.

30. On 30 July 2014, the Cassation Court set aside the Court of Appeal’s decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above), finding that the Court of Appeal had violated procedural rules and had not established all relevant facts. It remitted the case to the Court of Appeal.

31. On 5 September 2014, the Court of Appeal held that the child’s removal was not in dispute, since the father’s complaint concerned only the child’s allegedly wrongful retention in Ukraine. It then examined the applicant’s revised submissions. Rather than maintaining that the retention had been wrongful from 16 August 2011, he now argued that it had become wrongful on 20 June 2012, when he had first indicated his opposition to the child remaining in Ukraine. The court also established that, in August 2011, the applicant had sent parcels containing the child’s belongings to Ukraine.

32. With respect to the period beginning on 20 June 2012, the Court of Appeal concluded that the applicant had continued to consent to the child’s retention in Ukraine because he had raised no explicit objection before submitting the request under the Hague Convention. It further found that the applicant’s divorce claim had been delivered to S.’s representative on 20 June 2012.
In those proceedings, the applicant also requested sole custody of the child. That request, however, did not indicate that he opposed the child’s continued stay in Ukraine. In addition, the applicant had spent a holiday with S. and M. in Ukraine in July 2012. After returning to the United States in August 2012, he forwarded M.’s vaccination certificate to assist with M.’s enrolment in a child-care centre in Ukraine. In view of those circumstances, the Court of Appeal held that the applicant had custody rights in respect of M. but had not shown that those rights had been infringed. Accordingly, the child’s retention during that period could not be regarded as wrongful for the purposes of the Hague Convention.

33. The Court of Appeal further held that, even if the child’s retention were presumed to have been wrongful, the application for return could be refused under Articles 12, 13 and 20 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below). After reviewing the evidence concerning the child’s living arrangements and the social and medical care available to him in Ukraine, the court found that M. had all the conditions required for his proper development. Considering both the evidence and the total length of time M. had lived in Ukraine, it concluded that he had become fully settled in his present environment. The court also determined that returning M. to the United States without his mother—who no longer had a legal basis for entering or residing there—would be contrary to his best interests. It therefore set aside the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and rejected the applicant’s claim as unsubstantiated.

34. On 4 December 2014, the Cassation Court rejected the appeals on points of law lodged by the applicant and the Ministry of Justice and affirmed the decision of 5 September 2014 (see paragraphs 31–33 above).

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

35. Under section 7 § 1 of the Law of Ukraine on Ukrainian Citizenship of 18 January 2001 (“the Citizenship Act 2001”), a person is entitled to Ukrainian citizenship if, at the time of his or her birth, either or both parents were Ukrainian citizens.

36. By Resolution no. 952 of 10 July 2006, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted regulations governing the implementation of the Hague Convention in Ukraine. Those regulations designate the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine and its territorial departments to carry out the functions of the Ukrainian Central Authority. They also establish, among other matters, the procedure for processing applications seeking assistance with the return of children from Ukraine to other countries.
Under the applicable regulations, responsibility for initiating judicial proceedings to secure the child’s return rests with the Ministry of Justice. Where appropriate, the Ministry should inform the foreign Central Authority and/or the applicant that further information is required to support the application (paragraph 9).

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL LAW

37. The pertinent provisions of the Hague Convention, which entered into force with respect to Ukraine on 1 September 2006, provide as follows:

Article 3

A child’s removal or retention is wrongful if:

(a) it violates custody rights vested, either jointly or individually, in a person, institution, or other body under the law of the State where the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention; and

(b) those rights were being exercised, jointly or individually, at the time of the removal or retention, or would have been exercised had the removal or retention not occurred.

The custody rights referred to in subparagraph (a) may arise by operation of law, from a judicial or administrative decision, or under an agreement having legal effect pursuant to the law of that State.

Article 4

The Convention applies to every child who was habitually resident in a Contracting State immediately before custody or access rights were breached. It ceases to apply once the child reaches the age of 16.

Article 5

For the purposes of the Convention:

(a) “rights of custody” encompass rights concerning the child’s personal care and, in particular, the right to decide where the child shall live;

(b) “rights of access”
…includes the right to take the child, for a limited time, to a location other than the child’s habitual residence.

Article 11

The judicial and administrative authorities of the Contracting States must handle proceedings concerning the return of children without delay.

If the relevant judicial or administrative authority has not issued a decision within six weeks after the proceedings began, the applicant or the Central Authority of the requested State may seek an explanation for the delay. The Central Authority of the requested State may do so on its own initiative or at the request of the Central Authority of the requesting State.

Article 12

When a child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of Article 3, and fewer than twelve months have passed between the wrongful removal or retention and the commencement of proceedings before the judicial or administrative authority of the Contracting State in which the child is located, that authority must direct the child’s immediate return.

The authority must also order the child’s return when proceedings begin more than one year after the wrongful removal or retention, unless it is shown that the child has become settled in the new environment.

If the judicial or administrative authority in the requested State has grounds to believe that the child has been taken to a different State, it may suspend the proceedings or reject the application for the child’s return.

Article 13

Despite Article 12, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested State is not required to direct the child’s return if the person, institution, or other body opposing the return proves that:

(a) the person, institution, or other body responsible for the child’s care was not actually exercising custody rights when the removal or retention occurred, or had agreed to the removal or retention beforehand or accepted it afterward; or

(b) returning the child would create a grave risk of physical or psychological harm or would otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.

The judicial or administrative authority may also decline to order the return if the child objects and has reached an age and level of maturity at which it is appropriate to give weight to the child’s views.

When assessing the circumstances described in this Article, judicial and administrative authorities must consider information about the child’s social background supplied by the Central Authority or another competent authority in the State of the child’s habitual residence.

Article 16

Once notice has been received that a child was wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of Article 3, the judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child was taken, or in which the child…
“…the authorities of the State in which the child has been retained shall not rule on the substance of custody rights until it is established that the child will not be returned pursuant to this Convention, or unless no application under the Convention is submitted within a reasonable period after the notice is received….”

Article 19

“A ruling made under this Convention regarding the child’s return does not constitute a decision on the merits of any custody matter.”

Article 20

“The child’s return under Article 12 may be denied where it would be impermissible under the requested State’s fundamental principles concerning the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms….”
