On 24 September 2012, the Minnesota District Court terminated the marriage of the applicant and S. It left the question of M.’s custody unresolved, concluding that under Minnesota Statutes § 518D.201 it lacked jurisdiction to determine that matter.16.

Pursuant to section 7 § 1 of the Citizenship Act 2001, the Chernihiv Regional Department of the State Migration Service of Ukraine issued a certificate on 19 March 2013 confirming that M. was a Ukrainian citizen.17.

Acting on the applicant’s behalf, the Chernihiv Regional Chief Department of Justice brought proceedings before the Desnyansky District Court of Chernihiv (“the Desnyansky District Court”) on 10 April 2013. It claimed that M. had been unlawfully retained in Ukraine and sought his return to the USA under the Hague Convention.18.

According to the applicant, S. and M. had been due to return from Ukraine to the USA on 16 August 2011, but S. altered her plans and chose to remain in Ukraine with M. after that date. At the hearings, he said that, if S. were ordered to travel with the child to the USA, he was willing to pay both her and the child’s travel costs.19.

S. contested the claim, maintaining that the applicant himself had requested that she and the child remain in Ukraine beyond 16 August 2011. She stated that, on 9 August 2011, he had mailed four parcels from Minneapolis containing all of her and M.’s personal possessions, including clothes and toys. He had also sent M.’s vaccination record so that the child could be admitted to a child-care centre in Ukraine. Although the applicant had commenced divorce proceedings in the USA, S. agreed in July 2012 to take a holiday with him and their son in Ukraine in an effort to repair their relationship. She additionally asserted that, despite coming to Ukraine in 2013 and remaining there for a substantial period, the applicant had made no attempt to see the child. On that basis, S. argued that neither an actual abduction nor an unlawful retention had occurred and that no return order under the Hague Convention was therefore warranted.20.

In a decision of 19 June 2013, the Desnyansky District Court held that M. had initially travelled to Ukraine with the agreement of both parents, but that the mother had subsequently kept him there without the father’s consent. It ruled that this amounted to wrongful retention for the purposes of the Hague Convention and that M. had to be returned to his country of habitual residence, the USA. The court found that none of the Convention’s exceptions was applicable. Relying on the applicant’s oral assurances, it further concluded that there were no objective impediments preventing the mother from accompanying M. to the USA and having the custody dispute decided by the courts there. In the operative provisions, the court directed that M. be returned to the USA, specifically to the father’s residential address in Minneapolis, and stipulated that both parents were to accompany the child during the journey.21.
On 2 July 2013, the Desnyansky District Court delivered a supplementary decision providing that, unless the child was returned voluntarily, S. would be required to hand the child over to the applicant at his home address in Minneapolis.

22. S. challenged those decisions on appeal, arguing that the child had neither been abducted nor unlawfully retained. She further contended that, in any event, the exception under Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) applied because returning the child would create a risk of psychological harm and place him in an intolerable situation.

23. On 13 August 2013, the Municipal Centre of Social Services for Family, Children and Youth of Chernihiv issued a certificate recording its psychiatrist’s view that M. was “well settled in Ukraine and, having regard to the strong bond between the child and the mother and the need to avoid causing the child psychological trauma, it would be inappropriate to remove the child to the other place of residence”.

24. On 14 August 2013, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) set aside the decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and rejected the applicant’s claim as unsupported. Relying on Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention, it found a grave risk that returning M. to the USA would cause him psychological harm or otherwise place him in an intolerable situation. The Court of Appeal observed that M., who had lived in Ukraine since June 2011, had become fully settled in his new surroundings. It also noted that he had always resided with his mother and shared a close bond with her. There was no realistic prospect that the mother could travel with M. to the USA and remain near him there. The court additionally pointed out that the applicant had supplied no information about his actual residence in the USA, his present living conditions, or his income level.

25. On 20 November 2013, the Higher Specialised Court of Ukraine for Civil and Criminal Matters (“the Cassation Court”) overturned the decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above) and reinstated the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above). It held that those decisions were properly reasoned and had been adopted in accordance with the Hague Convention’s requirements. The Cassation Court was not persuaded by the arguments that M. would face a risk of psychological harm.

26. On 26 November 2013, the Desnyanskyy District Court issued a writ of execution concerning its decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013. That same day, S.’s lawyer approached the USA Embassy in Kyiv to ask about obtaining a USA visa under the particular circumstances.

27. On 27 November 2013, the Desnyanskyy District Department of the State Bailiffs Service opened enforcement proceedings, which led to fines being imposed on S. for failing to obey the return order.

28.
In February 2014, S. asked the Supreme Court to review the case, arguing that the Hague Convention had been interpreted differently during the cassation proceedings and had thus produced inconsistent judicial practice. On 28 April 2014, the Cassation Court found the request admissible and transferred the case to the Supreme Court.

29. On 18 June 2014, the Supreme Court examined S.’s application for review of the Cassation Court’s ruling of 20 November 2013 (see paragraph 25 above), which alleged that the cassation courts had applied the law inconsistently. After analysing domestic judicial practice, it concluded that Articles 3, 12 and 13 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below) had been subject to divergent application. The Supreme Court therefore identified the principles governing the interpretation and application of those provisions. Turning to the case at hand, it held that the domestic courts had not applied them correctly. In particular, the courts had failed to reach a clear position on whether the child’s removal or retention had been wrongful and, if so, when it had become wrongful. They had also failed to determine whether the father had consented to the child’s retention or subsequently acquiesced in it, and whether there were facts showing that the child had become settled in his current environment. Accordingly, the Supreme Court set aside the decision of 20 November 2013 and returned the case to the Cassation Court for reconsideration.

30. On 30 July 2014, the Cassation Court overturned the Court of Appeal’s decision of 14 August 2013 (see paragraph 24 above), finding that the Court of Appeal had violated procedural rules and had not established all relevant facts. It remitted the case to the Court of Appeal.

31. On 5 September 2014, the Court of Appeal held that the child’s removal was not in dispute, since the father’s complaint concerned only the allegedly wrongful retention of the child in Ukraine. It then examined the applicant’s revised submissions. Instead of maintaining that the retention had been wrongful from 16 August 2011, he now contended that it had become wrongful on 20 June 2012, when he had first communicated his opposition to the child remaining in Ukraine. The court also established that, in August 2011, the applicant had sent parcels to Ukraine containing the child’s possessions.

32. With respect to the period beginning on 20 June 2012, the Court of Appeal held that the applicant had continued to agree to the child’s retention in Ukraine because he had raised no explicit objection before lodging the request under the Hague Convention. It further found that the applicant’s divorce claim had been served on S.’s representative on 20 June 2012.
Although the applicant also sought sole custody of the child in that claim, this did not indicate that he objected to the child continuing to stay in Ukraine. Furthermore, in July 2012 he had spent a holiday in Ukraine with S. and M. After returning to the USA, he had sent M.’s vaccination certificate in August 2012 to facilitate the child’s admission to a child-care centre in Ukraine. The Court of Appeal held that, in those circumstances, the applicant had custody rights in respect of M. but had not shown that those rights had been breached. Accordingly, the child’s retention during that period could not be regarded as wrongful under the Hague Convention.

33. The Court of Appeal further held that, even if the child’s retention were assumed to have been wrongful, the request for return could be refused pursuant to Articles 12, 13 and 20 of the Hague Convention (see paragraph 37 below). Having examined the evidence concerning the child’s residence and the social and medical care available to him in Ukraine, it found that M. had all the conditions required for his proper development. In view of the evidence submitted and the total length of time M. had lived in Ukraine, the Court of Appeal concluded that he was fully settled in his present environment. It also found that returning M. to the USA without his mother, who no longer had any legal basis for entering or residing in the USA, would not serve the child’s best interests. It therefore set aside the Desnyansky District Court’s decisions of 19 June and 2 July 2013 (see paragraphs 20 and 21 above) and dismissed the applicant’s claim as unfounded.

34. On 4 December 2014, the Cassation Court rejected the appeals on points of law lodged by the applicant and the Ministry of Justice and upheld the decision of 5 September 2014 (see paragraphs 31–33 above).

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

35. Under section 7 § 1 of the Law of Ukraine on Ukrainian Citizenship of 18 January 2001 (“the Citizenship Act 2001”), a person is entitled to Ukrainian citizenship where, at the time of his or her birth, either one or both parents held Ukrainian citizenship.

36. By Resolution no. 952 of 10 July 2006, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine adopted regulations governing the implementation of the Hague Convention within Ukraine. Those regulations designate the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine and its territorial departments to carry out the functions of the Ukrainian Central Authority. In particular, they establish the procedure for processing applications for assistance in obtaining the return of children from Ukraine to foreign countries.
Under the applicable regulations, responsibility for bringing judicial proceedings to secure the child’s return rests with the Ministry of Justice. Where necessary, the Ministry should inform the foreign Central Authority and/or the applicant that further information must be submitted in support of the application (paragraph 9).

III. APPLICABLE INTERNATIONAL LAW

37. The pertinent provisions of the Hague Convention, which entered into force for Ukraine on 1 September 2006, provide:

Article 3

“A child’s removal or retention is wrongful if:

(a) it violates custody rights vested, whether jointly or individually, in a person, institution, or other body under the law of the State where the child was habitually resident immediately before being removed or retained; and

(b) those custody rights were being exercised, jointly or individually, when the removal or retention occurred, or would have been exercised had the removal or retention not taken place.

The custody rights referred to in subparagraph (a) may arise, in particular, directly under the law, from a judicial or administrative ruling, or from an agreement that has legal effect under the law of that State.”

Article 4

“This Convention applies to every child whose habitual residence was in a Contracting State immediately before custody or access rights were breached. Its application ends once the child reaches 16 years of age.”

Article 5

“For the purposes of the Convention:

(a) ‘custody rights’ encompass rights concerning the child’s personal care and, specifically, the right to decide where the child will reside;

(b) ‘access rights’”
shall encompass the right to take a child, for a limited period, to a location other than the child’s habitual residence....”

Article 11

In proceedings concerning the return of children, the judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States must proceed without delay.

If the relevant judicial or administrative authority has not issued a decision within six weeks after the proceedings began, the applicant or the Central Authority of the requested State—either acting on its own initiative or following a request from the Central Authority of the requesting State—may require an explanation of the reasons for the delay.

Article 12

When a child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of Article 3, and fewer than one year has passed between the wrongful removal or retention and the commencement of proceedings before the judicial or administrative authority of the Contracting State in which the child is located, that authority must order the child’s immediate return.

Even if proceedings begin after the one-year period identified in the preceding paragraph has expired, the judicial or administrative authority must still order the child’s return unless it is shown that the child has become settled in the new environment.

If the judicial or administrative authority in the requested State has grounds to believe that the child has been taken to another State, it may suspend the proceedings or reject the application seeking the child’s return.

Article 13

Despite the preceding Article, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested State is not required to order the child’s return when the person, institution, or other body opposing the return proves that—

(a) the person, institution, or other body responsible for the child’s care was not actually exercising custody rights when the removal or retention occurred, or had agreed to the removal or retention beforehand or subsequently accepted it; or

(b) returning the child would create a grave risk of exposing the child to physical or psychological harm or would otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.

The judicial or administrative authority may also decline to order the child’s return if it determines that the child objects to returning and has reached an age and level of maturity at which the child’s views should appropriately be considered.

When evaluating the circumstances described in this Article, judicial and administrative authorities must consider information about the child’s social background supplied by the Central Authority or another competent authority of the child’s habitual residence....

Article 16

Once notice has been received that a child was wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of Article 3, the judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child was taken or in which it
The authority before which the matter has been retained must not rule on the substance of custody rights until it is established either that the child will not be returned pursuant to this Convention or that no application under the Convention has been filed within a reasonable period after the notice was received....

Article 19

“An order made under this Convention regarding the child’s return does not constitute a ruling on the substance of any custody matter.”

Article 20

“Notwithstanding Article 12, the child’s return may be denied where it would be prohibited by the requested State’s fundamental principles concerning the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms....”

original: FOURTH SECTION      CASE OF SINKOVA v. UKRAINE (Application no. 39496/11)        JUDGMENT   STRASBOURG  27 February 2018  FINAL 02/07/2018 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision. In the case of Sinkova v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Vincent A. De Gaetano, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Faris Vehabović, Egidijus Kūris, Iulia Motoc, Georges Ravarani, Péter Paczolay, judges,and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 19 December 2017,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 39496/11) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Ms Anna Olegovna Sinkova (“the applicant”), on 21 June 2011.2. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Arkadiy Bushchenko, Ms Yana Zayikina and Ms Tetiana Zhurba, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr Ivan Lishchyna, of the Ministry of Justice.3. The applicant alleged that her detention had been in breach of Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 of the Convention. She also complained of a violation of her right to freedom of expression under Article 10.4. On 1 December 2014 the application was communicated to the Government.THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE5. The applicant was born in 1991 and lives in Kyiv.6. At the time of the events she belonged to an artistic group called the St Luke Brotherhood, which was known for its provocative public performances.7. On 16 December 2010 the applicant, together with three other members of the above-mentioned union, made what she described as an “act of performance”, which, according to both parties’ accounts, consisted of the following. They went to the Eternal Glory Memorial to those who perished in the Second World War, which contained the tombs of thirty-two soldiers, including that of an Unknown Soldier. The applicant took a frying pan prepared in advance, broke some eggs into it and fried them over the Eternal Flame at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Two of her friends joined her and fried sausages on skewers over the flame. Another member of the group filmed the event. Two police officers approached them and made a remark that their behaviour was inappropriate, without further interference. On the same day the applicant posted the video on the Internet on behalf of the St Luke Brotherhood. It was accompanied by the following statement:“Precious natural gas has been being burned, pointlessly, at the Glory Memorial in Kyiv for fifty-three years now. This pleasure costs taxpayers about 300,000 hryvnias [UAH] per month. And this is only one ‘eternal flame’ pagan temple, whereas there are hundreds or even thousands of them throughout Ukraine. On 16 December the St Luke Brotherhood reacted to this by an act of protest in the Glory Park in the capital. It showed that people should use the ‘eternal flame’.We suggest to the outraged representatives of the Communist Party of Ukraine to follow the example of ancient Roman vestal virgins and to carry out around-the-clock duty at the ‘eternal flames’, keeping the fire lit manually by wood. There is no doubt that communists will have no problems with fulfilling this task, because they already have experience of taking care of the Lenin monument in Kyiv and their financing is much better than that which the vestal virgins had.”8. While the parties did not provide a copy of the video in question to the Court, it was possible to view it on several publicly available websites. In addition to the factual account from the parties summarised above, the Court notes that the soundtrack to the video was a famous 1974 Soviet song “The battle is going on again” (devoted to the victory of the 1917 revolution and optimism about the future of the communist regime). The video started with the following opening titles: “The St Luke Brotherhood presents”, “Recipe of the day”, “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame”. The participants in the performance did not make any public address and their conversation was not audible. They had no posters or other visual aids, apart from the food and cooking utensils. It could be seen on the video that once the applicant had broken the eggs in the frying pan and was about to approach the fire, while her friends held skewers with sausages, the two police officers appeared and the applicant explained something to them and they left. In order to reach the flame the applicant had to step over a sculpture of a wreath of oak leaves and step on the words “Glory to the Unknown Soldier”.9. There were several complaints to the police that the action on the video had amounted to desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and called for criminal prosecution.10. On 21 December 2010 the police questioned D., one of the women who had participated in the performance. She submitted that she had not known the other members of the group and that she had met them by chance. As they had allegedly explained to her, they had been hungry and had intended to cook food in order to eat it.11. On the same day criminal proceedings were instituted against D. and three unidentified persons on suspicion of hooliganism.12. On 23 December 2010 D. wrote a confession that she had participated in a protest against inappropriate use of natural gas and that she regretted it. She knew only the first names of the other participants.13. On 24 December 2010 another criminal case was opened against her and three unidentified persons in respect of the same event, this time on suspicion of desecration of a tomb. It was joined to that opened earlier. Subsequently the charge of hooliganism was dropped.14. The police retrieved photos of several persons who might have been involved in the incident from the passport office’s database and showed them to D. She recognised the applicant.15. On 5 February 2011 the investigator questioned the applicant’s grandmother and mother, who lived at the address of the applicant’s registered residence. They submitted that they knew nothing about her involvement in the event in question. They also stated that the applicant did not in fact live there and denied knowing her whereabouts or having her contact details. They only knew that she had left for western Ukraine, without further details. The grandmother stated that the applicant had visited her about two weeks earlier. The applicant’s mother had seen her about a week earlier and had received a telephone call from her two days earlier.16. On 18 February 2011 the investigator severed the criminal case in respect of the applicant and two unidentified persons on suspicion of desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by a group following a prior conspiracy.17. On the same day the applicant was declared wanted by the police.18. On 17 March 2011 the investigator applied to the Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv (“the Pecherskyy Court”) for the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure pending trial. His arguments were as follows: the offence of which the applicant was suspected was punishable by a prison term of more than three years; the applicant had absconded, as a result of which she had been declared wanted by the police; and she could reoffend or hinder the establishment of the truth if at liberty.19. On 25 March 2011 a judge of the Pecherskyy Court allowed that application in part: he ordered the applicant’s arrest with a view to bringing her before the court for examination.20. On 29 March 2011 at 9 p.m. the applicant was arrested at the flat of a certain Z. in Kyiv. As the latter subsequently stated during her questioning, the applicant had been living there from 25 March 2011 at the request of an acquaintance.21. On 31 March 2011 the applicant was questioned as an accused in the presence of her lawyer. While insisting that her only intention had been to protest against the inappropriate use of natural gas, she confessed to the offence and expressed remorse.22. On the same day the investigator once again applied to the Pecherskyy Court for the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure. His reasoning was the same as before.23. On 31 March and 1 April 2011 two deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council applied to the Pecherskyy Court for the applicant’s release in exchange of their personal guarantee of her adequate procedural behaviour.24. On 1 April 2011 the Pecherskyy Court remanded the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial. It noted that she was accused of a serious offence punishable by imprisonment of from three to five years. Furthermore, the judge referred to the fact that the applicant had absconded and had therefore been put on the wanted list. It was also considered that she might hinder establishing the truth if at liberty. In so far as the applicant’s lawyer relied on her positive character references from various sources, the court noted that those could not guarantee her compliance with all the procedural requirements. While having noted that the applicant also relied on the letters of personal guarantee from the people’s deputies, the judge did not further comment on them. It was specified in the ruling that the term of the applicant’s detention was to be calculated from 29 March 2011. Under the applicable legislation, the duration of pre-trial detention was limited to two months, with the possibility of further extensions.25. The applicant’s lawyer appealed. He submitted that his client was willing to cooperate with the investigation and that there were no reasons for her detention. It was further pointed out in the appeal that the applicant had been declared wanted by the police on the very same day the criminal case against her had been opened. The lawyer noted that there had not been a single summons sent by the investigation to the applicant’s address prior to her arrest. According to her, she had found out about the charge against her only on the day of her arrest on 29 March 2011. Lastly, the lawyer submitted that the first-instance court had not considered any less intrusive preventive measures as an alternative to detention and that it had left without consideration the people deputies’ letters of guarantee.26. On 11 April 2011 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal rejected the above appeal. It noted that the Pecherskyy Court had already duly examined all the arguments raised in it.27. On 25 May 2011 the applicant was indicted. On the same day the case was sent to the Pecherskyy Court for trial.28. On 10 June 2011 the applicant applied to the court for release under an undertaking not to abscond. She submitted that she enjoyed positive character references, had no criminal record and had cooperated with the investigation. Furthermore, the applicant observed that by that time the investigation had already been completed and could not therefore be hampered. She emphasised that her actions had been nothing else than a protest driven by good motives. Several members of parliament and other prominent figures joined her in that application and expressed their wish to act as her personal guarantors.29. On 17 June 2011 the Pecherskyy Court held a preparatory hearing, during which it rejected the applicant’s application for release with reference to the seriousness of the charge against her, “the nature and the circumstances of the offence of which she [was] accused”, as well as the fact that she had been declared wanted by the police. The judge also stated, in general terms, that there were no grounds for the applicant’s release under a personal guarantee.30. On 30 June 2011 the applicant applied once again to be released. On the same day the Pecherskyy Court allowed that application and released her under an undertaking not to leave the town.31. On 4 October 2012 the Pecherskyy Court found the applicant guilty of the desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, acting as part of a group of persons following a prior conspiracy. The court noted that the applicant had convinced D. and two other people, whose identities remained unestablished, to carry out a performance at the “Eternal Glory” memorial aimed at protesting against the waste of natural gas caused by the burning of the Eternal Flame. D., who was questioned in court, confirmed that account of events. The court also questioned the memorial keeper, who had witnessed the performance from a distance, and the two police officers who had spoken to the applicant and her friends (see paragraph 7 above). Furthermore, the court examined the video-recording of the performance as material evidence.32. The judgment mentioned the statement made by the applicant during the hearing that in her opinion people bringing flowers to the memorial did not really understand what exactly it was dedicated to. She insisted that she had not committed any crime as her performance had not been meant to desecrate the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Furthermore, she maintained that there could not be a tomb beneath the Eternal Flame because of the gas pipe.33. The Pecherskyy Court held that the applicant’s arguments had no impact on the legal classification of her actions and that they were refuted by the evidence as a whole. The judgment further stated in that regard:“... the court considers that by committing deliberate acts in a group which showed disrespect for the burial place of the Unknown Soldier and for the public tradition of honouring the memory of soldiers who perished defending or liberating Kyiv and the lands of Ukraine from the fascist hordes, and by subsequently presenting those actions as a protest, [the applicant] has tried to escape social condemnation of her conduct and criminal liability for the offence.”34. Relying on local authority documents, the court dismissed the applicant’s submission that there was no established location for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.35. The court did not discern any aggravating or mitigating circumstances in the case. At the same time, in deciding on the penalty, it took into account, on the one hand, the fact that the applicant did not have a criminal record, that she was working as a political analyst and got positive character references by her place of residence and work. On the other hand, the court noted that the criminal offence in question was of medium gravity and that the applicant did not show any remorse for what she had done. As a result, she was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years.36. On the same date the Pecherskyy Court exempted D. from criminal liability under the surety of her employer.37. The applicant appealed. Relying on the definition of the desecration of a burial place under the Burial and Funeral Business Act (see paragraph 47 below), she maintained that in the absence of any intention by her to “defile the family or social memory of a deceased or to show contempt for a burial place, or social and religious principles and traditions”, there were no constituent elements of a crime in her actions. The applicant reiterated her argument that her performance had been nothing more than a protest. Lastly, she submitted that the criminal proceedings against her had violated her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.38. The prosecutor also appealed, considering the sentence to be too lenient.39. On 18 December 2012 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. It stated that desecration of a tomb could have different expressions, indicating an insulting attitude, mockery or disrespect towards a tomb or the person buried therein, regardless of the stated motives. As regards the applicant’s argument on her right to freedom of expression, the court noted that that right was not unlimited and that the restriction in the applicant’s case was in accordance with the law and pursued a legitimate aim. The appellate court also rejected the prosecutor’s appeal.40. The applicant further reiterated her arguments in an appeal on points of law lodged by her, which was, however, rejected by the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters on 11 April 2013.II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICEA. Applicable legislation and relevant legal opinions41. Article 9 § 1 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that international treaties which are in force and agreed on as binding by the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) of Ukraine are part of the national legislation.42. Article 34 of the Constitution, enshrining the right to freedom of expression, can be found in the Court’s judgment in the case of Lykin v. Ukraine (no. 19382/08, § 15, 12 January 2017).43. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1960 (in force and as worded at the material time) concerning preventive measures are quoted, in particular, in the Court’s judgment in the case of Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016).44. Article 297 of the Criminal Code of 2001 (as amended on 19 March 2009) read as follows:“1. Desecration of a tomb or other burial place, as well as defilement of a corpse (remains, ashes), desecration of an urn containing ashes of a deceased, or illegal seizure of a corpse (remains, ashes, of an urn containing ashes of a deceased, of objects from a tomb or from any other burial place or on a corpse (remains, ashes), shall be punished with a fine in the amount of up to two hundred non-taxable minimum [monthly salaries] or with arrest for up to six months, or with restriction of liberty for up to three years or imprisonment for that period.2. The same actions committed repeatedly, or following a prior conspiracy by a group of persons, or driven by lucrative or hooligan motives, or committed in respect of a common tomb or a Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, or combined with violence or its threat, shall be punishable with restriction of liberty for from three to five years or imprisonment for the same period.3. Actions referred to in the above paragraphs, if they led to serious consequences, shall be punished with imprisonment from five to twelve years.”45. Article 66 of the Criminal Code contains a non-exhaustive list of mitigating circumstances. It also states that a court may consider any other mitigating circumstance not indicated in that list when imposing a penalty. Under Article 69, a court may impose a more lenient penalty than that envisaged by law subject to several mitigating circumstances reducing the gravity of the offence and having regard to the offender’s character.46. The “Scientific and Practical Commentary on the Criminal Code of Ukraine” (Науково-практичний коментар Кримінального кодексу України, 7-ме вид., перероблене та доповнене / За ред. М.І. Мельника та М.І. Хавронюка. – Київ: Юридична думка, 2010) states, in respect of Article 297, in particular, as follows:“The object (target) of the crime is the moral foundations of society as regards respect towards the dead and their burial places. This crime causes non-pecuniary damage, in particular, to those who are close to the deceased, it violates public order, can entail interethnic and inter-confessional conflict, and has a negative impact on the education of teenagers. The attitude of people towards the dead is probably one of the most telling illustrations of the difference between civilisation and savagery, which also reflects a person’s attitude to other social values. ...The actus reus of the criminal offence is ... desecration of a tomb or other burial place ...Desecration is an insulting attitude, brutal mockery, or a demonstration of contempt towards a burial place or the ashes of the deceased. The law does not specify the ways in which desecration can be committed. It could be: profanation, including the placing of indecent inscriptions or drawings or soiling [the tomb] with excrement, the destruction of sepulchral constructions; the excavation of burial places, corpse dissection or destruction or tearing off its clothing. Desecration is characterised by an objective element – that is, the commission of certain acts in respect of a deceased or a burial place, and by a subjective element – that is, realising that those acts amount to contempt for the memory of the deceased which violate the principles of public life in that area. Most often, desecration takes the form of an action. However, it cannot be ruled out that it could stem from an omission – for example, not interfering with the behaviour of domestic animals digging into a tomb or relieving themselves on it.The mens rea of the crime is characterised by guilt in the form of intent. The guilty person realises that he/she: (a) is committing an infringement in relation to a tomb, other burial place or a corpse; (b) foresees that his/her actions will cause moral suffering to others and violate the moral foundations of society in respect of attitudes to the dead; (c) wishes to show his/her contempt for the memory of the deceased and to demonstrate his/her negative attitude towards the public principles prevailing in that area (that is, acts of direct intention); or is conscious of such an assumption (that is, acts of indirect intention).This crime is classified as aggravated if it has been committed:...- following a prior conspiracy by a group of persons;- for hooligan ... motives. ... Hooligan motives arise where the guilty person wishes to demonstrate his/her contempt for the generally recognised norms and rules of people’s attitudes towards the dead and their burial places, boasts of his/her pseudo-bravery, or seeks to assert himself/herself in the eyes of surrounding people by humiliating others and their feelings. In other words, they are motives which are considered, from the viewpoint of public morality, as disgraceful and ignoble, aiming to create conflict between an individual and society. Hooligan motives also stem from racial, ethnic or religious intolerance, different approaches to assessing historical events and so on;- in respect of ... a Tomb of an Unknown Soldier. ... A Tomb of an Unknown Soldier is a military memorial dedicated to those who perished in an armed conflict. It includes the place of burial itself and a memorial sign. ‘Soldier’ is a generic term referring to any military official, officer, sailor, or law-enforcement agent who died in action or in armed conflict. [It does not matter] on whose side the deceased participated in the events leading to their deaths. Nor is it of relevance how society or particular individuals assess the respective wars or other social cataclysms and the role of participants in them ...”47. Section 2 of the Burial and Funeral Business Act of 2003 (with further amendments) defines the desecration of a tomb or other burial place as follows:“- the placing of unauthorised inscriptions, drawings, symbols or other images at cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, on sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns with ashes, tombs and other burial places;- wilfully damaging, the excavation, demolition or destruction by other means of cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns with ashes, tombs and other burial places;- the use of cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns with ashes, tombs and other burial places for a purpose not envisaged by the legislation in force, their unauthorised use, or the commission of any other acts intended to defile the family or public memory of the deceased or to show contempt for the burial place, or the social and religious principles and traditions in that area; ...”48. Under section 32 of the law, persons guilty of desecrating a tomb or other burial place are held liable in accordance with the law.49. Under the Law On the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies in charge of Operational Enquiries, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts of 1994 (as worded at the material time, also known as “the Compensation Act”), a person was entitled to compensation for damage on account of, in particular, unlawful detention (section 1). A precondition for the entitlement to compensation was “a finding of ... unlawfulness of arrest and detention in a guilty verdict or other judicial decision” (section 2).B. Case-law of domestic courts cited by the applicant50. The applicant submitted to the Court copies of seven judgments delivered by local courts on various dates between 2007 and 2013, by which people had been found guilty of desecrating tombs after taking metal parts and trading them as scrap. The sentences were as follows (from the most lenient to the harshest):-  two years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for two years;-  three years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for one year;-  one year and six months’ restriction of liberty;-  one year and six months’ imprisonment, suspended for one year;-  three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years and six months;-  three years’ imprisonment; and-  three years and six months’ imprisonment.III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL TEXTS51. The summary of the position of the Supreme Court of the United States of America in respect of the controversial conduct of cross burning, as formulated in its decision on the case of Virginia v. Black, can be found in the Court’s judgment in the case of Fáber v. Hungary, no. 40721/08, § 18, 24 July 2012.

FOURTH SECTION      CASE OF SINKOVA v. UKRAINE (Application no. 39496/11)        JUDGMENT   STRASBOURG  27 February 2018  FINAL 02/07/2018 This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision. In the case of Sinkova v. Ukraine, the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Vincent A. De Gaetano, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Faris Vehabović, Egidijus Kūris, Iulia Motoc, Georges Ravarani, Péter Paczolay, judges, and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar, Having deliberated in private on 19 December 2017, Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 39496/11) against Ukraine lodged before the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Ms Anna Olegovna Sinkova (“the applicant”), on 21 June 2011.

2. The applicant, who was granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Arkadiy Bushchenko, Ms Yana Zayikina and Ms Tetiana Zhurba, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr Ivan Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant alleged that her detention had violated Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 of the Convention. She further complained of a breach of her right to freedom of expression under Article 10.

4. On 1 December 2014 the application was communicated to the Government.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1991 and resides in Kyiv.

6. At the relevant time, she belonged to an artistic group called the St Luke Brotherhood, which was known for its provocative public performances.

7. On 16 December 2010 the applicant, together with three other members of the above-mentioned group, carried out what she described as an “act of performance”, which, according to the accounts of both parties, consisted of the following. They went to the Eternal Glory Memorial to those who had perished in the Second World War, which contained the tombs of thirty-two soldiers, including that of an Unknown Soldier. The applicant took a frying pan prepared beforehand, broke several eggs into it and fried them over the Eternal Flame at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Two of her friends joined her, frying sausages on skewers over the flame. Another group member filmed the event. Two police officers approached them and remarked that their behaviour was inappropriate, but did not otherwise intervene. On the same day, the applicant posted the video online on behalf of the St Luke Brotherhood. It was accompanied by the following statement:

“Precious natural gas has been burned pointlessly at the Glory Memorial in Kyiv for fifty-three years now. This pleasure costs taxpayers approximately 300,000 hryvnias [UAH] per month.
And this is only one pagan temple with an ‘eternal flame’, whereas there are hundreds or even thousands of them across Ukraine. On 16 December the St Luke Brotherhood responded to this with an act of protest in the capital’s Glory Park. It demonstrated that people should make use of the ‘eternal flame’.

We suggest that the outraged representatives of the Communist Party of Ukraine follow the example of the ancient Roman vestal virgins and maintain around-the-clock duty at the ‘eternal flames’, keeping the fire burning manually with wood. There is no doubt that the communists will have no difficulty performing this task, since they already have experience of looking after the Lenin monument in Kyiv, and their funding is far better than that available to the vestal virgins.”

8. Although the parties did not submit a copy of the video in question to the Court, it could be viewed on several publicly accessible websites. In addition to the factual account provided by the parties and summarised above, the Court notes that the video’s soundtrack was the famous 1974 Soviet song “The battle is going on again” (dedicated to the victory of the 1917 revolution and expressing optimism about the future of the communist regime). The video began with the following opening titles: “The St Luke Brotherhood presents”, “Recipe of the day”, and “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame”. The participants in the performance did not make any public statements, and their conversation could not be heard. They had no posters or other visual materials apart from the food and cooking utensils. The video showed that, once the applicant had broken the eggs into the frying pan and was about to approach the fire, while her friends held skewers with sausages, two police officers appeared. The applicant explained something to them, after which they left. To reach the flame, the applicant had to step over a sculpture of a wreath of oak leaves and onto the words “Glory to the Unknown Soldier”.

9. Several complaints were made to the police alleging that the action shown in the video amounted to desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and calling for criminal prosecution.

10. On 21 December 2010 the police questioned D., one of the women who had taken part in the performance. She stated that she had not known the other members of the group and had met them by chance. According to what they had allegedly told her, they were hungry and intended to cook food to eat.

11. On the same day, criminal proceedings were brought against D. and three unidentified individuals on suspicion of hooliganism.

12. On 23 December 2010 D. wrote a confession stating that she had participated in a protest against the inappropriate use of natural gas and that she regretted doing so. She knew only the first names of the other participants.

13. On 24 December 2010 another criminal case was opened against her and three unidentified individuals concerning the same incident, this time on suspicion of desecrating a tomb.
It was joined to the case opened earlier. Subsequently, the charge of hooliganism was dropped.

14. The police obtained photos of several persons who might have been involved in the incident from the passport office’s database and showed them to D. She identified the applicant.

15. On 5 February 2011 the investigator questioned the applicant’s grandmother and mother, who lived at the address of the applicant’s registered residence. They stated that they knew nothing about her involvement in the event in question. They also said that the applicant did not actually live there and denied knowing her whereabouts or having her contact details. They knew only that she had left for western Ukraine, without any further details. The grandmother stated that the applicant had visited her about two weeks earlier. The applicant’s mother had seen her about a week earlier and had received a telephone call from her two days before.

16. On 18 February 2011 the investigator severed the criminal case concerning the applicant and two unidentified persons suspected of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier as a group following a prior conspiracy.

17. On the same day, the applicant was declared wanted by the police.

18. On 17 March 2011 the investigator applied to the Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv (“the Pecherskyy Court”) for the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure pending trial. His arguments were as follows: the offence of which the applicant was suspected was punishable by more than three years’ imprisonment; the applicant had absconded and, as a result, had been declared wanted by the police; and, if left at liberty, she could reoffend or hinder the establishment of the truth.

19. On 25 March 2011 a judge of the Pecherskyy Court allowed that application in part, ordering the applicant’s arrest with a view to bringing her before the court for examination.

20. On 29 March 2011 at 9 p.m. the applicant was arrested at the Kyiv flat of a certain Z. As the latter subsequently stated during questioning, the applicant had been living there since 25 March 2011 at the request of an acquaintance.

21. On 31 March 2011 the applicant was questioned as an accused in the presence of her lawyer. While maintaining that her sole intention had been to protest against the inappropriate use of natural gas, she confessed to the offence and expressed remorse.

22. On the same day, the investigator again applied to the Pecherskyy Court for the applicant’s detention as a preventive measure. His reasoning remained the same.

23. On 31 March and 1 April 2011, two deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council applied to the Pecherskyy Court for the applicant’s release in exchange for their personal guarantee of her proper procedural conduct.

24. On 1 April 2011 the Pecherskyy Court remanded the applicant in custody as a preventive measure pending trial. It observed that she was accused of a serious offence punishable by imprisonment for three to five years.
Furthermore, the judge referred to the fact that the applicant had absconded and had therefore been placed on the wanted list. It was also considered that, if at liberty, she might hinder the establishment of the truth. In so far as the applicant’s lawyer relied on positive character references from various sources, the court noted that these could not guarantee her compliance with all procedural requirements. Although the applicant also relied on letters of personal guarantee from the people’s deputies, the judge did not comment further on them. The ruling specified that the term of the applicant’s detention was to be calculated from 29 March 2011. Under the applicable legislation, pre-trial detention was limited to two months, with the possibility of further extensions.

25. The applicant’s lawyer appealed. He submitted that his client was willing to cooperate with the investigation and that there were no grounds for her detention. It was further pointed out in the appeal that the applicant had been declared wanted by the police on the very day the criminal case against her had been opened. The lawyer noted that not a single summons had been sent by the investigation to the applicant’s address before her arrest. According to the applicant, she had learned of the charge against her only on the day of her arrest, 29 March 2011. Lastly, the lawyer submitted that the first-instance court had not considered any less intrusive preventive measures as alternatives to detention and had failed to consider the letters of guarantee from the people’s deputies.

26. On 11 April 2011 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed the above appeal. It noted that the Pecherskyy Court had already duly examined all the arguments raised in it.

27. On 25 May 2011 the applicant was indicted. On the same day, the case was sent to the Pecherskyy Court for trial.

28. On 10 June 2011 the applicant applied to the court for release subject to an undertaking not to abscond. She submitted that she had positive character references, no criminal record, and had cooperated with the investigation. Furthermore, the applicant observed that by that time the investigation had already been completed and could therefore no longer be hampered. She emphasised that her actions had been nothing more than a protest driven by good motives. Several members of parliament and other prominent figures joined her application and expressed their willingness to act as her personal guarantors.

29. On 17 June 2011 the Pecherskyy Court held a preparatory hearing, during which it rejected the applicant’s application for release, referring to the seriousness of the charge against her, “the nature and the circumstances of the offence of which she [was] accused”, and the fact that she had been declared wanted by the police. The judge also stated, in general terms, that there were no grounds for the applicant’s release under a personal guarantee.

30.
On 30 June 2011 the applicant again applied for release. On the same day, the Pecherskyy Court granted that application and released her under an undertaking not to leave the town.

31. On 4 October 2012 the Pecherskyy Court found the applicant guilty of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, acting as part of a group pursuant to a prior conspiracy. The court noted that the applicant had persuaded D. and two other people, whose identities remained unknown, to stage a performance at the “Eternal Glory” memorial aimed at protesting against the waste of natural gas caused by the burning of the Eternal Flame. D., who was questioned in court, confirmed that version of events. The court also questioned the memorial keeper, who had witnessed the performance from a distance, and the two police officers who had spoken with the applicant and her friends (see paragraph 7 above). In addition, the court examined the video recording of the performance as material evidence.

32. The judgment referred to the applicant’s statement during the hearing that, in her opinion, people bringing flowers to the memorial did not truly understand what it was dedicated to. She insisted that she had not committed any crime, as her performance had not been intended to desecrate the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. She further maintained that there could not be a tomb beneath the Eternal Flame because of the gas pipe.

33. The Pecherskyy Court held that the applicant’s arguments had no bearing on the legal classification of her actions and were refuted by the evidence as a whole. In that regard, the judgment further stated:

“... the court considers that by committing deliberate acts in a group which showed disrespect for the burial place of the Unknown Soldier and for the public tradition of honouring the memory of soldiers who perished defending or liberating Kyiv and the lands of Ukraine from the fascist hordes, and by subsequently presenting those actions as a protest, [the applicant] has tried to escape social condemnation of her conduct and criminal liability for the offence.”

34. Relying on documents from the local authorities, the court rejected the applicant’s submission that there was no established location for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

35. The court found no aggravating or mitigating circumstances in the case. At the same time, when deciding on the penalty, it took into account, on the one hand, the fact that the applicant had no criminal record, worked as a political analyst and had received positive character references from her place of residence and work. On the other hand, the court observed that the criminal offence in question was of medium gravity and that the applicant had shown no remorse for her actions. Consequently, she was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years.

36. On the same date, the Pecherskyy Court exempted D.
from criminal liability under the surety of her employer.

37. The applicant appealed. Relying on the definition of desecration of a burial place under the Burial and Funeral Business Act (see paragraph 47 below), she argued that, in the absence of any intention on her part to “defile the family or social memory of a deceased or to show contempt for a burial place, or social and religious principles and traditions”, her actions did not contain the constituent elements of a crime. The applicant repeated her argument that her performance had been no more than a protest. Lastly, she submitted that the criminal proceedings against her had breached her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

38. The prosecutor also appealed, regarding the sentence as too lenient.

39. On 18 December 2012 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance court’s judgment. It stated that desecration of a tomb could take different forms, demonstrating an insulting attitude, mockery or disrespect towards a tomb or the person buried there, irrespective of the stated motives. As to the applicant’s argument concerning her right to freedom of expression, the court observed that that right was not unlimited and that the restriction in her case was in accordance with the law and pursued a legitimate aim. The appellate court also dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal.

40. The applicant again raised her arguments in an appeal on points of law, which was, however, dismissed by the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters on 11 April 2013.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Applicable legislation and relevant legal opinions

41. Article 9 § 1 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that international treaties which are in force and accepted as binding by the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) of Ukraine form part of national legislation.

42. Article 34 of the Constitution, which enshrines the right to freedom of expression, is reproduced in the Court’s judgment in Lykin v. Ukraine (no. 19382/08, § 15, 12 January 2017).

43. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1960 (in force and worded as at the material time) concerning preventive measures are set out, in particular, in the Court’s judgment in Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016).

44. Article 297 of the Criminal Code of 2001 (as amended on 19 March 2009) provided as follows:

“1.
Desecration of a tomb or other burial place, as well as defilement of a corpse (remains, ashes), desecration of an urn containing the ashes of a deceased person, or unlawful seizure of a corpse (remains, ashes), an urn containing the ashes of a deceased person, objects from a tomb or any other burial place, or objects on a corpse (remains, ashes), shall be punishable by a fine of up to two hundred non-taxable minimum [monthly salaries], arrest for up to six months, restriction of liberty for up to three years, or imprisonment for the same period.

2. The same actions, if committed repeatedly, pursuant to a prior conspiracy by a group of persons, for lucrative or hooligan motives, in respect of a common tomb or a Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, or in combination with violence or the threat of violence, shall be punishable by restriction of liberty for a term of three to five years or imprisonment for the same period.

3. Actions referred to in the preceding paragraphs, if they result in serious consequences, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to twelve years.”

45. Article 66 of the Criminal Code provides a non-exhaustive list of mitigating circumstances. It also states that, when imposing a penalty, a court may take into account any other mitigating circumstance not included in that list. Under Article 69, a court may impose a more lenient penalty than that prescribed by law where several mitigating circumstances reduce the gravity of the offence and having regard to the offender’s character.

46. The “Scientific and Practical Commentary on the Criminal Code of Ukraine” (Науково-практичний коментар Кримінального кодексу України, 7-ме вид., перероблене та доповнене / За ред. М.І. Мельника та М.І. Хавронюка. – Київ: Юридична думка, 2010) states, with respect to Article 297, in particular, as follows:

“The object (target) of the crime is the moral foundations of society concerning respect for the dead and their burial places. This crime causes non-pecuniary harm, particularly to those close to the deceased; it violates public order, may lead to interethnic and inter-confessional conflict, and has a negative impact on the education of teenagers. People’s attitude towards the dead is probably one of the clearest illustrations of the distinction between civilisation and savagery, and also reflects a person’s attitude towards other social values. ...

The actus reus of the criminal offence is ... the desecration of a tomb or other burial place ...

Desecration means an insulting attitude, brutal mockery, or a display of contempt towards a burial place or the ashes of the deceased. The law does not specify the means by which desecration may be committed. It may include profanation, such as placing indecent inscriptions or drawings or soiling [the tomb] with excrement; destroying sepulchral structures; excavating burial places; dissecting or destroying a corpse; or tearing off its clothing.
Desecration is characterised by an objective element – namely, the commission of certain acts in respect of a deceased person or a burial place – and by a subjective element – namely, awareness that those acts express contempt for the memory of the deceased and violate the principles of public life in that area. Most often, desecration takes the form of an action. However, it cannot be excluded that it may result from an omission – for example, failing to intervene when domestic animals dig into a tomb or relieve themselves on it.

The mens rea of the crime is characterised by guilt in the form of intent. The guilty person realises that he/she: (a) is committing an infringement in relation to a tomb, another burial place or a corpse; (b) foresees that his/her actions will cause moral suffering to others and violate society’s moral foundations concerning attitudes towards the dead; and (c) wishes to express his/her contempt for the memory of the deceased and demonstrate his/her negative attitude towards the public principles prevailing in that area (that is, acts with direct intent), or is conscious of such a possibility (that is, acts with indirect intent).

This crime is classified as aggravated if it has been committed:...

- following a prior conspiracy by a group of persons;
- for hooligan ... motives. ... Hooligan motives arise where the guilty person wishes to demonstrate his/her contempt for the generally recognised norms and rules governing people’s attitudes towards the dead and their burial places, boasts of his/her pseudo-bravery, or seeks to assert himself/herself in the eyes of others by humiliating them and their feelings. In other words, these are motives which, from the perspective of public morality, are regarded as disgraceful and ignoble and are aimed at creating conflict between an individual and society. Hooligan motives may also stem from racial, ethnic or religious intolerance, differing approaches to the assessment of historical events, and so on;
- in respect of ... a Tomb of an Unknown Soldier. ... A Tomb of an Unknown Soldier is a military memorial dedicated to those who died in an armed conflict. It includes the burial place itself and a memorial sign. ‘Soldier’ is a generic term referring to any military official, officer, sailor or law-enforcement agent who died in action or in armed conflict. [It does not matter] on which side the deceased took part in the events that led to their death. Nor is it relevant how society or particular individuals assess the wars or other social cataclysms concerned and the role of those who participated in them ...”47.
Section 2 of the Burial and Funeral Business Act of 2003 (as subsequently amended) defines the desecration of a tomb or other burial place as follows:

“- the placing of unauthorised inscriptions, drawings, symbols or other images on cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs and other burial places;

- wilfully damaging, excavating, demolishing or otherwise destroying cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs and other burial places;

- the use of cemetery facilities designated for burial and commemoration ceremonies, sepulchral constructions, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs and other burial places for a purpose not provided for by the legislation in force, their unauthorised use, or the commission of any other acts intended to defile the family or public memory of the deceased, show contempt for the burial place, or offend the social and religious principles and traditions of that area; ...”

48. Under section 32 of the Act, persons guilty of desecrating a tomb or other burial place are liable in accordance with the law.

49. Under the Law on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies in Charge of Operational Enquiries, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts of 1994 (as worded at the relevant time and also known as “the Compensation Act”), a person was entitled to compensation for damage arising, in particular, from unlawful detention (section 1). A prerequisite for entitlement to compensation was “a finding of ... unlawfulness of arrest and detention in a guilty verdict or other judicial decision” (section 2).

B. Case-law of the domestic courts cited by the applicant

50. The applicant submitted to the Court copies of seven judgments delivered by local courts on various dates between 2007 and 2013, in which individuals had been found guilty of desecrating tombs by taking metal parts and selling them as scrap. The sentences imposed were as follows (from the most lenient to the most severe):

- two years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for two years;

- three years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for one year;

- one year and six months’ restriction of liberty;

- one year and six months’ imprisonment, suspended for one year;

- three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years and six months;

- three years’ imprisonment; and

- three years and six months’ imprisonment.

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL TEXTS

51. A summary of the position of the Supreme Court of the United States of America concerning the controversial practice of cross burning, as set out in its decision in Virginia v. Black, can be found in the Court’s judgment in Fáber v. Hungary, no. 40721/08, § 18, 24 July 2012.
