FOURTH SECTION

CASE OF SINKOVA v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 39496/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

27 February 2018

FINAL

02/07/2018

This judgment became final pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention and may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Sinkova v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), convening as a Chamber composed of:

Vincent A. De Gaetano, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Faris Vehabović,
Egidijus Kūris,
Iulia Motoc,
Georges Ravarani,
Péter Paczolay, judges,

and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar,

Having held private deliberations on 19 December 2017,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case arose from application no. 39496/11, which Ms Anna Olegovna Sinkova (“the applicant”), a Ukrainian national, lodged against Ukraine with the Court on 21 June 2011 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. Having received legal aid, the applicant was represented by Mr Arkadiy Bushchenko, Ms Yana Zayikina and Ms Tetiana Zhurba, lawyers practising in Kharkiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent from the Ministry of Justice, most recently Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

3. The applicant claimed that her detention had contravened Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 of the Convention. She further alleged that her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 had been violated.

4. The application was communicated to the Government on 1 December 2014.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1991, the applicant resides in Kyiv.

6. At the relevant time, she was a member of an artistic group known as the St Luke Brotherhood, which had a reputation for staging provocative public performances.

7. On 16 December 2010, the applicant and three other members of that group carried out what she termed an “act of performance”. According to the accounts provided by both parties, the event unfolded as follows. The group visited the Eternal Glory Memorial dedicated to those who died in the Second World War. The memorial included the graves of thirty-two soldiers, among them the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Using a frying pan prepared beforehand, the applicant cracked eggs into it and cooked them over the Eternal Flame at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Two of her companions also used the flame to roast sausages on skewers, while another member filmed what occurred. Two police officers approached the group and commented that their conduct was inappropriate, but did not otherwise intervene. Later that day, acting on behalf of the St Luke Brotherhood, the applicant uploaded the recording to the Internet. The video appeared with the following statement:

“For fifty-three years, precious natural gas has been burned to no purpose at Kyiv’s Glory Memorial. This indulgence costs taxpayers approximately 300,000 hryvnias [UAH] every month.”
Yet this is merely one pagan temple built around an “eternal flame”; hundreds, if not thousands, exist across Ukraine. On 16 December, the St Luke Brotherhood responded by staging a protest in Kyiv’s Glory Park, demonstrating that the “eternal flame” should be put to use.

We invite the indignant representatives of the Communist Party of Ukraine to emulate the Vestal Virgins of ancient Rome by maintaining a twenty-four-hour vigil at the “eternal flames” and keeping them burning by hand with firewood. Communists should undoubtedly have no difficulty performing this task: they have already gained experience looking after the Lenin monument in Kyiv, and their funding is far more generous than that available to the Vestal Virgins.”

8. Although neither party supplied the Court with a copy of the video concerned, it was available for viewing on several publicly accessible websites. In addition to the parties’ factual account set out above, the Court observes that the video’s soundtrack featured the well-known 1974 Soviet song “The Battle Is Going On Again”, which celebrates the victory of the 1917 Revolution and expresses optimism about the communist regime’s future. The opening titles read: “The St Luke Brotherhood presents”, “Recipe of the day”, and “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame”. None of those taking part addressed the public, and their conversations could not be heard. Other than the food and cooking equipment, they displayed no posters or visual materials. The footage showed that, after the applicant had cracked the eggs into a frying pan and was preparing to move towards the flame while her companions held skewers of sausages, two police officers arrived. The applicant said something to them, after which they departed. To get to the flame, she had to climb over a sculpture depicting a wreath of oak leaves and tread on the inscription “Glory to the Unknown Soldier”.

9. The police received several complaints alleging that the act shown in the video constituted desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and demanding that those responsible be prosecuted.

10. On 21 December 2010, the police questioned D., one of the women involved in the performance. She stated that she did not know the other participants and had encountered them by chance. According to her, they had explained that they were hungry and planned to cook something to eat.

11. Later that day, criminal proceedings were initiated against D. and three unidentified individuals on suspicion of hooliganism.

12. On 23 December 2010, D. made a written confession acknowledging that she had taken part in a protest against the improper use of natural gas and expressing regret for doing so. She knew the other participants only by their first names.

13. On 24 December 2010, a further criminal case relating to the same incident was brought against D. and three unidentified persons, this time on suspicion of desecrating a tomb.
It was joined to the proceedings opened earlier. The hooliganism charge was subsequently dropped.

14. The police obtained from the passport office’s database photographs of several individuals who might have participated in the incident and showed them to D., who identified the applicant.

15. On 5 February 2011 the investigator interviewed the applicant’s mother and grandmother at her registered address, where they lived. Both said that they knew nothing about her involvement in the incident, that she did not actually reside there, and that they neither knew her whereabouts nor had her contact details. They were aware only that she had gone to western Ukraine, but had no further information. The grandmother added that the applicant had visited her approximately two weeks earlier. The applicant’s mother stated that she had seen her about a week earlier and had spoken to her by telephone two days earlier.

16. On 18 February 2011 the investigator separated the criminal proceedings against the applicant and two unidentified individuals, who were suspected of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier as a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy.

17. That same day, the police placed the applicant on the wanted list.

18. On 17 March 2011 the investigator asked the Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv (“the Pecherskyy Court”) to order the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure. He argued that the offence of which she was suspected carried a prison sentence exceeding three years; that she had absconded and had therefore been declared wanted by the police; and that, if left at liberty, she might reoffend or obstruct the establishment of the truth.

19. On 25 March 2011 a judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the request in part, ordering the applicant’s arrest so that she could be brought before the court for examination.

20. At 9 p.m. on 29 March 2011, the applicant was arrested in Z.’s flat in Kyiv. During subsequent questioning, Z. stated that the applicant had been staying there since 25 March 2011 at an acquaintance’s request.

21. On 31 March 2011, in the presence of her lawyer, the applicant was questioned as an accused. Although she maintained that her sole intention had been to protest against the inappropriate use of natural gas, she admitted committing the offence and expressed remorse.

22. Later that day, the investigator again requested that the Pecherskyy Court place the applicant in pre-trial detention as a preventive measure, relying on the same grounds as before.

23. On 31 March and 1 April 2011, two members of the Kyiv Regional Council asked the Pecherskyy Court to release the applicant in return for their personal guarantees that she would comply properly with procedural requirements.

24. On 1 April 2011 the Pecherskyy Court ordered the applicant’s remand in custody pending trial as a preventive measure. It observed that she had been charged with a serious offence carrying a sentence of three to five years’ imprisonment.
The judge further relied on the applicant’s having absconded, as a result of which she had been placed on the wanted list. The court also considered that, if released, she might obstruct efforts to establish the truth. As regards the favourable character references from various sources cited by the applicant’s lawyer, the court held that they could not ensure her compliance with all procedural obligations. Although the judge acknowledged the letters of personal guarantee submitted by people’s deputies on the applicant’s behalf, no further assessment of them was provided. The ruling stated that the applicant’s period of detention was to run from 29 March 2011. Under the relevant legislation, pre-trial detention was limited to two months, subject to possible extensions.

25. The applicant’s lawyer lodged an appeal, arguing that she was prepared to cooperate with the investigation and that there were no grounds for keeping her in detention. He also pointed out that the police had placed the applicant on the wanted list on the same day that the criminal proceedings against her had been instituted. Before her arrest, the investigating authorities had not sent a single summons to her address. Counsel maintained that the applicant had first learned of the charge against her when she was arrested on 29 March 2011. Finally, he contended that the first-instance court had neither considered less restrictive preventive measures as alternatives to detention nor examined the letters of guarantee provided by the people’s deputies.

26. On 11 April 2011 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding that the Pecherskyy Court had already given due consideration to all the arguments advanced in it.

27. The applicant was indicted on 25 May 2011, and the case was transmitted to the Pecherskyy Court for trial that same day.

28. On 10 June 2011 the applicant asked the court to release her subject to an undertaking not to abscond. She argued that she had favourable character references, no previous convictions, and a record of cooperation with the investigation. She further observed that the investigation had already been completed and therefore could no longer be obstructed. Emphasising that her conduct had amounted solely to a protest motivated by good intentions, she sought release. Several members of parliament and other prominent individuals supported the application and offered to serve as her personal guarantors.

29. At a preparatory hearing on 17 June 2011, the Pecherskyy Court refused the applicant’s request for release. It relied on the gravity of the charge, “the nature and the circumstances of the offence of which she [was] accused”, and the fact that the police had declared her wanted. The judge also stated in general terms that there were no grounds for releasing her under a personal guarantee.

30.
On 30 June 2011, the applicant again sought release. Later that day, the Pecherskyy Court granted her request and released her subject to an undertaking not to leave the town.

31. On 4 October 2012, the Pecherskyy Court convicted the applicant of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier as part of a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy. It found that she had persuaded D. and two other individuals, whose identities had not been established, to stage a performance at the “Eternal Glory” memorial in protest against the waste of natural gas resulting from the burning of the Eternal Flame. When questioned at trial, D. corroborated that version of events. The court also heard evidence from the memorial keeper, who had observed the performance from a distance, and from the two police officers who had spoken with the applicant and her friends (see paragraph 7 above). In addition, it examined the video recording of the performance as physical evidence.

32. The judgment referred to the applicant’s statement at the hearing that, in her view, people who laid flowers at the memorial did not truly understand what it commemorated. She maintained that she had committed no offence because the performance had not been intended to desecrate the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. She also argued that no tomb could exist beneath the Eternal Flame because a gas pipe ran there.

33. The Pecherskyy Court concluded that those arguments did not affect the legal characterisation of the applicant’s conduct and were contradicted by the evidence considered as a whole. In that connection, the judgment stated:

“... the court considers that by deliberately acting as part of a group in a manner demonstrating disrespect for the burial place of the Unknown Soldier and for the public tradition of commemorating the soldiers who died while defending or liberating Kyiv and the lands of Ukraine from the fascist hordes, and by later portraying those acts as a protest, [the applicant] sought to avoid public condemnation of her conduct and criminal responsibility for the offence.”

34. On the basis of documents issued by the local authorities, the court rejected the applicant’s argument that the location of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier had never been officially established.

35. The court found no aggravating or mitigating circumstances. When determining the sentence, however, it took account, on the one hand, of the applicant’s lack of a criminal record, her employment as a political analyst, and the positive character references provided by her workplace and from her place of residence. On the other hand, it observed that the offence was of medium gravity and that she had expressed no remorse for her actions. She was consequently sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for a period of two years.

36. On the same day, the Pecherskyy Court exempted D.
from criminal liability and placed her under her employer’s surety.

37. The applicant lodged an appeal. Referring to the definition of desecration of a burial place in the Burial and Funeral Business Act (see paragraph 47 below), she argued that her conduct did not contain the constituent elements of a criminal offence because she had not intended to “defile the family or social memory of a deceased or to show contempt for a burial place, or social and religious principles and traditions”. She repeated that her performance had been solely an act of protest. She further contended that the criminal proceedings against her had infringed her right to freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention.

38. The prosecutor appealed as well, arguing that the sentence was excessively lenient.

39. On 18 December 2012, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. It observed that desecration of a tomb could take various forms demonstrating an insulting attitude, ridicule or disrespect towards the tomb or the person buried there, irrespective of the motives claimed. Addressing the applicant’s freedom-of-expression argument, the court stated that this right was not absolute and that the restriction imposed in her case was prescribed by law and pursued a legitimate aim. The appellate court also dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal.

40. The applicant raised the same arguments in an appeal on points of law. On 11 April 2013, however, the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters dismissed that appeal.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Applicable legislation and relevant legal opinions

41. Under Article 9 § 1 of the Constitution of Ukraine, international treaties that are in force and whose binding nature has been approved by the Verkhovna Rada (the Ukrainian parliament) form part of domestic law.

42. Article 34 of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of expression, is reproduced in the Court’s judgment in Lykin v. Ukraine (no. 19382/08, § 15, 12 January 2017).

43. The pertinent provisions of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, as in force and worded at the relevant time, concerning preventive measures are set out, in particular, in the Court’s judgment in Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016).

44. Article 297 of the 2001 Criminal Code, as amended on 19 March 2009, provided:

“1.
Desecrating a tomb or any other burial site; defiling a corpse, human remains, or ashes; desecrating an urn holding a deceased person’s ashes; or unlawfully taking a corpse, remains, ashes, an urn containing such ashes, or objects located in a tomb, at another burial site, or on a corpse, remains, or ashes shall be punishable by a fine not exceeding two hundred non-taxable minimum [monthly salaries], arrest for a term of up to six months, restriction of liberty for up to three years, or imprisonment for the same term.

2. Where the same acts are committed repeatedly, by a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy, for financial gain or hooligan motives, against a common grave or the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, or in conjunction with violence or threats of violence, the punishment shall be restriction of liberty for three to five years or imprisonment for the same term.

3. If the acts specified in the preceding paragraphs result in serious consequences, they shall be punishable by imprisonment for five to twelve years.”

45. Article 66 of the Criminal Code sets out a non-exhaustive list of circumstances that mitigate punishment. It further provides that, when determining a sentence, a court may take into account mitigating circumstances not expressly included in that list. Pursuant to Article 69, where several mitigating circumstances lessen the seriousness of the offence, and after considering the offender’s character, a court may impose a penalty more lenient than that prescribed by law.

46. With regard to Article 297, the “Scientific and Practical Commentary on the Criminal Code of Ukraine” (Науково-практичний коментар Кримінального кодексу України, 7-ме вид., перероблене та доповнене / За ред. М.І. Мельника та М.І. Хавронюка. – Київ: Юридична думка, 2010) states, among other things:

“The object, or target, of the offence is society’s moral foundation concerning respect for the dead and their burial places. The offence inflicts non-pecuniary harm, particularly on persons close to the deceased; disrupts public order; may provoke interethnic and inter-confessional conflict; and adversely affects the upbringing of teenagers. The way in which people treat the dead is perhaps one of the clearest indications of the distinction between civilisation and savagery, while also revealing a person’s attitude towards other social values. ...

The actus reus of the criminal offence consists of ... desecrating a tomb or another burial place ...

Desecration means displaying contempt for a burial place or the deceased’s ashes, treating them insultingly, or subjecting them to brutal mockery. The law does not prescribe specific methods by which desecration may be carried out. Such conduct may include profanation—for example, placing indecent inscriptions or drawings on a tomb or soiling it with excrement—destroying sepulchral structures, excavating burial sites, dissecting or destroying a corpse, or tearing off its clothing.
Desecration comprises both an objective and a subjective component. The objective component consists of carrying out particular acts involving a deceased person or a burial site. The subjective component requires awareness that such conduct expresses contempt for the deceased’s memory and breaches the principles governing public life in that sphere. Although desecration is usually committed through positive action, it may also result from a failure to act—for instance, by not preventing domestic animals from digging into a grave or relieving themselves on it.

The mens rea required for this offence is intentional guilt. The perpetrator understands that he or she: (a) is infringing a tomb, another burial place, or a corpse; (b) anticipates that the conduct will inflict moral suffering on others and undermine society’s moral foundations concerning attitudes towards the dead; and (c) either seeks to express contempt for the deceased’s memory and a negative attitude towards the public principles applicable in this sphere, which constitutes direct intent, or is aware of and accepts that consequence, which constitutes indirect intent.

The offence is treated as aggravated where it is committed: ...

- by a group of persons acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy;

- for hooligan ... motives. ... Such motives exist when the perpetrator seeks to display contempt for generally accepted norms and rules concerning how people should treat the dead and their burial places, to boast of supposed bravery, or to gain standing in the eyes of others by humiliating people and offending their feelings. Put differently, these motives are regarded by public morality as shameful and base and are directed at creating conflict between the individual and society. Hooligan motives may also arise from racial, ethnic, or religious intolerance, divergent assessments of historical events, and similar considerations;

- in relation to ... a Tomb of an Unknown Soldier. ... A Tomb of an Unknown Soldier is a military memorial commemorating persons who died in an armed conflict. It encompasses both the burial site and the commemorative marker. The term “soldier” is used generically and includes any military servicemember, officer, sailor, or law-enforcement officer killed in combat or during an armed conflict. [It is immaterial] which side the deceased supported or fought for in the events that resulted in death. Equally irrelevant is how society or particular individuals evaluate the wars or other social upheavals concerned, or the roles played by those who participated in them ...”47.
Section 2 of the Burial and Funeral Business Act 2003, as subsequently amended, defines desecration of a tomb or another burial site as:

“- affixing, without authorisation, inscriptions, drawings, symbols or other images to cemetery facilities intended for burials and commemorative ceremonies, sepulchral structures, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or other burial places;

- intentionally damaging, excavating, demolishing or otherwise destroying cemetery facilities used for burials and commemorative ceremonies, sepulchral structures, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or other burial places;

- using cemetery facilities intended for burials and commemorative ceremonies, sepulchral structures, vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or other burial places for purposes not provided for by the legislation in force; using them without authorisation; or carrying out any other act aimed at insulting the family or public memory of the deceased, expressing contempt for the burial place, or showing disrespect for the social and religious principles and traditions of the locality; ...”

48. Section 32 of the Act provides that anyone responsible for desecrating a tomb or another burial place is liable in accordance with the law.

49. The 1994 Law on the Procedure for the Compensation of Damage caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies in charge of Operational Enquiries, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts, in the version applicable at the relevant time and also referred to as “the Compensation Act”, entitled a person to damages for harm resulting, among other things, from unlawful detention (section 1). Compensation was conditional upon “a finding of ... unlawfulness of arrest and detention in a guilty verdict or other judicial decision” (section 2).

B. Domestic case-law relied on by the applicant

50. The applicant provided the Court with copies of seven judgments issued by local courts on different dates from 2007 to 2013. In each case, individuals were convicted of desecrating tombs by removing metal components and selling them as scrap. Ranked from the least to the most severe, the sentences imposed were:

- two years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for two years;
- three years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for one year;
- one year and six months’ restriction of liberty;
- one year and six months’ imprisonment, suspended for one year;
- three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years and six months;
- three years’ imprisonment; and
- three years and six months’ imprisonment.

III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

51. A summary of the United States Supreme Court’s position on the controversial practice of cross-burning, as set out in Virginia v. Black, appears in the Court’s judgment in Fáber v. Hungary, no. 40721/08, § 18, 24 July 2012.

4. The application was communicated to the Government on 1 December 2014.

THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1991, the applicant resides in Kyiv.

6. When the events in question occurred, she was a member of an artistic group known as the St Luke Brotherhood, which had a reputation for staging provocative performances in public.

7. On 16 December 2010, the applicant and three other members of that group carried out what she termed an “act of performance”. According to the accounts given by both parties, it unfolded as follows. They visited the Eternal Glory Memorial commemorating those who died in the Second World War. The memorial contained the graves of thirty-two soldiers, among them the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Using a frying pan she had prepared beforehand, the applicant cracked several eggs into it and cooked them over the Eternal Flame at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Two of her companions also used the flame to grill sausages on skewers. A further member of the group recorded the incident on video. Two police officers approached and commented that the group’s conduct was inappropriate, but did not otherwise intervene. Later that day, acting on behalf of the St Luke Brotherhood, the applicant uploaded the video to the Internet together with the following statement:

“For fifty-three years, valuable natural gas has been burned to no purpose at Kyiv’s Glory Memorial. This indulgence costs taxpayers approximately 300,000 hryvnias [UAH] each month.”
This is merely one pagan temple with an ‘eternal flame’, although hundreds, perhaps even thousands, exist across Ukraine. On 16 December, the St Luke Brotherhood responded by staging a protest in the capital’s Glory Park, demonstrating that the ‘eternal flame’ should be put to use.

We propose that the indignant representatives of the Communist Party of Ukraine imitate the vestal virgins of ancient Rome by maintaining a twenty-four-hour watch over the ‘eternal flames’ and using wood to keep them burning manually. Communists will undoubtedly have no difficulty performing this duty: they already have experience caring for the Lenin monument in Kyiv, and their funding is far greater than that available to the vestal virgins.”

8. Although neither party submitted a copy of the video concerned to the Court, it could be watched on several publicly accessible websites. Beyond the parties’ factual account summarised above, the Court observes that the video’s soundtrack was the well-known 1974 Soviet song “The battle is going on again”, which celebrated the victory of the 1917 revolution and expressed optimism about the communist regime’s future. The video opened with the titles “The St Luke Brotherhood presents”, “Recipe of the day”, and “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame”. Those taking part made no public statement, and their conversation could not be heard. Other than the food and cooking utensils, they displayed no posters or visual materials. The footage showed that, after the applicant had cracked the eggs into the frying pan and was preparing to approach the flame, while her friends were holding skewers with sausages, two police officers arrived. The applicant explained something to them, after which they left. To access the flame, she had to cross over a sculpture representing a wreath of oak leaves and tread on the inscription “Glory to the Unknown Soldier”.

9. The police received several complaints alleging that the recorded action constituted desecration of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and demanding criminal prosecution.

10. On 21 December 2010, the police questioned D., one of the women involved in the performance. She stated that she had not known the other members of the group and had encountered them by chance. According to what they had allegedly told her, they were hungry and planned to prepare food to eat.

11. Later that same day, criminal proceedings were initiated against D. and three unidentified individuals on suspicion of hooliganism.

12. On 23 December 2010, D. made a written confession stating that she had participated in a protest against the improper use of natural gas and regretted doing so. She knew only the other participants’ first names.

13. On 24 December 2010, a second criminal case concerning the same incident was brought against D. and three unidentified persons, this time on suspicion of desecrating a tomb.

17. That same day, the police placed the applicant on the wanted list.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Applicable legislation and relevant legal opinions

41. Under Article 9 § 1 of the Constitution of Ukraine, international treaties that are in force and whose binding character has been approved by the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) of Ukraine form part of domestic legislation.

42. Article 34 of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of expression, is reproduced in the Court’s judgment in Lykin v. Ukraine (no. 19382/08, § 15, 12 January 2017).

43. The pertinent provisions on preventive measures in the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, in force and worded as applicable at the relevant time, are set out, in particular, in the Court’s judgment in Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016).

44. Article 297 of the 2001 Criminal Code, as amended on 19 March 2009, provided:

“1.
Desecrating a grave or any other place of burial; defiling a corpse, human remains, or ashes; profaning an urn holding a deceased person’s ashes; or unlawfully taking a corpse, remains, ashes, an urn containing the ashes of a deceased person, or items located in a grave, at another burial site, or on a corpse, remains, or ashes, is punishable by a fine not exceeding two hundred non-taxable minimum [monthly salaries], arrest for a term of up to six months, restriction of liberty for up to three years, or imprisonment for the same term.

2. Where those acts are committed repeatedly, by a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy, for profit or from hooligan motives, against a communal grave or the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, or together with violence or a threat of violence, the punishment shall be restriction of liberty for a period of three to five years or imprisonment for the same period.

3. If the conduct described in the preceding paragraphs results in serious consequences, it shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to twelve years.”

45. Article 66 of the Criminal Code provides a non-exhaustive catalogue of circumstances that mitigate punishment. It further permits a court, when determining a sentence, to take into account mitigating circumstances not included in that catalogue. Pursuant to Article 69, where several mitigating circumstances lessen the seriousness of the offence, and taking the offender’s personality into consideration, a court may impose a punishment more lenient than the one prescribed by law.

46. With regard to Article 297, the “Scientific and Practical Commentary on the Criminal Code of Ukraine” (Науково-практичний коментар Кримінального кодексу України, 7-ме вид., перероблене та доповнене / За ред. М.І. Мельника та М.І. Хавронюка. – Київ: Юридична думка, 2010) states, among other things:

“The protected object, or target, of the offence is society’s moral foundation concerning respect for deceased persons and their burial sites. The offence inflicts non-pecuniary harm, particularly on persons close to the deceased; disrupts public order; may provoke interethnic and inter-confessional conflict; and adversely affects the upbringing of teenagers. The way people treat the dead is perhaps among the clearest indications of the distinction between civilisation and savagery and also reveals an individual’s attitude towards other social values. ...

The actus reus of this criminal offence consists of ... the desecration of a grave or another burial place ...

Desecration means treating a burial site or the deceased’s ashes insultingly, subjecting them to brutal mockery, or openly displaying contempt for them. The legislation does not define the methods by which desecration may be carried out. Such methods may include profanation—for example, adding indecent words or images or fouling [the grave] with excrement—as well as destroying sepulchral structures, excavating burial sites, dissecting or destroying a corpse, or removing its clothing.
Desecration comprises both objective and subjective components. The objective component consists of particular conduct directed against a corpse or burial site. The subjective component requires awareness that such conduct expresses contempt for the deceased’s memory and breaches the principles governing public life in the relevant sphere. Desecration is usually committed through a positive act, although it may also result from a failure to act—for example, by allowing domestic animals to dig into a grave or relieve themselves on it without intervening.

The mens rea required for this offence is intentional guilt. The offender understands that he or she:

(a) is violating a tomb, another burial place, or a corpse;

(b) anticipates that the conduct will inflict moral suffering on others and undermine society’s moral foundations concerning attitudes towards the dead; and

(c) either seeks to express contempt for the deceased’s memory and display a negative attitude towards the public principles applicable in that sphere, which constitutes direct intent, or consciously accepts that outcome, which constitutes indirect intent.

The offence is treated as aggravated when it is committed:

...

- by a group of persons acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy;

- for hooligan ... motives. ...

Hooligan motives exist when an offender seeks to display contempt for the generally accepted norms and rules governing attitudes towards deceased persons and their burial places, to boast of supposed bravery, or to establish his or her status in the eyes of others by humiliating people and offending their feelings. Put differently, these motives are regarded by public morality as shameful and dishonourable and are intended to provoke conflict between the individual and society. They may also arise from racial, ethnic, or religious intolerance, divergent assessments of historical events, and similar considerations;

- in relation to ... a Tomb of an Unknown Soldier. ...

A Tomb of an Unknown Soldier is a military memorial honouring persons who died in an armed conflict. It encompasses both the burial site and a commemorative marker. The word “soldier” is used generically and includes any military servicemember, officer, sailor, or law-enforcement officer killed in action or during an armed conflict. [It is immaterial] which side the deceased supported or fought for in the events that caused his or her death. Equally irrelevant is the way in which society or particular individuals evaluate the wars or other social upheavals concerned, or the role played in them by their participants ...”47.
Section 2 of the Burial and Funeral Business Act 2003, as subsequently amended, characterises desecration of a tomb or another burial site as including:

“- affixing, without authorisation, inscriptions, drawings, symbols or other visual material to cemetery premises intended for burials and commemorative rites, sepulchral structures, burial vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or any other places of interment;

- intentionally damaging, excavating, demolishing or otherwise destroying cemetery premises intended for burials and commemorative rites, sepulchral structures, burial vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or any other places of interment;

- using cemetery premises intended for burials and commemorative rites, sepulchral structures, burial vaults, urns containing ashes, tombs or any other places of interment for purposes not provided for by the legislation in force; making unauthorised use of them; or carrying out any other act aimed at dishonouring the deceased’s family or public memory, expressing contempt for the burial site, or showing disregard for the social and religious principles and traditions observed in the locality; ...”

48. Section 32 of the Act provides that anyone responsible for desecrating a tomb or another burial site incurs liability as prescribed by law.

49. The 1994 Law on the Procedure for Compensation for Damage Caused to Citizens by the Unlawful Actions of Bodies Conducting Operational Enquiries, Pre-trial Investigation Authorities, Prosecutors or Courts—known also as “the Compensation Act” and cited in the version applicable at the relevant time—entitled individuals to compensation for harm resulting, among other things, from unlawful detention (section 1). Such entitlement arose only where “the unlawfulness of arrest and detention [had been established] in a guilty verdict or another judicial decision” (section 2).

B. Domestic judicial decisions relied on by the applicant

50. The applicant provided the Court with copies of seven judgments issued by local courts on different dates from 2007 to 2013. In those cases, individuals were convicted of desecrating tombs by removing metal components and selling them as scrap. Ranked from the least severe to the most severe, the penalties imposed were:

- restriction of liberty for two years, suspended for two years;
- restriction of liberty for three years, suspended for one year;
- restriction of liberty for one year and six months;
- imprisonment for one year and six months, suspended for one year;
- imprisonment for three years, suspended for two years and six months;
- imprisonment for three years; and
- imprisonment for three years and six months.

III. PERTINENT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

51. The Court’s judgment in Fáber v. Hungary, no. 40721/08, § 18, 24 July 2012, contains a summary of the position adopted by the Supreme Court of the United States of America regarding the controversial practice of cross burning, as set out in its ruling in Virginia v. Black.

original: FOURTH SECTION       CASE OF VOYKIN AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE (Application no. 47889/08)          JUDGMENT  STRASBOURG 27 March 2018 FINAL 27/06/2018 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of Voykin and Others v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Vincent A. De Gaetano, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Paulo Pinto de Albuquerque, Faris Vehabović, Egidijus Kūris, Iulia Motoc, Georges Ravarani, judges,and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 6 March 2018,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 47889/08) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Ukrainian nationals, Mr Valeriy Sergeyevich Voykin (the first applicant), Ms Marina Aleksandrovna Voykina (the second applicant), Ms Elleonora Nikolayevna Shupnyak (the third applicant), and Ms Valentina Borisovna Voykina (the fourth applicant). The first and second applicants lodged their applications on 11 November 2008. The third and fourth applicants joined them on 26 November 2008.The fourth applicant died after lodging her application. The first applicant, her son, expressed the wish to pursue her complaints in her stead.2. The applicants were represented by Mr Eduard Markov, a lawyer admitted to practice in Odessa. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr Ivan Lishchyna, of the Ministry of Justice.3. The applicants raised a number of complaints, in particular under Articles 3, 5, 8 and 13 of the Convention.4. On 6 January 2014 the application was communicated to the Government.5. On 10 July 2017 the Vice-President of the Section decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, that the parties should be invited to submit further written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application.THE FACTSI. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE6. The first applicant was born in 1978. At the time of the events he was a district police officer in the Kalyninskyy district police in Horlivka. As of February 2014, he has been serving a prison sentence in Menska prison no. 91. The second applicant is his wife who was born in 1984. She lives in Horlivka with her mother, the third applicant, who was born in 1951. The fourth applicant, the mother of the first applicant, was born in 1948 and died on 5 December 2010. The first applicant expressed wish to pursue his mother’s complaints on her behalf.A. Incident involving the second applicant and its investigation7. At the night from 18 to 19 June 2008, shortly after midnight, the second applicant had a conflict with a police officer, M., who was a colleague of her husband.8. The second applicant’s account of the events was as follows. When walking in the street with a friend, B., she heard somebody running after them. That person pushed her on the shoulder. Having turned, she saw M., whom she knew. He was wearing plain clothes and appeared to be heavily drunk. When she asked him what the matter was, M. shouted that he would subject her to a body search, without explanation. He snatched her bag from her. Having searched its contents, he threw it on the ground. Then M. grabbed the second applicant by the neck and started strangling her. In reply to her protests, he noted that the local prosecutor was there next to him and that it was pointless to complain. He hit the second applicant twice in the head with something heavy, which, in her opinion, could have been a mobile phone. At that moment the first applicant telephoned his wife’s friend B., who was then with her, to find out whether everything was fine (as his wife had not returned home at the expected time and was not answering his telephone calls). Having found out about the incident, the first applicant went there. M. threatened him in a rude manner with dismissal. He let the second applicant go only after two other police officers in plain clothes, who happened to be there, approached them.9. The second applicant’s friend B. supported the above version of events. However, eventually she specified that M. had not been strangling the second applicant, but had simply held her and not let her leave.10. M.’s version of the events was as follows. He was walking in the street with an acquaintance, P., a businessman, after the celebration of the professional holiday of police inspectors. They met two colleagues of M. and stopped to talk with them. Two women passed by. M. thought that one of them was a certain T., who was under administrative supervision and was not supposed to be out of her home so late. He went to ask her what she was doing there. However, having approached her, he realised that he had been mistaken. He recognised the second applicant and apologised for his mistake. The second applicant, who appeared to be heavily drunk, started insulting and pushing him. M. submitted that he had not touched her. As regards the possible origin of her injuries, he noted that she had had serious incidents in the past with her husband and that those injuries might have been inflicted by him. As regards the fact that the plastic bag that she had had in her hands had been torn, he explained it by her intense gesticulating.11. M.’s version was supported by the statements of his friend P. and the two police officers, who had been there.12. Having come home, the second applicant called an ambulance. She was diagnosed with several bruises on her neck and situational neurosis. She explained that she had been strangled by a police officer. In the presence of an ambulance paramedic, the second applicant called the police. According to the Government, she did not mention that M. was a law-enforcement official. The second applicant contested that submission.13. In the morning on 19 June 2008 the second applicant was examined by a neuropathologist who diagnosed her with concussion and bruises on her neck, and prescribed outpatient medical treatment.14. On 28 June 2008 the Kalyninskyy police issued a ruling refusing to institute criminal proceedings in respect of the second applicant’s complaint. It noted that she had complained to the police at 1.05 a.m. on 19 June 2008 of having been hit by an acquaintance. As further stated in the ruling, it had been impossible to question her, as she had never been at home when visited by the police.15. On 9 July 2008 the second applicant complained about the incident to the Horlivka town prosecutor’s office (“the Horlivka prosecutor’s office”). She requested that the investigation not be entrusted to the Kalyninskyy district prosecutor’s office (“the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office”), given that one of its officials had allegedly been with M. at the time of the events and that M. had referred to that fact as a guarantee of his impunity (see paragraph 8 above). The second applicant submitted that there had been no attempts by the authorities to contact them with a view to hearing their version of the events.16. On 15 July 2008 the Horlivka prosecutor’s office forwarded her complaint to the Kalyninskyy prosecutor.17. On 25 July 2008 the second applicant gave a written account of the incident to the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office. On the same date that authority quashed the refusal of 28 June 2008. It noted that the investigation had wrongly been entrusted to the Kalyninskyy police despite the fact that the second applicant’s complaint concerned her alleged ill-treatment by one of its officers.18. On 28 July 2008 the police officer who had been on duty during the night from 18 to 19 June 2008 was disciplined for not having followed up the second applicant’s call (see paragraph 12 above).19. On 1 August 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office refused to initiate criminal proceedings against M. under Article 365 § 2 of the Criminal Code (exceeding individual power by engaging in violent or degrading treatment of a victim), having held that there were no constituent elements of a crime discernible in his actions. The prosecutor noted that the second applicant’s allegation was supported by the statements of her husband and her friend. However, there were also statements of M. and the witnesses from his side, who denied any ill-treatment of the second applicant. The prosecutor therefore found her allegation to be unsubstantiated. It was also noted in the ruling that at the time of the events M. had been wearing civilian clothes and had not been acting as a law-enforcement official. Lastly, it was observed that the second applicant had ignored numerous summonses for questioning.20. On 4 August 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office annulled its refusal of 1 August 2008 as premature. It noted, in particular, that not all the relevant facts had been established. Furthermore, there had been no forensic medical expert examination of the second applicant.21. On 14 August 2008 the second applicant underwent such an examination, which documented no visible injuries. Having analysed her medical file, the expert concluded that she had sustained a bruise on her neck and a craniocerebral injury which led to concussion. Those injuries, assessed as insignificant, had resulted from “contact with blunt objects” at the time indicated by the second applicant.22. On the same day the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office once again refused to open a criminal case against M. for lack of the constituent elements of a crime in his actions. It relied, in particular, on the witnesses’ statements, according to which M. had not ill-treated the second applicant. Furthermore, the prosecutor noted that M. had not acted in his official capacity and that the injuries sustained by the second applicant had been insignificant.23. On 5 September 2008 a senior official of the same prosecutor’s office annulled the above ruling as premature. He noted, in particular, that an additional forensic medical examination was required with a view to verifying the second applicant’s allegation that she had been hit in the head with a mobile phone.24. On 15 September 2008 the prosecutor ordered such an examination of the second applicant with a view to answering the following questions: (1) how exactly could her injuries have been inflicted; (2) whether there were marks on her head possibly resulting from blows with a mobile phone; (3) whether she could have sustained the injuries in question in the circumstances as she alleged; and (4) when exactly she had sustained the injuries in question.25. On 9 October 2008 a forensic medical expert examination report was issued. It answered the above questions as follows: (1) the craniocerebral injury and the bruise on the neck had resulted from contact with blunt objects; (2) neither the examination of the second applicant nor the evaluation of the medical file had established any injuries to her head (apparently, implying visible injuries); (3) the second applicant’s injuries could have been inflicted on her in the circumstances described; and (4) according to the medical documents, the second applicant could have sustained the injuries on 19 June 2008.26. On 19 November 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office delivered yet another ruling refusing to open a criminal case in respect of the second applicant’s complaints. Having relied on the forensic medical examination reports and the witnesses’ statements, the prosecutor stated that her allegation had not been sufficiently corroborated.27. On 20 April 2009 the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office (“the regional prosecutor’s office”) annulled the above ruling as premature and based on an incomplete investigation.28. On 5 May 2009 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office again refused to institute criminal proceedings against M. It was stated in the ruling that the forensic medical expert evaluations of 14 August and 9 October 2008 refuted the second applicant’s allegations. Furthermore, the prosecutor noted that the second applicant had refused to give her account during the additional investigation.29. The second applicant challenged the above refusal before the Prosecutor General’s Office (“the PGO”) on at least three occasions (on 20 July and 8 October 2009 and on 4 January 2010). Her complaints were forwarded to the regional prosecutor’s office.30. On 21 February 2010 the regional prosecutor’s office wrote to her that it agreed with the lower prosecution authority’s decision. As further stated in the letter, it was open for her to challenge that decision before the courts if she so wished.B. Criminal proceedings against the first applicant31. In May 2008 the first applicant underwent knee surgery. From 8 August to 2 September 2008 he underwent a follow-up course of outpatient medical treatment in Horlivka Hospital.32. On an unspecified date (illegible in the available copy) the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office sent a summons to the first applicant at his registered residence (his mother’s home), instructing him to come to the prosecutor’s office on 5 September 2008. It is not clear whether it was issued in the context of the criminal investigation in respect of the complaints by the first applicant’s wife (see above) or whether it was rather related to the subsequent criminal proceedings against him.33. On 10 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office opened a criminal case against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and forgery committed in his capacity as a law-enforcement official in January 2008. More specifically, on 14 March 2008 the local court had informed the prosecutor of some factual inaccuracies in a report on an administrative (minor) offence, which had been drawn up by the first applicant. The latter was suspected of having forged that report.34. On the same date the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office informed the first applicant of the above decision by a letter sent to the address where he was de facto living with his wife (separately from their parents). It was also noted in the letter that he had to come to the prosecutor’s office to receive a copy of the decision and for questioning.35. Still on the same date, 10 September 2008, the prosecutor ordered the Kalyninskyy police to ensure the first applicant’s presence for investigative measures. On 12 September 2008 the police informed the investigator that it was impossible to comply with the above order given that the first applicant had been found neither at the address of his usual residence nor at his mother’s flat. When they had also gone to enquire about his whereabouts with his parents-in-law, the third applicant “had attacked them hysterically”, which made the police believe that the first applicant might be hiding there.36. On 13 September 2008 a judge of the Kalyninskyy Court ordered the first applicant’s arrest with a view to bringing him before the court to examine the issue of a preventive measure in his regard.37. On 19 September 2008 the first applicant was declared wanted by the police.38. On the same date he wrote to the regional prosecutor’s office that, following the incident with his wife, the Kalyninskyy police had been threatening him and his family with his dismissal, criminal prosecution, or even a fatal accident. He therefore sought that the Kalyninskyy prosecutor withdraw from the case. He also submitted that he was scared even to go to the hospital as some suspicious-looking persons had been loitering near his home. The first applicant indicated as his address that of his mother.39. On 22 September 2008 the investigator visited the first applicant’s mother (the fourth applicant) at her home and asked her whether she knew where the first applicant was. She stated that he had been living separately from her for about two years and that she was not aware of his whereabouts.40. On 24 September 2008 she sent to the investigator the first applicant’s request of 23 September 2008 to admit her to the proceedings as his representative and to give her a copy of the ruling of 10 September 2008 initiating the criminal investigation against him. In substantiation of that request, the first applicant stated that he was restricted in his movement following knee surgery.41. On 29 September 2008 the chief of medicine of Horlivka Hospital informed the investigator, in reply to the latter’s enquiry, that the last time the first applicant had come to the hospital had been 15 September 2008 and that the hospital administration did not know how he could be reached.42. On 1 October 2008 the internal security unit of the Kalyninskyy police wrote to the prosecutor that it had information that the first applicant had been secretly visiting the flats of his parents and parents-in-law.43. On 3 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor wrote to the first applicant at his mother’s address, indicating that the latter could not be admitted in the proceedings as his representative at such an early stage. The prosecutor indicated that the first applicant was on the wanted list and that he needed to show up to receive copies of the rulings in respect of the institution of the criminal proceedings against him and for his questioning.44. On 31 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor sent another letter to the first applicant, informing him that another criminal case had been opened against him on that date on suspicion of abuse of power by a law-enforcement official and forgery in office and that he had to come to the prosecutor’s office to get a copy of that decision and for questioning.45. During the period from October 2008 to January 2010 further eight criminal cases were opened against the first applicant on additional counts of abuse of office, as well as on suspicion of bribe-taking. He was suspected of having committed those offences in order to report better results to his superiors and thus be entitled to additional remuneration and promotions. The first applicant was informed of each such decision by a letter sent to his mother’s address.46. On 25 March 2009 the first applicant complained to the PGO that his numerous requests for the Kalyninskyy prosecutor to withdraw had been ignored. He further submitted that he required protection measures as “a person who had reported a crime”. Lastly, the first applicant requested that the prosecutor annul the decision on placing him on the wanted list “so that [he] could defend himself against the criminal charges and continue [his] medical treatment”.47. On 13 May and 26 June 2009 the regional prosecutor’s office wrote to the first applicant that his complaints had been dismissed as unsubstantiated.48. On 29 June 2009 the first applicant was arrested at the address where he lived with his wife. The investigator relied on Articles 106 and 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter “the CCP”, see paragraph 78 below) and substantiated the arrest as follows: the first applicant had been on the wanted list since 19 September 2008, had impeded the establishment of the truth and had committed serious criminal offences. It was also noted in the arrest report that the first applicant was suspected of offences under Articles 364 § 3 (abuse of power or office by a law-enforcement official), 366 § 1 (forgery in office) and 368 § 2 (bribe-taking) of the Criminal Code. The investigator drew up a report on the explanation to the first applicant of his procedural rights. The first applicant refused to sign it. He also refused to make any submissions as regards the charges against him.49. On 30 June 2009 the Kalyninskyy Court extended the term of the first applicant’s arrest to ten days on the grounds that the case file lacked information about his character. That ruling was not amenable to appeal.50. On 3 July 2009 the same court ordered the first applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure, “having regard to the seriousness and circumstances of the crimes committed and the character of [the first applicant]”, without further details.51. On 6 July 2009 the first applicant appealed. He submitted that his remand in custody was not based on sufficient and relevant reasons. He noted that he had been arrested at his home, where he had been living for over two years, and that he had not absconded. He noted that the reasoning in support of his pre-trial detention had been overly formalistic. Thus, although the court had referred to his character, it had failed to specify what exactly in his character had justified his detention as the most appropriate preventive measure.52. On 21 July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) quashed the ruling of 3 July 2009 and released the first applicant subject to an undertaking not to leave the town. It found that the first-instance court had not given reasons as to the necessity to choose the strictest preventive measure.53. On 17 November 2011 the Kalyninskyy Court found the first applicant guilty of fraud, abuse of power in his capacity of a law-enforcement official, forgery causing grave consequences, and bribe-taking, and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment with a ban to occupy posts in law-enforcement authorities, and confiscation of his personal property.54. On 6 March 2012 the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in the part concerning the forgery charge and remitted it to the first-instance court for a fresh examination. It upheld the judgment in the remaining part, having slightly reclassified some of the charges and having reduced the term of the first applicant’s imprisonment to six years.55. On 9 October 2012 the Kalyninskyy Court again found the applicant guilty of forgery causing grave consequences and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. The final sentence was six years’ imprisonment, as the most severe of the applicant’s punishments absorbed the more lenient one. In the absence of any appeals, the judgment became final.56. On 1 August 2013 the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters quashed the appellate court’s ruling of 6 March 2012 in the part concerning the first applicant’s conviction (the part concerning the remittal of the case to the first-instance court remained in force) and remitted the case for fresh appellate examination.57. On 3 December 2013 the appellate court upheld the judgment of 17 November 2011 in so far as it concerned the first applicant’s conviction for abuse of power in his capacity as a law-enforcement official and his sentencing to six years’ imprisonment. As regards the other charges (with the exception of that dealt with by the judgment of 9 October 2012 – see paragraph 55 above), they were slightly reclassified and the first applicant had the penalty in respect of that part removed.58. The case file does not contain any further information as regards the criminal proceedings against the first applicant.C. Police searches of the flats of the third and fourth applicants and related events59. On 10 September 2008 the investigator applied to the Kalyninskyy Court for authorisation to search the first applicant’s registered residence (the flat of the fourth applicant). It was stated in the application that on 27 January 2008 the first applicant had drawn up a report on an administrative (minor) offence in respect of unauthorised street trading by a private individual. As subsequently established, the information in that report had not been accurate, which had led to the institution of criminal proceedings against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and forgery. The investigator considered that “some items and documents relevant for establishing the truth” in the case could be found in the first applicant’s residence.60. On 11 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court in a final ruling, allowed the above application, having reiterated the investigator’s reasoning and description of the search’s scope. It relied on Article 177 of the CCP (follow the references in paragraph 78 below).61. On 12 September 2008 the investigator applied to the Kalyninskyy Court for authorisation to search the second applicant’s registered residence (the flat of the third applicant). The text of the application was identical to that submitted on 10 September 2008 (see paragraph 59 above).62. On the same day the police knocked at the third applicant’s door. She and her husband were at home, but did not let the police in.63. The third applicant’s account of the events of 12 September 2008 is as follows. A group of nine to ten persons, including police officers and some suspicious-looking persons, came to her flat. They knocked at the entrance door in a violent manner, demanding to be let in. The third applicant’s husband went out and asked them for a search warrant or another document authorising their actions, but no such document was produced. The police threatened the third applicant and her husband that they would break in and that they would find a pretext to criminally prosecute the entire family. They stayed on the stairs and in the yard and shouted for about three hours.64. According to the Government’s version, three police officers went to the third applicant’s flat. They informed her about the criminal proceedings against the first applicant and enquired as to his whereabouts. As she and her husband refused to cooperate, the police left.65. On 13 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court allowed the investigator’s application of 12 September 2008 (see paragraph 61 above). Its ruling was identical to that delivered on 11 September 2008 (see paragraph 60 above).66. On the same day the police carried out a search at the flat of the third applicant. According to her, they broke the entrance door using an electric saw. The third applicant further alleged that the police had not shown a search warrant to her. Two attesting witnesses were present. According to the third applicant, they were acquaintances of the police officers.67. As indicated in the search report, it lasted from 5.20 p.m. to 7.04 p.m. The police seized a number of documents related to the first applicant’s work. Furthermore, they seized a mobile telephone, which did not have a SIM card, together with its box. Lastly, they found and seized a package appearing to contain cannabis. According to the third applicant, it had been planted by the police.68. On 16 September 2008 the police conducted a search of the flat of the fourth applicant. They discovered and seized some documents which were deemed to be related to the criminal investigation in respect of the first applicant. According to the first and fourth applicants, those documents had been brought there by the police themselves the previous day. The fourth applicant submitted that the officers, whom she knew as colleagues of her son, had explained to her that, following an attack on their police station, they had not had a safe place to store the documents, which had been intended in any event for handing over to the first applicant.69. On 23 September 2008 an expert established that the package discovered in the third applicant’s flat on 13 September 2008 contained cannabis. On 2 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy police refused to institute criminal proceedings in that regard, having held that it had been impossible to establish to whom the cannabis might have belonged.70. On 7 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court allowed another application to search the first applicant’s registered residence (the flat of the fourth applicant) given that the investigator had information that the first applicant might be hiding there.71. On 11 February 2009 the police conducted a search of the fourth applicant’s flat on the basis of the court ruling of 7 October 2008. As indicated in the search report, the police were searching for “items, valuables and documents related to the criminal activity of [the first applicant]”. The search did not discover anything of interest for the investigation.72. The third and fourth applicants requested many times that the Kalyninskyy Court provide them with copies of the rulings authorising the searches of their flats. The president of the court replied that the searches had been carried out in compliance with the CCP and that sending a copy of the respective court rulings was not provided for by the legislation.73. The third and fourth applicants also complained many times to the prosecution authorities of the unlawfulness of the searches. They submitted, in particular, that the police had been rude and intrusive, that the attesting witnesses had not been independent, and that it was not clear what the police had actually been looking for.74. On 23 December 2008 the Horlivka prosecutor’s office refused to open a criminal case in respect of the police officers involved in the operation of 12 September and the searches of 13 and 16 September 2008, with the generally couched reasoning that there had been no violations of law. It appears that the applicants were unaware of that decision.75. On 17 June 2009, following complaints by the third and fourth applicants, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against the judge of the Kalyninskyy Court in respect of the rulings authorising the searches of their flats.76. On 20 November 2009 the third applicant got acquainted with the ruling of the Kalyninskyy Court of 13 September 2008 (see paragraph 65 above). It is not known whether, and if so when, the fourth applicant got access to the respective rulings of 11 September and 7 October 2008 (see paragraphs 60 and 70 above).D. Other facts77. On 5 June 2006 a local heating company initiated civil proceedings against the first and fourth applicants, who had their registered domicile at the same address, for debt recovery. The domestic courts found against the applicants. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016); and as regards search of a house or other property – in Vasylchuk v. Ukraine (no. 24402/07, §§ 28-30, 13 June 2013) and Bagiyeva v.
