FOURTH SECTION

CASE OF VOYKIN AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 47889/08)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

27 March 2018

FINAL

27/06/2018

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Voykin and Others v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Vincent A. De Gaetano, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Paulo Pinto de Albuquerque,
Faris Vehabović,
Egidijus Kūris,
Iulia Motoc,
Georges Ravarani, judges,

and Marialena Tsirli, Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 6 March 2018,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 47889/08) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Ukrainian nationals: Mr Valeriy Sergeyevich Voykin (the first applicant), Ms Marina Aleksandrovna Voykina (the second applicant), Ms Elleonora Nikolayevna Shupnyak (the third applicant), and Ms Valentina Borisovna Voykina (the fourth applicant). The first and second applicants submitted their applications on 11 November 2008. The third and fourth applicants joined them on 26 November 2008.

The fourth applicant died after lodging her application. The first applicant, her son, stated that he wished to pursue her complaints on her behalf.

2. The applicants were represented by Mr Eduard Markov, a lawyer authorised to practise in Odessa. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr Ivan Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicants made several complaints, notably under Articles 3, 5, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

4. On 6 January 2014, the application was communicated to the Government.

5. On 10 July 2017, the Vice-President of the Section decided, pursuant to Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit additional written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6. The first applicant was born in 1978. At the relevant time, he was a district police officer with the Kalyninskyy district police in Horlivka. Since February 2014, he has been serving a prison sentence in Menska Prison no. 91. The second applicant is his wife, who was born in 1984. She lives in Horlivka with her mother, the third applicant, who was born in 1951. The fourth applicant, the first applicant’s mother, was born in 1948 and died on 5 December 2010. The first applicant expressed a wish to pursue his mother’s complaints on her behalf.

A. Incident involving the second applicant and the ensuing investigation

7. During the night of 18 to 19 June 2008, shortly after midnight, the second applicant had an altercation with a police officer, M., who was her husband’s colleague.

8. The second applicant gave the following account of the events.
While walking along the street with her friend B., she heard someone running after them. That person pushed her on the shoulder. When she turned around, she saw M., whom she knew. He was dressed in plain clothes and appeared to be heavily drunk. When she asked what the matter was, M. shouted, without explanation, that he would subject her to a body search. He snatched her bag, searched its contents, and threw it on the ground. M. then grabbed the second applicant by the neck and began strangling her. In response to her protests, he stated that the local prosecutor was standing next to him and that there was no point in complaining. He struck the second applicant twice on the head with something heavy, which she believed might have been a mobile phone. At that moment, the first applicant telephoned his wife’s friend B., who was with her at the time, to check whether everything was all right, as his wife had not returned home when expected and was not answering his calls. After learning about the incident, the first applicant went there. M. rudely threatened him with dismissal. He released the second applicant only after two other plain-clothes police officers who happened to be there approached them.

9. The second applicant’s friend B. corroborated the above account of events. However, she later clarified that M. had not been strangling the second applicant, but had merely held her and prevented her from leaving.

10. M.’s account of the events was as follows. He was walking along the street with an acquaintance, P., a businessman, after celebrating the professional holiday of police inspectors. They encountered two of M.’s colleagues and stopped to speak with them. Two women walked past. M. thought that one of them was a certain T., who was under administrative supervision and was not permitted to be away from home so late. He went to ask what she was doing there. However, upon approaching her, he realised that he had been mistaken. He recognised the second applicant and apologised for his error. The second applicant, who appeared to be heavily drunk, began insulting and pushing him. M. maintained that he had not touched her. As to the possible origin of her injuries, he noted that she had previously had serious incidents with her husband and that he might have inflicted them. Regarding the torn plastic bag she had been holding, he attributed the damage to her vigorous gesticulation.

11. M.’s account was supported by statements from his friend P. and the two police officers who had been present.

12. After returning home, the second applicant called an ambulance. She was diagnosed with several bruises on her neck and situational neurosis. She stated that a police officer had strangled her. In the presence of an ambulance paramedic, the second applicant called the police. According to the Government, she did not say that M. was a law-enforcement official.
The second applicant disputed that submission.

13. On the morning of 19 June 2008, the second applicant was examined by a neuropathologist, who diagnosed her with concussion and bruising to her neck and prescribed outpatient medical treatment.

14. On 28 June 2008, the Kalyninskyy police issued a ruling refusing to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the second applicant’s complaint. It noted that, at 1.05 a.m. on 19 June 2008, she had complained to the police that she had been hit by an acquaintance. The ruling further stated that it had been impossible to question her because she had never been at home when the police visited.

15. On 9 July 2008, the second applicant complained about the incident to the Horlivka town prosecutor’s office (“the Horlivka prosecutor’s office”). She requested that the investigation not be assigned to the Kalyninskyy district prosecutor’s office (“the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office”), since one of its officials had allegedly been with M. at the time of the events and M. had referred to that fact as a guarantee of his impunity (see paragraph 8 above). The second applicant submitted that the authorities had made no attempt to contact them in order to hear their version of events.

16. On 15 July 2008, the Horlivka prosecutor’s office forwarded her complaint to the Kalyninskyy prosecutor.

17. On 25 July 2008, the second applicant provided the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office with a written account of the incident. On the same day, that authority quashed the refusal of 28 June 2008. It noted that the investigation had wrongly been entrusted to the Kalyninskyy police, even though the second applicant’s complaint concerned her alleged ill-treatment by one of its officers.

18. On 28 July 2008, the police officer who had been on duty during the night of 18 to 19 June 2008 was disciplined for failing to follow up on the second applicant’s call (see paragraph 12 above).

19. On 1 August 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office refused to initiate criminal proceedings against M. under Article 365 § 2 of the Criminal Code (exceeding individual power by engaging in violent or degrading treatment of a victim), finding that his actions disclosed no constituent elements of a crime. The prosecutor noted that the second applicant’s allegation was supported by statements from her husband and friend. However, M. and witnesses on his side had also given statements denying any ill-treatment of the second applicant. The prosecutor therefore considered her allegation unsubstantiated. The ruling also noted that, at the time of the events, M. had been wearing civilian clothes and had not been acting in his capacity as a law-enforcement official. Lastly, it observed that the second applicant had failed to comply with numerous summonses for questioning.

20. On 4 August 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office annulled its refusal of 1 August 2008 as premature.
It noted, in particular, that not all the relevant facts had been established. Moreover, no forensic medical expert examination of the second applicant had been conducted.

21. On 14 August 2008 the second applicant underwent such an examination, which revealed no visible injuries. Having reviewed her medical file, the expert concluded that she had sustained a bruise to her neck and a craniocerebral injury resulting in concussion. Those injuries, assessed as insignificant, had resulted from “contact with blunt objects” at the time indicated by the second applicant.

22. On the same day, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office again refused to open a criminal case against M. owing to the absence of the constituent elements of a crime in his actions. It relied, in particular, on witness statements according to which M. had not ill-treated the second applicant. The prosecutor further noted that M. had not acted in his official capacity and that the injuries sustained by the second applicant had been insignificant.

23. On 5 September 2008 a senior official from the same prosecutor’s office annulled the above ruling as premature. He noted, in particular, that an additional forensic medical examination was necessary to verify the second applicant’s allegation that she had been struck on the head with a mobile phone.

24. On 15 September 2008 the prosecutor ordered such an examination of the second applicant to answer the following questions: (1) how exactly her injuries could have been inflicted; (2) whether there were marks on her head that might have resulted from blows with a mobile phone; (3) whether she could have sustained the injuries in question in the circumstances alleged; and (4) when exactly she had sustained those injuries.

25. On 9 October 2008 a forensic medical expert report was issued. It answered the above questions as follows: (1) the craniocerebral injury and the bruise to the neck had resulted from contact with blunt objects; (2) neither the examination of the second applicant nor the review of her medical file had established any injuries to her head (apparently meaning visible injuries); (3) the second applicant’s injuries could have been inflicted in the circumstances described; and (4) according to the medical records, the second applicant could have sustained the injuries on 19 June 2008.

26. On 19 November 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office issued yet another ruling refusing to open a criminal case concerning the second applicant’s complaints. Relying on the forensic medical examination reports and witness statements, the prosecutor stated that her allegation had not been sufficiently substantiated.

27. On 20 April 2009 the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office (“the regional prosecutor’s office”) annulled the above ruling as premature and based on an incomplete investigation.

28.
On 5 May 2009 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office once again refused to institute criminal proceedings against M. The ruling stated that the forensic medical expert evaluations of 14 August and 9 October 2008 refuted the second applicant’s allegations. Moreover, the prosecutor noted that the second applicant had declined to give her account during the additional investigation.

29. The second applicant challenged that refusal before the Prosecutor General’s Office (“the PGO”) on at least three occasions: 20 July and 8 October 2009, and 4 January 2010. Her complaints were referred to the regional prosecutor’s office.

30. On 21 February 2010 the regional prosecutor’s office wrote to inform her that it agreed with the lower prosecution authority’s decision. The letter further stated that she could challenge that decision before the courts if she wished.

B. Criminal proceedings against the first applicant

31. In May 2008 the first applicant underwent knee surgery. From 8 August to 2 September 2008 he received a follow-up course of outpatient medical treatment at Horlivka Hospital.

32. On an unspecified date (illegible in the available copy), the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office sent a summons to the first applicant at his registered address (his mother’s home), instructing him to attend the prosecutor’s office on 5 September 2008. It is unclear whether the summons was issued in the context of the criminal investigation concerning the complaints made by the first applicant’s wife (see above) or was instead connected with the subsequent criminal proceedings against him.

33. On 10 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office instituted criminal proceedings against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and forgery committed in his capacity as a law-enforcement official in January 2008. More specifically, on 14 March 2008 the local court had informed the prosecutor of certain factual inaccuracies in a report concerning an administrative (minor) offence drawn up by the first applicant. He was suspected of having forged that report.

34. On the same day, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office notified the first applicant of that decision by letter sent to the address where he was actually living with his wife (separately from their parents). The letter also stated that he was required to attend the prosecutor’s office to receive a copy of the decision and to be questioned.

35. Also on 10 September 2008, the prosecutor instructed the Kalyninskyy police to ensure the first applicant’s attendance for investigative measures. On 12 September 2008 the police informed the investigator that they had been unable to comply with that order because the first applicant had been found neither at his usual residence nor at his mother’s flat.
When they had also gone to enquire about his whereabouts with his parents-in-law, the third applicant “had attacked them hysterically”, leading the police to believe that the first applicant might be hiding there.

36. On 13 September 2008 a judge of the Kalyninskyy Court ordered the first applicant’s arrest with a view to bringing him before the court for examination of the issue of a preventive measure in his regard.

37. On 19 September 2008 the police declared the first applicant wanted.

38. On the same day, he wrote to the regional prosecutor’s office stating that, following the incident with his wife, the Kalyninskyy police had been threatening him and his family with his dismissal, criminal prosecution or even a fatal accident. He therefore requested that the Kalyninskyy prosecutor withdraw from the case. He also submitted that he was afraid even to go to the hospital, as some suspicious-looking individuals had been loitering near his home. The first applicant gave his mother’s address as his own.

39. On 22 September 2008 the investigator visited the first applicant’s mother (the fourth applicant) at her home and asked whether she knew where he was. She stated that he had been living separately from her for approximately two years and that she was unaware of his whereabouts.

40. On 24 September 2008 she sent the investigator the first applicant’s request of 23 September 2008 to admit her to the proceedings as his representative and to provide her with a copy of the ruling of 10 September 2008 initiating the criminal investigation against him. In support of that request, the first applicant stated that his movement was restricted following knee surgery.

41. On 29 September 2008 the chief physician of Horlivka Hospital informed the investigator, in response to the latter’s enquiry, that the first applicant had last visited the hospital on 15 September 2008 and that the hospital administration did not know how to contact him.

42. On 1 October 2008 the internal security unit of the Kalyninskyy police informed the prosecutor in writing that it had information that the first applicant had been secretly visiting the flats of his parents and parents-in-law.

43. On 3 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor wrote to the first applicant at his mother’s address, explaining that she could not be admitted to the proceedings as his representative at such an early stage. The prosecutor stated that the first applicant was on the wanted list and that he needed to appear in order to receive copies of the rulings concerning the institution of criminal proceedings against him and to be questioned.

44.
On 31 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy prosecutor sent a further letter to the first applicant, informing him that another criminal case had been opened against him that day on suspicion of abuse of power by a law-enforcement official and forgery in office, and that he was required to attend the prosecutor’s office to receive a copy of that decision and to be questioned.

45. Between October 2008 and January 2010, a further eight criminal cases were opened against the first applicant on additional counts of abuse of office and on suspicion of bribe-taking. He was suspected of committing those offences in order to report better results to his superiors and thereby qualify for additional remuneration and promotions. The first applicant was notified of each such decision by a letter sent to his mother’s address.

46. On 25 March 2009 the first applicant complained to the PGO that his numerous requests for the withdrawal of the Kalyninskyy prosecutor had been ignored. He further submitted that he required protective measures as “a person who had reported a crime”. Lastly, the first applicant requested that the prosecutor annul the decision to place him on the wanted list “so that [he] could defend himself against the criminal charges and continue [his] medical treatment”.

47. On 13 May and 26 June 2009 the regional prosecutor’s office informed the first applicant in writing that his complaints had been dismissed as unsubstantiated.

48. On 29 June 2009 the first applicant was arrested at the address where he was living with his wife. The investigator relied on Articles 106 and 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter “the CCP”; see paragraph 78 below) and justified the arrest on the grounds that the first applicant had been on the wanted list since 19 September 2008, had obstructed the establishment of the truth, and had committed serious criminal offences. The arrest report also noted that the first applicant was suspected of offences under Articles 364 § 3 (abuse of power or office by a law-enforcement official), 366 § 1 (forgery in office), and 368 § 2 (bribe-taking) of the Criminal Code. The investigator drew up a report confirming that the first applicant’s procedural rights had been explained to him. The first applicant refused to sign it. He also declined to make any submissions concerning the charges against him.

49. On 30 June 2009 the Kalyninskyy Court extended the first applicant’s arrest to ten days on the ground that the case file contained insufficient information about his character. That ruling was not subject to appeal.

50. On 3 July 2009 the same court ordered the first applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure, “having regard to the seriousness and circumstances of the crimes committed and the character of [the first applicant]”, without providing further details.

51. On 6 July 2009 the first applicant lodged an appeal. He submitted that his remand in custody was not supported by sufficient and relevant reasons.
He stated that he had been arrested at his home, where he had lived for over two years, and that he had not absconded. He argued that the reasoning supporting his pre-trial detention had been excessively formalistic. Thus, although the court had referred to his character, it had failed to specify what aspect of his character had justified detention as the most appropriate preventive measure.

52. On 21 July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) quashed the ruling of 3 July 2009 and released the first applicant subject to an undertaking not to leave the town. It found that the first-instance court had failed to explain why it was necessary to impose the strictest preventive measure.

53. On 17 November 2011 the Kalyninskyy Court found the first applicant guilty of fraud, abuse of power in his capacity as a law-enforcement official, forgery causing grave consequences, and bribe-taking. It sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, banned him from holding posts in law-enforcement authorities, and ordered the confiscation of his personal property.

54. On 6 March 2012 the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment in so far as it concerned the forgery charge and remitted that charge to the first-instance court for fresh examination. It upheld the remainder of the judgment, while slightly reclassifying some charges and reducing the first applicant’s prison sentence to six years.

55. On 9 October 2012 the Kalyninskyy Court again found the applicant guilty of forgery causing grave consequences and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. The final sentence was six years’ imprisonment, as the more lenient punishment was absorbed by the most severe one. In the absence of any appeals, the judgment became final.

56. On 1 August 2013 the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters quashed the appellate court’s ruling of 6 March 2012 in so far as it concerned the first applicant’s conviction (the part concerning the remittal of the case to the first-instance court remained in force) and remitted the case for fresh appellate examination.

57. On 3 December 2013 the appellate court upheld the judgment of 17 November 2011 in so far as it concerned the first applicant’s conviction for abuse of power in his capacity as a law-enforcement official and his sentence of six years’ imprisonment. As regards the other charges (except for the charge dealt with in the judgment of 9 October 2012 – see paragraph 55 above), they were slightly reclassified and the penalty imposed on the first applicant in respect of that part was removed.

58. The case file contains no further information concerning the criminal proceedings against the first applicant.

C. Police searches of the flats of the third and fourth applicants and related events

59. On 10 September 2008 the investigator applied to the Kalyninskyy Court for authorisation to search the first applicant’s registered residence (the fourth applicant’s flat).
It was stated in the application that on 27 January 2008 the first applicant had drawn up a report concerning an administrative (minor) offence involving unauthorised street trading by a private individual. As was subsequently established, the information in that report had been inaccurate, which had led to criminal proceedings being instituted against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and forgery. The investigator considered that “some items and documents relevant to establishing the truth” in the case could be found at the first applicant’s residence.

60. On 11 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court, in a final ruling, allowed the above application, reiterating the investigator’s reasoning and description of the scope of the search. It relied on Article 177 of the CCP (see the references in paragraph 78 below).

61. On 12 September 2008 the investigator applied to the Kalyninskyy Court for authorisation to search the second applicant’s registered residence (the third applicant’s flat). The application was identical to that submitted on 10 September 2008 (see paragraph 59 above).

62. On the same day, the police knocked on the third applicant’s door. She and her husband were at home but did not allow the police to enter.

63. The third applicant’s account of the events of 12 September 2008 was as follows. A group of nine or ten persons, including police officers and several suspicious-looking individuals, came to her flat. They knocked violently on the entrance door and demanded to be let in. The third applicant’s husband went outside and asked them to produce a search warrant or another document authorising their actions, but no such document was provided. The police threatened the third applicant and her husband that they would break in and find a pretext to prosecute the entire family criminally. They remained on the stairs and in the yard, shouting for approximately three hours.

64. According to the Government’s account, three police officers went to the third applicant’s flat. They informed her of the criminal proceedings against the first applicant and asked about his whereabouts. When she and her husband refused to cooperate, the police left.

65. On 13 September 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court granted the investigator’s application of 12 September 2008 (see paragraph 61 above). Its ruling was identical to that delivered on 11 September 2008 (see paragraph 60 above).

66. On the same day, the police searched the third applicant’s flat. According to her, they broke down the entrance door using an electric saw. The third applicant further alleged that the police had not shown her a search warrant. Two attesting witnesses were present. According to the third applicant, they were acquaintances of the police officers.

67. As stated in the search report, the search lasted from 5.20 p.m. until 7.04 p.m. The police seized a number of documents relating to the first applicant’s work.
Furthermore, they seized a mobile telephone without a SIM card, together with its box. Lastly, they found and seized a package that appeared to contain cannabis. According to the third applicant, it had been planted by the police.

68. On 16 September 2008 the police searched the flat of the fourth applicant. They discovered and seized several documents deemed to be related to the criminal investigation concerning the first applicant. According to the first and fourth applicants, those documents had been brought there by the police themselves the previous day. The fourth applicant submitted that the officers, whom she knew as her son’s colleagues, had explained that, following an attack on their police station, they had had no safe place to store the documents, which had in any event been intended for delivery to the first applicant.

69. On 23 September 2008 an expert determined that the package found in the third applicant’s flat on 13 September 2008 contained cannabis. On 2 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy police refused to institute criminal proceedings in that regard, finding that it had been impossible to establish to whom the cannabis might have belonged.

70. On 7 October 2008 the Kalyninskyy Court granted another application to search the first applicant’s registered residence (the flat of the fourth applicant), given that the investigator had information suggesting that the first applicant might be hiding there.

71. On 11 February 2009 the police searched the fourth applicant’s flat on the basis of the court ruling of 7 October 2008. According to the search report, the police were looking for “items, valuables and documents related to the criminal activity of [the first applicant]”. The search did not uncover anything of interest to the investigation.

72. The third and fourth applicants repeatedly requested that the Kalyninskyy Court provide them with copies of the rulings authorising the searches of their flats. The president of the court replied that the searches had been conducted in compliance with the CCP and that the legislation did not provide for copies of the relevant court rulings to be sent.

73. The third and fourth applicants also complained repeatedly to the prosecution authorities that the searches had been unlawful. They submitted, in particular, that the police had been rude and intrusive, that the attesting witnesses had not been independent, and that it was unclear what the police had actually been searching for.

74. On 23 December 2008 the Horlivka prosecutor’s office refused to open a criminal case against the police officers involved in the operation of 12 September and the searches of 13 and 16 September 2008, giving the generalised reasoning that there had been no violations of the law. It appears that the applicants were unaware of that decision.

75.
On 17 June 2009, following complaints lodged by the third and fourth applicants, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office declined to institute criminal proceedings against the judge of the Kalyninskyy Court concerning the rulings authorising searches of their flats.

76. On 20 November 2009, the third applicant became acquainted with the Kalyninskyy Court’s ruling of 13 September 2008 (see paragraph 65 above). It is unclear whether, and if so when, the fourth applicant obtained access to the relevant rulings of 11 September and 7 October 2008 (see paragraphs 60 and 70 above).

D. Other facts

77. On 5 June 2006, a local heating company brought civil proceedings for debt recovery against the first and fourth applicants, whose registered domicile was at the same address. The domestic courts ruled against the applicants. On 19 May 2008, the Supreme Court declined to examine an appeal on points of law lodged by the first and fourth applicants because they had not paid the court fees.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

78. The relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (1960), as in force at the material time, can be found: regarding the obligation to investigate a crime, in Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012); regarding the arrest of a suspect by the body of inquiry, in Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016); and regarding searches of a house or other property, in Vasylchuk v. Ukraine (no. 24402/07, §§ 28-30, 13 June 2013) and Bagiyeva v. Ukraine (no. 41085/05, §§ 39 and 40, 28 April 2016).

79. The relevant provisions of the Civil Code (2003) and the Compensation Act (1994), as worded at the material time, are reproduced in the judgment in Yaroshovets and Others v. Ukraine (nos. 74820/10 and 4 others, §§ 60 and 62, 3 December 2015).

8. The second applicant described the events as follows.
While walking along the street with her friend B., the second applicant heard someone running behind them. The person shoved her shoulder. When she turned around, she recognised M., whom she knew. He was dressed in civilian clothes and appeared extremely intoxicated. She asked what was happening, but M., without offering any explanation, shouted that he intended to search her person. He seized her bag, rummaged through it, and threw it onto the ground. M. then took hold of the second applicant by the neck and began to strangle her. When she protested, he said that the local prosecutor was standing nearby and that there was no point in making a complaint. He struck her twice on the head with a heavy object, which she believed might have been a mobile telephone. Meanwhile, because his wife had neither returned home when expected nor answered his calls, the first applicant telephoned her friend B., who was with her, to check whether everything was all right. On learning what had happened, he went to the scene. M. crudely threatened to have him dismissed. The second applicant was released only after two other police officers in civilian clothing, who happened to be present, came over.

9. B., the second applicant’s friend, initially corroborated that account. She later clarified, however, that M. had not strangled the second applicant but had merely restrained her and prevented her from leaving.

10. M. gave a different account. He stated that, following celebrations marking the professional holiday of police inspectors, he had been walking along the street with an acquaintance, P., a businessman. They encountered two of M.’s colleagues and stopped to speak with them. Two women then walked past. M. mistook one of them for T., a woman subject to administrative supervision who was not permitted to be away from home at such a late hour. He approached her to ask why she was there, but then realised his error. After recognising the second applicant, he apologised. According to M., she appeared heavily intoxicated and began insulting and pushing him. He maintained that he had not touched her. As a possible explanation for her injuries, he referred to serious incidents that had previously occurred between her and her husband and suggested that her husband might have caused them. He attributed the tearing of the plastic bag she had been carrying to her vigorous gesticulation.

11. M.’s account was corroborated by his friend P. and by the two police officers who had been present.

12. After returning home, the second applicant summoned an ambulance. She was diagnosed with several bruises to her neck and situational neurosis. She told the medical personnel that a police officer had strangled her. In the presence of an ambulance paramedic, she telephoned the police. The Government stated that, during that call, she did not say that M. was a law-enforcement officer.
The second applicant disputed that assertion.

13. On the morning of 19 June 2008, a neuropathologist examined the second applicant, diagnosed her with concussion and bruising to her neck, and prescribed outpatient treatment.

14. On 28 June 2008, the Kalyninskyy police decided not to open criminal proceedings in connection with the second applicant’s complaint. The decision recorded that, at 1.05 a.m. on 19 June 2008, she had reported to the police that an acquaintance had struck her. It further stated that officers had been unable to question her because she had not been at home on any of the occasions when they had visited.

15. On 9 July 2008, the second applicant lodged a complaint concerning the incident with the Horlivka town prosecutor’s office (“the Horlivka prosecutor’s office”). She asked that the inquiry not be assigned to the Kalyninskyy district prosecutor’s office (“the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office”), alleging that one of its officials had been with M. when the events occurred and that M. had cited this circumstance as proof that he would enjoy impunity (see paragraph 8 above). She also maintained that the authorities had made no effort to contact them in order to obtain their account of the events.

16. On 15 July 2008, the Horlivka prosecutor’s office referred the complaint to the Kalyninskyy prosecutor.

17. On 25 July 2008, the second applicant provided the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office with a written description of the incident. That same day, the prosecutor’s office set aside the decision of 28 June 2008, observing that the inquiry had improperly been assigned to the Kalyninskyy police even though the complaint alleged that one of its officers had ill-treated her.

18. On 28 July 2008, disciplinary action was taken against the police officer who had been on duty during the night of 18 to 19 June 2008 for failing to follow up on the second applicant’s telephone call (see paragraph 12 above).

19. On 1 August 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office declined to institute criminal proceedings against M. under Article 365 § 2 of the Criminal Code, which concerned exceeding individual authority through the violent or degrading treatment of a victim. It concluded that M.’s conduct disclosed none of the constituent elements of that offence. The prosecutor acknowledged that the second applicant’s account was corroborated by statements from her husband and her friend. However, M. and the witnesses supporting his version denied that she had been ill-treated, leading the prosecutor to regard her allegation as unsubstantiated. The decision also noted that M. had been dressed in civilian clothes at the relevant time and had not been acting in his capacity as a law-enforcement officer. Finally, it stated that the second applicant had failed to comply with numerous summonses to attend for questioning.

20. On 4 August 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office quashed its decision of 1 August 2008 on the ground that it had been premature.
It observed, in particular, that the relevant facts had not all been established and that the second applicant had not undergone a forensic medical examination.

21. Such an examination was carried out on 14 August 2008 and revealed no visible injuries. After reviewing the second applicant’s medical records, the expert found that she had suffered a neck bruise and a craniocerebral injury resulting in concussion. The injuries, classified as insignificant, had been caused by “contact with blunt objects” at the time specified by her.

22. Later that day, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office again declined to institute criminal proceedings against M., finding that his conduct lacked the constituent elements of an offence. It relied primarily on witness statements indicating that M. had not ill-treated the second applicant. The prosecutor also noted that M. had not been acting in an official capacity and that the second applicant’s injuries were insignificant.

23. On 5 September 2008, a senior official from the same prosecutor’s office set aside that decision as premature. In particular, he found that a further forensic medical examination was necessary to verify the second applicant’s claim that she had been struck on the head with a mobile phone.

24. On 15 September 2008, the prosecutor ordered the additional examination to determine: (1) the precise manner in which the injuries could have been caused; (2) whether her head bore any marks potentially attributable to blows from a mobile phone; (3) whether the injuries could have occurred in the circumstances she described; and (4) when they had been sustained.

25. A forensic medical report was issued on 9 October 2008. It concluded that: (1) the craniocerebral injury and neck bruise had been caused by contact with blunt objects; (2) neither the physical examination nor the review of the medical records disclosed any head injuries—apparently meaning visible ones; (3) the injuries could have been inflicted in the circumstances alleged by the second applicant; and (4) the medical documentation indicated that they could have been sustained on 19 June 2008.

26. On 19 November 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office issued another decision refusing to open a criminal case concerning the second applicant’s complaints. Relying on the forensic medical reports and witness statements, the prosecutor concluded that her allegation had not been sufficiently substantiated.

27. On 20 April 2009, the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office (“the regional prosecutor’s office”) quashed that decision, finding it premature and based on an incomplete investigation.

28.
On 5 May 2009, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office once again declined to institute criminal proceedings against M. The decision stated that the forensic medical expert assessments of 14 August and 9 October 2008 contradicted the second applicant’s allegations. The prosecutor also observed that she had refused to provide her account during the supplementary investigation.

29. The second applicant contested that refusal before the Prosecutor General’s Office (“the PGO”) on at least three occasions: 20 July and 8 October 2009, and 4 January 2010. Her complaints were referred to the regional prosecutor’s office.

30. On 21 February 2010, the regional prosecutor’s office informed her in writing that it endorsed the decision taken by the lower-level prosecution authority. The letter further explained that she could challenge the decision in court if she wished.

B. Criminal proceedings against the first applicant

31. The first applicant had knee surgery in May 2008. Between 8 August and 2 September 2008, he received a follow-up course of outpatient treatment at Horlivka Hospital.

32. On a date that cannot be determined because it is illegible in the available copy, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office sent a summons to the first applicant at his registered address, which was his mother’s home, requiring him to appear at the prosecutor’s office on 5 September 2008. It remains uncertain whether the summons was issued as part of the criminal investigation concerning his wife’s complaints described above or in connection with the criminal proceedings subsequently brought against him.

33. On 10 September 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office instituted criminal proceedings against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of authority and forgery allegedly committed in January 2008 while he was acting as a law-enforcement officer. In particular, on 14 March 2008, the local court had notified the prosecutor of factual inaccuracies in a report concerning an administrative (minor) offence that the first applicant had prepared. He was suspected of falsifying that report.

34. That same day, the prosecutor’s office notified the first applicant of its decision by sending a letter to the address where he was actually residing with his wife, apart from their parents. The letter also instructed him to attend the prosecutor’s office to collect a copy of the decision and undergo questioning.

35. Also on 10 September 2008, the prosecutor directed the Kalyninskyy police to secure the first applicant’s attendance for investigative actions. On 12 September 2008, the police advised the investigator that they could not execute the order because the first applicant had been located neither at his usual place of residence nor at his mother’s apartment.
When the police also questioned his parents-in-law about his whereabouts, the third applicant “attacked them hysterically”, leading them to suspect that the first applicant might be hiding there.

36. On 13 September 2008, a judge of the Kalyninskyy Court ordered the first applicant’s arrest so that he could be brought before the court for consideration of the preventive measure to be applied to him.

37. The police placed the first applicant on the wanted list on 19 September 2008.

38. That same day, he informed the regional prosecutor’s office in writing that, after the incident involving his wife, the Kalyninskyy police had threatened him and his family with his dismissal, criminal prosecution, and even a fatal accident. He accordingly requested that the Kalyninskyy prosecutor withdraw from the case. He further stated that he was afraid even to attend the hospital because suspicious-looking individuals had been loitering near his home. He gave his mother’s address as his own.

39. On 22 September 2008, the investigator visited the home of the first applicant’s mother, the fourth applicant, and asked whether she knew his whereabouts. She replied that he had lived apart from her for approximately two years and that she did not know where he was.

40. On 24 September 2008, she forwarded to the investigator the first applicant’s request, dated 23 September 2008, that she be admitted to the proceedings as his representative and provided with a copy of the ruling of 10 September 2008 opening the criminal investigation against him. In support of the request, the first applicant explained that knee surgery had limited his mobility.

41. Responding to the investigator’s enquiry on 29 September 2008, the chief medical officer of Horlivka Hospital stated that the first applicant had last attended the hospital on 15 September 2008 and that the hospital administration did not know how to contact him.

42. On 1 October 2008, the Kalyninskyy police’s internal security unit advised the prosecutor in writing that it had information suggesting that the first applicant had been secretly visiting the flats of his parents and parents-in-law.

43. On 3 October 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor sent a letter to the first applicant at his mother’s address, explaining that she could not be admitted to the proceedings as his representative at such an early stage. The prosecutor also noted that the first applicant was wanted by the police and was required to appear in person to receive copies of the rulings concerning the institution of criminal proceedings against him and to undergo questioning.

44.
On 31 October 2008, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor again wrote to the first applicant, advising him that a further criminal case had been instituted against him that day on suspicion of abuse of power by a law-enforcement official and forgery in office. He was instructed to attend the prosecutor’s office to receive a copy of the relevant decision and to be questioned.

45. Between October 2008 and January 2010, eight more criminal cases were brought against the first applicant on further counts of abuse of office and suspicion of accepting bribes. It was alleged that he had committed those offences to present better performance results to his superiors and thereby qualify for additional remuneration and promotion. Notice of each decision was sent by letter to his mother’s address.

46. On 25 March 2009, the first applicant complained to the PGO that his repeated applications for the withdrawal of the Kalyninskyy prosecutor had received no response. He also claimed that he required protective measures as “a person who had reported a crime”. Finally, he asked for the decision placing him on the wanted list to be annulled “so that [he] could defend himself against the criminal charges and continue [his] medical treatment”.

47. By letters of 13 May and 26 June 2009, the regional prosecutor’s office informed the first applicant that his complaints had been rejected as unsubstantiated.

48. On 29 June 2009, the first applicant was arrested at the home where he resided with his wife. Relying on Articles 106 and 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“the CCP”; see paragraph 78 below), the investigator justified the arrest on the basis that the first applicant had been wanted since 19 September 2008, had obstructed efforts to establish the truth, and had committed serious criminal offences. The arrest report further recorded that he was suspected of offences under Articles 364 § 3 (abuse of power or office by a law-enforcement official), 366 § 1 (forgery in office), and 368 § 2 (bribe-taking) of the Criminal Code. The investigator prepared a report stating that the first applicant had been informed of his procedural rights, but he declined to sign it. He also refused to make any submissions concerning the charges.

49. On 30 June 2009, the Kalyninskyy Court extended the first applicant’s arrest to ten days because the case file contained insufficient information about his character. The ruling was not open to appeal.

50. On 3 July 2009, the same court ordered the first applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure, referring, without further elaboration, to “the seriousness and circumstances of the crimes committed and the character of [the first applicant]”.

51. The first applicant appealed on 6 July 2009, arguing that his detention on remand was unsupported by sufficient and relevant reasons.
He stated that he had been arrested at the home where he had resided for more than two years and had made no attempt to abscond. In his view, the justification for his pre-trial detention had been excessively formalistic: although the court had referred to his character, it had not identified any particular aspect of it that warranted detention as the most appropriate preventive measure.

52. On 21 July 2009, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Court of Appeal”) set aside the decision of 3 July 2009 and released the first applicant on an undertaking not to leave the town. It held that the first-instance court had failed to explain why the strictest preventive measure was necessary.

53. On 17 November 2011, the Kalyninskyy Court convicted the first applicant of fraud, abuse of power as a law-enforcement official, forgery resulting in grave consequences, and accepting bribes. It sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, barred him from holding positions within law-enforcement authorities, and ordered the confiscation of his personal property.

54. On 6 March 2012, the Court of Appeal set aside the judgment in respect of the forgery charge and returned that charge to the first-instance court for fresh consideration. It upheld the remainder of the judgment, while slightly reclassifying some charges and reducing the first applicant’s prison term to six years.

55. On 9 October 2012, the Kalyninskyy Court once again convicted the first applicant of forgery causing grave consequences and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. His final sentence remained six years because the more severe punishment absorbed the more lenient one. As no appeal was lodged, the judgment became final.

56. On 1 August 2013, the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters set aside the appellate court’s decision of 6 March 2012 insofar as it related to the first applicant’s conviction and remitted the case for a new appellate examination. The part of the decision ordering the case’s return to the first-instance court remained effective.

57. On 3 December 2013, the appellate court upheld the judgment of 17 November 2011 to the extent that it concerned the first applicant’s conviction for abuse of power as a law-enforcement official and his sentence of six years’ imprisonment. The remaining charges—apart from the charge addressed in the judgment of 9 October 2012 (see paragraph 55 above)—were slightly reclassified, and the penalty imposed on the first applicant in respect of that part was removed.

58. The case file contains no further information concerning the criminal proceedings against the first applicant.

C. Police searches of the third and fourth applicants’ flats and related events

59. On 10 September 2008, the investigator asked the Kalyninskyy Court to authorise a search of the first applicant’s registered residence, namely the fourth applicant’s flat.
The application stated that, on 27 January 2008, the first applicant had prepared a report concerning an administrative (minor) offence allegedly committed by a private individual through unauthorised street trading. It was later established that the report contained inaccurate information, prompting criminal proceedings against the first applicant on suspicion of abuse of power and forgery. The investigator believed that “some items and documents relevant for establishing the truth” in the case might be located at the first applicant’s residence.

60. In a final ruling of 11 September 2008, the Kalyninskyy Court granted the application. It repeated the investigator’s reasoning and description of the scope of the proposed search and relied on Article 177 of the CCP (see the references in paragraph 78 below).

61. On 12 September 2008, the investigator requested authorisation from the Kalyninskyy Court to search the second applicant’s registered residence, namely the third applicant’s flat. The application was worded identically to the one filed on 10 September 2008 (see paragraph 59 above).

62. Later that day, police officers knocked on the third applicant’s door. Although she and her husband were at home, they refused to allow the officers to enter.

63. The third applicant described the events of 12 September 2008 as follows. A group of nine or ten people, comprising police officers and several suspicious-looking individuals, arrived at her flat and violently pounded on the entrance door while demanding entry. Her husband went outside and asked them to produce a search warrant or some other document authorising their conduct, but they failed to do so. The police threatened to force their way in and to find grounds for bringing criminal proceedings against the entire family. They remained on the staircase and in the yard, shouting for approximately three hours.

64. The Government provided a different account. According to its version, three police officers visited the third applicant’s flat, informed her of the criminal proceedings against the first applicant, and asked where he was. When she and her husband declined to cooperate, the officers departed.

65. On 13 September 2008, the Kalyninskyy Court granted the investigator’s application of 12 September 2008 (see paragraph 61 above). The resulting ruling was identical to that issued on 11 September 2008 (see paragraph 60 above).

66. The police searched the third applicant’s flat later that same day. She alleged that they used an electric saw to break through the entrance door and did not show her a search warrant. Two attesting witnesses attended the search; according to the third applicant, both were acquaintances of the police officers.

67. The search report recorded that the operation took place between 5.20 p.m. and 7.04 p.m. During the search, the police seized several documents connected with the first applicant’s work.
In addition, the officers confiscated a mobile phone without a SIM card, along with its packaging. They also found and seized a packet that appeared to contain cannabis. The third applicant alleged that the police had planted it.

68. On 16 September 2008, the police searched the fourth applicant’s flat and seized several documents considered relevant to the criminal investigation concerning the first applicant. The first and fourth applicants maintained that the police themselves had brought those documents to the flat the day before. According to the fourth applicant, the officers, whom she knew as her son’s colleagues, had told her that an attack on their police station had left them without a secure place to keep the documents and that, in any event, the documents were intended to be handed over to the first applicant.

69. On 23 September 2008, an expert confirmed that the packet found in the third applicant’s flat on 13 September 2008 contained cannabis. However, on 2 October 2008, the Kalyninskyy police declined to institute criminal proceedings, concluding that it had been impossible to determine to whom the cannabis belonged.

70. On 7 October 2008, the Kalyninskyy Court granted a further request to search the first applicant’s registered address—the fourth applicant’s flat—because the investigator had received information suggesting that the first applicant might be hiding there.

71. Acting under the court order of 7 October 2008, the police searched the fourth applicant’s flat on 11 February 2009. The search report stated that the officers were looking for “items, valuables and documents related to the criminal activity of [the first applicant]”. Nothing relevant to the investigation was found.

72. The third and fourth applicants repeatedly asked the Kalyninskyy Court to provide copies of the decisions authorising the searches of their flats. The court’s president responded that the searches had been conducted in accordance with the CCP and that the law did not provide for copies of the relevant court decisions to be sent to them.

73. The third and fourth applicants also lodged repeated complaints with the prosecution authorities alleging that the searches had been unlawful. In particular, they claimed that the police officers had behaved rudely and intrusively, that the attesting witnesses had lacked independence, and that it had been unclear what the officers were actually seeking.

74. On 23 December 2008, the Horlivka prosecutor’s office declined to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers who had participated in the operation of 12 September and the searches conducted on 13 and 16 September 2008. Its decision relied on broadly worded reasoning that no breach of the law had occurred. The applicants appear not to have known about that decision.

75.
On 17 June 2009, after receiving complaints from the third and fourth applicants, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office declined to open criminal proceedings against the Kalyninskyy Court judge who had issued the rulings authorising searches of their flats.

76. The third applicant obtained access on 20 November 2009 to the Kalyninskyy Court’s ruling of 13 September 2008 (see paragraph 65 above). It remains unclear whether the fourth applicant was given access to the relevant rulings of 11 September and 7 October 2008 and, if so, when (see paragraphs 60 and 70 above).

D. Other facts

77. On 5 June 2006, a local heating company brought civil proceedings for recovery of a debt against the first and fourth applicants, whose registered domicile was at the same address. The domestic courts ruled against them. On 19 May 2008, the Supreme Court declined to consider their appeal on points of law because they had failed to pay the court fees.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

78. The pertinent provisions of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, in force at the relevant time, are set out in the following judgments: concerning the duty to investigate a crime, Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012); concerning the arrest of a suspect by the body of inquiry, Strogan v. Ukraine (no. 30198/11, § 45, 6 October 2016); and concerning searches of a home or other property, Vasylchuk v. Ukraine (no. 24402/07, §§ 28-30, 13 June 2013) and Bagiyeva v. Ukraine (no. 41085/05, §§ 39 and 40, 28 April 2016).

79. The relevant provisions of the 2003 Civil Code and the 1994 Compensation Act, in the versions applicable at the material time, are reproduced in Yaroshovets and Others v. Ukraine (nos. 74820/10 and four others, §§ 60 and 62, 3 December 2015).
