FOURTH SECTION

CASE OF BEKETOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 44436/09)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

19 February 2019

This judgment is final, but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Beketov v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Georges Ravarani, President,
Marko Bošnjak,
Péter Paczolay, judges,
and Andrea Tamietti, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 29 January 2019,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 44436/09) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Yuriy Oleksiyovych Beketov (“the applicant”), on 7 August 2009.

2. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms Olga Belyayeva, a lawyer practising in Dnipro. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

3. The applicant alleged under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been subjected to ill-treatment by the police, that no effective investigation into his complaints had been conducted, that the material conditions of his detention had been poor, that he had not been given food or water on hearing days, and that he had lacked access to adequate medical treatment while in detention. He also complained under Article 13 of the Convention that there had been no effective domestic remedies in respect of the above complaints.

4. On 5 June 2013, the application was communicated to the Government. The Government objected to the application being examined by a Committee. Having considered the Government’s objection, the Court dismisses it.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1970 and resides in Mankivka.

6. On 2 April 2007, the applicant underwent surgery for an umbilical hernia (exomphalos).

A. The applicant’s arrest, alleged ill-treatment by the police, and subsequent investigation

7. According to the applicant, on 9 February 2008, the police arrested him in Vinnytsya on suspicion of abduction and murder. That same day, he was transferred to Kyiv and detained in a cell at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station.

8. According to the Government, the applicant was arrested in Kyiv on 10 February 2008 on suspicion of abduction and murder and was placed that same day in a cell at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station.

9. According to the applicant, between 10 and 16 February 2008, he was beaten by police officers attempting to force him to confess to the abduction and murder.
In particular, Officer G., the first deputy head of the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy District Police Station, kicked the applicant in the face and abdomen, injuring the area where he had undergone surgery for an umbilical hernia (see paragraph 6 above). Following the beating, the applicant began suffering from constant abdominal pain.

10. On 16 February 2008, the applicant confessed to the murder and abduction and signed several undated documents. That same day, the police transferred him to the Kyiv Temporary Detention Facility (hereinafter “the ITT”). The ITT medical staff examined him and noted a bruise under his right eye.

11. According to the applicant, on 19 February 2008, the administration of the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (hereinafter “the SIZO”) refused to admit him because of his poor health. This was the second time the SIZO administration had refused him admission (see paragraph 39 below). The applicant was returned to the ITT, whose staff called an ambulance that transported him to the Kyiv Medical Emergency Hospital (“the Emergency Hospital”). According to a certificate issued by the Emergency Hospital, he remained there from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue”.

12. On 26 February 2008, the applicant was placed in the SIZO. He was examined by a SIZO doctor, who diagnosed him with a “post-operative condition” following his umbilical hernia operation in 2007.

13. On 16 May 2008, the applicant’s defence lawyer complained to the prosecutor’s office about the applicant’s ill-treatment by officers of the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy District Police Station between 10 and 16 February 2008.

14. On 24 June 2008, the investigator handling the criminal case against the applicant instructed a forensic medical expert to determine what injuries the applicant had sustained between 9 and 16 February 2008. The expert examined the applicant on 4 July 2008 and found no injuries that could have been inflicted during that period. The expert noted that fluid was leaking from the applicant’s navel and recommended that he be examined by a surgeon.

15. On 11 August 2008, the applicant’s lawyer lodged a petition with the prosecutor’s office stating that Officer G., the first deputy head of the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy District Police Station, had beaten the applicant.

16. On 16 September 2008, an investigating officer of the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office refused to institute criminal proceedings concerning the applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment, finding that there were no constituent elements of an offence. The investigating officer based that decision on statements from the investigator and the police officers involved in the initial investigative measures concerning the applicant.
Those questioned denied that the applicant had been subjected to ill-treatment.

17. On 29 September 2008 the applicant’s defence counsel lodged a complaint with the Kyiv City public prosecutor against the decision of 16 September 2008.

18. On 16 October 2008 the Kyiv City public prosecutor’s office found that there were no legal grounds for quashing the decision of 16 September 2008 (see paragraph 16 above).

19. On 18 November 2008 the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy District Court (hereinafter “the local court”) quashed the decision of 16 September 2008. It held that, during the inquiry, the investigating officer had failed to question the applicant and Officer G., the police officer identified by the applicant. The local court also found that the investigator had failed to add to the case file the results of the forensic examination of the applicant’s injuries to which his lawyer had referred in the application of 11 August 2008 (see paragraph 15 above).

20. On 19 December 2008, following an inquiry into the applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers on the grounds that there were no constituent elements of an offence. During that inquiry, Officer G. was questioned. He stated that he had not participated in the applicant’s arrest or in any other investigative activities concerning him.

21. On 1 December 2009 the local court quashed that decision and remitted the case file for a further inquiry. The local court noted that the investigating officer had failed to comply with the instructions set out in its decision of 18 November 2008 (see paragraph 19 above). In particular, the investigating officer had not questioned the applicant and had failed to substantiate his decision of 19 December 2008 (see paragraph 20 above).

22. On 30 January 2010, following a further inquiry into the applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers because there were no constituent elements of an offence. During that inquiry, Officers O., L., Psh. and S. were also questioned and denied having physically or psychologically coerced the applicant into confessing.

23. On 18 May 2010 the local court quashed that decision and remitted the case file for a further inquiry. The court noted that the investigating officer had not followed the instructions given in its decisions of 18 November 2008 and 1 December 2009 (see paragraphs 19 and 21 above).

24. On 23 August 2010, following a further inquiry into the applicant’s complaints, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against Officer G., who had allegedly ill-treated the applicant (see paragraph 9 above), because there were no constituent elements of an offence.
In the course of that further inquiry, the applicant was questioned and reiterated his account of the events concerning the ill-treatment. The investigating officer concluded that there was no evidence establishing Officer G.’s involvement in those events.

25. On 5 December 2010 and 30 March 2011, the applicant lodged petitions with the Prosecutor General of Ukraine in which he reiterated, inter alia, that he had been ill-treated by Officer G. and that the investigation into his complaints in that regard had been ineffective.

26. On 17 January 2011, a superior prosecutor quashed the decision of 23 August 2010 (see paragraph 24 above) and remitted the case file for further inquiry.

27. On 12 April 2011, following a further inquiry into the applicant’s complaints, the investigating officer refused to institute criminal proceedings against Officer G. on the grounds that there were no constituent elements of an offence. During that inquiry, the investigating officer questioned Officer Ovs., who had been on duty at the time of the applicant’s arrest. The officer denied that there had been blood on the applicant’s body in the stomach area. The investigating officer further noted that the applicant had not lodged any complaints either while at the police station or after his transfer to the Kyiv SIZO. On 30 March 2012, the local court quashed that decision and remitted the case file for further inquiry.

28. On 28 June 2012, following a further inquiry, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against Officer G. on the grounds that there were no constituent elements of an offence. The investigating officer concluded that it was impossible to question the individuals who had been at the police station with the applicant in February 2008. On an unspecified date, that decision was quashed and the case file was remitted for further inquiry.

29. On 7 September 2012, following a further inquiry, the investigating officer refused to institute criminal proceedings against Officer G. on the grounds that there were no constituent elements of an offence. On 17 September 2012, a superior prosecutor quashed that decision and remitted the case file for further inquiry.

30. On 27 September 2012, following a further inquiry into the applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment, the prosecutor’s office refused to institute criminal proceedings against Officer G. on the grounds that there were no constituent elements of an offence. During the inquiry, Inspector Ag., who had been on duty at the relevant time, was questioned and stated that he did not remember whether he had seen the applicant.

31. On 7 May 2013, the local court quashed the decision of 27 September 2012 (see paragraph 30 above) and remitted the case file for further inquiry.
The court held that the investigating officer had failed to question and/or properly analyse the statements of: the people who had been detained with the applicant in the cell at the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyy district police station in February 2008; the ITT and SIZO staff concerning the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment and the SIZO’s alleged refusal to admit him after the court had ordered his arrest; the emergency-service medical personnel who had provided the applicant with medical assistance in February 2008; the surgeon from Buchanska Prison Hospital who had operated on the applicant on 20 January 2010; and the police officers who had arrested the applicant in Vinnytsya on 9 February 2008.

32. On 21 May 2013, information concerning the physical injuries inflicted on the applicant was entered in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations, and the corresponding pre-trial investigation was opened in accordance with the provisions of the new Code of Criminal Procedure.

33. On 27 June 2013, following the pre-trial investigation, the prosecutor’s office decided to terminate the criminal proceedings on the ground that there were no constituent elements of an offence.

34. On 4 July 2013, a superior prosecutor quashed that decision, finding that the investigating officer had failed to follow the instructions issued by the local court in its decision of 7 May 2013 (see paragraph 31 above).

35. On 5 July 2013, the investigating officer questioned S., who had been detained with the applicant in the ITT cell. The witness stated that he did not recall the applicant being beaten.

36. On 29 August 2013, following the investigation, the prosecutor’s office decided to terminate the criminal proceedings because there were no constituent elements of an offence. On 18 February 2014, the local court upheld that decision.

37. On 15 April 2014, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal quashed the investigating officer’s decision of 29 August 2013 and the local court’s decision of 18 February 2014 (see paragraph 36 above), and remitted the case file for further pre-trial investigation. The court held that the investigating officer had failed to comply with the instructions issued by the local court in its decision of 7 May 2013 (see paragraph 31 above), and in particular had failed to establish the origin of the injuries sustained by the applicant in February 2008.

38. The parties provided no information about subsequent developments in the case.

B. The applicant’s detention and the medical assistance provided to him

39. Meanwhile, on 13 February 2008, the local court had ordered the applicant’s detention on remand and his transfer to the SIZO. As noted above (paragraph 11), according to the applicant, the SIZO administration refused to admit him because of his poor state of health. The police then took the applicant back to the Shevchenkivskyy district police station.

40.
On 16 February 2008 the applicant was placed in the ІТТ (see paragraph 10 above). A medical examination revealed a bruise under his right eye, which was classified as a minor physical injury.

41. Following a deterioration in the applicant’s health, the ITT staff called an ambulance, which took him to the Emergency Hospital. According to a certificate issued by the hospital, the applicant remained there from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue” (see paragraph 11 above).

42. On 26 February 2008 the applicant was transferred from the ITT to the SIZO. As noted in paragraph 12 above, on arrival he was examined by a SIZO doctor, who diagnosed a post-operative condition following his umbilical hernia operation in 2007 (see paragraph 6 above).

43. According to the applicant, on 29 February and 5, 10, and 16 March 2008 he complained to the SIZO staff of persistent abdominal pain. The SIZO doctors examined him and determined that the pain was caused by a post-operative navel fistula. On 21 March 2008 he was examined by a SIZO general practitioner, who administered an anaesthetic. Between 13 May and 2 July 2008 the applicant stayed in the SIZO medical unit and received the following treatment: lactulose, aloe, fluconazole, ascorbic acid, and Captopril. His navel injury was treated with hydrogen peroxide, vitamins В1 and В6, Thiotriazolin, Levomekol (an ointment), Riboxin, and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Following treatment, he was discharged and returned to a cell.

44. On 13 June 2008 the applicant was examined by a surgeon from the Emergency Hospital, who diagnosed a suture sinus (a type of wound complication) resulting from the umbilical hernia operation. He recommended applying a bandage to the applicant’s navel area, as well as treatment with antiseptics and antibiotics and elective surgery. The surgeon noted that the applicant did not require urgent inpatient treatment, and he was returned to the SIZO the same day.

45. On 22 October 2008 the applicant was examined at the SIZO by another surgeon, who noted that he did not require inpatient treatment or urgent surgery in connection with his navel fistula.

46. From 26 November to 15 December 2008 the applicant underwent examinations at the Emergency Hospital in connection with his persistent abdominal pain. He was diagnosed with omphalitis (inflammation of the navel and surrounding area) and a suture sinus following the 2007 umbilical hernia operation (see paragraph 6 above). He was also diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, myocardial cardiosclerosis, category II hypertension, hypertonic crises on 27 November and 1 and 4 December 2008, category I cardiac failure with cephalgia phenomena, asthenoneurotic syndrome, discirculatory encephalopathy, and chronic acute cholecystopancreatitis.
The applicant received the following treatment: antispasmodic drugs, hepatoprotectors, antibiotics, biocatalysts, antihypertensive drugs (inhibitors, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta-blockers and diuretics), and bandages to his umbilical area. On 5 December 2008 and 30 January 2009, the surgeon from the Emergency Hospital recommended that the applicant undergo elective surgery on the fistula and continue receiving care and symptomatic treatment from the surgeon, neuropathologist and cardiologist at the SIZO medical unit.

47. Between 9 February and 10 April 2009, the applicant stayed in the SIZO medical unit. He was diagnosed with and treated for omphalitis, a urachal cyst, a navel fistula and suture sinus, ischemic heart disease, encephalopathy, and an exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis. The treatment consisted of oral medication and the application of antiseptic to the applicant’s navel area.

48. On 6 and 7 May 2009, the applicant was examined by the SIZO cardiologist, neuropathologist and surgeon. He was diagnosed with a urachal cyst, a ligature fistula and category II hypertension. He was prescribed outpatient treatment for his symptoms.

49. On 31 July 2009, the SIZO surgeon recommended that the applicant undergo an operation on the fistula at a public hospital.

50. On 4 August 2009, the SIZO informed the applicant’s wife that the operation to remove his navel fistula would be arranged as soon as the court handling the criminal case against him authorised his transfer to an outside medical facility.

51. On 15 August 2009, the applicant was examined by the SIZO therapist. He was diagnosed with a urachal cyst, a ligature fistula and category II hypertension. It was recommended that he continue the prescribed outpatient treatment.

52. On 24 September 2009, during hearings at the Kyiv City Court of Appeal, an ambulance was called for the applicant. The ambulance team suspected that he had peritonitis and recommended his urgent hospitalisation. According to the ambulance team’s report, the person in charge of the prison escort refused to permit his hospitalisation. After the hearing, the applicant was returned to the SIZO medical unit. He remained there until 8 October 2009 and was treated for his navel fistula and inflammation of the navel. He received oral medication, and antiseptic was applied to his navel area.

53. On 29 September 2009, the applicant was transported to the Emergency Hospital because of constant abdominal pain. A duty surgeon and a supervising surgeon diagnosed him with omphalitis accompanied by a small amount of purulent discharge. The doctors did not prescribe emergency surgery, but recommended applying bandages with Levomekol and Ceftriakson. On the same day, the applicant was returned to the SIZO.

54. Between 24 September and 8 October 2009, the applicant remained in the SIZO medical unit, where he received the necessary treatment.
He was discharged with a recommendation that his health continue to be monitored by the therapist and surgeon of the SIZO medical unit.

55. On 30 October 2009 the Court granted the applicant’s request under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and indicated to the Government that he should be placed in a medical facility where he could receive appropriate treatment.

56. On 4 November 2009 the SIZO administration offered to place the applicant in the Emergency Hospital. He refused the proposal, explaining that he did not trust the hospital’s doctors. An ambulance team called for the applicant did not transfer him to the Emergency Hospital, but recommended that he consult a surgeon.

57. On the same day V., one of the applicant’s lawyers, asked the SIZO administration to transfer him to Public Hospital no. 6 for inpatient treatment of his fistula. Another of the applicant’s lawyers, A., requested that the SIZO place him in a private hospital. The applicant agreed to be admitted to that hospital. Ultimately, he was not placed in either hospital.

58. On the same day the SIZO staff called an ambulance for the applicant. The ambulance team found that he did not require urgent hospitalisation and recommended that he continue outpatient treatment for his fistula. The applicant was then placed in the SIZO medical unit.

59. On 9 and 16 November 2009, in response to requests from the applicant’s lawyers concerning his hospitalisation, the SIZO administration stated that it was not competent to decide on his placement in an outside medical facility and suggested that the lawyers submit their requests to the court dealing with his case.

60. On 10 November 2009 the applicant was taken to Public Hospital no. 9 for examination. The doctors recommended surgery on his navel fistula. On the same day, he was returned to the SIZO.

61. On 24 November 2009 an ambulance doctor examined the applicant in the hearing room of the Kyiv City Court of Appeal because of constant abdominal pain. The applicant received treatment for his symptoms.

62. On 26 November 2009 an ambulance doctor examined the applicant in the SIZO in connection with his constant abdominal pain and found that he did not require urgent hospitalisation.

63. On 27 November 2009 a surgeon from the Emergency Hospital examined the applicant and recommended that he continue outpatient treatment for his navel fistula.

64. On 4 December 2009, in view of additional information from the respondent Government concerning the applicant’s health and the treatment provided to him in the SIZO, the Court decided to lift the interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court (see paragraph 55 above).

65.
In December 2009 the applicant submitted several requests to the SIZO administration, asking to be transferred to any medical facility because of the serious deterioration in his health.

66. On 25 December 2009 the SIZO administration informed the applicant’s lawyer that the applicant did not need urgent hospitalisation in an outside medical facility and was receiving appropriate medical treatment for his fistula in the SIZO.

67. On 18 January 2010 the applicant was admitted to the surgery department of Buchanska Prison Hospital and diagnosed with a ligature fistula in the umbilical area.

68. On 20 January 2010 the applicant underwent surgery to remove the navel fistula. On 26 February 2010 he was discharged and returned to the SIZO.

69. The Government provided no information or supporting documents concerning the treatment given to the applicant after his discharge from the hospital. They stated that the medical records for the period from 26 February 2010 onwards had been lost.

C. Material conditions of the applicant’s detention in the SIZO

70. According to the applicant, the cells in which he was detained in the SIZO lacked natural light, while the electric lighting was dim and remained on constantly. The inmates slept on beds without mattresses or bed linen.

71. He further stated that the food was inadequate in both quality and quantity, and that prisoners were given tea and bread in the morning, porridge in the afternoon, and boiled water in the evening.

D. Provision of food and water to the applicant on hearing days

72. According to the applicant, he was not given food or water on hearing days, as Ukrainian legislation made no provision for this. It was not possible to obtain meals or drinks at the courts hearing his case.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

73. The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1960 relating to pre-investigation enquiries are set out in Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).

74. The Code of Criminal Procedure of 28 December 1960 was repealed with effect from 19 November 2012, when the new Code of Criminal Procedure of 2012 entered into force. The new Code abolished the pre-investigation enquiry stage. The relevant provisions of the new Code are set out in Nagorskiy v. Ukraine ((dec.), no. 37794/14, § 38, 4 February 2016).

III. RELEVANT MATERIAL OF THE COUNCIL OF EUROPE

75. The relevant Council of Europe and other material establishing standards for detention conditions, together with reports on conditions of detention in Ukraine, can be found in Davydov and Others v. Ukraine (nos. 17674/02 and 39081/02, §§ 101-108, 1 July 2010) and Gorbatenko v. Ukraine (no. 25209/06, §§ 97-100, 28 November 2013).

39. In the meantime, on 13 February 2008, the local court had ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody and transferred to the SIZO. 70. The applicant stated that the SIZO cells in which he was detained had no natural light, while the electric lighting was weak and remained switched on continuously. Detainees slept on beds that had neither mattresses nor bed linen.

72. The applicant alleged that he was given neither food nor water on days when hearings took place because Ukrainian law contained no provision requiring this. Nor was he able to obtain food or drink at the courts hearing his case.

73. The provisions of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure governing pre-investigation enquiries are set out in Kaverzin v. Ukraine (no. 23893/03, § 45, 15 May 2012).

74. The Code of Criminal Procedure of 28 December 1960 ceased to have effect on 19 November 2012, when the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure entered into force. 75. The pertinent Council of Europe and other materials setting standards for detention conditions, as well as reports addressing conditions of detention in Ukraine, are cited in Davydov and Others v. Ukraine (nos. 17674/02 and 39081/02, §§ 101-108, 1 July 2010) and Gorbatenko v. Ukraine (no. 25209/06, §§ 97-100, 28 November 2013).
