FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF KORBAN v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 26744/16)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

4 July 2019

FINAL

09/12/2019

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Korban v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Angelika Nußberger, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
André Potocki,
Síofra O’Leary,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer,
Lado Chanturia, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 28 May 2019,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 26744/16) against Ukraine lodged with the Court on 27 April 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Gennadiy Olegovych Korban (“the applicant”).

2. The applicant was represented by Mr N.S. Kulchytskyy, a lawyer practising in Kyiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

3. On 21 November 2016, at the applicant’s request, the President of the Section decided to give priority to the case under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court.

4. The applicant complained, in particular, under Article 3 of the Convention, about the conditions in which he had been transported on 2 November 2015; his participation in court hearings from 26 to 28 December 2015 despite being weak following a coronary angioplasty; and his confinement in a metal cage during the court hearings of 13, 22 and 25 January 2016. He also alleged a violation of his rights under Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 of the Convention. Under Article 18 of the Convention, taken together with Article 5, he complained that he had been deprived of his liberty for ulterior motives, namely political reasons. Lastly, he complained that public statements by high-ranking State officials concerning the criminal proceedings against him had breached his right to the presumption of innocence guaranteed by Article 6 § 2 of the Convention.

5. On 5 March 2018 the Government were given notice of the above complaints, and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6. The applicant was born in 1970 and resides in Dnipro (known as Dnipropetrovsk before June 2016).

A. The applicant’s involvement in Ukrainian politics

7. From 19 March 2014 until 24 March 2015, the applicant served as Deputy Head and Chief of Staff of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration (“the Regional Administration”). According to his account, following a deterioration in relations between the President of Ukraine and the then Head of the Regional Administration, the latter resigned together with his political team, including the applicant.

8.
On 15 September 2014 the applicant was awarded an “Order for Courage” by the President of Ukraine “for his commitment, active civic stance and high professionalism in carrying out his official duties”.

9. On 12 July 2015 the applicant became the leader of a new political party, the Ukrainian Union of Patriots (“UKROP” – Українське об’єднання патріотів — “УКРОП”), which strongly criticised those in power generally and President Poroshenko in particular.

10. On 26 July 2015 the applicant, as leader of UKROP, stood in the mid-term parliamentary elections in Chernigiv. Having secured 14.76% of the vote, he lost to the candidate from the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko” (35.90%).

11. In the local elections of 25 October 2015, the UKROP party received 7.43% of the nationwide vote and finished fourth (the three leading parties were the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko” (19.52%), “Batkivshchyna” (12.23%), and the “Opposition Bloc” (10.54%)). The applicant stood for the post of Kyiv mayor but lost the election, having obtained 2.61% of the vote.

B. Criminal proceedings against the applicant

12. On 14 August 2014 the Head of the State Agency of Land Resources (“the Agency”), R., was held against his will in the applicant’s office. The applicant demanded that R. appoint a particular person as head of the Agency’s regional department, after dismissing the incumbent from that post. R. reported the incident to the police.

13. On 15 August 2014 criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant and another person in connection with the above-mentioned events, on suspicion of kidnapping a public official and aggravated car theft (R.’s car had been moved without his consent). The relevant entry was made in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations (proceedings no. 12014040670002852, hereinafter “proceedings no. 52”).

14. On 25 February 2015 further criminal proceedings were brought against the applicant and another person. They were suspected of having organised the kidnapping, on that same day, of V., an official of the Dnipropetrovsk City Council, with the aim of forcing the acting head of that authority, Ro., to resign.

15. On 7 August 2015 another set of criminal proceedings was initiated against the applicant on suspicion of embezzling funds from a charitable organisation established in May 2014 to collect voluntary contributions in support of Ukrainian soldiers fighting in eastern Ukraine.

16. On 30 September 2015 the Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Election Commission received telephone threats of violence from someone who identified himself using the applicant’s name. On 1 October 2015 criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant in that connection, on suspicion of interfering with the work of an electoral officer.

17.
On 31 October 2015, an investigator from the Prosecutor General’s Office (“the PGO”) arrested the applicant and informed him that he was suspected of criminal offences under Article 191 § 5 (embezzlement of funds of a charity organisation by an organised group), Article 255 § 1 (creation of a criminal organisation), Article 289 § 2 (aggravated car theft) and Article 349 (two counts of taking a public official hostage) of the Criminal Code. It appears from the relevant notification that all the charges against the applicant were joined to proceedings no. 52 (see paragraph 13 above).

18. The circumstances surrounding the applicant’s arrest were as follows. At 8.40 a.m. on 31 October 2015, the PGO investigator, accompanied by a special forces unit, arrived at the applicant’s home in Dnipropetrovsk and demanded that he open the door, but the applicant refused. After forcing open the entrance door, the police entered the applicant’s flat. The applicant, who was inside behind the door, protested that the officers’ conduct failed to respect the privacy of his home. The police arrested him and took him to Kyiv (the reasons for the decision to handle the case in Kyiv are unknown).

19. At 8.37 p.m. that same day, the investigator drew up a report on the applicant’s arrest. According to the report, the applicant had been arrested under Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“the CCP”) (see paragraph 96 below) on suspicion of committing criminal offences under Articles 191 § 5, 255 § 1, 289 § 2 and 349 of the Criminal Code. The report template set out the following two pre-printed grounds for arrest: (1) where the person was caught in flagrante delicto; or (2) where, immediately after the criminal offence, eyewitnesses, including the victim, identified the person as the offender, or where this was indicated by the totality of obvious signs on that person’s body or clothing or at the scene of the events. The investigator underlined the second option as the grounds for the applicant’s arrest. The space in the report template for recording “specific facts and data” was left blank.

20. On 2 November 2015, the investigator applied to the investigating judge of the Chernigiv Novozavodskyy District Court (“the Novozavodskyy Court”) for the applicant to be placed in pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial (the case was heard in Chernigiv because the PGO had assigned the investigation to the Chernigiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office). The investigator referred to the seriousness of the charges against the applicant, which carried a potential sentence of up to fifteen years’ imprisonment. It was also noted that the applicant had friendly relations with officials from law-enforcement, judicial and other authorities.
The investigator therefore considered that the applicant might use his connections to influence witnesses, victims or other suspects in the proceedings, or to obstruct the investigation by destroying evidence, for example.

21. On the same day, the applicant was transported from Kyiv to Chernigiv (150 km) in a regular minibus. According to him, he was kept in the vehicle from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m., both during the journey and while waiting upon arrival in Chernigiv, without food or water and without access to a toilet. According to the Government, relying on information from the PGO, “the applicant had been provided with water and access to sanitary facilities at his requests”.

22. Later on 2 November 2015, the applicant complained to the Kyiv Pecherskyy District Court (“the Pecherskyy Court”, located near the PGO headquarters) that his arrest had been arbitrary and unlawful. In particular, he noted that the legal preconditions for arrest without a judicial warrant had not been satisfied in his case.

23. On the same date, another set of criminal proceedings was brought against the applicant on suspicion of aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer. Specifically, during the night of 30 to 31 October 2015, the applicant, together with several other persons, had allegedly obstructed the activities of a member of the Dnipropetrovsk City Election Commission “by violence and threats of violence and had demonstrated power by the presence of armed persons and military equipment near the electoral commission’s premises”. Those proceedings were joined to proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above).

24. At 8.40 a.m. on 3 November 2015, the time-limit for arrest without a judicial decision (seventy-two hours) expired, and the applicant was released in the hearing room of the Novozavodskyy Court. However, at 8.42 a.m., before he had even been able to leave the room, he was immediately re-arrested by decision of the investigator on suspicion of having committed a criminal offence under Article 157 § 3 of the Criminal Code (aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer). The applicant was immediately taken to Kyiv, where the investigator drew up a report on his arrest. As in the previous arrest report of 31 October 2015 (see paragraph 19 above), the investigator underlined the pre-printed phrase “where, immediately after the criminal offence, eyewitnesses including the victim pointed at the person as the offender, or this was suggested by the totality of obvious indications on that person’s body or clothes or at the site of the events” as the basis for the applicant’s re-arrest.

25. On the same day, the PGO decided that its Main Investigation Department would take over the investigation from the Chernigiv Prosecutor’s Office.

26. In addition to his complaint concerning his arrest (see paragraph 22 above), the applicant complained to the Pecherskyy Court that his re-arrest on 3 November 2015 had also been unlawful.

27.
On 4 November 2015 the PGO investigator applied to the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court for the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial. The new application reproduced the text of the one submitted earlier, on 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), adding a reference to the charge of interference with the work of an electoral officer (see paragraphs 23 and 24 above).

28. On the same date, in the light of the above-mentioned developments, the investigating judge of the Novozavodskyy Court decided to leave unexamined the investigator’s application of 2 November 2015 concerning the applicant’s pre-trial detention (see paragraph 20 above).

29. On 5 November 2015 the Pecherskyy Court decided to examine jointly the investigator’s application and the applicant’s complaints of 2 and 3 November 2015 concerning the lawfulness of his arrest and re-arrest (see paragraphs 22, 26 and 27 above).

30. On 6 November 2015 the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the investigator’s application of 4 November 2005 in part and ordered the applicant’s twenty-four-hour house arrest, with an obligation to wear an electronic tracking device, as a preventive measure for an initial period ending on 31 December 2015. She referred, in particular, to the gravity of the charges against the applicant and the seriousness of the potential penalties. At the same time, the ruling noted that the applicant had a permanent place of residence, elderly parents and three minor children. The judge also took into account that the applicant was the leader of a political party and had received numerous awards, including the presidential “Order for Courage” on 15 September 2014. It was further observed that he had positive character references and that numerous members of parliament had offered their personal surety as a guarantee that he would comply with his procedural obligations.

31. As to the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged unlawfulness of his arrest on 31 October 2015, the investigating judge concluded that, at the time of the impugned event, the applicant had been outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Pecherskyy Court and that she therefore lacked competence to rule on the matter.

32. In so far as the applicant had raised the same complaint regarding his re-arrest on 3 November 2015, the judge held, without giving further details, that it had complied with Article 208 of the CCP.

33. Both the applicant and the prosecutor appealed against the above ruling. The prosecutor maintained that the applicant’s pre-trial detention was the most appropriate preventive measure. The applicant’s lawyer argued that the investigating judge had failed to provide a single reason justifying such a restrictive preventive measure as twenty-four-hour house arrest.

34. On 1 December 2015 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals and upheld the ruling of 6 November 2015.
It agreed with the investigating judge that there were no grounds for applying pre-trial detention in the circumstances of the applicant’s case and that house arrest was sufficient. At the same time, the appellate court found that the case file contained material confirming the existence of a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed several serious criminal offences. The appellate court’s ruling also noted that the lawfulness of the applicant’s arrest had been duly examined by the first-instance court.

35. On 7 December 2015 an ambulance was called for the applicant, and he was admitted to the “Family Medicine Clinic”, a private hospital in Dnipropetrovsk. He received inpatient treatment for a hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris until 14 December 2015.

36. On 8 December 2015 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Police Department sent the PGO a report concerning the electronic tracking device which the applicant had been required to wear as part of his house arrest. It was noted that the device had generated thirty-eight alerts, thirty-five of which could be explained by “the technical imperfection of the device, the architectural particularities of the building, as well as the presence of a lift in the suspect’s flat”. Of the remaining alerts, two were explained by the applicant’s transportation to court hearings and one by his hospitalisation (see paragraph 35 above).

37. On 25 December 2015 the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office, to which the PGO had assigned the investigation, applied to the investigating judge of Kyiv Dniprovskyy District Court (“the Dniprovskyy Court”) to replace the applicant’s house arrest with pre-trial detention. In addition to the reasons put forward in the initial application of 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), the investigator submitted that, while under house arrest, the applicant had been avoiding various procedural measures by “abusing his right to medical assistance ... and continuously staying in private medical institutions”. The investigator noted that the applicant’s father was the founder of the “Family Medicine Clinic”. In the investigator’s view, the objectivity of any conclusions reached by that hospital’s staff was therefore open to question. The police had recorded thirty-eight alerts from the applicant’s electronic tracking device, which could suggest that he had been attempting to tamper with it. Moreover, according to the investigator, one of the witnesses had stated that the applicant, through his lawyers, had threatened him in an effort to make him change his statements in the applicant’s favour.

38.
38. On 28 December 2015 the Dniprovskyy Court granted the investigator’s application and ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention for an initial period ending on 25 February 2016 (for a detailed account of the events from 25 to 28 December 2015, see paragraphs 60-79 below). The ruling was limited to the operative part and a statement that the investigating judge required more time to prepare the reasoning.

39. It appears from certain documents in the case file that, immediately after the hearing on 28 December 2015, the applicant was placed in detention in the pre-trial investigation unit of the Security Service of Ukraine. At the same time, other documents suggest that he continued to receive inpatient medical treatment at the Amosov Institute (see paragraph 60 below) until 15 January 2016.

40. On 29 December 2015 the Dniprovskyy Court issued the full text of the ruling. In justifying the applicant’s remand in custody, the investigating judge repeated the investigator’s arguments concerning the existence of a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had been involved in a number of criminal offences, the seriousness of those offences, and the applicant’s friendly relations with officials of law-enforcement, judicial and other authorities (see paragraph 20 above). The judge further held as follows:

“... following the judicial examination [of the application], the investigating judge considers it established that the accused failed to comply with the obligations [inherent in] house arrest, which had [previously] been applied to him.

The prosecution’s arguments that none of the more lenient preventive measures ... would be capable of preventing the risks indicated in the application are well-founded.”

41. The applicant appealed. He argued that the above decision had been unlawful and arbitrary and that no alternative, less intrusive measures had been considered. He also complained that, although he was receiving inpatient medical treatment following an operation and there had been no urgency to examine the investigator’s application, the judge had held excessively lengthy hearings, including at weekends and during the night.

42. The applicant was held in a metal cage during the court hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016. The cage was subsequently replaced by a transparent box.

43. On 10 February 2016 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal partly allowed the applicant’s appeal: it quashed the ruling of 28 December 2015 and delivered a new ruling, again replacing the applicant’s house arrest with pre-trial detention, but this time until 23 February 2016. The appellate court upheld the findings and reasoning of the first-instance court. It considered, however, that the starting date of the applicant’s detention should be calculated from 26 December 2015 (see paragraph 66 below).

44. On 17 February 2016 the Dniprovskyy Court extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention until 15 April 2016.
It noted that the investigation had not yet been completed, while the seriousness of the charges against the applicant and the risks already established continued to justify his detention.

45. The applicant appealed. He argued, in particular, that the investigating judge had not considered any alternative, less intrusive preventive measures. Moreover, the applicant observed that not a single investigative measure had been carried out since he had been placed in pre-trial detention.

46. On 10 March 2016 the criminal charges against the applicant were slightly amended: namely, the charge of aggravated car theft (see paragraph 13 above) was removed from the indictment.

47. On the same date the applicant signed a friendly settlement agreement with R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). The applicant pleaded guilty to R.’s kidnapping on 14 August 2014 and expressed remorse. The parties considered the following penalty in respect of the applicant to be justified: three years’ restriction of liberty (that is, detention in a semi-open prison near his place of residence), suspended for a probation period of one year and six months. That agreement would later be approved by a court (see paragraph 51 below).

48. Still on 10 March 2016, the charge concerning R.’s kidnapping was severed into a separate set of proceedings. The other charges remained within proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13, 17 and 23 above).

49. On 15 March 2016 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decision of 17 February 2016 extending his pre-trial detention (see paragraph 44 above). According to the appellate court’s ruling, the fact that the investigating judge had decided that pre-trial detention was the most appropriate preventive measure did not mean that no alternative measures had been considered. As to the applicant’s submission that no investigative measures had been carried out for a long time, the Court of Appeal stated that this circumstance provided no grounds for quashing the investigating judge’s decision to extend the applicant’s detention. It observed that the applicant was free to complain of any omissions by the prosecution if he wished to do so.

50. On the same date the applicant applied to the Dniprovskyy Court for the preventive measure in respect of him to be changed from pre-trial detention to twenty-four-hour house arrest, on the ground that his elderly mother was seriously ill and required constant care. The investigating judge examined and granted that request on the same day. He noted that this new argument had been considered neither in the earlier decision of 17 February 2016 nor in the appellate court’s ruling of 15 March 2016 (see paragraphs 44 and 49 above). Accordingly, the Dniprovskyy Court placed the applicant under twenty-four-hour house arrest, without an electronic tracking device, until 15 April 2016. That decision was upheld on appeal on 14 April 2016.

51.
On 21 March 2016, the Dnipropetrovsk Kirovskyy District Court approved the friendly settlement agreement between the applicant and R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). Consequently, it found the applicant guilty of kidnapping R. following a prior conspiracy and sentenced him to three years’ restriction of liberty, suspended for a probationary period of one year and six months.

52. On 14 April 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court extended the applicant’s house arrest until 30 April 2016 in the context of the criminal proceedings against him, which remained ongoing (see paragraph 48 above). The ruling noted that a considerable number of investigative measures remained to be carried out and that the seriousness of the charges against the applicant and the risks identified earlier continued to justify his detention.

53. On 29 April 2016, the house arrest was extended again, this time until 27 June 2016.

54. On 7 June 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court replaced the applicant’s house arrest with an undertaking not to abscond, following his request for permission to undergo medical treatment in Israel. The new preventive measure remained applicable until 27 June 2016. On the same day, the investigating judge granted the applicant leave to travel to Israel.

55. On 16 June 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court extended the applicant’s undertaking not to abscond until 10 August 2016.

56. On 5 August 2016, the criminal charges under Article 255 § 1 (creation of a criminal organisation), Article 349 (taking a public official hostage), Article 191 § 5 (embezzlement of funds of a charity organisation by an organised group), and Article 157 § 3 of the Criminal Code (aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer) were severed into a separate set of proceedings, registered under no. 42016000000002043 in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations (hereinafter “no. 43”). No further information is available concerning that procedural step. Nor is it clear what charges, if any, remained pending in proceedings no. 52 (see, in particular, paragraph 48 above and paragraph 59 below).

57. On 11 August 2016, the Pecherskyy Court refused the PGO’s request to further extend the preventive measure imposed on the applicant (the undertaking not to abscond). The investigating judge observed that the measure had expired on 10 August 2016 and could therefore no longer be extended.

58. On 11 September 2017, the PGO discontinued criminal proceedings no. 43 against the applicant (see paragraph 56 above) for lack of evidence of his guilt. Specifically, the prosecution concluded that there was insufficient evidence to charge the applicant with creating and managing a criminal organisation, taking the public official V. hostage, embezzling funds from a charity organisation as part of an organised group, and aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer.

59.
The Government stated in their observations, without providing any details, that as of April 2018 criminal case no. 52, in which the applicant had “no procedural status”, remained ongoing. Without disputing that submission as such, the applicant noted that all charges against him had been dropped.

C. Events of 25 to 28 December 2015

1. 25 December 2015

60. The applicant was admitted to the Amosov National Institute of Cardiovascular Surgery (“the Amosov Institute”) for a medical assessment.

61. At approximately 2 p.m. the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute informed the media that the applicant’s examination would last about two hours. At around 3 p.m. a spokesperson for the UKROP party informed the public that an investigator was waiting for the applicant near the hospital ward in order to serve him with a copy of the application for a change of preventive measure (pre-trial detention instead of house arrest – see paragraph 37 above).

62. A panel of doctors examined the applicant and diagnosed ischemic heart disease, hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris. They concluded that an urgent coronary stent angioplasty (a percutaneous coronary procedure to reopen clogged arteries, combined with the insertion of a small wire-mesh tube called a stent to help keep the artery open) was necessary. The operation was performed immediately, and two stents were inserted into the applicant’s heart arteries.

63. By approximately 9 p.m. the operation had been completed, and the applicant was transferred to an intensive-care ward.

64. At 10.15 p.m., after the applicant had been transferred from intensive care to an ordinary ward, the investigator attempted to serve him with a copy of the application for a change of preventive measure. The applicant refused to accept it, citing his poor health, the late hour and the absence of his lawyers.

2. 26 December 2015

65. At 9.03 a.m. the investigating judge of the Dniprovskyy Court opened a hearing to examine the investigator’s application. The applicant’s lawyers informed the court that their client had undergone heart surgery and was receiving post-operative inpatient care at the Amosov Institute. They stated that the treatment would continue for approximately seven to ten days. The investigator, for his part, maintained that nothing prevented the applicant from appearing before the court.

66. At 11.47 a.m. the judge adjourned the hearing until 3 p.m. and ordered the applicant’s detention to secure his compulsory attendance.

67. At 3.07 p.m. the applicant was brought to the court premises in a wheelchair and with a medication infusion device. He was seated next to a metal cage in the hearing room. Doctors from the Amosov Institute and the emergency medical service were present and monitored his condition. At 3.30 p.m.
A doctor from the emergency medical service examined the applicant and reported that he had a rapid pulse and high blood pressure.

68. At 5.21 p.m. the investigating judge granted a request by the applicant’s lawyers for an immediate forensic medical examination of their client to establish his state of health and determine whether he was fit to participate in court hearings. Consequently, the hearing was adjourned until 8.30 p.m., and the applicant was taken back to the Amosov Institute.

69. At 8.30 p.m. the investigating judge resumed the hearing in the applicant’s absence. According to his lawyers, he was in an ambulance at that time because his health had worsened. Referring to that fact, as well as to the absence of any evidence that the court’s ruling on the applicant’s forensic medical examination had been implemented, the judge adjourned the hearing until 9.30 a.m. on 27 December 2015.

70. On 26 December 2015 the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute replied to an enquiry from the applicant’s lawyer, stating that the applicant required post-operative inpatient treatment and monitoring by a cardiologist. The doctor said that it was outside his competence to determine whether the applicant was fit to participate in court hearings. On the same date, the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute and his two deputies replied to a similar enquiry from the investigator, stating that the applicant’s health was satisfactory and that transferring him to the courtroom would not be “life-threatening”. At the same time, the doctors stated that they bore no responsibility for the health of their inpatients outside the Institute.

3. 27 December (Sunday) and 28 December 2015

71. According to media reports – journalists had been continuously present in the corridors of the Amosov Institute – at about 1.30 a.m. a group of prosecution officials attempted to enter the applicant’s ward. As it was locked, they read aloud to the applicant the ruling on his forensic medical examination and the summons for the court hearing on the morning of 27 December 2015. Two hospital attendants were required to sign a report to that effect as attesting witnesses.

72. Early on the morning of 27 December 2015 the investigator again went to the applicant’s ward. This time, he read the above-mentioned documents aloud directly to the applicant. The applicant replied that he would prefer not to leave the hospital before undergoing a forensic medical examination.

73. From about 8 to 9 a.m. on 27 December 2015 the investigator questioned three senior doctors at the Amosov Institute about the applicant’s health. The doctors answered affirmatively when asked whether the applicant could be moved in a wheelchair and accompanied by doctors without any risk to his life or health.

74. At 9.38 a.m. on 27 December 2015 the judge resumed the hearing. The applicant was absent.
The investigator referred to the questioning of the Amosov Institute doctors earlier that morning and requested that the applicant be forcibly brought before the court. The applicant’s lawyers objected, noting that their client had not undergone a forensic medical examination.

75. At 12.34 p.m. the judge adjourned the hearing until 3 p.m. that day and ordered the applicant’s detention to secure his compulsory attendance.

76. Early in the afternoon of 27 December 2015, the applicant underwent a medical examination lasting about half an hour by two senior doctors from the Amosov Institute, with the participation of a forensic medical expert and in the presence of the investigator and the applicant’s lawyer. In response to the investigator’s question whether the applicant could participate in court hearings in a wheelchair and accompanied by doctors without any risk to his life or health, the doctors replied in the affirmative. The forensic medical expert stated that he would refrain from answering that question. The details of the examination were recorded in “a medical examination report” prepared by the investigator and signed by all participants.

77. At 4.23 p.m. that day, the applicant was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair. The investigating judge ordered several short adjournments so that the applicant could receive medical care.

78. The courtroom was extremely crowded. At one point during the evening, clashes broke out in the public gallery. At about 9 p.m. on 27 December 2015, the judge decided to continue the hearing in camera.

79. The hearing continued until 1.35 p.m. on 28 December 2015. The mass media reported it as the longest court hearing ever held in Ukraine, having lasted about thirty hours in total.

D. Press statements concerning the criminal proceedings against the applicant

80. The applicant’s arrest and criminal prosecution attracted considerable media attention. The defence and the prosecution, as well as several politicians and non-governmental organisations, made press statements in that connection.

1. Press statements by the prosecution and other public officials

81. The applicant referred to the following statements made by high-ranking officials.

82. On 1 November 2015, the assistant to the Prosecutor General stated at a press briefing:

“Through the fault of these organisers [pointing at the screen showing the applicant’s photo], who created this criminal group, many people might come under investigation or become suspects today and later stand trial. I ask all those who have understood what happened to please come to the Security Service or the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine, share information with us, and paragraph 2 of Article 255 of the Criminal Code will be applied (that is to say, those who report a crime will be absolved of criminal liability).”

83.
The applicant also referred to another statement by the above-mentioned official: “This must be stopped. Fake stamps, creation of virtually private armies, fund-raising on that basis, kidnappings, possessing a private surveillance vehicle by these volunteers ...”84. Moreover, on 1 November 2015 the President of Ukraine stated during a televised interview: “The position is as follows. Nobody will stop on Korban. Nobody is immune to criminal liability for corruption-related offences. This concerns both the new team in power ... and the old team ... I underline that Ukraine will soon hear new names of those to face charges.”85. On 2 November 2015 the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine said during a press statement: “Why was that fund needed for the leaders of the organised criminal group, which included at the time, of course, Gennadiy Olegovych [the applicant], a respectful gentleman, together with [others]? ... This was a criminal group specialising in kidnappings ...”86. On 29 December 2015 the investigator stated at a briefing: “Please show the following slide. This is [a bakery plant], which has also been illegally seized by the criminal group under the leadership of Korban Gennadiy Olegovych.”87. On 22 January 2016 the assistant to the Prosecutor General told the press: “... the criminal group under Korban’s leadership, which, according to the information already provided to you, has been involved in a number of criminal activities, such as kidnappings, the embezzlement of funds, illegal arms handling and so on ...; While the entire country was consolidating forces in volunteer organisations and patriotic movements in order to help the Ukrainian military in the East ..., unfortunately, the criminal group, with Gennadiy Korban in the lead, was involved in the most grievous crimes, using as a cover patriotic or volunteering slogans; ... In fact, this criminal group under the leadership of Gennadiy Korban was financed in parallel with certain political projects.”

2. Press statements by Ukrainian political parties

88. On 31 October and 1 November 2015, three parliamentary political parties issued public statements concerning the applicant’s arrest on 31 October 2015.

89. The “Batkivshchyna” political party, led by Yuliya Tymoshenko (which remained in the ruling coalition until February 2016), stated as follows:

The All-Ukrainian Association ‘Batkivshchyna’ is concerned about the arrest of Gennadiy Korban, the leader of the ‘UKROP’ party

“‘Batkivshchyna’ is not a political ally of the ‘UKROP’ party. We do not share views on various matters.
Moreover, we strongly oppose mixing business with politics. However, given that those who shot the Maidan protesters and were involved in large-scale corruption under Yanukovych have still not been punished, the arrest of the leader of the ‘UKROP’ party, which entered several regional councils following the local elections, appears to constitute selective justice and political repression. We have information that searches are being conducted at [the offices of] members of parliament from the ‘UKROP’ party, which is inadmissible and unlawful. Such actions against a political force raise many questions in society that remain unanswered. In this context, ‘Batkivshchyna’ demands that the Prosecutor General and the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine attend the plenary session of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine on Tuesday. 90. The “Samopomich” political party led by Andriy Sadovyy (which belonged to the ruling coalition at the relevant time and left it in February 2016) stated as follows:

Return to political repression leads to collapse of the state – ‘Samopomich’

“The ‘Samopomich Union’ political party believes that the searches of the office of member of parliament Borys Filatov and the arrest of a fellow party member constitute an attempt to return Ukraine to the era of Viktor Yanukovych’s political repression. 91. The “Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko” (which had been part of the ruling coalition until September 2015) published the following statement on its website:

Lozovyy: Korban’s arrest signals the regime’s agony

“The People’s Deputy of Ukraine and deputy leader of the opposition faction of the ‘Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko’, Andriy Lozovyy, informed the ‘112’ [television] channel by telephone about the continuation of political repression in Ukraine.

3. Other public statements and newspaper articles

92. On 1 November 2015, the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group published an article on its website entitled “Ukrainian political party leader detained”. It stated, in particular:

“There may indeed be valid grounds for bringing criminal charges against Gennady Korban and for doing so specifically now. 93. The applicant also cited several articles in Ukrainian newspapers suggesting that his arrest had been politically motivated.

II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. Constitution of Ukraine 1996

94.
Article 29, which is relevant to the present case, reads as follows:

“Every person has the right to freedom and personal inviolability.

No one shall be arrested or held in custody except pursuant to a reasoned court decision and only on the grounds and in accordance with a procedure established by law.

Where there is an urgent need to prevent or stop a crime, bodies authorised by law may hold a person in custody as a temporary preventive measure, the reasonable grounds for which shall be reviewed by a court within seventy-two hours. The detained person shall be released immediately if, within seventy-two hours of detention, he or she has not been provided with a reasoned court decision concerning their being held in custody. ...

Everyone who has been detained has the right to challenge his or her detention before a court at any time. ...”

B. Criminal Code 2001

95. The relevant provisions may be summarised as follows:

- Article 157 § 3 provides that interference with the work of an electoral officer involving coercion, violence or threats of violence, committed pursuant to a conspiracy by a group of persons or by a public official using his or her position, is punishable by three to seven years’ imprisonment, together with disqualification from holding certain posts or carrying out certain activities for two to three years;

- Article 191 § 5 provides for seven to twelve years’ imprisonment, with confiscation of property and disqualification from holding certain posts or carrying out certain activities for up to three years, as punishment for embezzlement involving particularly large amounts or committed by an organised group;

- Article 255 § 1 provides for five to twelve years’ imprisonment as punishment for the creation of a criminal organisation;

- under Article 289 § 2, car theft committed, in particular, pursuant to a conspiracy or involving violence or threats of violence, is punishable by five to eight years’ imprisonment, with or without confiscation of property;

- Article 349 punishes the taking hostage of a public official by eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment.

C. Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

96. The relevant provisions state:

Article 176. General provisions on preventive measures

“1. Preventive measures are:

(1) a personal undertaking;

(2) a personal warranty;

(3) bail;

(4) house arrest; and

(5) pre-trial detention.

2. Arrest [without a court order] (затримання) is a provisional preventive measure that may be applied on the grounds and in accordance with the procedure set out in this Code.

3. The investigating judge or the court shall dismiss an application for a preventive measure if the investigator or prosecutor has not shown that there are sufficient grounds to believe that none of the more lenient preventive measures would be adequate to prevent the identified risk or risks. The most lenient preventive measure is a personal undertaking, while the most severe is pre-trial detention.

4.
Preventive measures shall be imposed: during the investigation – by the investigating judge at the request of a prosecutor, or at the request of an investigator approved by a prosecutor; and during the trial – by the court at the prosecutor’s request.”

Article 177. Purpose and grounds for applying preventive measures

“1. The purpose of a preventive measure is to ensure that a suspect or accused complies with his or her procedural obligations, as well as to prevent attempts to:

(1) abscond from the pre-trial investigation authorities and/or the court;

(2) destroy, conceal or damage any objects or documents essential for establishing the circumstances of the criminal offence;

(3) unlawfully influence the victim, witnesses, other suspects or accused persons, the expert or specialist ...;

(4) obstruct the criminal proceedings in any other manner;

(5) commit another criminal offence or continue the criminal offence of which he or she is suspected or accused.

2. A preventive measure shall be applied where there is a reasonable suspicion that the person has committed a criminal offence and where risks exist that give the investigating judge or the court sufficient grounds to believe that the suspect, accused or convicted person could carry out the actions specified in paragraph one of this Article ...”

Article 181. House arrest

“1. House arrest consists of prohibiting the suspect or accused from leaving his or her place of residence twenty-four hours a day or during specified hours.

2. House arrest may be applied to a person suspected or accused of committing a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment.

...

5. National police officers may visit the suspect or accused under house arrest at his or her domicile in order to monitor his or her behaviour. They may request verbal or written explanations concerning the suspect’s or accused’s compliance with his or her obligations. Electronic tracking devices may be used.

6. The period of validity of a ruling by the investigating judge placing a person under house arrest shall not exceed two months. Where necessary, the duration of house arrest may be extended at the prosecutor’s request within the limits of the pre-trial investigation .... The total duration of house arrest shall not exceed six months. Thereafter, the ruling applying that preventive measure shall be deemed to have expired, and the house arrest measure shall be considered lifted.”

Article 208. Arrest by a competent official [without a court order]

“1.
[In the absence of a court order, a] competent official may arrest (затримати) a person suspected of committing a crime punishable by imprisonment only in the following cases: (1) if the person has been caught while committing or attempting to commit a crime; or (2) if, immediately after a criminal offence, the statements of an eyewitness, including the victim, or the totality of obvious signs on the person’s body or clothing, or at the scene, indicate that the person has just committed an offence ...

4. A competent official who has made the arrest shall immediately inform the arrested person, in a language he or she understands, of the grounds for the arrest and the crime he or she is suspected of committing. The official shall also explain the arrested person’s rights: to legal representation; to receive medical assistance; to make statements or remain silent; to inform [third] persons ... of his or her arrest and whereabouts; to challenge the grounds for the arrest; and the other procedural rights set out in this Code.

5. A report shall be prepared concerning an individual’s arrest and shall contain, [in particular,] the following information: the place, date and exact time (hour and minute) of the arrest ...; the grounds for the arrest; the results of the personal search; any requests, statements or complaints made by the arrested person; and a comprehensive list of his or her procedural rights and duties. The arrest report shall be signed by the official who prepared it and by the arrested person. A copy shall be served on the arrested person immediately after his or her signature has been obtained ...”

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), convening as a Chamber consisting of:

Angelika Nußberger, President,
