PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 26744/16, brought against Ukraine before the Court on 27 April 2016 by Mr Gennadiy Olegovych Korban (“the applicant”), a Ukrainian national, under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. Mr N.S. Kulchytskyy, a lawyer practising in Kyiv, acted for the applicant. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

3. At the applicant’s request, the President of the Section decided on 21 November 2016 to accord the case priority under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court.

4. In particular, relying on Article 3 of the Convention, the applicant challenged the conditions in which he had been transported on 2 November 2015; his attendance at hearings between 26 and 28 December 2015 despite being in a weakened condition following coronary angioplasty; and his placement in a metal cage during hearings held on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016. He further alleged breaches of Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 of the Convention. Invoking Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5, he maintained that his deprivation of liberty had pursued ulterior, specifically political, purposes. Finally, he contended that public remarks concerning the criminal proceedings against him, made by senior State officials, had infringed the presumption of innocence secured by Article 6 § 2 of the Convention.

5. The Government were notified of those complaints on 5 March 2018. Under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, the balance of the application was declared inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6. Born in 1970, the applicant resides in Dnipro, which was known as Dnipropetrovsk until June 2016.

A. The applicant’s participation in Ukrainian political life

7. Between 19 March 2014 and 24 March 2015, the applicant served as Deputy Head and Chief of Staff of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration (“the Regional Administration”). According to his account, relations between the President of Ukraine and the Regional Administration’s then Head deteriorated, prompting the latter to resign along with his political team, of which the applicant was a member.

8.
On 15 September 2014, the President of Ukraine conferred the “Order for Courage” on the applicant in recognition of “his commitment, active civic stance and high professionalism in carrying out his official duties”.

9. On 12 July 2015, the applicant assumed the leadership of a newly established political party, the Ukrainian Union of Patriots (“UKROP” – Українське об’єднання патріотів — “УКРОП”). The party was strongly critical of the authorities generally and of President Poroshenko in particular.

10. In his capacity as UKROP leader, the applicant stood in the mid-term parliamentary elections held in Chernigiv on 26 July 2015. He secured 14.76% of the vote and was defeated by the candidate representing the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko”, who received 35.90%.

11. In the local elections on 25 October 2015, UKROP obtained 7.43% of the nationwide vote, placing fourth. The three parties ahead of it were the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko”, with 19.52%; “Batkivshchyna”, with 12.23%; and the “Opposition Bloc”, with 10.54%. The applicant also stood for election as mayor of Kyiv but was unsuccessful, receiving 2.61% of the vote.

B. Criminal proceedings brought against the applicant

12. On 14 August 2014, R., the Head of the State Agency of Land Resources (“the Agency”), was detained against his will in the applicant’s office. The applicant demanded that R. dismiss the incumbent head of the Agency’s regional department and appoint a specified individual in that person’s place. R. subsequently reported the incident to the police.

13. Criminal proceedings concerning those events were opened against the applicant and another person on 15 August 2014. They were suspected of kidnapping a public official and aggravated theft of a motor vehicle, as R.’s car had been moved without his permission. The case was entered in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations as proceedings no. 12014040670002852 (“proceedings no. 52”).

14. A further set of criminal proceedings was initiated against the applicant and another person on 25 February 2015. They were suspected of organising, on that date, the abduction of V., an official of the Dnipropetrovsk City Council, in order to compel Ro., the authority’s acting head, to resign.

15. Additional criminal proceedings were commenced against the applicant on 7 August 2015 on suspicion that he had embezzled money belonging to a charitable organisation. The organisation had been established in May 2014 to collect voluntary donations in support of Ukrainian soldiers fighting in eastern Ukraine.

16. On 30 September 2015, the Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Election Commission received telephone threats of violence from a caller who identified himself using the applicant’s name. Criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant on 1 October 2015 in connection with that incident, on suspicion of interfering with the work of an electoral officer.

17.
On 31 October 2015, an investigator from the Prosecutor General’s Office (“PGO”) arrested the applicant and informed him that he was suspected of offences under Article 191 § 5 of the Criminal Code (embezzlement of a charitable organisation’s funds by an organised group), Article 255 § 1 (creation of a criminal organisation), Article 289 § 2 (aggravated car theft), and Article 349 (two counts of taking a public official hostage). The relevant notification appears to show that all charges against the applicant were incorporated into proceedings no. 52 (see paragraph 13 above).

18. The applicant’s arrest took place in the following circumstances. At 8.40 a.m. on 31 October 2015, a PGO investigator, accompanied by a special forces unit, arrived at the applicant’s home in Dnipropetrovsk and ordered him to open the door. After he refused, the police forced open the entrance and entered the flat. Standing inside behind the door, the applicant objected that the officers’ actions infringed the privacy of his home. He was then arrested and transported to Kyiv; the reasons for handling the case there remain unknown.

19. At 8.37 p.m. that day, the investigator prepared an arrest report. It stated that the applicant had been apprehended pursuant to Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”) (see paragraph 96 below) on suspicion of committing offences under Articles 191 § 5, 255 § 1, 289 § 2, and 349 of the Criminal Code. The standard form listed two pre-printed grounds for arrest: (1) the person had been caught in flagrante delicto; or (2) immediately after the offence, eyewitnesses, including the victim, had identified the person as the offender, or the combined obvious signs found on the person’s body or clothing or at the scene pointed to that conclusion. The investigator underlined the second option as the basis for the applicant’s arrest but left blank the section designated for setting out “specific facts and data”.

20. On 2 November 2015, the investigator requested that the investigating judge of the Novozavodskyy District Court of Chernigiv (“the Novozavodskyy Court”) order the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial. The matter was heard in Chernigiv because the PGO had assigned the investigation to the Chernigiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office. In support of the application, the investigator cited the seriousness of the charges, which carried a potential sentence of up to fifteen years’ imprisonment, and noted that the applicant maintained friendly relations with officials in law-enforcement agencies, the judiciary, and other public authorities.
21. The investigator accordingly concluded that the applicant might exploit his connections to exert pressure on witnesses, victims, or other suspects in the proceedings, or otherwise obstruct the investigation, including by destroying evidence. Later that day, the applicant was taken approximately 150 km from Kyiv to Chernigiv in an ordinary minibus. He stated that he had remained inside the vehicle from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m., both during the journey and while waiting after reaching Chernigiv, and had been given neither food nor water nor access to a toilet. The Government, relying on information supplied by the PGO, maintained that “the applicant had been provided with water and access to sanitary facilities at his requests”.

22. Also on 2 November 2015, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Kyiv Pecherskyy District Court (“the Pecherskyy Court”), located near the PGO headquarters, alleging that his arrest had been arbitrary and unlawful. In particular, he argued that the statutory requirements permitting arrest without a judicial warrant had not been satisfied in his case.

23. On that same date, a separate set of criminal proceedings was opened against the applicant on suspicion of aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer. More specifically, it was alleged that, during the night of 30 to 31 October 2015, the applicant and several other individuals had obstructed a member of the Dnipropetrovsk City Election Commission “by violence and threats of violence and had demonstrated power by the presence of armed persons and military equipment near the electoral commission’s premises”. The new proceedings were subsequently joined to proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above).

24. At 8.40 a.m. on 3 November 2015, the seventy-two-hour maximum period of detention without a judicial decision came to an end, and the applicant was released in the hearing room of the Novozavodskyy Court. Two minutes later, at 8.42 a.m., before he had even been able to leave the room, he was immediately arrested again pursuant to an investigator’s decision. The new arrest concerned suspicion that he had committed an offence under Article 157 § 3 of the Criminal Code, namely aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer. He was promptly transported to Kyiv, where the investigator prepared an arrest report. As in the earlier report dated 31 October 2015 (see paragraph 19 above), the investigator indicated the grounds for the renewed arrest by underlining the pre-printed wording: “where, immediately after the criminal offence, eyewitnesses including the victim pointed at the person as the offender, or this was suggested by the totality of obvious indications on that person’s body or clothes or at the site of the events”.

25. That day, the PGO also decided to transfer responsibility for the investigation from the Chernigiv Prosecutor’s Office to its own Main Investigation Department.

26. In addition to challenging his initial arrest (see paragraph 22 above), the applicant lodged a further complaint with the Pecherskyy Court, contending that his re-arrest on 3 November 2015 had likewise been unlawful.
On 4 November 2015, the PGO investigator asked the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court to order the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial. The request repeated the application previously lodged on 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), but additionally referred to the charge of interfering with the work of an electoral officer (see paragraphs 23 and 24 above).

28. In view of those developments, the investigating judge of the Novozavodskyy Court decided that same day to leave unexamined the investigator’s application of 2 November 2015 concerning the applicant’s pre-trial detention (see paragraph 20 above).

29. On 5 November 2015, the Pecherskyy Court decided to consider together the investigator’s application and the applicant’s complaints of 2 and 3 November 2015 challenging the lawfulness of his arrest and subsequent re-arrest (see paragraphs 22, 26 and 27 above).

30. On 6 November 2015, the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the investigator’s application of 4 November 2005 in part. As an initial preventive measure, she placed the applicant under twenty-four-hour house arrest until 31 December 2015 and required him to wear an electronic tracking device. In reaching that decision, she referred in particular to the gravity of the charges and the severity of the possible penalties. The ruling also noted that the applicant had a permanent residence, elderly parents and three minor children. The judge further took account of his position as the leader of a political party, his numerous awards—including the presidential “Order for Courage”, conferred on 15 September 2014—and his positive character references. She also noted that numerous members of parliament had offered personal surety to guarantee his compliance with his procedural obligations.

31. Addressing the applicant’s allegation that his arrest on 31 October 2015 had been unlawful, the investigating judge found that, when the contested event occurred, he had been outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Pecherskyy Court. She therefore concluded that she lacked competence to determine the issue.

32. As to the identical complaint concerning the applicant’s re-arrest on 3 November 2015, the judge held, without further explanation, that it had complied with Article 208 of the CCP.

33. The prosecutor and the applicant both appealed against that ruling. The prosecutor maintained that pre-trial detention was the most appropriate preventive measure, while the applicant’s lawyer submitted that the investigating judge had given no reasons whatsoever to justify a measure as restrictive as twenty-four-hour house arrest.

34. On 1 December 2015, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals and upheld the ruling of 6 November 2015.
The appellate court concurred with the investigating judge that, in the circumstances of the applicant’s case, pre-trial detention was unwarranted and house arrest constituted a sufficient measure. Nevertheless, it found that the case file contained material supporting a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed several serious criminal offences. Its ruling also noted that the first-instance court had properly examined the lawfulness of the applicant’s arrest.

35. On 7 December 2015, an ambulance was summoned for the applicant, who was admitted to the “Family Medicine Clinic”, a private hospital in Dnipropetrovsk. He remained there as an inpatient until 14 December 2015, receiving treatment for a hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris.

36. On 8 December 2015, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Police Department submitted to the PGO a report concerning the electronic tracking device that the applicant was required to wear while under house arrest. The device had generated thirty-eight alerts. Thirty-five were attributed to “the technical imperfection of the device, the architectural particularities of the building, as well as the presence of a lift in the suspect’s flat”. Of the other three alerts, two occurred when the applicant was transported to attend court hearings, while the third was caused by his hospitalisation (see paragraph 35 above).

37. On 25 December 2015, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office, which had been assigned the investigation by the PGO, asked an investigating judge of the Kyiv Dniprovskyy District Court (“the Dniprovskyy Court”) to replace the applicant’s house arrest with pre-trial detention. Alongside the grounds set out in the original application of 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), the investigator alleged that, while under house arrest, the applicant had avoided various procedural measures by “abusing his right to medical assistance ... and continuously staying in private medical institutions”. The investigator further noted that the applicant’s father had founded the “Family Medicine Clinic” and, for that reason, questioned the objectivity of any conclusions reached by its staff. It was also argued that the thirty-eight alerts recorded by the police from the applicant’s electronic tracking device could suggest that he had attempted to tamper with it. In addition, according to the investigator, a witness had claimed that the applicant, acting through his lawyers, had threatened him in an effort to make him alter his statements in the applicant’s favour.

38.
On 28 December 2015, the Dniprovskyy Court granted the investigator’s application and remanded the applicant in pre-trial custody, initially until 25 February 2016 (a detailed account of the events between 25 and 28 December 2015 is provided in paragraphs 60-79 below). The ruling contained only its operative provisions, together with an indication that the investigating judge required additional time to prepare the reasons.

39. Certain documents in the case file indicate that, immediately after the hearing on 28 December 2015, the applicant was detained in the pre-trial investigation unit of the Security Service of Ukraine. Other records, however, suggest that he remained an inpatient at the Amosov Institute, where he was receiving medical treatment (see paragraph 60 below), until 15 January 2016.

40. The Dniprovskyy Court issued the full version of its ruling on 29 December 2015. In support of the decision to place the applicant in custody, the investigating judge repeated the investigator’s submissions concerning the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had participated in several criminal offences, the seriousness of those offences, and his friendly ties with officials in law-enforcement bodies, the judiciary and other public authorities (see paragraph 20 above). The judge further found that the judicial examination of the application had established that the applicant had failed to comply with the obligations arising from the house-arrest measure previously imposed on him. The judge also accepted as well-founded the prosecution’s contention that none of the less restrictive preventive measures would adequately address the risks identified in the application.

41. The applicant appealed, arguing that the decision was unlawful and arbitrary and that the court had failed to consider alternative, less intrusive measures. He further complained that, despite the absence of any urgency in examining the investigator’s application and the fact that he was receiving inpatient treatment following surgery, the judge had held excessively lengthy hearings, including at night and on weekends.

42. During the court hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016, the applicant was confined in a metal cage. The cage was later replaced with a transparent box.

43. On 10 February 2016, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal partly upheld the applicant’s appeal. It set aside the ruling of 28 December 2015 and issued a new decision which likewise replaced house arrest with pre-trial detention, although only until 23 February 2016. While endorsing the findings and reasoning of the first-instance court, the appellate court held that the applicant’s detention period had to be calculated as beginning on 26 December 2015 (see paragraph 66 below).

44. On 17 February 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged the applicant’s pre-trial detention until 15 April 2016.
It observed that the investigation remained ongoing and that, in view of the seriousness of the charges against the applicant and the risks already identified, his continued detention was still warranted.

45. The applicant lodged an appeal, arguing in particular that the investigating judge had failed to consider any less restrictive alternative preventive measures. He also pointed out that no investigative steps whatsoever had been taken since his placement in pre-trial detention.

46. On 10 March 2016 the charges against the applicant were amended slightly, with the aggravated car-theft charge (see paragraph 13 above) being removed from the indictment.

47. That same day, the applicant concluded a friendly-settlement agreement with R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). He admitted his guilt in relation to R.’s kidnapping on 14 August 2014 and expressed remorse. The parties agreed that an appropriate sentence would be three years’ restriction of liberty—that is, detention in a semi-open prison close to his place of residence—suspended subject to a probationary period of one year and six months. The agreement was subsequently to be approved by a court (see paragraph 51 below).

48. Also on 10 March 2016, the charge relating to R.’s kidnapping was separated into distinct proceedings. The remaining charges continued to be examined in proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13, 17 and 23 above).

49. On 15 March 2016 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decision of 17 February 2016 prolonging his pre-trial detention (see paragraph 44 above). According to its ruling, the investigating judge’s conclusion that pre-trial detention was the most suitable preventive measure did not imply that alternative measures had not been considered. Addressing the applicant’s argument that no investigative action had been taken for a prolonged period, the Court of Appeal held that this did not constitute a basis for setting aside the investigating judge’s decision to extend his detention. It added that the applicant remained free to complain about any omissions on the part of the prosecution if he so wished.

50. On the same day, the applicant asked the Dniprovskyy Court to replace his pre-trial detention with round-the-clock house arrest, explaining that his elderly mother was seriously ill and needed constant care. The investigating judge considered and granted the application that day. He noted that this new argument had been addressed neither in the earlier decision of 17 February 2016 nor in the appellate ruling of 15 March 2016 (see paragraphs 44 and 49 above). The Dniprovskyy Court therefore ordered the applicant’s placement under twenty-four-hour house arrest, without electronic monitoring, until 15 April 2016. That decision was upheld on appeal on 14 April 2016.

51.
On 21 March 2016, the Dnipropetrovsk Kirovskyy District Court approved the friendly settlement reached between the applicant and R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). It consequently convicted the applicant of kidnapping R. pursuant to a prior conspiracy and imposed a three-year restriction of liberty, suspended subject to a probationary period of one year and six months.

52. On 14 April 2016, in the still-pending criminal proceedings against the applicant (see paragraph 48 above), the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged his house arrest until 30 April 2016. The court observed that numerous investigative measures remained outstanding and held that both the seriousness of the charges and the previously identified risks continued to warrant that restriction.

53. The applicant’s house arrest was extended again on 29 April 2016, this time until 27 June 2016.

54. On 7 June 2016, following the applicant’s request for permission to receive medical treatment in Israel, the Dniprovskyy Court replaced house arrest with an undertaking not to abscond. That preventive measure was to remain in force until 27 June 2016. On the same date, the investigating judge granted the applicant leave to travel to Israel.

55. On 16 June 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged the undertaking not to abscond until 10 August 2016.

56. On 5 August 2016, the charges under Article 255 § 1 (creation of a criminal organisation), Article 349 (taking a public official hostage), Article 191 § 5 (embezzlement of funds belonging to a charity organisation by an organised group), and Article 157 § 3 of the Criminal Code (aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer) were separated into distinct proceedings. Those proceedings were entered in the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations under no. 42016000000002043 (“proceedings no. 43”). No additional information is available concerning that procedural decision. It is likewise unclear whether any charges remained pending in proceedings no. 52 and, if so, which ones (see, in particular, paragraph 48 above and paragraph 59 below).

57. On 11 August 2016, the Pecherskyy Court rejected the PGO’s application for a further extension of the preventive measure imposed on the applicant, namely the undertaking not to abscond. The investigating judge reasoned that the measure had expired on 10 August 2016 and was therefore no longer capable of being extended.

58. On 11 September 2017, the PGO terminated proceedings no. 43 against the applicant (see paragraph 56 above) because there was insufficient evidence of his guilt. More specifically, the prosecution found that the evidence did not suffice to charge him with creating and directing a criminal organisation, taking the public official V. hostage, embezzling a charity organisation’s funds as part of an organised group, or aggravated interference with an electoral officer’s work.

59.
In their observations, the Government stated, without giving any further information, that criminal case no. 52 remained pending as of April 2018 and that the applicant had “no procedural status” in those proceedings. Although the applicant did not dispute that assertion as such, he emphasised that all charges against him had been dropped.

C. Events from 25 to 28 December 2015

1. 25 December 2015

60. The applicant was admitted to the Amosov National Institute of Cardiovascular Surgery (“the Amosov Institute”) for a medical examination.

61. At approximately 2 p.m., the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute told the media that the applicant’s examination was expected to last about two hours. At around 3 p.m., a spokesperson for the UKROP party announced that an investigator was waiting outside the applicant’s hospital ward to serve him with a copy of the application seeking to replace house arrest with pre-trial detention (see paragraph 37 above).

62. After examining the applicant, a panel of doctors diagnosed ischemic heart disease, hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris. They concluded that he urgently required coronary stent angioplasty, a percutaneous coronary procedure in which blocked arteries are reopened and a small wire-mesh tube known as a stent is inserted to keep the artery open. The operation was performed immediately, and two stents were inserted into the applicant’s coronary arteries.

63. The procedure was completed by about 9 p.m., after which the applicant was transferred to an intensive-care ward.

64. At 10.15 p.m., following the applicant’s transfer from intensive care to an ordinary ward, the investigator attempted to give him a copy of the application for a change of preventive measure. The applicant declined to accept it, citing his poor state of health, the lateness of the hour and the absence of his lawyers.

2. 26 December 2015

65. At 9.03 a.m., an investigating judge of the Dniprovskyy Court began examining the investigator’s application. The applicant’s lawyers informed the court that their client had undergone heart surgery and remained at the Amosov Institute for post-operative inpatient care, which they said was expected to last between seven and ten days. The investigator maintained, however, that nothing prevented the applicant from attending the hearing.

66. At 11.47 a.m., the judge adjourned the proceedings until 3 p.m. and ordered that the applicant be detained to ensure his compulsory appearance.

67. At 3.07 p.m., the applicant was brought to the courthouse in a wheelchair and connected to a medication infusion device. He was positioned beside a metal cage in the courtroom. Doctors from the Amosov Institute and the emergency medical service attended and monitored his condition. At 3.30 p.m.
An emergency medical service doctor examined the applicant and noted that he had an elevated pulse and high blood pressure.

68. At 5.21 p.m., the investigating judge granted the applicant’s lawyers’ request that their client undergo an immediate forensic medical examination to assess his health and determine whether he was fit to attend court hearings. The proceedings were consequently postponed until 8.30 p.m., and the applicant was returned to the Amosov Institute.

69. When the investigating judge reconvened the hearing at 8.30 p.m., the applicant was absent. His lawyers stated that he was then in an ambulance following a deterioration in his condition. In view of that information and the absence of any evidence that the court’s order for a forensic medical examination had been carried out, the judge postponed the hearing until 9.30 a.m. on 27 December 2015.

70. On 26 December 2015, responding to an enquiry from the applicant’s lawyer, the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute stated that the applicant needed inpatient post-operative care and monitoring by a cardiologist. He added that determining whether the applicant was fit to take part in court hearings fell outside his competence. That same day, in response to a comparable enquiry from the investigator, the Institute’s chief doctor and his two deputies stated that the applicant’s condition was satisfactory and that transporting him to the courtroom would not be “life-threatening”. They nevertheless emphasised that they accepted no responsibility for the health of Institute inpatients while outside the facility.

3. 27 and 28 December 2015

71. According to media reports—the corridors of the Amosov Institute had been continuously occupied by journalists—a group of prosecution officials attempted to enter the applicant’s ward at approximately 1.30 a.m. Finding the door locked, they read aloud to him the order for his forensic medical examination and the summons requiring him to attend the court hearing on the morning of 27 December 2015. Two hospital attendants were required to sign a report confirming this as attesting witnesses.

72. Early on 27 December 2015, the investigator again visited the applicant’s ward and, on this occasion, read the aforementioned documents directly to him. The applicant replied that he would prefer not to leave the hospital before undergoing a forensic medical examination.

73. Between approximately 8 and 9 a.m. on 27 December 2015, the investigator questioned three senior doctors from the Amosov Institute regarding the applicant’s condition. When asked whether the applicant could be transported in a wheelchair under medical supervision without endangering his life or health, all three doctors answered affirmatively.

74. The judge resumed the hearing at 9.38 a.m. on 27 December 2015. The applicant was absent.
The investigator relied on the questioning of the Amosov Institute doctors conducted earlier that morning and sought an order compelling the applicant’s appearance in court. The applicant’s counsel opposed the request, noting that he had not yet been examined by a forensic medical expert.

75. At 12.34 p.m., the judge suspended the proceedings until 3 p.m. that day and ordered that the applicant be detained to ensure his compulsory attendance.

76. In the early afternoon of 27 December 2015, the applicant was examined for approximately thirty minutes by two senior doctors from the Amosov Institute. A forensic medical expert participated, while the investigator and the applicant’s lawyer were also present. When the investigator asked whether the applicant could attend court hearings in a wheelchair and under medical supervision without endangering his life or health, the doctors answered yes. The forensic medical expert declined to express an opinion on that question. The examination was documented in a “medical examination report” prepared by the investigator and signed by everyone present.

77. At 4.23 p.m. that day, the applicant was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair. The investigating judge ordered several short recesses to allow him to receive medical assistance.

78. The courtroom was severely overcrowded, and clashes broke out in the public gallery at one point during the evening. At approximately 9 p.m. on 27 December 2015, the judge ordered that the remainder of the hearing be held in camera.

79. The proceedings continued until 1.35 p.m. on 28 December 2015. The media described the hearing, which lasted about thirty hours in total, as the longest ever held in Ukraine.

D. Media statements concerning the criminal proceedings against the applicant

80. The applicant’s arrest and prosecution generated substantial media interest. Statements to the press were issued by both the defence and the prosecution, as well as by several politicians and non-governmental organisations.

1. Statements to the press by the prosecution and other public officials

81. The applicant relied on the following remarks by senior officials.

82. During a press briefing on 1 November 2015, the Prosecutor General’s assistant pointed to a screen displaying the applicant’s photograph and stated that, because of the organisers who had formed the criminal group, many people could be investigated or designated as suspects that day and might later face trial. He urged anyone who had understood what had occurred to approach either the Security Service or the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine and provide information, explaining that paragraph 2 of Article 255 of the Criminal Code would then apply, meaning that those who reported a crime would be exempted from criminal liability.

83.
The applicant additionally relied on another statement made by the same official: “This has to be brought to an end: forged stamps, the establishment of what are effectively private armies, fund-raising for those purposes, abductions, and these volunteers’ possession of a private surveillance vehicle ...”84. In a televised interview on 1 November 2015, the President of Ukraine further declared: “The position is this: the action will not end with Korban. No one is exempt from criminal responsibility for corruption offences. That applies both to the new team in government ... and to the old team ... I stress that Ukraine will shortly hear the names of other individuals who will be charged.”85. During a press statement on 2 November 2015, the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine said: “Why did the leaders of the organised criminal group need that fund? At the time, the group naturally included Gennadiy Olegovych [the applicant], a respectable gentleman, along with [others] ... It was a criminal group whose speciality was kidnapping ...”86. At a briefing held on 29 December 2015, the investigator stated: “Please display the next slide. This is [a bakery plant], which was likewise unlawfully taken over by the criminal group headed by Gennadiy Olegovych Korban.”87. Speaking to the press on 22 January 2016, the assistant to the Prosecutor General stated: “... the criminal group led by Korban, which, as you have already been informed, participated in numerous criminal activities, including abductions, misappropriation of funds, unlawful handling of weapons, and so forth ... While the whole country was joining forces through volunteer organisations and patriotic movements to support the Ukrainian armed forces in the East ..., regrettably, the criminal group headed by Gennadiy Korban committed the gravest offences while using patriotic and volunteer slogans as a cover; ... In reality, that criminal group, under Gennadiy Korban’s leadership, was financed alongside certain political projects.”

2. Public statements by Ukrainian political parties

88. Three political parties represented in Parliament issued public statements on 31 October and 1 November 2015 concerning the applicant’s arrest on 31 October 2015.

89. The “Batkivshchyna” political party, led by Yuliya Tymoshenko and a member of the governing coalition until February 2016, made the following statement:

The All-Ukrainian Association “Batkivshchyna” is concerned by the arrest of Gennadiy Korban, leader of the “UKROP” party

“‘Batkivshchyna’ is not politically allied with the ‘UKROP’ party. Our positions differ on a range of issues.
Furthermore, we firmly oppose any intermingling of business and politics. Nevertheless, given that those responsible for shooting Maidan protesters and those implicated in large-scale corruption under Yanukovych have still not been punished, the detention of the leader of the ‘UKROP’ party—which secured representation in several regional councils following the local elections—appears to constitute selective justice and political persecution.

We have received reports that searches are being conducted at the offices of members of parliament belonging to the ‘UKROP’ party. Such actions are unlawful and unacceptable. Measures of this kind against a political force have raised numerous questions within society, none of which have been answered.

Against this background, ‘Batkivshchyna’ demands that the Prosecutor General and the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine attend Tuesday’s plenary sitting of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. They must explain to parliament and the public the legal grounds for the arrest of ‘UKROP’ leader Gennadiy Korban and demonstrate that the actions of law-enforcement officials were not politically motivated. ...”

90. The ‘Samopomich’ political party, headed by Andriy Sadovyy—which belonged to the governing coalition at the relevant time before withdrawing from it in February 2016—issued the following statement:

A return to political repression will bring about the collapse of the state – ‘Samopomich’

“The ‘Samopomich Union’ political party considers the search of member of parliament Borys Filatov’s office and the detention of his fellow party member to be an attempt to drag Ukraine back to the era of political repression under Viktor Yanukovych.

Although the enemies of Ukrainian statehood have yet to be held accountable, law-enforcement agencies continue to detain dozens of volunteers defending Ukraine in its war for independence.

We categorically reject selective justice. The allegations now being made against Gennadiy Korban concern facts that have long been known both to the public and to law-enforcement bodies. Conduct for which he should have been punished was ignored by the prosecutor’s office and, in the public’s view, went unpunished. Yet it was only after Gennadiy Korban joined a political party that sharply criticises the President’s actions that his past became the basis for his arrest. It is therefore clear that his detention is, in reality, politically motivated persecution.

All individuals must answer for their conduct, but accountability must be imposed at the proper time, rather than only when it serves someone’s political interests. The principle that ‘friends receive assistance, while enemies are prosecuted’ was what brought about the former president’s downfall.
“Persisting with this policy while Ukraine remains engaged in an ongoing war for independence puts the country’s very statehood at risk. Samopomich calls on the President, the Prime Minister, and their parliamentary colleagues to remove the Prosecutor General without delay and ensure that an independent replacement is appointed to bring all corrupt officials and traitors in Ukraine to justice.”

91. The “Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko”, which had remained part of the governing coalition until September 2015, published the following statement on its website:

**Lozovyy: Korban’s detention signals the regime’s final agony**

“Andriy Lozovyy, a People’s Deputy of Ukraine and deputy leader of the opposition faction of the ‘Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko’, spoke by telephone to the ‘112’ television channel about the continuing political repression in Ukraine.

‘There can be no doubt that Gennadiy Korban’s arrest reflects the death throes of Poroshenko’s totalitarian regime’, Lozovyy said.

The parliamentarian stressed that criminal proceedings were being fabricated solely against patriots. Meanwhile, no one associated with the former ruling political party who had participated in plundering the country or killing the Heaven’s Hundred—the people who died during the 2013-14 protests—had been arrested. ...”

**3. Other public statements and newspaper reports**

92. On 1 November 2015, the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group posted an article on its website under the title “Ukrainian political party leader detained”. It included the following observations:

“There may indeed be legitimate reasons both for instituting criminal proceedings against Gennady Korban and for doing so at this particular time. Nevertheless, Ukrainians remain deeply distrustful following the politically motivated prosecutions conducted under Viktor Yanukovych, the continued failure to investigate properly the crimes committed during Euromaidan, and the authorities’ failure to ensure that individuals who gravely discredited themselves are, at a minimum, removed from positions of responsibility within the judiciary and law-enforcement agencies. In these circumstances, any prosecution is bound to provoke questions. It is therefore hoped that the authorities appreciate that a prompt and fully transparent investigation would contribute far more to rebuilding public confidence than official claims that the case contains not even the slightest trace of political motivation.”

93. The applicant further cited a number of Ukrainian newspaper articles asserting that political considerations had motivated his arrest.

**II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE**

**A. The 1996 Constitution of Ukraine**

94.
Article 29, insofar as relevant to the present case, provides:

“Everyone is entitled to liberty and personal security.

A person may be arrested or detained only on the basis of a reasoned judicial decision, on grounds prescribed by law and in accordance with the procedure established by law.

Where urgently necessary to prevent or halt an offence, legally authorised bodies may temporarily detain a person as a preventive measure. A court must review the existence of reasonable grounds for such detention within seventy-two hours. If, within seventy-two hours of being detained, the person has not been served with a reasoned court decision authorising continued detention, he or she must be released immediately. ...

Any detained person is entitled to contest the lawfulness of his or her detention before a court at any time. ...”

B. Criminal Code 2001

95. The relevant provisions may be outlined as follows:

- Under Article 157 § 3, obstructing the work of an electoral officer through coercion, violence or threats of violence, where the offence is committed by a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy or by a public official abusing his or her position, carries a sentence of three to seven years’ imprisonment and disqualification from holding specified posts or engaging in specified activities for two to three years;

- Article 191 § 5 makes embezzlement of particularly large amounts, or embezzlement committed by an organised group, punishable by seven to twelve years’ imprisonment, confiscation of property, and disqualification from holding specified posts or pursuing specified activities for up to three years;

- Pursuant to Article 255 § 1, establishing a criminal organisation is punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to twelve years;

- Article 289 § 2 provides that car theft committed, in particular, by persons acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy or accompanied by violence or threats of violence is punishable by five to eight years’ imprisonment, with or without confiscation of property;

- Under Article 349, taking a public official hostage is punishable by eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment.

C. Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

96. The relevant provisions state:

Article 176. General rules concerning preventive measures

“1. The available preventive measures are:

(1) a personal undertaking;

(2) a personal warranty;

(3) bail;

(4) house arrest; and

(5) pre-trial detention.

2. Arrest without a judicial order (затримання) constitutes a temporary preventive measure and may be applied only on the grounds and in accordance with the procedure laid down in this Code.

3. An investigating judge or court must dismiss an application for a preventive measure unless the investigator or prosecutor demonstrates sufficient grounds for concluding that no less restrictive measure would adequately avert the identified risk or risks. A personal undertaking is the least restrictive preventive measure, while pre-trial detention is the most severe.

4.
Preventive measures shall be ordered as follows: at the investigative stage, by the investigating judge upon an application from the prosecutor, or upon an investigator’s application endorsed by the prosecutor; and at the trial stage, by the court upon the prosecutor’s application.

Article 177. Aims and grounds for imposing preventive measures

1. A preventive measure is intended to secure the suspect’s or accused’s performance of his or her procedural duties and to avert any attempt to:

(1) evade the pre-trial investigative authorities and/or the court;

(2) destroy, hide, damage, or otherwise spoil objects or documents material to determining the circumstances of the criminal offence;

(3) unlawfully influence the victim, witnesses, other suspects or accused persons, an expert, or a specialist ...;

(4) interfere with the criminal proceedings by any other means;

(5) perpetrate a further criminal offence or continue the offence of which he or she is suspected or accused.

2. A preventive measure may be imposed where there is reasonable suspicion that the person committed a criminal offence and where identified risks provide the investigating judge or court with sufficient reason to believe that the suspect, accused, or convicted person may engage in any of the conduct listed in paragraph 1 of this Article ...

Article 181. House arrest

1. House arrest entails barring a suspect or accused from leaving his or her residence either throughout the entire day or during specified hours.

2. House arrest may be imposed on anyone suspected or accused of an offence for which imprisonment is a possible punishment.

...

5. To monitor the conduct of a suspect or accused subject to house arrest, national police officers may attend his or her residence. They may require oral or written explanations concerning compliance with the obligations imposed. Electronic monitoring equipment may also be employed.

6. An investigating judge’s order placing a person under house arrest shall remain valid for no longer than two months. Where necessary, house arrest may be extended at the prosecutor’s request, subject to the time limits of the pre-trial investigation .... In total, house arrest may not last more than six months. Once that period expires, the order imposing the preventive measure shall be regarded as no longer valid, and the house arrest shall be considered terminated.

Article 208. Arrest by an authorised official [in the absence of a court order]

1.
[Unless a court has issued an order, a] duly authorised official may arrest (затримати) an individual suspected of an offence punishable by imprisonment only where:

(1) the individual is apprehended while committing, or attempting to commit, the offence; or

(2) immediately after the offence, either an eyewitness—including the victim—identifies the individual as the perpetrator, or the combined effect of clear indications found on the individual’s body or clothing, or at the scene, shows that he or she has just committed the offence ...

4. The authorised official who made the arrest must promptly tell the arrested individual, in a language he or she understands, why the arrest was made and which offence he or she is suspected of committing. The official must also explain the individual’s rights, including the rights to legal representation and medical assistance; to give statements or remain silent; to notify [third] persons ... of the arrest and the individual’s whereabouts; to contest the grounds for the arrest; and to exercise the other procedural rights prescribed by this Code.

5. A written arrest report must be prepared. It must include, [among other things,] the place and date of the arrest; its precise time, stated to the hour and minute ...; the reasons for the arrest; the outcome of the personal search; any requests, statements, or complaints made by the arrested individual; and a complete list of his or her procedural rights and obligations. Both the official who prepared the report and the arrested individual must sign it. Once the arrested individual’s signature has been obtained, he or she must immediately be given a copy ...

CASE OF KORBAN v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 26744/16)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

4 July 2019

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Angelika Nußberger, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
André Potocki,
Síofra O’Leary,
Mārtiņš Mits,
