PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 26744/16, brought against Ukraine before the Court on 27 April 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Gennadiy Olegovych Korban, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”).

2. Mr N.S. Kulchytskyy, a lawyer practising in Kyiv, acted for the applicant. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

3. Following a request by the applicant, the President of the Section decided on 21 November 2016 to give the case priority under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court.

4. In particular, relying on Article 3 of the Convention, the applicant complained about the conditions of his transportation on 2 November 2015; his attendance at court hearings between 26 and 28 December 2015 despite being in a weakened condition following coronary angioplasty; and his placement in a metal cage during hearings held on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016. He further alleged violations of his rights under Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 of the Convention. Invoking Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5, he argued that his deprivation of liberty had pursued ulterior, specifically political, purposes. Finally, he claimed that public remarks concerning the criminal proceedings against him, made by senior State officials, had violated the presumption of innocence protected by Article 6 § 2 of the Convention.

5. The Government were notified of those complaints on 5 March 2018. Under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, the rest of the application was declared inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

6. Born in 1970, the applicant resides in Dnipro, which was known as Dnipropetrovsk until June 2016.

A. The applicant’s participation in Ukrainian politics

7. Between 19 March 2014 and 24 March 2015, the applicant served as Deputy Head and Chief of Staff of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration (“the Regional Administration”). According to his account, relations between the President of Ukraine and the person then heading the Regional Administration deteriorated, after which that official resigned along with his political team, including the applicant.

8.
On 15 September 2014, the President of Ukraine conferred the “Order for Courage” on the applicant in recognition of “his commitment, active civic stance and high professionalism in carrying out his official duties”.

9. The applicant became the head of a newly established political party, the Ukrainian Union of Patriots (“UKROP” – Українське об’єднання патріотів — “УКРОП”), on 12 July 2015. The party was strongly critical of the authorities generally and of President Poroshenko specifically.

10. Acting as UKROP’s leader, the applicant stood in the mid-term parliamentary elections in Chernigiv on 26 July 2015. He received 14.76% of the votes and was defeated by the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko” candidate, who secured 35.90%.

11. In the local elections held on 25 October 2015, UKROP obtained 7.43% of the nationwide vote and finished fourth. The top three parties were the “Bloc of Petro Poroshenko”, with 19.52%; “Batkivshchyna”, with 12.23%; and the “Opposition Bloc”, with 10.54%. The applicant also contested the election for mayor of Kyiv but was unsuccessful, receiving 2.61% of the vote.

B. Criminal cases concerning the applicant

12. On 14 August 2014, R., the Head of the State Agency of Land Resources (“the Agency”), was detained against his will in the applicant’s office. The applicant demanded that R. remove the incumbent head of the Agency’s regional department and appoint a specified individual in that person’s place. R. subsequently reported the incident to the police.

13. Criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant and another individual on 15 August 2014 in connection with those events. They were suspected of kidnapping a public official and aggravated theft of a vehicle, as R.’s car had been moved without his permission. The case was entered in the Unified Register of Pre-trial Investigations as proceedings no. 12014040670002852 (“proceedings no. 52”).

14. A further set of criminal proceedings was initiated against the applicant and another person on 25 February 2015. They were suspected of organising, on that date, the abduction of V., an official of the Dnipropetrovsk City Council, for the purpose of compelling Ro., the authority’s acting head, to resign.

15. On 7 August 2015, separate criminal proceedings were commenced against the applicant on suspicion that he had embezzled money belonging to a charitable organisation established in May 2014 to gather voluntary donations in support of Ukrainian soldiers fighting in eastern Ukraine.

16. On 30 September 2015, the Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Election Commission received telephone threats of violence from a caller who identified himself using the applicant’s name. Criminal proceedings were opened against the applicant on 1 October 2015 in relation to that incident, on suspicion of interfering with the duties of an electoral officer.

17.
On 31 October 2015, an investigator from the Prosecutor General’s Office (“the PGO”) took the applicant into custody and informed him that he was suspected of offences under Article 191 § 5 of the Criminal Code (embezzlement by an organised group of funds belonging to a charitable organisation), Article 255 § 1 (establishing a criminal organisation), Article 289 § 2 (aggravated theft of a car), and Article 349 (two instances of taking a public official hostage). The relevant notice indicates that all charges against the applicant were consolidated within proceedings no. 52 (see paragraph 13 above).

18. The applicant was arrested in the following circumstances. At 8.40 a.m. on 31 October 2015, a PGO investigator and a special forces unit came to his home in Dnipropetrovsk and ordered him to open the door. After he refused, the officers forced open the entrance door and entered the flat. The applicant, who was standing inside behind the door, objected that the officers’ actions failed to respect the privacy of his home. He was then arrested and transported to Kyiv. The reasons why it was decided to handle the case in Kyiv remain unknown.

19. At 8.37 p.m. that day, the investigator prepared an arrest report stating that the applicant had been detained under Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“the CCP”) (see paragraph 96 below) on suspicion of offences under Articles 191 § 5, 255 § 1, 289 § 2 and 349 of the Criminal Code. The report form listed two pre-printed grounds for arrest: (1) the person had been caught in flagrante delicto; or (2) immediately after the offence, eyewitnesses, including the victim, had identified the person as the perpetrator, or the overall set of obvious signs on the person’s body or clothing, or at the scene, indicated that the person was the offender. The investigator underlined the second option as the basis for the applicant’s arrest. However, the section intended for setting out “specific facts and data” was left empty.

20. On 2 November 2015, the investigator asked the investigating judge of the Chernigiv Novozavodskyy District Court (“the Novozavodskyy Court”) to order the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial. The proceedings were heard in Chernigiv because the PGO had assigned the investigation to the Chernigiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office. In support of the request, the investigator cited the seriousness of the charges, which carried a possible sentence of up to fifteen years’ imprisonment, and further noted that the applicant had friendly ties with officials in law-enforcement bodies, the judiciary and other authorities.
The investigator consequently believed that the applicant could exploit his connections to influence witnesses, victims, or other suspects involved in the proceedings, or otherwise obstruct the investigation, for instance by destroying evidence.

21. Later that same day, the applicant was taken from Kyiv to Chernigiv, a distance of 150 km, in an ordinary minibus. He stated that he had remained in the vehicle from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m., both during the trip and while awaiting further action after arriving in Chernigiv, and that he had been given neither food nor water and had not been allowed to use a toilet. The Government, referring to information supplied by the PGO, maintained that “the applicant had been provided with water and access to sanitary facilities at his requests”.

22. Subsequently, on 2 November 2015, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Kyiv Pecherskyy District Court (“the Pecherskyy Court”), located close to the PGO headquarters, alleging that his arrest had been arbitrary and unlawful. In particular, he argued that the statutory requirements permitting arrest without a court warrant had not been satisfied in his case.

23. On that date, a separate set of criminal proceedings was also opened against the applicant on suspicion of aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer. More specifically, it was alleged that, during the night of 30 to 31 October 2015, the applicant and several other individuals had obstructed the work of a member of the Dnipropetrovsk City Election Commission “by violence and threats of violence and had demonstrated power by the presence of armed persons and military equipment near the electoral commission’s premises”. Those proceedings were consolidated with proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above).

24. At 8.40 a.m. on 3 November 2015, the seventy-two-hour period during which the applicant could be detained without a judicial decision came to an end, and he was released in the Novozavodskyy Court’s hearing room. Nevertheless, at 8.42 a.m., before he had even been able to leave the room, he was immediately arrested again under an investigator’s decision on suspicion of an offence under Article 157 § 3 of the Criminal Code, namely aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer. He was taken to Kyiv without delay, where the investigator prepared a record of his arrest. As in the earlier arrest record dated 31 October 2015 (see paragraph 19 above), the investigator indicated the basis for the renewed arrest by underlining the pre-printed wording stating that, immediately following the offence, eyewitnesses, including the victim, had identified the person as the perpetrator, or that the combined obvious signs on the person’s body or clothing, or at the scene, pointed to that conclusion.

25. Also on 3 November 2015, the PGO decided to transfer responsibility for the investigation from the Chernigiv Prosecutor’s Office to its own Main Investigation Department.

26. Besides challenging his initial arrest (see paragraph 22 above), the applicant also complained to the Pecherskyy Court that his re-arrest on 3 November 2015 had been unlawful.

27.
On 4 November 2015, the PGO investigator asked the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court to place the applicant in pre-trial detention as a preventive measure pending trial. The request repeated the application lodged on 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), but additionally referred to the charge of interfering with the work of an electoral officer (see paragraphs 23 and 24 above).

28. That same day, in view of the developments outlined above, the investigating judge of the Novozavodskyy Court decided not to examine the investigator’s application of 2 November 2015 concerning the applicant’s pre-trial detention (see paragraph 20 above).

29. On 5 November 2015, the Pecherskyy Court resolved to consider together the investigator’s application and the applicant’s complaints of 2 and 3 November 2015 challenging the lawfulness of his arrest and subsequent re-arrest (see paragraphs 22, 26 and 27 above).

30. On 6 November 2015, the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court partly granted the investigator’s application of 4 November 2005. As an initial preventive measure lasting until 31 December 2015, she placed the applicant under twenty-four-hour house arrest and required him to wear an electronic tracking device. Her decision referred in particular to the gravity of the charges and the severity of the possible penalties. The ruling also recorded that the applicant had a permanent residence, elderly parents and three minor children. The judge further considered that he led a political party and had been granted numerous awards, including the presidential “Order for Courage” on 15 September 2014. She also noted his positive character references and the fact that numerous members of parliament had offered personal surety to guarantee his compliance with his procedural obligations.

31. Addressing the applicant’s allegation that his arrest on 31 October 2015 had been unlawful, the investigating judge found that, when the disputed event occurred, he had been outside the Pecherskyy Court’s territorial jurisdiction. She therefore concluded that she lacked competence to determine that issue.

32. Regarding the same allegation in connection with the applicant’s re-arrest on 3 November 2015, the judge stated, without giving any further details, that the re-arrest had complied with Article 208 of the CCP.

33. The applicant and the prosecutor both appealed against that ruling. The prosecutor maintained that pre-trial detention was the most suitable preventive measure. The applicant’s lawyer submitted that the investigating judge had not given a single reason capable of justifying a measure as restrictive as twenty-four-hour house arrest.

34. On 1 December 2015, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals and affirmed the ruling of 6 November 2015.
The appellate court concurred with the investigating judge that, in the particular circumstances of the applicant’s case, there were no grounds for imposing pre-trial detention and that house arrest constituted an adequate measure. Nevertheless, it found that the case-file materials supported a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed several serious criminal offences. Its ruling also noted that the first-instance court had properly considered the lawfulness of the applicant’s arrest.

35. On 7 December 2015 an ambulance was summoned for the applicant, who was then admitted to the “Family Medicine Clinic”, a private hospital in Dnipropetrovsk. He remained there as an inpatient until 14 December 2015, receiving treatment for a hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris.

36. On 8 December 2015 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Police Department submitted to the PGO a report concerning the electronic monitoring device that the applicant was required to wear while under house arrest. The device had generated thirty-eight alerts. Thirty-five were attributed to “the technical imperfection of the device, the architectural particularities of the building, as well as the presence of a lift in the suspect’s flat”. Of the other three alerts, two occurred when the applicant was transported to attend court hearings, while one resulted from his hospitalisation (see paragraph 35 above).

37. On 25 December 2015 the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office, which had been assigned the investigation by the PGO, asked the investigating judge of the Kyiv Dniprovskyy District Court (“the Dniprovskyy Court”) to replace the applicant’s house arrest with pre-trial detention. Alongside the grounds set out in the original application of 2 November 2015 (see paragraph 20 above), the investigator alleged that, during his house arrest, the applicant had avoided various procedural measures by “abusing his right to medical assistance ... and continuously staying in private medical institutions”. The investigator pointed out that the applicant’s father had founded the “Family Medicine Clinic” and argued that this cast doubt on the objectivity of any findings made by members of that hospital’s staff. The investigator further stated that the police had recorded thirty-eight alerts from the applicant’s electronic monitoring device, potentially indicating attempts to interfere with it. In addition, according to the investigator, a witness had claimed that the applicant had used his lawyers to threaten him and pressure him into changing his statements in the applicant’s favour.

38.
On 28 December 2015, the Dniprovskyy Court granted the investigator’s application and ordered that the applicant be held in pre-trial detention, initially until 25 February 2016. A detailed account of the events between 25 and 28 December 2015 appears in paragraphs 60-79 below. The ruling contained only its operative provisions and indicated that the investigating judge required additional time to prepare the reasons.

39. Certain documents in the case file indicate that, immediately after the hearing on 28 December 2015, the applicant was detained in the Security Service of Ukraine’s pre-trial investigation unit. Other documents, however, suggest that he remained an inpatient at the Amosov Institute, where he was receiving medical treatment (see paragraph 60 below), until 15 January 2016.

40. The Dniprovskyy Court issued the complete text of its ruling on 29 December 2015. In support of the decision to remand the applicant in custody, the investigating judge repeated the investigator’s submissions concerning the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had participated in several criminal offences, the seriousness of those offences, and his friendly relationships with officials in law-enforcement bodies, the judiciary and other authorities (see paragraph 20 above). The judge further stated:

“... after judicial examination [of the application], the investigating judge finds it established that the accused failed to comply with the obligations [arising from] the house arrest [previously] imposed on him.

The prosecution’s submissions that none of the more lenient preventive measures ... could avert the risks identified in the application are well-founded.”

41. The applicant lodged an appeal, arguing that the decision was arbitrary and unlawful and that no less intrusive alternative measures had been examined. He also complained that, despite his inpatient medical treatment following surgery and the absence of any urgency in considering the investigator’s application, the judge had held excessively lengthy hearings, including at night and on weekends.

42. During the hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016, the applicant was confined in a metal cage. The cage was later replaced with a transparent box.

43. On 10 February 2016, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal partly granted the applicant’s appeal. It set aside the ruling of 28 December 2015 and issued a new decision that likewise substituted pre-trial detention for house arrest, but ordered detention only until 23 February 2016. The appellate court endorsed the first-instance court’s findings and reasoning, although it held that the applicant’s detention period should be calculated as beginning on 26 December 2015 (see paragraph 66 below).

44. On 17 February 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged the applicant’s pre-trial detention until 15 April 2016.
It stated that, although the investigation remained unfinished, the seriousness of the accusations against the applicant and the risks previously identified continued to warrant his detention.

45. The applicant lodged an appeal, arguing in particular that the investigating judge had failed to examine any less restrictive alternative preventive measures. He also pointed out that no investigative action whatsoever had been conducted since his placement in pre-trial detention.

46. On 10 March 2016 the charges against the applicant were amended slightly: the aggravated car-theft charge (see paragraph 13 above) was removed from the indictment.

47. That same day, the applicant entered into a friendly settlement agreement with R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). He admitted his guilt in kidnapping R. on 14 August 2014 and expressed remorse. The parties agreed that the appropriate sentence would be three years’ restriction of liberty—meaning detention in a semi-open prison near his residence—suspended for a probationary period of one year and six months. The agreement was later to be approved by a court (see paragraph 51 below).

48. Also on 10 March 2016, the charge relating to R.’s kidnapping was separated into another set of proceedings. The remaining charges continued to be dealt with in proceedings no. 52 (see paragraphs 13, 17 and 23 above).

49. On 15 March 2016 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decision of 17 February 2016 extending his pre-trial detention (see paragraph 44 above). According to the appellate ruling, the investigating judge’s conclusion that pre-trial detention was the most suitable preventive measure did not indicate that alternative measures had not been considered. In response to the applicant’s argument that no investigative steps had been taken for a lengthy period, the Court of Appeal held that this did not justify setting aside the investigating judge’s decision to prolong his detention. It added that the applicant remained free to complain about any failure to act on the prosecution’s part.

50. On that same date, the applicant asked the Dniprovskyy Court to replace his pre-trial detention with twenty-four-hour house arrest because his elderly mother was seriously ill and needed constant care. The investigating judge considered and granted the application that day. He observed that this new argument had been addressed neither in the earlier decision of 17 February 2016 nor in the appellate ruling of 15 March 2016 (see paragraphs 44 and 49 above). The Dniprovskyy Court therefore ordered that the applicant be kept under twenty-four-hour house arrest, without an electronic monitoring device, until 15 April 2016. That ruling was upheld on appeal on 14 April 2016.

51.
51. On 21 March 2016, the Dnipropetrovsk Kirovskyy District Court endorsed the friendly-settlement agreement concluded by the applicant and R. (see paragraphs 12 and 13 above). Consequently, it convicted the applicant of kidnapping R. pursuant to a prior conspiracy and imposed a sentence of three years’ restriction of liberty, suspended subject to a probationary period of one year and six months.

52. On 14 April 2016, in the still-pending criminal proceedings against the applicant (see paragraph 48 above), the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged his house arrest until 30 April 2016. The ruling stated that a substantial number of investigative measures remained outstanding and that both the seriousness of the charges and the risks previously identified continued to warrant his detention.

53. On 29 April 2016, the same measure was extended again, until 27 June 2016.

54. On 7 June 2016, after the applicant sought permission to receive medical treatment in Israel, the Dniprovskyy Court substituted an undertaking not to abscond for his house arrest. That preventive measure was to remain in force until 27 June 2016. On the same date, the investigating judge granted the applicant permission to travel to Israel.

55. On 16 June 2016, the Dniprovskyy Court prolonged the applicant’s undertaking not to abscond until 10 August 2016.

56. On 5 August 2016, the charges under Article 255 § 1 of the Criminal Code (creation of a criminal organisation), Article 349 (taking a public official hostage), Article 191 § 5 (embezzlement of funds belonging to a charity organisation by an organised group), and Article 157 § 3 (aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer) were separated into distinct proceedings. Those proceedings were entered in the Unified Register of Pre-trial Investigations as no. 42016000000002043 (hereinafter “no. 43”). No additional information is available concerning that procedural step. It is likewise unclear which charges, if any, remained pending in proceedings no. 52 (see, in particular, paragraph 48 above and paragraph 59 below).

57. On 11 August 2016, the Pecherskyy Court rejected the PGO’s application for a further extension of the preventive measure imposed on the applicant, namely the undertaking not to abscond. The investigating judge observed that the measure had expired on 10 August 2016 and therefore was no longer capable of being extended.

58. On 11 September 2017, owing to the absence of evidence establishing the applicant’s guilt, the PGO terminated criminal proceedings no. 43 against him (see paragraph 56 above). More specifically, the prosecution found the evidence insufficient to charge him with creating and directing a criminal organisation, taking the public official V. hostage, embezzling a charity organisation’s funds as part of an organised group, and aggravated interference with the work of an electoral officer.

59.
In their observations, the Government stated, without giving further particulars, that criminal case no. 52 remained pending as of April 2018 and that the applicant had “no procedural status” in those proceedings. The applicant did not dispute that statement as such, but emphasised that every charge against him had been discontinued.

C. Events between 25 and 28 December 2015

1. 25 December 2015

60. The applicant was admitted to the Amosov National Institute of Cardiovascular Surgery (“the Amosov Institute”) to undergo a medical examination.

61. At approximately 2 p.m., the Amosov Institute’s chief doctor told the media that the examination would last about another two hours. At around 3 p.m., a spokesperson for the UKROP party announced that an investigator was waiting outside the applicant’s hospital ward to provide him with a copy of the application seeking to replace house arrest with pre-trial detention as the preventive measure (see paragraph 37 above).

62. After examining the applicant, a panel of doctors diagnosed ischemic heart disease, a hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina pectoris. They concluded that he urgently required coronary stent angioplasty—a percutaneous coronary procedure involving the reopening of blocked arteries and the insertion of a small wire-mesh tube, known as a stent, to keep the artery open. The operation was performed immediately, and two stents were inserted into the applicant’s coronary arteries.

63. The procedure was completed by approximately 9 p.m., after which the applicant was taken to an intensive-care ward.

64. At 10.15 p.m., once the applicant had been moved from intensive care to a regular ward, the investigator attempted to give him a copy of the application for a change of preventive measure. The applicant declined to receive it, citing his poor state of health, the lateness of the hour and the fact that his lawyers were not present.

2. 26 December 2015

65. At 9.03 a.m., an investigating judge of the Dniprovskyy Court began considering the investigator’s application. The applicant’s lawyers advised the court that their client had undergone heart surgery and remained at the Amosov Institute for post-operative inpatient treatment, which they said was expected to continue for approximately seven to ten days. The investigator maintained, however, that nothing prevented the applicant from attending court.

66. At 11.47 a.m., the judge postponed the hearing until 3 p.m. and ordered that the applicant be detained to ensure his compulsory appearance.

67. At 3.07 p.m., the applicant was brought to the courthouse in a wheelchair and connected to a medication infusion device. In the courtroom, he was positioned beside a metal cage. Doctors from the Amosov Institute and the emergency medical service attended and monitored his condition. At 3.30 p.m.
A doctor from the emergency medical service examined the applicant and found that his pulse was rapid and his blood pressure high.

68. At 5.21 p.m., the investigating judge granted the applicant’s lawyers’ request that their client undergo an immediate forensic medical examination to determine his state of health and whether he was fit to attend court hearings. The hearing was therefore postponed until 8.30 p.m., and the applicant was returned to the Amosov Institute.

69. When the investigating judge resumed the hearing at 8.30 p.m., the applicant was absent. His lawyers stated that he was then in an ambulance because his condition had worsened. In view of that information and the absence of any evidence that the court’s order for a forensic medical examination had been carried out, the judge adjourned the hearing until 9.30 a.m. on 27 December 2015.

70. On 26 December 2015, responding to an enquiry from the applicant’s lawyer, the chief doctor of the Amosov Institute stated that the applicant needed post-operative inpatient care and monitoring by a cardiologist. He added that deciding whether the applicant was fit to take part in court hearings fell outside his competence. That same day, in response to a similar enquiry from the investigator, the Institute’s chief doctor and his two deputies stated that the applicant’s condition was satisfactory and that transferring him to the courtroom would not be “life-threatening”. However, they also noted that they accepted no responsibility for the health of their inpatients while outside the Institute.

3. 27 December (Sunday) and 28 December 2015

71. According to mass-media reports—journalists having remained continuously in the corridors of the Amosov Institute—a group of prosecution officials attempted to enter the applicant’s ward at approximately 1.30 a.m. Finding the door locked, they read aloud to the applicant the order concerning his forensic medical examination and the summons requiring him to attend the court hearing on the morning of 27 December 2015. Two hospital attendants were required to sign a report confirming this as attesting witnesses.

72. Early on 27 December 2015, the investigator again visited the applicant’s ward. On this occasion, he read the aforementioned documents aloud directly to the applicant, who replied that he preferred not to leave the hospital before undergoing a forensic medical examination.

73. Between approximately 8 and 9 a.m. on 27 December 2015, the investigator questioned three senior doctors at the Amosov Institute about the applicant’s condition. When asked whether the applicant could be transported in a wheelchair under medical supervision without endangering his life or health, all three answered affirmatively.

74. At 9.38 a.m. on 27 December 2015, the judge reconvened the hearing. The applicant was absent.
Earlier that morning, the investigator had referred to the questioning of doctors from the Amosov Institute and asked that the applicant be forcibly brought before the court. The applicant’s counsel opposed that request on the ground that he had not yet been examined by a forensic medical expert.

75. At 12.34 p.m., the judge suspended the proceedings until 3 p.m. that day and ordered that the applicant be detained to ensure his compulsory appearance.

76. In the early afternoon of 27 December 2015, the applicant was medically examined for approximately half an hour by two senior doctors from the Amosov Institute. A forensic medical expert also took part, while the investigator and the applicant’s lawyer were present. When the investigator asked whether the applicant could attend court hearings in a wheelchair, accompanied by doctors, without endangering his life or health, the two doctors answered yes. The forensic medical expert declined to answer. The examination was documented in “a medical examination report”, which was prepared by the investigator and signed by everyone who had participated.

77. At 4.23 p.m. that day, the applicant was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair. The investigating judge briefly adjourned the proceedings several times to allow him to receive medical assistance.

78. The courtroom was exceptionally overcrowded. At one point during the evening, clashes broke out in the public gallery. At approximately 9 p.m. on 27 December 2015, the judge ordered that the remainder of the hearing be held in camera.

79. The proceedings continued until 1.35 p.m. on 28 December 2015. The mass media described them as the longest court hearing ever held in Ukraine, lasting approximately thirty hours in total.

D. Public statements concerning the criminal proceedings against the applicant

80. The applicant’s arrest and prosecution generated substantial media interest. Statements to the press were issued by both the defence and the prosecution, as well as by several politicians and non-governmental organisations.

1. Statements to the press by the prosecution and other public officials

81. The applicant relied on the following remarks by senior officials.

82. During a press briefing on 1 November 2015, the assistant to the Prosecutor General stated:

“Because of these organisers [pointing to the screen displaying the applicant’s photograph], who established this criminal group, many people may today come under investigation or be treated as suspects and may subsequently be tried. I ask everyone who has understood what occurred: please approach the Security Service or the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine, provide us with information, and paragraph 2 of Article 255 of the Criminal Code will be applied (in other words, individuals who report a crime will be exempted from criminal liability).”

83.
The applicant further relied on a statement made by the official referred to above, who declared that the situation had to be brought to an end, referring to counterfeit stamps, the establishment of what were effectively private armies, fundraising conducted on that basis, abductions, and the volunteers’ possession of a private surveillance vehicle.84

In a televised interview on 1 November 2015, the President of Ukraine stated that the action would not end with Korban and that no one—whether belonging to the new governing team or the previous one—was exempt from criminal responsibility for corruption-related offences. He emphasised that Ukraine would soon learn the names of additional persons who would be charged.85

During a press statement on 2 November 2015, the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine questioned why the leaders of the organised criminal group had needed that fund. He said that the group had, at the relevant time, included “the respectful gentleman” Gennadiy Olegovych—the applicant—and others, and described it as a criminal organisation specialising in kidnappings.86

At a briefing on 29 December 2015, the investigator asked for the next slide to be displayed and stated that it showed a bakery plant that had also been unlawfully taken over by the criminal group headed by Gennadiy Olegovych Korban.87

Speaking to the press on 22 January 2016, the assistant to the Prosecutor General described a criminal group led by Korban which, according to information already disclosed, had engaged in various offences, including kidnappings, embezzlement, unlawful handling of weapons, and other criminal activities. The assistant stated that, while the whole country had been mobilising through volunteer organisations and patriotic movements to support the Ukrainian military in the East, the group headed by Gennadiy Korban had unfortunately committed the gravest crimes under the guise of patriotic and volunteer slogans. The assistant added that this criminal organisation had, in fact, been financed alongside certain political projects.

2. Public statements by Ukrainian political parties88

On 31 October and 1 November 2015, three political parties represented in Parliament issued public statements concerning the applicant’s arrest on 31 October 2015.89

The All-Ukrainian Association “Batkivshchyna”, led by Yuliya Tymoshenko and part of the governing coalition until February 2016, expressed concern about the arrest of Gennadiy Korban, leader of the “UKROP” party. It stressed that “Batkivshchyna” was not a political ally of “UKROP” and that the two parties held differing views on a range of issues.
We also firmly oppose the mixing of business and politics. Nevertheless, given that those responsible for shooting Maidan protesters and participating in large-scale corruption under Yanukovych have still not been punished, the detention of the leader of the ‘UKROP’ party—which secured representation in several regional councils following the local elections—appears to constitute selective justice and political persecution.

We have received information that searches are being conducted at [the offices of] members of parliament belonging to the ‘UKROP’ party. Such measures are unlawful and unacceptable.

These actions against a political force have raised numerous questions in society, none of which have been answered.

Against this background, ‘Batkivshchyna’ demands that the Prosecutor General and the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine attend the plenary sitting of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine on Tuesday. They must explain to members of parliament and the public the grounds for arresting Gennadiy Korban, the leader of the ‘UKROP’ party, and demonstrate that the conduct of law-enforcement officials was not politically motivated. ...”

90. The ‘Samopomich’ political party, headed by Andriy Sadovyy—which belonged to the governing coalition at the relevant time and withdrew from it in February 2016—issued the following statement:

Political repression will cause the state to collapse – ‘Samopomich’

“The ‘Samopomich Union’ political party considers the search of member of parliament Borys Filatov’s office and the arrest of another party member to be an attempt to take Ukraine back to the era of political repression under Viktor Yanukovych.

Although the enemies of Ukrainian statehood have yet to be held responsible, law-enforcement bodies continue to arrest dozens of volunteers defending Ukraine in its war for independence.

We categorically reject selective justice. Both the public and law-enforcement authorities have long been aware of the facts on which the current accusations against Gennadiy Korban are based. The conduct for which [he] should have been punished was ignored by the prosecutor’s office and, in the public’s view, remained unpunished. Yet his past became grounds for arrest only after Gennadiy Korban joined a political party that sharply criticises the President’s actions. It is therefore clear that political persecution is the true reason for his detention.

All individuals must answer for their conduct, but accountability must be imposed at the proper time, rather than when it becomes politically advantageous to someone. The approach of ‘helping friends and prosecuting enemies’ brought about the former president’s downfall.
Persisting with this policy while Ukraine remains at war for its independence puts Ukrainian statehood at risk. ‘Samopomich’ calls on the President, the Prime Minister, and their fellow members of Parliament to remove the Prosecutor General without delay and ensure that an independent replacement is appointed to start bringing every corrupt official and traitor in Ukraine to justice.”91.

The “Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko”, which had participated in the governing coalition until September 2015, published the following announcement on its website:

Lozovyy: The detention of Korban signals the regime’s death throes

“Andriy Lozovyy, a People’s Deputy of Ukraine and deputy head of the opposition parliamentary faction of the ‘Radical Party of Oleh Lyashko’, told the ‘112’ television channel by telephone that political persecution in Ukraine was continuing.

‘There is no doubt that Gennadiy Korban’s arrest demonstrates the agony of Poroshenko’s totalitarian regime’, Lozovyy said.

The parliamentarian stressed that criminal proceedings were being fabricated exclusively against patriots .... Meanwhile, not one person from [the formerly governing political party] involved in plundering the country and killing the Heaven’s Hundred [those who died during the 2013-14 protests] had been arrested. ...”

3. Additional public comments and press reports

92. On 1 November 2015, the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group posted an article on its website under the headline “Ukrainian political party leader detained”. Among other things, it stated:

“There may indeed be legitimate reasons both for instituting criminal proceedings against Gennady Korban and for doing so at this particular time. Nevertheless, Ukrainians’ profound mistrust stems from the politically driven trials conducted under Viktor Yanukovych, the continuing failure to investigate properly the crimes perpetrated during Euromaidan, and the failure to ensure that individuals who seriously discredited themselves are, at a minimum, dismissed from positions of responsibility in the judiciary and law-enforcement agencies. In those circumstances, any prosecution will inevitably provoke doubts. It is therefore hoped that the authorities appreciate that a prompt and fully transparent investigation would contribute more to rebuilding public confidence than public declarations that politics played no part whatsoever.”

93. The applicant further cited several Ukrainian newspaper reports indicating that his arrest may have been politically motivated.

II. APPLICABLE DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

A. The 1996 Constitution of Ukraine

94.
Article 29, applicable to the present case, provides:

“Everyone is entitled to liberty and personal security.

A person may be arrested or detained only on the basis of a reasoned judicial decision and on the grounds and in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.

Where there is an urgent need to prevent or halt a criminal offence, legally authorised bodies may temporarily detain an individual as a preventive measure. A court must examine whether there were reasonable grounds for that detention within seventy-two hours. If, within seventy-two hours of being detained, the individual has not received a reasoned court decision authorising continued detention, he or she must be released immediately. ...

Any detained person is entitled to contest his or her detention before a court at any time. ...”

B. Criminal Code 2001

95. The pertinent provisions may be outlined as follows:

- Article 157 § 3 stipulates that interference with the activities of an electoral officer, when accompanied by coercion, violence or threats of violence and carried out either by a group acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy or by a public official abusing his or her position, is punishable by imprisonment for three to seven years, together with disqualification from holding specified posts or engaging in specified activities for two to three years;

- Article 191 § 5 prescribes imprisonment for seven to twelve years, confiscation of property and disqualification from holding certain posts or conducting certain activities for up to three years for embezzlement involving particularly large sums or perpetrated by an organised group;

- Article 255 § 1 makes the creation of a criminal organisation punishable by imprisonment for five to twelve years;

- pursuant to Article 289 § 2, theft of a car committed, in particular, by persons acting in conspiracy or involving violence or threats of violence carries a sentence of five to eight years’ imprisonment, with or without confiscation of property;

- Article 349 provides for a sentence of eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment for taking a public official hostage.

C. Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

96. The relevant provisions state:

Article 176. General rules concerning preventive measures

“1. The available preventive measures are:

(1) a personal undertaking;

(2) a personal warranty;

(3) bail;

(4) house arrest; and

(5) pre-trial detention.

2. Arrest without a judicial order (затримання) constitutes a temporary preventive measure that may be applied on the grounds and in accordance with the procedure laid down by this Code.

3. An investigating judge or a court must dismiss an application seeking a preventive measure where the investigator or prosecutor has failed to establish sufficient grounds for believing that no less restrictive measure would adequately prevent the identified risk or risks. A personal undertaking is the least restrictive preventive measure, while pre-trial detention is the most restrictive.

4.
Preventive measures may be imposed during an investigation by the investigating judge upon an application from the prosecutor, or upon an investigator’s application authorised by the prosecutor; during the trial, they may be imposed by the court upon the prosecutor’s application.

Article 177. Objectives and grounds for imposing preventive measures

1. A preventive measure is intended to secure the performance by a suspect or accused person of his or her procedural duties and to prevent that person from attempting to:

(1) evade the pre-trial investigation authorities and/or the court;

(2) damage, hide, or destroy any object or document essential to determining the circumstances of the criminal offence;

(3) unlawfully influence the victim, witnesses, other suspects or accused persons, an expert, or a specialist ...;

(4) interfere with the criminal proceedings by any other means;

(5) perpetrate another criminal offence or continue the offence of which he or she is suspected or accused.

2. A preventive measure may be imposed where there is a reasonable suspicion that the person committed a criminal offence and where risks exist that provide the investigating judge or the court with sufficient grounds to believe that the suspect, accused person, or convicted person may carry out any of the actions listed in paragraph one of this Article ...

Article 181. House arrest

1. House arrest means that a suspect or accused person is forbidden from leaving his or her residence either twenty-four hours a day or during specified hours.

2. This measure may be imposed on a person suspected or accused of committing a criminal offence for which imprisonment is a possible punishment.

...

5. Officers of the National Police may visit a suspect or accused person under house arrest at his or her residence to monitor his or her conduct. They may require oral or written explanations concerning the person’s compliance with his or her obligations. Electronic monitoring devices may also be employed.

6. An investigating judge’s ruling ordering house arrest shall remain valid for no longer than two months. Where necessary, house arrest may be extended at the prosecutor’s request, within the time limits of the pre-trial investigation .... In total, house arrest shall not last longer than six months. Once that period has elapsed, the ruling imposing the preventive measure shall be regarded as expired, and the house arrest shall be deemed terminated.

Article 208. Arrest by an authorised official [without a court order]

1.
[Where there is no court order, a] duly authorised official may arrest (затримати) an individual suspected of an offence punishable by imprisonment only where:

(1) the individual is apprehended while committing or attempting to commit the offence; or

(2) immediately after the offence, either an eyewitness account—including that of the victim—or the combination of readily apparent traces on the individual’s body or clothing, or at the location of the incident, indicates that the individual has just committed the offence ...

4. The authorised official effecting the arrest must promptly tell the arrested individual, in a language he or she understands, why the arrest has taken place and which offence he or she is suspected of committing. The official must also advise the individual of his or her rights, including the rights to legal representation and medical care; to give a statement or remain silent; to notify [third] parties ... of the arrest and his or her location; to contest the grounds for the arrest; and to exercise all other procedural rights established by this Code.

5. An arrest record must be prepared for every arrested individual. It must include, [among other matters,] the place and date of arrest; its precise time, stated by hour and minute ...; the reasons for the arrest; the outcome of the personal search; any requests, statements or complaints made by the arrested individual; and a complete list of his or her procedural rights and obligations. Both the official who prepared the record and the arrested individual must sign it. Once the arrested individual’s signature has been obtained, a copy must be given to him or her without delay ...”

original: FIFTH SECTION CASE OF RYABININ AND SHATALINA v. UKRAINE(Application no. 33006/07)    JUDGMENT STRASBOURG7 November 2019     This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision. In the case of Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Lado Chanturia, judges,and Milan Blaško, Deputy Section Registrar,Having deliberated in private on 15 October 2019,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:PROCEDURE1. The case originated in an application (no. 33006/07) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ukrainian nationals, Mr Valeriy Ivanovich Ryabinin (“the first applicant”) and Ms Yuliya Ignatyevna Shatalina (“the second applicant”), on 20 December 2006 or 12 July 2007 (the date is in dispute as regards the first applicant – see paragraphs 81 and 83 below) and 5 November 2009 respectively.2. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr A.S. Kychenok, a lawyer practising in Kyiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.3. The first applicant alleged, in particular: that he had been ill-treated by the police and that there had been no effective domestic investigation into the matter; that he had not had a fair trial; that his correspondence had been subjected to routine monitoring in detention; and that he had been unable to obtain copies of all the relevant documents from his case file in order to substantiate his application. The second applicant complained about the allegedly arbitrary seizure and retention of her property in the context of the criminal proceedings against her son and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard.4. On 20 June 2018 notice of the above complaints was given to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.THE FACTSTHE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE5. The first applicant was born in 1965 and is serving a life‑imprisonment sentence in Vinnytsya Prison no. 1. The second applicant is his mother. She was born in 1936 and lives in Kryvyy Rig.Background events6. On 13 November 2004 the first applicant was released from prison having served a twelve-year sentence for murder.7. In May 2005 he became acquainted with S. and they started a relationship. Shortly thereafter S. sold her flat and moved to a rented one.8. On 12 June 2005 she was seen alive for the last time.9. On 17 June 2005 the police extracted a leg and an arm from the local river Ingulets, later identified as being body parts of S.10. On 23 June 2005 the remaining parts of the body and its dissected head were retrieved from the river near the applicants’ house.Alleged ill-treatment of the first applicant and domestic investigation into the matter11. On 23 June 2005 the first applicant was arrested on suspicion of the murder of S. (see paragraph 29 below).12. The first applicant alleged that he had been ill-treated by the police following his arrest and provided the following account of events. The police beat him up by plastic bottles filled with sand and liquid, with a view to extracting his confession to the murder of S. and dissecting her corpse. As he refused, his ill-treatment is alleged to have continued until he fainted. When he regained his senses, he realised that his trousers and pants were lowered and that an electric cable was attached to his testicles. Another electric cable was attached to his lower lip. The police administered an electric current to the first applicant which made him faint several times. The officers also threatened him with rape. Eventually, the first applicant succumbed and wrote a statement of confession dictated to him. The police officer gave him some vodka, after which the first applicant vomited. Thereafter he was placed in a cell where there was another inmate. The first applicant had nausea and vomited. He was taken to the toilet several times at his request. Following one such request, a police officer took him out and shackled him to a motorcycle on a lorry outside. The first applicant spent the night outside. There was a fire hose from which cold water was pouring on him all the time.13. In the morning on 24 June 2005 the first applicant was allegedly made to change into clean clothes brought by his mother at the investigator’s instruction. According to the first applicant, the clothes which he had been wearing during his arrest were soiled with his blood following his ill-treatment. The investigator allegedly told the first applicant’s mother to destroy them, which she did.14. According to the Government, the first applicant was not subjected to any physical or moral coercion. They observed, however, that the documents pertaining to his detention in the Inguletskyy police station on 23 June 2005 had been destroyed in 2012 after the expiry of the period prescribed for their storage.15. On 25 June 2005 a judge of the Kryvyy Rig Inguletskyy District Court (“the Inguletskyy Court”) remanded the first applicant in custody. According to the first applicant, he was not given an opportunity to complain of his ill-treatment and the judge did not react to the visible injuries on his face (unspecified by the first applicant).16. On 1 July 2005 the first applicant was brought to the Kryvyy Rig pre‑trial detention facility (SIZO) where he was examined by a doctor. According to the Government, the examination did not reveal any injuries. According to the first applicant, his injuries were not documented. He did not, however, specify those injuries.17. On 25 August 2005 the first applicant complained to the Kryvyy Rig City Prosecutor’s Office that he had confessed to the murder “under moral coercion” by the investigator. He submitted that the investigator had instructed him what to say during the investigative measures under threat of harm to his relatives. Allegedly being afraid for his mother and daughter and feeling depressed, the first applicant had followed those instructions, even when represented by a lawyer.18. On 14 September 2005 the Inguletskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (“the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office”), to which the above-mentioned complaint had apparently been forwarded, wrote to the first applicant that his allegations had been investigated and had proved to be without basis.19. On an unspecified date after 23 September 2005 (see paragraph 41 below), during the first applicant’s trial, he complained to the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Dnipropetrovsk Court”), which was examining the case as a court of first instance, that he had been coerced into making self-incriminatory statements (see paragraph 43 below). On 1 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court instructed the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the matter.20. On 13 February 2006 the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office issued a ruling refusing to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers concerned, having found no indication of a criminal offence.21. The first applicant challenged the above refusal before the Inguletskyy Court. He submitted that on 23 June 2005 he had been subjected to “physical and psychological violence”. The first applicant noted that the clothes in which he had been arrested had been soiled with his blood and that the investigator had therefore instructed the first applicant’s mother to bring him similar clean clothes and to destroy the dirty ones. The first applicant further complained that the law enforcement officials had infringed the law by withdrawing from him a sum of money and a mobile phone belonging to his mother.22. On 16 March 2006 the Inguletskyy Court dismissed the first applicant’s complaint as unfounded. It noted that, apart from the vaguely expressed allegation of “physical and psychological violence”, the first applicant had not specified the circumstances of his alleged ill‑treatment. At the same time, the judge observed that in his complaint against the prosecutor’s refusal the first applicant had raised some new allegations, which had not been verified earlier. Namely, the first applicant additionally alleged that there had been various violations of the procedural rules in respect of the seizure of certain valuables. Accordingly, in so far as his complaint concerned other issues than his alleged ill-treatment, the Inguletskyy Court forwarded it to the local prosecutor.23. On 14 April 2006 the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office issued another ruling refusing to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers involved in the first applicant’s arrest and questioning, for the lack of the constituent elements of a crime. The officers had been questioned and had denied any wrongdoings. It appears that the issue of the first applicant’s alleged ill-treatment was also covered by that decision. Thus, the prosecutor referred to the statements by the officers who had submitted that the first applicant had not resisted his arrest and that immediately thereafter, in a conversation with the investigator, he had confessed to having murdered S. and to having dissected her body. The investigator had also denied having threatened the first applicant with rape.24. On 6 July 2006 the Inguletskyy Court upheld the above refusal.25. On 6 September 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court upheld the decision of the Inguletskyy Court of 16 March 2006 (see paragraph 22 above).26. On 13 September 2006 it also upheld the decision of the Inguletskyy Court of 6 July 2006 (see paragraph 24 above).Criminal proceedings against the first applicant27. On 23 June 2005, at 6 p.m., after having retrieved fragments of a corpse from the river near the applicants’ house (see paragraph 10 above), the police conducted a search at the applicants’ household, in the presence of the second applicant. They also documented her explanations as follows. In May 2005 her son had started a relationship with S., who had given him the key from her flat. Before 9 or 10 June 2005 S. had often come to see the first applicant. As he explained to his mother, thereafter S. had left for Kyiv. On 16 or 17 June 2005 the first applicant had brought a television set. On the following day he had left with a handcart and had come back some time later with a kitchen cabinet in that handcart.28. The police seized a hacksaw and four hacksaw blades, as well as the handcart, the TV-set and the kitchen cabinet referred to by the second applicant. The first applicant was not at home at that time.29. The investigator asked the second applicant to telephone her son and to tell him to come to the Inguletskyy district police station, which she did. According to the first applicant, he considered that the request was in connection with the usual police supervision following his release from prison. He therefore went to the police station, where, at 7.20 p.m., he was arrested on suspicion of the murder of S. The investigator indicated in the arrest report that evidence of the commission of a criminal offence had been discovered at the first applicant’s home and that there was a risk that he might abscond or reoffend.30. Shortly after his arrest on 23 June 2005 the first applicant gave written “explanations” to the chief of the Inguletskyy police department. The Government provided a copy thereof to the Court. That document was handwritten in Russian on fourteen pages, in simple words and without any references to legal provisions (see paragraph 84 below). The first applicant confessed to the murder of S. on 12 June 2005 and gave a detailed account of the events. He explained that they had had a dispute while drunk and that he had hit her several times in the head with an axe back. The first applicant emphasised that he had not meant to hurt S. and that she had provoked him. He went on to state that he could see her suffering and that he had realised that she would die anyway. To put an end to her suffering, he had smothered her with a pillow. On 13 and 14 June 2005 he had dissected the body and placed its parts in the refrigerator in the flat rented by S. Subsequently, he had drowned them in the river nearby. Following complaints from the neighbours about bad smells, the first applicant had sprayed several containers of air freshener in the flat of S. He admitted having taken some appliances and furniture from that flat and having withdrawn money from the deceased’s bank card on 12, 13 and 15 June 2005. He stated that he was confessing of his own free will and that he regretted what he had done.31. The same evening the first applicant signed “a report on the familiarisation of the suspect with his defence rights” with extensive relevant quotations from the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure. He also wrote that he wished to be represented by a lawyer as of his first questioning as a suspect.32. On 24 June 2005 a lawyer was appointed for the first applicant.33. On the same day he was questioned as a suspect in the presence of his lawyer and repeated his confession.34. Later on 24 June 2005 a reconstruction of the events was carried out in the lawyer’s presence. The first applicant maintained his confession. As it can be seen from the numerous photos included in the reconstruction report, the first applicant had no visible injuries.35. On 25 June 2005 the Inguletskyy Court remanded the first applicant in custody pending trial. On the same day he was questioned as an accused person in the presence of his lawyer and reiterated his previous confessions. The first applicant also wrote in the interview report that he fully admitted his guilt.36. On 10 August 2005 a forensic expert medical examination established that the victim’s body could have been dissected with the hacksaw seized in the applicants’ household on 23 June 2005 (see paragraph 28 above).37. On 23 August 2005 the first applicant underwent a forensic psychiatric examination with a view to establishing whether he could be held responsible for the criminal offence in question. In the course of that examination, he reiterated his confessions and raised no complaints. The experts concluded that the first applicant was aware of his actions and could control them. The first applicant signed the above-mentioned examination report with a note that he had no statements or requests to make.38. On 14 September 2005 the charges against the first applicant were modified. In addition to aggravated murder, he was charged with robbery and the unlawful possession of weapons (a home-made gun and a nunchaku had been found at his home). The first applicant was questioned in the presence of his lawyer and maintained his confession. He disagreed, however, with the charges of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons. The first applicant wrote in the interview report that he “partly” admitted his guilt. He stated that S. had herself given him her bank card and that he had killed her not for profit but as the result of a dispute. The first applicant also wrote that he had had the home-made weapons only for use in self-defence.39. On 15 September 2005 the pre-trial investigation was completed and the first applicant and his lawyer were given the opportunity to study the case file. As indicated in the report to that effect, the lawyer made a request that the charges against the first applicant be dropped, without further details.40. On the following day the investigator rejected that request on the grounds that the case file contained sufficient evidence to prove that the first applicant had committed the crimes of which he was accused. Furthermore, the investigator observed that the first applicant had not denied murdering S.41. On 23 September 2005 the case was sent to the Dnipropetrovsk Court for the trial.42. On an unspecified date the charges against the first applicant were modified: he was charged with murder as a repeat offence and theft.43. On 20 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court found the first applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The first applicant pleaded innocent in the court hearing. He retracted his confession made during the pre-trial investigation and alleged that it had been the result of his torture. The first applicant submitted that he had seen S. for the last time on 12 June 2005. While he admitted having used her bank card thereafter, he insisted that she had earlier entrusted it to him. The first applicant also admitted having taken some appliances and furniture from her flat as she “was not showing up”. Furthermore, he noted that he had been obliged to clean the flat and to spray several containers of air freshener because of the neighbours’ complaints about bad smell.44. The trial court did not consider plausible the first applicant’s submissions in the hearing and chose to rely on the statements he had made confessing his guilt during his numerous questionings as a suspect and subsequently as an accused, which had been conducted in the presence of his lawyer (see paragraphs 34, 35, 37 and 38 above). It was noted that the first applicant had consistently maintained his confessions throughout the pre-trial investigation. The Dnipropetrovsk Court observed, in particular, that, while he had disagreed with the charges of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, he had still admitted having killed S. arguing that it had not been for profit, but as the result of a dispute (see paragraph 38 above). Furthermore, the trial court examined the video record of the reconstruction of the events conducted on 24 June 2005, in the presence of the first applicant’s lawyer. It observed that the first applicant had no visible injuries and had been acting freely and giving detailed descriptions of how he had committed the crime in question. It was also noted in the judgment that, as confirmed by the case-file materials, the first applicant had been provided with the possibility to make handwritten comments and remarks in his questioning reports.45. The trial court relied on the following material evidence in convicting the first applicant: a pillow from the flat with traces of the deceased’s blood on it, as well as an axe and gloves with her blood and the first applicant’s fingerprints in that flat; the items seized from the applicants’ household on 23 June 2005 (see paragraphs 28 and 36 above); and the key of the victim’s flat and her bank card found on the first applicant. The court also heard a number of witnesses. One of them submitted that she had seen S. allow the first applicant use her bank card. Several neighbours of the victim stated that there had been a smell of rotting flesh coming from the flat of the deceased, about which they had complained to the first applicant. According to them, the latter had appeared nervous.46. It was noted in the judgment that the first applicant’s complaint of ill‑treatment by the police, confined to a vague allegation of “physical and psychological violence”, had been investigated and had been declared ill‑founded. During the hearing, the court questioned the principal investigator, who had arrested the first applicant.47. Lastly, the trial court observed a number of similarities between the murder, in respect of which the first applicant had already served his sentence (see paragraph 6 above), and that of S. Thus, the first applicant had abandoned the first victim’s body in the same river, not far from where he had dumped the corpse of S.48. It was noted in the judgment that the first applicant had thirty days to lodge an appeal on points of law starting from the date when the judgment was served on him.49. On 2 March 2006 a copy of the judgment was served on the first applicant.50. On 20 March 2006 the first applicant, who was no longer legally represented, lodged an appeal on points of law. He complained that he had been convicted in respect of crimes that he had not committed and that there was no conclusive evidence of his guilt. He alleged that he had incriminated himself “under physical and psychological duress” and under threats of rape. The first applicant alleged that he had been beaten in the Inguletskyy police station from 12.50 a.m. until 5 p.m. Having allegedly been threatened with rape, he had succumbed and had written a confession to the police. The first applicant noted that he had spent the night in a cell and that in the morning on 24 June 2005 he had been made to change into clean clothes brought by his mother. According to him, he continued to be afraid of being raped and had therefore maintained his confession even when represented by a lawyer. The first applicant further submitted that he had retracted his confession once the pre-trial investigation had been completed and his appointed lawyer had been replaced at his request. According to him, the investigation into his allegation of ill-treatment had been incomplete and superficial.51. On 17 June 2006 the first applicant submitted a request to be present during the hearing before the Supreme Court.52. On 24 July 2006 the Supreme Court rejected the above-mentioned request. It observed that, pursuant to Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 75 below), the time-limit for lodging such a request had been the same as for introducing an appeal on points of law (thirty days from the date of the service of the judgment on the first applicant). Given that the judgment of the trial court had been served on him on 2 March 2006 (see paragraph 49 above), the first applicant’s request had clearly been submitted out of time.53. On 15 August 2006, following a hearing with the participation of the prosecutor but in the absence of the first applicant or any person representing him, the Supreme Court upheld the judgment of 20 February 2006 and endorsed its reasoning. It held that the trial court had duly verified the first applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment and had rightly dismissed them as unfounded.54. The first applicant has not specified when the Supreme Court’s ruling was served on him. It appears from the case-file materials that he was informed of it on 5 December 2006 at the latest.The first applicant’s access to documents required for substantiation of his application before the Court55. According to the first applicant, on numerous occasions after the criminal proceedings against him were completed, he requested the trial court to provide him with copies of documents from his case file as required for substantiating his application before the Court. His requests were refused on the grounds that, firstly, he had already studied the case file in full (see paragraph 39 above) and, secondly, there was no legal basis for providing him with copies of documents from his case file. It was observed that the first applicant had already received copies of documents required by law (the bill of indictment and the judgment).56. The first applicant brought an administrative claim against the Deputy President of the trial court in respect of the above-mentioned refusals.57. On 21 May 2010 the Vinnytsya Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the first applicant’s claim. It concluded that the official’s refusals to provide the first applicant with the required copies of documents ran counter to the State’s obligations stemming from Article 34 of the Convention. Accordingly, the deputy president of the trial court was obliged to provide the first applicant with those copies. On 28 April 2011 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal quashed that ruling and rejected the first applicant’s claim. However, on 18 April 2013 the Higher Administrative Court quashed the appellate court’s ruling and upheld that of the first-instance court of 21 May 2010.58. The first applicant was provided with the requested copies of documents in 2013, which he confirmed in writing.Seizure of the second applicant’s mobile telephone and its retention by the investigator59. On 23 June 2005, following the first applicant’s arrest, the investigator seized, in particular, a mobile telephone from him. As it was eventually established, that telephone belonged to the second applicant, and her son had taken it on that day because his own telephone had not been charged. It was also later established that the investigator had requested the second applicant to bring the charger, which she did. The investigator explained to her that he needed to keep the telephone for some time.60. The verdict delivered by the Dnipropetrovsk Court in respect of the first applicant on 20 February 2006 did not mention the mobile telephone in question among the pieces of evidence. According to the second applicant, no procedural decision was ever taken in respect of that telephone.61. On 2 August 2007 the prosecutor returned to the second applicant her mobile telephone and its charger, and she wrote a receipt to that effect.62. The second applicant brought a civil claim against the investigator in respect of the delay in returning her mobile telephone.63. On 5 August 2008 the Inguletskyy Court refused to open proceedings following her claim, having concluded that it fell within the jurisdiction of the administrative rather than the civil courts.64. On 5 June 2009 the second applicant re-submitted her claim, this time before the administrative courts.65. On 8 June 2009 the Dnipropetrovsk Circuit Administrative Court refused to open proceedings, having concluded that the claim fell to be examined under criminal rather than administrative procedure.66. The second applicant complained about that matter to the prosecution authorities, but their constant reply was that there had been no violations of the law in her case.The first applicant’s correspondence with the Court67. On 20 July 2007 the Court received the first letter from the first applicant dated 12 July 2007, in which he complained, in particular: that he had been ill-treated by the police and that his complaints in that regard had not been duly investigated; that he had incriminated himself under duress and in the absence of legal assistance; and that he had not been present at the hearing before the Supreme Court. The first applicant noted that he had already sent a similar letter to the Court on 20 December 2006.68. The first applicant enclosed the following information note issued by the administration of the Ladyzhynska Prison in which he was detained at the material time:“According to the case-file materials, [the first applicant] did indeed apply to the European Court of Human Rights during his detention in the Dnipropetrovsk SIZO. That application was registered under no. P-714 of 20 December 2006.”69. Furthermore, according to the first applicant, on 16 February 2007 he had re-submitted his application to the Court from the Khmelnytskyy SIZO. However, it never reached the Court.70. On 24 December 2007 the first applicant sent a completed application form to the Court.71. The Government submitted that they were unable to provide any documents regarding the first applicant’s correspondence with the Court in 2005-2007 given that all the relevant records had been destroyed after the expiry of the mandatory period prescribed for their storage.RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICECriminal Code (2001)72. Under Article 115 § 2 (13), premeditated murder committed repeatedly (with some exceptions not applicable to the circumstances of the instant case) was punishable by imprisonment for a term of ten to fifteen years, or life imprisonment.Code of Criminal Procedure (1960, in force at the material time)73. Article 45 § 1 provided that legal representation during an inquiry, a pre-trial investigation and a trial before a court of first instance was obligatory if, inter alia, a life sentence was a possible penalty.74. According to Article 383 § 1, verdicts of appellate courts delivered at first instance could be reviewed under the cassation appeal procedure.75. Further relevant provisions concerning the cassation proceedings, including Article 391 (“Persons participating in the cassation proceedings”) are quoted in Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 2) (no. 15685/11, § 31, 1 June 2017).Code on the Enforcement of Sentences (2003)76. Article 113 of the Code on the Enforcement of Sentences (2003) stipulates that prisoners are allowed to correspond with relatives, other persons and organisations. All such correspondence, unless it is specifically exempted, is subject to automatic monitoring by the prison authorities.77. Prior to amendments introduced on 1 December 2005 and enacted on 21 December 2005, those exemptions had been limited to correspondence with the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights and prosecutors. The above-mentioned amendments exempted from monitoring all correspondence by prisoners addressed to the Court and other international institutions of which Ukraine was a member.78. Another round of amendments, which were introduced on 21 January 2010 and entered into force from 9 February 2010, added the following to the list of exemptions: (i) correspondence addressed to prisoners from previously exempt organisations and (ii) correspondence addressed to and received from prisoners’ lawyers.79. On 8 April 2014 correspondence between prisoners and all courts was added to the list of exemptions. That amendment was enacted on 7 May 2014.
