FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF RYABININ AND SHATALINA v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 33006/07)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

7 November 2019

This judgment is final, but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lado Chanturia, judges,

and Milan Blaško, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 15 October 2019,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 33006/07) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Valeriy Ivanovich Ryabinin (“the first applicant”) and Ms Yuliya Ignatyevna Shatalina (“the second applicant”), on 20 December 2006 or 12 July 2007 (the date is disputed in respect of the first applicant – see paragraphs 81 and 83 below) and 5 November 2009 respectively.

2. The applicants, who were granted legal aid, were represented by Mr A.S. Kychenok, a lawyer practising in Kyiv. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

3. The first applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been ill-treated by the police and that there had been no effective domestic investigation into the matter; that he had not received a fair trial; that his correspondence had been routinely monitored while he was in detention; and that he had been unable to obtain copies of all relevant documents from his case file in order to substantiate his application. The second applicant complained of the allegedly arbitrary seizure and retention of her property in connection with the criminal proceedings against her son and of the absence of an effective domestic remedy in that regard.

4. On 20 June 2018 notice of the above complaints was given to the Government, and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

THE FACTS

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The first applicant was born in 1965 and is serving a sentence of life imprisonment in Vinnytsya Prison no. 1. The second applicant is his mother. She was born in 1936 and resides in Kryvyy Rig.

Background events

6. On 13 November 2004 the first applicant was released from prison after serving a twelve-year sentence for murder.

7. In May 2005 he met S., and they began a relationship. Soon afterwards, S. sold her flat and moved into rented accommodation.

8. She was last seen alive on 12 June 2005.

9. On 17 June 2005 the police recovered a leg and an arm from the local Ingulets River, which were later identified as parts of S.’s body.

10.
On 23 June 2005, the remaining parts of the body and its severed head were recovered from the river near the applicants’ house.

Alleged ill-treatment of the first applicant and domestic investigation into the matter

11. On 23 June 2005, the first applicant was arrested on suspicion of murdering S. (see paragraph 29 below).

12. The first applicant alleged that he had been ill-treated by the police after his arrest and gave the following account of events. The police beat him with plastic bottles filled with sand and liquid in order to extract his confession to the murder of S. and the dissection of her corpse. When he refused, the ill-treatment allegedly continued until he fainted. Upon regaining consciousness, he realised that his trousers and underwear had been lowered and that an electric cable was attached to his testicles. Another electric cable was attached to his lower lip. The police applied an electric current to the first applicant, causing him to faint several times. The officers also threatened to rape him. Eventually, the first applicant gave in and wrote a confession dictated to him. A police officer gave him some vodka, after which he vomited. He was then placed in a cell with another inmate. The first applicant felt nauseous and vomited. He was taken to the toilet several times at his request. Following one such request, a police officer took him outside and shackled him to a motorcycle on a lorry. The first applicant spent the night outdoors, with cold water from a fire hose pouring over him the entire time.

13. On the morning of 24 June 2005, the first applicant was allegedly made to change into clean clothes brought by his mother at the investigator’s request. According to the first applicant, the clothes he had been wearing when arrested were stained with blood as a result of his ill-treatment. The investigator allegedly instructed the first applicant’s mother to destroy them, which she did.

14. According to the Government, the first applicant was not subjected to any physical or psychological coercion. They noted, however, that the documents relating to his detention at the Inguletskyy police station on 23 June 2005 had been destroyed in 2012 after the prescribed storage period had expired.

15. On 25 June 2005, a judge of the Kryvyy Rig Inguletskyy District Court (“the Inguletskyy Court”) remanded the first applicant in custody. According to the first applicant, he was not given an opportunity to complain about his ill-treatment, and the judge did not respond to the visible injuries on his face (which the first applicant did not specify).

16. On 1 July 2005, the first applicant was taken to the Kryvyy Rig pre-trial detention facility (SIZO), where he was examined by a doctor. According to the Government, the examination revealed no injuries. According to the first applicant, his injuries were not recorded.
He did not, however, specify the injuries.

17. On 25 August 2005 the first applicant complained to the Kryvyy Rig City Prosecutor’s Office that he had confessed to the murder “under moral coercion” from the investigator. He submitted that the investigator had told him what to say during the investigative measures, threatening harm to his relatives. Allegedly fearing for his mother and daughter and feeling depressed, the first applicant had complied with those instructions, even when represented by a lawyer.

18. On 14 September 2005 the Inguletskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (“the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office”), to which the above complaint had apparently been forwarded, informed the first applicant that his allegations had been investigated and found to be baseless.

19. On an unspecified date after 23 September 2005 (see paragraph 41 below), during the first applicant’s trial, he complained to the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Dnipropetrovsk Court”), which was hearing the case as a court of first instance, that he had been coerced into making self-incriminating statements (see paragraph 43 below). On 1 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court instructed the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the matter.

20. On 13 February 2006 the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office issued a ruling refusing to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers concerned, finding no indication that a criminal offence had been committed.

21. The first applicant challenged that refusal before the Inguletskyy Court. He submitted that on 23 June 2005 he had been subjected to “physical and psychological violence”. The first applicant stated that the clothes he had been wearing when arrested had been stained with his blood and that the investigator had therefore instructed his mother to bring him similar clean clothes and destroy the dirty ones. He further complained that law-enforcement officials had acted unlawfully by taking from him a sum of money and a mobile phone belonging to his mother.

22. On 16 March 2006 the Inguletskyy Court dismissed the first applicant’s complaint as unfounded. It noted that, apart from the vaguely worded allegation of “physical and psychological violence”, he had not specified the circumstances of his alleged ill-treatment. At the same time, the judge observed that, in his complaint against the prosecutor’s refusal, the first applicant had raised several new allegations that had not previously been verified. In particular, he additionally alleged that various procedural rules had been breached in connection with the seizure of certain valuables. Accordingly, in so far as his complaint concerned matters other than his alleged ill-treatment, the Inguletskyy Court forwarded it to the local prosecutor.

23.
On 14 April 2006 the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office issued another decision refusing to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers involved in the first applicant’s arrest and questioning, owing to the absence of the constituent elements of a crime. The officers had been questioned and denied any wrongdoing. It appears that the first applicant’s alleged ill-treatment was also addressed in that decision. Thus, the prosecutor referred to statements by the officers, who maintained that the first applicant had not resisted arrest and that immediately afterwards, during a conversation with the investigator, he had confessed to murdering S. and dissecting her body. The investigator also denied having threatened the first applicant with rape.

24. On 6 July 2006 the Inguletskyy Court upheld the above refusal.

25. On 6 September 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court upheld the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 16 March 2006 (see paragraph 22 above).

26. On 13 September 2006 it also upheld the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 6 July 2006 (see paragraph 24 above).

Criminal proceedings against the first applicant

27. On 23 June 2005, at 6 p.m., after retrieving fragments of a corpse from the river near the applicants’ house (see paragraph 10 above), the police searched the applicants’ household in the presence of the second applicant. They also recorded her explanations as follows. In May 2005 her son had begun a relationship with S., who had given him the key to her flat. Until 9 or 10 June 2005 S. had frequently visited the first applicant. As he later explained to his mother, S. had then left for Kyiv. On 16 or 17 June 2005 the first applicant had brought home a television set. The next day he had left with a handcart and returned some time later with a kitchen cabinet in it.

28. The police seized a hacksaw and four hacksaw blades, as well as the handcart, television set and kitchen cabinet mentioned by the second applicant. The first applicant was not at home at the time.

29. The investigator asked the second applicant to telephone her son and tell him to come to the Inguletskyy district police station, which she did. According to the first applicant, he believed that the request concerned the routine police supervision following his release from prison. He therefore went to the police station, where, at 7.20 p.m., he was arrested on suspicion of murdering S. The investigator stated in the arrest report that evidence of a criminal offence had been found at the first applicant’s home and that there was a risk that he might abscond or reoffend.

30. Shortly after his arrest on 23 June 2005, the first applicant provided written “explanations” to the chief of the Inguletskyy police department. The Government submitted a copy of them to the Court.
That document was handwritten in Russian over fourteen pages, in simple language and without any references to legal provisions (see paragraph 84 below). The first applicant confessed to murdering S. on 12 June 2005 and provided a detailed account of the events. He explained that they had had a dispute while intoxicated and that he had struck her several times on the head with the back of an axe. The first applicant stressed that he had not intended to hurt S. and that she had provoked him. He further stated that he could see her suffering and had realised that she would die anyway. To end her suffering, he had smothered her with a pillow. On 13 and 14 June 2005 he had dismembered the body and placed the parts in the refrigerator in the flat rented by S. He had subsequently drowned them in the nearby river. Following complaints from neighbours about unpleasant smells, the first applicant had sprayed several containers of air freshener in S.’s flat. He admitted taking some appliances and furniture from the flat and withdrawing money using the deceased’s bank card on 12, 13 and 15 June 2005. He stated that he was confessing of his own free will and regretted what he had done.

31. That same evening, the first applicant signed “a report on the familiarisation of the suspect with his defence rights”, containing extensive relevant quotations from the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure. He also wrote that he wished to be represented by a lawyer from his first questioning as a suspect.

32. On 24 June 2005 a lawyer was appointed to represent the first applicant.

33. On the same day, he was questioned as a suspect in the presence of his lawyer and repeated his confession.

34. Later on 24 June 2005, a reconstruction of the events was conducted in the lawyer’s presence. The first applicant maintained his confession. As can be seen from the numerous photographs included in the reconstruction report, the first applicant had no visible injuries.

35. On 25 June 2005 the Inguletskyy Court remanded the first applicant in custody pending trial. On the same day, he was questioned as an accused person in the presence of his lawyer and repeated his previous confessions. The first applicant also wrote in the interview report that he fully admitted his guilt.

36. On 10 August 2005 a forensic medical examination established that the victim’s body could have been dismembered using the hacksaw seized from the applicants’ household on 23 June 2005 (see paragraph 28 above).

37. On 23 August 2005 the first applicant underwent a forensic psychiatric examination to determine whether he could be held responsible for the criminal offence in question. During that examination, he repeated his confessions and raised no complaints. The experts concluded that the first applicant was aware of his actions and capable of controlling them.
The first applicant signed the above-mentioned examination report, noting that he had no statements or requests to make.

38. On 14 September 2005 the charges against the first applicant were amended. In addition to aggravated murder, he was charged with robbery and unlawful possession of weapons (a home-made gun and a nunchaku had been found at his home). The first applicant was questioned in the presence of his lawyer and maintained his confession. However, he disputed the charges of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons. The first applicant wrote in the interview report that he “partly” admitted his guilt. He stated that S. had given him her bank card herself and that he had killed her not for profit, but as a result of a dispute. The first applicant also wrote that he had kept the home-made weapons solely for self-defence.

39. On 15 September 2005 the pre-trial investigation was completed, and the first applicant and his lawyer were given an opportunity to examine the case file. According to the relevant report, the lawyer requested that the charges against the first applicant be dropped, without providing further details.

40. The following day, the investigator rejected that request on the ground that the case file contained sufficient evidence to establish that the first applicant had committed the crimes of which he was accused. Moreover, the investigator noted that the first applicant had not denied murdering S.

41. On 23 September 2005 the case was referred to the Dnipropetrovsk Court for trial.

42. On an unspecified date the charges against the first applicant were amended: he was charged with murder as a repeat offence and theft.

43. On 20 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court found the first applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. At the court hearing, the first applicant pleaded not guilty. He withdrew the confession he had made during the pre-trial investigation and alleged that it had resulted from torture. The first applicant submitted that he had last seen S. on 12 June 2005. Although he admitted using her bank card thereafter, he maintained that she had previously entrusted it to him. The first applicant also acknowledged taking some appliances and furniture from her flat because she “was not showing up”. Furthermore, he stated that he had been obliged to clean the flat and spray several containers of air freshener following the neighbours’ complaints about a bad smell.

44. The trial court did not find the first applicant’s submissions at the hearing plausible and instead relied on the statements in which he had confessed his guilt during his numerous questionings, first as a suspect and later as an accused, which had been conducted in the presence of his lawyer (see paragraphs 34, 35, 37 and 38 above). It noted that the first applicant had consistently maintained his confessions throughout the pre-trial investigation.
The Dnipropetrovsk Court noted, in particular, that, although he had denied the charges of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, he had nevertheless admitted to killing S., arguing that it had not been for profit but had resulted from a dispute (see paragraph 38 above). Furthermore, the trial court examined the video recording of the reconstruction of the events conducted on 24 June 2005 in the presence of the first applicant’s lawyer. It observed that the first applicant had no visible injuries, had acted freely, and had given detailed descriptions of how he had committed the crime in question. The judgment also noted that, as confirmed by the case-file materials, the first applicant had been given the opportunity to make handwritten comments and remarks in the records of his questioning.

45. In convicting the first applicant, the trial court relied on the following material evidence: a pillow from the flat bearing traces of the deceased’s blood, as well as an axe and gloves bearing her blood and the first applicant’s fingerprints in that flat; the items seized from the applicants’ household on 23 June 2005 (see paragraphs 28 and 36 above); and the key to the victim’s flat and her bank card found on the first applicant. The court also heard several witnesses. One of them stated that she had seen S. allow the first applicant to use her bank card. Several of the victim’s neighbours stated that there had been a smell of rotting flesh coming from the deceased’s flat, about which they had complained to the first applicant. According to them, he had appeared nervous.

46. The judgment noted that the first applicant’s complaint of ill-treatment by the police, limited to a vague allegation of “physical and psychological violence”, had been investigated and found to be ill-founded. During the hearing, the court questioned the principal investigator who had arrested the first applicant.

47. Lastly, the trial court identified a number of similarities between the murder for which the first applicant had already served his sentence (see paragraph 6 above) and the murder of S. In particular, the first applicant had abandoned the first victim’s body in the same river, not far from where he had disposed of S.’s corpse.

48. The judgment stated that the first applicant had thirty days from the date on which the judgment was served on him to lodge an appeal on points of law.

49. On 2 March 2006, a copy of the judgment was served on the first applicant.

50. On 20 March 2006, the first applicant, who was no longer legally represented, lodged an appeal on points of law. He complained that he had been convicted of crimes he had not committed and that there was no conclusive evidence of his guilt. He alleged that he had incriminated himself “under physical and psychological duress” and threats of rape.
The first applicant alleged that he had been beaten at the Inguletskyy police station from 12.50 a.m. until 5 p.m. Having allegedly been threatened with rape, he had given in and written a confession to the police. The first applicant stated that he had spent the night in a cell and that, on the morning of 24 June 2005, he had been made to change into clean clothes brought by his mother. According to him, he remained afraid of being raped and had therefore maintained his confession even when represented by a lawyer. The first applicant further submitted that he had retracted his confession once the pre-trial investigation had been completed and his appointed lawyer had been replaced at his request. In his view, the investigation into his allegation of ill-treatment had been incomplete and superficial.

51. On 17 June 2006 the first applicant requested permission to be present at the hearing before the Supreme Court.

52. On 24 July 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed that request. It noted that, under Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 75 below), the time-limit for lodging such a request was the same as that for introducing an appeal on points of law (thirty days from the date on which the judgment was served on the first applicant). Since the trial court’s judgment had been served on him on 2 March 2006 (see paragraph 49 above), the first applicant’s request had clearly been lodged out of time.

53. On 15 August 2006, following a hearing attended by the prosecutor but in the absence of the first applicant or anyone representing him, the Supreme Court upheld the judgment of 20 February 2006 and endorsed its reasoning. It found that the trial court had properly examined the first applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment and had correctly dismissed them as unfounded.

54. The first applicant has not indicated when the Supreme Court’s ruling was served on him. The case-file materials suggest that he was informed of it by 5 December 2006 at the latest.

The first applicant’s access to documents required to substantiate his application before the Court

55. According to the first applicant, on numerous occasions after the criminal proceedings against him had ended, he asked the trial court to provide him with copies of documents from his case file needed to substantiate his application before the Court. His requests were refused on the grounds that, first, he had already studied the case file in full (see paragraph 39 above) and, second, there was no legal basis for providing him with copies of documents from it. It was noted that the first applicant had already received copies of the documents required by law (the bill of indictment and the judgment).

56. The first applicant lodged an administrative claim against the Deputy President of the trial court concerning the above-mentioned refusals.

57.
On 21 May 2010 the Vinnytsya Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the first applicant’s claim. It found that the official’s refusals to provide the first applicant with the required copies of documents were contrary to the State’s obligations arising from Article 34 of the Convention. Accordingly, the deputy president of the trial court was required to provide the first applicant with those copies. On 28 April 2011 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal quashed that ruling and dismissed the first applicant’s claim. However, on 18 April 2013 the Higher Administrative Court quashed the appellate court’s ruling and upheld the first-instance court’s ruling of 21 May 2010.

58. The first applicant was provided with the requested copies of the documents in 2013, which he confirmed in writing.

Seizure of the second applicant’s mobile telephone and its retention by the investigator

59. On 23 June 2005, following the first applicant’s arrest, the investigator seized, among other things, a mobile telephone from him. As was eventually established, that telephone belonged to the second applicant, and her son had taken it that day because his own telephone was not charged. It was also subsequently established that the investigator had asked the second applicant to bring the charger, which she did. The investigator explained to her that he needed to retain the telephone for some time.

60. The verdict delivered by the Dnipropetrovsk Court in respect of the first applicant on 20 February 2006 did not list the mobile telephone in question among the items of evidence. According to the second applicant, no procedural decision was ever taken regarding that telephone.

61. On 2 August 2007 the prosecutor returned the second applicant’s mobile telephone and charger to her, and she signed a receipt to that effect.

62. The second applicant brought a civil claim against the investigator concerning the delay in returning her mobile telephone.

63. On 5 August 2008 the Inguletskyy Court refused to open proceedings in respect of her claim, having concluded that it fell within the jurisdiction of the administrative rather than the civil courts.

64. On 5 June 2009 the second applicant resubmitted her claim, this time before the administrative courts.

65. On 8 June 2009 the Dnipropetrovsk Circuit Administrative Court refused to open proceedings, having found that the claim was to be examined under criminal rather than administrative procedure.

66. The second applicant complained about the matter to the prosecution authorities, but their consistent response was that there had been no violations of the law in her case.

The first applicant’s correspondence with the Court

67.

4. On 20 June 2018 the Government were notified of the above complaints. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1965, the first applicant is currently serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison no. 1. The second applicant, his mother, was born in 1936 and resides in Kryvyy Rig.

Background events

6. On 13 November 2004 the first applicant was released from prison after completing a twelve-year sentence for murder.

7. He met S. in May 2005, and the two began a relationship. Soon afterwards, S. sold her flat and moved into rented accommodation.

8. S. was last seen alive on 12 June 2005.

9. On 17 June 2005 the police recovered a leg and an arm from the local Ingulets River. The remains were subsequently identified as body parts belonging to S.

10.
On 23 June 2005, the remaining body parts and the severed head were recovered from the river near the applicants’ home.

Alleged ill-treatment of the first applicant and the ensuing domestic investigation

11. On 23 June 2005, the first applicant was arrested on suspicion of murdering S. (see paragraph 29 below).

12. The first applicant alleged that, after his arrest, police officers had subjected him to ill-treatment. He gave the following account. To force him to confess to murdering S. and dismembering her body, the officers beat him with plastic bottles filled with sand and liquid. When he refused to confess, they allegedly continued until he lost consciousness. Upon coming round, he found that his trousers and underwear had been pulled down and that an electric cable had been attached to his testicles, while another had been fastened to his lower lip. The officers applied electric shocks, causing him to faint several times, and also threatened to rape him. He ultimately gave in and wrote out a confession dictated by the police. An officer then gave him vodka, after which he vomited. He was subsequently placed in a cell with another detainee, where he continued to feel nauseous and vomit. At his request, he was taken to the toilet several times. After one such request, an officer led him outside and handcuffed him to a motorcycle loaded on a lorry. He remained outdoors throughout the night while cold water continuously poured over him from a fire hose.

13. On the morning of 24 June 2005, the first applicant was allegedly required, on the investigator’s instructions, to put on clean clothes brought by his mother. He stated that the clothes worn at the time of his arrest had become stained with blood as a result of the ill-treatment. The investigator allegedly instructed his mother to destroy those clothes, and she complied.

14. The Government maintained that the first applicant had not been subjected to physical or psychological coercion. They noted, however, that the records relating to his detention at the Inguletskyy police station on 23 June 2005 had been destroyed in 2012 once the prescribed retention period had expired.

15. On 25 June 2005, a judge of the Kryvyy Rig Inguletskyy District Court (“the Inguletskyy Court”) ordered that the first applicant be remanded in custody. The first applicant asserted that he had not been afforded an opportunity to complain about the alleged ill-treatment and that the judge had failed to respond to the visible, though unspecified, injuries on his face.

16. On 1 July 2005, the first applicant was transferred to the Kryvyy Rig pre-trial detention facility (SIZO), where a doctor examined him. The Government stated that no injuries had been found, whereas the first applicant contended that his injuries had simply not been recorded.
He did not, however, identify the injuries in question.

17. On 25 August 2005, the first applicant complained to the Kryvyy Rig City Prosecutor’s Office that the investigator had subjected him to “moral coercion” to make him confess to the murder. He alleged that, under threats that his relatives would be harmed, the investigator had told him what to say during the investigative measures. Fearing for his mother and daughter and suffering from depression, he had allegedly complied with those instructions even in the presence of a lawyer.

18. On 14 September 2005, the Inguletskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (“the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office”), to which that complaint had apparently been transferred, informed the first applicant in writing that his allegations had been examined and found to be unsubstantiated.

19. During his trial, on an unspecified date after 23 September 2005 (see paragraph 41 below), the first applicant complained that he had been forced to make self-incriminating statements (see paragraph 43 below). He raised that complaint before the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Dnipropetrovsk Court”), which was hearing the case at first instance. On 1 February 2006, that court directed the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the allegation.

20. On 13 February 2006, the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office ruled that no criminal proceedings should be instituted against the police officers involved, as it had found no evidence of a criminal offence.

21. The first applicant contested that decision before the Inguletskyy Court, alleging that on 23 June 2005 he had been subjected to “physical and psychological violence”. He stated that the clothes he had been wearing when arrested were stained with his blood, prompting the investigator to tell his mother to bring him similar clean clothing and destroy the soiled garments. He also complained that law-enforcement officials had acted unlawfully by taking money from him, together with a mobile telephone belonging to his mother.

22. On 16 March 2006, the Inguletskyy Court rejected the first applicant’s complaint as unsubstantiated. It observed that, beyond his vaguely worded claim of “physical and psychological violence”, he had provided no details about the circumstances of the alleged ill-treatment. The judge nevertheless noted that, in challenging the prosecutor’s refusal, the first applicant had introduced additional allegations that had not previously been examined. In particular, he claimed that several procedural rules governing the seizure of certain valuables had been breached. Consequently, to the extent that the complaint raised matters other than the alleged ill-treatment, the Inguletskyy Court referred it to the local prosecutor.

23.
On 14 April 2006, the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office again declined to open criminal proceedings against the police officers involved in the first applicant’s arrest and questioning, finding no elements of a criminal offence. The officers had been interviewed and denied any misconduct. That ruling also appears to have addressed the first applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment. In particular, the prosecutor cited statements from the officers that the first applicant had not resisted arrest and that, in a conversation with the investigator immediately afterwards, he had admitted murdering S. and dismembering her body. The investigator likewise denied threatening the first applicant with rape.

24. On 6 July 2006, the Inguletskyy Court upheld that refusal.

25. On 6 September 2006, the Dnipropetrovsk Court affirmed the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 16 March 2006 (see paragraph 22 above).

26. On 13 September 2006, the Dnipropetrovsk Court also upheld the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 6 July 2006 (see paragraph 24 above).

27. At 6 p.m. on 23 June 2005, after recovering parts of a corpse from the river near the applicants’ home (see paragraph 10 above), the police searched their household in the second applicant’s presence. 32. A lawyer was appointed to represent the first applicant on 24 June 2005.

33. Later that day, he was interviewed as a suspect in the presence of his lawyer and repeated his confession.

35. On 25 June 2005, the Inguletskyy Court ordered that the first applicant be held in custody pending trial. He was questioned that day as an accused person, again in the presence of his lawyer, and reaffirmed his earlier confessions. In the interview record, he also wrote that he admitted his guilt in full.

37. On 23 August 2005, the first applicant was subjected to a forensic psychiatric assessment to determine whether he could be held criminally responsible for the offence concerned. During the assessment, he once again repeated his confessions and made no complaints. The experts found that he had understood his conduct and had been capable of controlling it.
The first applicant signed the aforementioned examination report, adding that he had no statements or requests to submit.

38. On 14 September 2005 the charges against him were amended. Alongside aggravated murder, he was accused of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, after a home-made gun and a nunchaku had been discovered at his residence. Questioned in the presence of his lawyer, the first applicant upheld his confession but disputed the robbery and weapons-possession charges. In the interview record, he wrote that he admitted his guilt “in part”. He maintained that S. had voluntarily given him her bank card and that he had killed her during a dispute, rather than for financial gain. He further stated that he had kept the home-made weapons solely for self-defence.

39. The pre-trial investigation concluded on 15 September 2005, after which the first applicant and his lawyer were allowed to examine the case file. According to the relevant report, the lawyer requested that the charges be dropped but provided no further details.

40. The next day, the investigator refused that request, finding that the case file contained sufficient evidence to establish that the first applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged. The investigator also noted that the first applicant had not denied killing S.

41. On 23 September 2005 the case was referred to the Dnipropetrovsk Court for trial.

42. At an unspecified later date, the charges were revised again, and the first applicant was charged with murder as a repeat offence and theft.

43. On 20 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court convicted the first applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. At trial, he pleaded not guilty, withdrew the confession he had given during the pre-trial investigation, and claimed that it had been extracted through torture. He stated that he had last seen S. on 12 June 2005. Although acknowledging that he had subsequently used her bank card, he insisted that she had previously entrusted it to him. He also admitted removing certain appliances and items of furniture from her flat because she “was not showing up”. In addition, he said that, following neighbours’ complaints about a foul smell, he had had to clean the flat and spray several containers of air freshener.

44. The trial court found the first applicant’s account at the hearing implausible. Instead, it relied on the confessions he had made during repeated questioning, initially as a suspect and later as an accused, in the presence of his lawyer (see paragraphs 34, 35, 37 and 38 above). The Dnipropetrovsk Court noted, in particular, that although the first applicant had contested the charges of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, he had acknowledged killing S. A number of the victim’s neighbours testified that the smell of decomposing flesh had emanated from the deceased’s flat and that they had complained about it to the first applicant, who, according to them, had appeared nervous.

46. The judgment recorded that the first applicant’s allegation of police ill-treatment, which consisted only of a general claim that he had been subjected to “physical and psychological violence”, had been investigated and found to be unsubstantiated. At the hearing, the court questioned the principal investigator who had arrested him.

47. Finally, the trial court identified several similarities between S.’s murder and the earlier murder for which the first applicant had already served a sentence (see paragraph 6 above). In particular, he had left the first victim’s body in the same river, close to the location where he had disposed of S.’s corpse.

48. The judgment stated that the first applicant had thirty days from the date on which it was served on him to lodge an appeal on points of law.

49. A copy of the judgment was served on the first applicant on 2 March 2006.

50. On 20 March 2006, by which time he was no longer represented by a lawyer, the first applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. He argued that he had been convicted of offences he had not committed and that no conclusive evidence established his guilt. He further alleged that he had incriminated himself “under physical and psychological duress” and following threats that he would be raped.
The first applicant claimed that he had been assaulted at the Inguletskyy police station from 12.50 a.m. to 5 p.m. He alleged that, after being threatened with rape, he had given in and written a confession for the police. He stated that he had spent the night in a cell and, on the morning of 24 June 2005, had been required to put on clean clothes brought by his mother. According to him, his continued fear of rape had led him to stand by the confession even after a lawyer began representing him. He further maintained that he had withdrawn the confession after the pre-trial investigation was completed and, at his request, his court-appointed lawyer was replaced. In his view, the investigation into his ill-treatment complaint had been cursory and incomplete.

Since the trial court’s judgment had been served on him on 2 March 2006 (see paragraph 49 above), his request was manifestly out of time.

On 15 August 2006, after holding a hearing attended by the prosecutor but not by the first applicant or any representative acting for him, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of 20 February 2006 and adopted its reasoning. 55. The first applicant stated that, following the conclusion of the criminal proceedings against him, he had repeatedly asked the trial court for copies of case-file documents necessary to support his application before the Court. Those requests were denied because he had already examined the entire case file (see paragraph 39 above) and because there was no legal basis for supplying him with copies of documents from it. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal set aside that judgment and dismissed the claim on 28 April 2011. On 18 April 2013, however, the Higher Administrative Court quashed the appellate decision and reinstated the first-instance judgment of 21 May 2010.

59. Following the first applicant’s arrest on 23 June 2005, the investigator seized several items from him, including a mobile telephone. It was subsequently established that the telephone belonged to the second applicant and that her son had borrowed it that day because his own telephone was not charged. It was also later determined that, at the investigator’s request, the second applicant had brought him the charger. He told her that the telephone would need to be retained for some time.

60. The Dnipropetrovsk Court’s verdict concerning the first applicant, delivered on 20 February 2006, did not list the mobile telephone among the evidence. The second applicant maintained that no procedural decision regarding the telephone had ever been issued.

61. On 2 August 2007, the prosecutor returned the mobile telephone and charger to the second applicant, who signed a receipt confirming their return.

62. The second applicant subsequently filed a civil claim against the investigator concerning the delay in returning her telephone.

63. On 5 August 2008, the Inguletskyy Court declined to institute proceedings, finding that the claim came within the jurisdiction of the administrative courts rather than the civil courts.

64. The second applicant lodged the claim again on 5 June 2009, this time before the administrative courts.

65. On 8 June 2009, the Dnipropetrovsk Circuit Administrative Court refused to open proceedings, holding that the claim had to be considered under criminal, not administrative, procedure.

66. The second applicant also raised the issue with the prosecution authorities, which repeatedly responded that no breach of the law had occurred in her case.

The first applicant’s correspondence with the Court

67.
On 20 July 2007, the Court received the first communication from the first applicant, in a letter dated 12 July 2007. He alleged, in particular, that the police had subjected him to ill-treatment and that his related complaints had not been properly investigated; that, without legal assistance and under duress, he had incriminated himself; and that he had not attended the hearing before the Supreme Court. He added that he had sent a similar letter to the Court on 20 December 2006.

68. The first applicant attached an information note from the administration of Ladyzhynska Prison, where he was being held at the relevant time. It stated:

“According to the case-file materials, [the first applicant] did indeed apply to the European Court of Human Rights while detained in the Dnipropetrovsk SIZO. That application was registered as no. P-714 on 20 December 2006.”

69. The first applicant further maintained that, on 16 February 2007, he had resubmitted his application to the Court from the Khmelnytskyy SIZO, but that it had never reached the Court.

70. On 24 December 2007, the first applicant forwarded a completed application form to the Court.

77. Before the amendments introduced on 1 December 2005 and brought into force on 21 December 2005, the only exemptions concerned correspondence with prosecutors and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights.
