15. On 25 June 2005, a judge of the Inguletskyy District Court of Kryvyy Rig (“the Inguletskyy Court”) ordered the first applicant’s detention on remand. The first applicant maintained that he had not been allowed to report the alleged ill-treatment and that the judge had ignored visible injuries to his face, which he did not specify.

16. On 1 July 2005, the first applicant was transferred to the Kryvyy Rig pre-trial detention centre (SIZO), where a doctor examined him. The Government stated that no injuries had been found, whereas the first applicant contended that his injuries had simply not been recorded.
He did not, however, provide details of those injuries.

17. On 25 August 2005, the first applicant lodged a complaint with the Kryvyy Rig City Prosecutor’s Office, alleging that the investigator had obtained his confession to the murder through “moral coercion”. According to him, the investigator had threatened to harm his relatives and directed him on what to say during the investigative procedures. Fearing for his mother and daughter and being depressed, the first applicant claimed that he had complied with those directions, including while assisted by a lawyer.

18. On 14 September 2005, the Inguletskyy District Prosecutor’s Office (“the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office”), to which that complaint had apparently been transferred, informed the first applicant in writing that his claims had been examined and found to be unsubstantiated.

19. At an unspecified time after 23 September 2005 (see paragraph 41 below), during his trial, the first applicant complained that he had been forced to make statements incriminating himself (see paragraph 43 below). He raised this complaint before the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal (“the Dnipropetrovsk Court”), which was hearing the case at first instance. On 1 February 2006, that court directed the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the allegation.

20. On 13 February 2006, after finding no evidence of a criminal offence, the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office decided not to open criminal proceedings against the police officers involved.

21. The first applicant appealed against that decision to the Inguletskyy Court. He alleged that on 23 June 2005 he had experienced “physical and psychological violence”. He stated that the clothing he had been wearing when arrested was stained with his blood; consequently, the investigator had told his mother to provide similar clean garments and destroy the bloodstained ones. He also alleged that law-enforcement officers had acted unlawfully by taking money from him, along with a mobile telephone belonging to his mother.

22. On 16 March 2006, the Inguletskyy Court rejected the first applicant’s complaint as lacking merit. It found that, beyond a vaguely formulated assertion of “physical and psychological violence”, he had given no details about the circumstances of the alleged ill-treatment. Nevertheless, the judge noted that his challenge to the prosecutor’s refusal included several new allegations that had not previously been examined. In particular, he additionally claimed that various procedural requirements had been breached when certain valuables were seized. The Inguletskyy Court therefore referred to the local prosecutor those parts of the complaint that concerned matters other than the alleged ill-treatment.

23.
On 14 April 2006, the Inguletskyy Prosecutor’s Office again declined to open criminal proceedings against the police officers involved in arresting and questioning the first applicant, finding that the constituent elements of a criminal offence were absent. The officers had been interviewed and denied any misconduct. That ruling also appears to have addressed the first applicant’s allegations of ill-treatment. In particular, the prosecutor cited statements from the officers indicating that the first applicant had not resisted arrest and that, immediately afterwards, during a conversation with the investigator, he had admitted murdering S. and dismembering her body. The investigator likewise denied threatening the first applicant with rape.

24. On 6 July 2006, the Inguletskyy Court upheld that refusal.

25. On 6 September 2006, the Dnipropetrovsk Court affirmed the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 16 March 2006 (see paragraph 22 above).

26. On 13 September 2006, the Dnipropetrovsk Court also affirmed the Inguletskyy Court’s decision of 6 July 2006 (see paragraph 24 above).

Criminal proceedings concerning the first applicant

27. On 23 June 2005, at 6 p.m., after recovering parts of a corpse from the river close to the applicants’ home (see paragraph 10 above), the police searched the applicants’ household in the second applicant’s presence. They also recorded her account. She stated that her son had begun a relationship with S. in May 2005 and that S. had given him a key to her flat. Until 9 or 10 June 2005, S. had frequently visited the first applicant. He subsequently told his mother that S. had gone to Kyiv. On 16 or 17 June 2005, the first applicant brought home a television set. The next day, he left with a handcart and returned after some time carrying a kitchen cabinet on it.

28. The police confiscated a hacksaw, four hacksaw blades, the handcart, the TV set and the kitchen cabinet mentioned by the second applicant. The first applicant was not at home during the search.

29. The investigator instructed the second applicant to call her son and ask him to report to the Inguletskyy district police station, and she complied. The first applicant stated that he believed the request concerned the routine police supervision imposed after his release from prison. He accordingly went to the police station, where he was arrested at 7.20 p.m. on suspicion of murdering S. In the arrest report, the investigator stated that evidence of a criminal offence had been found at the first applicant’s home and that he posed a risk of absconding or reoffending.

30. Soon after being arrested on 23 June 2005, the first applicant provided written “explanations” to the head of the Inguletskyy police department. The Government submitted a copy of that document to the Court.
The fourteen-page document was handwritten in Russian, used plain language and contained no references to any legal provisions (see paragraph 84 below). In it, the first applicant admitted murdering S. on 12 June 2005 and described the events in detail. He said that, while they were drunk, an argument had arisen between them and he had struck her several times on the head with the back of an axe. He stressed that he had not intended to harm S. and that she had provoked him. According to his account, he saw that she was suffering and understood that she would die in any event, so he smothered her with a pillow to end her suffering. On 13 and 14 June 2005, he dismembered her body and stored the body parts in the refrigerator of the flat rented by S. He later submerged them in a nearby river. After neighbours complained of an unpleasant smell, he sprayed several containers of air freshener inside S.’s flat. He further acknowledged taking furniture and household appliances from the flat and withdrawing money with the deceased’s bank card on 12, 13 and 15 June 2005. He declared that the confession was voluntary and expressed remorse for his actions.

31. That same evening, the first applicant signed “a report on the familiarisation of the suspect with his defence rights”, which reproduced extensive relevant passages from the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure. He also stated in writing that he wanted legal representation from the moment of his first questioning as a suspect.

32. A lawyer was appointed to represent the first applicant on 24 June 2005.

33. Later that day, he was interviewed as a suspect in his lawyer’s presence and repeated his confession.

34. A reconstruction of the events was also conducted on 24 June 2005 with the lawyer present. During it, the first applicant adhered to his confession. The numerous photographs attached to the reconstruction report show no visible injuries on him.

35. On 25 June 2005, the Inguletskyy Court ordered that the first applicant be held in custody pending trial. He was questioned that same day as an accused person, with his lawyer present, and again repeated his earlier confessions. In the interview report, he also wrote that he admitted his guilt in full.

36. On 10 August 2005, a forensic medical expert examination determined that the victim’s body could have been dismembered using the hacksaw seized from the applicants’ household on 23 June 2005 (see paragraph 28 above).

37. On 23 August 2005, the first applicant underwent a forensic psychiatric assessment to determine whether he could be held criminally responsible for the offence at issue. During the assessment, he once again repeated his confessions and made no complaints. The experts found that he had understood his conduct and had been capable of controlling it.
The first applicant signed the examination report referred to above, adding that he had no comments or requests.

38. On 14 September 2005 the charges against him were amended. Alongside aggravated murder, he was accused of robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, namely a home-made gun and a nunchaku discovered at his home. Questioned in his lawyer’s presence, he upheld his confession but disputed the robbery and weapons-possession charges. In the interview record, he wrote that he admitted his guilt “partly”. He claimed that S. had voluntarily given him her bank card and that he had killed her following a dispute, not for financial gain. He further stated that he had kept the home-made weapons solely for self-defence.

39. The pre-trial investigation ended on 15 September 2005, after which the first applicant and his lawyer were allowed to examine the case file. According to the corresponding report, the lawyer requested that the charges be discontinued but provided no further details.

40. The next day, the investigator dismissed that request, finding that the case file contained sufficient evidence that the first applicant had committed the offences with which he was charged. The investigator also observed that the first applicant had not denied killing S.

41. On 23 September 2005 the case was referred to the Dnipropetrovsk Court for trial.

42. On an unspecified date, the charges were revised again, and the first applicant was accused of murder as a repeat offence and theft.

43. On 20 February 2006 the Dnipropetrovsk Court convicted the first applicant on all charges and sentenced him to life imprisonment. At the hearing, he pleaded not guilty, withdrew the confession he had made during the pre-trial investigation, and alleged that it had been obtained through torture. He stated that he had last seen S. on 12 June 2005. Although he acknowledged subsequently using her bank card, he maintained that she had previously entrusted it to him. He also admitted removing certain appliances and furniture from her flat because she “was not showing up”. In addition, he said that neighbours had complained of a bad smell, forcing him to clean the flat and spray several containers of air freshener.

44. The trial court found the first applicant’s account at the hearing implausible. Instead, it relied on the admissions of guilt he had made during repeated questioning, first as a suspect and later as an accused, in the presence of his lawyer (see paragraphs 34, 35, 37 and 38 above). The court noted that throughout the pre-trial investigation he had consistently adhered to those confessions.
The Dnipropetrovsk Court noted, in particular, that although the first applicant had denied the robbery and unlawful possession of weapons charges, he had acknowledged killing S., maintaining that the killing had arisen from a dispute rather than being motivated by profit (see paragraph 38 above). The trial court also reviewed the video recording of the reconstruction carried out on 24 June 2005 in the presence of the first applicant’s lawyer. It found that he had shown no visible signs of injury, had behaved freely, and had described in detail how he had committed the offence at issue. The judgment further stated that the case-file materials confirmed that the first applicant had been given an opportunity to add handwritten observations and comments to the records of his questioning.

45. In finding the first applicant guilty, the trial court relied on the following physical evidence: a pillow from the flat bearing traces of the deceased’s blood; an axe and gloves found there that carried her blood and the first applicant’s fingerprints; the objects seized from the applicants’ home on 23 June 2005 (see paragraphs 28 and 36 above); and the victim’s flat key and bank card, which were discovered on the first applicant. The court additionally heard testimony from several witnesses. One witness stated that she had seen S. permit the first applicant to use her bank card. Several of the victim’s neighbours testified that the smell of decomposing flesh had been coming from the deceased’s flat and that they had complained about it to the first applicant. They said that he had appeared nervous.

46. According to the judgment, the first applicant’s complaint that the police had ill-treated him—consisting only of a general allegation of “physical and psychological violence”—had been investigated and dismissed as unfounded. At the hearing, the court questioned the principal investigator who had arrested him.

47. Finally, the trial court identified several similarities between S.’s murder and the murder for which the first applicant had previously served a sentence (see paragraph 6 above). In particular, he had left the first victim’s body in the same river, close to the location where he had disposed of S.’s corpse.

48. The judgment stated that the first applicant had thirty days from the date on which it was served on him to file an appeal on points of law.

49. The first applicant received a copy of the judgment on 2 March 2006.

50. On 20 March 2006, by which time he no longer had legal representation, the first applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. He argued that he had been convicted of offences he had not committed and that no conclusive evidence established his guilt. He claimed that he had incriminated himself “under physical and psychological duress” and because of threats that he would be raped.
The first applicant claimed that he had been assaulted at the Inguletskyy police station between 12.50 a.m. and 5 p.m. He alleged that threats of rape had compelled him to give in and write a confession for the police. He stated that he had remained in a cell overnight and that, on the morning of 24 June 2005, he had been required to put on clean clothing brought by his mother. He maintained that his continuing fear of rape had led him to stand by the confession even after a lawyer had begun representing him. He further asserted that, after the pre-trial investigation had ended and his court-appointed lawyer had been replaced at his request, he had withdrawn the confession. In his view, the inquiry into his ill-treatment complaint had been cursory and incomplete.

51. On 17 June 2006, the first applicant asked to attend the proceedings before the Supreme Court.

52. The Supreme Court dismissed that request on 24 July 2006. It noted that, under Article 391 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 75 below), a request of that kind had to be lodged within the same period applicable to an appeal on points of law, namely thirty days from the date on which the judgment was served on the first applicant. As the trial court’s judgment had been served on him on 2 March 2006 (see paragraph 49 above), his request was manifestly out of time.

53. Following a hearing on 15 August 2006, attended by the prosecutor but neither by the first applicant nor by anyone acting on his behalf, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of 20 February 2006 and adopted its reasoning. It found that the trial court had properly examined the first applicant’s ill-treatment allegations and had correctly rejected them as unsubstantiated.

54. The first applicant did not indicate when the Supreme Court’s decision had been served on him. The materials in the case file suggest that he had been notified of it no later than 5 December 2006.

The first applicant’s access to the documents needed to substantiate his application before the Court

55. The first applicant stated that, on many occasions after the criminal proceedings against him had concluded, he had asked the trial court for copies of case-file documents necessary to support his application before the Court. Those requests had been denied for two reasons: first, he had already examined the entire case file (see paragraph 39 above); and second, no legal provision entitled him to receive copies of documents from that file. It was also noted that he had already been given copies of the documents whose provision was required by law, namely the bill of indictment and the judgment.

56. In response to those refusals, the first applicant lodged an administrative claim against the Deputy President of the trial court.

57.
On 21 May 2010, the Vinnytsya Circuit Administrative Court granted the first applicant’s claim in part. It found that the official’s refusal to supply him with the requested document copies was incompatible with the State’s obligations under Article 34 of the Convention and therefore ordered the trial court’s deputy president to provide them. On 28 April 2011, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal set aside that judgment and dismissed the claim. On 18 April 2013, however, the Higher Administrative Court overturned the appellate judgment and reinstated the first-instance court’s decision of 21 May 2010.

58. In 2013, the first applicant received the requested copies and confirmed their receipt in writing.

The investigator’s seizure and retention of the second applicant’s mobile telephone

59. After the first applicant was arrested on 23 June 2005, the investigator seized, among other items, a mobile telephone from him. It was subsequently established that the device belonged to the second applicant and that her son had taken it that day because his own telephone was not charged. It was also later established that the investigator had asked the second applicant to bring in the charger, which she did. He told her that the telephone would need to be retained for a while.

60. The Dnipropetrovsk Court’s verdict concerning the first applicant, delivered on 20 February 2006, did not list the mobile telephone among the evidence. The second applicant maintained that no procedural decision concerning the device had ever been issued.

61. On 2 August 2007, the prosecutor gave the second applicant back both her mobile telephone and its charger, and she signed a receipt confirming their return.

62. The second applicant lodged a civil claim against the investigator over the delay in returning her mobile telephone.

63. On 5 August 2008, the Inguletskyy Court declined to institute proceedings on her claim, holding that it came within the jurisdiction of the administrative courts rather than the civil courts.

64. On 5 June 2009, the second applicant lodged the claim again, this time with the administrative courts.

65. On 8 June 2009, the Dnipropetrovsk Circuit Administrative Court refused to institute proceedings, finding that the claim had to be considered under criminal procedure instead of administrative procedure.

66. The second applicant raised the issue with the prosecution authorities, which repeatedly replied that no breach of the law had occurred in her case.

The first applicant’s correspondence with the Court

67.
The Court received the first applicant’s initial letter, dated 12 July 2007, on 20 July 2007. He alleged, in particular, that the police had ill-treated him and that his related complaints had not been properly investigated; that, under duress and without legal assistance, he had incriminated himself; and that he had been absent from the hearing before the Supreme Court. He stated that he had already dispatched a similar letter to the Court on 20 December 2006.

68. The first applicant attached an information note from the administration of Ladyzhynska Prison, where he was being held at the relevant time. It stated:

“The case-file materials confirm that [the first applicant], while detained in the Dnipropetrovsk SIZO, did apply to the European Court of Human Rights. The application was recorded under no. P-714 on 20 December 2006.”

69. The first applicant further maintained that he had sent his application to the Court again from the Khmelnytskyy SIZO on 16 February 2007, but that it had never arrived.

70. On 24 December 2007, he submitted a completed application form to the Court.

71. The Government stated that they could not produce any records relating to the first applicant’s correspondence with the Court between 2005 and 2007 because all relevant documents had been destroyed once the compulsory retention period had elapsed.

RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

Criminal Code (2001)

72. Article 115 § 2 (13) provided that repeated premeditated murder, subject to certain exceptions irrelevant to the present case, was punishable by imprisonment for ten to fifteen years or by life imprisonment.

Code of Criminal Procedure (1960, applicable at the relevant time)

73. Pursuant to Article 45 § 1, legal representation was mandatory during an inquiry, a pre-trial investigation, and proceedings before a first-instance court where, among other circumstances, life imprisonment was a possible sentence.

74. Article 383 § 1 provided that judgments delivered at first instance by appellate courts could be examined through cassation proceedings.

75. Additional pertinent rules governing cassation proceedings, including Article 391, entitled “Persons participating in the cassation proceedings,” are reproduced in Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 2) (no. 15685/11, § 31, 1 June 2017).

Code on the Enforcement of Sentences (2003)

76. Under Article 113 of the Code on the Enforcement of Sentences (2003), prisoners may exchange correspondence with relatives, other individuals, and organisations. Unless expressly exempted, all such correspondence is automatically monitored by the prison authorities.

77. Before the amendments introduced on 1 December 2005 and brought into force on 21 December 2005, the exemptions covered only correspondence with prosecutors and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights.
Under the amendments referred to above, all prisoners’ correspondence sent to the Court or to other international institutions of which Ukraine was a member was excluded from monitoring.78. Further amendments, adopted on 21 January 2010 and effective from 9 February 2010, extended the exemptions to include: (i) correspondence sent to prisoners by organisations already covered by the exemption and (ii) correspondence exchanged between prisoners and their lawyers.79. On 8 April 2014, correspondence between prisoners and all courts was also exempted; that amendment came into force on 7 May 2014.

original: FIFTH SECTIONCASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE(Application no. 17189/11) JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG11 June 2020 FINAL 11/09/2020 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Yonko Grozev, Alena Poláčková, Lәtif Hüseynov, Lado Chanturia, Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application against Slovakia and Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Afghan national, Mr M.S. (“the applicant”), on 16 March 2011;the decision to give notice of the complaints set out in paragraph 1 below to the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine and to strike out of the list and declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;the decision of the Section President to grant leave to intervene in written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2) to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovakian NGO;the decision not to have the applicant’s name disclosed;Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:INTRODUCTION1. The applicant complained that the Slovakian authorities, having arrested him after he had crossed from Ukraine, had failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, in violation of Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. They had then returned him to Ukraine, where he had been detained in inadequate conditions in disregard of his alleged status as a minor, in breach of Article 3. He had been unable to participate effectively in the proceedings concerning his detention, and had eventually been returned to Afghanistan in the absence of an adequate assessment of the risks he had faced there, in breach of Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Lastly, he alleged, under Article 34, that an NGO representative had been denied access to him in Ukraine, preventing him from lodging an application for an interim measure with the Court.THE FACTS2. The applicant lives in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, at the time the application was lodged, was employed by the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“the HIAS”) Representative Office in Ukraine.3. The Government of the Slovak Republic were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.4. The applicant alleged that he had been born in 1993 or 1994, whereas the authorities in Slovakia and Ukraine had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below). In support of his claim the applicant submitted to the Court, together with his application form, a photocopy of his Afghan identity document, in the original language, measuring 6 by 7 cm, and its “unofficial translation” into English by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to the translation, the field of the document marked “Date of birth and age” stated “age 8 years in year 2002”. The applicant also submitted to the Court a photograph which he considered showed that he looked like a teenager.The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia5. Prior to leaving Afghanistan the applicant lived in the Kunduz province, in the north of the country.6. According to the applicant, his father used to work with the National Security Department of Afghanistan. Having arrested some drug smugglers, he was killed in about 2005 by unknown people, possibly associated with the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. The applicant was unaware of its precise contents, but his uncle deduced that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and arranged for him to leave the country.7. Still according to the applicant, in May 2010 smugglers took the applicant to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. His passport was subsequently taken away by the smugglers. He then travelled onward to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He stayed in Moscow for one month and then entered Ukraine in early July 2010. He stayed in Kyiv for three months. During his journey to Ukraine the applicant was accompanied by his brother-in-law (his sister’s husband). In Ukraine the applicant and his brother-in-law separated. The brother-in-law managed to cross into Slovakia three days after the applicant, travelled to Spain and applied for asylum there.8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010 the applicant was arrested by the Slovakian border police while crossing into Slovakia illegally with three other Afghan nationals. He had no identity papers.9. According to records provided by the Government of Slovakia, at 7.25 p.m. on the same day the applicant was interviewed by border police officers to establish his identity and clarify the circumstances under which he had committed the offence of illegal entry to and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation from Slovak into English was provided. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently a member of the applicant’s group of Afghans, translated from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was noted as 14 January 1992. The applicant told the police that he wished to go to western Europe and live and work there, and that he was not requesting asylum in Slovakia.10. The record of the interview was signed by a police officer and the interpreter from Slovak into English, but not by the applicant or Mr Zazai. The Government of Slovakia submitted that the applicant had been asked to sign the record but had refused without providing a reason. By contrast, two other members of his group did sign similar records.11. On 24 September 2010 a decision to expel the applicant was issued. He was also banned from entering Slovakia for five years. He was given a Pashto translation of the guidelines on expulsion, summarising the relevant Slovakian legislation and procedures concerning expulsion of foreigners. According to the Government of Slovakia, the expulsion decision had been translated into Pashto. The document submitted by the Government is mainly in Pashto script. The parts containing general rules and quotes from legislation appear to be in that language, while certain case-specific details, such as the date and the country of destination, Ukraine, are written in Slovak.12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010 the applicant was handed over to the Ukrainian authorities.13. The applicant alleged that, throughout his time in Slovakia, he had not received any interpretation services or information about the asylum procedure in Slovakia and had had no access to a lawyer. As he spoke no European language, he had tried to ask for asylum with the help of a fellow Afghan who spoke some French. However, the Slovakian officials had not reacted. Despite his efforts to talk to them and to tell them that he was a minor, they had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. They had not provided him with any written decision concerning his return to Ukraine or explained to him any possible avenues of appeal.Return to Ukraine and detention there14. Following his expulsion to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was placed in the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He alleged that through other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had informed a guard, whom he had taken to be the supervisor, that he was fourteen years old. He also alleged that he had told a representative of Caritas, an NGO, that he was a minor and wished to apply for asylum, and that the Caritas representative had relayed that information to the border guards but that no action had been taken.15. According to the applicant, his conditions of detention in the Chop facility were unsatisfactory. The cells were overcrowded. Sometimes the detainees were not guaranteed daily exercise, and “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.16. On an unspecified date the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) issued an order directing the applicant to leave Ukraine voluntarily.17. On an unspecified date the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court, seeking the applicant’s forcible expulsion from Ukraine and his placement in detention pending expulsion. According to the court decision (see paragraph 18 below), the applicant agreed with the SBCS’s application. Also according to the court decision, on 1 October 2010 the SBCS and the applicant had asked the court to examine the case in their absence by way of a written procedure.18. On 13 October 2010 the court allowed the application and ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. The court stated that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992. It held that he had entered the territory of Ukraine illegally, had no means to return voluntarily and no relatives in Ukraine, and had crossed the border (with Slovakia) illegally. For the court, this showed that he was unlikely to comply with the order to leave the territory voluntarily.19. The court also referred to a United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”) publication entitled Сollection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН) published in February 2008, apparently in a Ukrainian translation. That publication has not been made available to the Court. According to the circuit court, the publication indicated that “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). It therefore concluded that in the event of return to Afghanistan, the applicant’s life would not be at risk. The court observed that the applicant had not lodged an application for asylum and did not wish to apply for asylum in Ukraine.20. According to the applicant, he was not aware of the proceedings, he did not have legal representation and did not understand his rights in the proceedings before the court. He had signed a document waiving his right to appear in court without understanding its contents. The court’s decision was not served on him and no information was provided to him on how to appeal. He therefore missed the ten-day time-limit for appeal (see the relevant provision of the domestic law in paragraph 37 below).21. On 14 October 2010 the applicant was transferred from the Border Guard temporary holding facility to temporary accommodation for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior at the time. He alleged that on arrival there, he had told the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. The officer allegedly informed the management of the facility but no action was taken.22. On 20 February 2011 the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv conducted a telephone interview with the applicant and on 22 February 2011 issued a travel document for him, indicating his date of birth as 14 January 1992.Asylum application in Ukraine23. On 19 October 2010 the applicant, along with three other Afghans, attended a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO, a local partner of the International Organization for Migration. One of the Afghans provided interpretation. Information on how to apply for refugee status was provided. The applicant did not contest that the session had been held, but stated that he had no recollection of it.24. On 23 February 2011 the applicant lodged an application for asylum in Ukraine. By way of reasoning he stated that he would be “immediately killed” if he were returned to Afghanistan.25. On 2 March 2011 an officer from the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”) interviewed the applicant concerning his asylum application. The applicant stated that in Afghanistan he used to live in Kunduz, had been studying and had been supported by his maternal uncle. When asked what had led him to leave Afghanistan, he stated that his father had been killed by the Taliban four years earlier and the Taliban had then started threatening him. His uncle had received a piece of paper, the contents of which were unknown to the applicant, and had said that the applicant had to leave the country. Afterwards, his uncle had obtained travel documents for him with which he had had no trouble leaving Afghanistan. The applicant was then asked what was his country of destination and responded that he wished to get to London where his sister lived. He explained that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan with his passport and an entry visa, but that the smugglers had then taken them away. He also stated that he had arrived in Ukraine from Russia and had travelled to the border with Slovakia through Kyiv. He had not sought help in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to get him to London where his sister was living.26. A questionnaire based on the same interview recorded the applicant’s answers to a number of standardised questions concerning his identity, history and background. It stated, in particular, that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992, that his mother tongue was Dari and that he also spoke Pashto.27. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the applicant’s asylum application as inadmissible (see paragraphs 34 and 35 below for the description of the two stages of the asylum procedure in Ukraine). The Regional Migration Service found that(i)  the facts on which his application was based were manifestly unfounded, as he could not be defined as a “refugee” under section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below);(ii)  since the applicant was not a member of any political, social or military organisation and had not been connected with any violent incidents associated with race, ethnicity, religion or political views, he did not qualify as a refugee under the Refugee Convention;(iii)  the fact that the country of origin had issued the applicant with a travel document demonstrated that he had benefited from protection in his country of origin, which, pursuant to Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, meant that the Refugee Convention did not apply to him;(iv)  the applicant had not applied for asylum while travelling through Tajikistan, Russia or Ukraine but had done so only after being returned from Slovakia to Ukraine. This showed that he had not intended to seek asylum in Ukraine but had meant to reach the United Kingdom, where his sister resided;(v)  since the applicant had no identity documents, it was not possible to identify him or his country of origin.Expulsion to Afghanistan28. According to the applicant, on 11 March 2011 in preparation for his expulsion to Afghanistan, he was transferred to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011 was notified to him.29. According to the applicant, on 12 March 2011, a Saturday, an NGO partner of the UNHCR attempted to contact him and other Afghan nationals facing expulsion to provide them with legal advice. However, it was denied access to them, preventing the applicant from applying for an interim measure with the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.30. On the same day the applicant was put on a train to Kyiv.31. On 14 March 2011 the applicant was expelled to Kabul.32. The applicant alleged that approximately three weeks after his expulsion to Afghanistan, some unknown people had looked for him at his home and left a threatening letter for him. His mother had arranged for him to leave Kunduz for Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. Since that time, he had been forced to change his place of residence frequently for fear of the people who had killed his father, and had been travelling frequently between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICERelevant domestic law in UkraineRefugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the material time)33. Under section 1 a refugee was defined as follows:“... a person who is not a citizen of Ukraine and who, due to a well‑founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality and is unable to avail himself of the protection of that country or, due to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of such protection, or who, not having a nationality and being outside the country of his former permanent residence, is unable or unwilling to return to it because of the said fear ...”34. Sections 12 to 14 and 16 of the Act provided for a two-stage asylum procedure: admissibility and merits stages. The regional migration services were responsible for examining the initial applications for asylum and decided on the admissibility. If a regional migration service found an application admissible, it instituted proceedings on the merits and made a recommendation to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions on the merits of the application. The Committee then took a final decision to grant or refuse asylum. Asylum-seekers could appeal against a negative decision taken by the regional migration service either to the Committee or to the courts. The lodging of an appeal constituted grounds for registration of the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.35. Section 12 provided that examination of an asylum application was to begin with an interview conducted in a language the asylum-seeker understood, if necessary with the assistance of an interpreter. An inadmissibility decision was to be taken if the applicant did not meet the definition of a refugee provided for in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above) or if an application was abusive: based on a false identity or lodged by an individual whose previous application had been rejected, unless circumstances had changed.Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)36. Section 32 of the Act laid down the procedure for expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It listed the grounds for compulsory expulsion, which included a serious breach of the legislation concerning foreign nationals and stateless persons, and provided that foreign nationals and stateless persons could be detained at temporary accommodation facilities for the period needed to organise their removal, which was not to exceed six months.Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)37. Under Article 186 of the Code an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the pronouncement of a judgment. If the judgment was delivered in writing, an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of receipt by the applicant of a copy of the judgment.International lawAgreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons38. The Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 2010, reads in the relevant parts as follows:Article 3Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons“1. The delegation noted that many foreign nationals lacked information on their legal status, the procedure applicable to them and their rights (including the right to lodge complaints). The internal regulations which were posted in the detention areas were, as a rule, available only in Ukrainian. Under the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are responsible for considering the initial applications for asylum and can decide on the admissibility. Regarding the quality of the asylum procedure, one of the main problems in Ukraine’s asylum management (as stated in paragraph 13 above) has been the constant reform of the asylum institutions which have been remodelled by successive governments, and in particular of the central executive body. FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11/09/2020

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Yonko Grozev,
Alena Poláčková,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Lado Chanturia,
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application against Slovakia and Ukraine submitted to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Afghan national, Mr M.S. (“the applicant”), on 16 March 2011;

the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, and to strike the remainder of the application out of the list and declare it inadmissible;

the decision of the Section President to grant the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovak NGO, leave to intervene in the written proceedings (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2);

the decision not to disclose the applicant’s name;

Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant complained that, after arresting him following his crossing from Ukraine, the Slovakian authorities had failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. They had subsequently returned him to Ukraine, where he had been held in inadequate conditions without due regard to his alleged status as a minor, in breach of Article 3. He had been unable to participate effectively in the proceedings relating to his detention and had ultimately been returned to Afghanistan without an adequate assessment of the risks he faced there, in breach of Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Lastly, he alleged under Article 34 that an NGO representative had been refused access to him in Ukraine, thereby preventing him from applying to the Court for an interim measure.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant resides in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, when the application was lodged, was employed by the Representative Office in Ukraine of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“HIAS”).

3. The Government of the Slovak Republic were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The applicant claimed that he had been born in 1993 or 1994, while the Slovakian and Ukrainian authorities had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
In support of his claim, the applicant submitted to the Court, together with his application form, a photocopy of his Afghan identity document in the original language, measuring 6 by 7 cm, and an “unofficial translation” into English prepared by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to that translation, the field marked “Date of birth and age” stated “age 8 years in year 2002”. The applicant also provided the Court with a photograph which he believed showed that he looked like a teenager.

The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia

5. Before leaving Afghanistan, the applicant lived in Kunduz province, in the north of the country.

6. According to the applicant, his father had worked with the National Security Department of Afghanistan. After arresting some drug smugglers, he was killed in about 2005 by unknown persons, possibly linked to the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. The applicant did not know its exact contents, but his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and arranged for him to leave the country.

7. Also according to the applicant, in May 2010 smugglers took him to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. The smugglers subsequently took his passport away. He then travelled on to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He remained in Moscow for one month before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He stayed in Kyiv for three months. During his journey to Ukraine, the applicant was accompanied by his brother-in-law (his sister’s husband). In Ukraine, the applicant and his brother-in-law parted ways. The brother-in-law managed to cross into Slovakia three days after the applicant, travelled to Spain and applied for asylum there.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, the applicant was arrested by the Slovak border police while illegally crossing into Slovakia with three other Afghan nationals. He had no identity documents.

9. According to records submitted by the Government of Slovakia, at 7.25 p.m. that same day the applicant was interviewed by border police officers to establish his identity and clarify the circumstances in which he had committed the offence of illegal entry into and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation from Slovak into English was provided. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently a member of the applicant’s group of Afghans, translated from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He told the police that he wished to travel to western Europe to live and work there and that he was not seeking asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record was signed by a police officer and the interpreter from Slovak into English, but not by the applicant or Mr Zazai.
The Government of Slovakia submitted that the applicant had been requested to sign the record but had refused without giving a reason. By contrast, two other members of his group signed similar records.

11. On 24 September 2010, a decision to expel the applicant was issued. He was also prohibited from entering Slovakia for five years. He was provided with a Pashto translation of the expulsion guidelines, summarising the relevant Slovak legislation and procedures concerning the expulsion of foreigners. According to the Government of Slovakia, the expulsion decision had been translated into Pashto. The document submitted by the Government is predominantly in Pashto script. The sections setting out general rules and quotations from legislation appear to be in that language, while certain case-specific information, such as the date and the destination country, Ukraine, is written in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010, the applicant was handed over to the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant alleged that throughout his time in Slovakia he had not received any interpretation services or information about the asylum procedure in Slovakia and had had no access to a lawyer. As he spoke no European language, he had attempted to request asylum with the assistance of a fellow Afghan who spoke some French. However, the Slovakian officials had not responded. Despite his attempts to speak to them and inform them that he was a minor, they had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. They had not provided him with any written decision regarding his return to Ukraine or explained any possible avenues of appeal.

Return to Ukraine and detention there

14. Following his expulsion to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was placed in the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He alleged that, through other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had informed a guard whom he believed to be the supervisor that he was fourteen years old. He also claimed that he had told a representative of Caritas, an NGO, that he was a minor and wished to apply for asylum, and that the Caritas representative had passed that information on to the border guards, but no action had been taken.

15. According to the applicant, the conditions of detention in the Chop facility were inadequate. The cells were overcrowded. At times, the detainees were not guaranteed daily exercise and “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. On an unspecified date, the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) issued an order requiring the applicant to leave Ukraine voluntarily.

17. On an unspecified date, the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court, seeking the applicant’s forcible expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. According to the court’s decision (see paragraph 18 below), the applicant agreed to the SBCS’s application.
According to the court decision, on 1 October 2010 the SBCS and the applicant had also asked the court to consider the case in their absence by way of written procedure.

18. On 13 October 2010 the court granted the application and ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. The court stated that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992. It found that he had entered Ukraine illegally, had no means to return voluntarily and no relatives in Ukraine, and had crossed the border with Slovakia illegally. In the court’s view, this demonstrated that he was unlikely to comply with an order to leave the territory voluntarily.

19. The court further referred to a publication by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”) entitled Collection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН), published in February 2008, apparently in a Ukrainian translation. That publication has not been submitted to the Court. According to the circuit court, it indicated that “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). The court therefore concluded that the applicant’s life would not be at risk if he returned to Afghanistan. It noted that the applicant had not lodged an asylum application and did not wish to seek asylum in Ukraine.

20. According to the applicant, he had been unaware of the proceedings, had no legal representation and did not understand his rights before the court. He had signed a document waiving his right to appear in court without understanding its contents. The court’s decision was not served on him, and he was given no information on how to appeal. As a result, he missed the ten-day time-limit for lodging an appeal (see the relevant provision of domestic law in paragraph 37 below).

21. On 14 October 2010 the applicant was transferred from the Border Guard temporary holding facility to temporary accommodation for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, which was then under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior. He alleged that, upon arrival, he had told the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. The officer allegedly notified the facility’s management, but no action was taken.

22. On 20 February 2011 the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv conducted a telephone interview with the applicant and, on 22 February 2011, issued him a travel document indicating his date of birth as 14 January 1992.

Asylum application in Ukraine

23. On 19 October 2010 the applicant, together with three other Afghans, attended a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO that was a local partner of the International Organization for Migration.
One of the Afghans acted as an interpreter. Information on how to apply for refugee status was given. The applicant did not dispute that the session had taken place, but stated that he had no recollection of it.

24. On 23 February 2011, the applicant lodged an asylum application in Ukraine. By way of reasoning, he stated that he would be “immediately killed” if returned to Afghanistan.

25. On 2 March 2011, an officer from the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”) interviewed the applicant regarding his asylum application. The applicant stated that he had lived in Kunduz, Afghanistan, where he had been studying and supported by his maternal uncle. When asked what had prompted him to leave Afghanistan, he stated that his father had been killed by the Taliban four years earlier and that the Taliban had subsequently begun threatening him. His uncle had received a piece of paper, the contents of which were unknown to the applicant, and had said that the applicant had to leave the country. His uncle had then obtained travel documents for him, with which he had had no difficulty leaving Afghanistan. The applicant was asked about his intended destination and replied that he wished to reach London, where his sister lived. He explained that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan using his passport and an entry visa, but that the smugglers had later taken them away. He also stated that he had entered Ukraine from Russia and travelled through Kyiv to the border with Slovakia. He had not sought assistance in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to take him to London, where his sister lived.

26. A questionnaire completed on the basis of the same interview recorded the applicant’s responses to a number of standardised questions concerning his identity, history and background. It stated, in particular, that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992, that Dari was his mother tongue and that he also spoke Pashto.

27. On 9 March 2011, the Regional Migration Service rejected the applicant’s asylum application as inadmissible (see paragraphs 34 and 35 below for a description of the two stages of the asylum procedure in Ukraine). The Regional Migration Service found that (i) the facts on which his application was based were manifestly unfounded, as he could not be regarded as a “refugee”
under section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below); (ii) since the applicant was not a member of any political, social or military organisation and had not been linked to any violent incidents associated with race, ethnicity, religion or political views, he did not qualify as a refugee under the Refugee Convention; (iii) the fact that the country of origin had provided the applicant with a travel document demonstrated that he had benefited from its protection, which, under Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, meant that the Convention did not apply to him; (iv) the applicant had not sought asylum while travelling through Tajikistan, Russia or Ukraine, but had done so only after being returned from Slovakia to Ukraine. This indicated that he had not intended to seek asylum in Ukraine, but had planned to reach the United Kingdom, where his sister lived; (v) as the applicant had no identity documents, it was not possible to establish his identity or country of origin.

Expulsion to Afghanistan

28. According to the applicant, on 11 March 2011, in preparation for his expulsion to Afghanistan, he was transferred to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where he was notified of the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011.

29. According to the applicant, on 12 March 2011, a Saturday, an NGO partner of the UNHCR tried to contact him and other Afghan nationals facing expulsion in order to provide them with legal advice. However, it was denied access to them, thereby preventing the applicant from applying to the Court for an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.

30. On the same day, the applicant was placed on a train to Kyiv.

31. On 14 March 2011, the applicant was expelled to Kabul.

32. The applicant alleged that about three weeks after his expulsion to Afghanistan, unknown individuals had searched for him at his home and left him a threatening letter. His mother had arranged for him to leave Kunduz for Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. Since then, he had been forced to change his place of residence frequently for fear of the people who had killed his father, and had travelled regularly between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant domestic law in Ukraine

Refugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the relevant time)

33. Section 1 defined a refugee as follows:

“... a person who is not a citizen of Ukraine and who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality and is unable to avail himself of that country’s protection or, owing to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of such protection, or who, being stateless and outside the country of his former permanent residence, is unable or unwilling to return to it because of the aforementioned fear ...”

34.
Sections 12 to 14 and 16 of the Act established a two-stage asylum procedure: admissibility and merits stages. The regional migration services were responsible for examining initial asylum applications and deciding on their admissibility. If a regional migration service found an application admissible, it opened proceedings on the merits and submitted a recommendation on the merits of the application to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions. The Committee then made a final decision to grant or refuse asylum. Asylum-seekers could appeal a negative decision by the regional migration service either to the Committee or to the courts. Lodging an appeal constituted grounds for registering the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.

35. Section 12 provided that the examination of an asylum application was to begin with an interview conducted in a language understood by the asylum-seeker, with the assistance of an interpreter if necessary. A decision of inadmissibility was to be taken if the applicant did not meet the definition of a refugee set out in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above) or if the application was abusive: based on a false identity or lodged by an individual whose previous application had been rejected, unless the circumstances had changed.

Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)

36. Section 32 of the Act set out the procedure for the expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It specified the grounds for compulsory expulsion, including a serious breach of the legislation concerning foreign nationals and stateless persons, and provided that they could be detained in temporary accommodation facilities for the period required to organise their removal, which was not to exceed six months.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)

37. Under Article 186 of the Code, an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the pronouncement of a judgment. If the judgment was issued in writing, an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the applicant’s receipt of a copy of the judgment.

International law

Agreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons

38. The Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 2010, provides in the relevant parts as follows:

Article 3

Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons

“1. The requested State, upon application by the requesting State and without any further formalities other than those provided for in this Agreement, shall readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons who do not, or no longer, fulfil the conditions in force for entry into or stay on the territory of the requesting State, provided that ...”
such persons: ...(a) had illegally entered the territory of the Member States directly from the territory of Ukraine, or had illegally entered the territory of Ukraine directly from the territory of the Member States;”

Relevant international materials concerning the situation in Slovakia and Ukraine

European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”)

39. The report on the CPT’s 2007 visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), published on 19 May 2009, states in the relevant parts as follows:

“A. Establishments under the authority of the State Border Service

...

39. As regards access to a lawyer, it was limited to visits by pro bono lawyers from NGOs, who assisted foreign nationals in filing asylum applications and provided them with information about the relevant legal procedures. However, the delegation was concerned to learn that, at Chop, NGO lawyers had restricted access to detained persons (i.e. they could meet only persons whose names they already knew). It should also be noted that the provision of legal advice was hampered by the lack of proper interpretation at Border Guard detention facilities (see also paragraph 41).

...

40. The delegation observed that many foreign nationals lacked information about their legal status, the procedure applicable to them and their rights (including the right to lodge complaints). As a rule, the internal regulations posted in the detention areas were available only in Ukrainian. Some other informational materials (e.g. the Law on refugees) were also available, but only in French or Russian; Border Guard staff stated that they had run out of materials in other languages. A positive feature was the involvement of NGOs in providing assistance and information to foreign nationals, pursuant to agreements with the State Border Service. However, the fact that external bodies were assisting foreign detainees does not relieve the State of its responsibility to provide information and assistance to those detainees.

The main complaint of detained foreign nationals was that they did not know what was happening in their case or how long they would remain in custody. This uncertainty significantly aggravated the experience of confinement and created tensions. The observations made during the visit indicate that Border Guard staff need to be more attentive to these concerns.

41. With regard to interpretation, several detained foreign nationals complained that, after being apprehended, they had been asked to sign documents in Ukrainian without understanding their contents. Even when interpretation had been provided, the information given was allegedly not always comprehensible.
The delegation was informed that there was a shortage of local interpreters for less common languages; to address the problem, plans were under way to establish distance-interpretation facilities at the main border units.

Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)

40. The UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers, dated October 2007, states, in so far as relevant:

“13. Under the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are responsible for examining initial asylum applications and deciding on their admissibility. If the Regional Migration Service decides to admit a case to the procedure, it will then consider the merits and make a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then issues a decision on the case. It may approve the RMS recommendation or adopt a different approach. Asylum-seekers may appeal a negative decision by the Regional Migration Service either to the SCNR or to the courts.

...

31. As regards the quality of the asylum procedure, one of the main problems in Ukraine’s asylum management (as noted in paragraph 13 above) has been the continual reform of asylum institutions, which have been reorganized by successive governments, particularly the central executive body. In March 2007, by decree of the Cabinet of Ministers (No. 201), the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions (formerly the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration) became the authorized central executive body responsible for asylum issues. Its activities are directed and coordinated by the Cabinet of Ministers through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine.

...

42. As concerns reception standards, neither asylum-seekers nor refugees have adequate access to State-sponsored accommodation, material support or employment. Under Article 20 of the Refugee Law, only recognized refugees are eligible for financial assistance and accommodation. Ukraine currently has only one operational temporary accommodation centre for asylum-seekers and refugees, with a capacity of up to 250 places. Under Article 7 of the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services should designate places for temporary accommodation and generally facilitate the provision of housing to refugees and asylum-seekers. In practice, however, they are unable to provide such services. Refugees and asylum-seekers must instead rent accommodation from private owners. As ‘foreigners’, they are asked to pay rents much higher than those charged to nationals. Private rents, particularly in cities, are high and continue to rise. Consequently, many refugees are forced to spend nearly all their income on accommodation. Many remain homeless or live in substandard conditions, putting their physical and psychological health at risk.

...

46.
The overall situation prompts some asylum-seekers to try to leave in search of better protection elsewhere. They are often apprehended while attempting to cross Ukraine’s western border illegally. Detention has consequently been increasing. Although detention conditions have improved in recent years, they remain poor because of the ever-growing number of irregular migrants and the State’s difficulty in coping with these increased numbers. Asylum-seekers are detained together with other foreigners and remain in detention for prolonged periods. This type of administrative detention may amount to a denial of the right to seek asylum....52. ... UNHCR advises States to refrain from returning third-country asylum-seekers to Ukraine, as at present no assurances can be given that the persons concerned: a) would be readmitted, b) would have access to a fair and efficient refugee status determination procedure, c) would be treated in accordance with international refugee standards, or d) would have effective protection against refoulement.”

Human Rights Watch

41. In a 124-page report published in December 2010, entitled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) presented the results of its research into the experiences of migrants and asylum-seekers returned to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.

42. According to the report, most of the fifty people interviewed who had been returned to Ukraine from Slovakia or Hungary said that they had requested asylum upon arrival in Slovakia or Hungary, but that their requests had been disregarded and they had been swiftly expelled back to Ukraine.

43. The report deplores the fact that, in December 2009, the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior terminated an agreement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League which, since 2007, had allowed NGO lawyers to monitor return procedures at the border.

44. Regarding the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, the report notes that many of the concerns previously raised by HRW have been addressed. In particular, material conditions at the centres have improved; all the facilities visited by HRW in 2010 appeared clean and well ordered, and none were overcrowded. Most detainees interviewed in most locations had no complaints about poor hygiene or overcrowding. However, former detainees at the temporary detention facility in Chop indicated that the institution was sometimes overcrowded. The most common complaints concerned the quality and quantity of food and the lack of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet, and television. HRW also observed that certain other problems persisted, particularly access to the asylum procedure, the detention of children, the mixing of children with adults, corruption, and the disproportionate use of migrant detention in general.

45.
According to the report, migration detainees in Ukraine lacked consistent and predictable access to a judge or other authority. Nor did they have access to legal representation that would enable them to challenge their detention. Moreover, there was generally no individualised assessment of whether the detention of migrants or asylum-seekers was necessary.

Relevant international materials concerning the situation in Afghanistan

46. The UNHCR’s Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Asylum-Seekers from Afghanistan, published on 17 December 2010, stated, insofar as relevant:

“I. Introduction

...

UNHCR considers that individuals with the profiles set out below require a particularly careful examination of possible risks. These risk profiles, while not necessarily exhaustive, include (i) individuals associated with, or perceived as supportive of, the Afghan Government...

In view of the worsening security environment in certain parts of the country and the increasing number of civilian casualties, UNHCR considers that the situation may be characterised as one of generalised violence in Helmand, Kandahar, Kunar, and parts of Ghazni and Khost provinces. Accordingly, Afghan asylum-seekers who formerly resided in these areas may require international protection under broader international protection criteria, including complementary forms of protection. In addition, given the fluid and volatile nature of the conflict, asylum applications by Afghans claiming to be fleeing generalised violence in other parts of Afghanistan should be assessed carefully on an individual basis, in light of the evidence presented by the applicant and other current and reliable information concerning the place of former residence. This determination will necessarily include an assessment of whether a situation of generalised violence exists in the place of former residence at the time of adjudication.

UNHCR generally considers internal flight to be a reasonable alternative where protection is available from the individual’s own extended family, community, or tribe in the area of prospective relocation. Single males and nuclear family units may, in some circumstances, subsist without family or community support in urban and semi-urban areas with established infrastructure and under effective Government control. Given the breakdown of the country’s traditional social fabric caused by decades of war, massive refugee flows, and increasing internal migration to urban areas, a case-by-case analysis will nevertheless be required.

...

III. Eligibility for International Protection

...

A. Potential Risk Profiles

1.
Individuals Associated with, or Perceived as Supporting, the Government and the International Community, Including the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF)

There is a systematic and ongoing campaign by armed anti-Government groups to target civilians associated with, or perceived as supportive of, the Afghan Government or the international community, particularly in areas where such groups operate....

Most targeted attacks on civilians by armed anti-Government groups have taken place in the groups’ strongholds. However, targeted assassinations and executions of civilians have also increased in other parts of the country previously regarded as more secure. In the south-eastern and central regions, the number of assassinations and executions allegedly carried out by armed anti-Government groups in 2010 increased compared with 2009. Such targeted attacks rose sharply in parts of the southern region, particularly in Kandahar, where the Taliban have conducted a systematic, targeted assassination campaign since the beginning of 2010. From June to mid-September 2010, an average of 21 assassinations per week was recorded—compared with seven per week during the same period in 2009—mostly in the southern and south-eastern regions.

UNHCR considers that individuals associated with, or perceived as supportive of, the Government and the international community and forces—including Government officials, Government-aligned tribal and religious leaders, judges, teachers, and workers on reconstruction and development projects—may, depending on the particular circumstances of the case, face risk on account of their actual or imputed political opinion, especially in areas where armed anti-Government groups operate or exercise control....

B. Eligibility Under Broader International Protection Criteria, Including Complementary Forms of Protection...

1. Civilian casualties...

In the first half of 2010, suicide attacks caused 183 civilian deaths, more than half of them in the southern region. This represents a 20 percent increase over the same period in 2009.

Although armed anti-Government groups primarily targeted military objectives during the first half of 2010, IED and suicide-attack tactics were also employed in civilian areas, including on roads used by civilians, near government buildings, outside hotels, in crowded markets, and in commercial areas.

Despite sustained efforts over the last decade to clear mines and unexploded ordnance (UXO), and a steady decline in the number of Afghan victims, mines and explosive remnants cause an average of 42 casualties each month, the vast majority of whom are children.
In addition to causing loss of life and serious injury, mine contamination has impeded livelihood activities, including by blocking access to agricultural land, water, healthcare and education.256 A further analysis by UNHCR of reported incidents involving civilian casualties during the period from 1 July 2010 to 8 October 2010 reveals that the provinces most affected by indiscriminate conflict-related violence are Helmand and Kandahar in the southern region and Kunduz in the north-eastern region....

3. Conflict-Induced Displacements and Voluntary Returns

Increasing insecurity and violence in certain parts of Afghanistan, resulting from fighting between anti-Government groups and pro-Government forces, continue to cause significant population displacement. The number of conflict-induced IDPs continues to increase, with displacement occurring largely in the southern and western regions of Afghanistan....

While conflict-induced displacement in Afghanistan has increased, it should also be noted that voluntary returns, particularly from Pakistan and Iran, are rising. Between March and October 2010, more than 100,000 Afghans returned, twice the number recorded during the same period in 2009. There are several reasons for return, including: (i) the perception that the security situation in some provinces has improved; (ii) economic factors; and (iii) increased insecurity and natural disasters in former settlement areas in Pakistan. While thousands of Afghans returned to their home areas, nearly one third currently live in informal IDP settlements or urban areas in Afghanistan. Some of these settlements are located in the provinces of Nagarhar, Laghman and Kunar, which continue to experience fluctuating but significant levels of civilian casualties and security incidents. It should be noted that many returns are taking place amid deteriorating conditions for Afghans outside the country, rather than significant improvements in security and human rights conditions in Afghanistan.”
