FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11/09/2020

Under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment has become final. It may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Yonko Grozev,
Alena Poláčková,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Lado Chanturia,
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application (no. 17189/11) brought against Slovakia and Ukraine before the Court on 16 March 2011 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr M.S., an Afghan national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, and to strike the remaining complaints out of the list or declare them inadmissible;

the Section President’s decision, pursuant to Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2, to allow the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovakian non-governmental organisation, to intervene in the written proceedings;

the decision to withhold the applicant’s name;

Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant alleged that, after arresting him following his crossing from Ukraine, the Slovakian authorities had not told him why he had been arrested, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. He was subsequently sent back to Ukraine, where, allegedly without regard to his claimed status as a minor, he was held in inadequate conditions, in violation of Article 3. He further maintained that he had been unable to participate effectively in the proceedings relating to his detention and that he had ultimately been returned to Afghanistan without a sufficient examination of the risks awaiting him there. In his view, those circumstances breached Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Finally, relying on Article 34, he complained that the Ukrainian authorities had refused an NGO representative access to him, thereby preventing him from applying to the Court for an interim measure.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant resides in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, when the application was submitted, worked for the Representative Office of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“HIAS”) in Ukraine.

3. Ms M. Pirošíková, acting as Agent, represented the Government of the Slovak Republic. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. According to the applicant, he was born in either 1993 or 1994. The Slovakian and Ukrainian authorities, however, registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
To substantiate his claim, the applicant enclosed with his application to the Court a photocopy, measuring 6 by 7 cm, of his Afghan identity document in the original language. He also provided an “unofficial translation” into English prepared by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. The translation indicated that the entry under “Date of birth and age” read “age 8 years in year 2002”. In addition, the applicant submitted a photograph which, in his view, showed that he appeared to be a teenager.

The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia

5. Before leaving Afghanistan, the applicant lived in Kunduz province in the north of the country.

6. The applicant stated that his father had worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department. After arresting several drug smugglers, his father was killed in or around 2005 by unidentified individuals who may have been associated with the Taliban. In 2010, the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. Although the applicant did not know its exact contents, his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and arranged for him to leave Afghanistan.

7. According to the applicant, smugglers took him to Tajikistan in May 2010, and he crossed the border using his passport. The smugglers subsequently confiscated the passport. He continued through Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia, spending one month in Moscow before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He then remained in Kyiv for three months. The applicant was accompanied on the journey to Ukraine by his brother-in-law, his sister’s husband, but they separated after arriving there. The brother-in-law crossed into Slovakia three days after the applicant, proceeded to Spain and applied for asylum there.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, the Slovakian border police arrested the applicant as he illegally entered Slovakia together with three other Afghan nationals. He was not carrying any identity documents.

9. Records submitted by the Slovak Government show that, at 7.25 p.m. that same day, border police officers interviewed the applicant to determine his identity and establish the circumstances surrounding the offence of illegal entry into and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation from Slovak into English was provided, while a certain Mr Zazai, apparently one of the Afghans travelling with the applicant, translated from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He informed the police that he intended to travel to western Europe to live and work and did not wish to seek asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record bore the signatures of a police officer and the Slovak-English interpreter, but was signed by neither the applicant nor Mr Zazai.
The Slovak Government stated that the applicant had been invited to sign the record but had declined to do so without giving any reason, whereas two other members of his group had signed comparable records.

11. On 24 September 2010, the authorities ordered the applicant’s expulsion and prohibited him from re-entering Slovakia for five years. He received a Pashto translation of the expulsion guidelines, which summarised the relevant Slovak legislation and procedures governing the removal of foreign nationals. The Slovak Government maintained that the expulsion decision itself had also been translated into Pashto. The document it produced is largely written in Pashto script: the general provisions and legislative quotations appear in Pashto, while some details specific to the applicant’s case—including the date and Ukraine as the destination country—are recorded in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. that same day, the applicant was transferred to the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant asserted that, during his entire stay in Slovakia, he had neither been provided with interpretation nor informed about the Slovak asylum procedure, and had been unable to consult a lawyer. Since he did not speak any European language, he had attempted to request asylum through another Afghan who knew some French, but the Slovak officials had failed to respond. Although he had tried to communicate with them and explain that he was a minor, they registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992. He was allegedly given no written decision regarding his return to Ukraine and received no explanation of any available appeal procedures.

Return to Ukraine and detention

14. After being expelled to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was held at the Border Guard’s temporary detention facility in Chop. He claimed that, with the assistance of other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had told a guard whom he believed to be the supervisor that he was fourteen. He further alleged that he had informed a representative of Caritas, a non-governmental organisation, that he was a minor and wanted to seek asylum. Although the Caritas representative had passed this information to the border guards, no steps had been taken.

15. In the applicant’s account, detention conditions at the Chop facility were inadequate. The cells were overcrowded, and detainees were not always allowed daily outdoor exercise; at times, they “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. On an unspecified date, the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) ordered the applicant to depart Ukraine voluntarily.

17. At a date that has not been specified, the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court for an order authorising the applicant’s forcible removal from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. The ensuing court decision indicated that the applicant had consented to the SBCS’s application (see paragraph 18 below).
According to the court’s decision, both the SBCS and the applicant requested on 1 October 2010 that the case be considered in their absence under a written procedure.

18. On 13 October 2010, the court granted the application, ordered the applicant’s removal from Ukraine, and directed that he remain in detention pending expulsion. It recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. The court found that he had entered Ukraine unlawfully, lacked the financial means to return voluntarily, had no relatives in the country, and had illegally crossed the border with Slovakia. In its view, those circumstances indicated that he was unlikely to comply voluntarily with an order to leave Ukraine.

19. The court further relied on a publication by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”), entitled Collection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН), issued in February 2008, apparently in Ukrainian translation. That publication has not been submitted to the Court. The circuit court stated that it indicated that “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). On that basis, it concluded that the applicant’s life would not be endangered if he were returned to Afghanistan. It also noted that he had neither applied for asylum nor wished to seek asylum in Ukraine.

20. The applicant maintained that he had been unaware of the proceedings, had not been legally represented, and had not understood his procedural rights before the court. He stated that he had signed a waiver of his right to attend the hearing without understanding what the document said. He was not served with the court’s decision and received no information about the procedure for lodging an appeal. As a result, he failed to comply with the ten-day appeal period provided for under domestic law (see paragraph 37 below).

21. On 14 October 2010, the applicant was moved from the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility to the temporary accommodation centre for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, which was then administered by the Ministry of the Interior. He alleged that, upon arrival, he had informed the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. Although the officer reportedly notified the facility’s management, no steps were taken.

22. On 20 February 2011, the Afghan Embassy in Kyiv interviewed the applicant by telephone. Two days later, on 22 February 2011, it issued him a travel document stating that he had been born on 14 January 1992.

Asylum application in Ukraine

23. On 19 October 2010, the applicant and three other Afghan nationals took part in a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO that was a local partner of the International Organization for Migration.
One of the Afghan nationals acted as an interpreter, and information was given on the procedure for applying for refugee status. Although the applicant did not deny that the session had taken place, he maintained that he could not remember it.

24. On 23 February 2011, the applicant submitted an asylum application in Ukraine, explaining that he would be “immediately killed” if sent back to Afghanistan.

25. On 2 March 2011, an officer of the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”) interviewed the applicant about his asylum claim. He said that he had lived in Kunduz, Afghanistan, where he had studied and received support from his maternal uncle. Asked why he had left the country, the applicant explained that the Taliban had killed his father four years earlier and had subsequently begun threatening him. According to the applicant, his uncle had received a document whose contents the applicant did not know and had then told him that he needed to leave Afghanistan. His uncle had later secured travel documents for him, enabling him to depart without difficulty. When questioned about his intended destination, the applicant replied that he wanted to reach London, where his sister lived. He stated that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan using his passport and an entry visa, but that smugglers had later confiscated both documents. He further indicated that he had entered Ukraine from Russia and had proceeded through Kyiv towards the Slovakian border. He had not sought assistance in Ukraine because the smugglers had assured him that they would take him to London to join his sister.

26. A questionnaire completed on the basis of the same interview documented the applicant’s responses to standard questions regarding his identity, personal history and background. Among other details, it recorded that he had been born on 14 January 1992, that Dari was his native language and that he also spoke Pashto.

27. On 9 March 2011, the Regional Migration Service declared the applicant’s asylum claim inadmissible (for an explanation of the two-stage asylum procedure in Ukraine, see paragraphs 34 and 35 below). It concluded that (i) the factual basis of the application was manifestly unfounded because the applicant could not be regarded as a “refugee”
for the purposes of section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below);

(ii) the applicant did not meet the criteria for refugee status under the Refugee Convention because he belonged to no political, social or military organisation and had no connection with any violent incident involving race, ethnicity, religion or political opinion;

(iii) the issuance of a travel document to the applicant by his country of origin showed that he had received that country’s protection. Consequently, under Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, the Convention was inapplicable to him;

(iv) although the applicant had travelled through Tajikistan, Russia and Ukraine, he had not sought asylum in any of those countries and had applied only after Slovakia returned him to Ukraine. This indicated that he had not intended to claim asylum in Ukraine, but had planned to travel to the United Kingdom, where his sister lived;

(v) because the applicant possessed no identity documents, neither his identity nor his country of origin could be established.

Expulsion to Afghanistan

28. The applicant stated that, on 11 March 2011, in preparation for his removal to Afghanistan, he had been transferred to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where he was informed of the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011.

29. According to the applicant, on Saturday, 12 March 2011, an NGO working in partnership with the UNHCR sought to contact him and other Afghan nationals who were facing expulsion in order to provide legal advice. The NGO was refused access to them, thereby preventing him from requesting an interim measure from the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.

30. Later that day, the applicant was placed on a train bound for Kyiv.

31. On 14 March 2011, he was expelled to Kabul.

32. The applicant alleged that, about three weeks after his removal to Afghanistan, unidentified individuals had come looking for him at his home and had left him a threatening letter. His mother had then arranged for him to leave Kunduz and travel to Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. From that point onward, fearing the people who had killed his father, he had been compelled to change his residence repeatedly and to travel frequently between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant domestic law in Ukraine

Refugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the material time)

33. Section 1 defined a refugee in the following terms:

“... an individual who is not a Ukrainian citizen and who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his or her nationality and cannot, or because of that fear does not wish to, seek the protection of that country; or an individual who is stateless and outside the country of his or her former permanent residence and who, because of that fear, is unable or unwilling to return there ...”

34.
Sections 12-14 and 16 of the Act established an asylum process comprising two phases: an admissibility assessment followed by consideration on the merits. Regional migration services examined asylum applications at first instance and determined whether they were admissible. When an application was declared admissible, the relevant regional migration service opened proceedings on the merits and submitted its recommendation to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions. The Committee subsequently issued the final decision granting or denying asylum. An asylum-seeker could challenge an adverse decision of a regional migration service before either the Committee or the courts. Filing such an appeal provided a basis for registering the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.

35. Under section 12, consideration of an asylum application had to commence with an interview in a language understood by the applicant, with interpretation provided where necessary. An application was to be declared inadmissible if the applicant did not satisfy the definition of a refugee set out in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above), or if the application amounted to an abuse. An application was considered abusive where it relied on a false identity or was submitted by a person whose earlier application had been refused, unless there had been a change in circumstances.

Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)

36. Section 32 governed the expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It specified the grounds on which compulsory expulsion could be ordered, including a serious violation of the legislation applicable to foreign nationals and stateless persons. It also authorised their detention in temporary accommodation facilities for the time required to arrange removal, subject to a maximum period of six months.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)

37. Article 186 required an appeal to be filed within ten days after a judgment was pronounced. Where the judgment was issued in written form, the ten-day period ran from the applicant’s receipt of a copy.

International law

Agreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons

38. The Agreement entered into force on 1 January 2010. Its relevant provisions state:

Article 3

Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons

1. At the request of the requesting State, and without formalities beyond those prescribed by the Agreement, the requested State must readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons who do not, or no longer, satisfy the applicable requirements for entering or remaining in the requesting State, provided that ...
such persons:

“...(a) entered the territory of the Member States unlawfully and directly from Ukrainian territory, or entered Ukrainian territory unlawfully and directly from the territory of the Member States;”

Relevant international materials concerning the situation in Slovakia and Ukraine

European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“CPT”)

39. The relevant sections of the report on the CPT’s 2007 visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), published on 19 May 2009, state:

“A. Facilities under the authority of the State Border Service

...

39. Access to legal counsel was confined to visits from NGO lawyers working pro bono. Those lawyers assisted foreign nationals in submitting asylum applications and informed them about the applicable legal procedures. The delegation was nevertheless concerned to discover that, in Chop, NGO lawyers’ access to detainees was restricted: they could meet only individuals whose names were already known to them. The absence of adequate interpretation services in Border Guard detention facilities also hindered the provision of legal advice (see paragraph 41 below).

...

40. The delegation observed that many foreign nationals had not been informed about their legal status, the procedures applicable to them, or their rights, including the right to submit complaints. As a rule, the internal regulations displayed in detention areas were available solely in Ukrainian. Certain other informational materials, including the Law on Refugees, were provided, but only in French or Russian. Border Guard personnel explained that materials in other languages had run out. One positive feature was that NGOs, acting under agreements with the State Border Service, helped and provided information to foreign nationals. However, assistance from external organisations did not relieve the State of its duty to provide foreign detainees with information and support.

The principal complaint among detained foreign nationals was that they did not know what was happening in their cases or how long they would remain in custody. The resulting uncertainty significantly worsened their experience of detention and created tension. The delegation’s observations indicated that Border Guard personnel needed to give greater attention to these concerns.

41. Regarding interpretation services, several detained foreign nationals complained that, after being apprehended, they had been required to sign documents written in Ukrainian without understanding what those documents said. They further alleged that, even where interpretation was provided, the information conveyed was not always comprehensible.”
The delegation found that interpreters for less widely spoken languages were in short supply locally. To address this difficulty, arrangements were being developed to provide remote interpretation facilities at the principal border units.

Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)

40. The UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers, issued in October 2007, states, where relevant:

“13. The Refugee Law assigns the Regional Migration Services responsibility for examining asylum applications at first instance and determining their admissibility. Where a Regional Migration Service admits an application to the procedure, it assesses the merits and submits a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then decides the case and may either endorse the RMS recommendation or reach a different conclusion. An asylum-seeker may challenge an adverse decision by the Regional Migration Service before either the SCNR or the courts.

...

31. As noted in paragraph 13 above, a principal weakness affecting the quality of asylum administration in Ukraine has been the repeated restructuring of the responsible institutions by successive governments, particularly the central executive authority. Pursuant to Cabinet of Ministers Decree No. 201 of March 2007, the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions—formerly the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration—was designated as the authorised central executive body for asylum matters. The Cabinet of Ministers directs and coordinates its work through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine.

...

42. As regards reception conditions, asylum-seekers and refugees lack adequate access to State-funded housing, material support and employment. Article 20 of the Refugee Law limits eligibility for financial assistance and accommodation to persons formally recognised as refugees. Ukraine currently has only one operational temporary accommodation centre serving asylum-seekers and refugees, with space for no more than 250 people. Under Article 7 of the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are expected to designate temporary accommodation and generally assist refugees and asylum-seekers in obtaining housing. In reality, however, they are unable to deliver these services. Refugees and asylum-seekers must therefore rent from private landlords. Because they are considered ‘foreigners’, they are asked to pay substantially more than Ukrainian nationals. Private rents—particularly in urban areas—are expensive and continue to rise. Consequently, many refugees must devote almost all of their income to housing, while many others remain homeless or live in inadequate conditions that endanger their physical and psychological well-being.

...

46.”
The circumstances as a whole lead some asylum-seekers to attempt to leave Ukraine in order to obtain better protection elsewhere. Many are arrested while trying to cross Ukraine’s western border unlawfully, and detention has consequently become increasingly common. Although conditions of detention have improved in recent years, they remain inadequate because the number of irregular migrants continues to rise and the State has difficulty managing the increased influx. Asylum-seekers are held together with other foreign nationals, often for extended periods. Such administrative detention may effectively deny them the right to seek asylum.

52. UNHCR therefore recommends that States refrain from returning third-country asylum-seekers to Ukraine, since no current guarantees can be provided that those concerned: (a) will be readmitted; (b) will have access to a fair and effective refugee-status determination procedure; (c) will be treated in accordance with international refugee standards; or (d) will receive effective protection from refoulement.

Human Rights Watch

41. In December 2010, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) published a 124-page report entitled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”. It presented the findings of HRW’s research into the experiences of migrants and asylum-seekers returned to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.

42. Most of the fifty interviewees who had been sent back to Ukraine from Slovakia or Hungary stated that, upon arriving in either country, they had requested asylum. According to them, those requests were disregarded, and they were rapidly expelled to Ukraine.

43. The report criticised the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior for terminating, in December 2009, an agreement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League. Since 2007, that agreement had allowed NGO lawyers to monitor border-return procedures.

44. With regard to the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, HRW acknowledged that many of its previously identified concerns had been addressed. Material conditions in the detention centres had notably improved. Every facility visited by HRW in 2010 appeared clean and orderly, and none was overcrowded. In most locations, the majority of detainees interviewed did not complain of overcrowding or inadequate hygiene. Former detainees from the temporary detention facility in Chop, however, reported that it was overcrowded at times. The most common complaints concerned the quality and quantity of food and the lack of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet and television. HRW further found that several other problems remained, particularly barriers to accessing the asylum procedure, the detention of children, the placement of children together with adults, corruption, and the generally disproportionate use of immigration detention.

45.
The report stated that migrants detained in Ukraine lacked regular and predictable access to a judge or another competent authority. They also had no access to legal counsel who could help them contest their detention. In addition, the authorities generally failed to conduct an individual assessment of whether detaining a particular migrant or asylum-seeker was necessary.

Relevant international materials on the situation in Afghanistan

46. The UNHCR’s Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Asylum-Seekers from Afghanistan, issued on 17 December 2010, stated, in the relevant parts:

“I. Introduction

...

UNHCR believes that possible risks must be examined with particular care in respect of individuals falling within the profiles identified below. Although the list is not necessarily exhaustive, these profiles include: (i) persons connected with, or regarded as supporting, the Afghan Government ...

Because of the deteriorating security situation in certain regions and the rising number of civilian casualties, UNHCR considers that generalized violence exists in Helmand, Kandahar and Kunar provinces, as well as in parts of Ghazni and Khost provinces. Afghan asylum-seekers who previously lived in those areas may therefore require international protection under broader protection criteria, including complementary forms of protection.

Moreover, since the conflict remains fluid and volatile, every application by an Afghan claiming to have fled generalized violence elsewhere in Afghanistan should be carefully evaluated on the basis of the evidence submitted by the applicant and other current, reliable information concerning the applicant’s former place of residence. That assessment must necessarily determine whether generalized violence existed in that location when the claim was adjudicated.

As a general rule, UNHCR regards internal relocation as a reasonable option when an individual can obtain protection from his or her extended family, community or tribe in the proposed area of relocation. In some circumstances, single men and nuclear families may be able to survive without family or community support in urban or semi-urban locations that have established infrastructure and are under effective Government control. Nevertheless, an individual assessment remains necessary, given the erosion of Afghanistan’s traditional social fabric following decades of war, large-scale refugee movements and increasing internal migration to urban areas.

...

III. Eligibility for International Protection

...

A. Potential Risk Profiles

1.
Individuals Linked to, or Regarded as Supporting, the Government and the International Community, Including the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF)

Armed anti-Government groups are carrying out a sustained and systematic campaign against civilians who are connected to, or believed to support, the Afghan Government or the international community, especially in locations where these groups operate....

Most deliberate attacks against civilians by armed anti-Government groups have taken place in the groups’ traditional strongholds. Nevertheless, targeted killings and executions of civilians have also become more frequent in other areas of the country that were previously viewed as relatively secure. In 2010, the number of assassinations and executions allegedly perpetrated by armed anti-Government groups in the south-eastern and central regions exceeded the figures recorded in 2009. Such attacks increased sharply in parts of the southern region, particularly Kandahar, where the Taliban had pursued a systematic campaign of targeted assassinations since the start of 2010. Between June and mid-September 2010, an average of 21 assassinations was documented each week—compared with seven per week during the corresponding period in 2009—with most occurring in the southern and south-eastern regions.

UNHCR considers that individuals associated with, or perceived as supporting, the Government, the international community, or international forces may, depending on the specific circumstances of each case, face risk because of their actual or imputed political opinion. Those potentially affected include Government officials, tribal and religious leaders aligned with the Government, judges, teachers, and employees working on reconstruction or development projects. The risk is particularly significant in areas where armed anti-Government groups are active or exercise control....

B. Eligibility Under Broader International Protection Standards, Including Complementary Forms of Protection

...1. Civilian Casualties...

Suicide attacks killed 183 civilians during the first six months of 2010, representing a 20 percent rise over the same period in 2009. More than half of these deaths occurred in the southern region.

Although armed anti-Government groups primarily attacked military targets during the first half of 2010, they also employed improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and suicide-attack tactics in civilian locations. These included roads used by civilians, areas surrounding government buildings, locations outside hotels, crowded markets, and commercial districts.

Despite continuing mine- and unexploded ordnance-clearing efforts over the preceding decade, as well as a steady decline in the number of Afghan victims, mines and explosive remnants still caused an average of 42 casualties each month. Children accounted for the large majority of those casualties.
Beyond causing deaths and severe injuries, landmine contamination has also disrupted livelihoods by restricting access to farmland, water, healthcare, and education.256 UNHCR’s further review of reported civilian-casualty incidents between 1 July and 8 October 2010 found that the provinces most affected by indiscriminate conflict-related violence were Helmand and Kandahar in the south and Kunduz in the north-east.

3. Conflict-Induced Displacement and Voluntary Returns

Growing insecurity and violence in parts of Afghanistan, driven by clashes between anti-Government groups and pro-Government forces, continue to displace substantial numbers of people. The conflict-induced IDP population is still increasing, with most displacement occurring in the country’s southern and western regions.

Despite the rise in conflict-related displacement within Afghanistan, voluntary returns—especially from Pakistan and Iran—have also grown. From March through October 2010, more than 100,000 Afghans returned, twice the number recorded during the corresponding period in 2009. Several factors prompted these returns: (i) a perception that security had improved in certain provinces; (ii) economic considerations; and (iii) worsening insecurity and natural disasters in former areas of settlement in Pakistan.

Although thousands of returnees went back to their home areas, almost one third now live in informal IDP settlements or urban locations in Afghanistan. Some such settlements are in Nagarhar, Laghman, and Kunar provinces, where civilian casualties and security incidents continue at fluctuating but significant levels. Many returns should therefore be understood as taking place amid deteriorating conditions for Afghans abroad, rather than as a consequence of substantial improvements in Afghanistan’s security and human rights situation.
