SECTION FIVE

M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11/09/2020

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment is final. Editorial amendments may still be made.

In the case concerning M.S. against Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of its Fifth Section, was constituted as follows:

Síofra O’Leary, President,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
Yonko Grozev,  
Alena Poláčková,  
Lәtif Hüseynov,  
Lado Chanturia,  
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar.

The Court took into consideration:

– the application brought against Slovakia and Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr M.S. (“the applicant”), an Afghan national, and lodged with the Court on 16 March 2011;

– the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, while striking the remaining parts of the application out of the list and declaring them inadmissible;

– the decision by the President of the Section to permit the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovakian NGO, to participate in the written proceedings as third-party interveners under Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2;

– the decision that the applicant’s identity should not be made public.

Following private deliberations on 17 March 2020,

The Court delivers the judgment below, adopted on that same date.

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant alleged that, after arresting him when he crossed the border from Ukraine, the Slovakian authorities did not tell him why he had been arrested, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. He further complained that they subsequently sent him back to Ukraine, where, despite his claimed status as a minor, he was held in unsuitable conditions, in violation of Article 3. According to the applicant, he was unable to participate effectively in the proceedings relating to his detention and was ultimately returned to Afghanistan without an adequate examination of the risks awaiting him there. He submitted that this breached Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Finally, relying on Article 34, he claimed that the Ukrainian authorities had refused an NGO representative access to him, thereby preventing him from applying to the Court for an interim measure.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant resides in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv. When the application was submitted, Mr Maksymov worked for the Representative Office in Ukraine of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“the HIAS”).

3. Ms M. Pirošíková, acting as Agent, represented the Government of the Slovak Republic. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The applicant maintained that his year of birth was either 1993 or 1994. By contrast, the Slovakian and Ukrainian authorities registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
To substantiate his claim, the applicant enclosed with his application form a photocopy of his Afghan identity document in its original language. The document measured 6 by 7 cm. He also provided an “unofficial translation” into English prepared by a lawyer at the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to that translation, the section headed “Date of birth and age” contained the entry “age 8 years in year 2002”. In addition, the applicant submitted a photograph which, in his view, showed that he had the appearance of a teenager.

The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia

5. Before departing from Afghanistan, the applicant resided in Kunduz province in the north of the country.

6. The applicant stated that his father had worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department. After arresting several drug smugglers, his father was killed in about 2005 by unidentified individuals who may have been linked to the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. Although the applicant did not know its exact contents, his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and made arrangements for him to leave Afghanistan.

7. The applicant further stated that, in May 2010, smugglers transported him to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. The smugglers later took the passport from him. He continued through Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia, spending one month in Moscow before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He remained in Kyiv for three months. On the way to Ukraine, he travelled with his brother-in-law, who was his sister’s husband. They separated while in Ukraine. Three days after the applicant, the brother-in-law succeeded in entering Slovakia, after which he went to Spain and sought asylum there.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, the Slovakian border police arrested the applicant as he was illegally entering Slovakia together with three other Afghan nationals. He was carrying no identity documents.

9. Records submitted by the Government of Slovakia indicate that, at 7.25 p.m. that same day, border police officers interviewed the applicant in order to determine his identity and establish the circumstances in which he had committed the offence of unlawfully entering and residing in Slovakia. Interpretation was provided from Slovak into English. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently one of the Afghans travelling with the applicant, interpreted from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He informed the police that he intended to travel to western Europe to live and work there and that he did not wish to seek asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record bore the signatures of a police officer and the Slovak-to-English interpreter, but it was not signed by either the applicant or Mr Zazai.
The Slovak Government stated that the applicant had been invited to sign the record but had declined to do so without giving any explanation. In contrast, two other people from his group signed comparable records.

11. On 24 September 2010, the authorities ordered the applicant’s expulsion and prohibited him from entering Slovakia for five years. He received a Pashto translation of the expulsion guidelines, which outlined the applicable Slovak legislation and procedures governing the removal of foreign nationals. The Slovak Government maintained that the expulsion decision itself had also been translated into Pashto. The document it produced is predominantly written in Pashto script: the sections setting out general rules and quoting legislation appear in Pashto, whereas some details specific to the applicant’s case—including the date and Ukraine as the destination country—are recorded in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010, the applicant was transferred into the custody of the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant claimed that during his entire stay in Slovakia he had been provided with neither interpretation nor information about the Slovak asylum process and had been unable to consult a lawyer. Since he did not speak any European language, he had attempted to request asylum with assistance from another Afghan who knew some French, but the Slovak officials had failed to respond. Although he had tried to communicate with them and explain that he was underage, they registered his birth date as 14 January 1992. He was not given any written decision regarding his return to Ukraine, nor was he informed about any available means of appeal.

Return to Ukraine and detention

14. After being expelled to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was detained at the Border Guard’s temporary holding centre in Chop. He alleged that, using other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian as intermediaries, he had told a guard whom he believed to be the person in charge that he was fourteen. He further claimed that he had informed a representative of Caritas, a non-governmental organisation, that he was a minor and wanted to seek asylum. Although the Caritas representative had passed this information to the border guards, they had taken no action.

15. In the applicant’s account, detention conditions at the Chop facility were inadequate. The cells were overcrowded, and detainees were not always assured of exercise every day; they “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. At an unspecified time, the Chop unit of Ukraine’s State Border Control Service (“the SBCS”) ordered the applicant to depart from Ukraine voluntarily.

17. On an unspecified date, the SBCS asked the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court to authorise the applicant’s compulsory expulsion from Ukraine and his detention while awaiting removal. As recorded in the court’s decision (see paragraph 18 below), the applicant consented to the SBCS’s request.
According to the court’s decision, both the SBCS and the applicant requested on 1 October 2010 that the case be considered in their absence under a written procedure.

18. On 13 October 2010, the court granted the application, ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine, and directed that he remain in detention pending expulsion. It recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. The court found that he had entered Ukraine unlawfully, lacked the financial means to return voluntarily, had no relatives in the country, and had illegally crossed the border with Slovakia. In its view, those circumstances demonstrated that he was unlikely to obey an order requiring him to leave voluntarily.

19. The court further relied on a February 2008 publication of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”), apparently available in Ukrainian translation, entitled Collection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН). That publication has not been submitted to the Court. The circuit court stated that, according to the publication, “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). On that basis, it concluded that the applicant’s life would not be endangered if he were returned to Afghanistan. It also noted that he had neither applied for asylum nor wished to seek asylum in Ukraine.

20. The applicant maintained that he had been unaware of the proceedings, had not been legally represented, and had not understood his rights during the court proceedings. He stated that he had signed a waiver of his right to attend the hearing without understanding what the document said. He was not served with the court’s decision and received no information about the appeal procedure. Consequently, he failed to comply with the ten-day time-limit for lodging an appeal (see the relevant provision of domestic law in paragraph 37 below).

21. On 14 October 2010, the applicant was moved from the Border Guard temporary holding facility to the temporary accommodation facility for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, which was then administered by the Ministry of the Interior. He alleged that, upon arriving, he informed the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. The officer reportedly notified the facility’s management, but no steps were taken.

22. On 20 February 2011, the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv interviewed the applicant by telephone. Two days later, on 22 February 2011, it issued him a travel document stating that he had been born on 14 January 1992.

Asylum application in Ukraine

23. On 19 October 2010, the applicant and three other Afghan nationals participated in a counselling session conducted by a lawyer from an NGO that was a local partner of the International Organization for Migration.
One Afghan acted as an interpreter, and instructions on applying for refugee status were given. Although the applicant did not dispute that the session had taken place, he said that he could not remember it.

24. On 23 February 2011, the applicant submitted an asylum application in Ukraine. In support of his claim, he asserted that he would be “immediately killed” if sent back to Afghanistan.

25. On 2 March 2011, the applicant was interviewed about his asylum claim by an official of the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”). He explained that he had lived in Kunduz, Afghanistan, where he had studied and received support from his maternal uncle. Asked why he had left Afghanistan, he said that the Taliban had killed his father four years earlier and had subsequently begun threatening him. His uncle had received a document whose contents the applicant did not know and had told him that he needed to leave the country. The uncle had then secured travel documents for him, which enabled him to depart Afghanistan without difficulty. When questioned about his intended destination, the applicant replied that he wanted to reach London, where his sister lived. He stated that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan using his passport and an entry visa, but that smugglers had later taken both documents from him. He further indicated that he had entered Ukraine from Russia and travelled through Kyiv towards the Slovakian border. He had not asked for assistance in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to take him to London, where his sister was residing.

26. A questionnaire completed on the basis of that same interview set out the applicant’s responses to various standard questions about his identity, personal history and background. Among other details, it recorded that he had been born on 14 January 1992, that Dari was his mother tongue and that he also spoke Pashto.

27. On 9 March 2011, the Regional Migration Service declared the applicant’s asylum claim inadmissible (for an explanation of the two stages of the Ukrainian asylum procedure, see paragraphs 34 and 35 below). It concluded that (i) the factual grounds advanced in support of the application were manifestly unfounded because the applicant could not be classified as a “refugee”
under section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below);

(ii) the applicant did not meet the Refugee Convention’s criteria for refugee status because he had never belonged to a political, social or military organisation and had no involvement in violent events linked to race, ethnicity, religion or political opinion;

(iii) the issuance of a travel document to the applicant by his country of origin established that he had received that country’s protection. Consequently, under Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, the Convention was inapplicable to him;

(iv) although the applicant had passed through Tajikistan, Russia and Ukraine, he had not sought asylum in any of those countries. He applied only after Slovakia had returned him to Ukraine. This indicated that he had not planned to claim asylum in Ukraine, but instead intended to travel to the United Kingdom, where his sister lived;

(v) because the applicant possessed no identity papers, neither his identity nor his country of origin could be established.

Expulsion to Afghanistan

28. The applicant stated that, on 11 March 2011, he had been moved to Mukacheve, Ukraine, in preparation for his removal to Afghanistan. There, he was informed of the Migration Service’s decision dated 9 March 2011.

29. The applicant further stated that, on Saturday, 12 March 2011, an NGO working in partnership with the UNHCR had tried to contact him and other Afghan nationals who were also facing expulsion, with a view to giving them legal advice. The NGO was refused access to them, however, and the applicant was therefore unable to request an interim measure from the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.

30. Later that same day, the applicant was placed on a train bound for Kyiv.

31. On 14 March 2011, he was removed to Kabul.

32. The applicant claimed that, around three weeks after his expulsion to Afghanistan, unidentified individuals had visited his home in search of him and had left him a threatening letter. His mother had then arranged for him to leave Kunduz and travel to Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. From that point onward, fearing those responsible for his father’s death, he had been compelled to relocate repeatedly and to travel frequently between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant Ukrainian domestic law

Refugees Act of 21 June 2001 (applicable at the relevant time)

33. Section 1 defined a refugee as:

“... an individual who is not a Ukrainian citizen and who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, remains outside the country of his or her nationality and cannot obtain that country’s protection or, because of that fear, does not wish to seek such protection; or an individual without a nationality who, while outside the country of his or her former permanent residence, cannot or, as a result of the same fear, does not wish to return there ...”

34.
Sections 12-14 and 16 of the Act established an asylum process consisting of two phases: an admissibility assessment followed by consideration of the merits. Regional migration services examined asylum applications at first instance and determined whether they were admissible. Where an application was declared admissible, the relevant regional migration service opened proceedings on the merits and submitted its recommendation to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions. The Committee subsequently issued the final decision either granting or denying asylum. An asylum-seeker could challenge an adverse decision by a regional migration service before either the Committee or the courts. Filing such an appeal provided a basis for registering the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.

35. Under section 12, consideration of an asylum application had to start with an interview held in a language understood by the asylum-seeker, with an interpreter’s assistance where necessary. An application was to be ruled inadmissible if the applicant did not fall within the definition of “refugee” set out in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above), or if the application amounted to an abuse of the procedure. An application was considered abusive if it relied on a false identity or had been submitted by a person whose earlier application had already been refused, unless there had been a change in circumstances.

Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)

36. Section 32 regulated the expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It specified the grounds on which compulsory expulsion could be ordered, including a serious violation of the law governing foreign nationals and stateless persons. It also permitted their detention in temporary accommodation facilities for as long as necessary to arrange their removal, subject to a maximum period of six months.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)

37. Article 186 required an appeal to be filed within ten days after a judgment was pronounced. Where the judgment was issued in written form, the ten-day period began when the applicant received a copy of it.

International law

Agreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons

38. The Agreement entered into force on 1 January 2010. Its relevant provisions stated:

Article 3

Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons

“1. At the requesting State’s request, and without any formalities beyond those prescribed by this Agreement, the requested State shall readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons who do not, or no longer, satisfy the applicable requirements for entering or remaining in the requesting State’s territory, provided that ...”
persons who: … (a) entered the territory of the Member States unlawfully after arriving directly from Ukrainian territory, or entered Ukrainian territory unlawfully after arriving directly from the territory of the Member States;”

Relevant international materials on the circumstances in Slovakia and Ukraine

European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”)

39. The pertinent sections of the report concerning the CPT’s 2007 visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), which was published on 19 May 2009, state:

“A. Facilities falling under the authority of the State Border Service

…

39. With respect to access to legal representation, this was confined to visits from NGO lawyers working pro bono. Those lawyers assisted foreign nationals in submitting asylum claims and informed them about the applicable legal processes. The delegation was nevertheless troubled to discover that, in Chop, NGO lawyers’ access to detainees was restricted: they were permitted to meet only individuals whose names they already knew. The absence of adequate interpretation services at Border Guard detention facilities also impeded the provision of legal advice (see also paragraph 41).

…

40. The delegation observed that numerous foreign nationals had not been informed about their legal position, the procedures governing their cases, or their rights, including the right to make complaints. As a general rule, the internal regulations displayed in detention areas were written only in Ukrainian. Certain additional informational documents, including the Law on refugees, were available, but solely in French or Russian. Border Guard personnel explained that materials in other languages had been exhausted. One positive feature was that, under agreements concluded with the State Border Service, NGOs participated in providing foreign nationals with information and assistance. Nonetheless, assistance from external organisations to foreign detainees does not relieve the State of its own duty to supply those detainees with information and support.

The principal grievance raised by detained foreign nationals was that they did not know what was occurring in their cases or how long their detention would last. That uncertainty significantly worsened their experience of being confined and generated tension. The findings from the visit indicate that Border Guard personnel should give greater attention to these issues.

41. Regarding interpretation services, several detained foreign nationals reported that, after being apprehended, they had been required to sign documents written in Ukrainian without understanding what those documents said. They further alleged that, even where interpretation was provided, the resulting information was not always understandable.
The delegation was informed that too few local interpreters were available for languages spoken less frequently. To address this shortage, arrangements were under consideration to establish remote-interpreting facilities at the principal border units.

Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)

40. The relevant portions of the UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers, issued in October 2007, state:

“13. The Refugee Law assigns the Regional Migration Services responsibility for examining asylum applications at first instance and determining whether they are admissible. Once a Regional Migration Service admits an application to the procedure, it assesses the merits and submits a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then decides the case and may either endorse the RMS recommendation or reach a different conclusion. An asylum-seeker may challenge an adverse Regional Migration Service decision before either the SCNR or the courts.

...

31. As concerns the standard of the asylum procedure, a major difficulty in Ukraine’s asylum system, as noted in paragraph 13 above, has been the repeated restructuring of the institutions responsible for asylum by successive governments, particularly the central executive authority. In March 2007, Cabinet of Ministers Decree No. 201 designated the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions—formerly known as the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration—as the authorised central executive body for asylum matters. The Cabinet of Ministers directs and coordinates its work through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine.

...

42. In relation to reception conditions, asylum-seekers and refugees lack sufficient access to State-funded housing, material support and work. Article 20 of the Refugee Law limits eligibility for financial assistance and accommodation to persons formally recognised as refugees. Only one temporary accommodation centre for asylum-seekers and refugees is currently operating in Ukraine, with space for up to 250 people. Under Article 7 of the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are required to identify temporary accommodation and, more generally, assist refugees and asylum-seekers in obtaining housing. In reality, however, they cannot provide these services. Refugees and asylum-seekers must therefore rent housing from private landlords. Because they are regarded as ‘foreigners’, they are asked to pay substantially higher rents than Ukrainian nationals. Private rental costs are high, particularly in urban areas, and continue to rise. Consequently, many refugees must devote nearly all their income to housing. Many others are homeless or reside in inadequate conditions that endanger their physical and psychological health.

...

46.”
The circumstances as a whole prompt some asylum-seekers to seek more effective protection in other countries. Many are arrested while trying to cross Ukraine’s western border unlawfully, and the number of detentions has consequently risen. Despite improvements in detention conditions over recent years, standards remain poor because irregular migrant numbers continue to grow and the State has difficulty managing the increase. Asylum-seekers are confined together with other foreign nationals and may be held for lengthy periods. Such administrative detention can effectively deny them the right to seek asylum....52. ... UNHCR recommends that States refrain from returning third-country asylum-seekers to Ukraine because it is currently impossible to guarantee that those concerned: (a) will be readmitted; (b) will be able to access a fair and effective refugee-status determination process; (c) will receive treatment consistent with international refugee standards; or (d) will benefit from effective safeguards against refoulement.”

Human Rights Watch41. In December 2010, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) issued a 124-page report titled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”. It presented findings from research into the experiences of migrants and asylum-seekers sent back to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.42. Of the fifty returnees interviewed after being transferred from Slovakia or Hungary, most stated that they had sought asylum upon reaching one of those countries. They said their applications were disregarded and that they were rapidly expelled to Ukraine.43. The report criticised the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior for terminating, in December 2009, an arrangement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League that had enabled NGO lawyers to monitor border-return procedures since 2007.44.

With regard to the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, HRW reported that numerous concerns it had previously identified had been remedied. Material conditions in the centres had improved in particular: every facility inspected by HRW in 2010 appeared clean and orderly, and none was overcrowded. Across most locations, the majority of interviewed detainees did not complain of poor hygiene or overcrowding. Nevertheless, former detainees at the temporary detention facility in Chop reported that it was overcrowded at times. The complaints raised most often concerned both the quality and quantity of food, as well as the absence of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet and television. HRW further found that several problems remained, notably obstacles to accessing asylum procedures, the detention of children, the placement of children together with adults, corruption, and the generally disproportionate reliance on migrant detention.45.
The report stated that migrants held in detention in Ukraine lacked regular and foreseeable access to a judge or another competent authority. They also had no access to legal representation through which they could contest their detention. Moreover, the need to detain individual migrants or asylum-seekers was generally not assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Relevant international materials on the situation in Afghanistan

46. In its Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Asylum-Seekers from Afghanistan, published on 17 December 2010, the UNHCR stated, in relevant part:

“I. Introduction

...

UNHCR considers that possible risks must be examined with particular care for individuals falling within the profiles identified below. Although these risk profiles are not necessarily exhaustive, they include: (i) persons connected with, or regarded as supporting, the Afghan Government ...

Considering the deteriorating security conditions in certain regions of the country and the rising number of civilian casualties, UNHCR considers the circumstances in Helmand, Kandahar, Kunar, and parts of Ghazni and Khost provinces to amount to generalized violence. Consequently, Afghan asylum-seekers who previously lived in those areas may require international protection under broader international protection standards, including complementary forms of protection. Furthermore, because the conflict remains fluid and volatile, every asylum application from an Afghan claiming to have escaped generalized violence elsewhere in Afghanistan should be carefully evaluated on the basis of the applicant’s evidence and other reliable, up-to-date information concerning the former place of residence. That assessment must, of course, determine whether generalized violence exists in that location when the claim is decided.

As a general rule, UNHCR regards internal flight as a reasonable alternative where the person can obtain protection from his or her extended family, community, or tribe in the proposed area of relocation. In some circumstances, single men and nuclear family units may be able to survive without family or community assistance in urban or semi-urban locations that have established infrastructure and are under effective Government control. Nevertheless, because decades of conflict, large-scale refugee movements, and increasing internal migration toward urban areas have disrupted Afghanistan’s traditional social fabric, each case must be assessed individually.

...

III. Eligibility for International Protection

...

A. Potential Risk Profiles

1.”
Individuals Linked to, or Regarded as Supporting, the Government and the International Community, Including the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF)

Armed anti-Government groups are conducting a sustained, systematic campaign against civilians who are connected to, or believed to support, the Afghan Government or the international community, especially in locations where these groups operate....

Most deliberate attacks by armed anti-Government groups against civilians have taken place in the groups’ strongholds. Nevertheless, targeted killings and executions of civilians have also become more frequent in other areas of the country that were previously viewed as relatively secure. In the south-eastern and central regions, assassinations and executions reportedly carried out by armed anti-Government groups occurred more often in 2010 than in 2009. Such attacks increased sharply in parts of the southern region, particularly Kandahar, where the Taliban have pursued a systematic, targeted assassination campaign since the start of 2010. Between June and mid-September 2010, an average of 21 assassinations per week was documented, compared with seven per week during the corresponding period in 2009. Most occurred in the southern and south-eastern regions.

UNHCR considers that, depending on the specific circumstances of each case, individuals associated with, or perceived as supporting, the Government, the international community, or international forces may face danger because of their actual or attributed political opinion. This category includes Government officials, tribal and religious leaders aligned with the Government, judges, teachers, and people employed on reconstruction or development projects. The risk is particularly significant in areas where armed anti-Government groups are active or exercise control....

B. Qualification Under Wider International Protection Standards, Including Complementary Forms of Protection

1. Civilian Casualties

During the first six months of 2010, suicide attacks killed 183 civilians. More than half of these deaths occurred in the southern region, and the total represented a 20 percent rise over the same period in 2009.

Although armed anti-Government groups focused mainly on military targets during the first half of 2010, they also used improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and suicide attacks in civilian locations. These included roads travelled by civilians, areas surrounding government buildings, sites outside hotels, crowded markets, and commercial districts.

Despite continuous mine- and unexploded ordnance-clearing efforts over the previous decade, as well as a steady decline in the number of Afghan victims, mines and explosive remnants still cause an average of 42 casualties each month. A large majority of those affected are children.
Mine contamination has not only caused deaths and severe injuries but has also disrupted livelihoods by restricting access to farmland, water supplies, healthcare and education.256 UNHCR’s additional review of reported civilian-casualty incidents between 1 July 2010 and 8 October 2010 indicates that indiscriminate conflict-related violence affected Helmand and Kandahar Provinces in the south, and Kunduz Province in the north-east, most severely.

3. Voluntary Returns and Displacement Caused by Conflict

Significant population displacement continues as insecurity and violence intensify in parts of Afghanistan amid clashes between anti-Government groups and pro-Government forces. The conflict-induced IDP population is continuing to grow, with most displacement occurring in Afghanistan’s southern and western regions.

At the same time as conflict-related displacement has increased within Afghanistan, voluntary returns—especially from Pakistan and Iran—have also risen. More than 100,000 Afghans returned between March and October 2010, twice the total recorded during the corresponding period in 2009. Several factors have prompted these returns: (i) a belief that security has improved in certain provinces; (ii) economic considerations; and (iii) worsening insecurity and natural disasters in their former areas of settlement in Pakistan.

Although thousands of returnees went back to their places of origin, almost one third now live in informal IDP settlements or urban locations within Afghanistan. Some such settlements are situated in Nagarhar, Laghman and Kunar Provinces, where civilian casualties and security incidents continue at significant, though fluctuating, levels. Many returns are taking place because conditions for Afghans outside the country are deteriorating, rather than because Afghanistan’s security and human rights situation has improved substantially.

original: FIFTH SECTIONCASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE(Application no. 17189/11) JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG11 June 2020 FINAL 11/09/2020 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Yonko Grozev, Alena Poláčková, Lәtif Hüseynov, Lado Chanturia, Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application against Slovakia and Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Afghan national, Mr M.S. (“the applicant”), on 16 March 2011;the decision to give notice of the complaints set out in paragraph 1 below to the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine and to strike out of the list and declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;the decision of the Section President to grant leave to intervene in written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2) to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovakian NGO;the decision not to have the applicant’s name disclosed;Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:INTRODUCTION1. The applicant complained that the Slovakian authorities, having arrested him after he had crossed from Ukraine, had failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, in violation of Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. They had then returned him to Ukraine, where he had been detained in inadequate conditions in disregard of his alleged status as a minor, in breach of Article 3. He had been unable to participate effectively in the proceedings concerning his detention, and had eventually been returned to Afghanistan in the absence of an adequate assessment of the risks he had faced there, in breach of Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Lastly, he alleged, under Article 34, that an NGO representative had been denied access to him in Ukraine, preventing him from lodging an application for an interim measure with the Court.THE FACTS2. The applicant lives in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, at the time the application was lodged, was employed by the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“the HIAS”) Representative Office in Ukraine.3. The Government of the Slovak Republic were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.4. The applicant alleged that he had been born in 1993 or 1994, whereas the authorities in Slovakia and Ukraine had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below). In support of his claim the applicant submitted to the Court, together with his application form, a photocopy of his Afghan identity document, in the original language, measuring 6 by 7 cm, and its “unofficial translation” into English by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to the translation, the field of the document marked “Date of birth and age” stated “age 8 years in year 2002”. The applicant also submitted to the Court a photograph which he considered showed that he looked like a teenager.The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia5. Prior to leaving Afghanistan the applicant lived in the Kunduz province, in the north of the country.6. According to the applicant, his father used to work with the National Security Department of Afghanistan. Having arrested some drug smugglers, he was killed in about 2005 by unknown people, possibly associated with the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. The applicant was unaware of its precise contents, but his uncle deduced that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and arranged for him to leave the country.7. Still according to the applicant, in May 2010 smugglers took the applicant to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. His passport was subsequently taken away by the smugglers. He then travelled onward to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He stayed in Moscow for one month and then entered Ukraine in early July 2010. He stayed in Kyiv for three months. During his journey to Ukraine the applicant was accompanied by his brother-in-law (his sister’s husband). In Ukraine the applicant and his brother-in-law separated. The brother-in-law managed to cross into Slovakia three days after the applicant, travelled to Spain and applied for asylum there.8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010 the applicant was arrested by the Slovakian border police while crossing into Slovakia illegally with three other Afghan nationals. He had no identity papers.9. According to records provided by the Government of Slovakia, at 7.25 p.m. on the same day the applicant was interviewed by border police officers to establish his identity and clarify the circumstances under which he had committed the offence of illegal entry to and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation from Slovak into English was provided. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently a member of the applicant’s group of Afghans, translated from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was noted as 14 January 1992. The applicant told the police that he wished to go to western Europe and live and work there, and that he was not requesting asylum in Slovakia.10. The record of the interview was signed by a police officer and the interpreter from Slovak into English, but not by the applicant or Mr Zazai. The Government of Slovakia submitted that the applicant had been asked to sign the record but had refused without providing a reason. By contrast, two other members of his group did sign similar records.11. On 24 September 2010 a decision to expel the applicant was issued. He was also banned from entering Slovakia for five years. He was given a Pashto translation of the guidelines on expulsion, summarising the relevant Slovakian legislation and procedures concerning expulsion of foreigners. According to the Government of Slovakia, the expulsion decision had been translated into Pashto. The document submitted by the Government is mainly in Pashto script. The parts containing general rules and quotes from legislation appear to be in that language, while certain case-specific details, such as the date and the country of destination, Ukraine, are written in Slovak.12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010 the applicant was handed over to the Ukrainian authorities.13. The applicant alleged that, throughout his time in Slovakia, he had not received any interpretation services or information about the asylum procedure in Slovakia and had had no access to a lawyer. As he spoke no European language, he had tried to ask for asylum with the help of a fellow Afghan who spoke some French. However, the Slovakian officials had not reacted. Despite his efforts to talk to them and to tell them that he was a minor, they had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. They had not provided him with any written decision concerning his return to Ukraine or explained to him any possible avenues of appeal.Return to Ukraine and detention there14. Following his expulsion to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was placed in the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He alleged that through other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had informed a guard, whom he had taken to be the supervisor, that he was fourteen years old. He also alleged that he had told a representative of Caritas, an NGO, that he was a minor and wished to apply for asylum, and that the Caritas representative had relayed that information to the border guards but that no action had been taken.15. According to the applicant, his conditions of detention in the Chop facility were unsatisfactory. The cells were overcrowded. Sometimes the detainees were not guaranteed daily exercise, and “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.16. On an unspecified date the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) issued an order directing the applicant to leave Ukraine voluntarily.17. On an unspecified date the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court, seeking the applicant’s forcible expulsion from Ukraine and his placement in detention pending expulsion. According to the court decision (see paragraph 18 below), the applicant agreed with the SBCS’s application. Also according to the court decision, on 1 October 2010 the SBCS and the applicant had asked the court to examine the case in their absence by way of a written procedure.18. On 13 October 2010 the court allowed the application and ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. The court stated that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992. It held that he had entered the territory of Ukraine illegally, had no means to return voluntarily and no relatives in Ukraine, and had crossed the border (with Slovakia) illegally. For the court, this showed that he was unlikely to comply with the order to leave the territory voluntarily.19. The court also referred to a United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”) publication entitled Сollection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН) published in February 2008, apparently in a Ukrainian translation. That publication has not been made available to the Court. According to the circuit court, the publication indicated that “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). It therefore concluded that in the event of return to Afghanistan, the applicant’s life would not be at risk. The court observed that the applicant had not lodged an application for asylum and did not wish to apply for asylum in Ukraine.20. According to the applicant, he was not aware of the proceedings, he did not have legal representation and did not understand his rights in the proceedings before the court. He had signed a document waiving his right to appear in court without understanding its contents. The court’s decision was not served on him and no information was provided to him on how to appeal. He therefore missed the ten-day time-limit for appeal (see the relevant provision of the domestic law in paragraph 37 below).21. On 14 October 2010 the applicant was transferred from the Border Guard temporary holding facility to temporary accommodation for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior at the time. He alleged that on arrival there, he had told the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. The officer allegedly informed the management of the facility but no action was taken.22. On 20 February 2011 the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv conducted a telephone interview with the applicant and on 22 February 2011 issued a travel document for him, indicating his date of birth as 14 January 1992.Asylum application in Ukraine23. On 19 October 2010 the applicant, along with three other Afghans, attended a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO, a local partner of the International Organization for Migration. One of the Afghans provided interpretation. Information on how to apply for refugee status was provided. The applicant did not contest that the session had been held, but stated that he had no recollection of it.24. On 23 February 2011 the applicant lodged an application for asylum in Ukraine. By way of reasoning he stated that he would be “immediately killed” if he were returned to Afghanistan.25. On 2 March 2011 an officer from the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”) interviewed the applicant concerning his asylum application. The applicant stated that in Afghanistan he used to live in Kunduz, had been studying and had been supported by his maternal uncle. When asked what had led him to leave Afghanistan, he stated that his father had been killed by the Taliban four years earlier and the Taliban had then started threatening him. His uncle had received a piece of paper, the contents of which were unknown to the applicant, and had said that the applicant had to leave the country. Afterwards, his uncle had obtained travel documents for him with which he had had no trouble leaving Afghanistan. The applicant was then asked what was his country of destination and responded that he wished to get to London where his sister lived. He explained that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan with his passport and an entry visa, but that the smugglers had then taken them away. He also stated that he had arrived in Ukraine from Russia and had travelled to the border with Slovakia through Kyiv. He had not sought help in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to get him to London where his sister was living.26. A questionnaire based on the same interview recorded the applicant’s answers to a number of standardised questions concerning his identity, history and background. It stated, in particular, that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992, that his mother tongue was Dari and that he also spoke Pashto.27. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the applicant’s asylum application as inadmissible (see paragraphs 34 and 35 below for the description of the two stages of the asylum procedure in Ukraine). The Regional Migration Service found that(i)  the facts on which his application was based were manifestly unfounded, as he could not be defined as a “refugee” under section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below);(ii)  since the applicant was not a member of any political, social or military organisation and had not been connected with any violent incidents associated with race, ethnicity, religion or political views, he did not qualify as a refugee under the Refugee Convention;(iii)  the fact that the country of origin had issued the applicant with a travel document demonstrated that he had benefited from protection in his country of origin, which, pursuant to Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, meant that the Refugee Convention did not apply to him;(iv)  the applicant had not applied for asylum while travelling through Tajikistan, Russia or Ukraine but had done so only after being returned from Slovakia to Ukraine. This showed that he had not intended to seek asylum in Ukraine but had meant to reach the United Kingdom, where his sister resided;(v)  since the applicant had no identity documents, it was not possible to identify him or his country of origin.Expulsion to Afghanistan28. According to the applicant, on 11 March 2011 in preparation for his expulsion to Afghanistan, he was transferred to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011 was notified to him.29. According to the applicant, on 12 March 2011, a Saturday, an NGO partner of the UNHCR attempted to contact him and other Afghan nationals facing expulsion to provide them with legal advice. However, it was denied access to them, preventing the applicant from applying for an interim measure with the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.30. On the same day the applicant was put on a train to Kyiv.31. On 14 March 2011 the applicant was expelled to Kabul.32. The applicant alleged that approximately three weeks after his expulsion to Afghanistan, some unknown people had looked for him at his home and left a threatening letter for him. His mother had arranged for him to leave Kunduz for Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. Since that time, he had been forced to change his place of residence frequently for fear of the people who had killed his father, and had been travelling frequently between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICERelevant domestic law in UkraineRefugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the material time)33. Under section 1 a refugee was defined as follows:“... a person who is not a citizen of Ukraine and who, due to a well‑founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality and is unable to avail himself of the protection of that country or, due to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of such protection, or who, not having a nationality and being outside the country of his former permanent residence, is unable or unwilling to return to it because of the said fear ...”34. Sections 12 to 14 and 16 of the Act provided for a two-stage asylum procedure: admissibility and merits stages. The regional migration services were responsible for examining the initial applications for asylum and decided on the admissibility. If a regional migration service found an application admissible, it instituted proceedings on the merits and made a recommendation to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions on the merits of the application. The Committee then took a final decision to grant or refuse asylum. Asylum-seekers could appeal against a negative decision taken by the regional migration service either to the Committee or to the courts. The lodging of an appeal constituted grounds for registration of the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.35. Section 12 provided that examination of an asylum application was to begin with an interview conducted in a language the asylum-seeker understood, if necessary with the assistance of an interpreter. An inadmissibility decision was to be taken if the applicant did not meet the definition of a refugee provided for in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above) or if an application was abusive: based on a false identity or lodged by an individual whose previous application had been rejected, unless circumstances had changed.Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)36. Section 32 of the Act laid down the procedure for expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It listed the grounds for compulsory expulsion, which included a serious breach of the legislation concerning foreign nationals and stateless persons, and provided that foreign nationals and stateless persons could be detained at temporary accommodation facilities for the period needed to organise their removal, which was not to exceed six months.Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)37. Under Article 186 of the Code an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the pronouncement of a judgment. If the judgment was delivered in writing, an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of receipt by the applicant of a copy of the judgment.International lawAgreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons38. The Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 2010, reads in the relevant parts as follows:Article 3Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons“1. The requested State, upon application by the requesting State and without further formalities other than those provided for by this Agreement, shall readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons which do not, or no longer, fulfill the conditions in force for entry to or stay on the territory of the requesting State provided that ... such persons:...(a)  illegally entered the territory of the Member States coming directly from the territory of Ukraine or illegally entered the territory of Ukraine coming directly from the territory of the Member States;”Relevant international material concerning the situation in Slovakia and UkraineEuropean Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”)39. The report on the 2007 CPT visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), published on 19 May 2009, reads in the relevant parts as follows:“A. Establishments under the authority of the State Border Service...39. Turning to access to a lawyer, it was limited to visits by pro-bono lawyers from NGOs, who helped foreign nationals file asylum applications and provided them with information on the relevant legal procedures. However, the delegation was concerned to learn that at Chop, the NGO lawyers had limited access to detained persons (i.e. they could only meet persons whose names they already knew). It should also be noted that the provision of legal consultations was hampered by the lack of proper interpretation at the Border Guard detention facilities (see also paragraph 41)....40. The delegation noted that many foreign nationals lacked information on their legal status, the procedure applicable to them and their rights (including the right to lodge complaints). The internal regulations which were posted in the detention areas were, as a rule, available only in Ukrainian. Some other information materials (e.g. the Law on refugees) were also available, but only in French or Russian; Border Guard staff indicated that they had run out of materials in other languages. A positive aspect was the involvement of NGOs in the provision of assistance and information to foreign nationals, on the basis of agreements with the State Border Service. However, the fact that outside bodies were helping foreign detainees does not discharge the State from its responsibility to provide information and assistance to such detainees.The major complaint of foreign nationals detained was the lack of knowledge of what was happening in their case and how long they would spend in custody. This uncertainty greatly exacerbated the experience of confinement and led to tensions. The observations made during the visit suggest that Border Guard staff need to be more attentive to these problems.41. As regards the provision of interpretation, a number of detained foreign nationals complained that, following their apprehension, they had been asked to sign documents in Ukrainian without understanding their content. Even when interpretation had been available, the information provided was allegedly not always comprehensible. The delegation learned that there was a shortage of local interpreters speaking the less common languages; to overcome the problem, plans were being made to set up facilities for distance interpretation at the main border units.”Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)40. The UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers, dated October 2007, reads, in so far as relevant:“13. Under the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are responsible for considering the initial applications for asylum and can decide on the admissibility. If the Regional Migration Service decides to admit a case into the procedure, it will then consider the substance and make a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then takes a decision on the case. The SCNR may approve the RMS recommendation or may take a different approach. Asylum‑seekers can appeal a negative decision from the Regional Migration Service either to the SCNR or to the courts....31. Regarding the quality of the asylum procedure, one of the main problems in Ukraine’s asylum management (as stated in paragraph 13 above) has been the constant reform of the asylum institutions which have been remodelled by successive governments, and in particular of the central executive body. In March 2007, by decree of the Cabinet of Ministers (No. 201), the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions (previously the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration) became the authorized central body of executive power to deal with asylum issues. Its activities are directed and coordinated by the Cabinet of Ministers through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine....42. With regard to reception standards, neither asylum-seekers nor refugees have adequate access to State-sponsored accommodation, material assistance or employment. According to Article 20 of the Refugee Law, only recognized refugees are eligible for financial aid and accommodation. In Ukraine, there is only one temporary accommodation centre for asylum-seekers and refugees currently in operation. It has a capacity of up to 250 places. According to Article 7 of the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services should determine places for temporary accommodation and generally facilitate the provision of housing to refugees and asylum-seekers. In practice, however, the Regional Migration Services are unable to provide such services. Instead, refugees and asylum-seekers have to rent accommodation from private owners. As “foreigners”, the rents requested from them are much higher than those charged to nationals. Rents for private accommodation, especially in the cities, are high and continue to increase. As a result, many refugees are obliged to spend almost their complete income on accommodation. Many remain homeless or live in sub-standard conditions, risking their physical and psychological health....46. The overall situation motivates some asylum-seekers to try to leave in search of better protection elsewhere. They are often apprehended for attempting to cross illegally the Western border of Ukraine. Detention has therefore been on the increase. Although detention conditions have improved in recent years, they are still poor due to the ever-growing number of irregular migrants and difficulties of the State to cope with the increased numbers. Asylum-seekers are detained jointly with other foreigners and remain in detention for protracted periods. This type of administrative detention may amount to a denial to the right to seek asylum....52.  ... UNHCR advises States, to refrain from returning third country asylum‑seekers to Ukraine as at present no assurances can be given that the persons in question: a) would be readmitted, b) would have access to a fair and efficient refugee status determination procedure, c) would be treated in accordance with international refugee standards or d) that there would be effective protection against refoulement.”Human Rights Watch41. In a 124-page report published in December 2010 and entitled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) described the results of their research on the experience of migrants and asylum-seekers returned to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.42. According to the report, most of the fifty people who were interviewed and who had been returned to Ukraine from Slovakia or Hungary said they had asked for asylum upon arrival in Slovakia or Hungary, but that their requests had been ignored and they had been swiftly expelled back to Ukraine.43. The report deplores the fact that in December 2009 the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior abrogated an agreement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League which since 2007 had permitted NGO lawyers to monitor return procedures at the border.44. Concerning the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, the report notes that many of the concerns previously noted by HRW have been addressed. In particular, the material conditions at the centres have improved, all of the facilities visited by the HRW in 2010 looked clean and well-ordered and none were overcrowded. Most of the detainees interviewed in most locations had no complaints regarding lack of hygiene or overcrowding. However, former detainees of the temporary detention facility at Chop indicated that the institution was sometimes overcrowded. The most frequent complaints were about the food, both quality and quantity, and lack of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet and television. HRW also observed that certain other problems persisted: particularly, access to the asylum procedure; detention of children; mixing of children with adults; corruption; and the disproportionate use of migrant detention in general.45.
