FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11/09/2020

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Yonko Grozev,
Alena Poláčková,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Lado Chanturia,
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application against Slovakia and Ukraine lodged with the Court on 16 March 2011 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Afghan national, Mr M.S. (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, and to strike the remainder of the application out of the list and declare it inadmissible;

the decision of the Section President to grant the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovak NGO, leave to intervene in the written proceedings (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2);

the decision not to disclose the applicant’s name;

Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant complained that, after arresting him following his crossing from Ukraine, the Slovakian authorities had failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. They had subsequently returned him to Ukraine, where he had been detained in inadequate conditions without regard to his alleged status as a minor, in breach of Article 3. He had been unable to participate effectively in the proceedings relating to his detention and had ultimately been returned to Afghanistan without an adequate assessment of the risks he faced there, in violation of Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Lastly, he alleged under Article 34 that an NGO representative had been refused access to him in Ukraine, thereby preventing him from lodging an application for an interim measure with the Court.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant lives in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, when the application was lodged, was employed by the Representative Office in Ukraine of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“HIAS”).

3. The Government of the Slovak Republic were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The applicant claimed that he had been born in 1993 or 1994, while the Slovakian and Ukrainian authorities recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
In support of his claim, the applicant submitted to the Court, together with his application form, a photocopy of his Afghan identity document in the original language, measuring 6 by 7 cm, and an “unofficial translation” into English prepared by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to that translation, the field marked “Date of birth and age” stated “age 8 years in year 2002”. The applicant also provided the Court with a photograph which he believed showed that he looked like a teenager.

The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia

5. Before leaving Afghanistan, the applicant lived in Kunduz province, in the north of the country.

6. According to the applicant, his father had worked with the National Security Department of Afghanistan. After arresting some drug smugglers, he was killed in around 2005 by unknown persons, possibly linked to the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. The applicant did not know its precise contents, but his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and arranged for him to leave the country.

7. Also according to the applicant, in May 2010 smugglers took him to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. The smugglers subsequently took his passport away. He then travelled on to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He remained in Moscow for one month before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He stayed in Kyiv for three months. During his journey to Ukraine, the applicant was accompanied by his brother-in-law (his sister’s husband). In Ukraine, the applicant and his brother-in-law parted ways. The brother-in-law managed to cross into Slovakia three days after the applicant, travelled to Spain and applied for asylum there.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, the applicant was arrested by the Slovak border police while illegally crossing into Slovakia with three other Afghan nationals. He had no identity documents.

9. According to records supplied by the Slovak Government, at 7.25 p.m. that same day the applicant was interviewed by border police officers to establish his identity and clarify the circumstances in which he had committed the offence of illegal entry into and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation from Slovak into English was provided. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently a member of the applicant’s group of Afghans, translated from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He told the police that he wished to travel to western Europe to live and work there, and that he was not seeking asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record was signed by a police officer and the interpreter from Slovak into English, but not by the applicant or Mr Zazai.
The Government of Slovakia submitted that the applicant had been asked to sign the record but had refused without giving a reason. By contrast, two other members of his group signed similar records.

11. On 24 September 2010, a decision to expel the applicant was issued. He was also prohibited from entering Slovakia for five years. He was provided with a Pashto translation of the guidelines on expulsion, summarising the relevant Slovak legislation and procedures concerning the expulsion of foreigners. According to the Government of Slovakia, the expulsion decision had been translated into Pashto. The document submitted by the Government is primarily in Pashto script. The sections setting out general rules and quotations from legislation appear to be in that language, while certain case-specific details, such as the date and the destination country, Ukraine, are written in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010, the applicant was handed over to the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant alleged that, throughout his stay in Slovakia, he had received no interpretation services or information about the asylum procedure in Slovakia and had had no access to a lawyer. As he spoke no European language, he had attempted to request asylum with the help of a fellow Afghan who spoke some French. However, the Slovak officials had not responded. Despite his attempts to speak to them and inform them that he was a minor, they had recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. They had not given him any written decision concerning his return to Ukraine or explained any possible avenues of appeal.

Return to Ukraine and detention there

14. Following his expulsion to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was placed in the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He alleged that, through other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had informed a guard, whom he believed to be the supervisor, that he was fourteen years old. He also alleged that he had told a representative of Caritas, an NGO, that he was a minor and wished to apply for asylum, and that the Caritas representative had passed that information on to the border guards, but no action had been taken.

15. According to the applicant, the conditions of detention in the Chop facility were unsatisfactory. The cells were overcrowded. At times, detainees were not guaranteed daily exercise and “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. On an unspecified date, the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) issued an order requiring the applicant to leave Ukraine voluntarily.

17. On an unspecified date, the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court, seeking the applicant’s forcible expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. According to the court’s decision (see paragraph 18 below), the applicant agreed to the SBCS’s application.
According to the court decision, on 1 October 2010 the SBCS and the applicant also asked the court to consider the case in their absence through a written procedure.

18. On 13 October 2010 the court granted the application and ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine and his detention pending expulsion. The court stated that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992. It found that he had entered Ukraine illegally, had no means to return voluntarily and no relatives in Ukraine, and had crossed the border with Slovakia illegally. In the court’s view, this showed that he was unlikely to comply with an order to leave the territory voluntarily.

19. The court further referred to a United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”) publication entitled Collection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН), published in February 2008, apparently in Ukrainian translation. That publication has not been made available to the Court. According to the circuit court, it indicated that “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). It therefore concluded that, if returned to Afghanistan, the applicant’s life would not be at risk. The court noted that the applicant had not lodged an asylum application and did not wish to apply for asylum in Ukraine.

20. According to the applicant, he was unaware of the proceedings, had no legal representation and did not understand his rights in the proceedings before the court. He had signed a document waiving his right to appear in court without understanding its contents. The court’s decision was not served on him, and he was not given any information on how to appeal. As a result, he missed the ten-day time-limit for lodging an appeal (see the relevant provision of domestic law in paragraph 37 below).

21. On 14 October 2010 the applicant was transferred from the Border Guard temporary holding facility to temporary accommodation for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, which was then under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior. He alleged that, on arrival, he had told the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. The officer allegedly notified the facility’s management, but no action was taken.

22. On 20 February 2011 the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv interviewed the applicant by telephone and, on 22 February 2011, issued him a travel document stating his date of birth as 14 January 1992.

Asylum application in Ukraine

23. On 19 October 2010 the applicant, together with three other Afghans, attended a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO that was a local partner of the International Organization for Migration.
One of the Afghans acted as an interpreter. Information on how to apply for refugee status was given. The applicant did not dispute that the session had taken place, but stated that he had no memory of it.

24. On 23 February 2011 the applicant submitted an application for asylum in Ukraine. In support of his application, he stated that he would be “immediately killed” if returned to Afghanistan.

25. On 2 March 2011 an officer from the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”) interviewed the applicant about his asylum application. The applicant stated that he had lived in Kunduz, Afghanistan, where he had been studying and was supported by his maternal uncle. When asked what had caused him to leave Afghanistan, he stated that his father had been killed by the Taliban four years earlier and that the Taliban had subsequently begun threatening him. His uncle had received a piece of paper, the contents of which were unknown to the applicant, and had told him that he had to leave the country. His uncle had then obtained travel documents for him, with which he had left Afghanistan without difficulty. When asked about his intended destination, the applicant replied that he wished to reach London, where his sister lived. He explained that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan using his passport and an entry visa, but that the smugglers had later taken those documents from him. He also stated that he had entered Ukraine from Russia and had travelled through Kyiv to the Slovakian border. He had not sought assistance in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to take him to London, where his sister was living.

26. A questionnaire based on the same interview recorded the applicant’s responses to several standardised questions about his identity, history and background. It stated, in particular, that the applicant had been born on 14 January 1992, that his mother tongue was Dari and that he also spoke Pashto.

27. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the applicant’s asylum application as inadmissible (see paragraphs 34 and 35 below for a description of the two stages of the asylum procedure in Ukraine). The Regional Migration Service found that (i) the facts on which his application was based were manifestly unfounded, since he could not be regarded as a “refugee”
under section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below); (ii) since the applicant was not a member of any political, social or military organisation and had no connection with any violent incidents involving race, ethnicity, religion or political views, he did not qualify as a refugee under the Refugee Convention; (iii) the fact that the country of origin had provided the applicant with a travel document showed that he had benefited from its protection, which, under Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, meant that the Convention did not apply to him; (iv) the applicant had not sought asylum while travelling through Tajikistan, Russia or Ukraine, but had done so only after being returned from Slovakia to Ukraine. This indicated that he had not intended to seek asylum in Ukraine, but rather to reach the United Kingdom, where his sister lived; (v) as the applicant had no identity documents, it was not possible to establish his identity or country of origin.

Expulsion to Afghanistan

28. According to the applicant, on 11 March 2011, in preparation for his expulsion to Afghanistan, he was transferred to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where he was notified of the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011.

29. According to the applicant, on 12 March 2011, a Saturday, an NGO partner of the UNHCR tried to contact him and other Afghan nationals facing expulsion in order to provide them with legal advice. However, it was denied access to them, thereby preventing the applicant from requesting an interim measure from the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.

30. On the same day, the applicant was placed on a train to Kyiv.

31. On 14 March 2011, the applicant was expelled to Kabul.

32. The applicant alleged that, approximately three weeks after his expulsion to Afghanistan, unknown individuals had come looking for him at his home and had left him a threatening letter. His mother had arranged for him to leave Kunduz for Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. Since then, he had been forced to change his place of residence frequently for fear of those who had killed his father, and had travelled regularly between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant domestic law in Ukraine

Refugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the material time)

33. Under section 1, a refugee was defined as follows:

“... a person who is not a citizen of Ukraine and who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality and is unable to avail himself of the protection of that country or, because of such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of such protection, or who, having no nationality and being outside the country of his former permanent residence, is unable or unwilling to return to it because of the said fear ...”

34.
Sections 12 to 14 and 16 of the Act established a two-stage asylum procedure: admissibility and merits stages. The regional migration services were responsible for examining initial asylum applications and determining their admissibility. If a regional migration service found an application admissible, it opened proceedings on the merits and submitted a recommendation on the merits of the application to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions. The Committee then made a final decision to grant or refuse asylum. Asylum-seekers could appeal against a negative decision by the regional migration service either to the Committee or to the courts. Lodging an appeal constituted grounds for registering the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.

35. Section 12 provided that the examination of an asylum application was to begin with an interview conducted in a language understood by the asylum-seeker, if necessary with the assistance of an interpreter. A decision of inadmissibility was to be taken if the applicant did not meet the definition of a refugee set out in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above), or if the application was abusive: based on a false identity or submitted by an individual whose previous application had been rejected, unless the circumstances had changed.

Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)

36. Section 32 of the Act set out the procedure for the expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It specified the grounds for compulsory expulsion, which included a serious breach of the legislation governing foreign nationals and stateless persons, and provided that such persons could be detained in temporary accommodation facilities for the period required to arrange their removal, not exceeding six months.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)

37. Under Article 186 of the Code, an appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the pronouncement of a judgment. If the judgment was issued in writing, the appeal had to be lodged within ten days of the applicant’s receipt of a copy of the judgment.

International law

Agreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons

38. The Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 2010, reads in its relevant parts as follows:

Article 3

Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons

“1. The requested State, upon application by the requesting State and without any further formalities other than those provided for in this Agreement, shall readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons who do not, or no longer, fulfil the conditions in force for entry into or stay on the territory of the requesting State, provided that ...”
such persons: ... (a) illegally entered the territory of the Member States directly from the territory of Ukraine, or illegally entered the territory of Ukraine directly from the territory of the Member States;”

Relevant international materials concerning the situation in Slovakia and Ukraine

European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“the CPT”)

39. The report on the CPT’s 2007 visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), published on 19 May 2009, states in the relevant parts as follows:

“A. Establishments under the authority of the State Border Service

...

39. As regards access to a lawyer, this was limited to visits by pro bono lawyers from NGOs, who assisted foreign nationals in filing asylum applications and provided information on the relevant legal procedures. However, the delegation was concerned to learn that, at Chop, NGO lawyers had restricted access to detained persons (that is, they could meet only persons whose names they already knew). It should also be noted that the provision of legal advice was hindered by the lack of adequate interpretation at Border Guard detention facilities (see also paragraph 41).

...

40. The delegation observed that many foreign nationals lacked information about their legal status, the procedure applicable to them, and their rights (including the right to lodge complaints). The internal regulations displayed in the detention areas were generally available only in Ukrainian. Some other information materials (for example, the Law on Refugees) were also available, but only in French or Russian; Border Guard staff stated that they had run out of materials in other languages. One positive aspect was the involvement of NGOs in providing assistance and information to foreign nationals, on the basis of agreements with the State Border Service. However, the assistance provided by outside bodies to foreign detainees does not relieve the State of its responsibility to provide such detainees with information and assistance.

The main complaint among detained foreign nationals was their lack of knowledge about what was happening in their case and how long they would remain in custody. This uncertainty significantly worsened the experience of confinement and caused tensions. The observations made during the visit indicate that Border Guard staff need to be more attentive to these issues.

41. Concerning the provision of interpretation, several detained foreign nationals complained that, after being apprehended, they had been asked to sign documents in Ukrainian without understanding their contents. Even where interpretation had been provided, the information given was allegedly not always comprehensible.
The delegation learned that there was a shortage of local interpreters who spoke the less common languages; to address the problem, plans were under way to establish facilities for remote interpretation at the main border units.”

Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)

40. The UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers, dated October 2007, states, in so far as relevant:

“13. Under the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services are responsible for reviewing initial asylum applications and may decide on their admissibility. If the Regional Migration Service decides to admit a case to the procedure, it will then examine the substance and make a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then makes a decision on the case. It may approve the RMS recommendation or adopt a different approach. Asylum-seekers may appeal a negative decision by the Regional Migration Service either to the SCNR or to the courts.

...

31. As regards the quality of the asylum procedure, one of the principal problems in Ukraine’s asylum management (as noted in paragraph 13 above) has been the continual reform of the asylum institutions, which have been restructured by successive governments, particularly the central executive body. In March 2007, by decree of the Cabinet of Ministers (No. 201), the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions (formerly the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration) became the authorized central executive body responsible for asylum matters. Its activities are directed and coordinated by the Cabinet of Ministers through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine.

...

42. Regarding reception standards, neither asylum-seekers nor refugees have adequate access to State-funded accommodation, material assistance or employment. Under Article 20 of the Refugee Law, only recognized refugees are eligible for financial assistance and accommodation. Ukraine currently has only one operational temporary accommodation centre for asylum-seekers and refugees, with a capacity of up to 250 places. Under Article 7 of the Refugee Law, the Regional Migration Services should designate places for temporary accommodation and generally facilitate the provision of housing to refugees and asylum-seekers. In practice, however, the Regional Migration Services are unable to provide these services. Refugees and asylum-seekers must instead rent accommodation from private owners. As ‘foreigners’, they are asked to pay rents much higher than those charged to nationals. Rents for private accommodation, particularly in cities, are high and continue to rise. Consequently, many refugees are forced to spend almost their entire income on accommodation. Many remain homeless or live in substandard conditions, putting their physical and psychological health at risk.

...

46.
The overall situation prompts some asylum-seekers to try to leave in search of better protection elsewhere. They are often apprehended while attempting to cross Ukraine’s western border illegally. Detention has consequently been increasing. Although detention conditions have improved in recent years, they remain poor because of the ever-growing number of irregular migrants and the State’s difficulties in coping with these increased numbers. Asylum-seekers are detained together with other foreigners and remain in detention for prolonged periods. This form of administrative detention may amount to a denial of the right to seek asylum....

52. ... UNHCR advises States to refrain from returning third-country asylum-seekers to Ukraine, as no assurances can currently be given that the persons concerned: (a) would be readmitted; (b) would have access to a fair and efficient refugee status determination procedure; (c) would be treated in accordance with international refugee standards; or (d) would have effective protection against refoulement.”

Human Rights Watch

41. In a 124-page report published in December 2010 entitled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) described the findings of its research into the experiences of migrants and asylum-seekers returned to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.

42. According to the report, most of the fifty interviewees who had been returned to Ukraine from Slovakia or Hungary said that they had requested asylum upon arriving in Slovakia or Hungary, but that their requests had been disregarded and they had been swiftly expelled back to Ukraine.

43. The report deplores that, in December 2009, the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior terminated an agreement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League which, since 2007, had allowed NGO lawyers to monitor return procedures at the border.

44. Regarding the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, the report notes that many of the concerns previously identified by HRW have been addressed. In particular, material conditions at the centres have improved; all facilities visited by HRW in 2010 appeared clean and orderly, and none were overcrowded. Most detainees interviewed in most locations had no complaints about poor hygiene or overcrowding. However, former detainees at the temporary detention facility in Chop indicated that the institution was sometimes overcrowded. The most common complaints concerned the quality and quantity of food and the lack of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet, and television. HRW also observed that certain other problems persisted, particularly access to the asylum procedure; the detention of children; the mixing of children with adults; corruption; and the disproportionate use of migrant detention in general.

45.
According to the report, migration detainees in Ukraine lacked consistent and predictable access to a judge or other authority. Nor did they have access to legal representation that would enable them to challenge their detention. Moreover, there was generally no individualised assessment of whether the detention of migrants or asylum-seekers was necessary.

Relevant international materials concerning the situation in Afghanistan

46. The UNHCR’s Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Asylum-Seekers from Afghanistan, published on 17 December 2010, state, insofar as relevant:

“I. Introduction

...

UNHCR considers that individuals with the profiles set out below require a particularly careful examination of possible risks. These risk profiles, while not necessarily exhaustive, include (i) individuals associated with, or perceived as supportive of, the Afghan Government...

In view of the worsening security environment in certain parts of the country and the increasing number of civilian casualties, UNHCR considers that the situation may be characterised as one of generalised violence in Helmand, Kandahar, Kunar, and parts of Ghazni and Khost provinces. Accordingly, Afghan asylum-seekers who formerly resided in these areas may require international protection under broader international protection criteria, including complementary forms of protection. In addition, given the fluid and volatile nature of the conflict, asylum applications by Afghans claiming to flee generalised violence in other parts of Afghanistan should be assessed carefully on an individual basis, in light of the evidence presented by the applicant and other current and reliable information concerning the place of former residence. This determination will clearly need to include an assessment of whether a situation of generalised violence exists in the place of former residence at the time of adjudication.

UNHCR generally considers internal flight to be a reasonable alternative where protection is available from the individual’s own extended family, community, or tribe in the prospective area of relocation. Single males and nuclear family units may, in certain circumstances, be able to subsist without family and community support in urban and semi-urban areas with established infrastructure and under effective Government control. Nevertheless, given the breakdown of the country’s traditional social fabric caused by decades of war, massive refugee flows, and increasing internal migration to urban areas, a case-by-case analysis will be necessary.

...

III. Eligibility for International Protection

...

A. Potential Risk Profiles

1.
Individuals Associated with, or Perceived as Supporting, the Government and the International Community, Including the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF)

There is a systematic and ongoing campaign by armed anti-Government groups to target civilians associated with, or perceived as supporting, the Afghan Government or the international community, particularly in areas where such groups operate....

Most targeted attacks on civilians by armed anti-Government groups have occurred in those groups’ strongholds. However, the number of targeted assassinations and executions of civilians has also risen in other parts of the country previously regarded as more secure. In the south-eastern and central regions, the number of assassinations and executions allegedly carried out by armed anti-Government groups in 2010 increased compared with 2009. Such targeted attacks rose sharply in parts of the southern region, particularly in Kandahar, where the Taliban have conducted a systematic and targeted assassination campaign since the beginning of 2010. From June to mid-September 2010, an average of 21 assassinations per week was recorded—compared with seven per week during the same period in 2009—mostly in the southern and south-eastern regions.

UNHCR considers that persons associated with, or perceived as supporting, the Government and the international community and forces—including Government officials, Government-aligned tribal and religious leaders, judges, teachers, and workers on reconstruction and development projects—may, depending on the individual circumstances of the case, be at risk on account of their actual or imputed political opinion, particularly in areas where armed anti-Government groups operate or exercise control....

B. Eligibility Under Broader International Protection Criteria, Including Complementary Forms of Protection

...1. Civilian casualties...

In the first half of 2010, suicide attacks caused 183 civilian deaths, more than half of which occurred in the southern region. This represents a 20 percent increase compared with the same period in 2009.

Although armed anti-Government groups predominantly targeted military objectives during the first half of 2010, IED and suicide-attack tactics were also used in civilian areas, including along roads used by civilians, around government buildings, outside hotels, in busy markets, and in commercial areas.

Despite sustained efforts over the last decade to clear mines and UXOs, and a steady decline in the number of Afghan victims, mines and explosive remnants cause an average of 42 casualties per month, the large majority of whom are children.
In addition to causing loss of life and serious injury, mine contamination has hindered livelihood activities, including by blocking access to agricultural land, water, healthcare and education.256 A further UNHCR analysis of reported incidents involving civilian casualties between 1 July 2010 and 8 October 2010 reveals that the provinces most affected by indiscriminate conflict-related violence are Helmand and Kandahar in the southern region and Kunduz in the north-eastern region....

3. Conflict-Induced Displacement and Voluntary Returns

Growing insecurity and violence in certain parts of Afghanistan, resulting from fighting between anti-Government groups and pro-Government forces, continue to cause significant population displacement. The number of conflict-induced IDPs continues to increase, with displacement occurring largely in Afghanistan’s southern and western regions....

While conflict-induced displacement in Afghanistan has increased, it should be noted that voluntary returns, particularly from Pakistan and Iran, are also rising. Between March and October 2010, more than 100,000 Afghans returned, twice the number recorded during the same period in 2009. There are several reasons for return, including: (i) the perception that the security situation in some provinces has improved; (ii) economic factors; and (iii) increased insecurity and natural disasters in former settlement areas in Pakistan. Although thousands of Afghans returned to their home areas, nearly one-third currently reside in informal IDP settlements or urban areas in Afghanistan. Some of these settlements are situated in the provinces of Nagarhar, Laghman and Kunar, which are experiencing fluctuating but still significant levels of civilian casualties and security incidents. It should be emphasized that many returns are taking place amid deteriorating conditions for Afghans outside the country rather than substantial improvements in security and human rights conditions in Afghanistan.”

FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF M.S. v. SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11/09/2020

This judgment became final pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention and may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Yonko Grozev,
Alena Poláčková,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Lado Chanturia,
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application (no. 17189/11) brought against Slovakia and Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr M.S., an Afghan national (“the applicant”), on 16 March 2011;

the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, and to strike the remaining complaints out of the list or declare them inadmissible;

the decision by the Section President to authorise the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovakian non-governmental organisation, to intervene in the written proceedings under Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2;

the decision to withhold the applicant’s identity;

Having deliberated in private on 17 March 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant submitted that, after arresting him following his crossing from Ukraine, the Slovakian authorities had not informed him of the grounds for his arrest, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. He was subsequently sent back to Ukraine, where, allegedly without due regard to his claimed status as a minor, he was held in inadequate conditions, in violation of Article 3. He further maintained that he had been unable to take an effective part in the proceedings relating to his detention and had ultimately been returned to Afghanistan without a sufficient assessment of the risks awaiting him there. In his view, this breached Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Finally, relying on Article 34, he alleged that an NGO representative had been refused access to him in Ukraine, thereby preventing him from applying to the Court for an interim measure.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant resides in Afghanistan. He was represented by Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv who, when the application was submitted, worked for the Representative Office of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“HIAS”) in Ukraine.

3. Ms M. Pirošíková acted as Agent for the Government of the Slovak Republic. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. According to the applicant, he was born in either 1993 or 1994. The Slovakian and Ukrainian authorities, however, registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
To substantiate his claim, the applicant enclosed with his application to the Court a photocopy of his Afghan identity document in its original language. The copy measured 6 by 7 cm. He also provided an English “unofficial translation” prepared by a lawyer from the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. The translation indicated that the entry under “Date of birth and age” read: “age 8 years in year 2002”. In addition, the applicant submitted a photograph which, in his view, showed him to be a teenager.

The events in Afghanistan and the applicant’s journey to Slovakia

5. Before leaving Afghanistan, the applicant lived in Kunduz province in the north of the country.

6. The applicant stated that his father had worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department. After arresting several drug smugglers, his father was killed in or around 2005 by unidentified individuals who may have been linked to the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. Although the applicant did not know its exact contents, his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and made arrangements for him to leave Afghanistan.

7. The applicant further stated that smugglers took him to Tajikistan in May 2010, where he used his passport to cross the border. The smugglers later confiscated the passport. He continued through Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia, spending one month in Moscow before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He remained in Kyiv for three months. On the journey to Ukraine, he was accompanied by his brother-in-law, who was married to his sister. The two separated in Ukraine. Three days after the applicant crossed into Slovakia, his brother-in-law succeeded in doing the same, then travelled to Spain and sought asylum there.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, Slovak border police arrested the applicant as he was entering Slovakia illegally with three other Afghan nationals. He was carrying no identity documents.

9. Records submitted by the Slovak Government show that, at 7.25 p.m. that same day, border police officers interviewed the applicant to determine his identity and clarify the circumstances surrounding the offence of unlawful entry into and residence in Slovakia. Interpretation was provided from Slovak into English. A Mr Zazai, apparently one of the Afghans travelling with the applicant, interpreted from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He informed the police that he intended to travel to western Europe to live and work and that he did not wish to seek asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record bore the signatures of a police officer and the Slovak-to-English interpreter, but was signed by neither the applicant nor Mr Zazai.
The Slovak Government stated that the applicant had been invited to sign the record but had declined to do so without giving any explanation. In contrast, two other members of his group signed comparable records.

11. On 24 September 2010, the authorities ordered the applicant’s expulsion and prohibited him from entering Slovakia for five years. He received a Pashto translation of the expulsion guidelines, which summarised the relevant Slovak legislation and procedures governing the removal of foreign nationals. The Slovak Government maintained that the expulsion decision itself had also been translated into Pashto. The document it submitted is predominantly written in Pashto script: the sections setting out general rules and quoting legislation appear in Pashto, whereas some details specific to the applicant’s case—including the date and Ukraine as the destination country—are recorded in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010, the applicant was transferred to the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant asserted that, during his entire stay in Slovakia, he had neither been provided with interpretation nor informed about the Slovak asylum procedure, and that he had been denied access to legal counsel. Since he spoke no European language, he had attempted to seek asylum through another Afghan national who knew some French, but the Slovak officials had failed to respond. Although he had tried to communicate with them and explain that he was a minor, they recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. He further claimed that he had received no written decision regarding his return to Ukraine and no explanation of any available appeal procedures.

Return to Ukraine and detention

14. After being expelled to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was detained at the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He alleged that, with the assistance of other Afghan detainees who spoke Russian, he had told a guard whom he believed to be the supervisor that he was fourteen years old. He also claimed to have informed a representative of Caritas, a non-governmental organisation, that he was a minor and intended to apply for asylum. Although the Caritas representative had passed this information to the border guards, no action had followed.

15. In the applicant’s account, detention conditions at the Chop facility were inadequate. The cells were overcrowded, and detainees were not always assured of daily outdoor exercise; at times, they “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. On an unknown date, the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) ordered the applicant to depart from Ukraine voluntarily.

17. Also on an unspecified date, the SBCS applied to the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court for an order authorising the applicant’s forcible removal from Ukraine and his detention while awaiting expulsion. The resulting court decision (see paragraph 18 below) states that the applicant consented to the SBCS’s application.
According to the court’s decision, both the SBCS and the applicant had requested on 1 October 2010 that the case be considered in their absence under a written procedure.

18. On 13 October 2010, the court granted the application, ordered the applicant’s expulsion from Ukraine, and directed that he remain in detention pending removal. It recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. The court found that he had entered Ukraine unlawfully, lacked the means to return voluntarily, had no relatives in the country, and had illegally crossed the border with Slovakia. In its view, those circumstances indicated that he was unlikely to comply voluntarily with an order to leave Ukraine.

19. The court further relied on a publication by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”), apparently translated into Ukrainian and issued in February 2008, entitled Collection of Country of Origin Information and Legal Materials to be used in Refugee Status Determination (Збірник інформації по країнах походження і юридичних матеріалів для використання в процедурі визначення статусу біженця УВКБ ООН). That publication has not been submitted to the Court. The circuit court stated that, according to the publication, “Afghanistan was not a country where crimes against the person occurred” (Афганістан не є країною де вчиняються злочини проти осіб). It consequently found that the applicant’s life would not be endangered if he were returned to Afghanistan. The court also noted that he had neither applied for asylum nor wished to seek asylum in Ukraine.

20. The applicant maintained that he had been unaware of the proceedings, had not been legally represented, and had not understood his procedural rights before the court. He had signed a waiver of his right to attend the hearing without comprehending what the document said. He was neither served with the court’s decision nor informed of the procedure for appealing it. As a result, he failed to lodge an appeal within the applicable ten-day time-limit (see the relevant provision of domestic law cited in paragraph 37 below).

21. On 14 October 2010, the applicant was moved from the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility to the temporary accommodation centre for foreign nationals and stateless persons in the Volyn Region, which was then administered by the Ministry of the Interior. He alleged that, upon arrival, he had informed the duty officer that he was fourteen years old. Although the officer reportedly notified the facility’s management, no measures were taken.

22. On 20 February 2011, the Embassy of Afghanistan in Kyiv interviewed the applicant by telephone. Two days later, on 22 February 2011, it issued him a travel document listing his date of birth as 14 January 1992.

Asylum application in Ukraine

23. On 19 October 2010, the applicant and three other Afghan nationals took part in a counselling session with a lawyer from an NGO that served as a local partner of the International Organization for Migration.
One of the Afghan nationals acted as an interpreter, and the participants were given information about the procedure for applying for refugee status. Although the applicant did not dispute that the session had taken place, he maintained that he could not remember it.

24. On 23 February 2011, the applicant submitted an asylum application in Ukraine. In support of his request, he asserted that, if returned to Afghanistan, he would be “immediately killed”.

25. On 2 March 2011, the applicant was interviewed about his asylum claim by an officer of the Volyn Regional Department of the Migration Service (“the Regional Migration Service”). He explained that he had lived in Kunduz, Afghanistan, where he had studied and received support from his maternal uncle. Asked why he had left the country, he said that the Taliban had killed his father four years previously and had subsequently begun threatening him. According to the applicant, his uncle had received a piece of paper whose contents the applicant did not know and had told him that he must leave Afghanistan. His uncle had then obtained travel documents for him, which enabled him to depart without difficulty. When questioned about his intended destination, the applicant replied that he wanted to reach London, where his sister lived. He stated that he had travelled from Afghanistan to Tajikistan using his passport and an entry visa, but that the smugglers had later confiscated both documents. He further indicated that he had entered Ukraine from Russia and travelled via Kyiv towards the Slovak border. He had not sought assistance in Ukraine because the smugglers had promised to take him to London to join his sister.

26. A questionnaire completed on the basis of that interview documented the applicant’s responses to standard questions about his identity, personal history and background. Among other things, it recorded that he had been born on 14 January 1992, that Dari was his mother tongue, and that he also spoke Pashto.

27. On 9 March 2011, the Regional Migration Service declared the applicant’s asylum application inadmissible (for an account of the two-stage asylum procedure in Ukraine, see paragraphs 34 and 35 below). It concluded that (i) the factual grounds advanced in support of the application were manifestly unfounded because the applicant could not be regarded as a “refugee”
within the meaning of section 1 of the Refugees Act (see paragraph 33 below);

(ii) As the applicant had never belonged to a political, social or military organisation and had no involvement in violent incidents linked to race, ethnicity, religion or political opinion, he did not meet the Refugee Convention’s criteria for refugee status;

(iii) The issuance of a travel document by his country of origin showed that he had received that country’s protection. Consequently, under Article 1.E of the Refugee Convention, the Convention was inapplicable to him;

(iv) Although the applicant had travelled through Tajikistan, Russia and Ukraine, he had not sought asylum in any of those countries. He applied only after Slovakia returned him to Ukraine. This indicated that he had not intended to claim asylum in Ukraine, but had instead planned to travel to the United Kingdom, where his sister lived;

(v) Because the applicant possessed no identity documents, neither his identity nor his country of origin could be established.

Expulsion to Afghanistan

28. The applicant stated that, in preparation for his removal to Afghanistan, he had been transferred on 11 March 2011 to Mukacheve, Ukraine, where he was informed of the Migration Service’s decision of 9 March 2011.

29. According to the applicant, on Saturday, 12 March 2011, an NGO working in partnership with the UNHCR tried to contact him and other Afghan nationals who were facing expulsion in order to provide legal assistance. The NGO was refused access to them, with the result that the applicant could not request an interim measure from the Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court.

30. Later that day, the applicant was placed on a train bound for Kyiv.

31. He was expelled to Kabul on 14 March 2011.

32. The applicant alleged that, about three weeks after his return to Afghanistan, unidentified individuals had visited his home looking for him and had left a threatening letter. His mother then arranged for him to leave Kunduz and travel to Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul. Fearing those responsible for his father’s death, he had since been compelled to move frequently and to travel repeatedly between Mazar-e Sharif and Kabul.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Relevant Ukrainian domestic law

Refugees Act of 21 June 2001 (in force at the relevant time)

33. Section 1 defined a refugee as:

“... a person who is not a Ukrainian citizen and who is outside the country of his or her nationality because of a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, and who is unable or, owing to that fear, unwilling to seek the protection of that country; or a stateless person who, being outside the country of his or her former permanent residence, is unable or unwilling to return there because of such fear ...”

34.
Sections 12-14 and 16 of the Act established an asylum process comprising two stages: admissibility and examination on the merits. Regional migration services considered asylum applications at first instance and determined whether they were admissible. When an application was declared admissible, the relevant regional service opened proceedings on the merits and submitted a recommendation to the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions. The Committee then issued the final decision granting or refusing asylum. An asylum-seeker could challenge an adverse decision by a regional migration service before either the Committee or the courts. Filing such an appeal provided a basis for registering the appellant’s temporary residence in Ukraine.

35. Under section 12, consideration of an asylum application had to commence with an interview held in a language understood by the asylum-seeker, with an interpreter’s assistance where necessary. An application was to be declared inadmissible if the applicant fell outside the definition of a refugee in section 1 of the Act (see paragraph 33 above), or if it amounted to an abuse—for example, because it relied on a false identity or had been submitted by a person whose earlier application had been rejected, unless the circumstances had subsequently changed.

Legal Status of Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons Act of 4 February 1994 (in force at the relevant time)

36. Section 32 governed the expulsion of foreign nationals and stateless persons from Ukraine. It specified the grounds for compulsory expulsion, including serious violations of the legislation applicable to foreign nationals and stateless persons. It also permitted their detention in temporary accommodation facilities for the time required to arrange removal, subject to a maximum period of six months.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as worded at the relevant time)

37. Article 186 required an appeal to be filed within ten days after a judgment was pronounced. Where the judgment was issued in writing, the ten-day period ran from the date on which the applicant received a copy.

International law

Agreement between the European Community and Ukraine on the Readmission of Persons

38. The Agreement entered into force on 1 January 2010. Its relevant provisions state:

Article 3

Readmission of third-country nationals and stateless persons

“1. At the requesting State’s request, and without any formalities beyond those prescribed by this Agreement, the requested State shall readmit to its territory third-country nationals or stateless persons who do not, or no longer, satisfy the applicable conditions for entry into or residence in the requesting State, provided that ...”
such persons: ... (a) entered the territory of the Member States unlawfully and directly from Ukraine, or entered Ukrainian territory unlawfully and directly from the territory of the Member States;”

Relevant international materials regarding the situation in Slovakia and Ukraine

European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“CPT”)

39. The relevant sections of the report concerning the CPT’s 2007 visit to Ukraine (CPT/Inf (2009) 15), which was published on 19 May 2009, state:

“A. Facilities administered by the State Border Service

...

39. Access to legal assistance was confined to visits from NGO lawyers working pro bono. Those lawyers assisted foreign nationals in submitting asylum applications and informed them about the applicable legal procedures. The delegation was nevertheless concerned to discover that, at Chop, NGO lawyers’ access to detainees was restricted: they were permitted to meet only individuals whose names they already knew. The lack of adequate interpretation services in Border Guard detention facilities also obstructed the provision of legal advice (see paragraph 41 below).

...

40. The delegation observed that many foreign nationals had not been informed about their legal status, the procedures applicable to them, or their rights, including the right to submit complaints. As a general rule, the internal regulations displayed in detention areas were available solely in Ukrainian. Although certain other informational documents, including the Law on Refugees, were provided, they were available only in French or Russian. Border Guard personnel explained that materials in other languages had been exhausted. One positive feature was the participation of NGOs, under agreements concluded with the State Border Service, in assisting foreign nationals and providing them with information. However, assistance from external organisations did not relieve the State of its own obligation to give foreign detainees the necessary information and support.

The principal complaint among detained foreign nationals was that they did not know what was happening in their cases or how long they would remain in custody. Such uncertainty substantially worsened the experience of detention and generated tension. The delegation’s observations during the visit indicated that Border Guard officials needed to pay greater attention to these concerns.

41. With respect to interpretation services, several detained foreign nationals complained that, after being apprehended, they had been required to sign documents written in Ukrainian without understanding their contents. It was further alleged that, even where interpretation had been provided, the information conveyed was not always comprehensible.
The delegation found that interpreters for less widely spoken languages were in short supply locally. To address this difficulty, arrangements were being developed to provide remote interpretation services at the principal border units.

Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”)

40. The October 2007 UNHCR Position on the Situation of Asylum in Ukraine in the Context of Return of Asylum-Seekers states, in relevant part:

“13. The Refugee Law assigns the Regional Migration Services responsibility for examining asylum applications at first instance and determining their admissibility. Where a Regional Migration Service admits an application to the procedure, it subsequently assesses the merits and submits a recommendation to the [State Committee for Nationalities and Religions]. The SCNR then decides the case and may either endorse the RMS recommendation or reach a different conclusion. An asylum-seeker may challenge an adverse decision by the Regional Migration Service before either the SCNR or the courts.

...

31. As regards the quality of the asylum procedure, a major difficulty affecting asylum administration in Ukraine, as noted in paragraph 13 above, has been the repeated restructuring of asylum institutions by successive governments, particularly the central executive authority. In March 2007, Cabinet of Ministers Decree No. 201 designated the State Committee for Nationalities and Religions—formerly the State Committee for Nationalities and Migration—as the central executive body authorized to handle asylum matters. The Cabinet of Ministers directs and coordinates its work through the Vice Prime Minister of Ukraine.

...

42. Reception conditions remain inadequate: neither asylum-seekers nor refugees have sufficient access to State-funded accommodation, material support, or employment. Under Article 20 of the Refugee Law, financial assistance and accommodation are available only to persons formally recognized as refugees. Ukraine currently has just one operational temporary accommodation centre for asylum-seekers and refugees, with capacity for no more than 250 people. Article 7 of the Refugee Law requires the Regional Migration Services to identify temporary accommodation and, more generally, to assist refugees and asylum-seekers in securing housing. In reality, however, those services lack the capacity to provide such support. Refugees and asylum-seekers must therefore rent privately. Because they are regarded as ‘foreigners’, landlords demand substantially higher rents from them than from Ukrainian nationals. Private-sector rents, particularly in urban areas, are expensive and continue to rise. Consequently, many refugees must devote nearly all their income to housing. Many others are left homeless or living in inadequate conditions that endanger their physical and psychological well-being.

...

46.
The broader circumstances lead some asylum-seekers to leave Ukraine in pursuit of more effective protection elsewhere. Many are apprehended while attempting to cross Ukraine’s western border unlawfully, resulting in a rise in detention. Although conditions have improved in recent years, they remain inadequate because the number of irregular migrants continues to grow and the State faces difficulties managing the increase. Asylum-seekers are held together with other foreign nationals, often for extended periods. Such administrative detention may effectively deny them the right to seek asylum.

52. UNHCR therefore recommends that States refrain from returning third-country asylum-seekers to Ukraine. At present, it cannot be guaranteed that those concerned: (a) will be readmitted; (b) will have access to a fair and effective refugee-status determination procedure; (c) will be treated in accordance with international refugee standards; or (d) will receive effective protection against refoulement.

Human Rights Watch

41. In December 2010, Human Rights Watch (“HRW”) published a 124-page report entitled “Buffeted in the Borderland: The Treatment of Migrants and Asylum Seekers in Ukraine”. It presented HRW’s research into the experiences of migrants and asylum-seekers returned to Ukraine from Hungary and Slovakia.

42. The report stated that most of the fifty interviewees returned from Slovakia or Hungary said that they had requested asylum upon reaching those countries. Their claims had allegedly been disregarded, and they had been rapidly expelled to Ukraine.

43. The report criticised the Slovakian Ministry of the Interior for terminating, in December 2009, an agreement with UNHCR and the Human Rights League. Since 2007, that agreement had allowed NGO lawyers to monitor border-return procedures.

44. Regarding the detention of asylum-seekers in Ukraine, HRW acknowledged that many of its previously identified concerns had been addressed. Material conditions in detention centres had improved: every facility visited by HRW in 2010 appeared clean and orderly, and none was overcrowded. In most locations, the majority of detainees interviewed raised no concerns about hygiene or overcrowding. Former detainees at the temporary detention facility in Chop, however, reported that it was overcrowded at times. The most common complaints concerned the quality and quantity of food and the lack of access to lawyers, telephones, the Internet, and television. HRW further found that several problems remained, notably barriers to the asylum procedure, the detention of children, the placement of children together with adults, corruption, and the generally disproportionate use of immigration detention.

45.
The report stated that immigration detainees in Ukraine lacked regular and foreseeable access to a court or another competent authority. They were also unable to obtain legal representation through which they could contest their detention. In addition, the necessity of detaining individual migrants or asylum-seekers was generally not assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Relevant international materials on the situation in Afghanistan

46. The UNHCR Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Asylum-Seekers from Afghanistan, issued on 17 December 2010, stated, to the extent relevant:

“I. Introduction

...

UNHCR considers that persons falling within the profiles set out below require particularly careful scrutiny of the risks they may face. Although these risk profiles are not necessarily exhaustive, they include: (i) persons associated with, or perceived to support, the Afghan Government ...

In view of the deteriorating security conditions in certain regions and the rising number of civilian casualties, UNHCR considers the situation in Helmand, Kandahar, Kunar, and parts of Ghazni and Khost provinces to amount to generalized violence. Afghans seeking asylum who previously lived in those areas may therefore require international protection under broader international-protection standards, including complementary forms of protection.

Moreover, because the conflict remains fluid and volatile, each asylum claim by an Afghan alleging flight from generalized violence elsewhere in Afghanistan must be examined carefully, taking account of the applicant’s evidence and other current, reliable information concerning the former place of residence. That assessment must necessarily determine whether generalized violence exists in the applicant’s former place of residence at the time the claim is decided.

As a general rule, UNHCR regards internal flight as a reasonable alternative when the individual can obtain protection from his or her extended family, community, or tribe in the proposed area of relocation. In some circumstances, single men and nuclear family units may be able to survive without family or community support in urban or semi-urban locations that have established infrastructure and are under effective Government control. Nevertheless, the erosion of Afghanistan’s traditional social fabric—resulting from decades of conflict, large-scale refugee movements, and increasing internal migration to cities—makes an individual assessment necessary in every case.

...

III. Eligibility for International Protection

...

A. Potential Risk Profiles

1.”
Individuals Associated with, or Perceived as Supporting, the Government and the International Community, Including the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF)

Armed anti-Government groups have engaged in a sustained, systematic campaign against civilians who are linked to, or believed to support, the Afghan Government or the international community, especially in areas where these groups operate....

Most targeted attacks against civilians have taken place in anti-Government groups’ strongholds. Nevertheless, targeted killings and executions of civilians have also become more frequent in other parts of the country that were previously regarded as relatively secure. In 2010, the south-eastern and central regions recorded more assassinations and executions allegedly carried out by armed anti-Government groups than in 2009. Such attacks increased particularly sharply in parts of the southern region, notably Kandahar, where the Taliban had pursued a systematic campaign of targeted assassinations since the start of 2010. Between June and mid-September 2010, an average of 21 assassinations was documented each week—up from seven per week during the corresponding period in 2009—with most incidents occurring in the southern and south-eastern regions.

UNHCR considers that individuals connected to, or perceived as supporting, the Government, the international community, or international forces may, depending on the specific circumstances of each case, face danger because of their actual or imputed political opinion. Those potentially at risk include Government officials, tribal and religious leaders aligned with the Government, judges, teachers, and employees working on reconstruction or development projects. The risk is especially pronounced in locations where armed anti-Government groups are active or exercise control....

B. Eligibility Under Broader International Protection Standards, Including Complementary Forms of Protection

1. Civilian Casualties

During the first six months of 2010, suicide attacks killed 183 civilians. More than half of these deaths occurred in the southern region, representing a 20 percent rise compared with the same period in 2009.

Although armed anti-Government groups primarily attacked military targets during the first half of 2010, they also employed improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and suicide attacks in civilian locations. These included roads used by civilians, areas surrounding Government buildings, sites outside hotels, crowded markets, and commercial districts.

Despite continuous mine- and unexploded-ordnance-clearing efforts over the previous decade, as well as a steady decline in Afghan victims, mines and explosive remnants continued to cause an average of 42 casualties each month. Children constituted the large majority of those casualties.
Mine contamination has not only caused deaths and severe injuries, but has also obstructed livelihoods by restricting access to farmland, water, healthcare and education.256 UNHCR’s additional analysis of reported civilian-casualty incidents between 1 July and 8 October 2010 indicates that indiscriminate conflict-related violence affected Helmand and Kandahar Provinces in the south, and Kunduz Province in the north-east, most severely.

3. Displacement Caused by Conflict and Voluntary Return

Significant population displacement continues as insecurity and violence intensify in parts of Afghanistan amid fighting between anti-Government groups and pro-Government forces. The conflict-induced IDP population is growing, with most displacement occurring in the country’s southern and western regions.

Despite this rise in conflict-related displacement, voluntary returns—especially from Pakistan and Iran—have also increased. More than 100,000 Afghans returned between March and October 2010, twice the number recorded during the equivalent period in 2009. Returns have been attributed to several factors: (i) perceptions of improved security in certain provinces; (ii) economic considerations; and (iii) worsening insecurity and natural disasters in former areas of settlement in Pakistan.

Although thousands of returnees went back to their places of origin, almost one third are now living in informal IDP settlements or urban areas within Afghanistan. Some settlements are situated in Nagarhar, Laghman and Kunar Provinces, where civilian casualties and security incidents continue at significant, though variable, levels. It is important to recognize that many Afghans are returning because conditions outside Afghanistan have deteriorated, rather than because security and human rights conditions inside the country have improved substantially.

SECTION FIVE

M.S. AGAINST SLOVAKIA AND UKRAINE

(Application no. 17189/11)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

11 June 2020

FINAL

11 September 2020

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment has become final. It remains subject to possible editorial amendment.

In the proceedings of M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of its Fifth Section, was composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
Yonko Grozev,  
Alena Poláčková,  
Lәtif Hüseynov,  
Lado Chanturia,  
Anja Seibert-Fohr, judges,

and Claudia Westerdiek, Section Registrar.

The Court took into consideration:

the application brought against Slovakia and Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”), which was lodged on 16 March 2011 by Mr M.S., an Afghan national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Governments of the Slovak Republic and Ukraine of the complaints described in paragraph 1 below, while striking the remaining parts of the application out of the list or declaring them inadmissible;

the Section President’s decision, under Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2, to permit the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Human Rights League, a Slovak NGO, to participate in the written proceedings as third-party interveners;

and the decision that the applicant’s identity should not be made public.

Following private deliberations held on 17 March 2020,

the Court gives the following judgment, adopted on that same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant alleged that, after arresting him when he crossed into Slovakia from Ukraine, the Slovak authorities had not told him why he was being arrested, contrary to Article 5 § 2 of the Convention. He was subsequently sent back to Ukraine, where, despite his asserted status as a minor, he was held in unsuitable conditions, allegedly in violation of Article 3. He further maintained that he had been unable to take an effective part in the proceedings relating to his detention and that, ultimately, he had been returned to Afghanistan without a proper evaluation of the dangers he claimed he would face there. In his view, those circumstances breached Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 4, and Article 13 of the Convention. Finally, relying on Article 34, he claimed that an NGO representative had been refused access to him in Ukraine, thereby preventing him from applying to the Court for an interim measure.

THE FACTUAL BACKGROUND

2. The applicant resides in Afghanistan. His representative was Mr A. Maksymov, a lawyer practising in Kyiv. When the application was submitted, Mr Maksymov worked for the Representative Office in Ukraine of the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (“HIAS”).

3. The Slovak Republic’s Government were represented by their Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. According to the applicant, he was born in either 1993 or 1994. By contrast, the Slovak and Ukrainian authorities registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992 (see paragraphs 9, 18 and 26 below).
To substantiate his claim, the applicant enclosed with his application to the Court a photocopy of his Afghan identity document. The copy, in the original language, measured 6 by 7 cm. He also provided an English “unofficial translation” prepared by a lawyer at the HIAS Representative Office in Ukraine. According to that translation, the section headed “Date of birth and age” contained the entry “age 8 years in year 2002”. In addition, the applicant submitted a photograph which, in his view, showed that he appeared to be a teenager.

The applicant’s departure from Afghanistan and journey to Slovakia

5. Before leaving Afghanistan, the applicant resided in Kunduz province in the north of the country.

6. The applicant stated that his father had worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department. After arresting several drug smugglers, his father was killed in about 2005 by unidentified persons who may have been connected to the Taliban. In 2010 the applicant’s maternal uncle received a threatening letter. Although the applicant did not know its exact contents, his uncle concluded that the applicant “also faced a risk related to the killing of his father” and made arrangements for him to leave Afghanistan.

7. The applicant further stated that, in May 2010, smugglers took him to Tajikistan, where he crossed the border using his passport. The smugglers later confiscated the passport. He continued through Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia, spending one month in Moscow before entering Ukraine in early July 2010. He remained in Kyiv for three months. On the journey to Ukraine, he was accompanied by his brother-in-law, who was his sister’s husband. They separated in Ukraine. The brother-in-law crossed into Slovakia three days after the applicant, then travelled to Spain, where he sought asylum.

8. At 4.10 p.m. on 23 September 2010, Slovakian border police arrested the applicant as he was illegally entering Slovakia together with three other Afghan nationals. He was carrying no identity documents.

9. Records submitted by the Slovak Government indicate that border police officers interviewed the applicant at 7.25 p.m. that same day to determine his identity and establish the circumstances in which he had committed the offence of illegally entering and residing in Slovakia. Interpretation was provided from Slovak into English. A certain Mr Zazai, apparently one of the Afghans travelling with the applicant, interpreted from English into Pashto. The applicant’s date of birth was recorded as 14 January 1992. He informed the police that he wanted to travel to western Europe to live and work there and that he did not wish to seek asylum in Slovakia.

10. The interview record bore the signatures of a police officer and the Slovak-to-English interpreter, but it was signed by neither the applicant nor Mr Zazai.
The Slovak Government stated that the applicant had been invited to sign the record but had declined to do so without giving any reason, whereas two other members of his group had signed comparable records.

11. On 24 September 2010, the authorities ordered the applicant’s expulsion and prohibited him from entering Slovakia for five years. He received a Pashto translation of the expulsion guidelines, which summarised the applicable Slovak legislation and procedures governing the expulsion of foreign nationals. The Slovak Government maintained that the expulsion decision itself had also been translated into Pashto. The document it submitted is predominantly written in Pashto script: the sections setting out general rules and quotations from legislation appear in Pashto, but some details specific to the applicant’s case—including the date and Ukraine as the destination country—are in Slovak.

12. At 2 p.m. on 24 September 2010, the applicant was transferred to the Ukrainian authorities.

13. The applicant asserted that, during his entire stay in Slovakia, he had neither been provided with interpretation nor informed about the Slovak asylum procedure, and had been unable to consult a lawyer. Since he spoke no European language, he had attempted to request asylum with assistance from another Afghan who spoke some French, but the Slovak officials had not responded. Although he had tried to communicate with them and explain that he was a minor, they had registered his date of birth as 14 January 1992. He had received no written decision regarding his return to Ukraine and no explanation of any available appeal procedures.

Return to Ukraine and detention

14. After being expelled to Ukraine on 24 September 2010, the applicant was detained in the Border Guard’s temporary holding facility in Chop. He claimed that, through other detained Afghans who spoke Russian, he had told a guard whom he believed to be the supervisor that he was fourteen years old. He further alleged that he had informed a representative of Caritas, a non-governmental organisation, that he was a minor and wanted to seek asylum. According to him, the Caritas representative passed this information to the border guards, but they took no action.

15. The applicant described the detention conditions at the Chop facility as inadequate. The cells were overcrowded, and detainees were not always assured of daily outdoor exercise; at times, they “had to make noise in order to be allowed their one-hour walk”.

16. On a date that has not been specified, the Chop unit of the State Border Control Service of Ukraine (“the SBCS”) ordered the applicant to depart from Ukraine voluntarily.
