FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF ROMANOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 63782/11)

JUDGMENT

This version was corrected on 24 August 2020 under Rule 81 of the Rules of Court.

STRASBOURG

16 July 2020

This judgment is final, but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Romanov v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Mārtiņš Mits, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lәtif Hüseynov, judges,
and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having deliberated in private on 23 June 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

PROCEDURE

1. The case originated in an application (no. 63782/11) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Russian national, Mr Ilya Eduardovich Romanov (“the applicant”), on 30 December 2005.

2. The applicant was initially represented by Mr V. Chernikov and subsequently by Mr V. Komarov, both lawyers practising in Moscow. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

3. On 9 February 2012 the Government were notified of the applicant’s complaints concerning the conditions of his detention in Odessa SIZO and of his transfer to Polytska[1] Prison; his right to adequate facilities for the preparation of his defence; his right to participate effectively in person and to legal representation in his criminal trial; his conviction on account of his political beliefs; and the absence of effective remedies for his complaints regarding the conditions of his detention and transfer.

4. The Government of the Russian Federation did not exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention).

THE FACTS

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. The applicant was born in 1967 and resides in Nizhniy Novgorod.

Background to the case

Dissemination of printed material

6. In 2001 Ya. formed a group of former Komsomol members whose aim was to restore the communist State through a communist revolution. Following arrangements between Ya. and his counterpart in Russia, various materials were printed in Russia, delivered to Ukraine and distributed in different towns during protest meetings taking place at the time as part of a mass campaign calling for President Kuchma’s resignation. The materials included, inter alia, issues 5 and 6 of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies (Совет рабочих депутатов) newspaper and issue 1 of the Rada of Workers’ Deputies (Рада робітничих депутатів) newspaper. The latter was a Ukrainian supplement to issue 5 of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper. Its front page indicated that it was the newspaper of revolutionary communists in Ukraine.

7. Issue 6 of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper contained, among other things, the following articles, some of which had been written by Ya.
under various pseudonyms: “Ukraine: from the tribunal to the revolution, or the people will not be fooled!” (“Украина: от трибунала к революции, или народ не пидмануть!”) concerned the ongoing protest movement against the President and included the following passages: “... But is it not Kuchma who should be found guilty of the genocide [of the Ukrainian people], but the entire capitalist order ... Only the establishment of a Soviet of workers’, peasants’ and soldiers’ deputies and an armed uprising will make it possible to overthrow the Kuchma regime and, thereafter, the [capitalist] order. And the opposition leaders, who are planning a superficial coup d’état, are well aware of this. But they pretend that once Kuchma is gone, the sun of freedom will rise over Ukraine. However, the majority [of the protesters] understand that it is not about Kuchma. The people cannot be fooled. This is why it is still too early to say what the eventual outcome of the anti-Kuchma movement will be ...”

“Is the Ukrainian opposition capable of victory?” (“Может ли украинская оппозиция добиться победы?”). This article criticised the opposition leaders, mainly for their vague actions against the existing political regime, and contained the following passages: “... This is why S. [the leader of the communist party] sided with an obvious criminal. He believed that he could use her [the criminal’s] energy and the people’s hatred of [the current President] to be ushered into power ... Yes, merely ushered in, because to seize power and establish new State bodies one would have to be a very brave and talented person. And if the creation [of new State bodies] required starting a civil war ... one would also have to be a GREAT STATE FIGURE ... Unfortunately, neither S. nor ... any other opposition leader is this kind of person ...

During the meetings on 16 and 24 September, the revolutionaries distributed a large amount of reading material calling on the people to launch a real uprising. Unfortunately, this call has not been heard ... But we remain optimistic ... Judging by how the protests are organised, Kuchma couldn’t care less about those meetings and collected signatures. In his address to the people, he had already stated clearly that he would not resign. He maintained that no revolution was possible in Ukraine because the people did not want unrest. Could [he] be right? Is it possible that the people are ready to die ... but are not taking up arms? We don’t believe it! Unfortunately, the people have not yet understood that only through fierce, bloody fighting will they gain real Freedom. But they certainly will!”

“This crazy, crazy ...” (“Этот безумный, безумный...”). Referring to the hardships of life under capitalism and giving several illustrative examples, the article concludes with the following passage: “... What would you call it? The outrage of those in power.”
Careful analysis of the situation would show that capitalism in Ukraine has become unstable; Kuchma’s power has almost disappeared ... Our main task now is to remain strong and focused. Although this is not an easy task! ... Many of my friends and comrades think I am out of my mind. That is because I propose eliminating the current regime of genocide through a powerful armed revolt by the people, since, on the one hand, the current impotent protests are pointless and, on the other, we cannot endure [the situation] any longer. And it is not only me and my comrades, but 90% of Ukrainians. Yet they are afraid to admit it.”

“...Genocide” (“... Геноцид”) discussed the State’s alleged overpricing of medication and contained the following passage:

“... The answer [as to why the overpricing was happening] is clear: capitalism and genocide are twin brothers in our country, and therefore accusations that [those in power] are committing genocide against our own people are logical ... There is only one solution—to overthrow the power of capitalism altogether, establish a people’s court and then prosecute officials for the genocide of [their] own people ....”

“Great job” (“Замечательная работа”) referred to the low standard of living in Ukraine following the collapse of the Soviet Union and, in particular, people’s dissatisfaction in the workplace. It included the following passages:

“... The lives of workers in the Soviet Union had been too free and easy, resulting in the loss of any notion of a class system. Having suddenly found themselves under capitalism, the people ... felt as though [they had been] knocked down. However, they still have the strength to rise and fight. You only need to be willing and determined ...

I am a professional revolutionary, part of a new generation of fighters against the capitalist order. We are, in fact, the same professionals as ... but we operate illegally. That is why we can call more openly for the overthrow of the regime through an armed revolt. You cannot do that! ... The joy we derive from knowing that we are hastening the fall of the capitalist order in the country is enormous! We are not afraid of repression. We are ordinary people, though just a little more determined. Anyone striving for the victory of workers in the State can do it. The principle is simple: the more of us there are, the faster we will destroy the capitalist order. We have experienced that happiness [from fighting] ... in practice. And we hope you feel the same.”

8. The Rada of Workers’ Deputies contained the following articles, two of which were written by Ya.:

“What the communist revolutionaries of Ukraine want” (“Чего хотят коммунисты-революционеры Украины”) was an introductory article containing the following passages:

“This new newspaper ...
is a printed platform for revolutionary communists whose aim is to develop the Soviet movement in Ukraine, organise a victorious uprising of the people, and declare Ukraine a republic of the Soviets of Workers’, Soldiers’, and Peasants’ Deputies.

A nation subjected to tyranny and oppression has the right to revolt. This international legal principle, long forgotten by the “civilised world,” must become law for the working people of Ukraine in their struggle against the Kuchma regime. Why is it needed?

It is important that working people—workers, peasants, soldiers, and honest officers—realise the full extent of the situation in Ukraine ... We declare that only the Soviets, elected by the working class and supported by armed working people, have the right to rule their country and govern its assets, created through the labour of many generations of workers and peasants.

One must understand that elections conducted under rules drafted by the CIA and Mossad are a deception of the people by those in power. The working class has never, anywhere, managed to improve its life substantially through peaceful means ...

Therefore, all parties that assure the people that the problem of a predatory government can be resolved by means of a “democratic election” are lying ...

Poor, hardworking people must understand that only a nationwide revolt can seize power from ... the capitalist oligarchs ... The truth is that it is impossible to remove those parasites hanging on our necks without bloodshed and victims. Therefore, there is only one way to save our children and grandchildren from death and shame—shed the blood of the parasites and your own in a civil war, win that war, and establish firm revolutionary power. This is the harsh truth, but we do not want to deceive the dying people by claiming that S. [the leader of the communist party] will come and put things right. The capitalists will not return what they have stolen without a fight ...

Therefore, the task of honest communists is to seize the initiative from the capitalists once the President has resigned and transform “the democratic coup” into a socialist revolution. This means that the revolutionaries [will] have to exploit the crisis among those in power and the people’s frustration to organise a victorious revolt.

How can it be won? ... Secondly, urgently establish armed groups. These groups must include former soldiers and officers capable of handling weapons, obeying discipline, and applying their knowledge of warfare. [Then] obtain information about the locations of ammunition and weapons warehouses ...

Thirdly, immediately launch widespread propaganda advocating revolt and calling on working people to join the armed groups ...

Fourthly, do not fear criminal responsibility and be prepared for unavoidable losses ...

[There is] no other way for communists to rid themselves of the stigma of traitors ...
and say to the people: “Our task is to fight for the happiness of the working class, and we are doing so by devoting all our efforts and lives!”

“Kuchma regime – regime of genocide” (“Режим Кучмы – режим геноцида”). In that article, the author mainly discussed the airshow disaster in Sknyliv, suggesting that it had occurred because of the financial greed of those in power. It contained the following passage:

“People must clearly understand that their enemies are not military officers ... Their enemy has settled in Kyiv ... Its name is the capitalist criminal order. There is only one way to defeat this enemy – a determined and offensive revolt. If we do not destroy this regime, it will slowly but surely destroy all of us ...”

“How to turn Ukraine upside down” (“Как перевернуть Украину”). The article discusses the defeat of the communist party in the parliamentary elections. The relevant parts read as follows:

“What lesson should be learned from the communist party’s defeat in the election? History gives a clear answer – we must begin serious preparations and propaganda for a revolt by the working people. We must use every protest movement against the government for this purpose. Nobody should fear civil war. It is already under way! ... This is your fault as well. For ten whole years, you remained far behind your ‘communist’ leaders! ...

Nowadays, the first groups of the military organisation of revolutionaries are already operating in Ukraine. The organisation’s aim is to arrange for armed working people to overthrow the regime of tyranny and oppression. It will be impossible to take power throughout the whole territory of Ukraine. Therefore, the first strategic goal ... is to detach from the capitalist centre the region (or regions) with the highest level of protest among the oppressed working people and to proclaim a Soviet republic of workers’, peasants’ and soldiers’ deputies ...”

“... thereafter [once the initial measures have been taken in the self-proclaimed Soviet Republic], groups of the revolutionary army will advance towards Kyiv in order to overthrow the anti-people regime and replace it with the power of the Soviets of Workers, Peasants and Soldiers.

The communists must be prepared for this and must also prepare the oppressed working people of Ukraine!”

“For the Soviet Republic of Crimea” (“За советскую республику Крым”). The article, which described current events in Crimea, included the following passages:

“... The communist party does not want to take power [in Crimea] except by winning elections ...

As a result, despite the fact that the communist movement is very active in Crimea, its people continue to live in the terrible conditions of modern Ukraine. Thus, the situation is this: whoever is more radical and determined will win. There is only one solution for ... the people: a revolt and the proclamation of a Soviet republic.”

Explosion

9.
On 21 October 2002, an explosive device was detonated in a rubbish bin outside the headquarters of the State Security Service (“the SBU”) in Kyiv. Criminal proceedings were opened in connection with the incident.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant

10. According to official records, on 8 December 2002, while the applicant was fishing in Kakhovka (Kherson Region), fishery workers called the police after finding a gun in his jacket. During an immediate police search, bullets, a homemade explosive device and a detonator were found in the applicant’s bag, while a gun and two passports in his name were discovered in his jacket. The applicant was taken to a police station in Kakhovka.

11. According to the applicant, the events in question occurred on 7 December 2002, and he was held by the police in unrecorded detention until 8 December.

12. On 8 December 2002, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. The copy of the arrest report provided to the Court was illegible. According to the applicant, he requested legal assistance in that report.

13. On 10 December 2002, the applicant was informed of his procedural rights and expressed his wish to be assisted by a lawyer, Chet. On the same day, Chet. was appointed to represent him in the proceedings. When questioned in Chet.’s presence, the applicant stated that he had come to Ukraine to gather material for “a journalism project”. He declined to give any further evidence, relying on his constitutional right to remain silent.

14. According to the applicant, the investigator had instructed him to request Chet.’s assistance.

15. On 11 December 2002, the applicant was charged with unlawful possession of firearms and explosives and was questioned. He denied his guilt and refused to provide any evidence. It does not appear from the relevant interview record that Chet. was present.

16. On 13 December 2002, several individuals were arrested at a flat in Mykolayiv on suspicion of involvement in a number of crimes committed as part of a criminal group led by Ya. (including unlawful possession of firearms, acts of terrorism, assault and robbery), with the aim of starting a communist revolution. The police seized firearms, ammunition, explosives, drugs, copies of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers, and other printed material from the flat. At some point following their arrest, one of the suspects told the police that the applicant might have made the explosive devices found in the flat, as well as the device detonated near the SBU headquarters (see paragraph 9 above). As the domestic courts subsequently established, some of the bullets seized from the flat were of the same calibre and bore the same identification code as those found in the applicant’s bag (see paragraph 10 above).

17.
On 14 and 15 December 2002, Sm., an acquaintance of the applicant who had been in police detention, was questioned as a witness by the Kakhovka police. During those interviews, he stated, among other things, that he belonged to a Russia-based non-governmental organisation that advocated the rights of political prisoners and promoted communist political views. He and two other members of the organisation had been sent to Ukraine to distribute the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and other materials, as well as to take part in public activities organised by opposition political forces in Ukraine and establish links with local leftist groups.

18. On 19 December 2002, the applicant was transferred from Kherson to Mykolayiv, where members of the alleged criminal group led by Ya. were being held pending the outcome of the investigations against them.

19. On 20 December 2002, the SBU instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant for membership of a criminal group. On the same day, that case was joined to the proceedings against those arrested on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above).

20. On 21 December 2002, at the SBU premises in Mykolayiv, the applicant made a handwritten statement (known as an “explanation” (oбъяснение)), stating, among other things, that he had travelled to Ukraine from Moscow to participate in the protest movement against the incumbent President and that, to demonstrate support for the protesters, he had decided to carry out an explosion near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv. According to him, another purpose of the explosion had been to divert suspicion from his wife, who was being prosecuted in Russia for carrying out a similar explosion near the Federal Security Service building in Moscow. The applicant provided details of how he had prepared and carried out the explosion, including the technical specifications of the explosive device he had used. He also confessed to having manufactured other explosive materials. He further stated that he had gone to Kakhovka to meet S., an activist in the communist movement, and to distribute the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers at a protest meeting there. The applicant concluded by stating that he did not believe he had committed any crime, as his actions had been taken in the interests of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, of which he considered himself a citizen and which, in his view, had temporarily fallen under the rule of global, primarily American, imperialism. He also wished to prevent the genocide of the Ukrainian people by the country’s current political regime.

21. According to the applicant, the text of the “explanation” had been dictated to him by the investigator. He agreed to make the statement because, one day earlier, he had been subjected to psychological ill-treatment at the detention facility.

22. According to the applicant, at 4.40 p.m.
On 21 December 2002, after drafting the “explanation”, he was informed of his procedural rights. He submitted that, in principle, he had wished to be represented by a lawyer during the investigation but was prepared to give some evidence, at his own discretion, without a lawyer present. At 5 p.m., when informed again of his defence rights, this time in the presence of a lawyer, Cheb., he repeated that statement.

23. At 5.10 p.m., the applicant was questioned as an accused by the SBU investigator. It appears from the relevant record that no lawyer was present during the interview, as the applicant had expressed a wish to be questioned without a lawyer before it began. Otherwise, the record is a printed version of the applicant’s “explanation” given earlier that day. It was signed by the applicant without remarks and included a handwritten declaration that all the evidence had been given of his own free will and without any pressure from the authorities.

24. On 22 December 2002, the applicant engaged two lawyers, Sk. and K., from a private law firm. On the same day, they were assigned to represent him in the proceedings. According to the applicant, they had been chosen by the investigator and, given his particular situation, he had no option but to enter into an agreement with them.

25. On the same day, a crime-scene reconstruction was carried out with the applicant’s participation and in the presence of Sk. The applicant confirmed his earlier statements concerning his involvement in the explosion near the SBU headquarters. He declined to answer certain questions, including those concerning his accomplices. The reconstruction record was signed by the applicant and Sk. without remarks.

26. On 23 December 2002, in the absence of a lawyer, Sm. provided the SBU investigator with a handwritten statement admitting, in particular, that he had distributed the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and other printed materials in Ukraine and had blown up the rubbish bin near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv in October 2002 together with the applicant and another accomplice.

27. On 25 December 2002, the applicant was questioned as an accused by the SBU investigator. No lawyer was present because, as noted in the relevant record, the applicant had stated that he did not wish to be assisted by a lawyer during the interview. The applicant confirmed that he had manufactured and detonated the explosive device near the SBU headquarters alone. When shown a number of items seized from the flat in Mykolayiv on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above), he confirmed that some belonged to him and had been used by him to manufacture different types of explosives.
He stated that he had no information regarding the ammunition and drugs found at the flat. The applicant also denied the allegations of unlawful possession of firearms and explosives for which he had initially been arrested, and maintained that the material evidence against him had been planted by the police. He further complained that he had been ill-treated by the police, who had attempted to force him to confess to that crime, and that he had instructed his lawyers to lodge a complaint against the officers involved. Lastly, he stated that he was willing to cooperate with the authorities regarding the crimes he had committed in Ukraine, but refused to give any evidence concerning his accomplices.

28. On 29 December 2002, after being informed of his right to legal assistance in the presence of Sk., the applicant expressed his wish to appoint Sk. as his lawyer. Thereafter, in Sk.’s presence, he was charged with membership of a criminal group led by Ya., whose aim had been to overthrow the constitutional order in Ukraine, including through terrorist acts such as the one that had occurred near the SBU headquarters. The applicant, for his part, challenged the legal classification of his actions and argued that they should have been classified either as a terrorism offence or as hooliganism. In doing so, he reiterated that his actions had been intended to prevent a more serious crime – the genocide of the Ukrainian people.

29. Later that day, the applicant was questioned as an accused in Sk.’s presence. During the interview, he again confirmed that he had carried out the explosion near the SBU premises and had manufactured the explosive material found at the flat in Mykolayiv. He maintained that he had acted alone and on his own initiative. The applicant also stated that Ya. had known of his intention to carry out the explosion and could have used that knowledge for his own purposes as a writer. According to the interview record, which was signed by the applicant and Sk. without comment, the applicant had, at his request, held a confidential meeting with Sk. before the interview began. In his submissions to the Court, the applicant denied that any such meeting had taken place.

30. On 3 February 2003, the applicant requested that Chep., a lawyer retained by his relatives, be admitted to the proceedings as his defence counsel, and refused the services of Sk. and K. His request was granted that same day.

31. On 16 and 18 February 2003, several notes addressed to various people were seized from the applicant during a routine search at Mykolayiv SIZO, where he was being detained at the time. No copies of the notes were submitted to the Court.
It appears from the case material that, in those notes, the applicant, among other things, demanded that witnesses in his wife’s case change their testimony, instructed various people on how to force the witnesses to do so, and provided details of the new defence strategy his wife should adopt in order to derail the investigation. He also asked that his lawyer, Chep., be involved in the process and that messages be sent to him through that lawyer. The applicant further assured the intended recipients of the notes that he was not a traitor, since he had confirmed only his own involvement in the explosion near the SBU headquarters and had refused to testify against anyone else. He also stated that the technical description of the explosive device was incorrect and that he would use this “tricky moment” in the future.

32. On 19 February 2003 the applicant was questioned in Chep.’s presence. He refused to give any evidence before the trial.

33. On 3 March 2003 the applicant was transferred to Odessa.

34. On 24 April 2003 the applicant was questioned in connection with his membership of a terrorist group and the distribution of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers. Before the questioning, he agreed in writing to take part in the investigative activity without his lawyer being present. During the interviews, the applicant refused to answer any of the investigator’s questions, relying on his right to remain silent.

35. On 21 May 2003 the original charges against the applicant were changed to dissemination, as part of a criminal group, of printed material containing calls for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order and seizure of power; banditry; terrorism; illegal production and possession of drugs; and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. The applicant was questioned in Chep.’s presence. He admitted his guilt in part but refused to give any evidence until the trial.

36. On 26 May 2003 the applicant was questioned about the notes seized from him at Mykolayiv SIZO on 16 and 18 February 2003 (see paragraph 31 above). He confirmed that he had written them but refused to provide any further evidence.

37. On 27 May 2003 the pre-trial investigation was completed, and from then until 24 July 2003 the applicant and Chep. studied the case file. Although the applicant signed a schedule confirming that he had familiarised himself with the file, he refused to sign a report confirming that he had fully done so. According to the applicant, he had not been given sufficient time to familiarise himself with all the material. Chep. stated that he had familiarised himself with all the material and signed the report without making any remarks.

38.
On an unspecified date, the applicant, together with ten other individuals implicated in the criminal activity carried out by the group headed by Ya., was committed to stand trial before the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Regional Court”), sitting as a first-instance court.

39. Between 2 and 11 September 2003, the applicant was granted additional time to study the case file.

40. On 24 September 2003, the Regional Court appointed A. (a lawyer engaged by the applicant to replace Chep., whose contract had expired) to represent him at trial. She was given until 13 October 2003 to familiarise herself with the case file.

41. During the trial, the applicant submitted that he shared communist beliefs with his co-defendants, whom he regarded as his political comrades, but denied carrying out any acts aimed at overthrowing the constitutional order. In that connection, he stated that he had taken eight issues of the Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspaper from Ya.’s flat in Mykolayiv, intending to use them for household purposes and to give them to Kakhovka residents as firelighters for their stoves. He emphasised that he had given the newspaper to S., whom he had met by chance at a protest meeting and who had expressed interest in its content, as well as to M.

With the exception of Sm., the applicant’s co-defendants admitted distributing the newspapers in question and other material as part of their activities aimed at restoring a Soviet republic. The editor of the newspapers and several other co-defendants acknowledged that the newspaper articles had contained incitement to violence, including calls for an armed revolt against the constitutional order in Ukraine and the seizure of power by revolutionary communists.

The applicant also denied involvement in any of the other criminal activity with which he had been charged and submitted that all his self-incriminating statements made during the pre-trial investigation had been obtained under duress and in violation of the privilege against self-incrimination. In particular, his “explanation” of 21 December 2002 had been dictated to him by the investigator, of whom he had been afraid. The investigator had also promised that, if he made a statement, he would have him declared insane and admitted to a psychiatric institution rather than a prison, as had occurred in the criminal proceedings against him in Russia (for the relevant facts, see Romanov v. Russia, no. 63993/00, 20 October 2005).

He further submitted to the trial court that he had not given any evidence during the subsequent investigative measures, but had merely signed all the documents presented to him by the investigator, without even reading them, because he feared ill-treatment. He also complained that Sk. had been an SBU agent rather than a lawyer of his choosing and had therefore failed to represent his interests effectively.

42. In November 2003, B., one of the applicant’s co-defendants, died in detention.
The remaining defendants alleged that he had died as a result of torture.43. The trial court ordered an inquiry into the circumstances of B.’s death. The prosecutor’s office reported that there was no case of torture to answer, since B. had died of cancer.44. On 19 July 2004 the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of terrorism, dissemination of printed material calling for an armed revolt against the constitutional order, banditry, and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. He was sentenced to ten years for terrorism, one year for distributing the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers, and five and six years respectively for the remaining offences. Applying the rule that a more lenient punishment is absorbed by a stricter one, the applicant’s final sentence was ten years’ imprisonment. He was acquitted of the illegal production and possession of drugs for lack of evidence. The Regional Court did not consider the applicant’s arguments concerning his non-involvement in the distribution of the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers convincing or credible, and gave detailed reasons for its conclusion. It referred, among other things, to the testimony given at trial by S. and M., who confirmed that the applicant had participated in the protest events in Kakhovka and had visited them twice during that period (on one occasion accompanied by Sm.); both times he had brought newspapers and discussed their content with them, maintaining, among other things, that there could be no revolution without victims. The trial court also referred to the content of several letters sent by the applicant from detention, including one to a co-defendant, in which he complained that Kakhovka’s Bolsheviks S. and R., who had been recommended to him as potential partisans, appeared to be the wrong people and had most likely assisted the police in arresting him. At the same time, the Regional Court held that there was insufficient evidence to establish that the applicant had disseminated the material outside Kakhovka or that he had acted on the instructions of Ya. or the newspapers’ editor. Referring further to the content of the articles in the newspapers distributed by the applicant (see paragraphs 7 and 8 above), the Regional Court found it established that they clearly called for an armed revolt in Ukraine aimed at overthrowing the existing legal order and seizing State power by Bolshevik revolutionaries. As regards the conviction for terrorism, the Regional Court relied mainly on the applicant’s confessions made during the pre-trial investigation, including the “explanation” of 21 December 2002, and on the testimony given by Sm. during the pre-trial investigation but retracted at trial.
The court also referred to the content of the notes seized from him at Mykolayiv SIZO; the trial testimony of one of his co-defendants that the applicant had confessed to carrying out the explosion near the SBU headquarters; and a forensic psychiatric report indicating that the applicant had also confirmed his involvement in the crime during the forensic examination.

The court found no evidence that the self-incriminating statements, including his “explanation”, had resulted from any pressure by the investigating authorities, and set out in detail the facts contradicting the applicant’s allegations. It noted, among other things, that when the applicant had given the “explanation”, the investigator had not yet been aware of his psychiatric treatment in Russia, but had known the technical characteristics of the explosive device used near the SBU. Thus, had he wished, the investigator could have ensured that the applicant gave the correct description of the explosive device in his testimony, rather than the one provided in his confession. The court further noted that the applicant’s intention to divert suspicion from his wife and the fact that he had deliberately given the police an incorrect description of the explosive device had also been confirmed in notes addressed to his friends that had been seized from him at Mykolayiv SIZO.

Regarding the applicant’s allegations against Sk., the trial court noted that, by signing the agreement with Sk. and the law firm, he had accepted Sk. as his legal representative. The court also observed that the applicant had wished to retain Sk. as his lawyer during certain investigative activities and, in letters sent from detention, had asked his friends to communicate with him through that lawyer, suggesting that a relationship of trust existed between them.

Referring to the results of an examination of the applicant by a panel of medical experts, which it had ordered, the Regional Court also found unsubstantiated the applicant’s complaint that physical and mental exhaustion had prevented him from participating effectively in the hearings.[2]

45. The applicant appealed. Before lodging the appeal, he was granted access to the case file. In his appeal, he admitted distributing several copies of the Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and discussing its content with those to whom he had given the material. However, he maintained that those actions did not constitute a criminal offence because he had not intended to overthrow the constitutional order in Ukraine, and the newspaper was legally published in Russia and was not banned in Ukraine.
He submitted that it was only during the pre-trial investigation that he had begun to think that a change in the constitutional order in Ukraine – which he understood as the resignation of its President – would be a good thing. The applicant further submitted that his conviction in respect of the other crimes had been based on inconsistent, partly falsified, and insufficient evidence. In particular, as regards his conviction for terrorism, he challenged the admissibility of all confessions he had made during the pre-trial investigation, maintaining that they had been obtained under duress and in breach of his defence rights. In relation to the latter issue, he noted that his “explanation” of 21 December 2002 had been obtained without a lawyer present, despite the fact that shortly after his arrest he had expressly stated his wish to be represented by Chet., who had already been assigned to represent him in the proceedings. He further submitted that the subsequent investigative activities had taken place either without a lawyer present or in the presence of lawyers selected for him by the investigator, including Sk. He also complained that, during the trial, his lawyer A. had been prevented by rules imposed by the convoy service from speaking to him before the hearing of 24 September 2003, and that during the hearing of 5 February 2004 he had been instructed to keep his hands behind his back while replying to the prosecutor’s questions, without being able to consult his notes. Lastly, the applicant complained that he had not been given sufficient time to study the case file.

46. On 26 July 2005, the Supreme Court of Ukraine, sitting as a court of last instance, quashed the applicant’s conviction for banditry and acquitted him of that charge for lack of evidence. In all other respects, the court upheld his conviction and sentence. It found, in particular, that the testimony of various witnesses, including some of the applicant’s co-defendants, given both during the pre-trial investigation and at trial, together with the applicant’s letters sent from detention, confirmed that he had been involved in disseminating material unequivocally calling for the violent removal of the existing political regime.

The Supreme Court also held that there was sufficient evidence that the applicant had unlawfully possessed firearms and explosives, including statements from lay witnesses who had been present when those items were seized from him.

As regards the applicant’s involvement in a terrorist act, the Supreme Court found that his guilt had been established by the confessions made by him and Sm. during the pre-trial investigation, “including during the [crime scene] reconstruction [conducted] with [the applicant’s] participation and in the presence of a lawyer”. It held that those pieces of evidence had been correctly assessed and declared admissible by the Regional Court and endorsed the latter’s findings in that respect.
The Supreme Court further noted that there was other evidence of the applicant’s guilt, including the contents of the notes seized from him in detention and incriminating statements made by his co-defendants at trial. The Supreme Court found no violation of the defence rights of the applicant and his co-defendants, observing that its analysis of the case file indicated that all matters relating to access to lawyers during the proceedings and their replacement had been addressed by the authorities in accordance with the law. Acknowledging that some investigative activities had been carried out without lawyers present, the Supreme Court found that the verbatim records of those activities indicated that the defendants had agreed to testify in the absence of a lawyer. Lastly, the Supreme Court held that the applicant had had sufficient time to prepare his defence, as demonstrated by the numerous references to various pages of the case file in his extensive appeal on points of fact and law. It also observed that the applicant and his lawyer had been granted access to the case file on several occasions, including at the applicant’s request.

47. On 7 December 2012 the applicant was released from prison after serving his sentence in full. The following day, pursuant to a decision by the SBU, he was expelled from Ukraine and banned from re-entering the country for the next three years.

Conditions of Detention in Odessa SIZO

48. From 3 March 2003 until 3 November 2005 the applicant was held in Odessa pre-trial detention facility no. 21 (“the SIZO”).

Material conditions of detention

49. In his initial submissions, the applicant complained that, upon arrival at the detention facility, he had been placed for two months in cell no. 4-133, which had been extremely cold because the window was not glazed. The cell had housed five detainees despite having only four sleeping places. Consequently, he had been forced to sleep on a cold floor during that period. The sanitary facilities at the SIZO had also been very poor. In particular, detainees had had no access to washing facilities for two to three weeks in spring, and hot water had not always been available during the summer. Other than mattresses and covers, detainees had had no additional items in their cells. For seven days in September 2003 the applicant had been confined in a disciplinary cell. It had been flooded, leaving him standing in water up to his ankles.

50. The Government submitted that the conditions of the applicant’s detention had been adequate. Referring to information supplied by the relevant authorities on 14 May 2012, they stated that he had never been held in a disciplinary cell and had been detained in cells nos. 4-133, 4-135, 4-249, 4-244, 4-245, 4-261, 2-73, 2-74, 2-94, 2-303, 2-295, 2-296 and 2-298. These were ordinary cells fitted with a toilet, central water and heating, and artificial and natural lighting. The cells measured between 7.6 and 8.5 sq. m and were intended to accommodate four inmates.
Pursuant to the relevant regulations, detainees were entitled to a one-hour daily walk in the courtyard and weekly access to the shower facility.

51. In his comments in response to the Government’s observations, the applicant maintained his complaint, further submitting that the conditions in all the cells in which he had been detained had been poor. According to him, the cells measured between 8 and 10 sq. m and contained four sleeping places. The toilet was merely a hole in the floor, which was not separated from the living area and was situated one metre from the place where detainees ate their food; there was no artificial ventilation, and the natural airflow was insufficient, resulting in the cell being filled with the smell of excrement, especially during summer; there was no water supply for most of the day; and detainees were provided with no bedding, crockery or personal hygiene items.

Medical assistance

52. Documents submitted by the Government show that, upon his arrival at the SIZO, the applicant underwent a medical examination which revealed no particular health problems. On several occasions during his detention there, he was examined by various medical specialists, including a panel of civilian doctors (comprising an ophthalmologist, a urologist, a general practitioner, a pulmonologist, a cardiologist and a neurologist) on 12 March 2004, following an order by the trial court. He was diagnosed with hypertension, chronic bronchitis (in remission), neurocirculatory dystonia and chronic pharyngitis. The appropriate treatment was prescribed and provided. He was also diagnosed with a congenital cataract, a hereditary condition not amenable to conservative treatment.

53. On 19 March 2004, the applicant made a written statement indicating that he had no complaints regarding his state of health.

54. In October 2005, before his release from the SIZO, the applicant was examined and the previous diagnoses (see paragraph 52 above) were confirmed.

55. While in prison, the applicant complained of back pain. On 14 February 2006, following an examination, he was found to be suffering from severe myopia, astigmatism, cataracts and the aftereffects of a spinal injury sustained in the 1980s. Owing to his health conditions, he was recognised as falling within the third (mildest) category of disability.

56. According to the applicant, his medical examinations at the SIZO were infrequent and superficial. Although he had a long history of spinal problems—for which he was later recognised as having a disability—his condition was neither recorded nor treated at the SIZO. Medical recommendations concerning his other health problems were not followed by the authorities, and no medical treatment was provided, resulting in a deterioration in his health. No medication or equipment was available at the SIZO, and only blood and urine tests were carried out. Detainees were required to provide their own paper and pens for record-keeping.

Transfer between the SIZO and the court

57.
Between 24 September 2003 and 2 July 2004, during the proceedings before the Regional Court, the applicant was transported from the SIZO to the court and back.

58. According to the applicant, on hearing days, which sometimes ran for several consecutive days, and when he was familiarising himself with the case file, he was taken from his cell at about 6 a.m., according to his initial submissions, and at 5 a.m., according to his comments in response to the Government’s observations. He was then placed with other detainees in a special “assembly cell” without windows or heating. They remained there for more than three hours before being taken to court. In the court building, after the hearings and until 3 or 4 p.m., the detainees were kept in a holding cell in the basement. They were generally not provided with hot meals, except for a short period following complaints by detainees. The so-called “packed lunches” consisted only of bread. After returning from court, the applicant had to wait in the same “assembly cell” until 8 p.m. before being escorted to his regular cell. Consequently, he missed mealtimes and was unable to wash, as no water was available at that time of day. These conditions left him exhausted and hungry and prevented him from properly preparing for and participating in the court hearings.

59. According to the Government, most hearings in the applicant’s case lasted no more than three hours per day. As a rule, hearings were held over three consecutive days, followed by three or four days of rest. The SIZO administration always ensured that he received three meals a day. Pursuant to an order issued by the SIZO governor on 11 August 2003, during trial weeks involving more than three consecutive hearing days, the applicant received hot lunches arranged on the court premises by officer K. When the court weeks were shorter, he was provided with packed lunches. His other meals were served at the SIZO.

Transit between prisons

60. In the summer of 2006, the applicant was transferred from Yenakieve Correctional Colony in the Donetsk Region (“Yenakieve Prison”) to Polytska Correctional Colony no. 76 in the Rivne Region (“Polytska Prison”), a lower-security facility, to continue serving his sentence.[3]

61. After leaving Yenakieve Prison on 29 July 2006, the applicant arrived at Polytska[4] Prison on 22 September 2006. While in transit, he was held at Donetsk SIZO until 3 August 2006, Kharkiv SIZO from 3 to 14 August 2006, Dnipropetrovsk SIZO from 14 August to 14 September 2006, and Lviv SIZO from 14 September 2006 until his departure for the final destination prison.

62. According to the applicant, he was subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment during the several weeks of transfer. In particular, the train compartments were overcrowded and lacked ventilation. For lengthy periods, he was provided with no food or drink and had no access to sanitary facilities.
The transit cells at the pre-trial detention facilities where he was held between trains, except for Kharkiv SIZO, had inadequate sanitary conditions, with toilets not separated from the living area and poor lighting and ventilation. He was often deprived of basic necessities, such as bedsheets. Detention facility staff treated the prisoners without respect, forcing them to mop the floors and squat when outside their cells, and beating them for not shaving. Prisoners’ correspondence was often not sent out. 63. According to the Government, the travel documents containing information relevant to the conditions of the applicant’s transit had been destroyed. However, they maintained that the conditions of his transport and detention at transit points had been reasonably adapted to meet his needs. Prison train carriages were of a standard size and designed to accommodate up to eighty people. They contained large compartments measuring 3.5 sq. m, designed for twelve people, and smaller compartments measuring 2.5 sq. m, designed for five people.
