CASE OF ROMANOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 63782/11)

JUDGMENT

This version was corrected on 24 August 2020 pursuant to Rule 81 of the Rules of Court.

STRASBOURG

16 July 2020

The judgment is final, although it may undergo editorial revision.

In Romanov v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), convening as a Committee composed of:

Mārtiņš Mits, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lәtif Hüseynov, judges,

and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having considered the case in private on 23 June 2020,

Gives the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings arose from application no. 63782/11, which Mr Ilya Eduardovich Romanov (“the applicant”), a Russian national, lodged against Ukraine with the Court on 30 December 2005 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”).

2. Mr V. Chernikov initially acted for the applicant and was subsequently replaced by Mr V. Komarov; both were lawyers practising in Moscow. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

3. On 9 February 2012 notice was given to the Government of the applicant’s complaints regarding the conditions in which he had been detained at Odessa SIZO and transferred to Polytska[1] Prison; his right to adequate facilities for preparing his defence; his rights to participate effectively and in person in his criminal trial and to legal representation; his conviction on account of his political beliefs; and the absence of effective remedies in respect of his complaints about the conditions of his detention and transfer.

4. The Government of the Russian Federation chose not to exercise their right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1967, the applicant resides in Nizhniy Novgorod.

Background

Distribution of printed publications

6. In 2001 Ya. established a group made up of former Komsomol members. Its objective was to restore the communist State by means of a communist revolution. Under arrangements made between Ya. and his counterpart in Russia, various materials were printed in Russia, transported to Ukraine, and distributed in several towns during protest rallies then being held as part of a large-scale campaign demanding President Kuchma’s resignation. Among the publications circulated were issues 5 and 6 of the newspaper Soviet of Workers’ Deputies (Совет рабочих депутатов) and issue 1 of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies (Рада робітничих депутатів). The latter publication was a Ukrainian supplement to issue 5 of Soviet of Workers’ Deputies, and its front page presented it as the newspaper of revolutionary communists in Ukraine.

7. Issue 6 of Soviet of Workers’ Deputies included, among other content, the following articles, several of which had been authored by Ya.
Published under various pseudonyms, “Ukraine: From the Tribunal to the Revolution, or the People Will Not Be Fooled!” (“Украина: от трибунала к революции, или народ не пидмануть!”) discussed the ongoing protest movement against the President and included the following statements:

“... Yet it is not Kuchma alone who should be held responsible for the genocide [of the Ukrainian people], but the entire capitalist system ... The Kuchma regime—and subsequently [the capitalist] order itself—can be overthrown only by establishing a Soviet of workers’, peasants’ and soldiers’ deputies and launching an armed uprising. The opposition leaders, who are preparing a superficial coup d’état, know this perfectly well. Nevertheless, they pretend that Kuchma’s departure will cause the sun of freedom to rise over Ukraine. Most [protesters], however, understand that the issue goes beyond Kuchma. The people will not be deceived. It is therefore still too soon to predict the ultimate outcome of the anti-Kuchma movement ...”

“Is the Ukrainian Opposition Capable of Winning?” (“Может ли украинская оппозиция добиться победы?”) criticized opposition leaders, chiefly for the lack of clarity in their actions against the existing political regime. It contained these passages:

“... That is why S. [the leader of the communist party] aligned himself with an obvious criminal. He thought he could exploit her [the criminal’s] energy and the people’s hatred of [the current President] to be ushered into power ... Yes, merely ushered in, because taking power and building new State institutions would require exceptional courage and talent. And if establishing [those new State bodies] meant initiating a civil war ... it would also require a GREAT STATESMAN ... Regrettably, neither S. nor ... any other opposition leader possesses such qualities ...

“At the meetings held on 16 and 24 September, revolutionaries distributed a large quantity of literature urging the people to begin a genuine uprising. Unfortunately, that appeal went unheard ... Even so, we remain optimistic ... Judging by the way the protests are being organised, Kuchma could not care less about these gatherings or the signatures collected. In his address to the nation, he had already made it clear that he would not step down. He maintained that a revolution could not occur in Ukraine because the people did not want turmoil. Could [he] have been right? Could it be that the people are prepared to die ... yet unwilling to take up arms? We do not believe so! Unfortunately, the people have not yet understood that true Freedom can be won only through fierce and bloody struggle. But they certainly will!”

“This Crazy, Crazy...” (“Этот безумный, безумный...”) described the hardships of life under capitalism and offered several illustrative examples before ending with the following words:

“... What else could this be called? An outrage committed by those in power.”
“On close examination, it becomes clear that capitalism in Ukraine has grown unstable and Kuchma’s power has nearly disappeared ... Our principal objective now is to remain strong and resolute, although that is far from easy! ... Many of my friends and comrades believe that I have lost my mind. They think so because I propose ending the present genocidal regime through a powerful armed uprising by the people. On the one hand, the current ineffectual protests are pointless; on the other, we can no longer tolerate [the situation]. This view is shared not only by my comrades and me, but by 90% of Ukrainians, although they are afraid to acknowledge it.”

“...Genocide” (“... Геноцид”) addressed the State’s alleged inflation of medicine prices and contained the following passage:

“... The reason [for the overpricing] is obvious: in our country, capitalism and genocide are twin brothers. It is therefore logical to accuse [those in power] of committing genocide against our own people ... There is only one remedy—to overthrow capitalist rule in its entirety, establish a people’s court, and then prosecute officials for the genocide of [their] own people ....”

“Great job” (“Замечательная работа”) discussed Ukraine’s low standard of living following the collapse of the Soviet Union, focusing particularly on people’s dissatisfaction in the workplace. It included these passages:

“... Workers in the Soviet Union had lived too freely and comfortably, causing them to lose their awareness of the class system. When the people suddenly found themselves living under capitalism, they ... felt as though [they had been] struck down. Nevertheless, they still possess the strength to get back up and fight. All that is required is willingness and determination ...

I am a professional revolutionary, part of a new generation fighting against the capitalist order. In reality, we are the same kind of professionals as ..., but we operate illegally. For that reason, we are able to call more openly for the regime to be overthrown through armed revolt. You cannot do that! ... The tremendous joy we experience comes from knowing that we are hastening the collapse of the country’s capitalist order. We fear no repression. We are ordinary people, only somewhat more determined. Anyone seeking the victory of the State’s workers is capable of doing the same. The principle is straightforward: the more numerous we become, the sooner we will destroy the capitalist order. We have experienced that happiness [of fighting] ... in practice, and we hope that you experience it too.”

8. The Rada of Workers’ Deputies published the following articles, two of which were written by Ya.:

“What the communist revolutionaries of Ukraine want” (“Чего хотят коммунисты-революционеры Украины”) served as an introductory article and included the following passage:

“This new newspaper ...”
It is a printed forum for revolutionary communists seeking to expand the Soviet movement in Ukraine, organise a successful popular uprising, and proclaim Ukraine a Soviet republic governed by Workers’, Soldiers’, and Peasants’ Deputies.

Any nation subjected to oppression and tyranny is entitled to rebel. Although this principle of international law has long been forgotten by the “civilised world,” it must become the guiding law for Ukraine’s working people in their struggle against the Kuchma regime. Why is this necessary?

Workers, peasants, soldiers, and honest officers must recognise the full reality of Ukraine’s situation ... We maintain that the country and the assets produced through generations of labour by workers and peasants may legitimately be governed only by Soviets elected by the working class and backed by an armed working population.

It must also be understood that elections held according to rules devised by the CIA and Mossad amount to those in power deceiving the people. Nowhere has the working class ever achieved a substantial improvement in its living conditions through peaceful means ...

Consequently, every party claiming that a predatory government can be removed through a “democratic election” is lying ...

Impoverished working people must understand that the power of ... the capitalist oligarchs can be seized only through a nationwide revolt. The reality is that the parasites clinging to our necks cannot be removed without bloodshed and casualties. There is therefore only one way to spare our children and grandchildren from humiliation and death: spill both the parasites’ blood and your own in a civil war, emerge victorious, and establish strong revolutionary authority. This is a harsh truth, but we refuse to deceive a dying population by pretending that S. [the leader of the communist party] will arrive and set everything right. The capitalists will not surrender what they have stolen without resisting ....

The duty of honest communists, therefore, is to wrest the initiative from the capitalists after the President resigns and transform “the democratic coup” into a socialist revolution. In practical terms, revolutionaries [will] need to exploit the crisis among those holding power, along with popular frustration, to organise a victorious uprising.

How can victory be achieved? ...

Second, armed groups must be formed without delay. Their ranks should include former soldiers and officers who know the art of warfare, can handle weapons, and are capable of following discipline. [They must then] obtain information about the locations of weapons and ammunition warehouses ...

Third, a broad propaganda campaign must begin immediately, promoting revolt and urging working people to enter the armed groups ...

Fourth, participants must not fear criminal liability and must prepare themselves for inevitable losses ...

[There is] no other means by which communists can free themselves from the stigma of betrayal ...
and tell the people: “Our mission is to struggle for the happiness of the working class, and we are devoting all our strength—and our lives—to that cause!”

“Kuchma’s regime—a regime of genocide” (“Режим Кучмы – режим геноцида”). This article focused primarily on the Sknyliv air-show disaster, which the author claimed had resulted from the financial greed of those in power. It included the following passage:

“People must clearly understand that military officers are not their enemies ... Their true enemy is based in Kyiv ... It is called the capitalist criminal order. There is only one means of defeating it: a resolute, offensive uprising. Unless we destroy this regime, it will slowly but surely destroy us all ...”

“How to turn Ukraine upside down” (“Как перевернуть Украину”). This article discussed the Communist Party’s defeat in the parliamentary elections. The relevant passages stated:

“What lesson should be drawn from the Communist Party’s electoral defeat? History provides an unequivocal answer: we must begin serious preparations and propaganda efforts for an uprising by working people. Every protest movement directed against the government must be used to advance this purpose. No one should fear civil war—it is already taking place! ... You are also to blame. For an entire decade, you lagged far behind your ‘communist’ leaders! ...

The first units of a military organisation of revolutionaries are already active in Ukraine. Its objective is to enable armed working people to overthrow the regime of tyranny and oppression. Seizing power throughout the entire territory of Ukraine will be impossible. Accordingly, the first strategic objective ... is to detach from the capitalist centre the region—or regions—where oppressed working people display the strongest level of protest, and there proclaim a Soviet republic governed by deputies representing workers, peasants and soldiers ...”

“... After the initial measures have been implemented in the self-proclaimed Soviet Republic, units of the revolutionary army will launch an advance on Kyiv to overthrow the anti-people regime and replace it with the authority of the Soviets of Workers, Peasants and Soldiers.

Communists must be ready for this and must also prepare Ukraine’s oppressed working people!”

“For the Soviet Republic of Crimea” (“За советскую республику Крым”). Describing contemporary events in Crimea, the article contained the following passages:

“... The Communist Party is unwilling to assume power [in Crimea] by any means other than an electoral victory ...

Consequently, although the communist movement is highly active in Crimea, the population continues to endure the appalling conditions of present-day Ukraine. The situation is therefore clear: victory will belong to whoever is more radical and determined. The people have only one solution: an uprising followed by the proclamation of a Soviet republic.”

Explosion

9.
On 21 October 2002, an explosive device placed in a rubbish bin outside the headquarters of the State Security Service (“the SBU”) in Kyiv was detonated. Criminal proceedings were subsequently opened in relation to the incident.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant

10. Official records state that on 8 December 2002, while the applicant was fishing in Kakhovka, Kherson Region, fishery workers contacted the police after discovering a gun in his jacket. The police immediately searched him and found bullets, a homemade explosive device and a detonator in his bag, together with a gun and two passports issued in his name in his jacket. He was then taken to a police station in Kakhovka.

11. The applicant maintained that these events had occurred on 7 December 2002 and that the police had held him in unrecorded detention until 8 December.

12. On 8 December 2002, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of unlawfully possessing firearms and explosives. The copy of the arrest report provided to the Court was illegible. The applicant alleged that he had requested legal assistance in that report.

13. On 10 December 2002, the applicant was advised of his procedural rights and stated that he wished to be represented by a lawyer, Chet. Chet. was appointed to act for him in the proceedings that same day. During questioning in Chet.’s presence, the applicant explained that he had travelled to Ukraine to gather material for “a journalism project”. Invoking his constitutional right to remain silent, he declined to provide any further evidence.

14. The applicant asserted that the investigator had instructed him to ask for Chet.’s assistance.

15. On 11 December 2002, the applicant was charged with unlawful possession of firearms and explosives and was questioned. He pleaded not guilty and refused to provide any evidence. The relevant interview record does not indicate that Chet. attended the questioning.

16. On 13 December 2002, several individuals were arrested at a flat in Mykolayiv on suspicion of participating in various offences committed by a criminal group led by Ya., including unlawful possession of firearms, terrorist acts, assault and robbery, with the aim of launching a communist revolution. The police seized firearms, ammunition, explosives, drugs, copies of the newspapers Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies, and other printed materials from the flat. At some stage following the arrests, one suspect informed the police that the applicant might have manufactured both the explosive devices recovered from the flat and the device detonated outside the SBU headquarters (see paragraph 9 above). The domestic courts later established that some bullets seized from the flat had the same calibre and identification code as those discovered in the applicant’s bag (see paragraph 10 above).

17.
On 14 and 15 December 2002, the Kakhovka police questioned Sm., an acquaintance of the applicant who was being held in police custody, as a witness. During questioning, Sm. stated, among other things, that he belonged to a Russia-based non-governmental organisation that defended the rights of political prisoners and promoted communist political views. He explained that he and two other members had been sent to Ukraine to distribute the newspaper Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and other materials, take part in public events organised by Ukrainian opposition political forces, and establish links with local left-wing groups.

18. On 19 December 2002, the applicant was moved from Kherson to Mykolayiv, where members of the alleged criminal group led by Ya. were being held while the investigations against them were pending.

19. On 20 December 2002, the SBU opened criminal proceedings against the applicant on suspicion of membership of a criminal group. That same day, the case was joined to the proceedings concerning the persons arrested on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above).

20. On 21 December 2002, while at the SBU premises in Mykolayiv, the applicant wrote a statement by hand, referred to as an “explanation” (oбъяснение). In it, he stated, among other matters, that he had travelled from Moscow to Ukraine to participate in the protest movement against the incumbent President. To demonstrate his support for the protesters, he had decided to detonate an explosive device near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv. He further stated that the explosion was intended to deflect suspicion from his wife, who was facing prosecution in Russia for a similar explosion near the Federal Security Service building in Moscow. The applicant described in detail the preparation and execution of the explosion, including the technical specifications of the explosive device used. He also admitted that he had manufactured other pieces of explosive material. According to the statement, he had travelled to Kakhovka to meet S., an activist in the communist movement, and to distribute the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers at a protest rally there. In conclusion, the applicant asserted that he did not consider his conduct criminal because he had acted in the interests of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, of which he regarded himself as a citizen and which, in his view, was temporarily under the domination of global, predominantly American, imperialism. He also stated that he had sought to prevent the current political regime from committing genocide against the Ukrainian people.

21. The applicant alleged that the investigator had dictated the wording of the “explanation”. He maintained that he had agreed to write it because, on the previous day, he had been subjected to psychological ill-treatment at the detention facility.

22. According to the applicant, at 4.40 p.m.
On 21 December 2002, after preparing the “explanation”, the applicant was advised of his procedural rights. He stated that, although he had generally wished to have legal representation during the investigation, he had been willing to provide certain evidence, at his own discretion, without a lawyer. At 5 p.m., when his defence rights were explained to him again, he repeated that position in the presence of a lawyer, Cheb.

23. Ten minutes later, at 5.10 p.m., an SBU investigator questioned the applicant as an accused. The relevant record indicates that no lawyer attended the interview because, before it began, the applicant had expressed a wish to be questioned without legal assistance. Otherwise, the record consisted of a printed version of the “explanation” he had provided earlier that day. The applicant signed it without comment and added a handwritten declaration stating that he had given all the evidence voluntarily and without pressure from the authorities.

24. On 22 December 2002, the applicant retained two lawyers, Sk. and K., from a private law firm, and they were appointed to represent him in the proceedings that same day. He alleged that the investigator had selected them and that, in view of his particular circumstances, he had had no alternative but to conclude an agreement with them.

25. Later that day, a reconstruction of the crime scene was carried out with the applicant participating and Sk. present. The applicant reaffirmed his earlier statements concerning his involvement in the explosion near the SBU headquarters, but declined to answer some questions, including those relating to his accomplices. Both he and Sk. signed the reconstruction record without making any remarks.

26. On 23 December 2002, without a lawyer present, Sm. gave the SBU investigator a handwritten statement. Among other things, he admitted distributing the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and other printed materials in Ukraine and stated that, in October 2002, he, the applicant, and another accomplice had blown up the rubbish bin near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv.

27. On 25 December 2002, the SBU investigator again questioned the applicant as an accused. No lawyer attended because, according to the interview record, the applicant had stated that he did not wish to receive legal assistance during the questioning. He confirmed that he had acted alone in manufacturing and detonating the explosive device near the SBU headquarters. After being shown several items seized from the Mykolayiv flat on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above), he acknowledged that some belonged to him and that he had used them to manufacture various types of explosives.
He stated that he had no knowledge of the ammunition or drugs discovered in the flat. The applicant also denied unlawfully possessing the firearms and explosives for which he had originally been arrested, alleging that the police had planted the incriminating evidence. He further complained that officers had ill-treated him in an attempt to extract a confession to that offence and said that he had instructed his lawyers to file a complaint against those involved. Finally, he declared that he was willing to cooperate with the authorities concerning the crimes he had committed in Ukraine, but would not provide evidence about his accomplices.

28. On 29 December 2002, after being advised of his right to legal assistance in Sk.’s presence, the applicant indicated that he wished to retain Sk. as his lawyer. He was then charged, with Sk. present, with belonging to a criminal group led by Ya. whose objective had been to overthrow Ukraine’s constitutional order, including through terrorist acts such as the explosion near the SBU headquarters. The applicant disputed the legal characterisation of his conduct, arguing that it should instead have been classified as either terrorism or hooliganism. He repeated that his actions had been intended to avert a graver crime, namely the genocide of the Ukrainian people.

29. Later the same day, the applicant was questioned as an accused person in the presence of Sk. During the interview, he once more acknowledged that he had caused the explosion near the SBU premises and produced the explosive material found in the Mykolayiv flat. He insisted that he had acted alone and on his own initiative. He also stated that Ya. had known of his plan to carry out the explosion and might have exploited that knowledge for his own purposes as a writer. The interview record, signed without comment by both the applicant and Sk., indicated that, at the applicant’s request, he had met privately with Sk. before questioning began. In his submissions to the Court, however, the applicant denied that any such confidential meeting had occurred.

30. On 3 February 2003, the applicant asked for Chep., a lawyer retained by his relatives, to be admitted to the proceedings as his defence counsel, while declining further representation by Sk. and K. The request was approved that same day.

31. During routine searches at Mykolayiv SIZO, where the applicant was then detained, several notes addressed to various individuals were confiscated from him on 16 and 18 February 2003. Copies of those notes were not submitted to the Court.
The case material indicates that, in those notes, the applicant sought, inter alia, to have witnesses in his wife’s case alter their testimony. He instructed various individuals on how to compel the witnesses to do so and outlined a new defence strategy for his wife aimed at obstructing the investigation. He also requested that his lawyer, Chep., participate in the process and that messages be conveyed to him through Chep. The applicant further reassured the notes’ intended recipients that he was not a traitor, explaining that he had admitted only his own involvement in the explosion near the SBU headquarters and had declined to testify against anyone else. He added that the technical description of the explosive device was incorrect and that he intended to exploit this “tricky moment” later.

32. On 19 February 2003, the applicant was interviewed in Chep.’s presence. He declined to give any evidence before the trial.

33. On 3 March 2003, the applicant was transferred to Odessa.

34. On 24 April 2003, he was questioned regarding his membership of a terrorist group and the distribution of the newspapers Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies. Before the questioning began, he consented in writing to take part in the investigative measure without his lawyer. During the interviews, however, he invoked his right to remain silent and declined to answer any of the investigator’s questions.

35. On 21 May 2003, the initial charges against the applicant were amended to include the dissemination, as a member of a criminal group, of printed material calling for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order and the seizure of power; banditry; terrorism; the unlawful manufacture and possession of drugs; and the illegal possession of firearms and explosives. When questioned in Chep.’s presence, the applicant partially admitted his guilt but refused to provide any evidence before trial.

36. On 26 May 2003, the applicant was questioned about the notes confiscated from him at Mykolayiv SIZO on 16 and 18 February 2003 (see paragraph 31 above). He acknowledged having written them but declined to give any additional evidence.

37. The pre-trial investigation concluded on 27 May 2003. Between that date and 24 July 2003, the applicant and Chep. examined the case file. The applicant signed a schedule acknowledging that he had reviewed the file, but refused to sign a report stating that he had familiarised himself with it in full. He maintained that he had not been given enough time to examine all the material. Chep., by contrast, confirmed that he had reviewed the entire file and signed the report without comment.

38.
On an unspecified date, the applicant and ten other persons accused of involvement in criminal activities carried out by the group led by Ya. were sent for trial before the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Regional Court”), sitting as a first-instance court.

39. From 2 to 11 September 2003, the applicant was granted additional time to examine the case file.

40. On 24 September 2003, the Regional Court appointed A. to represent the applicant at trial. The applicant had retained her to replace Chep., whose contract had expired. A. was allowed until 13 October 2003 to acquaint herself with the case materials.

41. At trial, the applicant acknowledged that he shared communist views with his co-defendants, whom he regarded as his political comrades, but denied participating in any attempt to overthrow the constitutional order. He stated that he had taken eight copies of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies from Ya.’s flat in Mykolayiv, intending to use them for domestic purposes and to give them to Kakhovka residents as kindling for their stoves. He emphasised that he had passed copies to S., whom he had encountered by chance at a protest meeting and who had expressed interest in the newspaper’s contents, and also to M.

Except for Sm., the applicant’s co-defendants admitted distributing the newspapers in question and other materials as part of activities intended to restore a Soviet republic. The newspaper editor and several other co-defendants acknowledged that the articles had incited violence, including by calling for an armed uprising against Ukraine’s constitutional order and the seizure of power by revolutionary communists.

The applicant also denied taking part in any of the other criminal conduct with which he had been charged. He maintained that all his self-incriminating statements during the pre-trial investigation had been obtained under duress and in violation of his privilege against self-incrimination. In particular, he alleged that the investigator, of whom he had been afraid, had dictated his “explanation” of 21 December 2002. The investigator had also promised that, if the applicant made a statement, he would arrange for him to be declared insane and placed in a psychiatric institution rather than imprisoned, as had occurred in the criminal proceedings against him in Russia (for the relevant facts, see Romanov v. Russia, no. 63993/00, 20 October 2005).

He further told the trial court that he had provided no evidence during the later investigative measures and had merely signed every document presented to him by the investigator, without reading any of them, because he feared ill-treatment. He also complained that Sk. had been an SBU agent rather than counsel of his own choosing and had therefore failed to represent his interests effectively.

42. In November 2003, B., one of the applicant’s co-defendants, died while in detention.
The other defendants claimed that B. had died from torture.43. The trial court directed that the circumstances of his death be investigated. The prosecutor’s office subsequently concluded that there was no basis for a torture case because B. had died of cancer.44.

On 19 July 2004, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of terrorism, distributing printed materials advocating an armed uprising against the constitutional order, banditry, and the unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. It imposed sentences of ten years for terrorism, one year for distributing the newspapers Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies, and five and six years respectively for the other offences. Applying the rule under which the more severe penalty absorbs the more lenient one, the court fixed the applicant’s final sentence at ten years’ imprisonment. Owing to insufficient evidence, it acquitted him of the unlawful production and possession of drugs.

The Regional Court rejected as unconvincing and lacking credibility the applicant’s denial of involvement in distributing the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies, giving detailed reasons for that finding. Among other evidence, it relied on the trial testimony of S. and M. They confirmed that the applicant had taken part in the protest events in Kakhovka and had visited them twice during that period, accompanied by Sm. on one occasion. On both visits, he had brought newspapers and discussed their contents with them, stating, among other things, that a revolution could not occur without victims. The court also cited the contents of several letters written by the applicant while in detention, including one addressed to a co-defendant. In that letter, he complained that S. and R., the Kakhovka Bolsheviks who had been recommended to him as potential partisans, appeared to be the wrong people and had most likely helped the police arrest him. Nevertheless, the Regional Court found the evidence insufficient to establish either that he had distributed the materials outside Kakhovka or that he had acted on instructions from Ya. or the newspapers’ editor.

Having further examined the articles published in the newspapers distributed by the applicant (see paragraphs 7 and 8 above), the Regional Court concluded that they plainly advocated an armed uprising in Ukraine aimed at overthrowing the existing legal order and enabling Bolshevik revolutionaries to seize State power.

In convicting the applicant of terrorism, the Regional Court relied primarily on the confessions he had made during the pre-trial investigation, including his “explanation” of 21 December 2002, as well as on the statement given by Sm. during the pre-trial investigation, which Sm. later withdrew at trial.
The court further relied on the contents of notes seized from the applicant at Mykolayiv SIZO; the trial testimony of a co-defendant, who stated that the applicant had admitted to carrying out the explosion near the SBU headquarters; and a forensic psychiatric report indicating that, during his forensic examination, the applicant had again acknowledged his involvement in the offence.

Having detailed the circumstances that contradicted the applicant’s allegations, the court found no evidence that pressure from the investigating authorities had induced any of his self-incriminating statements, including his “explanation”. Among other things, it observed that, when the applicant gave that “explanation”, the investigator was not yet aware that he had undergone psychiatric treatment in Russia. The investigator did, however, know the technical specifications of the explosive device used near the SBU and could therefore, had he wished, have ensured that the applicant’s testimony accurately described the device rather than providing the account contained in his confession. The court also noted that the applicant’s intention to deflect suspicion from his wife, as well as his deliberate provision of an inaccurate description of the explosive device to the police, had been corroborated by notes addressed to his friends and seized from him at Mykolayiv SIZO.

Regarding the applicant’s allegations against Sk., the trial court held that, by signing the agreement with Sk. and the law firm, the applicant had accepted Sk. as his legal representative. It further observed that the applicant had wanted Sk. to continue representing him during certain investigative measures and, in letters sent from detention, had asked his friends to communicate with him through that lawyer. In the court’s view, those circumstances indicated that their relationship had been based on trust.

Relying on the findings of a medical examination conducted by a panel of experts at its request, the Regional Court also rejected as unsubstantiated the applicant’s claim that physical and mental exhaustion had prevented him from participating effectively in the hearings.[2]

45. The applicant appealed and was given access to the case file before submitting his appeal. He acknowledged that he had distributed several copies of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies and discussed its contents with the recipients. He nevertheless maintained that this conduct did not amount to a criminal offence, as he had not intended to overthrow Ukraine’s constitutional order and the newspaper was lawfully published in Russia and was not prohibited in Ukraine.
He argued that only during the pre-trial investigation had he begun to consider that changing Ukraine’s constitutional order—which, in his understanding, meant the resignation of the President—would be desirable. He further maintained that his convictions for the remaining offences rested on contradictory, partly fabricated, and inadequate evidence. Regarding the terrorism conviction in particular, he contested the admissibility of all confessions he had made during the pre-trial investigation, alleging that they had been extracted under duress and in violation of his defence rights. In that connection, he pointed out that his “explanation” of 21 December 2002 had been taken without a lawyer present, even though, shortly after his arrest, he had expressly requested representation by Chet., who had already been appointed to act for him in the proceedings. He also asserted that subsequent investigative measures had been conducted either without legal counsel or in the presence of lawyers selected for him by the investigator, including Sk.

The applicant additionally complained that, at trial, rules imposed by the convoy service had prevented his lawyer, A., from speaking with him before the hearing on 24 September 2003. During the hearing on 5 February 2004, he had also allegedly been instructed to keep his hands behind his back while answering the prosecutor’s questions, leaving him unable to consult his notes. Finally, he contended that he had not been given adequate time to examine the case file.

46. On 26 July 2005, the Supreme Court of Ukraine, acting as the court of final instance, set aside the applicant’s conviction for banditry and acquitted him of that charge because of insufficient evidence. It upheld the remainder of his convictions and sentence. In particular, the Supreme Court held that the testimony of several witnesses, including some of the applicant’s co-defendants, given both during the pre-trial investigation and at trial, together with letters written by the applicant while in detention, established his involvement in distributing material that unequivocally advocated the violent removal of the existing political regime.

The Supreme Court further concluded that sufficient evidence demonstrated that the applicant had unlawfully possessed firearms and explosives. That evidence included statements from lay witnesses who had been present when those items were seized from him.

Concerning the applicant’s participation in a terrorist act, the Supreme Court found his guilt established by the confessions made by him and Sm. during the pre-trial investigation, “including during the [crime scene] reconstruction [conducted] with [the applicant’s] participation and in the presence of a lawyer”. It held that the Regional Court had properly evaluated those items of evidence and correctly found them admissible, and it endorsed that court’s conclusions on the matter.
The Supreme Court further observed that additional evidence supported the applicant’s guilt, notably the contents of notes confiscated from him while in detention and incriminating testimony given by his co-defendants during the trial. It concluded that neither the applicant’s defence rights nor those of his co-defendants had been violated. Its examination of the case file indicated that the authorities had dealt with all matters relating to access to and replacement of legal counsel in accordance with the law. Although certain investigative measures had taken place without lawyers present, the Supreme Court considered that the verbatim records of those measures showed that the defendants had consented to give evidence without legal representation. Finally, it held that the applicant had been afforded adequate time to prepare his defence, as demonstrated by the numerous citations to different pages of the case file in his detailed appeal on issues of fact and law. The court also noted that both the applicant and his lawyer had been granted access to the file on several occasions, including in response to the applicant’s own requests.

47. Having served his sentence in full, the applicant was released from prison on 7 December 2012. The following day, pursuant to a decision of the SBU, he was expelled from Ukraine and prohibited from re-entering the country for three years.

Conditions of Detention in Odessa SIZO

48. Between 3 March 2003 and 3 November 2005, the applicant was held in Odessa pre-trial detention facility no. 21 (“the SIZO”).

Material conditions of detention

49. In his original submissions, the applicant alleged that, upon arriving at the facility, he had spent two months in cell no. 4-133. The cell had been extremely cold because its window had no glass. Although it contained only four sleeping places, it had housed five detainees, forcing him to sleep on the cold floor throughout that period. He further maintained that sanitary conditions in the SIZO had been very poor. In particular, during the spring, detainees had gone without access to washing facilities for two to three weeks, while hot water had not always been available in the summer. Other than mattresses and covers, no additional items had been provided in the cells. The applicant also stated that he had spent seven days in a disciplinary cell in September 2003. That cell had been flooded, leaving him standing in water reaching his ankles.

50. The Government maintained that the applicant had been detained in satisfactory conditions. Referring to information supplied by the competent authorities on 14 May 2012, they asserted that he had never been placed in a disciplinary cell. Instead, he had been held in ordinary cells nos. 4-133, 4-135, 4-249, 4-244, 4-245, 4-261, 2-73, 2-74, 2-94, 2-303, 2-295, 2-296 and 2-298. Those cells had toilets, central heating and running water, together with both natural and artificial lighting. Measuring between 7.6 and 8.5 sq. m, each cell was intended for four inmates.
Under the applicable regulations, detainees were entitled to spend one hour each day walking in the courtyard and to use the shower facilities once a week.

51. In his reply to the Government’s observations, the applicant reiterated his complaint and further alleged that conditions had been poor in every cell in which he had been held. He stated that the cells were between 8 and 10 sq. m in size and contained four sleeping places. The toilet consisted merely of a hole in the floor, with no partition separating it from the living space, and was situated only one metre from the area where detainees ate. There was no mechanical ventilation, while the supply of fresh air was inadequate; as a result, particularly in summer, the cells were permeated by the smell of excrement. Water was unavailable for most of the day, and detainees were not provided with bedding, tableware or personal-hygiene items.

Medical assistance

52. The documents submitted by the Government indicate that the applicant was medically examined upon admission to the SIZO and that no specific health issues were detected. During his detention there, he was examined on several occasions by various medical specialists. In particular, pursuant to an order of the trial court, a panel of civilian doctors examined him on 12 March 2004. The panel included an ophthalmologist, a urologist, a general practitioner, a pulmonologist, a cardiologist and a neurologist. The applicant was diagnosed with hypertension, chronic bronchitis in remission, neurocirculatory dystonia and chronic pharyngitis. Appropriate treatment was prescribed and administered. He was also found to have a congenital cataract, a hereditary condition that could not be treated conservatively.

53. On 19 March 2004, the applicant signed a written statement confirming that he had no health-related complaints.

54. Before his release from the SIZO in October 2005, the applicant underwent another examination, which confirmed the earlier diagnoses referred to in paragraph 52 above.

55. While serving time in prison, the applicant complained of back pain. Following an examination on 14 February 2006, he was diagnosed with severe myopia, astigmatism, cataracts and residual effects of a spinal injury sustained in the 1980s. In view of those conditions, he was classified as having a third-category disability, the least severe category.

56. The applicant contended that the medical examinations conducted at the SIZO had been sporadic and cursory. Although he had suffered from spinal problems for many years—and was subsequently recognised as having a disability on that basis—those problems had neither been documented nor treated while he was held at the SIZO. He further alleged that the authorities had failed to follow medical recommendations concerning his other health conditions and had provided no treatment, causing his health to deteriorate. According to him, the SIZO had neither medication nor medical equipment, and the only procedures carried out were blood and urine tests. Detainees themselves were required to supply the paper and pens needed for medical record-keeping.

Transfer between the SIZO and the court

57.
Between 24 September 2003 and 2 July 2004, while the proceedings before the Regional Court were ongoing, the applicant was transported from the SIZO to the courthouse and back.

58. The applicant stated that, on hearing days—which sometimes occurred several days consecutively—and when he was reviewing the case file, he was removed from his cell at approximately 6 a.m. according to his initial submissions, or at 5 a.m. according to his response to the Government’s observations. He was then confined with other detainees in a designated “assembly cell” without windows or heating, where they waited for over three hours before being transported to court. At the courthouse, after the hearings and until between 3 and 4 p.m., they were kept in a basement holding cell. As a general rule, they received no hot food, apart from a brief period following complaints by detainees; the purported “packed lunches” contained only bread. After returning from court, the applicant remained in the same assembly cell until 8 p.m., when he was escorted back to his regular cell. Consequently, he missed scheduled meals and was unable to wash because water was unavailable at that time. These conditions allegedly left him hungry and exhausted and prevented him from preparing adequately for, and participating properly in, the hearings.

59. The Government submitted that most hearings in the applicant’s case lasted no longer than three hours per day. They were generally scheduled for three successive days, after which there was a break of three or four days. The SIZO administration consistently ensured that the applicant received three daily meals. Under an order issued by the SIZO governor on 11 August 2003, officer K. arranged hot lunches at the courthouse during trial weeks involving more than three consecutive hearing days. During shorter court weeks, the applicant was provided with packed lunches, while his other meals were served at the SIZO.

Transit between prisons

60. In the summer of 2006, the applicant was moved from Yenakieve Correctional Colony in the Donetsk Region (“Yenakieve Prison”) to the lower-security Polytska Correctional Colony no. 76 in the Rivne Region (“Polytska Prison”), where he was to continue serving his sentence.[3]

61. The applicant departed Yenakieve Prison on 29 July 2006 and reached Polytska[4] Prison on 22 September 2006. During the transfer, he was detained at Donetsk SIZO until 3 August 2006; at Kharkiv SIZO from 3 to 14 August 2006; at Dnipropetrovsk SIZO from 14 August to 14 September 2006; and at Lviv SIZO from 14 September 2006 until he left for the final destination.

62. The applicant alleged that he was subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment throughout the transfer, which lasted several weeks. In particular, the train compartments were overcrowded and lacked ventilation, and for prolonged periods he was provided with neither food nor drink and was denied access to sanitary facilities.
Except at Kharkiv SIZO, the transit cells in the pre-trial detention centres where he stayed while changing trains were poorly lit and ventilated and had unsanitary conditions, including toilets that were not partitioned off from the living space. He was frequently denied essentials such as bedsheets. Detention-facility staff showed prisoners no respect: outside their cells, detainees were made to squat and clean the floors, and they were beaten if they had not shaved. Prisoners’ letters were also often not dispatched.

63. The Government stated that the travel records containing details relevant to the applicant’s conditions in transit had been destroyed. Nevertheless, they maintained that both his transportation and his detention at transit facilities had been reasonably adjusted to his needs. Prison-train carriages were standard-sized and intended to carry up to eighty people. Each had larger compartments measuring 3.5 sq. m and designed for twelve people, as well as smaller 2.5 sq. m compartments intended for five. For journeys lasting under four hours, the larger compartments could hold sixteen people and the smaller ones six. Every train

ROMANOV v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 63782/11)

JUDGMENT
