STRASBOURG

16 July 2020

The judgment is final, although it remains subject to possible editorial amendments.

In Romanov v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee consisting of:

Mārtiņš Mits, President,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
Lәtif Hüseynov, judges,  
and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having considered the case in private on 23 June 2020,

Gives the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

PROCEDURE

1. The proceedings began with application no. 63782/11, brought against Ukraine before the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”). The application was lodged on 30 December 2005 by Mr Ilya Eduardovich Romanov (“the applicant”), a Russian national.

2. The applicant was first represented by Mr V. Chernikov and subsequently by Mr V. Komarov, both lawyers practising in Moscow. The Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

3. On 9 February 2012, notice was given to the Government of the applicant’s complaints relating to: the conditions in which he had been held in Odessa SIZO; the conditions of his transfer to Polytska[1] Prison; his right to adequate facilities for preparing his defence; his rights to participate effectively and in person in his criminal trial and to receive legal representation; his conviction on account of his political beliefs; and the absence of effective remedies in respect of his complaints concerning the conditions of his detention and transfer.

4. The Government of the Russian Federation chose not to exercise their right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

5. Born in 1967, the applicant lives in Nizhniy Novgorod.

Background to the proceedings

Distribution of printed publications

6. In 2001, Ya. established a group made up of former Komsomol members. Its objective was to restore the communist State by means of a communist revolution. Under arrangements made between Ya. and his Russian counterpart, various materials were printed in Russia, transported to Ukraine and distributed in several towns during protest gatherings then being held as part of a large-scale campaign demanding President Kuchma’s resignation. Among those materials were issues 5 and 6 of the newspaper Soviet of Workers’ Deputies (Совет рабочих депутатов) and issue 1 of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies (Рада робітничих депутатів). The latter publication was a Ukrainian supplement to issue 5 of Soviet of Workers’ Deputies. Its front page presented it as the newspaper of Ukraine’s revolutionary communists.

7. Issue 6 of Soviet of Workers’ Deputies included, among other material, the following articles, several of which had been authored by Ya.
Published under various assumed names, the writings included the following:

“Ukraine: From Tribunal to Revolution — the People Cannot Be Deceived!” (“Украина: от трибунала к революции, или народ не обмануть!”) discussed the ongoing protest campaign against the President and stated:

“... Responsibility for the genocide [of the Ukrainian people] lies not merely with Kuchma, but with the capitalist system as a whole ... The Kuchma regime—and subsequently [the capitalist] order—can be brought down only through an armed uprising and the establishment of a Soviet of workers’, peasants’ and soldiers’ deputies. The opposition leaders, who intend to stage only a superficial coup d’état, understand this perfectly well. Yet they act as though Kuchma’s departure would cause the sun of freedom to shine over Ukraine. Most [protesters], however, realise that the issue goes beyond Kuchma. The people cannot be deceived. It is therefore still too soon to predict the final result of the anti-Kuchma movement ...”

“Can Ukraine’s Opposition Achieve Victory?” (“Способна ли украинская оппозиция победить?”) criticised the opposition leadership, chiefly because its campaign against the existing political regime lacked a clear course. It included these passages:

“... That is why R. [the leader of the communist party] joined forces with an obvious criminal. He thought that her [the criminal’s] energy, together with the people’s hatred of [the current President], would carry him into office ... Yes—merely carry him there, because taking power and establishing new State institutions would require exceptional courage and talent. If creating [those new State bodies] also meant launching a civil war ... then one would need to be a GREAT STATESMAN as well ... Regrettably, neither R. nor ... any other opposition leader possesses such qualities ...

At the demonstrations held on 16 and 24 September, revolutionaries distributed large quantities of literature urging the population to begin a genuine uprising. Sadly, that appeal went unanswered ... Nevertheless, we remain hopeful ... Judging by the way the protests are being conducted, Kuchma is completely unconcerned by either the rallies or the signatures gathered. In his speech to the population, he had already made it unmistakably clear that he would not step down. He argued that revolution could not happen in Ukraine because the people did not want disorder. Could [he] have been correct? Could it be that people are prepared to die ... yet still refuse to take up arms? We do not believe so! Unfortunately, the people have not yet understood that true Freedom can be won only through fierce and bloody struggle. But they will certainly come to understand it!”

“This Mad, Mad...” (“Этот сумасшедший, сумасшедший...”) described the hardships of life under capitalism and gave several illustrative examples before concluding:

“... What name can be given to this? It is the lawlessness of those who hold power.”
A close examination of the circumstances would show that Ukrainian capitalism had grown unstable and that Kuchma’s authority had nearly disappeared. “… Our principal objective at this point is to remain resolute and concentrated, although doing so is far from simple! … Many friends and comrades believe that I have lost my mind. They think this because I propose ending the existing genocidal regime through a powerful armed uprising by the people. On the one hand, the present ineffective demonstrations are pointless; on the other, we can no longer tolerate [the situation]. This view is shared not only by me and my comrades, but by 90% of Ukrainians, although they are frightened to acknowledge it.”

The article “… Genocide” (“… Геноцид”) discussed claims that the State was charging excessively high prices for medicines. It included this passage:

“… The explanation [for the excessive pricing] is obvious: in our country, capitalism and genocide are twin brothers, making accusations that [those in power] are committing genocide against our own population entirely logical … Only one remedy exists—to bring down capitalist power in its entirety, establish a people’s court, and then put officials on trial for the genocide of [their] own people ….”

“Great Job” (“Замечательная работа”) addressed Ukraine’s poor standard of living following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, focusing particularly on people’s dissatisfaction at work. It contained the following passages:

“… Workers’ lives in the Soviet Union had been so comfortable and unrestricted that they lost any understanding of the class system. When the people suddenly found themselves living under capitalism, they … felt as though [they had been] struck down. Nevertheless, they retain the strength to get back up and struggle. All that is required is willingness and determination …

I am a revolutionary by profession, belonging to a new generation that fights the capitalist system. In reality, we are professionals just like …, except that we operate illegally. For that reason, we are able to call more openly for the regime to be overthrown through armed rebellion. You cannot do so! … The tremendous joy comes from knowing that we are helping to bring about the collapse of the country’s capitalist system! No form of repression frightens us. We are ordinary individuals, merely somewhat more determined. Anyone seeking the triumph of the State’s workers is capable of doing this. The principle is straightforward: the greater our numbers, the sooner we will demolish the capitalist system. We have felt that happiness [derived from the struggle] … through actual experience, and we hope that you experience it too.”

8. The Rada of Workers’ Deputies published the following articles, two of which were written by Ya.:

“What the Communist Revolutionaries of Ukraine Want” (“Чего хотят коммунисты-революционеры Украины”) served as an introductory article and included the following passage:

“This new newspaper …”
serves as the print forum of revolutionary communists seeking to build the Soviet movement in Ukraine, organise a successful popular uprising, and proclaim Ukraine a Soviet republic governed by Workers’, Soldiers’, and Peasants’ Deputies.

Any nation suffering under oppression and tyranny is entitled to rebel. Although the “civilised world” has long forgotten this principle of international law, it must become the guiding law of Ukraine’s working people in their struggle against the Kuchma regime. Why is this necessary?

Workers, peasants, soldiers, and honourable officers must grasp the full reality of Ukraine’s situation ... We maintain that the country and its wealth—created through the labour of generations of workers and peasants—may legitimately be governed only by Soviets elected by the working class and backed by armed working people.

It must be recognised that elections held according to rules devised by the CIA and Mossad amount to those in power deceiving the people. Nowhere, at any time, has the working class succeeded in substantially improving its conditions peacefully ... Consequently, every party claiming that a predatory government can be dealt with through a “democratic election” is lying ...

Impoverished workers must understand that the power of ... the capitalist oligarchs can be taken only through a nationwide uprising ... The reality is that these parasites clinging to our necks cannot be removed without bloodshed and casualties. Thus, only one path can rescue our children and grandchildren from humiliation and death: spill both the parasites’ blood and your own in a civil war, achieve victory, and install strong revolutionary rule. This truth is harsh, but we refuse to deceive a dying people by promising that S. [the leader of the communist party] will arrive and set everything right. The capitalists will not surrender their stolen property without fighting....

The duty of honest communists, therefore, is to wrest the initiative from the capitalists after the President resigns and transform “the democratic coup” into a socialist revolution. In other words, revolutionaries [will] need to exploit the rulers’ crisis and popular discontent to organise a victorious uprising.

What is required for victory?...

Secondly, armed groups must be formed without delay. Their members should include former officers and soldiers who can handle weapons, submit to discipline, and understand warfare. [Then] obtain information on the locations of weapons and ammunition depots ...

Thirdly, immediately launch propaganda on a broad scale that promotes rebellion and urges working people to enter the armed groups ...

Fourthly, do not fear criminal prosecution, and remain ready for inevitable losses ...

[There is] no other means by which communists can free themselves from the stigma of betrayal ...
and tell the people: “Our mission is to struggle for the working class’s happiness, and we are pursuing it with all our strength and with our very lives!”

“Kuchma’s regime—a regime of genocide” (“Pежим Kучмы – режим геноцида»). This article focused primarily on the Sknyliv air-show catastrophe and alleged that it had occurred because of the financial avarice of those in power. It included the following statements:

“People must understand clearly that military officers are not their enemies ... Their true enemy is based in Kyiv ... It is called the capitalist criminal order. This enemy can be defeated in only one way—through a resolute and offensive uprising. Unless we destroy this regime, it will destroy every one of us, slowly but surely ...”

“How Ukraine can be turned upside down” (“Как перевернуть Украину”). This article discussed the communist party’s loss in the parliamentary elections. Its pertinent passages stated:

“What conclusion should be drawn from the communist party’s electoral defeat? History provides an unequivocal answer: we must start making serious preparations and conducting propaganda for an uprising by working people. Every protest movement against the government must be used toward that end. No one should fear civil war. It has already begun! ... You also bear responsibility for this. Throughout all ten years, you remained far behind your ‘communist’ leaders! ...

The first units of the revolutionaries’ military organisation are already active in Ukraine today. The organisation seeks to bring about the overthrow of the regime of oppression and tyranny by armed working people. Seizing power across the entirety of Ukraine will not be possible. Consequently, the initial strategic objective ... is to separate from the capitalist centre the region, or regions, where oppressed working people display the greatest degree of protest, and to declare a Soviet republic governed by deputies representing workers, peasants and soldiers ...

... after the immediate measures have been implemented in the self-proclaimed Soviet Republic, units of the revolutionary army will launch an advance toward Kyiv, overthrow the anti-people regime and replace it with the authority of the Soviets of Workers, Peasants and Soldiers.

The communists must ready themselves for this and must likewise prepare Ukraine’s oppressed working people!”

“For a Soviet Republic of Crimea” (“За советскую республику Крым”). Describing contemporary developments in Crimea, this article contained the following passages:

“... The communist party is unwilling to assume power [in Crimea] except by securing victory in elections ...

Accordingly, despite the communist movement’s high level of activity in Crimea, the population there continues to endure the dreadful conditions found in present-day Ukraine. The circumstances are therefore as follows: victory will belong to whoever is more resolute and radical. For ... the people, only one answer exists: an uprising followed by the declaration of a Soviet republic.”

Explosion

9.
On 21 October 2002, an explosive device placed in a waste bin outside the Kyiv headquarters of the State Security Service (“the SBU”) was detonated. Criminal proceedings were opened in respect of that event.

Criminal case against the applicant

10. Official records state that on 8 December 2002, while the applicant was fishing in Kakhovka, Kherson Region, fishery officers discovered a gun in his jacket and alerted the police. The police immediately searched him and found bullets, a homemade explosive device and a detonator in his bag, together with a gun and two passports issued in his name in his jacket. The applicant was then taken to a police station in Kakhovka.

11. The applicant maintained that these events had occurred on 7 December 2002 and that the police had detained him without recording his detention until 8 December.

12. On 8 December 2002, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of illegally possessing firearms and explosives. The copy of the arrest record provided to the Court was illegible. The applicant asserted that he had requested legal assistance in that document.

13. On 10 December 2002, the applicant was advised of his procedural rights and stated that he wished to be represented by a lawyer, Chet. Chet. was appointed that same day to act for him in the proceedings. During questioning conducted in Chet.’s presence, the applicant said that he had travelled to Ukraine to gather material for “a journalism project”. Invoking his constitutional right to silence, he declined to provide any additional evidence.

14. The applicant alleged that the investigator had instructed him to ask for Chet.’s assistance.

15. On 11 December 2002, the applicant was formally charged with unlawful possession of firearms and explosives and was questioned. He pleaded not guilty and refused to give evidence. The relevant questioning record does not indicate that Chet. attended.

16. On 13 December 2002, several people were arrested in a flat in Mykolayiv on suspicion of participating in various offences committed by a criminal group led by Ya., whose aim was to launch a communist revolution. The suspected offences included unlawful possession of firearms, terrorism, assault and robbery. During the search of the flat, the police seized firearms, ammunition, explosives, drugs, copies of the newspapers Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies, and other printed materials. At an unspecified time following the arrests, one suspect informed the police that the applicant might have manufactured both the explosive devices recovered from the flat and the device detonated outside the SBU headquarters (see paragraph 9 above). The domestic courts later established that some of the bullets seized from the flat had the same calibre and identification code as those discovered in the applicant’s bag (see paragraph 10 above).

17.
On 14 and 15 December 2002, the Kakhovka police questioned the applicant’s acquaintance, Sm., as a witness while he was in police custody. Among other matters, Sm. stated that he belonged to a Russia-based non-governmental organisation that defended the rights of political prisoners and promoted communist political views. He and two other members had been dispatched to Ukraine to distribute the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and other materials, take part in public events organised by Ukrainian opposition political forces, and establish contacts with local left-wing groups.

18. The applicant was moved on 19 December 2002 from Kherson to Mykolayiv, where members of the alleged criminal group led by Ya. were being held while the investigations against them remained pending.

19. On 20 December 2002, the SBU opened criminal proceedings against the applicant on suspicion of belonging to a criminal group. That same day, the case was consolidated with the proceedings against the persons arrested on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above).

20. While at the SBU premises in Mykolayiv on 21 December 2002, the applicant wrote a statement by hand, referred to as an “explanation” (oбъяснение). In it, he stated, among other things, that he had travelled from Moscow to Ukraine to participate in the protest movement against the incumbent President. To demonstrate his support for the protesters, he had decided to cause an explosion near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv. He said that the explosion had also been intended to deflect suspicion from his wife, who was facing prosecution in Russia for a similar explosion near the Federal Security Service building in Moscow. The applicant described in detail his preparation and execution of the explosion, including the technical specifications of the explosive device used. He also admitted manufacturing other items of explosive material. He further explained that he had travelled to Kakhovka to meet S., an activist in the communist movement, and to distribute the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers during a protest meeting there. In conclusion, the applicant maintained that he did not consider his conduct criminal because he had acted in the interests of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, of which he believed himself to be a citizen and which, in his view, was temporarily ruled by global imperialism, primarily American. He also wished to stop the current political regime from committing genocide against the people of Ukraine.

21. The applicant alleged that the investigator had dictated the wording of the “explanation”. He agreed to write it because, one day earlier, he had been subjected to psychological ill-treatment at the detention facility.

22. According to the applicant, at 4.40 p.m.
On 21 December 2002, after preparing the “explanation”, the applicant was advised of his procedural rights. He stated that, although he generally wished to have legal representation during the investigation, he was willing, at his own discretion, to provide certain evidence without a lawyer. At 5 p.m., in the presence of a lawyer, Cheb., he repeated this position when his defence rights were explained to him again.

23. At 5.10 p.m., an SBU investigator questioned the applicant as an accused. According to the interview record, no lawyer attended because, before questioning began, the applicant had indicated that he wished to proceed without legal assistance. Otherwise, the record was a typed version of the “explanation” he had provided earlier that day. The applicant signed it without comments and added a handwritten declaration confirming that he had given all the evidence voluntarily and without pressure from the authorities.

24. On 22 December 2002, the applicant retained two lawyers, Sk. and K., from a private law firm, and they were appointed to represent him in the proceedings that same day. The applicant maintained that the investigator had selected them and that, in view of his particular circumstances, he had no option but to conclude an agreement with them.

25. Also on 22 December 2002, a reconstruction of the crime scene was carried out with the applicant participating and Sk. present. The applicant reaffirmed his earlier statements concerning his involvement in the explosion near the SBU headquarters. He declined to answer some questions, including those relating to his accomplices. Both the applicant and Sk. signed the reconstruction record without making any comments.

26. On 23 December 2002, without a lawyer present, Sm. gave the SBU investigator a handwritten statement. Among other things, he admitted that he had distributed the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies newspaper and other printed materials in Ukraine and that, in October 2002, he, the applicant, and another accomplice had blown up the rubbish bin near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv.

27. On 25 December 2002, the SBU investigator again questioned the applicant as an accused. No lawyer attended because, as recorded in the relevant document, the applicant had stated that he did not want legal assistance during the interview. He confirmed that he had acted alone in making and detonating the explosive device near the SBU headquarters. After being shown several objects seized from the flat in Mykolayiv on 13 December 2002 (see paragraph 16 above), he acknowledged that some belonged to him and that he had used them to manufacture various kinds of explosives.
He stated that he knew nothing about the ammunition and drugs discovered in the flat. The applicant also rejected the accusations of unlawful possession of firearms and explosives on which his initial arrest had been based, alleging that the police had planted the physical evidence against him. He further claimed that police officers had subjected him to ill-treatment in an attempt to compel him to confess to that offence and that he had instructed his lawyers to file a complaint against the officers involved. Finally, he declared that he was willing to cooperate with the authorities concerning the crimes he had committed in Ukraine, but would not provide evidence about his accomplices.

28. On 29 December 2002, in Sk.’s presence and after being advised of his right to legal assistance, the applicant indicated that he wished to appoint Sk. as his lawyer. He was subsequently charged, with Sk. present, with belonging to a criminal group led by Ya. that had sought to overthrow Ukraine’s constitutional order, including through terrorist acts such as the incident near the SBU headquarters. The applicant disputed the legal characterisation of his conduct, arguing that it should instead have been treated either as terrorism or as hooliganism. He repeated that his actions had been intended to avert a more serious offence—the genocide of the Ukrainian people.

29. Later on the same date, the applicant was interviewed as an accused person in the presence of Sk. He once more acknowledged that he had caused the explosion near the SBU premises and produced the explosive material discovered in the Mykolayiv flat. He insisted that he had acted alone and on his own initiative. He further stated that Ya. had known of his plan to carry out the explosion and, as a writer, might have exploited that information for his own purposes. The interview record, signed without comments by both the applicant and Sk., stated that, at the applicant’s request, he had met privately with Sk. before questioning began. In his representations to the Court, however, the applicant denied that any such meeting had occurred.

30. On 3 February 2003, the applicant asked for Chep., a lawyer retained by his relatives, to be admitted to the proceedings as defence counsel, while declining the services of Sk. and K. That request was approved on the same day.

31. During a routine search at Mykolayiv SIZO, where the applicant was then detained, several notes addressed to various individuals were confiscated from him on 16 and 18 February 2003. The Court was not provided with copies of those notes.
The case materials indicate that, in those notes, the applicant demanded, among other things, that witnesses in his wife’s case alter their statements. He instructed various individuals on how to pressure those witnesses into changing their testimony and outlined a new defence strategy for his wife aimed at obstructing the investigation. He also requested the involvement of his lawyer, Chep., and asked that messages be conveyed to him through that lawyer. The applicant assured the notes’ intended recipients that he was not a traitor, explaining that he had acknowledged only his own role in the explosion near the SBU headquarters and had refused to testify against anyone else. He further asserted that the technical description of the explosive device was incorrect and that he intended to exploit this “tricky moment” later.

32. On 19 February 2003, the applicant was questioned in Chep.’s presence. He declined to give any evidence before trial.

33. On 3 March 2003, the applicant was moved to Odessa.

34. On 24 April 2003, he was questioned regarding his membership of a terrorist group and the distribution of the newspapers Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies. Before the questioning, he consented in writing to take part in the investigative measure without his lawyer. During the interviews, he invoked his right to remain silent and refused to answer any questions from the investigator.

35. On 21 May 2003, the initial charges against the applicant were replaced with charges of disseminating, as a member of a criminal group, printed materials calling for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order and the seizure of power; banditry; terrorism; the illegal manufacture and possession of drugs; and the unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. Questioned in Chep.’s presence, the applicant partially admitted his guilt but refused to provide any evidence until trial.

36. On 26 May 2003, the applicant was questioned about the notes confiscated from him at Mykolayiv SIZO on 16 and 18 February 2003 (see paragraph 31 above). He acknowledged writing them but declined to give any additional evidence.

37. The pre-trial investigation ended on 27 May 2003. From that date through 24 July 2003, the applicant and Chep. reviewed the case file. Although the applicant signed a timetable confirming that he had examined the file, he declined to sign a report stating that he had reviewed it in full. He maintained that he had not been given enough time to examine all the materials. Chep. confirmed that he had reviewed everything and signed the report without comments.

38.
On an unspecified date, the applicant and ten other people alleged to have participated in criminal activities carried out by the group led by Ya. were sent for trial before the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal (“the Regional Court”), sitting as a court of first instance.

39. From 2 to 11 September 2003, the applicant was afforded additional time to examine the case file.

40. On 24 September 2003, the Regional Court appointed A. to represent the applicant at trial. The applicant had retained her to replace Chep., whose contract had expired. A. was allowed until 13 October 2003 to acquaint herself with the case materials.

41. At trial, the applicant acknowledged that he and his co-defendants shared communist beliefs and that he regarded them as his political comrades, but denied having engaged in any conduct intended to overthrow the constitutional order. He stated that he had removed eight copies of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies from Ya.’s apartment in Mykolayiv, intending to use them for domestic purposes and to distribute them to Kakhovka residents as firelighters for their stoves. He emphasised that he had handed the newspaper to S., whom he had encountered by chance at a protest meeting and who had expressed interest in its contents, and also to M.

Except for Sm., the applicant’s co-defendants admitted distributing the newspapers concerned and other materials as part of their efforts to restore a Soviet republic. The newspapers’ editor and several other co-defendants acknowledged that the articles had incited violence, including by calling for an armed uprising against Ukraine’s constitutional order and for revolutionary communists to seize power.

The applicant also denied taking part in any of the other criminal activities with which he had been charged. He maintained that all self-incriminating statements he had made during the pre-trial investigation had been obtained under duress and in violation of his privilege against self-incrimination. In particular, he claimed that the investigator, whom he feared, had dictated his “explanation” of 21 December 2002. The investigator had also promised that, if the applicant gave a statement, he would arrange for him to be declared insane and placed in a psychiatric institution rather than prison, as had occurred in the criminal proceedings against him in Russia (for the relevant facts, see Romanov v. Russia, no. 63993/00, 20 October 2005).

He further told the trial court that he had provided no evidence during the later investigative measures and had merely signed every document presented to him by the investigator, without reading them, because he feared ill-treatment. He also alleged that Sk. had been an SBU agent rather than a lawyer of his choosing and had therefore failed to represent his interests effectively.

42. In November 2003, B., one of the applicant’s co-defendants, died while in detention.
43. The other defendants claimed that B. had died from torture. The trial court ordered an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding his death. The prosecutor’s office concluded that there was no case of torture to pursue because B. had died of cancer.

44. On 19 July 2004, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of terrorism; distributing printed material advocating an armed uprising against the constitutional order; banditry; and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. It imposed sentences of ten years for terrorism, one year for distributing the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers, and five and six years respectively for the other offences. Applying the rule under which the more severe penalty absorbs the more lenient one, the court fixed the applicant’s overall sentence at ten years’ imprisonment. Owing to insufficient evidence, it acquitted him of the unlawful production and possession of drugs.

The Regional Court rejected as unpersuasive and lacking credibility the applicant’s denial that he had taken part in distributing the Soviet of Workers’ Deputies and Rada of Workers’ Deputies newspapers, giving detailed reasons for that finding. Among other evidence, it relied on the trial testimony of S. and M. They confirmed that the applicant had participated in the protest events in Kakhovka and had visited them twice during that period, accompanied by Sm. on one occasion. On both visits, he had brought newspapers and discussed their contents with them, asserting, among other things, that a revolution could not occur without victims. The trial court also relied on passages from letters the applicant had sent while in detention, including one addressed to a co-defendant. In those letters, he complained that S. and R., the Kakhovka Bolsheviks who had been recommended to him as potential partisans, appeared to be the wrong people and had most likely helped the police arrest him. However, the Regional Court found insufficient evidence that the applicant had distributed the material beyond Kakhovka or had acted on instructions from Ya. or the newspapers’ editor.

Having further examined the articles published in the newspapers distributed by the applicant (see paragraphs 7 and 8 above), the Regional Court found it established that they expressly advocated an armed uprising in Ukraine aimed at overthrowing the existing legal order and enabling Bolshevik revolutionaries to seize State power.

In convicting the applicant of terrorism, the Regional Court relied primarily on his confessions during the pre-trial investigation, including his “explanation” of 21 December 2002, and on Sm.’s pre-trial testimony, which Sm. later withdrew at trial.
The court further relied on the notes confiscated from the applicant at Mykolayiv SIZO; trial testimony from one of his co-defendants stating that the applicant had admitted to carrying out the explosion near the SBU headquarters; and a forensic psychiatric report indicating that, during the forensic examination, the applicant had likewise acknowledged his involvement in the offence.

It found no proof that pressure from the investigating authorities had induced any of the applicant’s self-incriminating statements, including his “explanation”, and detailed the circumstances that contradicted his claims. In particular, when the applicant gave the “explanation”, the investigator was not yet aware that he had received psychiatric treatment in Russia. The investigator did, however, know the technical specifications of the explosive device used near the SBU and, had he wished, could therefore have ensured that the applicant’s testimony contained an accurate description of the device rather than the description given in his confession. The court also observed that the notes addressed to the applicant’s friends and seized at Mykolayiv SIZO confirmed both his intention to deflect suspicion from his wife and his deliberate provision of an incorrect description of the explosive device to the police.

Concerning the applicant’s accusations against Sk., the trial court held that, by entering into the agreement with Sk. and the law firm, the applicant had accepted Sk. as his legal representative. It further noted that the applicant had wanted Sk. to remain his lawyer during certain investigative measures and, in letters sent from detention, had instructed his friends to communicate with him through that lawyer. These circumstances indicated that their relationship had been based on trust.

Relying on the findings of an examination of the applicant conducted by a panel of medical experts at its request, the Regional Court also rejected as unsubstantiated his complaint that physical and mental exhaustion had prevented him from participating effectively in the hearings.[2]

45. The applicant lodged an appeal after being given access to the case file. In his appeal, he acknowledged that he had distributed several copies of the newspaper Rada of Workers’ Deputies and discussed its contents with the recipients. Nevertheless, he argued that this conduct was not a criminal offence because he had not intended to overthrow Ukraine’s constitutional order, while the newspaper was lawfully published in Russia and was not prohibited in Ukraine.
He stated that he had begun to consider a change in Ukraine’s constitutional order—which he understood to mean the resignation of its President—as desirable only during the pre-trial investigation.

The applicant further argued that his convictions for the remaining offences rested on contradictory, partly fabricated and inadequate evidence. Concerning the terrorism conviction in particular, he disputed the admissibility of every confession he had made during the pre-trial investigation, alleging that they had been extracted under duress and in violation of his defence rights. In that connection, he pointed out that his “explanation” of 21 December 2002 had been obtained without a lawyer present, even though, shortly after his arrest, he had expressly requested representation by Chet., who had already been appointed to act for him in the proceedings. He also claimed that subsequent investigative measures had been conducted either without legal counsel or with lawyers selected for him by the investigator, among them Sk.

In addition, he complained that, during the trial, rules imposed by the convoy service had prevented his lawyer, A., from speaking with him before the hearing on 24 September 2003. At the hearing on 5 February 2004, he had allegedly been ordered to keep his hands behind his back while answering the prosecutor’s questions, leaving him unable to consult his notes. Finally, the applicant maintained that he had not been given enough time to examine the case file.

46. On 26 July 2005, acting as the final-instance court, the Supreme Court of Ukraine set aside the applicant’s conviction for banditry and acquitted him of that charge because of insufficient evidence. It upheld the remainder of his convictions and his sentence.

In particular, the Supreme Court held that statements from several witnesses, including some of the applicant’s co-defendants, made both during the pre-trial investigation and at trial, together with letters the applicant had sent while in detention, established his participation in distributing materials that unequivocally advocated the violent removal of the existing political regime.

The Supreme Court further concluded that sufficient evidence proved the applicant’s unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. That evidence included statements by lay witnesses who had been present when those items were seized from him.

Regarding the applicant’s participation in a terrorist act, the Supreme Court found his guilt established by the confessions made by him and Sm. during the pre-trial investigation, “including during the [crime scene] reconstruction [conducted] with [the applicant’s] participation and in the presence of a lawyer”. It held that the Regional Court had properly evaluated and admitted that evidence and endorsed the Regional Court’s conclusions on that issue.
The Supreme Court further observed that additional evidence supported the applicant’s guilt, notably the contents of notes confiscated from him while in detention and incriminating testimony given by his co-defendants during the trial. It concluded that neither the applicant’s defence rights nor those of his co-defendants had been violated. Its examination of the case file indicated that the authorities had dealt with all questions relating to access to and replacement of lawyers during the proceedings in accordance with the law. Although certain investigative measures had taken place without lawyers present, the Supreme Court considered that the verbatim records of those measures showed that the defendants had consented to testify without legal assistance.

Finally, the Supreme Court held that the applicant had been afforded adequate time to prepare his defence, as demonstrated by the numerous citations to different pages of the case file contained in his detailed appeal on points of fact and law. It also observed that both the applicant and his lawyer had been granted access to the case file on several occasions, including in response to the applicant’s own request.

47. The applicant was released from prison on 7 December 2012 after completing his sentence in full. On the following day, pursuant to an SBU decision, he was expelled from Ukraine and prohibited from re-entering the country for the next three years.

Conditions of Detention in Odessa SIZO

48. Between 3 March 2003 and 3 November 2005, the applicant was held in Odessa pre-trial detention facility no. 21 (“the SIZO”).

Material conditions of detention

49. In his original submissions, the applicant alleged that, on arriving at the detention facility, he had been placed in cell no. 4-133 for two months. The cell had been extremely cold because its window had no glass. Although it contained only four sleeping places, five detainees had been accommodated there, forcing him to sleep on the cold floor throughout that period. He further maintained that sanitary conditions in the SIZO had been very poor. In particular, during spring, detainees had gone without access to washing facilities for two to three weeks, while hot water had not always been available in summer. Their cells had contained no items other than mattresses and covers. The applicant also stated that, for seven days in September 2003, he had been confined in a disciplinary cell that was flooded, with water reaching his ankles.

50. The Government maintained that the applicant’s conditions of detention had been fair. Referring to information supplied by the competent authorities on 14 May 2012, they stated that he had never been placed in a disciplinary cell. Instead, he had been held in ordinary cells nos. 4-133, 4-135, 4-249, 4-244, 4-245, 4-261, 2-73, 2-74, 2-94, 2-303, 2-295, 2-296 and 2-298. Those cells were equipped with a toilet, central heating and water, and both natural and artificial lighting. Each measured between 7.6 and 8.5 sq. m and was intended for four inmates.
Under the applicable regulations, detainees were entitled to spend one hour each day walking in the courtyard and to use the shower facilities once a week.

51. In his response to the Government’s observations, the applicant reiterated his complaint and further alleged that conditions had been poor in every cell in which he had been held. He stated that the cells were between 8 and 10 sq. m in size and contained four sleeping places. The toilet consisted merely of a hole in the floor. It was not partitioned off from the living space and was situated one metre from the area where detainees ate. There was no mechanical ventilation, while the supply of fresh air was inadequate, leaving the cells permeated by the smell of excrement, particularly in summer. Running water was unavailable for most of the day, and detainees were not provided with bedding, crockery or personal-hygiene items.

Medical care

52. The documents submitted by the Government indicate that the applicant underwent a medical examination upon admission to the SIZO, and no significant health issues were identified. During his detention there, he was examined on several occasions by various medical specialists. Following an order by the trial court, on 12 March 2004 he was assessed by a panel of civilian doctors consisting of an ophthalmologist, a urologist, a general practitioner, a pulmonologist, a cardiologist and a neurologist. He was diagnosed with hypertension, chronic bronchitis in remission, neurocirculatory dystonia and chronic pharyngitis. Appropriate treatment was prescribed and administered. He was also found to have a congenital cataract, a hereditary condition that could not be treated conservatively.

53. On 19 March 2004, the applicant submitted a written declaration stating that he had no complaints concerning his health.

54. In October 2005, before his release from the SIZO, he was examined again, and the earlier diagnoses referred to in paragraph 52 above were confirmed.

55. While detained in prison, the applicant reported back pain. After an examination on 14 February 2006, he was diagnosed with severe myopia, astigmatism, cataracts and residual effects of a spinal injury sustained in the 1980s. Owing to those medical conditions, he was placed in the third and least severe category of disability.

56. The applicant asserted that medical examinations at the SIZO had been sporadic and cursory. Despite his longstanding spinal problems—for which he was subsequently granted disability status—the condition was neither documented nor treated while he was in the SIZO. He further claimed that the authorities had failed to follow medical recommendations concerning his other health issues and had provided no treatment, causing his health to worsen. According to him, the SIZO had neither medication nor medical equipment, and the only procedures carried out were blood and urine tests. Detainees themselves had to supply the paper and pens used for medical records.

Transport between the SIZO and the court

57.
From 24 September 2003 to 2 July 2004, while the case was being heard by the Regional Court, the applicant was transported between the SIZO and the courthouse.

58. The applicant stated that, on hearing days—which sometimes occurred on several consecutive days—and when he examined the case file, he was removed from his cell at approximately 6 a.m. according to his original submissions, or at 5 a.m. according to his comments responding to the Government’s observations. He was then confined with other detainees in a designated “assembly cell” without windows or heating, where they waited for over three hours before being transported to court. After the hearings, they were kept until 3 or 4 p.m. in a holding cell in the courthouse basement. As a general rule, they received no hot food, apart from a brief period following complaints by detainees. The purported “packed lunches” contained only bread. On returning from court, the applicant was again held in the “assembly cell” until 8 p.m., when he was escorted back to his regular cell. Consequently, he missed scheduled meals and was unable to wash because water was unavailable at that hour. These conditions caused him to be hungry and exhausted and prevented him from adequately preparing for and participating in the hearings.

59. The Government maintained that most hearings in the applicant’s case lasted no longer than three hours each day. They were normally scheduled for three successive days, after which there was a break of three or four days. The SIZO authorities consistently ensured that the applicant received three daily meals. Under an order issued by the SIZO governor on 11 August 2003, during trial weeks involving more than three consecutive hearing days, officer K. organised hot lunches for the applicant at the courthouse. In shorter court weeks, he was supplied with packed lunches, while his remaining meals were provided at the SIZO.

Transit between prisons

60. During the summer of 2006, the applicant was moved from Yenakieve Correctional Colony in the Donetsk Region (“Yenakieve Prison”) to the lower-security Polytska Correctional Colony no. 76 in the Rivne Region (“Polytska Prison”), where he was to continue serving his sentence.[3]

61. The applicant departed Yenakieve Prison on 29 July 2006 and reached Polytska[4] Prison on 22 September 2006. During the journey, he was detained at Donetsk SIZO until 3 August 2006; at Kharkiv SIZO from 3 to 14 August 2006; at Dnipropetrovsk SIZO from 14 August to 14 September 2006; and at Lviv SIZO from 14 September 2006 until he left for the prison that was his final destination.

62. The applicant alleged that he was subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment throughout the transfer, which lasted several weeks. Specifically, the railway compartments were overcrowded and lacked ventilation, and for prolonged periods he was provided with neither food nor drink and had no access to sanitary facilities.
Except at Kharkiv SIZO, the transit cells in the pre-trial detention centres where he stayed between train journeys were unsanitary, poorly lit and inadequately ventilated, and their toilets were not partitioned off from the living space. He was frequently denied basic items, including bedsheets. Detention-facility staff showed prisoners no respect: when outside their cells, inmates were made to squat and clean the floors, and they were beaten if they had not shaved. Prisoners’ letters were often not dispatched.

63. The Government stated that the travel records containing relevant details about the conditions experienced by the applicant in transit had been destroyed. Nevertheless, they maintained that both his transportation conditions and his detention at transit locations had been reasonably adjusted to his needs. The railway carriages used for prisoners were standard-sized and intended to hold as many as eighty people. Each carriage had larger compartments measuring 3.5 sq. m and designed for twelve occupants, as well as smaller compartments measuring 2.5 sq. m and intended for five occupants. On journeys lasting under four hours, the larger compartments could hold sixteen people and the smaller ones six. All train

original: FIFTH SECTIONCASE OF LEVCHUK v. UKRAINE(Application no. 17496/19)   JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG3 September 2020FINAL 03/12/2020  This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of Levchuk v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer, Ganna Yudkivska, Mārtiņš Mits, Lәtif Hüseynov, Anja Seibert-Fohr, Mattias Guyomar, judges,and Victor Soloveytchik, Deputy Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application (no. 17496/19) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Ukrainian national, Ms Iryna Mykolayivna Levchuk (“the applicant”), on 20 March 2019;the decision to give notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”);the decision to grant priority to the case under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court;the parties’ observations;Having deliberated in private on 30 June 2020,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:INTRODUCTION1. The case concerns alleged breaches of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention on account of the dismissal of an eviction claim brought by the applicant against her ex-husband as he had repeatedly subjected her to psychological and physical violence in the presence of their minor children.THE FACTS2. The applicant was born in 1982 and lives in Rivne. She is a registered disabled person with a category 3 disability[1] who lives off her disability pension and child support allowances. She was granted legal aid and was represented by Ms N.A. Bukhta, a lawyer practising in Rivne.3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.4. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.5. In 2002 the applicant had a son.6. On 26 May 2006 the applicant married O.L. The couple installed themselves in a flat in Rivne co-owned by O.L. and his mother.7. In January 2007 the applicant and O.L. had triplets (three girls).8. In view of the multiple birth, in February 2008 the Rivne City Council provided the applicant and O.L. with social housing – a flat which they could occupy as protected tenants, together with their triplets and the applicant’s son.9. According to the applicant, her relationship with O.L. gradually deteriorated because he abused alcohol and, under its influence, started arguments, harassed and threatened her and the children, and sometimes resorted to physical violence against her. On various occasions the applicant was so afraid of his violent outbursts that she fled to stay with relatives or acquaintances for periods of time.10. On 18 March 2009 the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had a broken nose and haemorrhages around her eyes. According to the applicant, these injuries were the result of one of her arguments with O.L. It appears from the case file that this incident generated no formal follow-up proceedings.11. On 13 January 2011 an acquaintance of the applicant, S.L., lodged a complaint with the Rivne police, informing them that O.L. had hit the applicant during an argument at home. The police refused to institute criminal proceedings, on the grounds that there was no corpus delicti in O.L.’s actions. That decision was not appealed against.12. In April 2015 the applicant instituted civil proceedings, complaining that O.L. had not been contributing to meet the financial needs of their children.13. In June 2015 the Rivne Town Court issued a judgment establishing how much O.L. should pay the applicant in child support.14. On 10 June 2015 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the police, informing them that at about 9 p.m. on 31 May 2015 O.L. had kicked her during an argument at home.15. On 11 June 2015 criminal proceedings were initiated against O.L. under Article 125 of the Criminal Code (“the CC”) in relation to the alleged assault on the applicant.16. On 16 June 2015 the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had a subcutaneous haemorrhage on her right thigh.17. On 23 September 2015 the marriage between the applicant and O.L. was dissolved. Custody of all the children was given to the applicant. After the divorce, all the family members and O.L. remained living in the same flat.18. On 16 October 2015 the Rivne police closed the criminal proceedings initiated against O.L. in June because the applicant had withdrawn her complaint. The relevant decision stated that while it appeared that O.L.’s conduct fell within the ambit of Article 125 of the CC, in view of the applicant’s decision not to pursue her complaint as the injured party, the case material would be sent to a different police department for a decision on whether O.L. should be charged with an administrative offence. It appears that no further decision was taken in respect of this incident.19. On 11 November 2015 the applicant complained to the Rivne police that O.L. had not been paying child support. She presented a certificate from the State Bailiffs Service indicating that O.L. was seven months in arrears with regard to these payments. She alleged that although O.L. was officially unemployed, in fact he regularly performed odd jobs and was concealing his income. On the same date criminal proceedings were instituted in relation to this matter.20. When questioned by the police (in December 2015), O.L. acknowledged that he had not been paying child support. He explained that he was unable to make the payments which were due as he was unemployed and had no income. He assured the police that he would pay the arrears once he found a source of income and obtained the necessary means. It appears that the proceedings against O.L. were subsequently either closed or abandoned.21. On 23 November 2015 and 2 February 2016 the applicant made further calls to the police complaining that O.L. was harassing and mistreating her at their home. In response, the police authorities visited the applicant’s and O.L.’s home and carried out pre-emptive conversations.22. On 23 February 2016 the applicant made a further call to the police, complaining that O.L. was behaving aggressively under the influence of alcohol.23. On 12 March 2016 the applicant made a further call to the police, complaining that her husband had been harassing her. This call generated another police inspection and another oral warning for O.L., as indicated in a police report of 16 March 2016.24. On 18 March 2016 the chief of Rivne police decided that O.L.’s actions on 23 February 2016 (insulting and threatening the applicant and piercing a blanket with a knife) could be categorised as psychological harassment. He charged O.L. with the administrative offence of domestic violence under Article 173-2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (“the CAO”) and referred the case to the Rivne Town Court. It appears that no further decision was taken in respect of this police report.25. On 14 March 2016 the applicant complained to the Rivne municipal family, child and youth welfare service (“the family welfare service”) that her husband frequently acted abusively under the influence of alcohol, and she solicited their help in finding a structured solution.26. Between 14 and 22 March 2016 a group of people from the family welfare service conducted an assessment of the needs of the applicant’s family, during which they visited her flat and interviewed the triplets. According to the interview records, one of the girls stated that she loved both her parents, yet she was very distressed when her father came home drunk and became involved in arguments with her mother. Another girl stated that she had no respect for her father and hated it when he came home drunk. The third girl stated that she loved her mother, and she attempted to avoid speaking about her father. According to further records, the social workers were unable to interview O.L., as he was not at home during their visits. Their attempts to set up a separate appointment with him failed, as he either did not pick up the telephone or refused to meet the social workers, saying that he was very busy at work. As a result of the assessment, the welfare service drafted a report indicating that the children had generally been provided with the conditions necessary for their upbringing. However, their father neglected his parental responsibilities and engaged in violent arguments with the mother, which was intimidating and distressing for the children. The applicant was offered counselling support, which she declined at that time.27. On 24 March 2016 the family welfare service asked the police to follow up on the applicant’s family situation, in particular by having a pre-emptive conversation with O.L. and identifying whether there were any grounds for prosecuting him for domestic violence.28. On 5 April 2016 a police inspector who had been assigned that task reported that he had not been able to reach O.L. to schedule a meeting.29. In April 2016 staff members from the triplets’ primary school – the principal, the school psychologist and the girls’ class teacher – reported to the welfare service that the girls had generally integrated well into their school and social life. However, their home environment was distressing. The girls reported that their parents argued often. They enjoyed a good and trusting relationship with their mother and maternal relatives. As regards their father, they reported difficulties in trusting him, and felt that he often paid little attention to matters relating to them. They regularly saw him under the influence of alcohol, and were scared of his appearance and his unpredictable and sometimes violent conduct. The staff members were unaware of any incidents where the girls had been physically ill-treated by their father. However, they considered that the combination of his disengaged attitude and aggressive outbursts towards the mother had led to the girls being victims of “psychological ill-treatment”.30. On 13 April 2016 the applicant lodged a fresh complaint with the police, alleging that at about 10 p.m. on that date O.L. had had a new violent outburst: he had sworn at her, and had threatened and pushed her.31. On 18 April 2016 the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had haemorrhages on her right wrist, arm and leg, and a sprain of the aponeurosis in her right foot.32. On 5 July 2016, with respect to his conduct on 13 April 2016, the Rivne Town Court found O.L. guilty of an act of domestic violence within the meaning of Article 173-2 of the CAO. O.L., who took part in the hearing, acknowledged that he was guilty of the offence in question. The court also decided that O.L. could be relieved of formal liability for the offence and given only an oral reprimand, in view of the fact that the applicant had asked for this, as the parties had already resolved their differences.33. In the meantime, on 22 June 2016 the applicant had instituted civil proceedings in the Rivne Town Court, seeking to evict O.L. from their flat. Referring to Article 116 of the Housing Code, she alleged that living with him was impossible, as he was systematically abusing alcohol, mistreating, threatening and harassing her and the children, disrespecting their interests and having violent outbursts. Continuing to live with him would mean that she and her children, who were minors, would be at constant risk of being subjected to psychological harassment and physical violence. The applicant also argued that eviction would not place O.L. in a precarious situation, as he and his mother co-owned a flat in the same town.34. During the hearings concerning the eviction claim, three witnesses (the applicant’s sister and two friends) who were questioned by the court confirmed the applicant’s version of events and testified that O.L. had been abusing alcohol and mistreating his former spouse and children. In contrast, three other witnesses (O.L.’s brother and two people who were either his friends or relatives) suggested that the arguments had been caused by the applicant, who wanted to get rid of O.L. in order to gain full control of the flat. These witnesses also alleged that O.L. cared about the children and was a thoughtful father.35. In support of his case, O.L. also submitted two character references. The first one was from the management body of the building in which his and the applicant’s flat was located. This reference indicated that no complaints against him had ever been lodged by any building residents. The second was from a limited liability company called R., which indicated that O.L., one of their independent contractors, was highly esteemed as a diligent construction worker and a good team member.36. The applicant adduced documents concerning all her previous complaints of harassment and violence, and a new certificate from the State Bailiffs Service indicating that O.L. was at the material time eighteen months in arrears with regard to his child support payments.37. On 4 April 2017 the Rivne Town Court allowed the applicant’s claim and ordered O.L.’s eviction. In its judgment, the court noted, in particular, as follows:“... The court, having heard the [parties and their representatives], [and] the witnesses ..., [and] having examined the written evidence, has come to the following [conclusions]:...... the respondent abuses alcohol, constantly makes scenes and causes arguments, [and] intimidates [the applicant] in the presence of the children. [The respondent] behaves aggressively, [and] threatens the claimant with physical violence. [The claimant], along with her children, who are minors, has sometimes been forced to sleep at her acquaintances’ homes, as she has been afraid to stay at home with the respondent. The claimant has repeatedly appealed to the law-enforcement bodies for the protection of her rights and those of her minor children. ... The respondent was subjected to ... measures to correct his behaviour in the form of pre-emptive conversations and warnings concerning the unacceptability of domestic violence, and a decision of the Rivne Town Court of 5 July 2016 found [him] guilty of an administrative offence under Article 173-2 [of the CAO]. The respondent was also prosecuted under Article 125 [of the CC] for a criminal offence, for inflicting minor injuries on the claimant.The above measures to correct [the respondent’s] behaviour did not bring about the desired result ...”38. O.L. appealed. He argued that the applicant had been causing arguments in order to separate him from the children and obtain pecuniary benefits from the flat. For the same reason, she had been exaggerating the situation and submitting vexatious complaints containing accusations which were not supported by evidence. Moreover, Article 116 of the Housing Code provided for the eviction of a resident whose misconduct was systematic, where less stringent measures in respect of that resident had proved to be ineffective. In his case, there was no evidence of systematic misconduct and several witnesses had testified in his favour. While some fights had taken place occasionally, all the evidence against him pertained to either 2011 or 2015-16. No fresh evidence of any arguments between him and his former spouse had been provided. As regards the flat which he co-owned, that flat was occupied by his mother and his brother’s family, and there was therefore no room for him.39. On 14 June 2017 the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal quashed the Town Court’s judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim, finding that there were no grounds for applying such a radical measure as eviction, and that the conditions required by Article 116 of the Housing Code had not been fulfilled. The relevant part of the court’s ruling reads as follows:“It is apparent from the case-file material that on a number of occasions the applicant called the police to her home address and accused the defendant of having committed unlawful acts in respect of her and in respect of her family members; however, it has not been demonstrated that [O.L.] systematically breached the rules on living together and was found liable [on this account]....Of and by itself, addressing the competent authorities with complaints concerning a breach of the rules on living together, without those authorities applying measures to correct the behaviour of the [guilty] party concerned, is not grounds for eviction.Having evaluated every piece of evidence separately and jointly, the judicial panel concludes that the evidence provided by the parties demonstrates the existence of hostile, conflictual relations between the former spouses.In such circumstances, the judicial panel considers that the grounds for applying such an extreme measure as eviction in respect of the defendant are insufficient. At the same time, the judicial panel considers it necessary to warn [O.L.] that he needs to change his attitude towards the rules on living together with the members of his family [after the divorce]. ...”40. The applicant appealed on points of law. In particular, she argued that O.L. had already been found guilty of domestic violence in administrative proceedings, and had been prosecuted under Article 125 of the CC for a criminal offence for having assaulted her. She argued that O.L. had not corrected his conduct or attitude, and that living with him exposed her and the children to a considerable risk of harassment and violence. She also reiterated that he had another dwelling available.41. On 20 August 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law, endorsing the findings of the Court of Appeal.42. On 11 October 2018 that decision was sent to the applicant by post.43. On 28 May 2019 the applicant, O.L., their daughters and the applicant’s son were granted ownership of the family flat under the national scheme allowing protected tenants to become the owners of their residences.44. At present, all of them still share the flat.45. In December 2019 the applicant filed a fresh criminal complaint against O.L. concerning a further violent outburst.46. On 26 November 2019 the applicant also initiated proceedings to deprive O.L. of his parental rights over their triplets, alleging that he systematically neglected their needs and avoided paying child support. Those proceedings are currently ongoing.RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORKRelevant domestic lawThe Criminal Code (2002)47. Article 125 of the Code, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:Article 125. Intentional minor physical injury“1. Intentional minor physical injury shall be punishable by a fine of up to fifty times the non-taxable minimum income for citizens, or up to two hundred hours of community service, or correctional labour for up to one year. ...”The Code of Administrative Offences (1984)48. The relevant provision of the Code, Article 173-2, as worded at the material time, read as follows:Article 173-2. Act of domestic violence, failure to abide by a restraining order or evasion of a correctional programme“The commission of an act of domestic violence, that is, the intentional commission of any acts of a physical, psychological or economic nature (the use of physical force which does not result in physical pain and does not cause physical injuries; threats; insults; stalking; depriving a victim of his or her dwelling, food, clothes, other effects or funds to which he or she is entitled by law; and so on) which results in or could result in harm being caused to the victim’s physical or psychological health, as well as a person’s failure to abide by a restraining order issued in respect of him or her, [and] a person’s evasion of a correctional programme where that person has committed an act of domestic violenceshall be punishable by thirty to forty hours of community service, or administrative detention for up to seven days. ...”The Housing Code (1983)49. Article 116 of the Code, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:Article 116. Eviction without the provision ... of another dwelling“If the tenant, members of his or her family, or others living with him or her ... systematically ... break the rules on ... living together, making it impossible for the other [people in the dwelling] to live with them in the same flat or house, and if measures of pre-emption and measures involving public pressure have not produced any positive result, those responsible shall be evicted at the request of ... interested persons, without another dwelling being provided for them. ...”Law of Ukraine “On the prevention and combatting domestic violence” (no. № 2229-VIII of 7 December 2017; “The Domestic Violence Act”)50. The Domestic Violence Act of 2017 entered into force on 7 January 2018, having replaced the preceding Law “On the prevention of family violence” (2001). According to Section 5 of the Act, the objectives of the State policy on prevention and combatting domestic violence were defined as follows:“1. State policy in the sphere of prevention and combatting domestic violence shall aim to ensure a comprehensive integrated approach towards eradication of domestic violence, provision of comprehensive assistance to the victims and affirmation of non-violent character of private relations.2. Main directions of the realisation of the State policy for prevention and combatting domestic violence shall be as follows:1)  prevention of domestic violence;2)  effective response to the incidents of domestic violence by way of development of the mechanism of interaction between the authorities exercising power in the sphere of prevention and combatting of the domestic violence;3)  provision of assistance and protection to the victims, ensuring compensation of damage suffered as a result of domestic violence;4)  proper investigation of the incidents of domestic violence, imposition of liability on offenders in accordance with the law and the modification of their conduct.”51. The Act provided, inter alia, for the creation of a Unified State Register of the incidents of domestic and gender-based violence (Section 16) and stipulated a series of “special measures on combatting domestic violence” for addressing victims’ complaints. These measures included, in particular, urgent injunctive police order; restraining court order; placement of the offender on the preventive measures record; and placement of the offender into the special corrective programme (Sections 24 – 28).Resolution no. 2 of 12 April 1985 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine on issues arising in the courts’ implementation of the Housing Code of Ukraine52. The Resolution, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:“17. When resolving cases [brought] under Article 116 of the [Housing Code] concerning the eviction of persons who systematically breach the rules on living together and make it impossible for others to live with them in one flat or house, it should be taken into account that where the person in question is guilty of persistent antisocial conduct, the eviction may take place, for instance, after a repeated breach, if pre-emptive measures (попередження) or measures involving public pressure have not brought about a positive result. [The measures to take into consideration include]..., in particular, pre-emptive measures applied by the courts, prosecutors, law-enforcement bodies [or] administrative commissions of executive committees, as well as measures involving public pressure applied at the meetings of residents of the apartment block or members of the housing cooperative, ... and [those applied] by other public organisations [operating] at the respondent’s place of employment or residence (regardless of whether an express warning has been given concerning a possible eviction). ...”Relevant domestic case-law concerning restraining ordersRuling of the Supreme Court of Ukraine of 4 December 2019 in case no. 607/10122/1953. In its ruling in the aforementioned case, the Supreme Court noted, in particular, as follows:“In April 2019 [the complainant] instituted proceedings seeking a restraining order on [her former husband]. ... [She] noted that [the respondent] had been subjecting her and their minor child to psychological [and] physical violence manifested through constant threats, intimidation, harassment, application of physical force, as well as interference with their use of [the room in the accommodation hall, in which the three of them resided].... The notion of gender is clearly defined in the Convention, which holds that, while the term "sex" refers to the biological characteristics that define humans as female and male, gender "shall mean the socially constructed roles, behaviours, activities and attributes that a society considers appropriate for women and men." This definition is also used by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and other UN bodies. This meaning also enters into play in the term "gender stereotypes".-  Some critics acknowledge that violence against women is a problem, but wish to prevent governments from challenging traditional gender roles and stereotypes, due to a cultural affirmation that men and women should play very different roles in public life and within the family.
