CASE OF LEVCHUK v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 17496/19)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

3 September 2020

FINAL

03/12/2020

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Levchuk v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Anja Seibert-Fohr,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 17496/19) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Ms Iryna Mykolayivna Levchuk (“the applicant”), on 20 March 2019;

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the decision to give priority to the case under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court;

the parties’ submissions;

Having deliberated in private on 30 June 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case concerns alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the dismissal of an eviction claim brought by the applicant against her ex-husband, who had repeatedly subjected her to psychological and physical violence in the presence of their minor children.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1982 and resides in Rivne. She is registered as a person with a category 3 disability[1] and lives on her disability pension and child support allowances. She was granted legal aid and represented by Ms N.A. Bukhta, a lawyer practising in Rivne.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

5. In 2002 the applicant gave birth to a son.

6. On 26 May 2006 the applicant married O.L. The couple settled in a flat in Rivne co-owned by O.L. and his mother.

7. In January 2007 the applicant and O.L. had triplets, all girls.

8. In light of the multiple birth, in February 2008 the Rivne City Council provided the applicant and O.L. with social housing—a flat which they could occupy as protected tenants together with their triplets and the applicant’s son.

9. According to the applicant, her relationship with O.L. gradually worsened because he abused alcohol and, while under its influence, started arguments, harassed and threatened her and the children, and at times used physical violence against her. On several occasions, the applicant was so frightened by his violent outbursts that she fled and stayed with relatives or acquaintances for periods of time.

10. On 18 March 2009 the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had sustained a broken nose and haemorrhaging around her eyes. According to the applicant, those injuries resulted from one of her arguments with O.L.
It appears from the case file that this incident resulted in no formal follow-up proceedings.

11. On 13 January 2011 an acquaintance of the applicant, S.L., filed a complaint with the Rivne police, informing them that O.L. had struck the applicant during an argument at home. The police refused to institute criminal proceedings on the grounds that O.L.’s actions disclosed no corpus delicti. That decision was not appealed.

12. In April 2015 the applicant brought civil proceedings, complaining that O.L. had failed to contribute to the financial needs of their children.

13. In June 2015 the Rivne Town Court issued a judgment determining how much O.L. should pay the applicant in child support.

14. On 10 June 2015 the applicant filed a criminal complaint with the police, stating that at about 9 p.m. on 31 May 2015 O.L. had kicked her during an argument at home.

15. On 11 June 2015 criminal proceedings were opened against O.L. under Article 125 of the Criminal Code (“the CC”) in connection with the alleged assault on the applicant.

16. On 16 June 2015 the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had sustained a subcutaneous haemorrhage on her right thigh.

17. On 23 September 2015 the marriage between the applicant and O.L. was dissolved. The applicant was granted custody of all the children. Following the divorce, all the family members, including O.L., continued to live in the same flat.

18. On 16 October 2015 the Rivne police discontinued the criminal proceedings initiated against O.L. in June because the applicant had withdrawn her complaint. The relevant decision stated that, although O.L.’s conduct appeared to fall within the scope of Article 125 of the CC, in view of the applicant’s decision not to pursue her complaint as the injured party, the case material would be forwarded to another police department for a decision on whether O.L. should be charged with an administrative offence. It appears that no further decision was made concerning this incident.

19. On 11 November 2015 the applicant complained to the Rivne police that O.L. had failed to pay child support. She submitted a certificate from the State Bailiffs Service indicating that O.L. was seven months in arrears on those payments. She alleged that, although O.L. was officially unemployed, he regularly performed odd jobs and concealed his income. Criminal proceedings concerning this matter were instituted on the same date.

20. When questioned by the police in December 2015, O.L. acknowledged that he had not paid child support. He explained that he was unable to make the payments due because he was unemployed and had no income. He assured the police that he would pay the arrears once he found a source of income and obtained the necessary funds. It appears that the proceedings against O.L. were subsequently either discontinued or abandoned.

21.
On 23 November 2015 and 2 February 2016, the applicant made further calls to the police, complaining that O.L. was harassing and mistreating her at their home. In response, the police visited the home shared by the applicant and O.L. and conducted pre-emptive conversations.

22. On 23 February 2016, the applicant again called the police, complaining that O.L. was behaving aggressively while under the influence of alcohol.

23. On 12 March 2016, the applicant made another call to the police, complaining that her husband had been harassing her. This call led to another police inspection and a further oral warning for O.L., as recorded in a police report dated 16 March 2016.

24. On 18 March 2016, the chief of Rivne police determined that O.L.’s actions on 23 February 2016—insulting and threatening the applicant and piercing a blanket with a knife—could be categorised as psychological harassment. He charged O.L. with the administrative offence of domestic violence under Article 173-2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (“the CAO”) and referred the case to the Rivne Town Court. It appears that no further decision was made regarding this police report.

25. On 14 March 2016, the applicant complained to the Rivne municipal family, child and youth welfare service (“the family welfare service”) that her husband frequently behaved abusively while under the influence of alcohol, and she requested their assistance in finding a structured solution.

26. Between 14 and 22 March 2016, a group from the family welfare service assessed the needs of the applicant’s family, during which they visited her flat and interviewed the triplets. According to the interview records, one of the girls said that she loved both parents but was very distressed when her father came home drunk and argued with her mother. Another girl stated that she had no respect for her father and hated when he came home drunk. The third girl said that she loved her mother and attempted to avoid talking about her father. Further records indicated that the social workers were unable to interview O.L. because he was not at home during their visits. Their attempts to arrange a separate appointment with him were unsuccessful, as he either did not answer the telephone or refused to meet them, stating that he was very busy at work. Following the assessment, the welfare service prepared a report indicating that the children had generally been provided with the conditions necessary for their upbringing. However, their father neglected his parental responsibilities and engaged in violent arguments with their mother, which intimidated and distressed the children. The applicant was offered counselling support, which she declined at that time.

27. On 24 March 2016, the family welfare service asked the police to follow up on the applicant’s family situation, particularly by conducting a pre-emptive conversation with O.L.
and determining whether there were grounds for prosecuting him for domestic violence.

28. On 5 April 2016, a police inspector assigned to that task reported that he had been unable to contact O.L. to arrange a meeting.

29. In April 2016, staff members from the triplets’ primary school – the principal, the school psychologist and the girls’ class teacher – informed the welfare service that the girls had generally integrated well into school and social life. However, their home environment was distressing. The girls stated that their parents argued frequently. They had a good and trusting relationship with their mother and maternal relatives. As for their father, they found it difficult to trust him and felt that he often paid little attention to matters concerning them. They regularly saw him under the influence of alcohol and were frightened by his appearance and his unpredictable and sometimes violent behaviour. The staff members were not aware of any incidents in which the girls had been physically ill-treated by their father. However, they considered that his disengaged attitude, combined with his aggressive outbursts towards the mother, had caused the girls to become victims of “psychological ill-treatment”.

30. On 13 April 2016, the applicant lodged a new complaint with the police, alleging that at about 10 p.m. that day O.L. had had another violent outburst: he had sworn at her, threatened her and pushed her.

31. On 18 April 2016, the Rivne regional forensic bureau certified that the applicant had haemorrhages on her right wrist, arm and leg, as well as a sprain of the aponeurosis in her right foot.

32. On 5 July 2016, in relation to his conduct on 13 April 2016, the Rivne Town Court found O.L. guilty of an act of domestic violence within the meaning of Article 173-2 of the CAO. O.L., who participated in the hearing, admitted that he was guilty of the offence in question. The court also decided that O.L. could be exempted from formal liability for the offence and given only an oral reprimand, given that the applicant had requested this, as the parties had already resolved their differences.

33. Meanwhile, on 22 June 2016, the applicant had instituted civil proceedings before the Rivne Town Court, seeking O.L.’s eviction from their flat. Referring to Article 116 of the Housing Code, she alleged that living with him was impossible because he systematically abused alcohol, mistreated, threatened and harassed her and the children, disregarded their interests and had violent outbursts. Continuing to live with him would mean that she and her minor children would remain at constant risk of psychological harassment and physical violence. The applicant further argued that eviction would not leave O.L. in a precarious situation, since he and his mother co-owned a flat in the same town.

34.
During the hearings concerning the eviction claim, three witnesses questioned by the court—the applicant’s sister and two friends—confirmed the applicant’s account of events and testified that O.L. had abused alcohol and mistreated his former spouse and children. By contrast, three other witnesses—O.L.’s brother and two people who were either his friends or relatives—suggested that the arguments had been provoked by the applicant, who wanted to remove O.L. in order to gain full control of the flat. Those witnesses also alleged that O.L. cared for the children and was a considerate father.

35. In support of his case, O.L. also submitted two character references. The first came from the management body of the building in which his and the applicant’s flat was situated. It stated that no building residents had ever lodged any complaints against him. The second came from a limited liability company called R., which indicated that O.L., one of its independent contractors, was highly regarded as a diligent construction worker and a good team member.

36. The applicant submitted documents relating to all her previous complaints of harassment and violence, as well as a new certificate from the State Bailiffs Service indicating that, at the relevant time, O.L. was eighteen months in arrears on his child-support payments.

37. On 4 April 2017, the Rivne Town Court allowed the applicant’s claim and ordered O.L.’s eviction. In its judgment, the court noted, in particular, as follows:

“... The court, having heard the [parties and their representatives] [and] the witnesses ..., and having examined the written evidence, has reached the following [conclusions]:

...

The respondent abuses alcohol, constantly makes scenes and starts arguments, [and] intimidates [the applicant] in the presence of the children. [The respondent] behaves aggressively [and] threatens the claimant with physical violence. [The claimant], together with her minor children, has sometimes been forced to sleep at her acquaintances’ homes because she has been afraid to remain at home with the respondent. The claimant has repeatedly applied to the law-enforcement authorities for protection of her rights and those of her minor children. ...

The respondent was subjected to ... measures aimed at correcting his behaviour, in the form of pre-emptive conversations and warnings about the unacceptability of domestic violence, and a decision of the Rivne Town Court of 5 July 2016 found [him] guilty of an administrative offence under Article 173-2 [of the CAO]. The respondent was also prosecuted under Article 125 [of the CC] for a criminal offence involving the infliction of minor injuries on the claimant.

The above measures aimed at correcting [the respondent’s] behaviour did not achieve the desired result ...”

38. O.L. appealed. He argued that the applicant had been provoking arguments in order to separate him from the children and obtain financial benefits from the flat.
For the same reason, she had been overstating the situation and lodging vexatious complaints containing allegations unsupported by evidence. Moreover, Article 116 of the Housing Code provided for the eviction of a resident whose misconduct was systematic, where less stringent measures taken in respect of that resident had proved ineffective. In his case, there was no evidence of systematic misconduct, and several witnesses had testified in his favour. Although some fights had occasionally occurred, all the evidence against him related to either 2011 or 2015-16. No new evidence of any arguments between him and his former spouse had been submitted. As regards the flat which he co-owned, it was occupied by his mother and his brother’s family, and there was therefore no room for him.

39. On 14 June 2017, the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal quashed the Town Court’s judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim, finding that there were no grounds for applying such a drastic measure as eviction and that the conditions required by Article 116 of the Housing Code had not been met. The relevant part of the court’s ruling reads as follows:

“It is apparent from the case-file material that on a number of occasions the applicant called the police to her home address and accused the defendant of committing unlawful acts against her and her family members; however, it has not been shown that [O.L.] systematically breached the rules on living together and was found liable [on this account].

...

In and of itself, addressing the competent authorities with complaints concerning a breach of the rules on living together, without those authorities taking measures to correct the behaviour of the [guilty] party concerned, does not constitute grounds for eviction.

Having assessed each item of evidence separately and as a whole, the judicial panel concludes that the evidence submitted by the parties demonstrates the existence of hostile and conflictual relations between the former spouses.

In these circumstances, the judicial panel considers that there are insufficient grounds for applying such an extreme measure as eviction to the defendant. At the same time, the judicial panel considers it necessary to warn [O.L.] that he needs to change his attitude towards the rules on living together with the members of his family [after the divorce]. ...”

40. The applicant appealed on points of law. In particular, she argued that O.L. had already been found guilty of domestic violence in administrative proceedings and had been prosecuted under Article 125 of the CC for the criminal offence of assaulting her. She maintained that O.L. had not corrected his conduct or attitude and that living with him exposed her and the children to a significant risk of harassment and violence. She also reiterated that another dwelling was available to him.

41.
On 20 August 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law and upheld the findings of the Court of Appeal.42. On 11 October 2018 that decision was sent to the applicant by post.43. On 28 May 2019 the applicant, O.L., their daughters and the applicant’s son were granted ownership of the family flat under the national scheme enabling protected tenants to become owners of their residences.44. At present, they all continue to share the flat.45. In December 2019 the applicant lodged a new criminal complaint against O.L. concerning another violent outburst.46. On 26 November 2019 the applicant also brought proceedings to deprive O.L. of his parental rights over their triplets, alleging that he systematically neglected their needs and evaded payment of child support. Those proceedings remain ongoing.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Relevant domestic law

The Criminal Code (2002)

47. Article 125 of the Code, in so far as relevant, provides as follows:

Article 125. Intentional minor physical injury

“1. Intentional minor physical injury shall be punishable by a fine of up to fifty times the non-taxable minimum income for citizens, or up to two hundred hours of community service, or correctional labour for a period of up to one year. ...”

The Code of Administrative Offences (1984)

48. The relevant provision of the Code, Article 173-2, as worded at the relevant time, provided as follows:

Article 173-2. Act of domestic violence, failure to comply with a restraining order or evasion of a correctional programme

“The commission of an act of domestic violence, that is, the intentional commission of any acts of a physical, psychological or economic nature (the use of physical force which does not result in physical pain or cause physical injuries; threats; insults; stalking; depriving a victim of his or her dwelling, food, clothing, other effects or funds to which he or she is entitled by law; and so on) which results in or could result in harm to the victim’s physical or psychological health, as well as a person’s failure to comply with a restraining order issued in respect of him or her, [and] a person’s evasion of a correctional programme where that person has committed an act of domestic violence

shall be punishable by thirty to forty hours of community service, or administrative detention for up to seven days. ...”

The Housing Code (1983)

49. Article 116 of the Code, in so far as relevant, provides as follows:

Article 116. Eviction without the provision ... of another dwelling

“If the tenant, members of his or her family, or others living with him or her ... systematically ... breach the rules on ... living together, making it impossible for the other [people in the dwelling] to live with them in the same flat or house, and if preventive measures and measures involving public pressure have not produced any positive result, those responsible shall be evicted at the request of ... interested persons, without being provided with another dwelling.
Law of Ukraine “On the Prevention and Combatting of Domestic Violence” (no. 2229-VIII of 7 December 2017; “the Domestic Violence Act”)

50. The Domestic Violence Act of 2017 entered into force on 7 January 2018, replacing the previous Law “On the Prevention of Family Violence” (2001). Under Section 5 of the Act, the objectives of State policy on preventing and combatting domestic violence were defined as follows:

“1. State policy in the sphere of preventing and combatting domestic violence shall seek to ensure a comprehensive and integrated approach to the eradication of domestic violence, the provision of comprehensive assistance to victims, and the affirmation of the non-violent nature of private relations.

2. The main directions for implementing State policy on preventing and combatting domestic violence shall be as follows:

1) prevention of domestic violence;

2) effective response to incidents of domestic violence through the development of a mechanism for interaction between the authorities exercising powers in the sphere of preventing and combatting domestic violence;

3) provision of assistance and protection to victims, ensuring compensation for damage suffered as a result of domestic violence;

4) proper investigation of incidents of domestic violence, holding offenders liable in accordance with the law, and modification of their conduct.”

51. The Act provided, among other things, for the establishment of a Unified State Register of incidents of domestic and gender-based violence (Section 16) and laid down a series of “special measures for combatting domestic violence” to address victims’ complaints. These measures included, in particular, an urgent injunctive police order; a restraining court order; placement of the offender on the preventive-measures record; and placement of the offender in a special corrective programme (Sections 24-28).

Resolution no. 2 of 12 April 1985 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine on issues arising from the courts’ application of the Housing Code of Ukraine

52. The Resolution, in so far as relevant, provides as follows:

“17. When deciding cases brought under Article 116 of the Housing Code concerning the eviction of persons who systematically breach the rules of communal living and make it impossible for others to live with them in the same flat or house, account should be taken of the fact that, where the person concerned is guilty of persistent antisocial conduct, eviction may take place, for example, following a repeated breach, if preventive measures (попередження) or measures involving public pressure have failed to produce a positive result.”
[The measures to be taken into account include] ..., in particular, pre-emptive measures applied by the courts, prosecutors, law-enforcement bodies [or] administrative commissions of executive committees, as well as measures involving public pressure imposed at meetings of residents of the apartment block or members of the housing cooperative, ... and [those applied] by other public organisations [operating] at the respondent’s place of employment or residence (regardless of whether an explicit warning has been given concerning possible eviction). ...”

Relevant domestic case-law on restraining orders

Ruling of the Supreme Court of Ukraine of 4 December 2019 in case no. 607/10122/19

53. In its ruling in the above-mentioned case, the Supreme Court noted, in particular, as follows:

“In April 2019 [the complainant] instituted proceedings seeking a restraining order against [her former husband]. ... [She] stated that [the respondent] had subjected her and their minor child to psychological [and] physical violence, manifested through constant threats, intimidation, harassment, the use of physical force, as well as interference with their use of [the room in the accommodation hall in which the three of them resided].

... [the complainant] requested that a restraining order be issued in respect of [the respondent] for a period of six months ... in particular, by enjoining him from interfering with the use of the room [by herself and her minor son] and prohibiting him from accessing [or residing in] ... the aforementioned room.

...

When examining such applications, the courts should comprehensively assess all the circumstances and evidence in the case, giving due consideration to the rights and interests of the children and the parents, while also ensuring that no unjustified restriction of one parent’s rights concerning the children occurs where the other parent’s claims are unfounded and unjustified.

...

In the case at issue, it has been established that [the complainant] and [the respondent] have a hostile relationship; conflicts frequently arise concerning residence in and use of the room in the accommodation hall ...

[The respondent] stated that he did not intend to allow his former spouse ... and their minor son to use the room ...

Having established these circumstances, the first-instance court, whose conclusions were upheld by the court of appeal, correctly concluded that there were lawful grounds for issuing a restraining order requiring [the respondent] to cease interfering with the complainant’s and her minor son’s use of the dwelling, as well as the household items located therein. Similarly, the lower courts correctly concluded that there were no grounds for ...
prohibiting [the respondent] from accessing [or residing in] the room ..., as [the complainant] had not submitted unequivocal proof that [the respondent] had committed domestic violence ...”

Ruling of the Supreme Court of Ukraine of 28 April 2020 in case no. 754/11171/19⁵⁴. In its ruling in the above-mentioned case, the Supreme Court noted, in particular, as follows:

“In July 2019 [the complainant] brought proceedings seeking a restraining order against [her former husband], alleging that he had systematically subjected her and their children to violence and intimidation. Those acts took the form of assaults involving physical, psychological and sexual violence. ...

... When deciding whether to apply such a measure, the courts ... must assess the proportionality of the interference with the rights and freedoms of the individual, taking into account that those measures are prompted by the unlawful conduct of [the offender].

Accordingly, the conclusion of [the lower courts] that it was not possible to grant the victim’s request concerning ... the temporary restriction of [the respondent’s] right to [use] the flat of which he is a co-owner ... is erroneous, since it deprives the complainant of the guarantees ... afforded by the [Domestic Violence Act].

In the present case, the [lower] courts ... concluded that there was a high risk of [repeated violence] ...

In these circumstances, the judicial panel ... considers that [the complainant’s] requests ... to prohibit [the respondent] from staying in the ... flat ... [and] from approaching within two kilometres of [the flat] should be granted. ...”

Relevant international material

55. A summary of the relevant international material may be found in Volodina v. Russia, no. 41261/17, §§ 51-60, 9 July 2019.

56. In Recommendation Rec(2002)5 of 30 April 2002 on the protection of women against violence, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe stated, inter alia, that member States should introduce, develop and/or improve, where necessary, national policies against violence based on: ensuring the maximum safety and protection of victims; providing support and assistance; adapting criminal and civil law; raising public awareness; training professionals who encounter violence against women; and prevention.

57. With regard to domestic violence, the Committee of Ministers recommended that member States classify all forms of violence within the family as criminal offences and provide for the possibility of taking measures to, inter alia: enable the judiciary to adopt interim measures intended to protect victims; prohibit the perpetrator from contacting, communicating with or approaching the victim, or from residing in or entering specified areas; penalise all breaches of measures imposed on the perpetrator; and establish a compulsory operating protocol for the police and medical and social services.

Material concerning violence against women in Ukraine

58.
The Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (the Istanbul Convention) was signed by Ukraine on 7 November 2011 but has not yet been ratified. On 14 November 2017, Mr N. Muiznieks, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, sent a letter to Mr A. Parubiy, the Speaker of the Ukrainian Parliament, urging him to facilitate the ratification of the Istanbul Convention. The letter stated, in particular, as follows:

“During my country visits, I have encountered several objections and/or misconceptions concerning the Convention. Those arguments can be summarised—and countered—as follows:

- Objections to the use of the word ‘gender’ because of its purported ‘ideological’ connotations. The notion of gender is clearly defined in the Convention, which provides that, while the term ‘sex’ refers to the biological characteristics that define humans as female and male, gender ‘shall mean the socially constructed roles, behaviours, activities and attributes that a society considers appropriate for women and men.’ This definition is also used by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and other UN bodies. The same meaning applies to the term ‘gender stereotypes.’

- Some critics acknowledge that violence against women is a problem but seek to prevent governments from challenging traditional gender roles and stereotypes, based on the cultural belief that men and women should play very different roles in public life and within the family. This approach confines women to the stereotypical role of mothers, giving birth and remaining at home to raise children.

- Others go so far as to argue that the Istanbul Convention should not be ratified because it would endanger societies based on traditional families. I would like to reassure everyone that there is no such danger, since all the measures set out in the Istanbul Convention strengthen family foundations and ties by preventing and combating the main cause of family breakdown, namely violence.

- Another criticism of the Convention concerns its allegedly ‘unjustified’ focus on women, even though men can also be victims of violence. However, data collected in various CoE member states—including Ukraine—show that, in the vast majority of domestic violence cases, women are subjected to violence inflicted by men. More broadly, numerous studies demonstrate that women and girls face a higher risk of gender-based violence than men and that violence specifically targeting women remains widespread. That said, the Istanbul Convention recognises that men and children are also victims of domestic violence and that this issue must likewise be addressed.

The Istanbul Convention seeks to eradicate violence against women and domestic violence by requiring the establishment of a comprehensive system to combat these phenomena effectively.”
Individual victims, families, and society as a whole will all benefit if everyone’s fundamental rights to life, security, freedom, dignity, and physical and emotional integrity are upheld. I would be grateful if you could bring my letter to the attention of all members of the Ukrainian Parliament, and I look forward to receiving further information about the ratification process.”

59. In March 2017, in its concluding observations on Ukraine’s eighth periodic report, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) noted, in particular, as follows:

“26. The Committee remains concerned about the persistence, in political discourse, the media, and society, of deep-rooted patriarchal attitudes and discriminatory stereotypes regarding the roles and responsibilities of women and men in the family. These perpetuate women’s subordination within the family and society and are reflected, inter alia, in women’s educational and professional choices, their limited participation in political and public life, their unequal participation in the labour market, and their unequal status in family relations. The Committee recalls that such discriminatory stereotypes are also root causes of violence against women and expresses concern that, to date, the State party has not taken sustained measures to modify or eliminate discriminatory stereotypes and negative traditional attitudes.

...

29. Recalling its general recommendation No. 19 (1992) on violence against women, the Committee recommends that the State party:

(a) ... expedite the ratification of the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence [the Istanbul Convention];

(b) Take comprehensive measures to prevent and address violence against women and girls and ensure that perpetrators are prosecuted and appropriately punished; ...”

60. According to the OSCE-led 2018 survey on violence against women in Ukraine, most women interviewed were concerned about the issue, with 64% stating that it was a common occurrence. Some of the Survey’s key conclusions and recommendations were as follows:

“...

VAW (violence against women) is highly prevalent, but women are reluctant to report it or seek help.

More than one-quarter of women (26%) in Ukraine have experienced physical and/or sexual violence by a current or former partner. Two-thirds of women (65%) have experienced psychological violence by an intimate partner, a rate significantly higher than the EU average of 43% and higher than in any EU country. However, only 7% of women who survived violence by a current partner and 12% of those who survived violence by a former partner reported their experiences to the police.
Considering that 52% of women survivors of intimate partner violence suffered physical consequences from their most serious incident of violence, it is likely that other serious violence goes unreported. Women in the qualitative research said that psychological violence is viewed as normal, while 26% of women also believed that domestic violence is a private matter. The experts interviewed for this report said that there is a collective tolerance of violence, and women surveyed indicated that feelings of shame create barriers to reporting. In relation to current partner violence, more than four-fifths of women (81%) who identified a most serious incident did not contact the police or any other organization; the same was true of 67% of women regarding previous partner violence and 52% regarding non-partner violence.”61.

The U.K. Home Office’s Country Policy and Information Note on Ukraine concerning gender-based violence (May 2018) included, in particular, the following information:

“4.2.3. ... Kateryna Levchenko, President of the NGO ‘La Strada – Ukraine,’ presented statistical data collected from a survey of police and prosecutors and an analysis of court decisions in cases involving violence against women and domestic violence. Some cases of family violence are justified by 10% of prosecutors, 11% of judges, and 12% of police officers. Among criminal justice officers, 39% consider domestic violence to be a private matter, while 60% blame victims for sexual violence.

During judicial proceedings in domestic violence cases, 77% of prosecutors, 81% of police officers, and 84% of judges consider reconciliation [between] partners and family preservation to be the ... top priority, with violence being underestimated and treated as a minor dispute.

Courts often approach violence cases from a formal point of view. Monitoring of 77 hearings revealed that meetings lasted an average of 4 to 23 minutes. Offenders often do not appear in court. Only one in six abusers appeared in court, frequently resulting in the cancellation of hearings. ...”

FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF LEVCHUK v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 17496/19)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

3 September 2020

FINAL

03/12/2020

This judgment became final pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention and may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Levchuk v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Lәtif Hüseynov,
Anja Seibert-Fohr,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application against Ukraine (no. 17496/19), submitted to the Court on 20 March 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Iryna Mykolayivna Levchuk, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the decision to accord the case priority under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court;

the observations filed by the parties;

Having deliberated in private on 30 June 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the dismissal of her claim seeking the eviction of her former husband, who had repeatedly inflicted psychological and physical violence on her in the presence of their minor children.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant, who was born in 1982, resides in Rivne. She is officially registered as having a category 3 disability[1] and relies on her disability pension and child-support benefits for her livelihood. After being granted legal aid, she was represented by Ms N.A. Bukhta, a lawyer practising in Rivne.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. On the basis of the parties’ submissions, the relevant facts may be outlined as follows.

5. The applicant gave birth to a son in 2002.

6. On 26 May 2006 she married O.L. They moved into a flat in Rivne jointly owned by O.L. and his mother.

7. In January 2007 the couple had triplet daughters.

8. Because of the multiple birth, the Rivne City Council allocated social housing to the applicant and O.L. in February 2008. The accommodation consisted of a flat which they, their triplets and the applicant’s son were entitled to occupy as protected tenants.

9. The applicant stated that her relationship with O.L. progressively worsened owing to his alcohol abuse. When intoxicated, he provoked arguments, harassed and threatened both her and the children, and at times physically assaulted her. On several occasions, fear of his violent episodes drove her to seek temporary refuge with relatives or acquaintances.

10. On 18 March 2009 the Rivne Regional Forensic Bureau confirmed that the applicant had sustained a fractured nose and haemorrhaging around her eyes. She maintained that those injuries had been caused during one of her altercations with O.L.
The case file suggests that the incident did not result in any formal follow-up proceedings.

11. On 13 January 2011 S.L., an acquaintance of the applicant, reported to the Rivne police that O.L. had struck the applicant during an argument in their home. The police declined to open criminal proceedings, finding no corpus delicti in O.L.’s conduct. No appeal was lodged against that decision.

12. In April 2015 the applicant brought civil proceedings, alleging that O.L. had failed to contribute financially to the children’s needs.

13. In June 2015 the Rivne Town Court delivered a judgment determining the amount of child support that O.L. was required to pay the applicant.

14. On 10 June 2015 the applicant filed a criminal complaint with the police, alleging that O.L. had kicked her during an argument at home at approximately 9 p.m. on 31 May 2015.

15. The following day, 11 June 2015, criminal proceedings were opened against O.L. under Article 125 of the Criminal Code (“the CC”) concerning the alleged assault.

16. On 16 June 2015 the Rivne regional forensic bureau confirmed that the applicant had sustained a subcutaneous haemorrhage on her right thigh.

17. The applicant’s marriage to O.L. was dissolved on 23 September 2015, and she was granted custody of all the children. Despite the divorce, O.L. and the other family members continued to reside together in the same flat.

18. On 16 October 2015 the Rivne police discontinued the criminal proceedings opened against O.L. in June after the applicant withdrew her complaint. The discontinuation decision noted that O.L.’s actions appeared to fall within the scope of Article 125 of the CC. However, because the applicant, as the injured party, no longer wished to pursue the complaint, the material in the case was to be forwarded to another police department to determine whether O.L. should instead face administrative charges. It appears that no subsequent decision concerning that incident was made.

19. On 11 November 2015 the applicant informed the Rivne police that O.L. had failed to pay child support. She submitted a certificate issued by the State Bailiffs Service showing that his payments were seven months in arrears. According to the applicant, although O.L. was officially unemployed, he regularly undertook odd jobs and concealed the income he earned from them. Criminal proceedings concerning the matter were instituted that same day.

20. During police questioning in December 2015, O.L. admitted that he had not paid child support. He stated that he could not make the required payments because he was unemployed and had no income. He promised to settle the arrears once he found a source of income and had sufficient funds. The proceedings against him appear subsequently to have been either discontinued or abandoned.

21.
On 23 November 2015 and again on 2 February 2016, the applicant contacted the police, alleging that O.L. was harassing and mistreating her in their home. Police officers responded by visiting the couple’s residence and holding preventive discussions.

22. On 23 February 2016, the applicant called the police once more, reporting that O.L. was intoxicated and behaving aggressively.

23. The applicant made another police call on 12 March 2016, alleging harassment by her husband. The complaint prompted a further police inspection and another oral warning to O.L., as recorded in a police report dated 16 March 2016.

24. On 18 March 2016, the chief of the Rivne police concluded that O.L.’s conduct on 23 February—insulting and threatening the applicant and stabbing a blanket with a knife—could be classified as psychological harassment. O.L. was charged with the administrative offence of domestic violence under Article 173-2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (“the CAO”), and the matter was referred to the Rivne Town Court. It appears that no subsequent decision was issued concerning that police report.

25. On 14 March 2016, the applicant approached the Rivne municipal family, child and youth welfare service (“the family welfare service”), stating that her husband frequently became abusive when under the influence of alcohol and requesting assistance in finding a structured solution.

26. From 14 to 22 March 2016, representatives of the family welfare service assessed the needs of the applicant’s family. They visited her flat and interviewed the triplets. The interview records indicate that one daughter loved both parents but became deeply distressed when her father returned home drunk and argued with her mother. A second daughter said that she did not respect her father and hated his coming home intoxicated. The third stated that she loved her mother and tried to avoid discussing her father.

The records further show that the social workers could not interview O.L. because he was absent during their visits. Efforts to arrange a separate meeting were unsuccessful: he either failed to answer the telephone or declined to meet them, explaining that he was extremely busy at work. Following the assessment, the family welfare service prepared a report concluding that, overall, the children had been provided with the conditions required for their upbringing. Nevertheless, their father failed to fulfil his parental responsibilities and engaged in violent arguments with their mother, causing the children fear and distress. The applicant was offered counselling but declined it at that time.

27. On 24 March 2016, the family welfare service asked the police to continue monitoring the applicant’s family circumstances, particularly by conducting a preventive discussion with O.L.
and determining whether any grounds existed for prosecuting him for domestic violence.

28. On 5 April 2016, the police inspector entrusted with that task reported that he had been unable to contact O.L. to arrange a meeting.

29. In April 2016, the principal, psychologist and class teacher at the triplets’ primary school informed the welfare service that the girls had, overall, adapted well to school and social life. Their home situation, however, was troubling. The girls said that their parents frequently argued. They had a close and trusting relationship with their mother and maternal relatives. By contrast, they found it difficult to trust their father and felt that he often showed little concern for matters affecting them. They regularly saw him intoxicated and were frightened by his appearance, as well as by his unpredictable and at times violent behaviour. The school staff knew of no occasion on which the father had physically ill-treated the girls. Nevertheless, they considered that his detached attitude, combined with his aggressive outbursts towards their mother, amounted to “psychological ill-treatment” of the girls.

30. On 13 April 2016, the applicant filed another police complaint, alleging that O.L. had had a further violent outburst at approximately 10 p.m. that day, during which he had sworn at her, threatened her and pushed her.

31. On 18 April 2016, the Rivne Regional Forensic Bureau issued a certificate recording haemorrhages on the applicant’s right wrist, arm and leg, together with a sprain of the aponeurosis in her right foot.

32. On 5 July 2016, in relation to the events of 13 April 2016, the Rivne Town Court found O.L. guilty of domestic violence within the meaning of Article 173-2 of the CAO. O.L. attended the hearing and admitted committing the offence. The court nevertheless decided to exempt him from formal liability and impose only an oral reprimand, since the applicant had requested that outcome and the parties had already settled their differences.

33. Meanwhile, on 22 June 2016, the applicant had brought civil proceedings before the Rivne Town Court seeking O.L.’s eviction from their flat. Relying on Article 116 of the Housing Code, she maintained that living with him had become impossible because he systematically abused alcohol, mistreated, threatened and harassed her and the children, disregarded their interests, and engaged in violent outbursts. She argued that, if they continued living together, she and her minor children would remain at constant risk of psychological harassment and physical violence. The applicant further submitted that eviction would not leave O.L. in a precarious position because he co-owned another flat in the same town with his mother.

34.
In the proceedings relating to the eviction claim, the court examined six witnesses. Three of them—the applicant’s sister and two of her friends—corroborated her account, stating that O.L. abused alcohol and ill-treated his former wife and children. The remaining witnesses—O.L.’s brother and two individuals who were either his friends or relatives—gave a different account. They maintained that the applicant had instigated the disputes because she wished to remove O.L. and secure exclusive control over the flat. They further described O.L. as a caring and considerate father.

35. O.L. also produced two character references in support of his position. One had been issued by the management body responsible for the building where the parties’ flat was situated and stated that none of the building’s residents had ever complained about him. The other came from R., a limited liability company for which O.L. worked as an independent contractor. It described him as a highly regarded, diligent construction worker and a good member of the team.

36. The applicant submitted records of all her earlier complaints concerning violence and harassment. She also provided a new certificate from the State Bailiffs Service showing that, at the relevant time, O.L. was eighteen months behind on his child-support payments.

37. On 4 April 2017, the Rivne Town Court upheld the applicant’s claim and ordered O.L. to be evicted. Its judgment included the following findings:

“... After hearing the [parties and their representatives] and the witnesses ..., and after considering the documentary evidence, the court has reached the following [conclusions]:

... the respondent misuses alcohol, continually creates scenes and starts arguments, and intimidates [the applicant] in front of the children. He acts aggressively and threatens the claimant with physical violence. At times, the claimant and her minor children have had to spend the night at the homes of acquaintances because she was afraid to remain in the flat with the respondent. The claimant has repeatedly sought assistance from the law-enforcement authorities to protect her own rights and those of her minor children. ...

Measures aimed at correcting the respondent’s conduct were taken, including preventive discussions and warnings that domestic violence was unacceptable. Moreover, by a decision of 5 July 2016, the Rivne Town Court found [him] guilty of an administrative offence under Article 173-2 [of the CAO]. The respondent was also prosecuted under Article 125 [of the CC] for the criminal offence of causing minor injuries to the claimant.

Those attempts to correct [the respondent’s] behaviour failed to achieve the intended result ...”

38. O.L. lodged an appeal, contending that the applicant had deliberately provoked the disputes in order to distance him from the children and obtain financial advantages from the flat.
For that same reason, she had overstated the circumstances and lodged vexatious complaints containing allegations unsupported by evidence. Furthermore, Article 116 of the Housing Code permitted the eviction of a resident only where that person’s misconduct was systematic and less severe measures had failed. In his situation, there was no proof of systematic misconduct, while several witnesses had given evidence in his favour. Although occasional fights had occurred, all the evidence against him related either to 2011 or to 2015-16. No new evidence had been submitted of any disputes between him and his former wife. As for the flat of which he was a co-owner, his mother and his brother’s family lived there, leaving no room for him.

39. On 14 June 2017, the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal set aside the Town Court’s judgment and rejected the applicant’s claim. It held that there was no basis for imposing eviction, such a drastic measure, and that the requirements of Article 116 of the Housing Code had not been satisfied. The relevant portion of its ruling stated:

“The material in the case file shows that the applicant contacted the police at her home address on several occasions, alleging that the defendant had committed unlawful acts against her and members of her family. However, it has not been established that [O.L.] systematically violated the rules governing communal living or that he was held liable [on that basis]....

Merely submitting complaints to the competent authorities about breaches of the rules on living together, where those authorities have not taken measures to correct the conduct of the [guilty] person concerned, does not constitute a basis for eviction.

Having assessed each item of evidence both individually and as a whole, the judicial panel finds that the evidence submitted by the parties establishes the existence of hostile and conflict-ridden relations between the former spouses.

In those circumstances, the judicial panel considers that there are insufficient grounds for imposing on the defendant the extreme measure of eviction. Nevertheless, the panel finds it necessary to warn [O.L.] that he must change his attitude towards the rules governing cohabitation with members of his family [following the divorce]. ...”

40. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. She argued, in particular, that O.L. had previously been found guilty of domestic violence in administrative proceedings and had also been prosecuted under Article 125 of the CC for the criminal offence of assaulting her. In her submission, O.L. had altered neither his conduct nor his attitude, and continuing to live with him placed her and the children at substantial risk of harassment and violence. She further repeated that alternative accommodation was available to him.

41.
42. On 20 August 2018 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law and upheld the Court of Appeal’s conclusions.

43. The decision was mailed to the applicant on 11 October 2018.

44. On 28 May 2019, under the national scheme enabling protected tenants to acquire ownership of their homes, title to the family flat was granted to the applicant, O.L., their daughters and the applicant’s son.

45. They all continue to live together in the flat.

46. On 26 November 2019 the applicant brought proceedings seeking to have O.L. deprived of his parental rights in respect of their triplets. She alleged that he consistently failed to attend to their needs and evaded payment of child support. Those proceedings remain pending. In December 2019, following another violent outburst, the applicant lodged a new criminal complaint against O.L.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Relevant domestic law

The Criminal Code (2002)

47. In its relevant part, Article 125 provides:

Article 125. Intentional infliction of minor physical injury

“1. Anyone who intentionally causes minor physical injury shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty times the non-taxable minimum income for citizens, up to two hundred hours of community service, or correctional labour for a maximum period of one year. ...”

The Code of Administrative Offences (1984)

48. At the relevant time, Article 173-2 of the Code provided, in so far as pertinent:

Article 173-2. Domestic violence, non-compliance with a restraining order, or avoidance of a correctional programme

“An act of domestic violence means the deliberate commission of conduct of a physical, psychological or economic nature, including the use of physical force that neither causes physical pain nor results in bodily injury; threats; insults; stalking; or depriving a victim of housing, food, clothing, other belongings or funds to which he or she is legally entitled, and similar conduct, where such acts cause or may cause harm to the victim’s physical or psychological health.

The same applies where a person fails to comply with a restraining order issued against him or her or, after committing an act of domestic violence, avoids participation in a correctional programme.

Such conduct shall be punishable by thirty to forty hours of community service or by administrative detention for a period not exceeding seven days. ...”

The Housing Code (1983)

49. The relevant portion of Article 116 states:

Article 116. Eviction without the provision ... of alternative accommodation

“Where a tenant, a member of his or her family, or another person residing with the tenant systematically breaches the rules governing communal living, thereby making it impossible for the other occupants to continue living with that person in the same flat or house, and where preventive measures and measures involving public pressure have failed to achieve a positive outcome, the person responsible shall, at the request of ... interested persons, be evicted without being provided with another dwelling.”
Law of Ukraine “On the Prevention and Combating of Domestic Violence” (no. 2229-VIII of 7 December 2017; “the Domestic Violence Act”)

50. The 2017 Domestic Violence Act came into effect on 7 January 2018 and superseded the 2001 Law “On the Prevention of Family Violence”. Section 5 set out the aims of State policy concerning the prevention and combating of domestic violence as follows:

“1. State policy in the field of preventing and combating domestic violence shall seek to establish a comprehensive and integrated approach to eliminating domestic violence, providing victims with comprehensive assistance, and affirming the non-violent nature of private relationships.

2. The principal areas for implementing State policy on the prevention and combating of domestic violence shall be:

1) preventing domestic violence;

2) responding effectively to incidents of domestic violence by developing a mechanism for cooperation among the authorities exercising powers in this field;

3) providing victims with assistance and protection and ensuring compensation for damage sustained as a result of domestic violence;

4) properly investigating incidents of domestic violence, holding perpetrators liable in accordance with the law, and modifying their conduct.”

51. Among other provisions, the Act required the establishment of a Unified State Register of incidents of domestic and gender-based violence (section 16). It also introduced a range of “special measures for combating domestic violence” to address victims’ complaints. In particular, these comprised an urgent police injunction, a court-issued restraining order, the placing of the perpetrator on the preventive-measures register, and the perpetrator’s enrolment in a special corrective programme (sections 24-28).

Resolution no. 2 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine of 12 April 1985 concerning issues arising from the courts’ application of the Housing Code of Ukraine

52. In so far as relevant, the Resolution provided:

“17. In determining cases brought under Article 116 of the Housing Code concerning the eviction of persons who repeatedly violate the rules of communal living and thereby make it impossible for others to reside with them in the same flat or house, courts should bear in mind that eviction may be ordered, for example, following a repeated violation where the individual concerned is responsible for persistent antisocial conduct and prior preventive measures (попередження) or measures involving public pressure have failed to produce a positive result.”
[The measures that should be considered include] ... notably, preventive action taken by courts, prosecutors, law-enforcement authorities [or] the administrative commissions of executive committees; measures of public pressure adopted at meetings of apartment-block residents or housing-cooperative members; ... and [measures taken] by other public organisations [active] at the respondent’s place of work or residence, irrespective of whether the respondent has been expressly warned of the possibility of eviction. ...”

Relevant domestic case-law on restraining orders

Supreme Court of Ukraine ruling of 4 December 2019 in case no. 607/10122/19

53. In that case, the Supreme Court stated, among other things:

“In April 2019, [the complainant] brought proceedings seeking a restraining order against [her former husband]. ... [She] alleged that [the respondent] had inflicted psychological [and] physical violence on her and their minor child through persistent threats, intimidation and harassment, the use of physical force, and obstruction of their use of [the room in the accommodation hall where all three lived].

... [The complainant] sought a restraining order against [the respondent] for six months ... requiring him, in particular, not to obstruct [her and her minor son’s] use of the room and prohibiting him from entering [or living in] ... that room.

... When examining applications of this kind, courts must conduct a comprehensive assessment of all the evidence and circumstances of the case. They must give appropriate weight to the rights and interests of both the children and the parents and ensure that one parent’s rights in relation to the children are not unjustifiably restricted where the other parent’s claims are unfounded and unjustified.

... In the present case, it was established that relations between [the complainant] and [the respondent] were hostile and that disputes frequently arose over occupation and use of the room in the accommodation hall ...

[The respondent] declared that he did not intend to allow his former spouse ... or their minor son to use the room ...

In view of those findings, the first-instance court—whose conclusions were upheld by the appellate court—correctly determined that there were lawful grounds for making a restraining order requiring [the respondent] to stop obstructing the complainant and her minor son in their use of the dwelling and the household items kept there. The lower courts were likewise correct in finding that there were no grounds for ...”
barring [the respondent] from entering [or living in] the room ..., because [the complainant] had failed to submit unequivocal evidence that [the respondent] had perpetrated domestic violence ...”

Ruling of the Supreme Court of Ukraine of 28 April 2020 in case no. 754/11171/1954. In that ruling, the Supreme Court observed, among other things:

“In July 2019 [the complainant] commenced proceedings for a restraining order against [her former husband], claiming that he had repeatedly subjected her and their children to intimidation and violence. The alleged conduct included physical assaults and psychological and sexual violence.

...

In determining whether to impose such a measure, the courts ... are required to evaluate whether the interference with the person’s rights and freedoms is proportionate, bearing in mind that the need for those measures arises from [the offender’s] unlawful behaviour.

Accordingly, [the lower courts] erred in concluding that they could not grant the victim’s request to ... temporarily restrict [the respondent’s] right to [use] the flat that he co-owned ..., as that conclusion deprived the complainant of the safeguards ... afforded by the [Domestic Violence Act].

In the present case, the [lower] courts ... found that there was a high risk of [further violence] ...

Against that background, the judicial panel ... considers that [the complainant’s] requests ... to prohibit [the respondent] from remaining in the ... flat ... [and] from coming within two kilometres of [the flat] should be granted. ...”

Relevant international material

55. The relevant international material is summarised in Volodina v. Russia, no. 41261/17, §§ 51-60, 9 July 2019).

56. In Recommendation Rec(2002)5 of 30 April 2002 concerning the protection of women against violence, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe stated, inter alia, that member States should introduce, develop and, where required, improve national policies to combat violence. Such policies should be founded on ensuring the highest possible degree of safety and protection for victims; providing support and assistance; adapting criminal and civil law; increasing public awareness; training professionals who encounter violence against women; and prevention.

57. As regards domestic violence, the Committee of Ministers recommended that member States make every form of violence within the family a criminal offence and allow measures to be taken that would, inter alia: empower the judiciary to order interim protection for victims; prohibit perpetrators from contacting, communicating with or approaching victims, or from living in or entering specified locations; impose penalties for every breach of measures ordered against perpetrators; and create a mandatory operational protocol for the police and for medical and social services.

Material concerning violence against women in Ukraine

58.
Ukraine signed the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (the Istanbul Convention) on 7 November 2011, but has yet to ratify it. On 14 November 2017, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr N. Muiznieks, wrote to Mr A. Parubiy, Speaker of the Ukrainian Parliament, urging him to help advance the Convention’s ratification. The letter stated, among other things:

“During my visits to different countries, I have come across a number of objections to, and misconceptions about, the Convention. These arguments, together with responses to them, can be outlined as follows:

- Some object to the word ‘gender’ because of its alleged ‘ideological’ implications. Yet the Convention defines the concept clearly: whereas ‘sex’ denotes the biological characteristics distinguishing human beings as female or male, gender ‘shall mean the socially constructed roles, behaviours, activities and attributes that a society considers appropriate for women and men.’ The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and other United Nations bodies use the same definition. It is also the meaning applied in the expression ‘gender stereotypes.’

- Certain critics accept that violence against women is a serious issue but, based on the cultural belief that women and men should fulfil sharply different functions in family and public life, oppose government efforts to challenge traditional gender roles and stereotypes. Such an approach confines women to the stereotypical position of mothers whose role is to give birth, remain at home and raise children.

- Some even contend that ratifying the Istanbul Convention would threaten societies founded on traditional families. I wish to assure everyone that it poses no such risk. On the contrary, every measure contained in the Convention strengthens family ties and foundations by preventing and addressing violence, the principal cause of family breakdown.

- The Convention has also been criticised for what is described as an ‘unjustified’ emphasis on women, given that men may also experience violence. Nevertheless, evidence gathered across various Council of Europe member states, Ukraine included, demonstrates that women subjected to violence by men constitute the overwhelming majority of domestic-violence cases. More broadly, many studies establish that women and girls face a greater risk of gender-based violence than men and that violence directed specifically against women remains widespread. At the same time, the Istanbul Convention acknowledges that men and children can also be victims of domestic violence and that their experiences must likewise be addressed.

The purpose of the Istanbul Convention is to eliminate violence against women and domestic violence by requiring the creation of a comprehensive framework capable of combating these phenomena effectively.”
Respect for every person’s fundamental rights—including the rights to life, security, liberty, dignity, and physical and emotional integrity—would benefit individual victims, their families, and society at large. I would appreciate it if you could circulate my letter to all members of the Ukrainian Parliament, and I look forward to receiving additional information about the ratification process.”

59. In its March 2017 concluding observations on Ukraine’s eighth periodic report, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) stated, in particular:

“26. The Committee continues to be concerned that deeply entrenched patriarchal attitudes and discriminatory stereotypes about the respective roles and responsibilities of women and men within the family persist in political debate, the media, and society. These attitudes maintain women’s subordinate position in both family and society and are evident, among other areas, in women’s educational and career choices, their limited involvement in political and public life, their unequal position in the labour market, and their unequal status in family relationships. The Committee reiterates that such discriminatory stereotypes are also among the root causes of violence against women. It is concerned that the State party has not yet adopted sustained measures to change or eliminate discriminatory stereotypes and harmful traditional attitudes.

...

29. With reference to its general recommendation No. 19 (1992) on violence against women, the Committee recommends that the State party:

(a) ... expedite ratification of the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence [the Istanbul Convention];

(b) Adopt comprehensive measures to prevent and respond to violence against women and girls, while ensuring that perpetrators are prosecuted and receive appropriate punishment; ...”

60. The 2018 OSCE-led survey on violence against women in Ukraine found that most women interviewed were concerned about the problem, and 64% considered it a common occurrence. Among the survey’s principal findings and recommendations were the following:

“... Violence against women (VAW) is highly prevalent, yet women are hesitant to report it or seek assistance.

In Ukraine, more than one woman in four (26%) has experienced physical and/or sexual violence by a current or former partner. Psychological violence by an intimate partner has affected almost two-thirds of women (65%), a figure substantially above the EU average of 43% and higher than that recorded in any EU country. Nevertheless, only 7% of women who survived violence by a current partner and 12% of those who experienced violence by a former partner reported it to the police.”
Given that 52% of female survivors of intimate partner violence experienced physical harm during the most severe incident they endured, other forms of serious violence are also likely to be underreported. Women participating in the qualitative study stated that psychological abuse is widely regarded as normal, while 26% of surveyed women believed domestic violence to be a private matter. Experts interviewed for the report described a collective tolerance of violence, and survey respondents identified shame as an obstacle to reporting abuse. Among women who identified a most serious incident involving a current partner, more than four in five (81%) did not approach the police or any other organization. The corresponding figures were 67% for violence by a former partner and 52% for non-partner violence.”61.

The U.K. Home Office’s May 2018 Country Policy and Information Note on gender-based violence in Ukraine included the following information:

“4.2.3. ... Kateryna Levchenko, President of the NGO ‘La Strada – Ukraine,’ presented statistical findings drawn from a survey of police officers and prosecutors, together with an analysis of court decisions in cases involving violence against women and domestic violence. Certain instances of family violence were justified by 10% of prosecutors, 11% of judges, and 12% of police officers. Among criminal justice officials, 39% regarded domestic violence as a private issue, while 60% blamed victims for sexual violence.

During court proceedings in domestic violence cases, preserving the family and achieving reconciliation [between] partners were viewed as the ... highest priorities by 77% of prosecutors, 81% of police officers, and 84% of judges. As a result, the violence was minimized and treated as a minor disagreement.

Courts frequently approach violence cases as a formality. Monitoring of 77 hearings found that proceedings lasted an average of between 4 and 23 minutes. Perpetrators commonly failed to attend court, with only one in six abusers appearing. Their absence often led to hearings being cancelled. ...”
