FIFTH SECTION

LEVCHUK v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 17496/19)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

3 September 2020

FINAL

03/12/2020

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment is final. It may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Levchuk v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), convening as a Chamber consisting of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,  
Gabriele Kucsko-Stadlmayer,  
Ganna Yudkivska,  
Mārtiņš Mits,  
Lәtif Hüseynov,  
Anja Seibert-Fohr,  
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application against Ukraine (no. 17496/19), submitted to the Court on 20 March 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Iryna Mykolayivna Levchuk, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the decision, under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court, to accord the case priority;

the observations filed by the parties;

Having held private deliberations on 30 June 2020,

Gives the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. This case relates to alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the rejection of the applicant’s claim seeking the eviction of her former husband, who had repeatedly inflicted psychological and physical violence on her in the presence of their minor children.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1982, the applicant resides in Rivne. She is officially registered as having a category 3 disability[1] and supports herself through a disability pension and child-support benefits. She received legal aid and was represented by Ms N.A. Bukhta, a lawyer practising in Rivne.

3. Mr I. Lishchyna, acting as Agent, represented the Government.

4. The parties’ accounts permit the relevant circumstances to be summarised as set out below.

5. The applicant gave birth to a son in 2002.

6. She married O.L. on 26 May 2006. They moved into a flat in Rivne jointly owned by O.L. and his mother.

7. In January 2007, the applicant and O.L. became parents to triplet daughters.

8. Because of the multiple birth, the Rivne City Council allocated social housing to the applicant and O.L. in February 2008. The accommodation was a flat which they, their triplets and the applicant’s son were entitled to occupy as protected tenants.

9. The applicant stated that her relationship with O.L. progressively worsened as a result of his alcohol abuse. When intoxicated, he initiated arguments, harassed and threatened both her and the children, and occasionally used physical violence against her. On a number of occasions, his violent episodes frightened her to such an extent that she left the home and stayed temporarily with relatives or acquaintances.

10. On 18 March 2009, the Rivne regional forensic bureau recorded that the applicant had sustained a fractured nose and haemorrhaging around both eyes. She maintained that those injuries had been caused during one of her disputes with O.L.
The case file indicates that no formal follow-up proceedings arose from this incident.

11. On 13 January 2011, S.L., an acquaintance of the applicant, reported to the Rivne police that O.L. had struck the applicant during an argument at home. The police declined to open criminal proceedings because they found no corpus delicti in O.L.’s conduct. No appeal was lodged against that decision.

12. In April 2015, the applicant brought civil proceedings, alleging that O.L. had failed to contribute to the financial support of their children.

13. In June 2015, the Rivne Town Court delivered a judgment determining the amount of child support that O.L. was required to pay the applicant.

14. On 10 June 2015, the applicant filed a criminal complaint with the police, stating that O.L. had kicked her during a domestic argument at approximately 9 p.m. on 31 May 2015.

15. On 11 June 2015, criminal proceedings concerning the alleged assault on the applicant were opened against O.L. under Article 125 of the Criminal Code (“the CC”).

16. On 16 June 2015, the Rivne regional forensic bureau confirmed that the applicant had sustained a subcutaneous haemorrhage on her right thigh.

17. The marriage between the applicant and O.L. was dissolved on 23 September 2015, and the applicant was granted custody of all the children. Following the divorce, O.L. and all the family members continued to reside in the same flat.

18. On 16 October 2015, the Rivne police discontinued the criminal proceedings opened against O.L. in June after the applicant withdrew her complaint. The decision noted that O.L.’s actions appeared to fall within the scope of Article 125 of the CC. However, because the applicant, as the injured party, had chosen not to pursue the complaint, the case materials were to be transferred to another police department to determine whether O.L. should face an administrative-offence charge. It appears that no subsequent decision was made regarding this incident.

19. On 11 November 2015, the applicant reported to the Rivne police that O.L. had failed to pay child support. She submitted a certificate issued by the State Bailiffs Service showing that his payments were seven months in arrears. She maintained that, despite being officially unemployed, O.L. regularly undertook odd jobs and concealed the income he earned from them. Criminal proceedings concerning the matter were instituted that same day.

20. During police questioning in December 2015, O.L. admitted that he had not paid child support. He stated that he could not make the required payments because he was unemployed and had no income. He promised to clear the arrears once he had found a source of income and acquired the necessary funds. It appears that the proceedings against him were later either discontinued or abandoned.

21.
On 23 November 2015 and again on 2 February 2016, the applicant telephoned the police to report that O.L. was harassing and mistreating her in their home. Police officers responded by visiting the couple’s residence and holding preventive discussions.

On 23 February 2016, the applicant called the police once more, alleging that O.L. was acting aggressively while under the influence of alcohol.

She made another call on 12 March 2016, reporting harassment by her husband. As recorded in a police report dated 16 March 2016, the police conducted a further inspection and issued O.L. another oral warning.

On 18 March 2016, the head of the Rivne police concluded that O.L.’s conduct on 23 February 2016—insulting and threatening the applicant and stabbing a blanket with a knife—could be classified as psychological harassment. O.L. was charged with the administrative offence of domestic violence under Article 173-2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (“the CAO”), and the matter was referred to the Rivne Town Court. No subsequent decision appears to have been made concerning that police report.

On 14 March 2016, the applicant contacted the Rivne municipal family, child and youth welfare service (“the family welfare service”), stating that her husband frequently behaved abusively when under the influence of alcohol and requesting assistance in finding a structured solution.

From 14 to 22 March 2016, representatives of the family welfare service assessed the needs of the applicant’s family by visiting her flat and interviewing the triplets. The interview records show that one daughter said she loved both parents but became very distressed when her father returned home drunk and argued with her mother. A second daughter stated that she did not respect her father and hated his coming home intoxicated. The third said that she loved her mother and tried to avoid discussing her father.

Additional records indicate that the social workers could not interview O.L. because he was absent during their visits. Efforts to arrange a separate meeting were unsuccessful: he either failed to answer the telephone or refused to meet them, explaining that he was extremely busy at work.

Following the assessment, the family welfare service prepared a report concluding that the children had generally been provided with the conditions required for their upbringing. Nevertheless, their father was neglecting his parental duties and engaging in violent disputes with their mother, causing the children fear and distress. Counselling was offered to the applicant, but she declined it at that stage.

On 24 March 2016, the family welfare service requested that the police continue monitoring the applicant’s family circumstances, specifically by conducting a preventive discussion with O.L.
and determining whether any basis existed for prosecuting him for domestic violence.

28. On 5 April 2016, the police inspector entrusted with that task stated that he had been unable to contact O.L. to arrange a meeting.

29. In April 2016, the principal, psychologist and the girls’ class teacher at the triplets’ primary school informed the welfare service that the girls had, overall, adapted well to school and social life. Their situation at home, however, was troubling. They said that their parents frequently argued. They had a close, trusting relationship with their mother and maternal relatives. By contrast, they found it difficult to trust their father and believed that he often showed little interest in matters concerning them. They regularly saw him intoxicated and were frightened by his appearance and by his unpredictable, at times violent, behaviour. The school staff knew of no occasion on which the father had physically mistreated the girls. Nevertheless, they concluded that his detached attitude, together with his aggressive outbursts against the mother, had made the girls victims of “psychological ill-treatment”.

30. On 13 April 2016, the applicant filed another police complaint, claiming that at approximately 10 p.m. that day O.L. had again erupted violently by swearing at her, threatening her and pushing her.

31. On 18 April 2016, the Rivne regional forensic bureau confirmed that the applicant had haemorrhages on her right wrist, arm and leg, as well as a sprain of the aponeurosis in her right foot.

32. On 5 July 2016, concerning O.L.’s behaviour on 13 April 2016, the Rivne Town Court convicted him of domestic violence under Article 173-2 of the CAO. O.L. attended the hearing and admitted committing the offence. The court further ruled that he could be exempted from formal liability and receive only an oral reprimand because the applicant had requested that outcome and the parties had already settled their differences.

33. Meanwhile, on 22 June 2016, the applicant had brought civil proceedings before the Rivne Town Court seeking O.L.’s eviction from their flat. Relying on Article 116 of the Housing Code, she maintained that cohabitation with him had become impossible because he systematically misused alcohol, mistreated, threatened and harassed her and the children, disregarded their interests and had violent outbursts. If they continued living together, she and her minor children would remain under constant threat of psychological harassment and physical violence. She further submitted that eviction would not leave O.L. in a vulnerable position because he co-owned another flat in the same town with his mother.

34.
In the proceedings on the eviction claim, the court examined three witnesses—the applicant’s sister and two friends—who corroborated her account and stated that O.L. had abused alcohol and mistreated his former wife and children. Three other witnesses, consisting of O.L.’s brother and two individuals who were either his friends or relatives, gave a different account. They claimed that the applicant had provoked the disputes because she wished to remove O.L. and secure complete control over the flat. They further asserted that O.L. was concerned about the children and was a considerate father.

35. O.L. also produced two character references in support of his position. One had been issued by the management body responsible for the building where the flat occupied by him and the applicant was situated. It stated that none of the building’s residents had ever made a complaint about him. The other reference came from R., a limited liability company, and described O.L., who worked for the company as an independent contractor, as a highly regarded, diligent construction worker and a good member of the team.

36. The applicant submitted documents relating to all of her earlier complaints about violence and harassment. She also provided a new certificate issued by the State Bailiffs Service, according to which O.L. was, at the relevant time, eighteen months behind in his child-support payments.

37. On 4 April 2017, the Rivne Town Court upheld the applicant’s claim and ordered O.L. to be evicted. Its judgment included, in particular, the following findings:

“... After hearing [the parties and their representatives] and the witnesses ..., and after reviewing the written evidence, the court has reached the following [conclusions]:

... the respondent abuses alcohol, repeatedly creates scenes and starts arguments, and intimidates [the applicant] in front of the children. He acts aggressively and threatens the claimant with physical violence. On some occasions, [the claimant] and her minor children have had to spend the night at the homes of acquaintances because she was afraid to remain at home with the respondent. The claimant has repeatedly sought assistance from the law-enforcement authorities to protect both her own rights and those of her minor children. ... Measures intended to correct the respondent’s conduct were imposed on him, including preventive discussions and warnings that domestic violence was unacceptable. Furthermore, in a decision dated 5 July 2016, the Rivne Town Court found [him] guilty of an administrative offence under Article 173-2 [of the CAO]. He was also prosecuted for a criminal offence under Article 125 [of the CC] for causing minor injuries to the claimant.

Those measures aimed at correcting [the respondent’s] conduct failed to achieve the intended outcome ...”

38. O.L. lodged an appeal, maintaining that the applicant had deliberately instigated disputes in order to distance him from the children and derive financial advantages from the flat.
For the same reasons, she had overstated the circumstances and lodged vexatious complaints based on allegations unsupported by evidence. Furthermore, Article 116 of the Housing Code allowed the eviction of a resident only where that person’s misconduct was systematic and less severe measures had failed. In his case, there was no proof of repeated misconduct, and several witnesses had given evidence in his support. Although occasional fights had occurred, all evidence against him related either to 2011 or to 2015-16. No new evidence had been submitted showing any arguments between him and his former wife. As for the flat he co-owned, it was occupied by his mother and his brother’s family, leaving no space for him.

39. On 14 June 2017, the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal set aside the Town Court’s judgment and rejected the applicant’s claim. It held that there was no basis for imposing eviction, such a drastic measure, because the requirements of Article 116 of the Housing Code had not been met. The pertinent part of its ruling stated:

“The case-file materials show that the applicant repeatedly called the police to her home, alleging that the defendant had committed unlawful acts against her and members of her family. However, it has not been established that [O.L.] systematically violated the rules of cohabitation or was held liable [in that connection]....

Merely submitting complaints to the competent authorities about breaches of the rules of cohabitation, where those authorities have not imposed measures intended to correct the conduct of the [guilty] person concerned, does not constitute grounds for eviction.

After assessing each item of evidence individually and all the evidence collectively, the judicial panel finds that the material submitted by the parties establishes the existence of hostile and conflict-ridden relations between the former spouses.

Against that background, the judicial panel considers the grounds insufficient to impose on the defendant such an extreme measure as eviction. Nevertheless, the panel finds it necessary to caution [O.L.] that he must alter his attitude towards the rules governing cohabitation with members of his family [following the divorce]. ...”

40. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. She submitted, in particular, that O.L. had previously been found guilty of domestic violence in administrative proceedings and had been prosecuted under Article 125 of the CC for the criminal offence of assaulting her. She maintained that he had neither changed his behaviour nor corrected his attitude, and that continuing to live with him placed her and the children at substantial risk of violence and harassment. She further repeated that another dwelling was available to him.

41.
On 20 August 2018, the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law and upheld the Court of Appeal’s findings.

42. The decision was mailed to the applicant on 11 October 2018.

43. On 28 May 2019, under the national scheme enabling protected tenants to acquire ownership of their homes, ownership of the family flat was granted to the applicant, O.L., their daughters and the applicant’s son.

44. They all continue to live together in the flat.

45. On 26 November 2019, the applicant brought proceedings seeking to have O.L. deprived of his parental rights in respect of their triplets. She alleged that he persistently failed to attend to their needs and avoided paying child support. Those proceedings remain pending.

46. In December 2019, following another violent outburst, the applicant lodged a new criminal complaint against O.L.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Relevant domestic law

The Criminal Code (2002)

47. In its relevant part, Article 125 of the Code provides:

Article 125. Intentional infliction of minor physical injury

“1. Anyone who intentionally causes minor physical injury shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty times the non-taxable minimum income for citizens, community service of up to two hundred hours, or correctional labour for a period of up to one year. ...”

The Code of Administrative Offences (1984)

48. At the relevant time, Article 173-2 of the Code provided, in so far as pertinent:

Article 173-2. Domestic violence, non-compliance with a restraining order, or avoidance of a correctional programme

“An act of domestic violence means the intentional commission of conduct of a physical, psychological or economic nature—including the use of physical force that neither causes physical pain nor results in physical injury; threats; insults; stalking; or depriving a victim of housing, food, clothing, other belongings or money to which he or she is legally entitled, and so forth—where such conduct causes or may cause harm to the victim’s physical or psychological health.

The same provision applies where a person fails to comply with a restraining order issued against him or her or, after committing an act of domestic violence, evades participation in a correctional programme.

Such conduct shall be punishable by thirty to forty hours of community service or by administrative detention for a maximum of seven days. ...”

The Housing Code (1983)

49. The relevant part of Article 116 of the Code states:

Article 116. Eviction without provision ... of alternative housing

“Where a tenant, a member of his or her family, or another person residing with him or her ... systematically ... breaches the rules governing ... cohabitation, thereby making it impossible for the other [occupants of the dwelling] to live with that person in the same flat or house, and where measures of pre-emption and public-pressure measures have failed to achieve a positive outcome, the persons responsible shall, at the request of ... interested persons, be evicted without being provided with another dwelling.”
Law of Ukraine “On Preventing and Combating Domestic Violence” (No. 2229-VIII of 7 December 2017; “the Domestic Violence Act”)

50. The 2017 Domestic Violence Act took effect on 7 January 2018 and superseded the 2001 Law “On the Prevention of Family Violence”. Section 5 set out the aims of State policy on preventing and combating domestic violence in the following terms:

“1. State policy concerning the prevention of and response to domestic violence shall seek to establish a comprehensive and integrated approach to eliminating domestic violence, providing victims with comprehensive assistance, and affirming the non-violent nature of private relationships.

2. State policy on preventing and combating domestic violence shall be implemented in the following principal areas:

1) preventing domestic violence;

2) responding effectively to incidents of domestic violence by developing a mechanism for cooperation among the authorities exercising powers in the field of preventing and combating domestic violence;

3) assisting and protecting victims and ensuring compensation for harm sustained as a consequence of domestic violence;

4) duly investigating incidents of domestic violence, holding offenders liable in accordance with the law, and changing their behaviour.”

51. Among other things, the Act envisaged establishing a Unified State Register of incidents of domestic and gender-based violence (Section 16). It also laid down a number of “special measures for combating domestic violence” to address complaints by victims. In particular, those measures comprised an urgent injunctive police order, a court restraining order, registration of the offender in preventive-measures records, and enrolment of the offender in a special corrective programme (Sections 24-28).

Resolution No. 2 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine, dated 12 April 1985, concerning issues arising from the courts’ application of the Housing Code of Ukraine

52. In its relevant part, the Resolution provided:

“17. In determining cases brought under Article 116 of the [Housing Code] seeking the eviction of individuals who repeatedly violate the rules of communal living and thereby make it impossible for others to reside with them in the same flat or house, regard must be had to the fact that, where the individual concerned is responsible for persistent antisocial behaviour, eviction may occur, for example, following a repeated violation, provided that preventive measures (попередження) or measures of public pressure have failed to produce a positive result.”
[Among the measures that should be considered are] ..., notably preventive measures imposed by courts, prosecutors, law-enforcement agencies [or] administrative commissions of executive committees; measures of public pressure adopted at meetings of apartment-block residents or housing-cooperative members; ... and [measures imposed] by other public organisations [active] at the respondent’s workplace or place of residence, irrespective of whether the respondent has been expressly warned of possible eviction. ...”

Relevant national case-law on restraining orders

Supreme Court of Ukraine ruling of 4 December 2019 in case no. 607/10122/1953

In that ruling, the Supreme Court observed, inter alia:

“In April 2019, [the complainant] brought proceedings requesting that a restraining order be issued against [her former husband]. ...

[She] alleged that [the respondent] had committed psychological [and] physical violence against her and their minor child through persistent threats, intimidation and harassment, the use of physical force, and obstruction of their use of [the room in the accommodation hall where all three resided].

... [The complainant] sought a restraining order against [the respondent] for six months ..., including an injunction preventing him from obstructing [her and her minor son’s] use of the room and a prohibition on his entering [or residing in] ... that room.

...

When determining applications of this kind, courts must conduct a comprehensive assessment of all the facts and evidence, duly respecting the rights and interests of both the children and the parents. They must also ensure that, where one parent’s claims are unfounded and unjustified, those claims do not result in an unwarranted restriction of the other parent’s rights in relation to the children.

...

It has been established in the present case that relations between [the complainant] and [the respondent] are hostile and that disputes frequently occur over residence in and use of the room in the accommodation hall ...

[The respondent] declared that he did not intend to permit his former spouse ... or their minor son to use the room ...

On the basis of those established facts, the first-instance court—whose findings were upheld by the appellate court—correctly found lawful grounds for issuing a restraining order requiring [the respondent] to stop obstructing the complainant and her minor son in their use of the dwelling and of the household items situated there. The lower courts were likewise correct in finding that there were no grounds for ...
“barring [the respondent] from entering [or living in] room ..., because [the complainant] had failed to submit unambiguous evidence that [the respondent] had perpetrated domestic violence ...”

54. In its ruling of 28 April 2020 in case no. 754/11171/19, the Supreme Court of Ukraine stated, among other things:

“In July 2019, [the complainant] initiated proceedings for a restraining order against [her former husband], claiming that he had repeatedly subjected both her and their children to intimidation and violence. The alleged conduct included physical attacks and psychological and sexual violence.

...

In determining whether to impose such a measure, the courts ... are required to evaluate whether the resulting restriction of the person’s rights and freedoms is proportionate, bearing in mind that the need for those measures arises from [the offender’s] unlawful behaviour.

Accordingly, [the lower courts] were wrong to find that the victim’s request could not be granted in so far as it concerned ... temporarily limiting [the respondent’s] right to [use] the flat that he co-owns ..., since that finding denies the complainant the safeguards ... guaranteed by the [Domestic Violence Act].

In the present case, the [lower] courts ... found that there was a high risk of [further violence] ...

Against that background, the judicial panel ... considers that [the complainant’s] requests ... to prohibit [the respondent] from remaining in the ... flat ... [and] from coming within two kilometres of [the flat] should be granted. ...”

Relevant international materials

55. The pertinent international materials are summarised in Volodina v. Russia, no. 41261/17, §§ 51-60, 9 July 2019.

56. In Recommendation Rec(2002)5 of 30 April 2002 concerning the protection of women against violence, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe stated, inter alia, that member States should establish, expand and/or, where needed, strengthen national policies to combat violence. Such policies should be founded on ensuring the highest possible level of victim safety and protection; providing support and assistance; adapting criminal and civil law; increasing public awareness; training professionals who encounter violence against women; and prevention.

57. As regards violence in the family, the Committee of Ministers recommended that member States make every form of domestic violence a criminal offence and allow measures to be taken that would, inter alia: empower the judiciary to order interim measures for the protection of victims; prohibit perpetrators from contacting, communicating with or approaching victims, or from living in or entering specified places; impose penalties for any violation of measures ordered against perpetrators; and introduce a mandatory operational protocol for the police and for medical and social services.

Materials concerning violence against women in Ukraine

58.
Ukraine signed the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, known as the Istanbul Convention, on 7 November 2011, but has not yet ratified it.

On 14 November 2017, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Mr N. Muiznieks wrote to Mr A. Parubiy, Speaker of the Ukrainian Parliament, urging him to help advance the Convention’s ratification. In particular, the Commissioner addressed several objections and misconceptions he had encountered during country visits.

One objection concerned the word “gender” and its alleged “ideological” implications. The Commissioner noted that the Convention defines the concept clearly: whereas “sex” denotes the biological characteristics by which human beings are defined as female or male, gender “shall mean the socially constructed roles, behaviours, activities and attributes that a society considers appropriate for women and men.” The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and other United Nations bodies use the same definition, which is also relevant to the expression “gender stereotypes.”

Some critics accepted that violence against women was a problem but opposed allowing governments to challenge traditional gender roles and stereotypes. Their position was based on the cultural belief that women and men should have sharply different functions both in public life and in the family. According to the Commissioner, this outlook confines women to the stereotypical role of mothers who give birth and remain at home to raise children.

Other opponents argued that ratifying the Istanbul Convention would threaten societies founded on traditional families. The Commissioner reassured them that no such risk existed. On the contrary, all measures established by the Convention strengthen family ties and foundations by preventing and combating violence, the principal cause of family breakdown.

A further criticism was that the Convention placed an allegedly “unjustified” emphasis on women even though men could also experience violence. The Commissioner responded that data gathered in various Council of Europe member states, including Ukraine, showed that women subjected to violence by men accounted for the overwhelming majority of domestic-violence cases. Numerous studies likewise demonstrated that women and girls faced a greater risk of gender-based violence than men and that violence specifically directed against women remained widespread. At the same time, the Istanbul Convention acknowledged that men and children could also be victims of domestic violence and that their experiences must be addressed as well.

The Istanbul Convention seeks to eliminate violence against women and domestic violence by requiring the creation of a comprehensive framework capable of combating both phenomena effectively.
Respecting every person’s fundamental rights to life, security, liberty, dignity, and physical and emotional integrity would benefit individual victims, their families, and society at large. I would appreciate it if you could circulate my letter to every member of the Ukrainian Parliament, and I await further information about the ratification process.”59.

In March 2017, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) issued its concluding observations on Ukraine’s eighth periodic report. It stated, among other things:

“26. The Committee continues to be concerned that deeply entrenched patriarchal attitudes and discriminatory stereotypes about the respective roles and responsibilities of women and men within the family remain widespread in political discourse, the media, and society. These views reinforce the subordinate position of women in both family and society and are evident, inter alia, in women’s choices in education and employment, their restricted involvement in political and public life, their unequal position in the labour market, and their unequal status in family relationships. Recalling that such discriminatory stereotypes are also underlying causes of violence against women, the Committee is concerned that the State party has not yet adopted sustained measures to change or eradicate discriminatory stereotypes and harmful traditional attitudes.

...

29. With reference to its general recommendation No. 19 (1992) concerning violence against women, the Committee recommends that the State party:

(a) ... expedite ratification of the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence [the Istanbul Convention];

(b) Adopt comprehensive measures to prevent and respond to violence against women and girls, while ensuring that perpetrators are prosecuted and receive appropriate punishment; ...”60.

The 2018 OSCE-led survey on violence against women in Ukraine found that most women interviewed were concerned about the problem, and 64% described it as common. Its principal findings and recommendations included the following:

“... Violence against women (VAW) is highly prevalent, yet women are hesitant to report it or ask for assistance.

In Ukraine, more than one in four women (26%) have been subjected to physical and/or sexual violence by a current or former partner. Psychological violence by an intimate partner has affected two-thirds of women (65%), a rate substantially above the EU average of 43% and higher than that recorded in every EU country. Nevertheless, only 7% of women who survived violence by a current partner and 12% of those who experienced violence by a former partner reported it to the police.
Given that 52% of female survivors of intimate partner violence experienced physical harm from the most severe incident they endured, other forms of serious violence are also likely to be underreported. Women participating in the qualitative study stated that psychological abuse is regarded as normal, while 26% of women believed domestic violence to be a private issue. Experts interviewed for the report described a collective tolerance of violence, and surveyed women identified shame as an obstacle to reporting abuse. Among women who identified a most serious incident involving a current partner, more than four-fifths (81%) contacted neither the police nor any other organization. The corresponding proportions were 67% for violence by a former partner and 52% for non-partner violence.”61.

The U.K. Home Office’s May 2018 Country Policy and Information Note on gender-based violence in Ukraine included the following information:

“4.2.3. ... Kateryna Levchenko, President of the NGO ‘La Strada – Ukraine,’ presented statistical findings drawn from a survey of police officers and prosecutors, along with an analysis of court rulings in cases involving violence against women and domestic violence. Certain instances of family violence are justified by 10% of prosecutors, 11% of judges, and 12% of police officers. Domestic violence is viewed as a private matter by 39% of criminal justice officials, while 60% blame victims for sexual violence.

In court proceedings concerning domestic violence, reconciliation [between] partners and preservation of the family are treated as the ... highest priorities by 77% of prosecutors, 81% of police officers, and 84% of judges; violence is consequently minimized and characterized as a minor dispute.

Courts frequently address violence cases in a formalistic manner. Monitoring of 77 hearings found that meetings lasted an average of between 4 and 23 minutes. Perpetrators fail to attend court, with only every 6th abuser appearing. As a result, hearings are often cancelled. ...”

Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of: Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, President, Ganna Yudkivska, Lado Chanturia, judges,and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Ukrainian national, Ms Tetyana Vasylivna Kornilova (“the applicant”), on 27 June 2014;the decision to give notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”);the parties’ observations;the decision to reject the Government’s objection to examination of the application by a Committee;Having deliberated in private on 13 October 2020,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:INTRODUCTION1. The applicant was hit by a man whom she had been attempting to invite to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. The individual was eventually convicted of infliction of a minor injury, sentenced to a fine and ordered to pay damages. The applicant complained that the authorities had not sufficiently taken into account the alleged motive of religious prejudice behind the violence. She relied on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.THE FACTS2. The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Nosivka. She was represented by Mr K. Chernychenko, Mr R. Cook and Mr A. Carbonneau, lawyers practising in Lviv, London and Paris respectively.3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.4. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.5. On 7 March 2013 the applicant, a Jehovah’s Witness, and her co-religionist, Ms N.S., were conducting door-to-door visits in the town of Nosivka, distributing printed invitations to a religious service. On the front of the invitations was an image of Jesus Christ and the words “One Died for All” in large print; on the back there was some text mentioning, in smaller print, that the invitation was to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting.6. At about 1 p.m. the applicant and N.S. called at the house of V.S., a fifty-year-old man with whom they were unacquainted. He met them at the front gate of the house. According to the applicant, V.S. noticed the invitations and the Bible in the women’s hands and immediately punched the applicant in the head and started cursing at the two women, using obscenities and also calling them “shtundas” (штунди). Also according to the applicant, she and N.S. walked away as V.S. had threatened to unleash his dog.7. Shtunda or shtundist is a colloquial term used in Ukraine to denote evangelical Protestants of various denominations. It is derived from the term shtundism, used to describe evangelical protestant groups active in the Ukraine in the 19th century, focused on evangelisation by spreading knowledge of the Bible.[1]8. On 9 March 2013 the applicant was admitted to the neurology department of the Nosivka District Central Hospital in connection with her complaints of dizziness and nausea. She was diagnosed with concussion. A bruise on the face was also noted. She received inpatient treatment until 19 March 2013 and was authorised to return to work the following day.9. Also on 9 March 2013 the applicant complained to the Nosivka District Police Department. The police opened a criminal investigation and notified her of that fact, also indicating that the alleged offence had been classified, on a preliminary basis, under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code (intentional infliction of minor injuries, see paragraph 45 below).10. On the same day the police questioned the applicant. She stated that she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that on 7 March she and a fellow believer, N.S., had been distributing invitations to a religious service. When they had called at one particular house, a fifty-year old man had come out and started cursing at them and calling them shtundas. He had then hit the applicant in the head without any reason (безпричинно).11. Still on the same day, V.S. was questioned as a witness, in the absence of a lawyer. He stated that two previously unknown women had come to his property and offered him Jehovah’s Witnesses’ literature. He had refused to take it and had demanded that they leave and not visit his property again. They had refused to leave and “continued to try to recruit him into their fraternity” (продовжували агітувати у своє братство). At that point, V.S. had become angry and had slapped one of the women on the face. He stated that, even if he had uttered obscenities, they had not been addressed to the women.12. On 12 March 2013 N.S. was questioned. She stated that V.S. had hit the applicant right away, as soon as he had seen her, before any words had been exchanged. N.S. had not seen whether he had slapped or punched her. She did remember, however, that V.S. had cursed constantly and had called the applicant and her “shtundas”.13. On 18 March 2013, the local hospital informed the police investigator in charge of the case, in response to a request from him, that V.S. was not under medical supervision for any psychiatric or addiction problems. The investigator also requested background information about V.S. from the local council, which responded that there had been no complaints about him. Lastly, the investigator established that V.S. had no criminal record.14. On 25 March 2013 the applicant was recognised as an aggrieved party (victim) in the proceedings and given information on her procedural rights in that capacity under the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 48 below).15. On the same day the applicant was questioned and made a detailed statement setting out the events in terms similar to those described in paragraph 6 above. She stressed in great detail, making reference to Articles 3 and 9 of the Convention, how she had felt humiliated and traumatised by the experience and how that had interfered with her religious practice.16. On 1 and 12 April 2013 the police questioned a member of the council of elders of the Jehovah’s Witnesses community to which the applicant belonged, the applicant’s daughter (also a Jehovah’s Witness) and two other members of the community. Those witnesses, based on conversations they had had with the applicant, repeated her account of the incident set out in paragraph 6 above.17. On 2 April 2013 a forensic medical expert determined that the applicant had suffered minor bodily injuries which had had short-term implications on her health, defined in the relevant regulations as health problems lasting from six to twenty-one days. The expert concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have been inflicted either by a slap (the defendant’s version) or by a punch (the applicant’s version).18. On 9 April 2013 the head of the district police informed the investigator that, at his request, police detectives had canvassed V.S.’s neighbours in an attempt to identify possible witnesses to the incident. However, nothing of relevance had been found.19. On 25 April 2013 the applicant’s husband, who was not a Jehovah’s Witness, was questioned. He stated that the applicant had not told him about the incident with V.S. on the same day (7 March) or the following day, and he had only learned about it from her on 9 March at the hospital. According to the applicant’s account, V.S. had come out of his house to meet the applicant and her fellow believer N.S., and, as soon as he had seen in their hands printed material with the picture of Jesus Christ and the Bible, he had started shouting and cursing, and had hit the applicant.20. On 14 May 2013 the investigator formally notified V.S. that he was suspected of having committed an offence under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Questioned on that day, V.S. submitted that he could not remember whether the women had been holding anything in their hands or what they had been talking about; he could, however, remember that they had invited him somewhere; despite his requests, the women would not leave, so he had then slapped one of them. V.S denied any possible element of religious intolerance in his conduct.21. On the same day the investigator organised a confrontation between the applicant and V.S. The applicant gave the account set out in paragraph 6 above. V.S. largely confirmed it, but stated that he had hit the applicant not out of a desire to offend her religious convictions but on account of the “sudden emergence of hostility” (із раптово виниклих неприязних відносин). V.S. repeated that formula when asked by the applicant why he had hit her (see paragraph 41 below for an explanation of the meaning of that formula).22. On 15 May 2013 the applicant asked the investigator to reclassify the offence with which V.S. was charged from intentional infliction of minor injuries under Article 125 to discriminatory acts, an offence under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 46 below). She claimed that V.S. had known that she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that he had hit her for that reason.23. On 16 May 2013 the investigator again questioned the applicant and N.S. They reiterated their previous accounts.24. On 17 May 2013 the investigator refused the applicant’s reclassification request, stating that it had been established that V.S. had reacted to the “sudden emergence of hostility”. It had not been established that he had acted out of a desire to incite religious hatred.25. On 20 May 2013 V.S. was questioned again. He stated that he had slapped the applicant on account of the “sudden emergence of hostility”, because she and N.S. had distracted him from his housework. They had insistently invited him to a meeting, indicating that there would be a lot of women there. The applicant had then humiliated him concerning his “man’s health” (Корнілова Т.В. тоді навіть образила мене з приводу мого чоловічого здоров’я), which was why he had hit her. He explained that he had not mentioned that aspect of the incident before because he had been too embarrassed. It had not been his intention to create religious hostility or offend the applicant’s religious convictions. V.S. insisted that he had respect for all religions. He had not known that the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness, as there had been no signs of her belonging to that group. He had indeed uttered obscenities, but those words had not been addressed to the applicant and her companion. He might have uttered the word “shtundas”, but that had had no religious connotations. He had then swung at her and, because she had been standing close, had ended up slapping her.29. On 16 July 2013 the Nosivka District Court found V.S. guilty of intentional infliction of a minor physical injury under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code and fined him the equivalent of 78 euros (EUR). The court found that he had inflicted minor physical injuries on the applicant “due to the sudden emergence of hostility” (на ґрунті раптово виниклих неприязних відносин); no aggravating circumstances could be established. The court noted that V.S. had already paid the amount claimed in respect of pecuniary damage (notably the costs of the applicant’s hospital treatment). In addition, she argued that the crime had been committed on grounds of religious enmity, which was an aggravating circumstance under Article 67 of the Criminal Code.35. The prosecutor responded, arguing that the defendant had been correctly charged and convicted of an offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code, rather than of discriminatory acts based on religious prejudice. The prosecutor pointed out that the investigation had been unable to identify a religious motive in the defendant’s actions, referring in this respect to the defendant’s account of the events (see paragraph 25 above).36. The defendant also appealed, arguing that the award in respect of non-pecuniary damage was excessive.37. At the close of the hearing the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s allegation that the crime had been committed on account of her religion, noting that no such motive had been established in the course of the investigation or court proceedings. The classification of the offence had been correct and the applicant had failed to point to any evidence which would support reclassification of the offence as hooliganism or discriminatory acts, as she had requested, beyond her initial statement to the police indicating that she had been attacked for no reason (see paragraph 10 above). In the Ukrainian legal context, the term “sudden emergence of hostility” is used to refer to a motive arising out of personal conflict or animosity. It is intended to distinguish offences arising out of such personal conflict or animosity from offences driven by other motives, such as financial gain or hooliganism, which may change the legal classification of an offence or can constitute an aggravating circumstance. For instance, if an assault causing a minor injury was motivated by such personal hostility, it can be classified under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. However, if the same assault was motivated by hooliganism, it can be classified as hooliganism, an offence against public order under Article 296 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 47 below).42. The elements of the offence of hooliganism, in particular the motives for an act of hooliganism, are explained in paragraph 47 below.Criminal Code 200143. Article 67 of the Code lists, among various circumstances to be taken into account as aggravating factors in sentencing, the commission of a crime on grounds of racial, national or religious enmity or hostility.44. The part of the Criminal Code dedicated to particular offences classifies them by chapter based on the societal value that a given offence is considered to be directed against.45. Article 125 of the Code, which is located in the chapter entitled “Offences against another person’s life and health”, criminalises the offence of “intentional infliction of a minor physical injury” with short-term health implications. The relevant regulations define “short-term health implications” as inability to work for six to twenty-one days. Article 125 makes this offence punishable by one of the following: (i) a fine of between the equivalent of EUR 58 and EUR 158; (ii) community work for a period of between 150 and 240 hours; (iii) the withholding of ten to twenty percent of wages for up to one year; (iv) short-term detention for up to six months; or (v) placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to two years.46. Article 161 of the Code, which is located in the chapter entitled “Offences against electoral, labour and other human and civil rights and freedoms”, criminalises the offence of “violation of the equality of citizens on grounds of race, ethnicity or religious beliefs”. At the relevant time it was punishable by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 790 or by placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years and, if the same acts were accompanied by violence, deception or threats or were committed by a person exercising official authority, by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 1,580 or by imprisonment for a period of between two and five years.47. Article 296, which is located in the chapter entitled “Offences against public order and morals”, criminalises “hooliganism” (хуліганство – sometimes also translated as “disorderly acts”), which is defined as “a serious breach of public order motivated by flagrant disrespect for society, combined with particular effrontery or exceptional cynicism”. At the relevant time that offence was punishable by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 1,580, short-term detention for up to six months or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years. The same acts committed in a group were punishable by placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years or imprisonment for up to four years. If combined with the use of an instrument adjusted specifically or constructed beforehand to inflict bodily harm, hooliganism was punishable by imprisonment for between three and seven years.A commentary to the Criminal Code, summarising the relevant case-law and established academic opinion, explains that the key element of the offence of hooliganism is that it must be motivated by “flagrant disrespect for society”. This is defined as a desire to show disregard for the established social rules of conduct, to reaffirm oneself at the expense of others, and to put oneself in opposition to others, society and the State.[2]Code of Criminal Procedure 201248. Article 56 of the Code confers a range of rights on an aggrieved party (victim) in criminal proceedings, most notably the right:(i)  to have the complaint about the crime committed promptly registered;(ii)  to submit evidence in support of such a complaint and submit any other relevant evidence in the proceedings;(iii)  to be notified of one’s rights as an aggrieved party;(iv)  to be informed of the nature of the charges or suspicion against the defendant, the imposition or removal of restrictions on the defendant and completion of the investigation;(v)  to lodge requests and applications and to challenge judges and other officials in charge of the case;(vi)  where merited, to benefit from police protection;(vii)  to make statements and testify in a language the victim understands or to refuse to do so and to use the services of an interpreter;(viii)  to challenge the decisions of the investigator, prosecutor and the court;(ix)  to be represented;(x)  to claim and recover damages caused by the crime;(xi)  to examine the case-file material concerning the crime committed against him or her at the time of completion of the investigation or its discontinuation and to obtain copies of such material;(xii)  to participate in investigative actions, put questions to the participants, make requests and objections concerning the procedure observed in the course of the action, examine records of such actions and propose corrections to them;(xiii)  to use recording devices in the course of investigative actions in which the aggrieved party takes part, unless the authority in charge of the proceedings bans such use in order to protect the confidentiality of certain information;(xiv)  to be notified in advance of the time of court hearings, take part in them, and participate in the examination of the evidence;(xv)  to continue to pursue the prosecution in lieu of the prosecutor if the prosecutor decides to withdraw charges;(xvi)  to be heard on the matters of sentencing;(xvii)  to examine the trial records and audio recordings; and(xviii)  to appeal against court decisions.

In the case of Kornilova v. Ukraine,

the parties’ observations;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee;

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant was struck by a man whom she had been trying to invite to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. The man was eventually convicted of inflicting a minor injury, sentenced to a fine and ordered to pay damages. The applicant complained that the authorities had failed to take sufficient account of the alleged religious prejudice motivating the violence. She relied on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1973 and resides in Nosivka. She was represented by Mr K. Chernychenko, Mr R. Cook and Mr A. Carbonneau, lawyers practising in Lviv, London and Paris respectively.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

5. On 7 March 2013 the applicant, a Jehovah’s Witness, and her fellow believer, Ms N.S., were making door-to-door visits in the town of Nosivka and distributing printed invitations to a religious service. The front of the invitations featured an image of Jesus Christ and the words “One Died for All” in large print; the back contained text stating, in smaller print, that the invitation was to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting.

6. At approximately 1 p.m. the applicant and N.S. called at the home of V.S., a fifty-year-old man whom they did not know. He met them at the front gate. According to the applicant, V.S. saw the invitations and the Bible in the women’s hands and immediately punched her in the head. He then began cursing at both women, using obscenities and calling them “shtundas” (штунди). The applicant further stated that she and N.S. walked away after V.S. threatened to unleash his dog.

7. Shtunda or shtundist is a colloquial expression used in Ukraine to refer to evangelical Protestants of various denominations.
It derives from the term shtundism, used to describe evangelical Protestant groups active in Ukraine in the 19th century and focused on evangelisation through spreading knowledge of the Bible.[1]

8. On 9 March 2013, the applicant was admitted to the neurology department of the Nosivka District Central Hospital following complaints of dizziness and nausea. She was diagnosed with a concussion. A bruise on her face was also noted. She received inpatient treatment until 19 March 2013 and was cleared to return to work the next day.

9. Also on 9 March 2013, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Nosivka District Police Department. The police opened a criminal investigation and informed her accordingly, also indicating that the alleged offence had been provisionally classified under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code (intentional infliction of minor injuries; see paragraph 45 below).

10. On the same day, the police questioned the applicant. She stated that she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that, on 7 March, she and a fellow believer, N.S., had been distributing invitations to a religious service. When they called at a particular house, a fifty-year-old man came out and began cursing at them and calling them shtundas. He then struck the applicant on the head without any reason (безпричинно).

11. Still on the same day, V.S. was questioned as a witness without a lawyer present. He stated that two women previously unknown to him had come to his property and offered him Jehovah’s Witnesses’ literature. He had refused to accept it and demanded that they leave and not visit his property again. They had refused to leave and “continued to try to recruit him into their fraternity” (продовжували агітувати у своє братство). At that point, V.S. became angry and slapped one of the women in the face. He stated that, even if he had used obscenities, they had not been directed at the women.

12. On 12 March 2013, N.S. was questioned. She stated that V.S. had struck the applicant immediately upon seeing her, before any words were exchanged. N.S. had not seen whether he had slapped or punched her. She did recall, however, that V.S. had cursed continuously and called both her and the applicant “shtundas”.

13. On 18 March 2013, in response to a request, the local hospital informed the police investigator handling the case that V.S. was not under medical supervision for any psychiatric or addiction-related problems. The investigator also requested background information on V.S. from the local council, which replied that no complaints had been made against him. Lastly, the investigator established that V.S. had no criminal record.

14. On 25 March 2013, the applicant was formally recognised as an aggrieved party (victim) in the proceedings and informed of her procedural rights in that capacity under the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 48 below).

15.
On the same day, the applicant was questioned and gave a detailed statement describing the events in terms similar to those set out in paragraph 6 above. Referring to Articles 3 and 9 of the Convention, she emphasised in considerable detail how humiliated and traumatised she had felt by the experience and how it had interfered with her religious practice.

16. On 1 and 12 April 2013, the police questioned a member of the council of elders of the Jehovah’s Witnesses community to which the applicant belonged, the applicant’s daughter (also a Jehovah’s Witness), and two other members of the community. Based on conversations they had had with the applicant, those witnesses repeated her account of the incident as set out in paragraph 6 above.

17. On 2 April 2013, a forensic medical expert determined that the applicant had sustained minor bodily injuries with short-term consequences for her health, defined in the relevant regulations as health problems lasting between six and twenty-one days. The expert concluded that the applicant’s injuries could have been caused either by a slap (the defendant’s version) or by a punch (the applicant’s version).

18. On 9 April 2013, the head of the district police informed the investigator that, at his request, police detectives had canvassed V.S.’s neighbours in an effort to identify possible witnesses to the incident. However, nothing relevant had been discovered.

19. On 25 April 2013, the applicant’s husband, who was not a Jehovah’s Witness, was questioned. He stated that the applicant had not told him about the incident with V.S. either on the same day (7 March) or the following day, and that he had learned of it from her only on 9 March at the hospital. According to the applicant’s account, V.S. had come out of his house to meet the applicant and her fellow believer, N.S., and, as soon as he saw printed material bearing an image of Jesus Christ and the Bible in their hands, he began shouting and cursing and struck the applicant.

20. On 14 May 2013, the investigator formally notified V.S. that he was suspected of committing an offence under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code. When questioned that day, V.S. stated that he could not remember whether the women had been holding anything or what they had been discussing; he could, however, recall that they had invited him somewhere. Despite his requests, the women had refused to leave, so he had slapped one of them. V.S. denied that his conduct involved any element of religious intolerance.

21. On the same day, the investigator arranged a confrontation between the applicant and V.S. The applicant gave the account set out in paragraph 6 above. V.S. largely confirmed it, but stated that he had struck the applicant not out of a desire to offend her religious convictions, but because of the “sudden emergence of hostility” (із раптово виниклих неприязних відносин). V.S.
He repeated that formula when the applicant asked why he had hit her (see paragraph 41 below for an explanation of its meaning).

22. On 15 May 2013 the applicant requested that the investigator reclassify the offence with which V.S. had been charged from intentional infliction of minor injuries under Article 125 to discriminatory acts, an offence under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 46 below). She alleged that V.S. had known she was a Jehovah’s Witness and had hit her for that reason.

23. On 16 May 2013 the investigator questioned the applicant and N.S. again. They repeated their previous accounts.

24. On 17 May 2013 the investigator rejected the applicant’s reclassification request, stating that it had been established that V.S. had reacted to the “sudden emergence of hostility”. It had not been shown that he had acted with the intention of inciting religious hatred.

25. On 20 May 2013 V.S. was questioned once more. He stated that he had slapped the applicant owing to the “sudden emergence of hostility”, because she and N.S. had distracted him from his housework. They had repeatedly invited him to a meeting, indicating that many women would be there. The applicant had then humiliated him regarding his “man’s health” (Корнілова Т.В. тоді навіть образила мене з приводу мого чоловічого здоров’я), which was why he had struck her. He explained that he had not previously mentioned that aspect of the incident because he had been too embarrassed. He had not intended to create religious hostility or offend the applicant’s religious beliefs. V.S. maintained that he respected all religions. He had not known that the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness, since there had been no indication that she belonged to that group. He had indeed used obscenities, but those words had not been directed at the applicant or her companion. He might have used the word “shtundas”, but it had carried no religious connotations. V.S. stated that he sometimes used that word when angry with women. Lastly, V.S. denied threatening to set his dog on the women. He stated that he regretted committing the offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code with which he had been charged.

26. In the criminal proceedings, the applicant brought a civil claim for damages against V.S.

27. On 20 May 2013 the investigation was completed and the applicant reviewed the case file. She made no comments.

28. During the trial, the defendant pleaded guilty as charged. He testified that the applicant and N.S. had invited him to some celebration (на якусь гулянку), though he could not recall what kind, where there would be many women. He had declined. The applicant had told him that he was probably not interested because he was “not capable of anything with women” (що він з жінками не способен). He had then swung at her and, as she had been standing nearby, had ended up slapping her.

29.
The applicant, represented by a lawyer, maintained that she had been ill-treated on account of her religion. She described the events as set out in paragraph 6 above, except that she had not herself heard V.S. threaten to set his dog on her but had learned of the threat from N.S.’s account of the events. When asked why she had waited two days before seeking medical attention, she explained that she had not known how to tell her husband about the incident.

30. The other witnesses who had provided statements during the pre-trial investigation were also examined at trial.

31. On the final day of the trial, 15 July 2013, the applicant submitted a formal application to the trial court requesting that the offence be reclassified as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code, or as hooliganism under Article 296 (see paragraph 47 below). She relied on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention and, citing the Court’s judgment in Milanović v. Serbia (no. 44614/07, § 96, 14 December 2010), stressed that the State had a duty to take all reasonable steps to uncover any religious motive behind violent acts. She argued that it was unlikely that the defendant had been motivated by “personal hostility”, since he had not known her, had acted violently without provocation, had cursed at her, thereby showing his contempt for social rules, and had used the word “shtunda”.

32. On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court found V.S. guilty of intentionally inflicting a minor physical injury under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code and fined him the equivalent of 78 euros (EUR). The court held that he had inflicted minor physical injuries on the applicant “due to the sudden emergence of hostility” (на ґрунті раптово виниклих неприязних відносин); no aggravating circumstances were established. In reaching its judgment, the court relied on the statements of V.S., N.S. and the applicant, together with medical and other documentary evidence.

33. The court observed that V.S. had already paid the amount claimed for pecuniary damage, notably the costs of the applicant’s hospital treatment. Regarding the claim for non-pecuniary damage, the court took into consideration the defendant’s monthly income of 1,200 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) and awarded the applicant UAH 3,000 (equivalent to approximately EUR 278) of the UAH 5,000 claimed.

34. The applicant appealed, contending that the investigating authorities and the trial court had failed to examine the religious hatred underlying the defendant’s criminal conduct and that her freedom of religion had not been protected. She maintained that the case should have been classified under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code. She further argued that the offence had been committed on grounds of religious enmity, constituting an aggravating circumstance under Article 67 of the Criminal Code.

35.
The prosecutor responded that the defendant had been properly charged and convicted of an offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code, rather than of discriminatory acts motivated by religious prejudice. The prosecutor noted that the investigation had been unable to establish a religious motive for the defendant’s actions, referring in that regard to the defendant’s account of the events (see paragraph 25 above).

36. The defendant also appealed, submitting that the award for non-pecuniary damage was excessive.

37. On 26 September 2013 the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal, following a hearing attended by the applicant and the defendant, upheld the judgment of 16 July 2013.

38. At the end of the hearing, the Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s allegation that the crime had been committed because of her religion, observing that no such motive had been established during the investigation or the court proceedings. The offence had been correctly classified, and the applicant had failed to identify any evidence supporting its reclassification as hooliganism or discriminatory acts, as she had requested, other than her initial statement to the police that she had been attacked for no reason (see paragraph 10 above). She had not requested that the Court of Appeal re-examine the evidence relating to the offence.

39. The applicant appealed on points of law, reiterating her argument that the issue of religious intolerance had not been properly examined.

40. On 8 January 2014 the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters upheld the lower courts’ decisions, finding them lawful and well-founded. In light of the facts established by the courts, the legal classification of the defendant’s actions had been correct.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Criminal law

Terminology

41. In the Ukrainian legal context, the expression “sudden emergence of hostility” refers to a motive arising from personal conflict or animosity. It is intended to distinguish offences resulting from such personal conflict or animosity from offences driven by other motives, such as financial gain or hooliganism, which may alter the legal classification of an offence or constitute an aggravating circumstance. For example, if an assault causing a minor injury was motivated by such personal hostility, it may be classified under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. However, if the same assault was motivated by hooliganism, it may be classified as hooliganism, an offence against public order under Article 296 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 47 below).

42. The elements of the offence of hooliganism, particularly the motives underlying an act of hooliganism, are set out in paragraph 47 below.

Criminal Code 2001

43.
Article 67 of the Code lists, among the various circumstances to be considered as aggravating factors in sentencing, the commission of an offence on grounds of racial, national or religious enmity or hostility.

44. The part of the Criminal Code devoted to specific offences classifies them by chapter according to the societal value against which a given offence is considered to be directed.

45. Article 125 of the Code, found in the chapter entitled “Offences against another person’s life and health”, criminalises the “intentional infliction of a minor physical injury” with short-term health consequences. The relevant regulations define “short-term health consequences” as incapacity for work lasting between six and twenty-one days. Article 125 makes this offence punishable by one of the following: (i) a fine of between the equivalent of EUR 58 and EUR 158; (ii) community work for a period of between 150 and 240 hours; (iii) the withholding of ten to twenty percent of wages for up to one year; (iv) short-term detention for up to six months; or (v) placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to two years.

46. Article 161 of the Code, which appears in the chapter entitled “Offences against electoral, labour and other human and civil rights and freedoms”, criminalises the “violation of the equality of citizens on grounds of race, ethnicity or religious beliefs”. At the relevant time, it was punishable by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 790 or by placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years and, where the same acts were accompanied by violence, deception or threats or committed by a person exercising official authority, by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 1,580 or by imprisonment for a period of between two and five years.

47. Article 296, located in the chapter entitled “Offences against public order and morals”, criminalises “hooliganism” (хуліганство – also sometimes translated as “disorderly acts”), defined as “a serious breach of public order motivated by flagrant disrespect for society, combined with particular effrontery or exceptional cynicism”. At the relevant time, the offence was punishable by a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 1,580, short-term detention for up to six months, or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years. The same acts, when committed by a group, were punishable by placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years or imprisonment for up to four years. Where combined with the use of an instrument specifically adapted or constructed beforehand to inflict bodily harm, hooliganism was punishable by imprisonment for between three and seven years.

A commentary on the Criminal Code, summarising the relevant case-law and established academic opinion, explains that the central element of the offence of hooliganism is that it must be motivated by “flagrant disrespect for society”.
This is defined as a desire to disregard established social rules of conduct, to assert oneself at the expense of others, and to place oneself in opposition to other people, society, and the State.[2]

Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

48. Article 56 of the Code grants a range of rights to an aggrieved party (victim) in criminal proceedings, most notably the right:

(i) to have a complaint concerning the crime committed promptly registered;

(ii) to submit evidence supporting such a complaint and any other relevant evidence in the proceedings;

(iii) to be informed of one’s rights as an aggrieved party;

(iv) to be informed of the nature of the charges or suspicion against the defendant, the imposition or lifting of restrictions on the defendant, and the completion of the investigation;

(v) to lodge requests and applications and challenge judges and other officials responsible for the case;

(vi) where warranted, to receive police protection;

(vii) to make statements and testify in a language the victim understands, or to refuse to do so, and to use the services of an interpreter;

(viii) to challenge decisions made by the investigator, prosecutor, and court;

(ix) to be represented;

(x) to claim and recover damages caused by the crime;

(xi) to examine the case-file material concerning the crime committed against him or her upon completion or discontinuation of the investigation and to obtain copies of that material;

(xii) to participate in investigative actions, question the participants, make requests and objections regarding the procedure followed during the action, examine records of such actions, and propose corrections to them;

(xiii) to use recording devices during investigative actions in which the aggrieved party participates, unless the authority responsible for the proceedings prohibits such use to protect the confidentiality of certain information;

(xiv) to receive advance notice of the time of court hearings, attend them, and participate in the examination of evidence;

(xv) to continue pursuing the prosecution in place of the prosecutor if the prosecutor decides to withdraw the charges;

(xvi) to be heard on sentencing matters;

(xvii) to examine the trial records and audio recordings; and

(xviii) to appeal against court decisions.

CASE OF KORNILOVA v. UKRAINE
