JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

12 November 2020

This judgment is final, although it may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Kornilova v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee consisting of:

Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lado Chanturia, judges,

and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application (no. 47283/14) against Ukraine submitted to the Court on 27 June 2014 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Tetyana Vasylivna Kornilova, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the observations filed by the parties;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the application being considered by a Committee;

Having deliberated in private on 13 October 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant was struck by a man whom she had sought to invite to a meeting of Jehovah’s Witnesses. The man was ultimately found guilty of causing a minor injury, fined and ordered to pay compensation. The applicant alleged that the authorities had failed to give adequate consideration to the purported religiously prejudiced motive for the attack. She relied on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1973, the applicant resides in Nosivka. She was represented by Mr K. Chernychenko, Mr R. Cook and Mr A. Carbonneau, lawyers practising in Lviv, London and Paris respectively.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. On the basis of the parties’ submissions, the relevant facts may be summarised as follows.

5. On 7 March 2013, the applicant, who is a Jehovah’s Witness, and Ms N.S., a fellow member of her faith, went from door to door in Nosivka distributing printed invitations to a religious service. The front of each invitation displayed an image of Jesus Christ together with the prominently printed words “One Died for All”. The reverse contained text which stated, in smaller lettering, that the invitation concerned a meeting of Jehovah’s Witnesses.

6. At approximately 1 p.m., the applicant and N.S. approached the home of V.S., a fifty-year-old man whom they did not know. He met them at the property’s front gate. The applicant stated that, upon seeing the invitations and the Bible carried by the women, V.S. immediately punched her in the head. He then swore at both women, using obscene language and referring to them as “shtundas” (штунди). According to the applicant, she and N.S. left after V.S. threatened to release his dog.

7. In Ukraine, “shtunda” or “shtundist” is a colloquial label for evangelical Protestants belonging to various denominations.
The word originates from “shtundism”, a term applied to evangelical Protestant groups active in Ukraine during the nineteenth century whose activities centred on evangelisation through disseminating knowledge of the Bible.[1]

8. On 9 March 2013, following complaints of dizziness and nausea, the applicant was admitted to the neurology department of Nosivka District Central Hospital. She was diagnosed with concussion, and a facial bruise was also recorded. She remained in hospital until 19 March 2013 and was cleared to resume work the next day.

9. That same day, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Nosivka District Police Department. The police initiated a criminal investigation and informed her accordingly, stating that the alleged offence had provisionally been classified under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code as the intentional infliction of minor injuries (see paragraph 45 below).

10. When interviewed by the police later that day, the applicant explained that she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that, on 7 March, she and N.S., a fellow believer, had been handing out invitations to a religious service. At one house, a man aged about fifty had emerged, sworn at them and called them “shtundas”. According to the applicant, he had then struck her on the head for no reason (безпричинно).

11. V.S. was also questioned as a witness that day, without a lawyer present. He said that two women whom he had never met before had entered his property and offered him Jehovah’s Witnesses’ literature. After refusing the literature, he had told them to leave and not to return to his property. They had nevertheless declined to go and had “continued to try to recruit him into their fraternity” (продовжували агітувати у своє братство). V.S. had then lost his temper and slapped one of the women across the face. He added that, although he might have used obscene language, it had not been directed at the women.

12. During questioning on 12 March 2013, N.S. stated that V.S. had struck the applicant immediately upon seeing her, before anyone had spoken. She could not tell whether the blow had been a slap or a punch. She did, however, recall that V.S. had sworn continuously and had referred to both her and the applicant as “shtundas”.

13. On 18 March 2013, responding to an enquiry from the police investigator responsible for the case, the local hospital reported that V.S. was not receiving medical supervision for any psychiatric condition or addiction. The investigator also sought background information from the local council, which indicated that no complaints had been made against V.S. Finally, the investigator confirmed that V.S. had no criminal record.

14. On 25 March 2013, the applicant was formally granted the status of an aggrieved party (victim) in the proceedings and was informed of the procedural rights attaching to that status under the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 48 below).

15.
That same day, the applicant was interviewed and provided a detailed account of the events broadly corresponding to the version summarised in paragraph 6 above. Referring specifically to Articles 3 and 9 of the Convention, she described at length the humiliation and trauma she had experienced and explained how the incident had disrupted her religious practice.

16. On 1 and 12 April 2013, the police interviewed a council member from the congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses to which the applicant belonged, as well as the applicant’s daughter, who was also a Jehovah’s Witness, and two other members of the community. Drawing on their conversations with the applicant, those witnesses reiterated her account of the incident as presented in paragraph 6 above.

17. A forensic medical expert concluded on 2 April 2013 that the applicant had sustained minor bodily injuries resulting in short-term effects on her health. Under the applicable regulations, such effects were defined as health problems lasting between six and twenty-one days. The expert found that the injuries could have been caused either by a slap, as maintained by the defendant, or by a punch, as alleged by the applicant.

18. On 9 April 2013, the head of the district police advised the investigator that police detectives, acting at the investigator’s request, had questioned V.S.’s neighbours in an effort to locate potential witnesses to the incident. Their inquiries had produced no relevant information.

19. The applicant’s husband, who was not a Jehovah’s Witness, was interviewed on 25 April 2013. He said that the applicant had not mentioned the incident involving V.S. either on 7 March, the day it occurred, or on the following day. He had learned of it only when she told him at the hospital on 9 March. According to the version she gave him, V.S. had left his house to approach the applicant and N.S., a fellow believer. Upon seeing printed material bearing images of Jesus Christ and the Bible in their hands, he had immediately begun shouting and swearing before striking the applicant.

20. On 14 May 2013, the investigator formally informed V.S. that he was suspected of an offence under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code. During questioning that day, V.S. stated that he could not recall whether the women had been carrying anything or what they had been discussing, although he did remember that they had invited him somewhere. He further stated that they had refused to leave despite his requests, prompting him to slap one of them. V.S. denied that religious intolerance had played any part in his actions.

21. Later that day, the investigator arranged a confrontation between the applicant and V.S. The applicant repeated the account summarised in paragraph 6 above. While V.S. confirmed that account in large part, he maintained that he had struck her not to insult her religious beliefs, but because of the “sudden emergence of hostility” (із раптово виниклих неприязних відносин). V.S.
When the applicant asked why he had struck her, he repeated the same formula (its meaning is explained in paragraph 41 below).

22. On 15 May 2013, the applicant requested that the investigator reclassify the charge against V.S. from intentional infliction of minor injuries under Article 125 of the Criminal Code to discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 (see paragraph 46 below). She maintained that V.S. had known she was a Jehovah’s Witness and had assaulted her for that reason.

23. The investigator questioned the applicant and N.S. again on 16 May 2013. Both repeated their earlier accounts.

24. On 17 May 2013, the investigator rejected the reclassification request. The decision stated that V.S. had acted in response to the “sudden emergence of hostility” and that there was no evidence that he had intended to incite religious hatred.

25. During further questioning on 20 May 2013, V.S. said that he had slapped the applicant because of the “sudden emergence of hostility”, explaining that she and N.S. had interrupted his housework. According to him, they had persistently invited him to a meeting, mentioning that many women would be present. He alleged that the applicant had then insulted him about his “man’s health” (Корнілова Т.В. тоді навіть образила мене з приводу мого чоловічого здоров’я), prompting him to strike her. He said that embarrassment had prevented him from disclosing this aspect of the incident earlier. He denied intending either to create religious hostility or to offend the applicant’s religious beliefs and asserted that he respected all religions. V.S. further claimed that he had not known the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness because nothing had indicated her affiliation with that group. Although he acknowledged using obscenities, he maintained that they had not been directed at the applicant or her companion. He conceded that he might have used the word “shtundas”, but denied that it carried any religious meaning, explaining that he sometimes used it when angry with women. Lastly, he denied threatening to set his dog on them and expressed regret for committing the offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code with which he had been charged.

26. In the course of the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim for damages against V.S.

27. The investigation ended on 20 May 2013, after which the applicant reviewed the case file and made no comments.

28. At trial, the defendant pleaded guilty to the charge. He testified that the applicant and N.S. had invited him to some kind of celebration (на якусь гулянку), though he could not recall its nature, telling him that many women would be there. After he declined, the applicant allegedly remarked that he was probably uninterested because he was “not capable of anything with women” (що він з жінками не способен). He then swung at her and, as she was standing nearby, ended up slapping her.

29.
Represented by counsel, the applicant maintained that she had been subjected to ill-treatment because of her religion. Her account corresponded to the events described in paragraph 6 above, except that she had not personally heard V.S. threaten to set his dog on her; rather, she had learned of that threat from N.S.’s description of the incident. Asked why she had waited two days before seeking medical care, she said that she had not known how to explain the incident to her husband.

30. The remaining witnesses who had provided statements during the pre-trial investigation were likewise questioned at trial.

31. On 15 July 2013, the final day of the proceedings, the applicant formally requested that the trial court reclassify the offence either as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code or as hooliganism under Article 296 (see paragraph 47 below). Relying on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention and referring to the Court’s judgment in Milanović v. Serbia (no. 44614/07, § 96, 14 December 2010), she submitted that the State was required to take every reasonable measure to uncover any religious motive underlying acts of violence. In her view, “personal hostility” was an implausible explanation because the defendant did not know her, had acted violently without provocation, had sworn at her—thereby showing contempt for social norms—and had used the term “shtunda”.

32. On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code of intentionally causing a minor physical injury and imposed a fine equivalent to 78 euros (EUR). It concluded that he had caused the applicant minor physical injuries “due to the sudden emergence of hostility” (на ґрунті раптово виниклих неприязних відносин) and found no aggravating circumstances. Its decision was based on the testimony of V.S., N.S. and the applicant, together with medical records and other documentary material.

33. The court observed that V.S. had already paid the sum sought for pecuniary damage, particularly the applicant’s hospital-treatment expenses. In determining compensation for non-pecuniary damage, it considered the defendant’s monthly income of 1,200 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) and awarded the applicant UAH 3,000—approximately EUR 278—out of the UAH 5,000 claimed.

34. On appeal, the applicant contended that neither the investigating authorities nor the trial court had addressed the religious hatred underlying the defendant’s criminal actions, and that they had failed to safeguard her freedom of religion. She maintained that the offence should have been legally classified under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code. She further argued that religious enmity had motivated the crime and therefore constituted an aggravating circumstance under Article 67 of the Criminal Code.

35.
The prosecutor submitted in response that the defendant had properly been charged with and convicted of an offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code, rather than of discriminatory conduct motivated by religious prejudice. Referring to the defendant’s version of events (see paragraph 25 above), the prosecutor emphasised that the investigation had found no evidence of a religious motive behind her actions.

36. The defendant lodged an appeal as well, contending that the amount awarded for non-pecuniary damage was excessive.

37. On 26 September 2013, following a hearing attended by both the applicant and the defendant, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of 16 July 2013.

38. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s claim that the offence had been religiously motivated, observing that neither the investigation nor the judicial proceedings had established such a motive. It held that the offence had been correctly classified and that, apart from her initial statement to the police that she had been attacked without any reason (see paragraph 10 above), the applicant had identified no evidence supporting her requested reclassification of the conduct as either hooliganism or discriminatory acts. She had not asked the Court of Appeal to reassess the evidence relating to the offence.

39. The applicant appealed on points of law, reiterating that the question of religious intolerance had not been adequately examined.

40. On 8 January 2014, the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters affirmed the lower courts’ decisions, holding that they were lawful and properly reasoned. In view of the facts established by those courts, it found that the defendant’s conduct had been correctly classified in law.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Criminal law

Terminology

41. In Ukrainian law, the expression “sudden emergence of hostility” denotes a motive stemming from personal conflict or animosity. The term serves to differentiate offences arising from such personal hostility or conflict from those prompted by other motives, including financial gain or hooliganism, which may alter the legal classification of the conduct or amount to an aggravating circumstance. Thus, an assault causing a minor injury may be classified under Article 125 of the Criminal Code where it was motivated by personal hostility. If the same assault was instead driven by hooligan motives, it may be classified as hooliganism—an offence against public order under Article 296 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 47 below).

42. Paragraph 47 below sets out the constituent elements of hooliganism, including the motives underlying an act of hooliganism.

Criminal Code 2001

43.
Article 67 of the Code identifies, among the circumstances regarded as aggravating for sentencing purposes, the commission of an offence motivated by racial, national or religious enmity or hostility.44.

The section of the Criminal Code dealing with specific offences is divided into chapters according to the societal value against which each offence is deemed to be directed.45.

Article 125 appears in the chapter entitled “Offences against another person’s life and health” and criminalises the “intentional infliction of a minor physical injury” resulting in short-term health consequences. Under the applicable regulations, “short-term health implications” means incapacity for work lasting between six and twenty-one days. The offence is punishable by one of the following penalties: (i) a fine equivalent to between EUR 58 and EUR 158; (ii) 150 to 240 hours of community work; (iii) the withholding of ten to twenty percent of wages for a period of up to one year; (iv) short-term detention for no more than six months; or (v) placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to two years.46.

Article 161, contained in the chapter headed “Offences against electoral, labour and other human and civil rights and freedoms”, makes it a criminal offence to “violate the equality of citizens on grounds of race, ethnicity or religious beliefs”. At the material time, this offence carried either a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 790 or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for a maximum of five years. Where the same conduct involved violence, deception or threats, or was perpetrated by a person acting in an official capacity, the available penalties were a fine of up to the equivalent of EUR 1,580 or imprisonment for two to five years.47.

Article 296 falls within the chapter entitled “Offences against public order and morals” and criminalises “hooliganism” (хуліганство, also sometimes rendered as “disorderly acts”). It defines the offence as “a serious breach of public order motivated by flagrant disrespect for society, combined with particular effrontery or exceptional cynicism”. At the relevant time, hooliganism was punishable by a fine not exceeding the equivalent of EUR 1,580, short-term detention for up to six months, or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for a maximum of five years. When committed by a group, the same conduct attracted placement in such an institution for up to five years or imprisonment for up to four years. Where hooliganism involved the use of an instrument specially adapted or prepared in advance to cause bodily injury, the prescribed punishment was imprisonment for a term of three to seven years.

A commentary on the Criminal Code, reflecting the relevant case-law and settled academic understanding, states that an essential element of hooliganism is the requirement that the conduct be motivated by “flagrant disrespect for society”.
It is understood as the intention to flout accepted social norms of behaviour, assert oneself to the detriment of others, and set oneself against other people, society, and the State.[2]

Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

48. Article 56 of the Code grants an aggrieved party (victim) numerous rights in criminal proceedings. In particular, the victim is entitled:

(i) to have a complaint concerning the offence promptly recorded;

(ii) to provide evidence supporting the complaint, as well as any other evidence relevant to the proceedings;

(iii) to be advised of the rights attaching to the status of an aggrieved party;

(iv) to receive information about the nature of the charges or suspicions against the defendant, the imposition or lifting of restrictions on the defendant, and the conclusion of the investigation;

(v) to file requests and applications and seek the disqualification of judges or other officials responsible for the case;

(vi) to receive police protection where the circumstances warrant it;

(vii) to give statements and testimony in a language the victim understands, or to decline to do so, and to obtain the assistance of an interpreter;

(viii) to contest decisions made by the investigator, the prosecutor, or the court;

(ix) to have legal representation;

(x) to seek and obtain compensation for damage resulting from the offence;

(xi) upon completion or discontinuation of the investigation, to inspect the case-file materials relating to the offence committed against the victim and obtain copies of those materials;

(xii) to take part in investigative measures, question participants, submit requests and objections regarding the procedure followed, review the records of those measures, and propose amendments to them;

(xiii) to use recording equipment during investigative measures in which the victim participates, unless the authority conducting the proceedings prohibits its use to preserve the confidentiality of particular information;

(xiv) to receive advance notice of court hearings, attend those hearings, and participate in the examination of evidence;

(xv) to carry on the prosecution in place of the prosecutor if the prosecutor withdraws the charges;

(xvi) to present views on sentencing;

(xvii) to inspect the records and audio recordings of the trial; and

(xviii) to appeal judicial decisions.
heavy:
FIFTH SECTION

KORNILOVA v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 47283/14)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

12 November 2020

This judgment is final, although it may undergo editorial revision.

In Kornilova v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee consisting of:

Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, President,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lado Chanturia, judges,

and Anne-Marie Dougin, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having considered:

the application against Ukraine submitted to the Court on 27 June 2014 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Tetyana Vasylivna Kornilova, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the observations filed by the parties;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the application being considered by a Committee;

Having deliberated in private on 13 October 2020,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. A man struck the applicant while she was trying to invite him to a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. He was ultimately convicted of causing a minor injury, fined and directed to pay compensation. The applicant alleged that the authorities had failed to give adequate consideration to the purported religiously prejudiced motive for the assault. She invoked Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1973, the applicant resides in Nosivka. She was represented by Mr K. Chernychenko, Mr R. Cook and Mr A. Carbonneau, lawyers practising in Lviv, London and Paris, respectively.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The parties’ accounts of the relevant circumstances may be summarised as set out below.

5. On 7 March 2013, the applicant, who is a Jehovah’s Witness, and Ms N.S., a fellow believer, went from door to door in Nosivka distributing printed invitations to a religious service. The invitations displayed on the front an image of Jesus Christ together with the large-print phrase “One Died for All”. The reverse contained text stating, in smaller print, that the invitation concerned a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting.

6. At approximately 1 p.m., the applicant and N.S. approached the home of V.S., a fifty-year-old man whom they did not know. He encountered them at the property’s front gate. In the applicant’s account, V.S. saw the invitations and the Bible the women were holding, immediately punched her in the head, and began directing curses and obscenities at both women, also referring to them as “shtundas” (штунди). The applicant further stated that she and N.S. left after V.S. threatened to release his dog.

7. In Ukraine, “shtunda” or “shtundist” is an informal expression referring to evangelical Protestants belonging to various denominations.
The word originates from “shtundism”, a term applied to evangelical Protestant groups operating in Ukraine during the 19th century whose activities centred on evangelisation through the dissemination of biblical knowledge.[1]

8. Following complaints of nausea and dizziness, the applicant was admitted to the neurology department of Nosivka District Central Hospital on 9 March 2013. She was diagnosed with concussion, and a facial bruise was also recorded. She remained an inpatient until 19 March 2013 and was cleared to resume work the next day.

9. On 9 March 2013, the applicant also lodged a complaint with the Nosivka District Police Department. The police initiated a criminal investigation and informed her accordingly. They further indicated that the alleged offence had been provisionally classified under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code as the intentional infliction of minor injuries (see paragraph 45 below).

10. The police interviewed the applicant that same day. She explained that she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that, on 7 March, she and another believer, N.S., had been handing out invitations to a religious service. At one house, a man aged fifty had emerged, sworn at them and referred to them as “shtundas”. According to the applicant, he then struck her on the head without any reason (безпричинно).

11. Also that day, V.S. was questioned as a witness without a lawyer present. He said that two women whom he had not previously known had entered his property and offered him Jehovah’s Witnesses’ literature. He had declined it and ordered them to leave and never return to his property. The women had refused to go and had “continued attempting to recruit him into their fraternity” (продовжували агітувати у своє братство). V.S. had then become angry and slapped one of them across the face. He added that, even if he had used obscene language, it had not been directed at the women.

12. When questioned on 12 March 2013, N.S. stated that V.S. had struck the applicant immediately upon seeing her, before anyone had spoken. Although N.S. could not tell whether the blow had been a slap or a punch, she recalled that V.S. had sworn continuously and had called both her and the applicant “shtundas”.

13. On 18 March 2013, replying to a request from the police investigator responsible for the case, the local hospital reported that V.S. was not medically supervised for any psychiatric condition or addiction. The investigator additionally sought background information about V.S. from the local council, which stated that no complaints had been made against him. The investigator also confirmed that V.S. had no criminal record.

14. On 25 March 2013, the applicant was formally granted the status of aggrieved party (victim) in the proceedings and was informed of the procedural rights attached to that status under the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 48 below).

15.
On the same day, the applicant was interviewed and provided a detailed description of the events that broadly corresponded to the account given in paragraph 6 above. Referring specifically to Articles 3 and 9 of the Convention, she explained at length that the incident had left her feeling humiliated and traumatised and had disrupted her religious practice.

16. On 1 and 12 April 2013, the police interviewed a member of the council of elders of the Jehovah’s Witnesses community to which the applicant belonged, her daughter, who was also a Jehovah’s Witness, and two other community members. Relying on their conversations with the applicant, they reiterated her version of the incident as described in paragraph 6 above.

17. On 2 April 2013, a forensic medical expert found that the applicant had sustained minor bodily injuries with short-term effects on her health, which the applicable regulations defined as health problems lasting between six and twenty-one days. The expert determined that those injuries could have resulted either from a slap, as claimed by the defendant, or from a punch, as alleged by the applicant.

18. On 9 April 2013, the head of the district police advised the investigator that, in response to the investigator’s request, police detectives had questioned V.S.’s neighbours in an effort to locate potential witnesses to the incident. No relevant information had been discovered.

19. The applicant’s husband, who was not a Jehovah’s Witness, was interviewed on 25 April 2013. He said that the applicant had not mentioned the incident involving V.S. either on 7 March, the day it occurred, or on the following day. He had first heard about it from her at the hospital on 9 March. According to what the applicant told him, V.S. had left his house to approach her and N.S., a fellow believer. Upon noticing that they were carrying printed materials depicting Jesus Christ and the Bible, he had begun shouting and swearing and had struck the applicant.

20. On 14 May 2013, the investigator formally informed V.S. that he was suspected of committing an offence under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code. During questioning that day, V.S. stated that he could not recall whether the women had been carrying anything or what they had been discussing, although he remembered that they had invited him somewhere. He said that they had refused to leave despite his requests, after which he had slapped one of them. V.S. denied that his actions had involved any element of religious intolerance.

21. Later that same day, the investigator arranged a confrontation between V.S. and the applicant. She repeated the version of events described in paragraph 6 above. V.S. confirmed most of her account but maintained that he had struck her not because he wished to insult her religious beliefs, but because of the “sudden emergence of hostility” (із раптово виниклих неприязних відносин).
When the applicant asked why he had struck her, he repeated the same formula (for its meaning, see paragraph 41 below).

22. On 15 May 2013, the applicant requested that the investigator change the legal classification of the charge against V.S. from intentional infliction of minor injuries under Article 125 of the Criminal Code to discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of that Code (see paragraph 46 below). She maintained that V.S. had known she was a Jehovah’s Witness and had assaulted her for that reason.

23. On 16 May 2013, the investigator questioned the applicant and N.S. once more. Both repeated their earlier versions of events.

24. On 17 May 2013, the investigator rejected the applicant’s request for reclassification. The decision stated that V.S. had been found to have acted in response to the “sudden emergence of hostility”, while there was no evidence that he had intended to incite religious hatred.

25. On 20 May 2013, V.S. underwent further questioning. He said that he had slapped the applicant because of the “sudden emergence of hostility”, explaining that she and N.S. had interrupted his household chores. According to him, they had persistently invited him to a meeting and had said that many women would be present. He alleged that the applicant had then insulted him about his “man’s health” (Корнілова Т.В. тоді навіть образила мене з приводу мого чоловічого здоров’я), prompting him to strike her. He said that embarrassment had prevented him from mentioning that part of the incident earlier. He denied intending to cause religious hostility or insult the applicant’s religious beliefs and asserted that he respected every religion. V.S. also claimed that he had not known the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness because nothing had indicated her membership of that group. Although he acknowledged using obscene language, he maintained that it had not been directed at the applicant or her companion. He accepted that he might have used the word “shtundas”, but said that it carried no religious meaning and that he sometimes used it when angry with women. Lastly, he denied threatening to set his dog on the women. He expressed regret for committing the offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code with which he had been charged.

26. In the course of the criminal proceedings, the applicant brought a civil claim for damages against V.S.

27. The investigation ended on 20 May 2013, after which the applicant reviewed the case file and made no comments.

28. At trial, the defendant admitted his guilt on the charge. He testified that the applicant and N.S. had invited him to some kind of celebration (на якусь гулянку), although he could not recall what type, and had told him that many women would attend. He had declined the invitation. The applicant had then suggested that he was probably uninterested because he was “not capable of anything with women” (що він з жінками не способен). He had swung at her and, as she was standing nearby, ultimately slapped her.

29.
Represented by counsel, the applicant maintained that she had been subjected to ill-treatment because of her religion. Her account corresponded to the events described in paragraph 6 above, except that she had not personally heard V.S. threaten to set his dog on her; rather, she had learned of that threat from N.S.’s version of events. Asked why she had waited two days before obtaining medical care, she said that she had not known how to explain the incident to her husband.

30. At trial, the court also heard the other witnesses who had provided statements during the pre-trial investigation.

31. On 15 July 2013, the final day of the trial, the applicant formally requested that the trial court reclassify the offence either as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code or as hooliganism under Article 296 (see paragraph 47 below). Relying on Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention and referring to the Court’s judgment in Milanović v. Serbia (no. 44614/07, § 96, 14 December 2010), she submitted that the State was required to take every reasonable measure to uncover any religious motive underlying acts of violence. In her view, “personal hostility” was an implausible explanation for the defendant’s conduct because he had not known her, had acted violently despite the absence of any provocation, had sworn at her—thereby showing disregard for social norms—and had used the term “shtunda”.

32. On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. of intentionally causing a minor physical injury under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code and imposed a fine equivalent to 78 euros (EUR). It concluded that he had caused the applicant minor physical injuries “due to the sudden emergence of hostility” (на ґрунті раптово виниклих неприязних відносин), and found that no aggravating circumstances had been established. The judgment was based on the accounts given by V.S., N.S. and the applicant, together with medical records and other documentary material.

33. The court observed that V.S. had already paid the sum sought for pecuniary damage, in particular the expenses associated with the applicant’s hospital treatment. Regarding non-pecuniary damage, it considered the defendant’s monthly earnings of 1,200 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) and awarded the applicant UAH 3,000—approximately EUR 278—out of the UAH 5,000 requested.

34. In her appeal, the applicant contended that neither the investigative authorities nor the trial court had addressed the religious hatred underlying the defendant’s criminal actions, and that they had failed to safeguard her freedom of religion. She maintained that the offence should have been legally characterised under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code. She further argued that the crime had been motivated by religious enmity, constituting an aggravating circumstance under Article 67 of the Criminal Code.

35.
The prosecutor maintained that the defendant had been properly charged with and convicted of an offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code, rather than of discriminatory conduct motivated by religious prejudice. In support of that position, the prosecutor noted that the investigation had found no religious motive behind the defendant’s actions and referred to the defendant’s account of the incident (see paragraph 25 above).

36. The defendant lodged an appeal as well, contending that the amount awarded for non-pecuniary damage was excessive.

37. On 26 September 2013, following a hearing attended by both the applicant and the defendant, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment delivered on 16 July 2013.

38. At the end of the hearing, the Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s claim that the offence had been religiously motivated, observing that neither the investigation nor the judicial proceedings had established such a motive. It found that the offence had been correctly classified and that, apart from her initial statement to the police that she had been attacked without any reason (see paragraph 10 above), the applicant had identified no evidence capable of supporting her requested reclassification of the offence as either hooliganism or discriminatory acts. She had not requested that the Court of Appeal reassess the evidence relating to the offence.

39. The applicant appealed on points of law, reiterating that the question of religious intolerance had not been adequately examined.

40. On 8 January 2014, the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters affirmed the lower courts’ decisions, holding that they were lawful and sufficiently reasoned. In view of the facts established by those courts, the defendant’s conduct had been legally classified correctly.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Criminal law

Terminology

41. Within Ukrainian law, the expression “sudden emergence of hostility” denotes a motive stemming from personal conflict or animosity. Its purpose is to differentiate offences resulting from such conflict or animosity from those prompted by other motives, including financial gain or hooliganism, which may alter the legal classification of the offence or amount to an aggravating circumstance. Thus, an assault causing a minor injury and motivated by personal hostility may be classified under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. By contrast, where the same assault is motivated by hooliganism, it may be classified as hooliganism—an offence against public order—under Article 296 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 47 below).

42. Paragraph 47 below sets out the constituent elements of hooliganism, including the motives underlying an act of hooliganism.

Criminal Code 2001

43.
Among the circumstances identified in Article 67 of the Code as aggravating factors for sentencing purposes is the perpetration of an offence motivated by racial, national or religious enmity or hostility.44.

The section of the Criminal Code dealing with specific offences is divided into chapters according to the societal value against which each offence is regarded as being directed.45.

Within the chapter headed “Offences against another person’s life and health”, Article 125 prohibits the “intentional infliction of a minor physical injury” that has short-term consequences for health. Under the applicable regulations, “short-term health implications” means incapacity for work lasting from six to twenty-one days. The penalties available under Article 125 are: (i) a fine equivalent to between EUR 58 and EUR 158; (ii) between 150 and 240 hours of community work; (iii) deduction of ten to twenty percent of wages for a period not exceeding one year; (iv) short-term detention for no more than six months; or (v) placement in a semi-open correctional institution for a maximum of two years.46.

Article 161 appears in the chapter entitled “Offences against electoral, labour and other human and civil rights and freedoms” and establishes the offence of “violation of the equality of citizens on grounds of race, ethnicity or religious beliefs”. At the material time, the offence carried either a fine equivalent to no more than EUR 790 or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years. Where the same conduct involved violence, deception or threats, or was carried out by a person acting in an official capacity, it was punishable by a fine equivalent to a maximum of EUR 1,580 or by imprisonment for between two and five years.47.

Located in the chapter headed “Offences against public order and morals”, Article 296 criminalises “hooliganism” (хуліганство, also sometimes rendered as “disorderly acts”). It defines that offence as “a serious breach of public order motivated by flagrant disrespect for society, combined with particular effrontery or exceptional cynicism”. At the relevant time, the available sanctions were a fine equivalent to up to EUR 1,580, short-term detention for a maximum of six months, or placement in a semi-open correctional institution for no more than five years. If the same conduct was committed by a group, the penalty was placement in a semi-open correctional institution for up to five years or imprisonment for up to four years. Hooliganism involving the use of an instrument specially adapted or prepared in advance to cause bodily injury was punishable by imprisonment for a term of between three and seven years.

A commentary on the Criminal Code, reflecting the relevant judicial decisions and settled academic opinion, states that the defining component of hooliganism is the requirement that the conduct be driven by “flagrant disrespect for society”.
This refers to an intention to defy accepted social standards of conduct, assert oneself at other people’s expense, and position oneself against other individuals, society, and the State.[2]

Code of Criminal Procedure 2012

48. Article 56 of the Code grants an aggrieved party (victim) numerous rights in criminal proceedings. In particular, the victim has the right:

(i) to have a complaint concerning the offence promptly recorded;

(ii) to provide evidence supporting the complaint and any other evidence relevant to the proceedings;

(iii) to receive notification of his or her rights as an aggrieved party;

(iv) to be informed about the nature of the accusation or suspicion against the defendant, the introduction or lifting of restrictions imposed on the defendant, and the conclusion of the investigation;

(v) to file requests and applications and seek the recusal of judges or other officials responsible for the case;

(vi) when justified, to receive police protection;

(vii) to make statements and give testimony in a language understood by the victim, or to decline to do so, and to use an interpreter’s services;

(viii) to contest decisions made by the investigator, the prosecutor, or the court;

(ix) to have legal representation;

(x) to seek and obtain compensation for damage resulting from the offence;

(xi) upon completion or discontinuation of the investigation, to inspect the case-file materials relating to the offence committed against him or her and obtain copies of those materials;

(xii) to take part in investigative measures, question participants, raise requests and objections regarding the procedure followed during those measures, review the resulting records, and suggest corrections;

(xiii) to use recording equipment during investigative measures in which the aggrieved party participates, unless the authority conducting the proceedings prohibits its use to preserve the confidentiality of particular information;

(xiv) to receive advance notice of the date and time of court hearings, attend them, and participate in the consideration of evidence;

(xv) if the prosecutor withdraws the charges, to continue pursuing the prosecution in the prosecutor’s place;

(xvi) to present views on sentencing issues;

(xvii) to review the trial records and audio recordings; and

(xviii) to appeal court rulings.

original: FIFTH SECTIONCASE OF YUKHYMOVYCH v. UKRAINE(Application no. 11464/12) JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG17 December 2020FINAL 17/03/2021  This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of Yukhymovych v. Ukraine,The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Mārtiņš Mits, Ganna Yudkivska, Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström, Jovan Ilievski, Lado Chanturia, Ivana Jelić, judges, and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application (no. 11464/12) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Leontiy Ivanovych Yukhymovych (“the applicant”), on 6 January 2012;the decision to give notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”);the parties’ observations;Having deliberated in private on 24 November 2020,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:THE FACTS2. The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in Lviv.3. The applicant was initially represented by Mr A. Buryy, a lawyer practising in Lviv, and subsequently represented himself. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna from the Ministry of Justice.4. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.Background to the case and events of 4 March 19995. On 25 February 1999 B. complained to the Lviv Regional Department for Combatting Organised Crime of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (“the DCOC”) that unknown persons had threatened her and extorted the sum of 25,000 United States dollars (USD).6. According to the Government, an inquiry into B.’s allegations was conducted and it was established that the unknown persons were the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, and his friend Z., both alleged members of an organised criminal group which had been extorting money and property from residents of Mykolayiv with the use of weapons.7. On 1 March 1999 the DCOC approved an operation plan to arrest the alleged extortionists by the “Sokil” special police unit of the DCOC, which was composed of senior police detective Zar., detective M., and assistant detectives O. and G.8. On 2 March 1999 the above-mentioned police officers, who were wearing civilian clothes, commenced an operation to ambush the alleged extortionists in B.’s house. B.’s 22-year-old daughter and 16-year-old son were with B. at home.9. On 3 March 1999 criminal proceedings were instituted in respect of the financial extortion from B.10. According to the parties’ submissions, it appears that at around 2 p.m. on 4 March 1999 a private taxi driver Tz. drove the applicant’s son and Z. to B.’s house. The two men approached the house and the driver stayed in the car. B.’s daughter opened the door. Z. was the first to enter, and the applicant’s son followed him. Police officer M. yelled “Freeze, police!” and officers Zar., M. and G. arrested Z. The applicant’s son, who was at the entrance to the hallway at the time, disobeyed the order and started to flee. Officers M. and O. ran after him to the garden gate to arrest him. In the course of the operation, the applicant’s son was shot twice by O. He died from his injuries.Criminal investigation into the death of the applicant’s son11. Between 3.40 and 8.20 p.m. on 4 March 1999 an investigator from the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office, in the presence of two witnesses, F. and Mar., conducted an on-site inspection at the scene of the incident. Two partial video recordings of the inspection were made.12. On 15 March 1999 experts from the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations examined the body of the applicant’s son and drew up a report stating that his death had been caused by a gunshot wound to the chest. The injuries found on his left side turned out to be a perforating gunshot wound. The experts also discovered other injuries on his body, such as a bruise on his forehead and superficial wounds and subcutaneous haemorrhages on the occipital part of the head and the lower lip.13. On 24 March 1999 the internal inquiry conducted by the DCOC established that O. had used his service gun lawfully and in compliance with the requirements of the Police Act. The report noted that during the on-site inspection a “Valtro” gas gun had been found near the applicant’s son’s body.14. On 25 March 1999 the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office, after conducting a pre-investigation inquiry, refused to institute a criminal investigation into the death of the applicant’s son. The relevant decision referred to the results of the forensic examination of the body, witness statements and the results of the internal inquiry and stated that the police officers’ actions had disclosed no indication of an offence, since they had acted in an appropriate manner.15. On 31 March 1999 the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office set aside the decision of 25 March 1999 and opened criminal proceedings into alleged abuse of power by the police causing serious harm, reasoning that it had been impossible to establish the circumstances of the use of the weapon in the course of the pre-investigation inquiry and that an investigation was required.16. On 15 April and 23 September 1999 forensic fingerprint examinations found a fingerprint on the left side of the “Valtro” gun belonging to the same group as the left thumbprint of the applicant’s son. Three more of his fingerprints were found on the side of the gun’s magazine.17. On 16 April 1999 the prosecutor questioned the police officers who had participated in the operation.18. B. and her daughter testified that from 1996 the applicant’s son and Z. had been extorting money from their family by force. This had led B. to lodge a complaint with the police. On 2 March 1999 four police officers had organised an ambush at B.’s house. On 3 March 1999 they had seen the extortionists driving past in their car checking if there was anyone at home. At around 2 p.m. on 4 March 1999 they had heard knocking at the door and Z. calling for B.’s daughter to open the door. As she had been scared, B. had escaped into the bathroom and her daughter had opened the door. The latter further testified that Z. had grabbed her arm and tried to pull her out of the house, and that the applicant’s son had been standing behind him on the steps. She had managed to break away and run inside the house into one of the rooms. The women further stated that after the extortionists had entered the house, they had heard one of the police officers shouting “Freeze, police!” followed by the sounds of fighting and a gunshot. They had then heard another gunshot outside the house. When the police officers had returned to the house, they had told B. to calm down because they had “gunned down” one of the extortionists.19. Police officer M. testified that the ambush had been planned by an officer of the DCOC, K. He stated, inter alia, that K. had not informed them whether or not the alleged racketeers were armed. On 2 or 3 March 1999, while M. and his colleagues had been lying in wait at B.’s house, the latter had told them the names of the racketeers and that one of them had a gun. On 4 March 1999, while they had all been having lunch, someone had knocked on the door. B., who had had a recording device on her to record the extortion, had been too scared to open the door, and they had convinced her daughter to do it. M. stated that he and his colleagues had spontaneously spread out around the house since they had not had time to think, and M. had stayed in the kitchen. He further testified that on being noticed by Z., who had entered the house, he had jumped out and yelled “Freeze, police!” Z. had not complied, so he had hit him in the chest. Immediately after this he had heard a shot in the hallway. He had turned around and seen the back of someone escaping from the house. He had yelled “Don’t shoot!” and run after the person. At the gate, the absconder, who later turned out to be the applicant’s son, had tried to open it. At that time M., who had caught up with the applicant’s son and tried to arrest him, had kicked him in the back with his right foot. The applicant’s son had then started to turn towards M. and the latter had noticed a gun in his hand, pointed at him. At the same moment, M. had heard a shot and seen O. with his service gun in his hand. After the shot, the applicant’s son had fallen onto the concrete pavement of the yard and started to convulse, with the gun on his left side. Afterwards, police detective Zar. had left to call an ambulance and inform the police authorities of the incident. In order to save the physical evidence, as a crowd had been gathering at the scene, M. had taken the gun to B.’s house, put it in a plastic bag and left it on the coffee table in the living room.In further statements given on unspecified dates M. changed his testimony and stated that in the course of the operation he and O. had stayed in the kitchen in accordance with the agreed operation plan.20. Police officer O. testified that when Z. had entered the house he had been hiding in the kitchen with M. When the latter had yelled “Freeze, police!” he had jumped out into the hallway with his weapon ready to shoot and had tried to arrest the second man, who had taken out his gun and pointed it at him. O., after assessing the situation as one entitling a police officer to use firearms, had shot at the applicant’s son, who had ducked behind the door to try to avoid the bullet. After being wounded, the applicant’s son had run out into the yard. M. and O. had run after the applicant’s son to the gate to arrest him. M. had reached the applicant’s son first and kicked him in the back. At that point O. had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand pointed at M. and, to defend his colleague, he had run towards the applicant’s son and shot him in the back almost at point-blank range. After the applicant’s son had fallen down, he had pushed the gun away from him. He had wanted to turn the applicant’s son onto his back, but he had heard rattling noises from him and had decided to leave him in the same position.21. Police officer Zar. testified that after the second shot he had run out to the yard and had seen the applicant’s son lying face down on the ground. He did not remember seeing a gun near the body. After he had called the ambulance and returned to the house he had seen a big black gun in a plastic bag in the living room. Police officer G. provided a similar testimony.22. When questioned on 3 May 1999 Tz., the taxi driver, testified that he had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand both during his struggle with the police officers and later near his body.23. When questioned on 4 June 1999 Z., the alleged accomplice, testified that the applicant’s son had not had a weapon, since he had left his gun in his car before going to B.’s house. After the applicant’s son had been shot, the police officers had forced him to tell them about the gun and its whereabouts. Z. further stated that when he had been escorted out of the building, he had noticed a gun in a plastic bag on a coffee table, but that it had not been the applicant’s son’s gun.He later changed his testimony, stating that he did not know if the applicant’s son had had a gun during the shooting.24. According to results of forensic medical examinations dated 30 June and 6 October 1999, two gunshot wounds were inflicted on the applicant’s son: one to the back of his right shoulder fired from a certain distance, which was impossible to establish since the bullet had gone through an obstacle – the door – before entering his body, and another to the back fired at point-blank range or from a distance of no more than two centimetres. The death of the applicant’s son was caused by the first wound to the back of his right shoulder. The experts also stated that the applicant’s son could have carried out certain actions after receiving the first wound, that is, he could have run a distance of about sixteen metres, fought back and pointed a gun.25. On 20 August 1999 the case was transferred to the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office.26. On 19 and 21 October 1999 the witnesses to the on-site inspection were questioned. F. testified that he had not seen a gun at the scene of the incident, but that he could not rule out the possibility of one being there. Another witness to the on-site inspection, Mar., stated that he could not remember if he had seen a gun.27. On 28 December 1999 a forensic examination of metallic residues found that the jacket and trousers of the applicant’s son had traces of such residues, caused by contact with a steel object, possibly the “Valtro” gun allegedly found at the scene of the incident.28. On 28 January 2000 the investigator of the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office terminated the proceedings for lack of any evidence of a crime. His decision referred to the statements of Tz., B., B.’s daughter, police officers who had participated in the operation (see paragraphs 19-21 above) and law enforcement agents who had arrived at the scene of the incident. On 25 December 2000 the Regional Court of Lviv set aside the above-mentioned decision and ordered the proceedings to be reopened. The court noted, inter alia, that the evidence as to whether the applicant’s son had been in possession of a gun at the time of the shooting was controversial; in particular, on 21 April 2000 Tz. had made a statement virtually withdrawing his previous testimony and submitting that the applicant’s son had not had a weapon when he had been shot. On 27 December 2001 the proceedings were again terminated, but on 12 February 2002 they were reopened as the investigator had failed to establish all the circumstances of the case.32. The proceedings were again terminated on 19 August 2002. This decision was set aside on 9 December 2002 by the Uzhgorod Local Court of the Zakarpattya Region. The court reasoned that when terminating the proceedings the investigator had relied on the conclusion of the internal inquiry conducted by the DCOC (see paragraph 13 above), breaching the principle of the objective evaluation of evidence, the DCOC being an interested party. The court again pointed out the importance of establishing whether or not the applicant’s son had had a gun during the shooting, and listed a number of investigative actions which had to be taken, such as a repeated reconstruction of events with the participation of Tz.33. On 10 March 2004 the Zakarpattya Regional Court of Appeal set aside the decision to terminate the proceedings of 30 September 2003. The court noted that the investigative authority had failed to comply with instructions issued by higher prosecutors and to answer the applicant’s complaints. The court further noted that the investigator had failed to demonstrate the existence of any evidence which would unequivocally prove that O. had used his weapon against the applicant’s son in compliance with the law. The court also pointed out procedural shortcomings in the investigation, such as the failure of the police officers to secure the scene of the incident and the towing of the applicant’s son’s car without the investigator’s permission. In particular, it had to be checked whether police officers had access to the car as, according to Z., the applicant’s son had left his gun in it. The court further referred to the inconsistencies in the witness statements, in particular concerning F.’s statement that he had not seen a gun at the scene of the incident (see paragraph 26 above). Lastly, the court questioned the manner in which B.’s statement concerning the alleged racketeering had been dealt with and ordered the investigator to ascertain why the identities of the alleged racketeers had not been established and why they had not been questioned by the police once B. had given her statement.34. On 28 May 2004 the Prosecutor General’s Office transferred the case to the Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office.35. On 31 August 2004 a forensic examination of the video recordings of the on-site inspection was conducted, which found no signs that the examined parts of the video recording had been manually or electronically edited. Furthermore, video recordings on video cassettes from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office and the DCOC showed a gun on a table inside the house similar to the “Valtro” gun given for examination, in terms of its brand, size and manufacturing characteristics. However, the expert noted that it had been impossible to establish if the gun on the recording was identical to the “Valtro” gun due to the poor quality of the recordings.36. On 8 November 2004 the proceedings were again terminated. On 7 October 2005 this decision was set aside by the Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court, which reasoned that the investigator had failed to reconcile the inconsistencies in the witness statements and once again raised the question of the manner in which B.’s statement had been dealt with concerning the alleged racketeering. On several occasions the Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court ruled on complaints by the applicant challenging the termination, but its rulings were quashed by the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court of Appeal. On 15 January 2008 the investigator terminated the proceedings without any additional investigative measures. On 12 March 2008 the Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office set aside this decision as premature and reopened the proceedings.39. On 7 April 2008 the case was transferred to the Rogatyn district prosecutor’s office and on 23 December 2008 to the Pustomyty district prosecutor’s office.40. On 6 August 2009, following a forensic medical examination, a report was drawn up stating that the applicant’s son had sustained two gunshot wounds: one to his back and another to the back of his right shoulder. According to the results of the examination, it had been impossible to definitively establish the order of the shots.41. According to the results of a forensic ballistic examination of 19 August 2009, the first gunshot wound was inflicted on the applicant’s son’s back at point-blank range in the hallway of the house; after leaving the body the bullet went through the door. On 25 October 2012 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv set aside this decision, reasoning that an additional investigation after the reopening of the proceedings in 2008 had been conducted with a formalistic approach and that a number of investigative actions and forensic examinations had not been carried out. The court also pointed out that some evidence had been lost and that its location had not been established. On 23 November 2012 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal dismissed a prosecutor’s appeal against that decision.45. On 28 February 2014 a follow-up ballistic and forensic medical examination was conducted. It confirmed the findings of the examinations of 30 June and 6 October 1999 (see paragraph 24 above). The court further noted that the investigation had not established the circumstances in which the applicant’s son had received the additional injuries indicated on 15 March 1999 by the experts of the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations (see paragraph 12 above).49. On 16 May and 31 August 2017 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv set aside the decisions to terminate the criminal proceedings, reasoning that the investigator had failed to address the shortcomings outlined in the decision of the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv of 18 June 2015.50. The relevant provisions, as in force at the material time, provided:Article 4Obligation to institute criminal proceedings and investigate a crime“A court, prosecutor, investigator or body of inquiry shall, to the extent that it is within their power to do so, institute criminal proceedings in every case where signs of a crime have been discovered, take all necessary measures provided by law to establish the circumstances surrounding the crime, identify those guilty of the crime and punish them.”Article 97Obligation to accept allegations or notifications of crimes and the procedure for their examination“A prosecutor, investigator, body of inquiry or judge shall accept allegations or notifications of crimes [which have been] committed or [are] being prepared, including in cases that are outside their jurisdiction.Upon receipt of an allegation or notification of a crime, the prosecutor, investigator, body of inquiry or judge shall adopt, within three days, one of the following decisions:(1)  to institute criminal proceedings;(2)  to refuse to institute criminal proceedings;(3)  to remit the allegation or notification for examination in accordance with [the rules of] jurisdiction.Simultaneously, all possible measures shall be applied to prevent the further commission of the crime or to put an end to it ...Before instituting criminal proceedings, the prosecutor, investigator or body of inquiry shall conduct an inquiry, if it is necessary to verify [information contained in] an allegation or notification of a crime. THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1949 and resides in Lviv.

3. The applicant was initially represented by Mr A. Buryy, a lawyer practising in Lviv, and later represented himself. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

Background to the case and events of 4 March 1999

5. On 25 February 1999 B. complained to the Lviv Regional Department for Combatting Organised Crime of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (“the DCOC”) that unknown individuals had threatened her and extorted 25,000 United States dollars (USD).

6. According to the Government, an inquiry into B.’s allegations was carried out, and it was established that the unknown individuals were the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, and his friend Z., both alleged members of an organised criminal group that had been extorting money and property from residents of Mykolayiv using weapons.

7. On 1 March 1999 the DCOC approved an operational plan for the arrest of the alleged extortionists by the DCOC’s “Sokil” special police unit, which consisted of senior police detective Zar., detective M., and assistant detectives O. and G.

8. On 2 March 1999 the above-mentioned police officers, dressed in civilian clothes, began an operation to ambush the alleged extortionists in B.’s house. B.’s 22-year-old daughter and 16-year-old son were at home with her.

9. On 3 March 1999 criminal proceedings were instituted concerning the financial extortion of B.

10. According to the parties’ submissions, it appears that at around 2 p.m. on 4 March 1999 a private taxi driver, Tz., drove the applicant’s son and Z. to B.’s house. The two men approached the house while the driver remained in the car. B.’s daughter opened the door. Z. entered first, followed by the applicant’s son. Police officer M.
shouted, “Freeze, police!” and officers Zar., M. and G. arrested Z. The applicant’s son, who was standing at the entrance to the hallway at the time, disobeyed the order and began to flee. Officers M. and O. pursued him to the garden gate to arrest him. During the operation, the applicant’s son was shot twice by O. He died from his injuries.

Criminal investigation into the death of the applicant’s son

11. Between 3.40 and 8.20 p.m. on 4 March 1999, an investigator from the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office, in the presence of two witnesses, F. and Mar., carried out an on-site inspection at the scene of the incident. Two partial video recordings of the inspection were made.

12. On 15 March 1999, experts from the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations examined the body of the applicant’s son and prepared a report stating that his death had resulted from a gunshot wound to the chest. The injuries found on his left side proved to be a perforating gunshot wound. The experts also found other injuries on his body, including a bruise on his forehead, as well as superficial wounds and subcutaneous haemorrhages on the occipital part of the head and the lower lip.

13. On 24 March 1999, the internal inquiry conducted by the DCOC concluded that O. had used his service gun lawfully and in accordance with the requirements of the Police Act. The report noted that a “Valtro” gas gun had been found near the applicant’s son’s body during the on-site inspection.

14. On 25 March 1999, after conducting a pre-investigation inquiry, the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office declined to open a criminal investigation into the death of the applicant’s son. The relevant decision referred to the forensic examination results, witness statements and the findings of the internal inquiry, and stated that the police officers’ actions had disclosed no indication of an offence, as they had acted appropriately.

15. On 31 March 1999, the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office overturned the decision of 25 March 1999 and opened criminal proceedings into alleged abuse of power by the police causing serious harm. It reasoned that the circumstances surrounding the use of the weapon could not be established during the pre-investigation inquiry and that an investigation was therefore necessary.

16. On 15 April and 23 September 1999, forensic fingerprint examinations identified a fingerprint on the left side of the “Valtro” gun belonging to the same group as the applicant’s son’s left thumbprint. Three additional fingerprints belonging to him were found on the side of the gun’s magazine.

17. On 16 April 1999, the prosecutor questioned the police officers who had taken part in the operation.

18. B. and her daughter testified that, since 1996, the applicant’s son and Z. had been forcibly extorting money from their family. This had prompted B. to file a complaint with the police. On 2 March 1999, four police officers had set up an ambush at B.’s house.
On 3 March 1999 they had seen the extortionists drive past in their car to check whether anyone was at home. At around 2 p.m. on 4 March 1999 they had heard knocking at the door and Z. calling for B.’s daughter to open it. As she had been frightened, B. had retreated into the bathroom and her daughter had opened the door. The latter also testified that Z. had grabbed her arm and tried to pull her out of the house, while the applicant’s son had been standing behind him on the steps. She had managed to break free and run back inside the house into one of the rooms. The women further stated that after the extortionists had entered the house, they had heard one of the police officers shout “Freeze, police!”, followed by the sounds of fighting and a gunshot. They had then heard another gunshot outside the house. When the police officers had returned to the house, they had told B. to calm down because they had “gunned down” one of the extortionists.

19. Police officer M. testified that the ambush had been planned by K., an officer of the DCOC. He stated, inter alia, that K. had not told them whether the alleged racketeers were armed. On 2 or 3 March 1999, while M. and his colleagues had been lying in wait at B.’s house, the latter had given them the names of the racketeers and told them that one of them had a gun. On 4 March 1999, while they had all been having lunch, someone had knocked on the door. B., who had been wearing a recording device to record the extortion, had been too afraid to open the door, and they had persuaded her daughter to do so. M. stated that he and his colleagues had spontaneously spread out around the house, as they had not had time to plan, and M. had remained in the kitchen. He further testified that, upon being noticed by Z., who had entered the house, he had jumped out and shouted “Freeze, police!” Z. had not complied, so he had struck him in the chest. Immediately afterwards, he had heard a shot in the hallway. He had turned around and seen the back of someone fleeing the house. He had shouted “Don’t shoot!” and run after the person. At the gate, the fleeing person, who later turned out to be the applicant’s son, had tried to open it. At that point M., who had caught up with the applicant’s son and attempted to arrest him, had kicked him in the back with his right foot. The applicant’s son had then started turning towards M., who had noticed a gun in his hand pointed at him. At the same moment, M. had heard a shot and seen O. holding his service gun. After the shot, the applicant’s son had fallen onto the concrete pavement in the yard and begun to convulse, with the gun on his left side. Afterwards, police detective Zar. had gone to call an ambulance and inform the police authorities about the incident. In order to preserve the physical evidence, as a crowd had been gathering at the scene, M.
had taken the gun to B.’s house, placed it in a plastic bag and left it on the coffee table in the living room. In further statements given on unspecified dates, M. altered his testimony and stated that during the operation he and O. had remained in the kitchen in accordance with the agreed plan.

20. Police officer O. testified that when Z. had entered the house, he had been hiding in the kitchen with M. When M. had yelled, “Freeze, police!”, he had jumped into the hallway with his weapon ready to fire and had tried to arrest the second man, who had drawn his gun and pointed it at him. O., having assessed the situation as one entitling a police officer to use firearms, had fired at the applicant’s son, who had ducked behind the door to avoid the bullet. After being wounded, the applicant’s son had run out into the yard. M. and O. had chased him to the gate to arrest him. M. had reached the applicant’s son first and kicked him in the back. At that point, O. had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand pointed at M. and, in order to defend his colleague, had run towards the applicant’s son and shot him in the back from almost point-blank range. After the applicant’s son had fallen, he had pushed the gun away from him. He had intended to turn the applicant’s son onto his back, but had heard rattling noises from him and decided to leave him in the same position.

21. Police officer Zar. testified that after the second shot, he had run into the yard and seen the applicant’s son lying face down on the ground. He did not recall seeing a gun near the body. After calling an ambulance and returning to the house, he had seen a large black gun in a plastic bag in the living room. Police officer G. gave similar testimony.

22. When questioned on 3 May 1999, Tz., the taxi driver, testified that he had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand both during his struggle with the police officers and later near his body.

23. When questioned on 4 June 1999, Z., the alleged accomplice, testified that the applicant’s son had not been armed, since he had left his gun in his car before going to B.’s house. Z. further stated that when he had been escorted out of the building, he had noticed a gun in a plastic bag on a coffee table, but it had not been the applicant’s son’s gun. He later changed his testimony, stating that he did not know whether the applicant’s son had had a gun during the shooting.

According to the results of forensic medical examinations dated 30 June and 6 October 1999, the applicant’s son sustained two gunshot wounds: one to the back of his right shoulder, fired from a distance that could not be established because the bullet had passed through an obstacle – the door – before entering his body, and another to the back, fired at point-blank range or from no more than two centimetres away. The death of the applicant’s son was caused by the first wound to the back of his right shoulder. The experts also stated that, after receiving the first wound, the applicant’s son could have performed certain actions, namely, he could have run about sixteen metres, fought back and pointed a gun.

25. On 20 August 1999 the case was transferred to the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office.

26. On 19 and 21 October 1999 the witnesses to the on-site inspection were questioned. F. testified that he had not seen a gun at the scene of the incident, although he could not rule out the possibility that one had been there. Another witness to the on-site inspection, Mar., stated that he could not recall whether he had seen a gun.

28. On 28 January 2000 the investigator from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office terminated the proceedings for lack of evidence of a crime. His decision referred to the statements of Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers who had participated in the operation (see paragraphs 19-21 above), and the law-enforcement agents who had arrived at the scene of the incident.

On 25 December 2000 the Regional Court of Lviv quashed the above-mentioned decision and ordered that the proceedings be reopened.
