45. On 28 February 2014 a follow-up ballistic and forensic medical examination was carried out. It confirmed the findings of the examinations of 30 June and 6 October 1999 (see paragraph 24 above). The experts also noted that there were no forensic indications enabling the order of the shots to be established.

46. On 28 March 2014 the proceedings were again terminated. That decision was upheld by the Galytskyy District Court on 24 December 2014; however, on 21 January 2015 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal set it aside as unsubstantiated.

47. On 26 March 2015 the investigator of the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office terminated the proceedings for lack of any evidence of a crime. His decision referred, among other evidence, to the statements of Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers who had participated in the operation (see paragraphs 18-22 above), and the law-enforcement agents who had arrived at the scene of the incident. The witnesses had testified either that the applicant’s son had had a gun during his arrest or that they had later seen a gun in B.’s house. The investigator further concluded that the witness statements were supported by the crime-scene reconstructions and the results of the forensic examinations conducted.

48. On 18 June 2015 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv set aside that decision, finding that the investigator had failed to resolve the inconsistencies between the statements of Tz., Zar. and other witnesses (the police officers) concerning whether the applicant’s son had had a gun when he was shot and whether the gun had been near his body (see paragraphs 21 and 29 above). The court also noted that the investigation had not established the circumstances in which the applicant’s son had sustained the additional injuries identified on 15 March 1999 by the experts of the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations (see paragraph 12 above).

49. The proceedings were again terminated on 30 September 2015 and 29 July 2017. On 16 May and 31 August 2017 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv set aside the decisions terminating the criminal proceedings, finding that the investigator had failed to address the shortcomings identified in the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv’s decision of 18 June 2015.

50. As at 13 March 2018, the proceedings remained pending. No further information has been provided.

Code of Criminal Procedure of 28 December 1960

51.
The relevant provisions, as in force at the material time, stated:

Article 4  
Obligation to institute criminal proceedings and investigate a crime

“A court, prosecutor, investigator or body of inquiry shall, to the extent within their power, institute criminal proceedings whenever signs of a crime have been discovered, take all necessary measures provided for by law to establish the circumstances surrounding the crime, identify those responsible and punish them.”

Article 97

“A prosecutor, investigator, body of inquiry or judge shall accept allegations or notifications of crimes [which have been] committed or [are] being prepared, including where they fall outside their jurisdiction.

(1)  to institute criminal proceedings;

(2)  to refuse to institute criminal proceedings;

(3)  to remit the allegation or notification for examination in accordance with [the rules of] jurisdiction.

At the same time, all possible measures shall be taken to prevent the further commission of the crime or to put an end to it ...

Before instituting criminal proceedings, the prosecutor, investigator or body of inquiry shall conduct an inquiry where necessary to verify [information contained in] an allegation or notification of a crime. [The inquiry] shall be completed within ten days by obtaining explanations from individual citizens or officials or by securing the necessary documents.

[Information contained in] an allegation or notification of a crime may be verified before criminal proceedings are instituted by means of operational-search activities ...”

Article 15  
Use of firearms

“Police officers shall be entitled to use firearms as a last resort in the following cases:

(1)  to protect citizens from an attack threatening their life and health, as well as to secure the release of hostages;

(5)  to apprehend a person offering armed resistance or attempting to escape from custody, as well as an armed person threatening to use weapons or other life-threatening items that endanger the life and health of police officers;

(6)  to stop a vehicle by damaging it if the driver poses a threat to the life or health of citizens or police officers ...”

THE FACTS

2. The applicant, who was born in 1949, resides in Lviv.

3. He was initially represented by Mr A. Buryy, a lawyer practising in Lviv, but later acted on his own behalf. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna of the Ministry of Justice.

4. The circumstances of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as set out below.

Background and the events of 4 March 1999

5. On 25 February 1999, B. reported to the Lviv Regional Department for Combatting Organised Crime of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (“the DCOC”) that unidentified individuals had threatened her and demanded 25,000 United States dollars (USD) from her.

6. The Government stated that an inquiry into B.’s complaint had identified those individuals as the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, and his friend Z. Both men were alleged to belong to an organised criminal group that had used weapons to extort money and property from inhabitants of Mykolayiv.

7. On 1 March 1999, the DCOC authorised an operational plan under which its “Sokil” special police unit would arrest the suspected extortionists. The unit comprised senior police detective Zar., detective M., and assistant detectives O. and G.

8. On 2 March 1999, those officers, dressed in civilian clothing, began an operation in which they lay in wait for the suspected extortionists at B.’s home. B. was in the house with her 22-year-old daughter and her 16-year-old son.

9. Criminal proceedings concerning the extortion of money from B. were opened on 3 March 1999.

10. The parties’ submissions indicate that, at approximately 2 p.m. on 4 March 1999, Tz., a private taxi driver, took the applicant’s son and Z. to B.’s house. While Tz. remained in the vehicle, the two men walked towards the house. B.’s daughter answered the door. Z. entered first, followed by the applicant’s son. Police officer M.
shouted, “Freeze, police!” Officers Zar., M. and G. then arrested Z. The applicant’s son, who was standing at the entrance to the hallway, ignored the command and attempted to escape. Officers M. and O. pursued him as far as the garden gate in order to apprehend him. During the operation, O. shot the applicant’s son twice. He subsequently died from his wounds.

Criminal investigation into the death of the applicant’s son

11. On 4 March 1999, between 3.40 and 8.20 p.m., an investigator from the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office inspected the scene in the presence of two witnesses, F. and Mar. The inspection was partially recorded in two videos.

12. On 15 March 1999, experts from the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations performed an examination of the applicant’s son’s body. Their report concluded that he had died from a gunshot wound to the chest. The injuries on the left side of his body were identified as a perforating gunshot wound. The experts also recorded a forehead bruise, as well as superficial wounds and subcutaneous haemorrhaging on the occipital area of the head and the lower lip.

13. An internal DCOC inquiry concluded on 24 March 1999 that O.’s use of his service weapon had been lawful and consistent with the Police Act. According to the inquiry report, a “Valtro” gas gun had been discovered near the body of the applicant’s son during the inspection of the scene.

14. Following a pre-investigation inquiry, the Mykolayiv district prosecutor’s office decided on 25 March 1999 not to open a criminal investigation into the applicant’s son’s death. Relying on the forensic examination findings, witness testimony and the conclusions of the internal inquiry, it found no indication that the police officers had committed an offence, as their conduct had been appropriate.

15. On 31 March 1999, the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office overturned the decision of 25 March 1999 and instituted criminal proceedings concerning alleged abuse of power by the police resulting in serious harm. It considered that the pre-investigation inquiry had been unable to determine the circumstances in which the weapon had been used and that a full investigation was therefore necessary.

16. Forensic fingerprint examinations carried out on 15 April and 23 September 1999 identified, on the left side of the “Valtro” gun, a fingerprint belonging to the same group as the applicant’s son’s left thumbprint. Three additional fingerprints belonging to him were detected on the side of the gun’s magazine.

17. On 16 April 1999, the prosecutor interviewed the police officers involved in the operation.

18. B. and her daughter stated that, beginning in 1996, the applicant’s son and Z. had used force to extort money from their family. As a result, B. had filed a complaint with the police. On 2 March 1999, four police officers had set up an ambush at B.’s home.
On 3 March 1999, they had observed the extortionists drive past the house in their car to check whether anyone was home. At approximately 2 p.m. the following day, they had heard someone knocking on the door and Z. calling on B.’s daughter to open it. Frightened, B. had hidden in the bathroom, while her daughter had answered the door. The daughter also testified that Z. had seized her by the arm and attempted to drag her out of the house; the applicant’s son had been standing behind him on the steps. She had succeeded in freeing herself and had run back inside, taking refuge in one of the rooms. The women further stated that, once the extortionists had entered the house, they had heard a police officer shout, “Freeze, police!”, followed by sounds of a struggle and a gunshot. A second shot had then been heard outside. When the officers returned to the house, they told B. to calm down because they had “gunned down” one of the extortionists.

19. Police officer M. testified that K., an officer from the DCOC, had devised the ambush. Among other things, he stated that K. had not told the officers whether the suspected racketeers were armed. On 2 or 3 March 1999, while M. and his colleagues had been waiting at B.’s home, B. had given them the racketeers’ names and informed them that one of the men had a gun. On 4 March 1999, as everyone was eating lunch, there had been a knock at the door. B. had been wearing a recording device intended to capture the extortion, but she had been too frightened to answer, and the officers had persuaded her daughter to do so instead. According to M., he and the other officers had dispersed spontaneously throughout the house because there had been no time to plan their positions; he had remained in the kitchen. He further testified that, when Z. entered and noticed him, M. had leapt out and shouted, “Freeze, police!” When Z. failed to obey, M. had struck him in the chest. Immediately afterward, M. had heard a shot in the hallway. Turning around, he had seen the back of a person fleeing the house. He had shouted, “Don’t shoot!”, and pursued him.

At the gate, the fleeing man—later identified as the applicant’s son—had attempted to open it. M. had caught up with him and, while trying to arrest him, had kicked him in the back with his right foot. The applicant’s son had then begun turning toward M., who noticed that he was holding a gun pointed in M.’s direction. At that same instant, M. had heard a shot and had seen O. holding his service weapon. Following the shot, the applicant’s son had fallen onto the yard’s concrete pavement and begun convulsing, with the gun lying to his left. Police detective Zar. had then gone to summon an ambulance and notify the police authorities about the incident. As a crowd was gathering at the scene, M., seeking to preserve the physical evidence,
had brought the gun to B.’s house, placed it inside a plastic bag, and left it on the living-room coffee table. In additional statements made on unspecified dates, M. altered his account, asserting that, in accordance with the agreed operational plan, he and O. had remained in the kitchen throughout the operation.

20. Police officer O. stated that he and M. had been concealed in the kitchen when Z. entered the house. After M. shouted, “Freeze, police!”, O. emerged into the hallway with his firearm ready to discharge and attempted to arrest the second man. That man drew a gun and aimed it at O. Having concluded that the circumstances justified a police officer’s use of firearms, O. fired at the applicant’s son, who tried to evade the bullet by ducking behind the door. Although wounded, the applicant’s son ran into the yard. M. and O. pursued him as far as the gate in order to arrest him. M. reached him first and kicked him in the back. O. then saw a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand aimed at M. To protect his colleague, O. ran towards the applicant’s son and shot him in the back from almost point-blank range. Once the applicant’s son had fallen, O. pushed the gun away from him. O. intended to turn him onto his back but, upon hearing rattling sounds coming from him, decided not to move him.

21. Police officer Zar. testified that, following the second shot, he ran into the yard and saw the applicant’s son lying face down. He could not recall seeing a firearm near the body. After calling an ambulance and returning inside the house, he observed a large black gun in a plastic bag in the living room. Police officer G. gave a similar account.

22. During questioning on 3 May 1999, Tz., the taxi driver, stated that he had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand both while he was struggling with the police officers and subsequently near his body.

23. Questioned on 4 June 1999, Z., the alleged accomplice, stated that the applicant’s son had been unarmed because he had left his gun in his car before entering B.’s house. According to Z., after the applicant’s son was shot, the police officers compelled him to tell them about the firearm and where it was located. Z. also said that, as he was escorted from the building, he noticed a gun inside a plastic bag on a coffee table, but it was not the weapon belonging to the applicant’s son. He later revised his account, saying that he did not know whether the applicant’s son had been carrying a gun during the shooting.

24.
Forensic medical examinations completed on 30 June and 6 October 1999 established that the applicant’s son had sustained two gunshot wounds. One bullet struck the back of his right shoulder and had been fired from an indeterminate distance, which could not be calculated because it had first passed through an obstacle—the door—before entering his body. The second shot hit him in the back and was discharged either at point-blank range or from no more than two centimetres away. His death resulted from the first wound, to the back of the right shoulder. The experts further concluded that, after sustaining that injury, he could still have performed certain actions, including running approximately sixteen metres, resisting, and pointing a gun.

25. On 20 August 1999 the case was reassigned to the Lviv Regional Prosecutor’s Office.

26. The witnesses present during the on-site inspection were interviewed on 19 and 21 October 1999. F. said that he had not observed a gun at the scene, although he could not exclude the possibility that one had been there. Mar., another inspection witness, stated that he did not recall whether he had seen a firearm.

27. A forensic analysis of metallic residues conducted on 28 December 1999 detected traces on the jacket and trousers worn by the applicant’s son. Those traces were attributed to contact with a steel object, potentially the “Valtro” gun purportedly discovered at the scene.

28. On 28 January 2000 an investigator from the Lviv Regional Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the proceedings on the ground that there was no evidence that a criminal offence had been committed. The decision relied on statements given by Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers involved in the operation (see paragraphs 19-21 above), and the law-enforcement personnel who subsequently arrived at the scene.

On 25 December 2000 the Lviv Regional Court quashed that decision and directed that the investigation be resumed. Among other matters, it observed that the evidence concerning whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun when the shooting occurred was inconsistent. In particular, on 21 April 2000 Tz. had made a statement that effectively retracted his earlier testimony, asserting that the applicant’s son had been unarmed when he was shot. In view of those contradictions, the court ordered the investigator to conduct further questioning of the witnesses.

30. The Prosecutor General’s Office transferred the case to the Zakarpattya Regional Prosecutor’s Office on 19 April 2001.

31. Although the proceedings were discontinued once more on 27 December 2001, they were reopened on 12 February 2002 because the investigator had not established all the relevant circumstances.

32. A further decision terminating the proceedings was issued on 19 August 2002. On 9 December 2002 the Uzhgorod Local Court of the Zakarpattya Region set that decision aside.
The court found that, in discontinuing the proceedings, the investigator had based his decision on the findings of the DCOC’s internal inquiry (see paragraph 13 above). Since the DCOC was an interested party, this reliance was incompatible with the principle requiring an objective assessment of the evidence. The court reiterated that it was essential to determine whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun at the time of the shooting and specified several investigative measures that remained necessary, including a further reconstruction of the events involving Tz.

33. On 10 March 2004 the Zakarpattya Regional Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 30 September 2003 discontinuing the proceedings. It observed that the investigative authority had neither followed the directions given by higher-ranking prosecutors nor addressed the applicant’s complaints. It also found that the investigator had failed to identify any evidence conclusively establishing that O. had acted lawfully when using his weapon against the applicant’s son. The court highlighted additional procedural defects, including the police officers’ failure to secure the scene and the removal by tow truck of the applicant’s son’s car without the investigator’s authorisation. In particular, it was necessary to determine whether police officers had had access to the vehicle, given Z.’s statement that the applicant’s son had left his gun inside it. The court also drew attention to contradictions in the witness testimony, notably F.’s assertion that he had seen no gun at the scene (see paragraph 26 above). Finally, it criticised the handling of B.’s allegations of racketeering and directed the investigator to establish why the alleged racketeers had not been identified and why the police had failed to question them after B. made her statement.

34. On 28 May 2004 the Prosecutor General’s Office referred the case to the Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office.

35. A forensic analysis of the video recordings of the on-site inspection was carried out on 31 August 2004. It revealed no indication that the portions examined had been altered, either manually or electronically. Recordings on videotapes supplied by the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office and the DCOC also depicted a gun lying on a table inside the house which, in its make, dimensions and manufacturing features, resembled the “Valtro” gun submitted for examination. Owing to the poor quality of the footage, however, the expert could not determine whether the gun shown was the same “Valtro” gun.

36. The proceedings were discontinued once again on 8 November 2004.
On 7 October 2005, the Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court overturned that decision. It found that the investigator had not resolved the discrepancies among the witness statements and again questioned how B.’s statement regarding the alleged racketeering had been handled. The court further observed that the reconstruction of events involving Tz. had been conducted superficially and that the applicant’s complaints remained unanswered.

37. After conducting further interviews with witnesses F. and Mar., the investigator discontinued the proceedings once more on 30 December 2005. The Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court examined the applicant’s challenges to the discontinuation on several occasions, but its rulings were subsequently quashed by the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court of Appeal. In a final decision of 17 December 2007, the appellate court upheld the Local Court’s ruling of 25 October 2007, which had annulled the decision to terminate the criminal proceedings. It concluded that the investigator had not remedied the deficiencies identified in the Local Court’s decision of 7 October 2005.

38. On 15 January 2008, without undertaking any further investigative steps, the investigator again discontinued the proceedings. The Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office found that decision premature, set it aside on 12 March 2008, and reopened the case.

39. The case was transferred to the Rogatyn district prosecutor’s office on 7 April 2008 and subsequently to the Pustomyty district prosecutor’s office on 23 December 2008.

40. A report prepared on 6 August 2009 following a forensic medical examination recorded that the applicant’s son had suffered two gunshot wounds, one to his back and the other to the rear of his right shoulder. The examination did not permit a definitive determination of the sequence in which the shots had been fired.

41. A forensic ballistic examination dated 19 August 2009 concluded that the first shot had struck the applicant’s son in the back at point-blank range in the hallway of the house, with the bullet passing through his body and then through the door. The second shot, which caused his death, struck the back of his right shoulder in the front yard near the gate and was fired from a distance of at least two metres.

42. On 13 February 2010, the case was transferred to the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office.

43. A further forensic examination was ordered to resolve the inconsistencies among the earlier findings concerning the manner and sequence in which the applicant’s son had sustained his injuries (see paragraphs 24, 40 and 41 above). It could not be carried out, however, because the victim’s clothing had been returned to his father, who had destroyed it.

44. The proceedings were discontinued on 17 February 2012.
On 25 October 2012, the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv quashed that decision. It found that, following the reopening of the proceedings in 2008, the additional investigation had been conducted in a merely formalistic manner and that several investigative measures and forensic examinations had not been undertaken. The court also observed that certain evidence had gone missing and that its whereabouts had not been ascertained. On 23 November 2012, the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal rejected the prosecutor’s appeal against that ruling.

45. A supplementary ballistic and forensic medical examination was carried out on 28 February 2014. It corroborated the conclusions reached in the examinations of 30 June and 6 October 1999 (see paragraph 24 above). The experts additionally stated that no forensic indications existed from which the sequence of the shots could be established.

46. The proceedings were discontinued once more on 28 March 2014. Although the Galytskyy District Court upheld that decision on 24 December 2014, the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal quashed it as unsubstantiated on 21 January 2015.

47. On 26 March 2015, an investigator from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office discontinued the proceedings on the ground that there was no evidence that a crime had been committed. In reaching that decision, he relied, among other material, on statements given by Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers involved in the operation (see paragraphs 18-22 above), and the law-enforcement officers who had subsequently arrived at the scene. Those witnesses had stated either that the applicant’s son had been carrying a gun when he was arrested or that they had later seen a gun in B.’s house. The investigator also concluded that their accounts were corroborated by the reconstructions of the crime scene and the findings of the forensic examinations.

48. The Galytskyy District Court of Lviv overturned that decision on 18 June 2015. It held that the investigator had not reconciled the inconsistencies between the accounts of Tz., Zar. and the other witnesses, namely the police officers, as to whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun when he was shot and whether a gun had been lying near his body (see paragraphs 21 and 29 above). The court further observed that the investigation had failed to determine how the applicant’s son had sustained the additional injuries identified on 15 March 1999 by experts from the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations (see paragraph 12 above).

49. Further decisions discontinuing the proceedings were issued on 30 September 2015 and 29 July 2017. On 16 May and 31 August 2017, the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv quashed the respective discontinuation decisions, finding that the investigator had not remedied the deficiencies identified in that court’s ruling of 18 June 2015.

50. As of 13 March 2018, the proceedings remained pending. No subsequent information has been submitted.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Code of Criminal Procedure of 28 December 1960

51.
At the relevant time, the applicable provisions stated as follows:

Article 4  
Duty to initiate criminal proceedings and investigate offences

“Whenever indications of a crime are identified, a court, prosecutor, investigator or inquiry body shall, insofar as it lies within its authority, open criminal proceedings and take every measure prescribed by law to determine the circumstances of the offence, identify those responsible and ensure that they are punished.”

Article 97  
Duty to receive allegations or reports of crimes and the procedure for examining them

“A prosecutor, investigator, inquiry body or judge shall receive allegations or reports concerning crimes that have been committed or are being planned, even where the matter falls outside that authority’s jurisdiction.

Within three days of receiving an allegation or report of a crime, the prosecutor, investigator, inquiry body or judge shall decide:

(1) to open criminal proceedings;

(2) not to open criminal proceedings; or

(3) to refer the allegation or report for examination in accordance with the applicable jurisdictional rules.

At the same time, every possible measure shall be taken to prevent the crime from continuing or to bring it to an end ...

Where verification of the information contained in an allegation or report is required, the prosecutor, investigator or inquiry body shall carry out a preliminary inquiry before criminal proceedings are opened. That inquiry shall be completed within ten days by obtaining explanations from private individuals or officials, or by securing the necessary documents.

Before criminal proceedings are instituted, the information contained in an allegation or report of a crime may also be verified through operational-search measures ...”

Police Act of 20 December 1990

52. At the material time, the relevant provisions were worded as follows:

Article 15  
Use of firearms

“Police officers may resort to firearms only as a last measure and solely in the following circumstances:

(1) to defend citizens against an attack endangering their life or health, or to secure the release of hostages;

(2) to repel an attack on a police officer or members of that officer’s family where their life or health is at risk;

(3) to repel attacks against protected facilities, convoys, citizens’ homes, or the premises of State or public enterprises, institutions and organisations, and to recover such places if they have been seized;

(4) to arrest a person who has been caught committing a serious criminal offence and is attempting to flee;

(5) to arrest a person who offers armed resistance or attempts to escape from custody, as well as an armed person who threatens to use weapons or other life-threatening objects in a manner endangering the life or health of police officers;

(6) to bring a vehicle to a halt by damaging it where its driver poses a danger to the life or health of citizens or police officers ...”

Referring to the body’s forensic examination, witness testimony and the findings of the internal inquiry, the decision concluded that the police officers’ conduct showed no sign of a criminal offence because their actions had been appropriate.

15. The Lviv regional prosecutor’s office overturned the decision of 25 March 1999 on 31 March 1999 and commenced criminal proceedings concerning suspected abuse of power by the police resulting in serious harm. It found that the circumstances in which the weapon had been used could not be determined through the pre-investigation inquiry and therefore required a full investigation.

16. Forensic fingerprint examinations conducted on 15 April and 23 September 1999 identified, on the left side of the “Valtro” gun, a print belonging to the same group as the applicant’s son’s left thumbprint. Three additional fingerprints belonging to him were detected on the side of the gun’s magazine.

17. On 16 April 1999, the prosecutor interviewed the police officers involved in the operation.

18. B. and her daughter stated that, beginning in 1996, the applicant’s son and Z. had forcibly extorted money from their family, prompting B. to file a police complaint. On 2 March 1999, four police officers had set up an ambush at B.’s home.
On 3 March 1999, they had observed the extortionists driving by in their car to check whether anyone was home. At approximately 2 p.m. the following day, 4 March 1999, they had heard someone knock at the door and Z. call on B.’s daughter to open it. B., frightened, had hidden in the bathroom, while her daughter had answered the door. According to the daughter, Z. had seized her by the arm and attempted to drag her out of the house; the applicant’s son had been standing behind Z. on the steps. She had broken free and fled back inside, taking refuge in one of the rooms. The women also stated that, once the extortionists had entered the house, they had heard a police officer shout, “Freeze, police!”, followed by sounds of a struggle and a gunshot. A second gunshot had then been heard outside. When the officers came back into the house, they had reassured B. and told her to calm down because they had “gunned down” one of the extortionists.

19. Police officer M. testified that K., an officer of the DCOC, had devised the ambush. Among other things, he stated that K. had not told the officers whether the suspected racketeers were armed. While M. and his colleagues were waiting at B.’s home on 2 or 3 March 1999, B. had given them the racketeers’ names and said that one of them possessed a gun. On 4 March 1999, as everyone was eating lunch, there had been a knock at the door. B. had been wearing a recording device intended to capture the extortion, but she had been too frightened to answer, so the officers had persuaded her daughter to do so. M. explained that, because there had been no time to plan, he and his colleagues had instinctively taken positions throughout the house, with M. remaining in the kitchen.

M. further testified that, after Z. entered the house and noticed him, he had leapt out and shouted, “Freeze, police!” When Z. failed to obey, M. had struck him in the chest. Immediately afterward, M. had heard a gunshot in the hallway. Turning around, he had seen the back of a person fleeing the house. He had called out, “Don’t shoot!”, and pursued the individual. At the gate, the fleeing person—later identified as the applicant’s son—had attempted to open it. By then, M. had caught up with him and, while trying to arrest him, had kicked him in the back with his right foot. The applicant’s son had begun turning toward M., who then saw a gun in his hand aimed at him. At that same instant, M. had heard a shot and observed O. holding his service weapon. Following the shot, the applicant’s son had collapsed onto the yard’s concrete pavement and begun convulsing, with the gun lying to his left. Police detective Zar. had subsequently left to summon an ambulance and notify the police authorities about the incident. Because a crowd was assembling at the scene, M., in order to preserve the physical evidence,
He had brought the gun to B.’s house, placed it inside a plastic bag, and left it on the living-room coffee table. In later statements made on dates that were not specified, M. altered his account, claiming that, in line with the agreed operational plan, he and O. had remained in the kitchen throughout the operation.

20. Police officer O. stated that, when Z. entered the house, he and M. had been concealed in the kitchen. After M. shouted, “Freeze, police!”, O. emerged into the hallway with his weapon ready to fire and attempted to arrest the second man. That man drew a gun and aimed it at O. Having concluded that the circumstances justified a police officer’s use of firearms, O. fired at the applicant’s son, who tried to evade the bullet by ducking behind the door. Although wounded, the applicant’s son ran into the yard. M. and O. pursued him as far as the gate in order to arrest him. M. reached him first and kicked him in the back. O. then saw a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand aimed at M. To protect his colleague, O. ran towards the applicant’s son and shot him in the back from almost point-blank range. Once the applicant’s son had fallen, O. pushed the gun away from him. He intended to turn him onto his back but, after hearing rattling sounds coming from him, decided to leave him in the same position.

21. Police officer Zar. testified that, following the second shot, he ran into the yard and saw the applicant’s son lying face down on the ground. He could not recall seeing a gun near the body. After calling an ambulance and going back inside the house, he noticed a large black gun inside a plastic bag in the living room. Police officer G. gave a similar account.

22. During questioning on 3 May 1999, the taxi driver, Tz., stated that he had seen a gun in the applicant’s son’s hand while he was struggling with the police officers and had later seen it near his body.

23. When interviewed on 4 June 1999, Z., the alleged accomplice, stated that the applicant’s son had not been armed because he had left his gun in his car before entering B.’s house. According to Z., after the applicant’s son was shot, the police officers compelled him to disclose the existence and location of the gun. Z. also said that, while being escorted from the building, he noticed a gun in a plastic bag on a coffee table, but it was not the applicant’s son’s weapon. He subsequently revised his evidence and said that he did not know whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun during the shooting.

24.
Forensic medical examinations completed on 30 June and 6 October 1999 established that the applicant’s son had sustained two gunshot wounds. One bullet struck the back of his right shoulder and had been fired from an undetermined distance, which could not be ascertained because it had first passed through an obstacle—the door—before entering his body. The second shot hit him in the back and was discharged either at point-blank range or from no more than two centimetres away. His death resulted from the first wound, to the back of his right shoulder. The experts further concluded that, after sustaining that wound, he could still have performed certain actions, including running approximately sixteen metres, resisting and pointing a gun.

25. The case was transferred to the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office on 20 August 1999.

26. The witnesses who had attended the on-site inspection were interviewed on 19 and 21 October 1999. F. said that he had not observed a gun at the scene, although he could not exclude the possibility that one had been present. Mar., another witness to the inspection, stated that he did not remember whether he had seen a gun.

27. A forensic analysis of metallic residues, conducted on 28 December 1999, detected traces of such material on the jacket and trousers worn by the applicant’s son. The residues had resulted from contact with a steel object, possibly the “Valtro” gun allegedly discovered at the scene.

28. On 28 January 2000, an investigator from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office discontinued the proceedings on the ground that there was no evidence that a crime had been committed. In reaching that decision, the investigator relied on statements from Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers involved in the operation (see paragraphs 19-21 above), and law-enforcement officers who had subsequently arrived at the scene. On 25 December 2000, the Regional Court of Lviv quashed that decision and directed that the proceedings be resumed. Among other things, the court observed that the evidence concerning whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun when the shooting occurred was contradictory. In particular, on 21 April 2000, Tz. had given a statement that effectively retracted his earlier testimony and asserted that the applicant’s son had been unarmed when he was shot. The court therefore ordered the investigator to conduct further questioning of the witnesses in order to address those inconsistencies.

30. On 19 April 2001, the Prosecutor General’s Office referred the case to the Zakarpattya regional prosecutor’s office.

31. The proceedings were discontinued once more on 27 December 2001. They were reopened on 12 February 2002 because the investigator had not established all the circumstances surrounding the case.

32. Another decision terminating the proceedings was issued on 19 August 2002. On 9 December 2002, the Uzhgorod Local Court of the Zakarpattya Region set that decision aside.
The court found that, in discontinuing the proceedings, the investigator had based the decision on the findings of the DCOC’s internal inquiry (see paragraph 13 above). Since the DCOC was an interested party, that reliance violated the principle requiring an objective assessment of evidence. The court reiterated that it was essential to determine whether the applicant’s son had possessed a gun at the time of the shooting and identified several investigative measures that remained necessary, including another reconstruction of the events involving Tz.

33. On 10 March 2004 the Zakarpattya Regional Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 30 September 2003 discontinuing the proceedings. It observed that the investigative authority had neither followed the instructions of higher-ranking prosecutors nor addressed the applicant’s complaints. It also stated that the investigator had failed to identify any evidence conclusively establishing that O. had acted lawfully when using his weapon against the applicant’s son. The court highlighted procedural defects in the investigation, including the police officers’ failure to preserve the scene and the removal by tow truck of the applicant’s son’s car without the investigator’s authorisation. In particular, it was necessary to determine whether police officers had had access to the vehicle because, according to Z., the applicant’s son had left his gun inside it. The court additionally cited contradictions between witness statements, especially F.’s assertion that he had not seen a gun at the scene (see paragraph 26 above). Finally, it questioned how B.’s statement about the alleged racketeering had been handled and instructed the investigator to establish why the alleged racketeers had not been identified and why the police had not questioned them after B. made her statement.

34. On 28 May 2004 the Prosecutor General’s Office referred the case to the Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office.

35. A forensic analysis of the video footage from the on-site inspection was carried out on 31 August 2004. It revealed no indication that the portions examined had been edited either manually or electronically. Moreover, footage on video cassettes originating from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office and the DCOC depicted a gun lying on a table inside the house which, in its make, dimensions and manufacturing features, resembled the “Valtro” gun submitted for examination. Nevertheless, because the recordings were of poor quality, the expert was unable to determine whether the weapon shown was the same “Valtro” gun.

36. The proceedings were once more discontinued on 8 November 2004.
On 7 October 2005, the Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court quashed that decision. It found that the investigator had not resolved discrepancies in the witness testimony and again questioned how B.’s statement regarding the alleged racketeering had been handled. The court further observed that the reconstruction involving Tz. had been conducted superficially and that no responses had been given to the applicant’s complaints.

37. After questioning the witnesses F. and Mar. further, the investigator discontinued the proceedings again on 30 December 2005. The Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court ruled several times on the applicant’s challenges to that discontinuance, but the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court of Appeal overturned those rulings. In a final decision of 17 December 2007, the appellate court upheld the Ivano-Frankivsk Local Court’s ruling of 25 October 2007, which had annulled the decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings. It held that the investigator had not remedied the deficiencies identified in the Local Court’s decision of 7 October 2005.

38. On 15 January 2008, without taking any further investigative steps, the investigator once more discontinued the proceedings. The Ivano-Frankivsk regional prosecutor’s office annulled that decision as premature on 12 March 2008 and reopened the case.

39. The case was transferred to the Rogatyn district prosecutor’s office on 7 April 2008 and subsequently to the Pustomyty district prosecutor’s office on 23 December 2008.

40. A report prepared on 6 August 2009 following a forensic medical examination recorded that the applicant’s son had suffered two gunshot wounds, one in his back and the other in the rear of his right shoulder. The examination could not conclusively determine the sequence in which the shots had been fired.

41. A forensic ballistic examination dated 19 August 2009 concluded that the first wound had been caused by a point-blank shot to the applicant’s son’s back in the hallway of the house, with the bullet passing through the door after exiting his body. The second shot struck the back of his right shoulder and resulted in his death; it was fired in the front yard near the gate from a distance of at least two metres.

42. On 13 February 2010, the case was reassigned to the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office.

43. A further forensic examination was commissioned to resolve the inconsistencies among the earlier examinations regarding the manner and sequence in which the applicant’s son had sustained his injuries (see paragraphs 24, 40 and 41 above). However, it could not be performed because the son’s clothing had been returned to his father, who had destroyed it.

44. The proceedings were discontinued on 17 February 2012.
On 25 October 2012, the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv annulled the decision. It found that the additional investigation carried out after the proceedings had been reopened in 2008 had been merely formalistic, and that several investigative measures and forensic examinations had not been conducted. It also observed that certain evidence had disappeared and that its whereabouts had not been determined. A prosecutor’s appeal was rejected by the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal on 23 November 2012.

45. A further ballistic and forensic medical examination took place on 28 February 2014. It corroborated the conclusions reached in the examinations of 30 June and 6 October 1999 (see paragraph 24 above). The experts also stated that no forensic indications existed from which the sequence of the shots could be established.

46. The proceedings were discontinued once more on 28 March 2014. Although the Galytskyy District Court upheld that decision on 24 December 2014, the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal quashed it as unsubstantiated on 21 January 2015.

47. On 26 March 2015, an investigator from the Lviv regional prosecutor’s office closed the proceedings because there was no evidence that a crime had been committed. Among the evidence cited in the decision were statements by Tz., B., B.’s daughter, the police officers involved in the operation (see paragraphs 18-22 above), and the law-enforcement officers who had subsequently reached the scene. Those witnesses stated either that the applicant’s son had possessed a gun when he was arrested or that they had later seen a gun in B.’s house. The investigator also concluded that their accounts were corroborated by the crime-scene reconstructions and the findings of the forensic examinations.

48. The Galytskyy District Court of Lviv quashed that decision on 18 June 2015. It held that the investigator had not reconciled the inconsistencies between the accounts given by Tz., Zar. and the other witnesses—the police officers—regarding whether the applicant’s son had been carrying a gun when he was shot and whether a gun had been lying near his body (see paragraphs 21 and 29 above). The court additionally found that the investigation had failed to clarify how the applicant’s son had sustained the further injuries identified on 15 March 1999 by experts from the Lviv Bureau of Forensic Medical Examinations (see paragraph 12 above).

49. The proceedings were discontinued again on 30 September 2015 and on 29 July 2017. On 16 May and 31 August 2017, the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv annulled the respective decisions terminating the criminal proceedings, finding that the investigator had not remedied the deficiencies identified in that court’s decision of 18 June 2015.

50. The proceedings remained pending as of 13 March 2018. No additional information has been submitted.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Code of Criminal Procedure of 28 December 1960

51.
At the relevant time, the applicable provisions stated as follows:

**Article 4 — Duty to open criminal proceedings and investigate an offence**

Whenever indications of a crime are identified, a court, prosecutor, investigator or inquiry body must, insofar as this lies within its authority, commence criminal proceedings, take every measure required by law to determine the circumstances of the offence, establish the identity of those responsible and ensure their punishment.

**Article 97 — Duty to receive reports or information concerning offences and the procedure for examining them**

A prosecutor, investigator, inquiry body or judge must receive reports or information about offences that have been committed or are being planned, even where the matter falls outside that authority’s jurisdiction.

Within three days after receiving such a report or information, the prosecutor, investigator, inquiry body or judge must decide to:

(1) commence criminal proceedings;

(2) decline to commence criminal proceedings; or

(3) forward the report or information for consideration under the applicable jurisdictional rules.

At the same time, every possible measure must be taken to prevent the offence from continuing or to bring it to an end ...

Before criminal proceedings are commenced, the prosecutor, investigator or inquiry body must carry out an inquiry where this is necessary to verify the information contained in the report or notification. That inquiry must be completed within ten days by obtaining explanations from private individuals or officials, or by securing the necessary documents.

Before proceedings are instituted, the information in a report or notification of an offence may also be checked through operational-search measures ...

**Police Act of 20 December 1990**

**52.** At the material time, the relevant provisions were worded as follows:

**Article 15 — Resort to firearms**

Police officers may use firearms only as a measure of last resort and solely in the following circumstances:

(1) to defend citizens against an attack endangering their life or health, or to free hostages;

(2) to repel an attack against a police officer or members of that officer’s family where their life or health is at risk;

(3) to repel attacks against protected facilities, convoys, citizens’ homes, or the premises of State or public enterprises, institutions and organisations, and to recover them if they have been seized;

(4) to arrest a person who has been caught while committing a serious criminal offence and is attempting to flee;

(5) to arrest a person who offers armed resistance or attempts to escape from custody, or an armed person who threatens to use weapons or other life-threatening objects that endanger the life or health of police officers;

(6) to bring a vehicle to a halt by damaging it where the driver presents a danger to the life or health of citizens or police officers ...

original: FIFTH SECTIONCASE OF SHABELNIK v. UKRAINE (NO. 3)(Application no. 54806/18)   JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG4 November 2021 FINAL 04/02/2022 This judgment has become final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.In the case of Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 3),The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of: Síofra O’Leary, President, Mārtiņš Mits, Ganna Yudkivska, Lətif Hüseynov, Jovan Ilievski, Ivana Jelić, Mattias Guyomar, judges,and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,Having regard to:the application (no. 54806/18) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Dmitriy Grigoryevich Shabelnik (“the applicant”), on 13 November 2018;the decision to give notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”);the observations submitted by the Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant;the written comments submitted by the Lviv Forum of Criminal Justice (“the third party”), who was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3);Having deliberated in private on 12 October 2021,Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:INTRODUCTION1. The case deals with the applicant’s complaint under Article 7 of the Convention that the judicial review of his previous conviction had resulted in a new punishment being imposed on him outside the statutory time-limit.THE FACTS2. The applicant was born in 1979. He is currently serving a life sentence in Zhytomyr, Ukraine. The applicant, who was granted legal aid, was represented by Mr M.O. Tarakhkalo and Ms V. Lebid, lawyers practising in Kyiv, Ukraine.3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.4. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.Criminal proceedings against the applicant5. In October 2001 Ms K., an elderly person, was found murdered in her flat. In December 2001 Ms S., a minor, was abducted and murdered.6. On 10 December 2001 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of abduction of S. in order to extort money from her parents and of S.’s subsequent murder.7. On 17 December 2001 the applicant appointed a lawyer.8. On 19 December 2001 the applicant was charged with the above-mentioned crime, following an investigation during which the applicant showed the police the places in which he had hidden S.’s corpse and some of her belongings. The banknotes received as a ransom from the parents of S. were found in his possession.9. On 15 February 2002, apparently at his own request, the applicant, was questioned as a witness regarding the circumstances of K.’s death. During the questioning, which took place without the presence of a lawyer, the applicant confessed to K.’s murder. The next day, still acting in the capacity of a witness, the applicant participated without the presence of a lawyer in an on-site reconstruction of the attack on K. On 18 and 22 February 2002 he was again questioned, without a lawyer, about the attack.10. On 25 February 2002 the investigating prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant in respect of K.’s murder and joined them with the criminal case concerning the abduction and murder of S.11. On 11 July 2002 the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal, acting as a trial court, convicted the applicant of the abduction, hostage-taking, extortion and murder of S., and of the robbery and murder of K. The court decided that the applicant’s actions in respect of K. had had the following qualifying features (кваліфікуючі ознаки) under the respective Articles of the Criminal Code: robbery (Article 187 § 4) and murder committed in order to conceal a robbery (Article 115 § 2 (9)) (aggravated by the fact that the murder had been committed against an elderly person (Article 67 § 1 (6)). According to the verdict, the qualifying features of the applicant’s actions with respect to S. were: the abduction of a person leading to grave consequences (Article 146 § 3), the taking of a hostage (Article 147 § 2), extortion with the threat of murder (Article 189 § 4), murder of a minor (Article 115 § 2 (2)), murder of a hostage (Article 115 § 2 (3)), murder based on motives of personal gain (Article 115 § 2 (6)), and murder committed by a person who had previously committed a murder (Article 115 § 2 (13)). The court sentenced him to life imprisonment for the murders under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13), and imposed further punishments for the less severe crimes (under Articles 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4) ranging from ten to fifteen years of imprisonment; those sentences were absorbed by the life sentence (see “Relevant legal framework” below for details). The court furthermore allowed a civil claim for damages lodged by S.’s father and awarded him compensation.12. Following an appeal by the applicant, on 10 October 2002 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld the decision of the trial court of 11 July 2002.The applicant’s first case before the Court13. On 2 April 2003 the applicant lodged an application with the Court (no. 16404/03) alleging that his conviction for the murder of K. had been based on incriminating evidence that had been obtained in violation of his right to remain silent and his right not to incriminate himself and that he had been hindered in the effective exercise of his right to benefit from the assistance of a lawyer when he had been questioned at the pre-trial stage of the proceedings (see paragraph 9 above).14. On 19 February 2009 the Court declared the application partly admissible and found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine, no. 16404/03, 19 February 2009).15. The Shabelnik judgment became final on 19 May 2009.Re-examination of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik judgment16. The applicant’s lawyer lodged an application with the Supreme Court for a review of the applicant’s criminal case in view of the first Shabelnik judgment (cited above). He asked the Supreme Court to quash the trial court’s judgment and its own 2002 decision upholding the original conviction. He asked that he and the applicant be present during the examination of the request.17. The prosecutor’s office also applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the case. It asked the court to amend the trial court’s judgment and the Supreme Court’s 2002 decision by striking out references to the records of the questioning of the applicant as a witness about K.’s murder and to the findings of the on-site reconstruction of that murder.18. On 30 April 2010 the Supreme Court allowed the above requests in part, quashed its own 2002 decision and remitted the case to a panel of three judges of the Supreme Court for a fresh examination in cassation proceedings.19. On 9 September 2010 the Supreme Court examined the case in the absence of the applicant but in the presence of his lawyer and a prosecutor. The Supreme Court excluded the applicant’s original confessions from the body of evidence but found that the rest of the evidence in the case file was sufficient to support the trial court’s finding that the applicant had murdered K. while trying to cover up an attempted robbery.The applicant’s second case before the Court20. On 28 February 2011 the applicant lodged his second application with the Court (no. 16404/03), alleging that the Supreme Court, in the course of re-examining his case in cassation proceedings, had breached a number of provisions of Article 6 of the Convention.21. On 1 June 2017 the Court declared the application admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court found in particular that “the Supreme Court’s reasoning and the procedure it [had] followed did not meet the requirements of fairness inherent in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention” and that there had therefore been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 2), no. 15685/11, §§ 54 and 55, 1 June 2017). It furthermore stated:“56. In view of the above conclusions the Court considers that ... only a full retrial could have provided, given the particular circumstances of the case, an appropriate forum for an adequate examination of the impact of the exclusion of the applicant’s confessions on the conclusiveness of the remaining evidence about the attack on K.”22. The Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment became final on 1 September 2017.Re-examination of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment23. On 5 December 2017 the applicant’s lawyer lodged an application with the Supreme Court for a review of the applicant’s criminal case in view of the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment. The applicant’s representative requested a full review of the trial court’s judgment of 11 July 2002 and the decision of the Supreme Court of 9 September 2010 on the grounds that those judicial decisions had been rendered as a result of an unfair trial. The lawyer furthermore requested that the applicant’s detention be substituted with a less strict preventive measure.24. On 16 May 2018 the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court, composed of sixteen judges, held a hearing in respect of the applicant’s case, with the participation of the applicant’s lawyer and a prosecutor. Having reiterated the circumstances of the applicant’s case and the findings of the domestic courts and of this Court in its judgments in respect of Shabelnik and Shabelnik (no. 2) and having concluded that it had the authority to quash in part the previous decisions delivered in respect of the applicant’s criminal case, it allowed the application of 5 December 2017 in part.25. The Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court held, in particular that:“... D.G. Shabelnik was convicted of a set of crimes, classified under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9), (13), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The murder of a minor, preceded by her abduction, and ... [followed by] a demand for ransom ... is covered by the following [provisions]: Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, and 189 § 4. The convict was found guilty under item 2 [of paragraph 2 of Article 115] because he had committed the murder of a minor S. (a ten-year-old), under item 3 because the murdered child had been taken as a hostage, under item 6 because by committing the murder the guilty person had [aimed] to obtain property (money in the amount of twenty thousand [US] dollars). These factual circumstances were established by the first-instance court.The ... murder and robbery of K. shall be excluded from the ultimate classification of the actions of D.G. Shabelnik, since the case in this part must be reviewed in its entirety, as the ECHR provided in [its] judgment in the case of Shabelnik v. Ukraine (No. 2) taking into account the conclusions of the ECHR in the judgment in the case of Shabelnik v. Ukraine.... in exercising such authority as the quashing of a judicial decision in part, a court shall decide on the punishment of a convicted person, taking into account any reduction in the number of acts [of which that person has been accused of], the exclusion of certain criminal activities, reclassification of actions, etc....The murder of a minor, S., by D.G. Shabelnik, namely the nature and location of the bodily injuries, the method of murder chosen by D.G. Shabelnik, the clearly [planned nature] of his actions, [and] the motive of personal gain that [he] placed above the life of a young child testify in sum to [the fact] that D.G. Shabelnik poses a special danger to society.D.G. Shabelnik, being a young, physically healthy, able-bodied man who did not accord to human life the highest possible value, ruthlessly and cold-bloodedly, by suffocation, killed his neighbour – young S., who had been on her way to school, luring her into his apartment. D.G. Shabelnik was aware that the victim was physically weaker because she had [only] reached the age of ten at the time of the crime and would not have been able to resist an adult, physically healthy man, owing to [her] physical helplessness. Killing the victim, D.G. Shabelnik put his motives of personal gain above the child’s life.The court did not establish any circumstances mitigating or aggravating [D.G. Shabelnik’s] liability for the criminal actions against S..Given these circumstances, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court concludes that the isolation of D.G. Shabelnik by means of life imprisonment meets the requirements of justice in the application of punishment and reflects the proportionality of the crime and punishment, and that only [the imposition of] such necessary and sufficient punishment can rectify him and prevent him from committing new crimes....... the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court:DECIDES:1. To allow in part the application of the defence counsel, M.O. Tarakhkalo, [lodged] in the interests of the convicted D.G. Shabelnik.2. To quash the sentence of the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal of 11 July 2002 and the decision of the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of 9 September 2010 concerning D.G. Shabelnik in the part concerning his conviction for robbery and the murder of K., [and], in this part, to remit the case for fresh judicial examination to the relevant court of first instance.3. To consider D.G. Shabelnik sentenced under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine to imprisonment for [the following] terms:under Article 146 § 3 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of ten years’ [imprisonment];under Article 147 § 2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of fifteen years’ [imprisonment];under Article 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of ten years’ [imprisonment], with confiscation of all property that the convicted person owns;under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6) of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to life imprisonment, with confiscation of all property that the convicted person owns.4. Under Article 70 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine to determine D.G. Shabelnik’s final punishment for a set of crimes by way of merging milder punishments into one heavier [punishment] in the form of life imprisonment, with confiscation of all property that the convicted person owns....”26. Three judges of the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court wrote a separate opinion in which they disagreed with the majority opinion in respect of the separation of the punishments.
