FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF SHABELNIK v. UKRAINE (NO. 3)

(Application no. 54806/18)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

4 November 2021

FINAL

04/02/2022

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 3),

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Lətif Hüseynov,
Jovan Ilievski,
Ivana Jelić,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 54806/18) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Dmitriy Grigoryevich Shabelnik (“the applicant”), on 13 November 2018;

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the observations submitted by the Government and the applicant’s observations in reply;

the written comments submitted by the Lviv Forum of Criminal Justice (“the third party”), which was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3);

Having deliberated in private on 12 October 2021,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 7 of the Convention that judicial review of his previous conviction resulted in a new punishment being imposed on him after the expiry of the statutory time-limit.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1979 and is currently serving a life sentence in Zhytomyr, Ukraine. Having been granted legal aid, he was represented by Mr M.O. Tarakhkalo and Ms V. Lebid, lawyers practising in Kyiv, Ukraine.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant

5. In October 2001, Ms K., an elderly woman, was found murdered in her flat. In December 2001, Ms S., a minor, was abducted and murdered.

6. On 10 December 2001, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of abducting S. in order to extort money from her parents and subsequently murdering her.

7. On 17 December 2001, the applicant appointed a lawyer.

8. On 19 December 2001, the applicant was charged with the above-mentioned offence, following an investigation during which he showed the police where he had hidden S.’s body and some of her belongings. Banknotes received as ransom from S.’s parents were found in his possession.

9. On 15 February 2002, apparently at his own request, the applicant was questioned as a witness about the circumstances of K.’s death. During the questioning, which took place without a lawyer present, he confessed to K.’s murder.
The following day, still acting as a witness, the applicant took part, without a lawyer present, in an on-site reconstruction of the attack on K. On 18 and 22 February 2002 he was questioned again, without a lawyer, concerning the attack.

10. On 25 February 2002 the investigating prosecutor opened criminal proceedings against the applicant in relation to K.’s murder and joined them to the criminal case concerning the abduction and murder of S.

11. On 11 July 2002 the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal, sitting as a trial court, convicted the applicant of the abduction, hostage-taking, extortion and murder of S., as well as the robbery and murder of K. The court found that the applicant’s actions in relation to K. had the following qualifying features (кваліфікуючі ознаки) under the relevant Articles of the Criminal Code: robbery (Article 187 § 4) and murder committed to conceal a robbery (Article 115 § 2 (9)), aggravated by the fact that the murder had been committed against an elderly person (Article 67 § 1 (6)). According to the judgment, the qualifying features of the applicant’s actions concerning S. were: abduction of a person leading to grave consequences (Article 146 § 3), hostage-taking (Article 147 § 2), extortion accompanied by a threat of murder (Article 189 § 4), murder of a minor (Article 115 § 2 (2)), murder of a hostage (Article 115 § 2 (3)), murder motivated by personal gain (Article 115 § 2 (6)), and murder committed by a person who had previously committed murder (Article 115 § 2 (13)). The court sentenced him to life imprisonment for the murders under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13), and imposed additional sentences for the less serious offences (under Articles 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4), ranging from ten to fifteen years’ imprisonment; those sentences were absorbed into the life sentence (see “Relevant legal framework” below for details). The court also allowed a civil claim for damages brought by S.’s father and awarded him compensation.

12. Following an appeal by the applicant, on 10 October 2002 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld the trial court’s decision of 11 July 2002.

The applicant’s first case before the Court

13. On 2 April 2003 the applicant lodged an application with the Court (no. 16404/03), alleging that his conviction for the murder of K. had been based on incriminating evidence obtained in breach of his right to remain silent and his right not to incriminate himself, and that he had been prevented from effectively exercising his right to legal assistance when questioned during the pre-trial stage of the proceedings (see paragraph 9 above).

14. On 19 February 2009 the Court declared the application partly admissible and found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine, no. 16404/03, 19 February 2009).

15.
The Shabelnik judgment became final on 19 May 2009.

Re-examination of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik judgment

16. The applicant’s lawyer applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the applicant’s criminal case in light of the first Shabelnik judgment (cited above). He requested that the Supreme Court quash the trial court’s judgment and its own 2002 decision upholding the original conviction. He also asked that both he and the applicant be present during the examination of the request.

17. The prosecutor’s office likewise applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the case. It requested that the court amend the trial court’s judgment and the Supreme Court’s 2002 decision by removing references to the records of the applicant’s questioning as a witness concerning K.’s murder and to the findings of the on-site reconstruction of that murder.

18. On 30 April 2010 the Supreme Court granted the above requests in part, quashed its own 2002 decision, and remitted the case to a panel of three Supreme Court judges for a fresh examination in cassation proceedings.

19. On 9 September 2010 the Supreme Court examined the case in the applicant’s absence but in the presence of his lawyer and a prosecutor. It excluded the applicant’s original confessions from the body of evidence but held that the remaining evidence in the case file was sufficient to support the trial court’s finding that the applicant had murdered K. while attempting to conceal an attempted robbery.

The applicant’s second case before the Court

20. On 28 February 2011 the applicant lodged his second application with the Court (no. 16404/03), claiming that, in re-examining his case in cassation proceedings, the Supreme Court had breached several provisions of Article 6 of the Convention.

21. On 1 June 2017 the Court declared the application admissible and found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In particular, it held that “the Supreme Court’s reasoning and the procedure it [had] followed did not meet the requirements of fairness inherent in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention” and that there had accordingly been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 2), no. 15685/11, §§ 54 and 55, 1 June 2017). It further stated:

“56. In view of the above conclusions the Court considers that ... only a full retrial could have provided, given the particular circumstances of the case, an appropriate forum for an adequate examination of the impact of the exclusion of the applicant’s confessions on the conclusiveness of the remaining evidence about the attack on K.”

22. The Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment became final on 1 September 2017.

Re-examination of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment

23. On 5 December 2017 the applicant’s lawyer applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the applicant’s criminal case in light of the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment.
The applicant’s representative sought a full review of the trial court’s judgment of 11 July 2002 and the Supreme Court’s decision of 9 September 2010 on the ground that those judicial decisions had resulted from an unfair trial. The lawyer also requested that the applicant’s detention be replaced with a less stringent preventive measure.24. On 16 May 2018 the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court, sitting as a panel of sixteen judges, held a hearing in the applicant’s case, with the participation of the applicant’s lawyer and a prosecutor. Having restated the circumstances of the applicant’s case and the findings of the domestic courts and of this Court in its judgments concerning Shabelnik and Shabelnik (no. 2), and having concluded that it had the authority to quash in part the previous decisions delivered in the applicant’s criminal case, it allowed the application of 5 December 2017 in part.25. The Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court held, in particular, that:“... D.G. Shabelnik was convicted of a series of crimes classified under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9), (13), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The murder of a minor, preceded by her abduction and ... [followed by] a demand for ransom ... is covered by the following [provisions]: Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, and 189 § 4. The convict was found guilty under item 2 [of paragraph 2 of Article 115] because he had murdered a minor, S. (a ten-year-old); under item 3 because the murdered child had been taken hostage; and under item 6 because, by committing the murder, the guilty person had [intended] to obtain property (money in the amount of twenty thousand [US] dollars). These factual circumstances were established by the first-instance court.The ... murder and robbery of K. shall be removed from the ultimate classification of the actions of D.G. Shabelnik, since this part of the case must be reviewed in its entirety, as the ECHR provided in [its] judgment in Shabelnik v. Ukraine (No. 2), taking into account the conclusions of the ECHR in its judgment in Shabelnik v. Ukraine.... when exercising the authority to quash a judicial decision in part, a court shall determine the punishment of a convicted person, taking into account any reduction in the number of acts [of which that person has been accused], the exclusion of certain criminal activities, the reclassification of actions, etc....The murder of the minor S. by D.G. Shabelnik, namely the nature and location of the bodily injuries, the method of murder selected by D.G. Shabelnik, the clearly [planned nature] of his actions, [and] the motive of personal gain that [he] placed above the life of a young child, demonstrate, taken together, [the fact] that D.G. Shabelnik poses a particular danger to society.D.G.
Shabelnik, being a young, physically healthy, able-bodied man who did not attach the highest possible value to human life, ruthlessly and cold-bloodedly killed his neighbour – young S., who had been on her way to school – by suffocating her after luring her into his apartment. D.G. Shabelnik was aware that the victim was physically weaker, as she had [only] reached the age of ten at the time of the crime and would have been unable to resist an adult, physically healthy man owing to [her] physical helplessness. In killing the victim, D.G. Shabelnik placed his motives of personal gain above the child’s life.

The court did not establish any circumstances mitigating or aggravating [D.G. Shabelnik’s] liability for the criminal acts against S.

Given these circumstances, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court concludes that the isolation of D.G. Shabelnik through life imprisonment meets the requirements of justice in the imposition of punishment and reflects the proportionality between the crime and the punishment, and that only [the imposition of] such necessary and sufficient punishment can reform him and prevent him from committing further crimes.

... the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court:

DECIDES:

1. To allow in part the application of defence counsel M.O. Tarakhkalo, [lodged] in the interests of the convicted D.G. Shabelnik.

2. To quash the judgment of the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal of 11 July 2002 and the decision of the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of 9 September 2010 concerning D.G. Shabelnik in so far as they relate to his conviction for the robbery and murder of K., [and], in this part, to remit the case for fresh judicial examination by the relevant court of first instance.

3. To consider D.G. Shabelnik sentenced under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine to imprisonment for [the following] terms:

under Article 146 § 3 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of ten years’ [imprisonment];

under Article 147 § 2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of fifteen years’ [imprisonment];

under Article 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to a term of ten years’ [imprisonment], with confiscation of all property owned by the convicted person;

under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6) of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – to life imprisonment, with confiscation of all property owned by the convicted person.

4. Under Article 70 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, to determine D.G. Shabelnik’s final punishment for the set of crimes by merging the milder punishments into the heavier [punishment] of life imprisonment, with confiscation of all property owned by the convicted person.

...”

26. Three judges of the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court issued a separate opinion in which they disagreed with the majority’s position concerning the separation of the punishments. They noted, in particular:

“...
In our opinion, it is erroneous to split the case and quash the court decisions only in the part concerning the conviction for the robbery and murder of K[...], as this resulted in an incorrect determination of the punishment in respect of the acts [committed] against S. attributed to D.G. Shabelnik....... The text of the judgment [of 11 July 2002] states: “Since D.G. Shabelnik did not obtain any money as a result of the robbery of K., he planned a new crime.” Thus, the court established a certain connection between the crimes against the two persons on account of a consistent motive of personal gain.... However, the Grand Chamber determined [that] the same punishment [should be imposed on] D.G. Shabelnik under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6) of the Criminal Code, despite the absence of an aggravating circumstance – [namely] the commission of a crime against an elderly person, K. – which worsened his situation compared with that before the case was split, because the scope of the charges had in fact been reduced (the classification no longer included two of the qualifying features [set out in] Article 115 § 2 of the Criminal Code) and there were no aggravating circumstances ...”

04/02/2022

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Mārtiņš Mits,

Ivana Jelić,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

the application (no. 54806/18) brought against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Dmitriy Grigoryevich Shabelnik (“the applicant”), on 13 November 2018;

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the Government’s observations and the applicant’s submissions in response;

the written observations provided by the Lviv Forum of Criminal Justice (“the third party”), which the President of the Section authorised to intervene under Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3;

Having deliberated in private on 12 October 2021,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 7 of the Convention that judicial reconsideration of his earlier conviction led to the imposition of a new punishment after the statutory time-limit had expired.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1979, the applicant is currently serving a life sentence in Zhytomyr, Ukraine. He was granted legal aid and represented by Mr M.O. Tarakhkalo and Ms V. Lebid, lawyers practising in Kyiv, Ukraine.

3. The Government’s Agent was Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The parties’ accounts of the relevant facts may be summarised as set out below.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant

5. In October 2001, Ms K., an elderly woman, was discovered murdered in her apartment. In December of the same year, Ms S., a minor, was abducted and killed.

6. On 10 December 2001, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of abducting S. for the purpose of extorting money from her parents and subsequently murdering her.

7. The applicant retained a lawyer on 17 December 2001.

8. On 19 December 2001, after an investigation in which he directed the police to the locations where he had concealed S.’s body and some of her possessions, the applicant was formally charged with the offence described above. Banknotes paid by S.’s parents as ransom were also found in his possession.

9. On 15 February 2002, apparently at his own request, the applicant was questioned as a witness about the circumstances surrounding K.’s death. During that interview, which was conducted without a lawyer present, he confessed to murdering K.
The following day, the applicant, who continued to be treated as a witness, took part in an on-site reconstruction of the attack on K. without legal representation. He was questioned again about the attack on 18 and 22 February 2002, on both occasions without a lawyer.

10. On 25 February 2002 the investigating prosecutor opened criminal proceedings against the applicant for K.’s murder and joined those proceedings to the criminal case relating to S.’s abduction and murder.

11. On 11 July 2002 the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal, sitting as a court of first instance, found the applicant guilty of abducting, taking hostage, extorting and murdering S., as well as robbing and murdering K. In relation to K., the court held that the applicant’s conduct had the following qualifying features (кваліфікуючі ознаки) under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code: robbery under Article 187 § 4 and murder committed to conceal a robbery under Article 115 § 2 (9), with the additional aggravating circumstance that the victim was elderly under Article 67 § 1 (6).

As stated in the judgment, the conduct concerning S. was legally characterised as abduction resulting in grave consequences under Article 146 § 3; hostage-taking under Article 147 § 2; extortion accompanied by a threat to kill under Article 189 § 4; murder of a minor under Article 115 § 2 (2); murder of a hostage under Article 115 § 2 (3); murder motivated by personal gain under Article 115 § 2 (6); and murder committed by a person who had previously committed murder under Article 115 § 2 (13).

For the murders, classified under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13), the applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment. The court also imposed prison terms ranging from ten to fifteen years for the less serious offences under Articles 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4, but those penalties were absorbed by the life sentence (see “Relevant legal framework” below for details). In addition, the court upheld a civil claim for damages brought by S.’s father and awarded him compensation.

12. The applicant appealed, but on 10 October 2002 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld the trial court’s judgment of 11 July 2002.

The applicant’s first case before the Court

13. On 2 April 2003 the applicant submitted an application to the Court (no. 16404/03). He alleged that his conviction for K.’s murder had relied on incriminating evidence obtained in breach of his right to remain silent and his privilege against self-incrimination. He further complained that, when questioned during the pre-trial proceedings, he had been prevented from effectively exercising his right to legal assistance (see paragraph 9 above).

14. In its judgment of 19 February 2009, the Court declared the application partly admissible and held that Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention had been violated (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine, no. 16404/03, 19 February 2009).

15.
The Shabelnik judgment became final on 19 May 2009.

Reconsideration of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik judgment

16. Relying on the first Shabelnik judgment (cited above), the applicant’s lawyer requested that the Supreme Court review the applicant’s criminal case. He sought the quashing of both the trial court’s judgment and the Supreme Court’s 2002 decision affirming the original conviction. He also requested that both he and the applicant be allowed to attend the examination of the application.

17. The prosecutor’s office likewise asked the Supreme Court to review the case. It sought amendments to the trial court’s judgment and the Supreme Court’s 2002 decision, specifically requesting the removal of references to the records of the applicant’s questioning as a witness concerning K.’s murder and to the findings obtained during the on-site reconstruction of the killing.

18. On 30 April 2010 the Supreme Court partly granted those requests. It set aside its 2002 decision and referred the case to a three-judge panel of the Supreme Court for a fresh examination in cassation proceedings.

19. On 9 September 2010 the Supreme Court considered the case without the applicant being present, although his lawyer and a prosecutor attended. While removing the applicant’s initial confessions from the body of evidence, it concluded that the remaining material in the case file was sufficient to uphold the trial court’s finding that the applicant had killed K. while attempting to conceal an attempted robbery.

The applicant’s second case before the Court

20. On 28 February 2011 the applicant submitted his second application to the Court (no. 16404/03), claiming that, during the cassation re-examination of his case, the Supreme Court had infringed several guarantees under Article 6 of the Convention.

21. On 1 June 2017 the Court declared the application admissible and held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention had been violated. In particular, it concluded that “the Supreme Court’s reasoning and the procedure it [had] followed did not meet the requirements of fairness inherent in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention” and, accordingly, found a breach of that provision (see Shabelnik v. Ukraine (no. 2), no. 15685/11, §§ 54 and 55, 1 June 2017). The Court further observed:

“56. In view of the above conclusions the Court considers that ... only a full retrial could have provided, given the particular circumstances of the case, an appropriate forum for an adequate examination of the impact of the exclusion of the applicant’s confessions on the conclusiveness of the remaining evidence about the attack on K.”

22. The judgment in Shabelnik (no. 2) became final on 1 September 2017.

Reconsideration of the applicant’s case following the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment

23. On 5 December 2017 the applicant’s lawyer applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the applicant’s criminal case in light of the Shabelnik (no. 2) judgment.
The applicant’s representative sought a comprehensive review of the trial court’s judgment dated 11 July 2002 and the Supreme Court’s decision of 9 September 2010, arguing that both rulings had resulted from unfair proceedings. Counsel also asked that the applicant’s detention be replaced by a more lenient preventive measure.

24. On 16 May 2018, the sixteen-judge Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court held a hearing in the applicant’s case, attended by the applicant’s lawyer and a prosecutor. After restating the circumstances of the case and reviewing the conclusions reached by the domestic courts and by this Court in Shabelnik and Shabelnik (no. 2), the Grand Chamber found that it was empowered to set aside parts of the earlier decisions in the applicant’s criminal proceedings. It therefore granted the application of 5 December 2017 in part.

25. In particular, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court stated:

“... D.G. Shabelnik was convicted of several offences classified under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 187 § 4 and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The murder of a minor, preceded by her abduction and ... [followed by] a ransom demand ..., falls within Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2 and 189 § 4. The conviction under item 2 [of paragraph 2 of Article 115] was based on the fact that the victim, S., was a ten-year-old minor; item 3 applied because the murdered child had been taken hostage; and item 6 applied because the offender had committed the murder with the aim of obtaining property, namely twenty thousand [United States] dollars. The first-instance court established those factual circumstances.

The ... murder and robbery of K. must be removed from the final legal classification of D.G. Shabelnik’s conduct because that part of the case requires a complete review, as indicated by the ECHR in Shabelnik v. Ukraine (No. 2), with due regard to the ECHR’s conclusions in Shabelnik v. Ukraine.

... when exercising its power to quash part of a judicial decision, a court must determine the convicted person’s punishment in light of any decrease in the number of alleged acts, the removal of particular criminal acts, the reclassification of conduct, and other relevant changes....

Taken together, the nature and location of the injuries inflicted during D.G. Shabelnik’s murder of the minor S., the method of killing he selected, the clearly [premeditated nature] of his conduct, and the profit-driven motive that [he] placed above the life of a young child demonstrate [that] D.G. Shabelnik presents a particular danger to society.

D.G.”
Shabelnik, a young, physically fit and able-bodied man who failed to place the highest value on human life, lured his neighbour, ten-year-old S., into his apartment while she was on her way to school and killed her by suffocation in a ruthless and cold-blooded manner. D.G. Shabelnik knew that, because of her age and resulting physical helplessness, the victim was weaker than he was and could not resist a healthy adult man. In killing the child, he placed his motives of personal gain above her life.

The court found no circumstances that either mitigated or aggravated D.G. Shabelnik’s liability for the criminal acts committed against S.

In view of those considerations, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court finds that isolating D.G. Shabelnik from society through life imprisonment satisfies the requirements of justice in sentencing and appropriately reflects the proportionality between the offence and the punishment. It further considers that only such a necessary and sufficient sentence is capable of reforming him and preventing him from committing further offences.

...

The Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court

DECIDES:

1. To grant in part the application submitted by defence counsel M.O. Tarakhkalo on behalf of the convicted person, D.G. Shabelnik.

2. To set aside the judgment of the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal dated 11 July 2002 and the decision of the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court dated 9 September 2010, in so far as they concern D.G. Shabelnik’s conviction for the robbery and murder of K., and to remit that part of the case to the competent first-instance court for a fresh judicial examination.

3. To regard D.G. Shabelnik as having been sentenced under Articles 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6), 146 § 3, 147 § 2, and 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine to the following terms of imprisonment:

under Article 146 § 3 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – ten years’ imprisonment;

under Article 147 § 2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – fifteen years’ imprisonment;

under Article 189 § 4 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – ten years’ imprisonment, together with confiscation of all property belonging to the convicted person;

under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6) of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – life imprisonment, together with confiscation of all property belonging to the convicted person.

4. Pursuant to Article 70 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, to determine D.G. Shabelnik’s final aggregate sentence by absorbing the lesser penalties into the more severe one, resulting in life imprisonment and confiscation of all property belonging to the convicted person.

...”

26. Three judges of the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court issued a separate opinion, disagreeing with the majority’s position regarding the separation of the sentences. In particular, they stated:

“...
In our view, it was wrong to sever the case and set aside the judicial decisions only insofar as they concerned the conviction for the robbery and murder of K[...]. That approach also resulted in an incorrect determination of the punishment for the acts against S. attributed to D.G. Shabelnik.......

The judgment of 11 July 2002 stated: “Because D.G. Shabelnik obtained no money from the robbery of K., he devised a plan to commit another offence.” The court thus found that the offences against the two victims were linked by a continuing motive of personal gain....

Nevertheless, the Grand Chamber imposed the same sentence on D.G. Shabelnik under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6) of the Criminal Code, despite the absence of the aggravating circumstance—namely, the commission of an offence against an elderly person, K. This left him in a worse position than before the case was severed, even though the scope of the charges had in fact been reduced: the legal classification no longer contained two of the qualifying elements provided for in Article 115 § 2 of the Criminal Code, and no aggravating circumstances remained ...”

Criminal proceedings brought against the applicant

5. In October 2001, an elderly woman, Ms K., was discovered murdered in her apartment. In December 2001, Ms S., who was a minor, was abducted and killed.

6. The applicant was arrested on 10 December 2001 on suspicion of having abducted S. to extort money from her parents and of subsequently murdering her.

8. On 19 December 2001, the applicant was formally charged with that offence. During the investigation, he had shown the police where he had concealed S.’s body and certain items belonging to her. Banknotes paid by S.’s parents as ransom were also found in his possession.

9. On 15 February 2002, apparently at the applicant’s own request, he was interviewed as a witness about the circumstances surrounding K.’s death. No lawyer was present during that questioning, in the course of which he admitted murdering K.

10. On 25 February 2002, the investigating prosecutor opened criminal proceedings against the applicant for K.’s murder and combined them with the criminal case relating to S.’s abduction and murder.

11. Sitting as a trial court, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal convicted the applicant on 11 July 2002 of abducting S., taking S. hostage, extorting and murdering S., and robbing and murdering K.
