SECOND SECTION

CASE OF GRAŽULEVIČIŪTĖ v. LITHUANIA

(Application no. 53176/17)


JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

14 December 2021


FINAL

14/03/2022


This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Gražulevičiūtė v. Lithuania,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Jon Fridrik Kjølbro, President,
Marko Bošnjak,
Aleš Pejchal,
Egidijus Kūris,
Branko Lubarda,
Pauliine Koskelo,
Saadet Yüksel, judges,

and Stanley Naismith, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 53176/17) against the Republic of Lithuania lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Lithuanian national, Ms Edita Gražulevičiūtė (“the applicant”), on 21 July 2017;

the decision to notify the Lithuanian Government (“the Government”) of the complaints concerning the right to a fair hearing, the right to respect for private life, and the right to an effective domestic remedy, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ submissions;

Having deliberated in private on 9 November 2021,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant is a doctor and clinical researcher. Following the death of one of her patients, she was suspended. The applicant complains that the final court decision exonerating her was overturned, in breach of the principle of res judicata and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. She further complains that she received no compensation for the damage caused by her suspension, in breach of Article 8.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1971 and resides in Vilnius. She was represented by Ms L. Meškauskienė, a lawyer practising in Vilnius.

3. The Government were represented by their Acting Agent, Ms L. Urbaitė.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

5. The applicant is a rheumatologist and has worked in that capacity since 2004. According to what appears to be an extract from a tax declaration submitted by the applicant, she had been working as a clinical researcher (tyrėja) since 12 November 2004. According to a separate document issued by a private company, the Centre for Clinical and Basic Research, the applicant worked for that company from May 2007 until July 2011 as a “consulting doctor”.

The applicant’s work as a clinical researcher and her suspension
6. In 2011, the applicant was conducting several clinical trials as part of a team of clinical researchers. At a certain stage, she was on maternity leave. One of the trials concerned a drug, tocilizumab, and during that trial, on 14 April 2011, a patient, V.S., died. On 27 September 2011, V.S.’s daughters asked the State Medicines Control Agency (Valstybinė vaistų kontrolės tarnyba – hereinafter “the SMCA”) to investigate whether the applicant had properly performed her duties during the clinical trial.

7. On 11 October 2011, the head of the SMCA ordered an unscheduled good clinical practice inspection (hereinafter – “the inspection”).

8. The inspection was conducted on 16 December 2011 and identified certain shortcomings, two of which were considered critical (dangerous) (kritiniai (pavojingi)) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraphs 53 and 54 below): firstly, failure to see the patient for an unscheduled appointment and, secondly, failure to report serious side-effects of the medicine being tested. In addition, the inspectors found ten significant (reikšmingi) and six minor (nereikšmingi) violations of those rules. They further concluded that the researchers’ actions might have harmed the health of the patient, V.S., leading to her death. According to the inspectors, V.S.’s welfare had not been ensured during the trial, thereby breaching her rights. The inspectors recommended that the measures set out in point 78 of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below) be imposed on the principal researcher, A.V., and the applicant.

9. By order (įsakymas) no. 1A-29 of 10 January 2012, issued by the head of the SMCA, the applicant and A.V. were suspended (nušalinti) from the clinical trial of tocilizumab being conducted at the Santariškės Clinics of Vilnius University Hospital (hereinafter – the first clinical trial). They were also prohibited from taking up new clinical trials. The order was to be published on the SMCA website.

10. By order (įsakymas) no. 1A-45 of 12 January 2012, issued by the head of the SMCA, the applicant, acting as the principal researcher (a status granted to her by the SMCA on 25 July 2011), was suspended from the clinical trial of tocilizumab conducted at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic (Vilniaus rajono centrinė poliklinika, hereinafter – the second clinical trial). The head of the SMCA annulled that order on 29 May 2012.

11. On 27 August 2011, the authorities opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances surrounding V.S.’s death. A forensic examination was ordered. On 11 October 2012, the experts issued report no. DM 6 (76)/13 (01), stating that V.S. had died of “sepsis which [had] developed as fast as lightning” (žaibiškai išsivystęs sepsis), rather than as a result of the applicant’s actions. The report also stated that sepsis could develop irrespective of whether tocilizumab was being taken.
It was also noted that, once informed of the deterioration in V.S.’s health, the applicant suspected that it was not due to rheumatologic causes but rather to other medical issues (complications), such as torn tendons or an infection, and had advised V.S. to consult a traumatology specialist. Administrative court proceedings concerning the applicant’s suspension as a researcher
12. On an unspecified date, the applicant challenged the suspension decisions (see paragraphs 9 and 10 above). She argued, among other things, that in reaching their conclusion the SMCA inspectors had failed to properly assess all the information and that the suspension decisions had therefore been unlawful and unfounded. As regards the circumstances surrounding V.S.’s death, the applicant argued that the relevant legal provisions did not impose an obligation to arrange an unscheduled diagnostic appointment [at the patient’s home] if the patient refused to attend a medical institution. The applicant stated that, after learning by telephone on 11 April 2011 that V.S.’s health had deteriorated, she had suspected complications. After consulting several other doctors, she had recommended that V.S. come to the hospital immediately, but V.S. had failed to do so. Consequently, it had become impossible to examine V.S. in a timely manner, which had ultimately resulted in her death.

13. In its response to the applicant’s action, the SMCA maintained that the findings set out in the inspection report had been objective. It also pointed out that the orders suspending the applicant had been issued “only because” two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below) had been established, and that only those two violations were therefore relevant to the court proceedings. Any other significant or minor violations had not formed the basis of the orders suspending the applicant.

14. On 6 December 2013 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court allowed the applicant’s claim in full. At the outset, the court clarified that, since the administrative courts examine disputes concerning actions or decisions affecting a claimant’s rights or obligations, the inspection report and the circumstances established therein (see paragraph 8 above) had not, as such, had any consequences for the applicant, meaning that the report could not be challenged in court. In other words, only the suspension orders had affected her rights or obligations, not the inspection report. Accordingly, the court would rule only on the circumstances referred to in the inspection report that had led to the orders suspending the applicant. Given that the applicant’s suspension and removal from clinical trials had been based on the two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 8 above), the court decided to confine its assessment to those matters.

15. Regarding the circumstances leading to V.S.’s death, the court established that, before the clinical trial, V.S. had signed an agreement to participate and had been informed whom to contact in the event of complications. The agreement had not included the applicant’s contact details, but only those of doctor J.R. and the principal researcher, A.V.
Although V.S.’s daughters had complained about the applicant’s actions, they had been unable to explain why V.S. had failed to contact the other researchers (J.R. or A.V.). The court also noted that, although V.S. had been required to inform the researchers of any possible deterioration in her health, once her condition began worsening on 9 April 2011, she had instead contacted an outside doctor whom she “personally knew” (asmeniškai pažįstamo gydytojo), had taken medication prescribed by that doctor, and had also taken methadone. She had contacted the applicant only several days later.

16. The court took into account the expert medical report obtained in the criminal proceedings, which had found that V.S. had died from acute sepsis and not because of the applicant’s actions (see paragraph 11 above). The court also questioned as a witness doctor J.R., who had participated in the same clinical trial and had been named as one of the contact persons in the event of complications. J.R. confirmed that she had heard the telephone conversation between V.S. and the applicant on 12 April 2011, during which the applicant “had insisted” (primygtinai liepė) that V.S. go to hospital to see a traumatology specialist. J.R. stated that when V.S. had ultimately been taken to hospital by ambulance on 13 April 2011, she had examined V.S. together with the applicant, and they had observed that V.S.’s leg was dark grey and that the complication was at least four days old. The court established that both the applicant and J.R. had examined V.S.; thus, one of the inspection’s conclusions against the applicant – that she had not participated in that examination – was unfounded.

17. The court further found that the inspectors had based their findings on the explanations provided by V.S.’s daughters, presuming that the applicant might have intentionally completed the medical and other records incorrectly in order to avoid trouble. However, that conclusion had no factual basis and rested solely on the daughters’ subjective view, expressed in testimony given after V.S.’s death, possibly in order to support their claims against the applicant.

18. Contrary to the suggestion made by V.S.’s daughters, the fact that the applicant had been on maternity leave (vaiko priežiūros atostogos) (see paragraph 6 above) was not significant because she had not been the only researcher involved in that clinical trial. Another doctor, J.R., had also participated and had the same responsibilities as the applicant. The court also expressly held that the applicant had not been an “irreplaceable person” during the clinical trial and that her maternity leave, in itself, had neither complicated the situation nor directly affected the conduct of the clinical trial.

19.
In light of the above, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court held that the inspectors’ conclusions concerning the breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, which had been characterised as the inappropriate organisation of unscheduled appointments, were incorrect and contradicted the factual circumstances.

20. The court then considered the second critical (dangerous) violation of the Good Clinical Practice Rules attributed to the applicant’s actions, namely her alleged failure to inform the sponsor of the clinical trial (užsakovas), within twenty-four hours, of any “serious side-effects” (sunkus nepageidaujamas reiškinys) which had resulted in death or disability or had had other serious consequences. Having examined the medical records and questioned an expert in clinical trials, the court established that the applicant had not breached this reporting requirement, since V.S. had initially experienced pain in her ankle, which was not a serious side-effect of the medication being trialled. The applicant had also promptly informed the sponsor when septic arthritis had been suspected in V.S.

21. The court therefore held that the inspectors’ conclusions had been based on their subjective assessment of the circumstances, without explaining why they had rejected the applicant’s arguments. In the court’s view, there was no evidence supporting a categorical conclusion that the applicant’s arguments had been unfounded. Accordingly, the court concluded that the applicant’s actions in reporting negative side-effects had been unjustifiably classified as a critical (dangerous) violation.

22. Having found that the inspectors had incorrectly concluded that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) violations, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court held that restrictions on the applicant’s work as a researcher had been imposed “unjustly” (neteisingai). The court therefore annulled the orders suspending the applicant from the clinical trials and barring her from taking part in new ones (see paragraphs 9 and 10 above).

23. This decision was not appealed and became final on 21 December 2013.

Administrative court proceedings concerning damage sustained as a result of the suspension
24. The applicant subsequently lodged a claim against the State, represented by the SMCA, seeking compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage which she maintained she had sustained as a result of her suspension from the clinical trials. The applicant submitted, among other things, that she had worked as a clinical researcher since 12 November 2004. She argued that she had suffered damage as a result of the SMCA’s unlawful actions in ordering her suspension, which had been annulled by the court in the earlier set of proceedings (see paragraphs 12-23 above). The applicant contended that, had she not been suspended, she would have received income from the first and second trials. She emphasised the “particularly high requirements of care and professionalism” (ypač aukšti atidumo ir rūpestingumo reikalavimai) applicable to the medical profession and submitted that any doubts as to her competence had tarnished her reputation and caused her considerable stress. The applicant specified that the first clinical trial had taken place from 11 October 2010 to 19 August 2013. In response to the applicant’s claim, the SMCA referred to the two critical violations identified by the inspectors: obligatory medical assistance had not been provided to V.S., in breach of the clinical trial protocol and the relevant regulations, and systemic failures to report serious side-effects had undermined the integrity of the critical trial data. Those two critical violations had formed the basis for the applicant’s suspension by the SMCA, and there had been nothing unlawful in the SMCA’s adoption of that measure.

25. On 4 November 2015 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court allowed the applicant’s claim in part. The court first noted that the applicant had claimed, as pecuniary damage, the income she would have received had the SMCA not issued the orders of 10 and 12 January 2012 suspending her from conducting the first and second clinical trials. The court also referred to Article 6.249 § 1 of the Civil Code concerning the concept of damage, and Articles 6.246 and 6.271 thereof (see paragraph 56 below), which provided that unlawful action was one of the necessary conditions for civil liability.

26. The court further pointed out that, under Article 58 § 2 of the Law on Administrative Proceedings (see paragraph 55 below), facts established in one administrative case by a court decision that had entered into force did not need to be proved again in other administrative cases involving the same parties. The court then referred to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court’s decision of 6 December 2013 concerning the dispute between the applicant and the SMCA, which had not been appealed against and had entered into force (see paragraphs 14-23 above).
The court pointed out that in the instant (second) set of proceedings “essentially the same parties [had been] involved”, and accordingly there was no need to prove again the conditions for public liability (viešosios atsakomybės sąlygos) in respect of the applicant. 27. As regards the first clinical trial, the court established that on 17 August 2010 an agreement had been concluded setting specific amounts to be paid per person for a complete trial. The court noted that the applicant had de facto conducted that clinical trial until she had been suspended from it by the SMCA order of 10 January 2012, which had subsequently been annulled by the administrative court. Given that one of the patients had died, the applicant had continued the clinical trial with the remaining five patients. On the basis of the case-file material, the court also established that the first clinical trial had been completed and documented as planned. There was no information in the file that could raise doubts as to whether the clinical trial would not have taken place because of the applicant’s actions. Moreover, contrary to what had been suggested by the defendant in those court proceedings, the medical records showed that it had been the applicant who had conducted the clinical trials with those five patients and that the trials had been completed in respect of them. 28. In the court’s view, it had to be emphasised that, as had been stated in the court decision of 6 December 2013, the inspectors’ conclusions concerning violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules had been erroneous, and that the SMCA order of 10 January 2012 suspending the applicant from the first trial had therefore been annulled. In the view of the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, this meant that the SMCA order removing the applicant from the first clinical trial had caused her pecuniary damage. 29. Lastly, the administrative court referred to the Supreme Court’s ruling of 13 November 2006 in civil case no. 3K-3-585/2006, in which it had held that the amount of income not received had to be proved by the plaintiff and had to be real. In determining whether the unreceived income could be regarded as pecuniary damage, it was necessary to consider whether that income had been planned, whether the plaintiff could reasonably have expected to receive it, and whether he or she had not received it because of unlawful actions by the defendant. In the instant case, had the applicant not been suspended from conducting the first clinical trial for the remaining five patients, she would have received 6,128 euros (EUR), a sum calculated in advance in the contract with the pharmaceutical company and which she had not received because of the “unlawful actions” (neteisėti veiksmai) of the SMCA. The court therefore awarded the applicant EUR 6,128 in respect of pecuniary damage. 30.
Regarding the second clinical trial, the court observed that on 26 August 2011 the applicant had entered into a clinical trial contract with a pharmaceutical company, under which she was to act as the principal researcher. She was later suspended from conducting that trial by the decision of 12 January 2012 (see paragraph 10 above). That being so, the court also noted that, as the applicant herself had confirmed in court, she had declined to participate in that second clinical trial, and therefore the trial had not taken place at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic. Although at the hearing the applicant had argued that she had withdrawn from the second clinical trial because of the psychological stress she had experienced as a result of the inspection of the first clinical trial, there was no evidence to support that assertion. It was also noteworthy that the pharmaceutical company had informed the SMCA that no patients had participated in or had even been selected for the second clinical trial. It followed that the applicant’s claim for pecuniary damage sustained in connection with the second clinical trial had to be dismissed.

31. Lastly, with regard to non-pecuniary damage, the court noted the applicant’s complaint that she had been suspended from conducting the first clinical trial and had been unable to engage in research activity for nearly two years, between 10 January 2012 and 6 December 2013 (see paragraphs 9 and 23 above), and that any doubts concerning her competence as a medical professional had damaged her reputation, particularly given that information about her suspension and about critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules had been published on the SMCA’s website. The court reiterated that the decision of 10 January 2012 suspending the applicant had been annulled as unlawful. It considered that the nearly two-year suspension from clinical trials could objectively have caused the applicant a “negative experience” (neigiami išgyvenimai), and decided to award her EUR 200 in compensation.

32. The applicant appealed, seeking an award of pecuniary damages in connection with the second clinical trial. She also challenged the failure to grant her claim for non-pecuniary damage in full. The SMCA likewise appealed, arguing that the applicant had failed to substantiate her claim for pecuniary damage in respect of the first clinical trial and was therefore not entitled to have that claim granted. It further submitted that the applicant should not receive a monetary award for non-pecuniary damage. The SMCA also argued that, in the second set of court proceedings, the first-instance court had not assessed the factual and legal aspects of the SMCA’s actions that were relevant to the issue of the State’s tortious liability.
In the SMCA’s view, the first-instance court had failed to consider that the head of the SMCA had issued the orders suspending the applicant on the basis of inspection findings revealing two critical violations – harm to a patient’s health and damage to the integrity of the trial data. The SMCA further argued that, in taking action against the applicant by adopting the decisions to suspend her, it had sought to protect the health of those participating in the clinical trials.

33. By a ruling of 30 January 2017, delivered in written proceedings, the Supreme Administrative Court allowed the SMCA’s appeal, rejected the applicant’s civil claim for damages and dismissed her appeal.

34. At the outset, the Supreme Administrative Court referred to its settled case-law concerning liability for damage caused by the unlawful actions of State institutions (Article 15 § 1 (3) of the Law on Administrative Proceedings, see paragraph 55 below), according to which the annulment of an administrative decision did not, in itself, provide a basis for finding that the actions of a State institution had been unlawful and that civil liability under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code therefore arose. The court also noted that, when determining the question of a State institution’s civil liability, Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code had to be applied as the “special norm” (specialioji norma), rather than the general norm laid down in the first paragraph of that Article (see paragraph 56 below).

35. The Supreme Administrative Court held that, in accordance with the principle of res judicata, factual and legal elements established in another judicial decision had to be accepted and could be relied on by the parties to the proceedings or by another interested party. Nevertheless, this did not mean that, in cases concerning damages, the court was not entitled to examine allegedly unlawful actions in the context of the State’s tortious liability. In the Supreme Administrative Court’s view, a legal assessment (teisinis vertinimas) of the circumstances established by a judicial decision was not to be regarded as denying the binding and res judicata effect of that decision. Moreover, disputes in administrative cases concerning the annulment of administrative decisions differed from disputes concerning compensation for damage caused by unlawful actions of the State (the Supreme Administrative Court referred to its earlier ruling of 14 July 2011 in case no. A502-3034/2011, delivered by an enlarged chamber). Similarly, the “verification”
(patikra) by the court of allegedly unlawful actions in the context of tortious liability constituted an assessment of the relevant factual and legal elements within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code, and such verification in proceedings for compensation for damage could be carried out without calling into question the facts established and assessed in another (previous) case (the Supreme Administrative Court referred to the same ruling and to its ruling of 8 October 2015 in case no. A3155-624/2015, also delivered by an enlarged chamber). The Supreme Administrative Court held that the first-instance court had failed to take all this case-law into consideration when examining the applicant’s claim for damages (see paragraphs 25-31 above) and had therefore adopted an unreasoned and unlawful decision.

36. The Supreme Administrative Court further pointed out that, when examining whether the State had incurred civil liability in the present case, account had to be taken not only of domestic legal regulations but also of international and European Union law. First, it cited the principle that a person’s interests and well-being take precedence over the interests of society and science. In that connection, it also referred to the general rule that scientific research was to be conducted freely, subject to legal rules protecting human rights, as set out, respectively, in Articles 2 and 15 of the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (see paragraph 48 below). The court noted that the principle enshrined in Article 2 of that Convention had been reflected in Article 5 § 1 of the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below) and point 2.3 of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below).

37. Second, at the material time, the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 (hereinafter “the Directive”; see paragraph 49 below) had applied and were relevant. In Lithuania, the Directive had been implemented through the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below), the Law on Pharmacy (see paragraph 52 below), and other relevant legal acts. The Directive established the principle of protecting individuals participating in clinical trials (point 2 of its preamble). It also laid down “core provisions” (esminės nuostatos), including that a clinical trial, once commenced, should be verified and supervised, that compliance with Good Clinical Practice standards should be monitored, and that, where objective evidence was identified, Member States had the right to suspend or discontinue the trial (point 18 of the preamble and Article 12 of the Directive; see paragraph 49 below). Lastly, a clinical trial could not begin until the ethics committee had given its approval.
In Lithuania, the authorities responsible for approving clinical trials were the SMCA and the Bioethics Committee (Article 18 § 4 of the Law on Pharmacy; see paragraph 52 below).

38. In the present case, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court had annulled the relevant part of the order concerning the applicant because it considered the findings of the investigation against her insufficient to substantiate the two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules and held that excessive weight had been given to the subjective explanations provided by V.S.’s daughters (see paragraph 17 above). For the Supreme Administrative Court, it was important to determine whether the authorities’ approvals for conducting the two clinical trials had complied with the law.

39. The Supreme Administrative Court held that the findings reached by the first-instance court in the first set of administrative proceedings, which had resulted in the annulment of the decision of 10 January 2012, “in themselves [had] not constitute[d] a basis” (savaime nėra pagrindas) for ruling that the SMCA’s actions had been unlawful within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. For the purposes of Article 6.271 § 4 of that Code, in assessing the State’s possible tortious liability, it was necessary to conduct a “broader legal assessment of the circumstances pertinent to the case and from a broader legal viewpoint” (turi būti atliktas platesnis bylai aktualių aplinkybių teisinis vertinimas platesniu teisiniu aspektu). When examining the damages claim, it was necessary to verify whether the SMCA’s decision to order the inspection, as well as the manner in which that inspection had been conducted, complied with the letter of the law: whether the SMCA and its employees had acted lawfully, since any essential violations of the rules applicable to such an inspection could provide a basis for finding that the individual administrative decision adopted on the basis of its conclusions had resulted in an unlawful action within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. For the Supreme Administrative Court, when examining whether the State incurred tortious liability, the relevant court also had to consider whether, in adopting the decision to suspend the applicant, the SMCA had acted as required by law with regard, firstly, to protecting individuals participating in the clinical trial and, secondly, to verifying the reliability of the data obtained during that trial.

40. Over several pages of its decision, the Supreme Administrative Court then analysed the SMCA’s actions in detail against the background of the applicable legal framework, particularly the Good Clinical Practice Rules. Ultimately, it concluded that, within the meaning of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, the SMCA had acted within its competence and as required by law.

41.
In light of the aforementioned legal regulations and the factual circumstances of the case, the Supreme Administrative Court shared the SMCA’s view that the agency, in applying to the applicant the measure prescribed in point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure, on the basis of the inspectors’ conclusion, had acted within the limits of its competence and pursued aims prescribed by law – to prevent violations of individuals’ rights; to guarantee their safety and well-being; to ensure that the clinical trial would be conducted in accordance with the Good Clinical Practice Rules and other legal acts; and to ensure that the data obtained during clinical trials would be reliable and of good quality. The Supreme Administrative Court saw no reason to disagree with those arguments of the SMCA.

42. The Supreme Administrative Court further noted that the relevant legal acts did not grant the head of the SMCA discretion to “revise” (revizuoti) the inspectors’ conclusions or to “correct them” (atitinkamai jas koreguoti). Likewise, in performing his function, the head of the SMCA had no right to disregard those conclusions. The inspectors’ conclusions, set out in the relevant report (see paragraph 8 above), therefore constituted the factual basis for applying measures to the clinical researcher. The lawfulness and reasonableness of the inspectors’ conclusions could be reviewed only “in court” (tik teismine tvarka), by challenging a decision imposing measures on a researcher.

43. The Supreme Administrative Court also agreed with the defendant’s position that, once the inspectors’ conclusions unfavourable to the applicant had been received and specified – namely, that she had committed two critical (dangerous) violations – the head of the SMCA could only adopt the decision to suspend her. The mere fact that the order suspending the applicant had subsequently been annulled by the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court did not mean that the SMCA’s actions in adopting that order had been unlawful within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. It had to be stressed that, during the first set of court proceedings, the order of 10 January 2012 concerning the applicant had been annulled not because the court had established any of the absolute grounds for annulment set out in Article 89 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (see paragraph 55 below), but because it had disagreed with the inspectors’ reasoning that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules. This meant that the order of 10 January 2012 concerning the applicant’s suspension had not been unlawful ab initio.

44. The Supreme Administrative Court also reconsidered the factual circumstances relating to the two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules attributed to the applicant by the inspection.
Regarding the first critical violation, the Supreme Administrative Court reviewed the sequence of events leading to S.V.’s death and how those events had been recorded in the inspection report. The court found that the facts established by the inspection had not been contradicted by any other information in the case file, and that they showed that the applicant had failed to ensure that, when side-effects occurred on 11 April 2011, V.S. would receive proper medical care. The applicant had also failed to take effective measures to ensure that unscheduled medical appointments would take place, as required by the Good Clinical Practice Rules.

45. In its reasoning, the Supreme Administrative Court also referred to the addendum to the agreement to participate in the clinical trial, signed by both V.S. and the applicant on 6 April 2011, which partly amended the initial clinical trial agreement concluded on 9 November 2010. The addendum warned of a potentially higher risk of serious, and sometimes fatal, infection from the medication tested during that clinical trial. In the Supreme Administrative Court’s view, that addendum had imposed on the applicant, as a researcher, an “increased duty of care” (reikalavo iš tyrėjo padidinto budrumo) to ensure that the rights and well-being of the patients participating in the clinical trial, including V.S., remained protected. The Supreme Administrative Court therefore considered that the SMCA had acted within its competence in imposing measures on the applicant.

46. As regards the second critical (dangerous) violation of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, concerning the reporting of serious side-effects (see paragraph 8 above), the Supreme Administrative Court also held that “there were data in the case file” indicating that the inspection had established that the applicant had not taken measures to guarantee the “quality, completeness and reliability” of the clinical trial documents (dokumentų kokybę, pilnumą ir patikimumą). The Supreme Administrative Court further considered that, under point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure, the first critical (dangerous) violation of the Good Clinical Practice Rules alone had been sufficient to suspend the applicant, and that the second critical violation identified during the inspection had essentially been connected to the first violation and had had no bearing on the decision to suspend the applicant.

47. In light of the foregoing, the Supreme Administrative Court concluded that the SMCA, in adopting order no.
1A-29, within the meaning of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, had acted in compliance with Article 18 § 1 of the Law on Pharmacy and points 78, 79 and 791 of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below), as it had sought to protect the rights and well-being of individuals participating in clinical trials, as well as to ensure that the data gathered during those trials were reliable and of high quality. Contrary to the findings of the first-instance court (see paragraphs 25-31 above), there were no grounds for concluding that the SMCA had acted improperly. This also meant that the State could not be held civilly liable under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code, since there had been no unlawful actions on the part of the SMCA – an indispensable element for such a finding.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Council of Europe instruments and European Union law

48. The Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Dignity of the Human Being with regard to the Application of Biology and Medicine: Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (known as the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine), which entered into force in respect of Lithuania on 1 February 2003, reads, in so far as relevant, as follows:

Article 2 – Primacy of the human being

“The interests and welfare of the human being shall prevail over the sole interest of society or science.”

Article 15 – General rule

“Scientific research in the field of biology and medicine shall be carried out freely, subject to the provisions of this Convention and the other legal provisions ensuring the protection of the human being.”

49. Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in conducting clinical trials on medicinal products for human use reads, in so far as relevant, as follows:

“Whereas:

... (2) The accepted basis for conducting clinical trials in humans is founded on the protection of human rights and the dignity of the human being with regard to the application of biology and medicine ...

... (18) It is also necessary to provide for the monitoring of adverse reactions occurring in clinical trials ... in order to ensure the immediate cessation of any clinical trial involving an unacceptable level of risk ...”

Article 3

Protection of clinical trial subjects

“1. This Directive shall apply without prejudice to national provisions on the protection of clinical trial subjects where they are more comprehensive than the provisions of this Directive ...

2. A clinical trial may be undertaken only if, in particular:
(a) the foreseeable risks and inconveniences have been balanced against the anticipated benefit for the individual trial subject and other current and future patients. A clinical trial may be started only if the Ethics Committee and/or the competent authority concludes that the expected therapeutic and public-health benefits justify the risks, and may continue only if compliance with this requirement is continuously monitored;

(b) the trial subject ... has had the opportunity, during a prior interview with the investigator or a member of the investigating team, to understand the trial’s objectives, risks and inconveniences, and the conditions under which it is to be conducted, and has also been informed of his right to withdraw from the trial at any time;

(c) the subject’s rights to physical ... integrity ... are protected;

(d) the trial subject ... has provided written consent after being informed of the nature, significance, implications and risks of the clinical trial ...;

... 3. The medical care provided to subjects, and medical decisions made on their behalf, shall be the responsibility of an appropriately qualified doctor ... 4. The subject shall be given a contact point from which he may obtain further information.”

Article 12

Suspension of the trial or infringements

“1. Where a Member State has objective grounds to consider that the conditions in the request for authorisation ... are no longer fulfilled, or has information giving rise to doubts about the safety or scientific validity of the clinical trial, it may suspend or prohibit the clinical trial and shall notify the sponsor accordingly. ... 2. Where a competent authority has objective grounds to consider that the sponsor, investigator, or any other person involved in conducting the trial no longer fulfils the obligations laid down, it shall immediately inform that person, specifying the action to be taken to remedy the situation. The competent authority concerned shall immediately inform the Ethics Committee, the other competent authorities and the Commission of that course of action.”

CASE OF GRAŽULEVIČIŪTĖ v. LITHUANIA

(Application no. 53176/17)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

14 December 2021

FINAL

14 March 2022

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment is final. It may nevertheless undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Gražulevičiūtė v. Lithuania,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Jon Fridrik Kjølbro, President,  
Marko Bošnjak,  
Aleš Pejchal,  
Egidijus Kūris,  
Branko Lubarda,  
Pauliine Koskelo,  
Saadet Yüksel, judges,

and Stanley Naismith, Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the application against the Republic of Lithuania (no. 53176/17), lodged with the Court on 21 July 2017 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Edita Gražulevičiūtė, a Lithuanian national (“the applicant”);

the decision to notify the Lithuanian Government (“the Government”) of the complaints relating to the right to a fair hearing, respect for private life, and an effective domestic remedy, while declaring the rest of the application inadmissible;

the observations submitted by the parties;

Having held private deliberations on 9 November 2021,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant is a physician and clinical researcher. She was suspended after one of her patients died. Relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the principle of res judicata, she complains that the final judicial decision exonerating her was subsequently overturned. She further alleges a violation of Article 8 because she received no compensation for the harm caused by her suspension.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1971, the applicant resides in Vilnius. She was represented by Ms L. Meškauskienė, a lawyer practising in Vilnius.

3. The Government’s representative was their Acting Agent, Ms L. Urbaitė.

4. The parties’ accounts allow the relevant circumstances to be summarised as follows.

5. The applicant is a rheumatologist and has practised in that field since 2004. A document submitted by her, apparently an extract from a tax declaration, indicates that she had worked as a clinical researcher (tyrėja) since 12 November 2004. A separate document issued by a private company, the Centre for Clinical and Basic Research, states that she was employed there as a “consulting doctor” between May 2007 and July 2011.

The applicant’s activities as a clinical researcher and her suspension
6. In 2011, the applicant worked as a clinical researcher alongside a team of other researchers, conducting several clinical trials. For part of that period, she was on maternity leave. One trial involved the drug tocilizumab. On 14 April 2011, V.S., a patient participating in that trial, died. On 27 September 2011, V.S.’s daughters requested that the State Medicines Control Agency (Valstybinė vaistų kontrolės tarnyba – hereinafter “the SMCA”) investigate whether the applicant had properly discharged her duties in connection with the trial.

7. On 11 October 2011, the head of the SMCA ordered an unscheduled good clinical practice inspection (hereinafter “the inspection”).

8. Conducted on 16 December 2011, the inspection identified a number of shortcomings. Two were classified as critical (dangerous) (kritiniai (pavojingi)) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraphs 53 and 54 below): the failure to see the patient at an unscheduled appointment and the failure to report serious side-effects of the medicine under investigation. The inspectors also recorded ten significant (reikšmingi) and six minor (nereikšmingi) violations of those rules. They further considered that the researchers’ conduct might have harmed V.S.’s health and contributed to her death. In their view, V.S.’s welfare had not been safeguarded during the trial, thereby violating her rights. They recommended that the measures provided for in point 78 of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below) be applied to the principal researcher, A.V., and to the applicant.

9. By order (įsakymas) no. 1A-29, issued by the head of the SMCA on 10 January 2012, the applicant and A.V. were suspended (nušalinti) from the tocilizumab trial taking place at the Santariškės Clinics of Vilnius University Hospital (hereinafter “the first clinical trial”). They were also barred from undertaking new clinical trials. The order was to be published on the SMCA’s website.

10. In a further order (įsakymas), no. 1A-45 of 12 January 2012, the head of the SMCA suspended the applicant, in her capacity as principal researcher—a status granted to her by the SMCA on 25 July 2011—from the tocilizumab trial being conducted at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic (Vilniaus rajono centrinė poliklinika, hereinafter “the second clinical trial”). On 29 May 2012, the head of the SMCA annulled that order himself.

11. Meanwhile, on 27 August 2011, the authorities had opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances surrounding V.S.’s death and ordered a forensic examination. The experts issued report no. DM 6 (76)/13 (01) on 11 October 2012. It concluded that V.S. had died from “sepsis which [had] developed as fast as lightning” (žaibiškai išsivystęs sepsis), rather than as a result of the applicant’s actions. The report added that sepsis could arise irrespective of whether tocilizumab was being taken.
It was further observed that, after learning that V.S.’s health had worsened, the applicant suspected that the decline was attributable not to rheumatologic causes but to other medical problems or complications, such as torn tendons or an infection. She therefore advised V.S. to consult a traumatology specialist.

Administrative court proceedings concerning the applicant’s suspension from her research position
12. On an unspecified date, the applicant contested the suspension decisions referred to in paragraphs 9 and 10 above. She submitted, inter alia, that the SMCA inspectors had failed to assess all the available information properly and that the decisions were consequently unlawful and unfounded. With regard to the circumstances of V.S.’s death, she maintained that the applicable legal framework did not require an unscheduled diagnostic visit to be arranged at a patient’s home where the patient had refused to attend a medical institution. The applicant stated that, after learning by telephone on 11 April 2011 that V.S.’s condition had deteriorated, she had suspected complications. Following consultations with several other doctors, she had advised V.S. to come to the hospital immediately, but V.S. had failed to do so. It had therefore become impossible to examine her promptly, ultimately resulting in her death.

13. In response to the applicant’s action, the SMCA maintained that the findings recorded in the inspection report were objective. It further stated that the suspension orders had been issued “only because” the inspectors had identified two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below). Accordingly, only those two breaches were relevant to the judicial proceedings; the suspension orders had not been based on any of the other violations classified as significant or minor.

14. On 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court allowed the applicant’s claim in full. It first explained that administrative courts adjudicated disputes concerning actions or decisions affecting a claimant’s rights or obligations. The inspection report and the circumstances recorded in it (see paragraph 8 above) had not, in themselves, produced any consequences for the applicant and were therefore not open to judicial challenge. Only the suspension orders, rather than the report, had affected her rights or obligations. The court would thus rule solely on those findings in the inspection report that had given rise to the suspension orders. Since the applicant’s suspension and exclusion from clinical trials had rested on two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 8 above), the court confined its examination to those matters.

15. In examining the circumstances preceding V.S.’s death, the court found that, before the clinical trial began, V.S. had signed an agreement to participate and had been told whom she should contact if complications arose. The agreement did not contain the applicant’s contact details; it listed only those of Dr J.R. and the principal researcher, A.V.
Although V.S.’s daughters had raised complaints about the applicant’s conduct, they could not explain why V.S. had not contacted either of the other researchers, J.R. or A.V. The court further observed that V.S. had been required to notify the researchers of any deterioration in her health. Nevertheless, when her condition began to worsen on 9 April 2011, she consulted an outside doctor whom she “personally knew” (asmeniškai pažįstamo gydytojo), took medication prescribed by that doctor, and also used methadone. She did not contact the applicant until several days later.

16. The court considered the expert medical report prepared during the criminal proceedings, which concluded that V.S. had died from acute sepsis rather than as a result of the applicant’s actions (see paragraph 11 above). It also heard evidence from J.R., a doctor who had participated in the same clinical trial and was listed as one of the persons to be contacted if complications arose. J.R. confirmed that she had overheard the telephone conversation between V.S. and the applicant on 12 April 2011, during which the applicant “had insisted” (primygtinai liepė) that V.S. attend hospital and consult a traumatology specialist. According to J.R., when an ambulance eventually brought V.S. to hospital on 13 April 2011, she and the applicant examined V.S. together. They observed that V.S.’s leg was dark grey and that the complication had existed for at least four days. The court therefore determined that both J.R. and the applicant had examined V.S. and that the inspection’s finding against the applicant—that she had not participated in the examination—was unfounded.

17. The court additionally found that the inspectors had relied on statements made by V.S.’s daughters and had assumed that the applicant might deliberately have entered inaccurate information in the medical and other records to avoid trouble. That conclusion, however, had no factual foundation. It reflected only the daughters’ subjective opinion, expressed in testimony after V.S.’s death, possibly to support their claims against the applicant.

18. Contrary to the assertions of V.S.’s daughters, the applicant’s maternity leave (vaiko priežiūros atostogos) (see paragraph 6 above) was immaterial, since she was not the sole researcher involved in the clinical trial. J.R., another doctor, had participated in the trial and bore the same responsibilities as the applicant. The court expressly found that the applicant had not been an “irreplaceable person” in the trial and that her maternity leave had neither complicated the circumstances nor directly affected the conduct of the clinical trial.

19.
In view of the foregoing, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court found that the inspectors’ conclusions concerning a breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, characterised as the improper organisation of unscheduled appointments, were erroneous and inconsistent with the facts.

20. The court next examined the second critical (dangerous) breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules attributed to the applicant: her alleged failure to notify the clinical-trial sponsor (užsakovas), within twenty-four hours, of any “serious side-effects” (sunkus nepageidaujamas reiškinys) resulting in death, disability, or other serious consequences. After reviewing the medical records and questioning a clinical-trials expert, the court determined that the applicant had not violated the reporting requirement. V.S. had initially suffered ankle pain, which did not constitute a serious side-effect of the medication under trial. Moreover, as soon as septic arthritis was suspected, the applicant informed the sponsor.

21. The court therefore concluded that the inspectors’ findings had rested on their subjective assessment of the circumstances and that they had failed to explain why the applicant’s arguments had been rejected. In the court’s view, no evidence supported a definitive finding that those arguments were unfounded. It accordingly held that the applicant’s conduct in reporting adverse side-effects had been unjustifiably classified as a critical (dangerous) violation.

22. Having found that the inspectors had wrongly determined that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) violations, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court ruled that the restrictions placed on her work as a researcher had been imposed “unjustly” (neteisingai). It consequently annulled the orders suspending her from the clinical trials and barring her from participation in new trials (see paragraphs 9 and 10 above).

23. No appeal was lodged against that decision, which became final on 21 December 2013.

Administrative court proceedings concerning damage sustained as a result of the suspension
24. The applicant subsequently brought a claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage against the State, represented by the SMCA, alleging that she had suffered such damage as a result of her suspension from the clinical trials. She stated, among other things, that she had worked as a clinical researcher since 12 November 2004. In her view, the damage had resulted from the SMCA’s unlawful decisions to suspend her, which had been annulled by the court in the previous proceedings (see paragraphs 12-23 above). She maintained that, but for the suspension, she would have earned income from both the first and the second trials. Emphasising the “particularly high requirements of care and professionalism” (ypač aukšti atidumo ir rūpestingumo reikalavimai) governing the medical profession, she asserted that doubts cast on her competence had harmed her reputation and caused her considerable stress. She further specified that the first clinical trial had run from 11 October 2010 until 19 August 2013. In reply, the SMCA relied on the two critical violations identified by the inspectors: the failure to provide V.S. with mandatory medical assistance, contrary to the clinical-trial protocol and the applicable regulations, and systemic failures to report serious side-effects, which had undermined the integrity of the critical trial’s data. The SMCA contended that those two critical violations had justified the applicant’s suspension and that its decision to impose that measure had not been unlawful.

25. On 4 November 2015 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court upheld the applicant’s claim in part. It first observed that the pecuniary damage sought by the applicant represented the income she would have earned had the SMCA not issued the orders of 10 and 12 January 2012 suspending her from conducting the first and second clinical trials. The court also cited Article 6.249 § 1 of the Civil Code, concerning the concept of damage, together with Articles 6.246 and 6.271 of that Code (see paragraph 56 below), under which unlawful conduct constituted one of the necessary conditions for civil liability.

26. The court further noted that, pursuant to Article 58 § 2 of the Law on Administrative Proceedings (see paragraph 55 below), facts established by a final judicial decision in one administrative case did not have to be proved again in another administrative case involving the same parties. It then referred to the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court’s decision of 6 December 2013 in the dispute between the applicant and the SMCA. That decision had not been appealed against and had become final (see paragraphs 14-23 above).
The court observed that “essentially the same parties [had been] taking part” in the present, second set of proceedings. It was therefore unnecessary to establish anew whether the conditions for public liability (viešosios atsakomybės sąlygos) had been met in the applicant’s case.

27. As regards the first clinical trial, the court found that an agreement had been concluded on 17 August 2010 specifying the amount payable per participant upon completion of the trial. The applicant had, in practice, conducted the trial until the SMCA suspended her by an order of 10 January 2012, which was subsequently annulled by the administrative court. After one patient died, she continued the trial with the other five participants. The case-file material further demonstrated that the first trial had been completed and documented in accordance with the plan. Nothing in the file suggested that the trial might not have taken place because of the applicant’s conduct. Furthermore, contrary to the defendant’s submissions in those proceedings, the medical records confirmed that the applicant herself had conducted and completed the clinical trials involving the five remaining patients.

28. The court stressed that, as stated in the decision of 6 December 2013, the inspectors’ findings concerning breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules had been incorrect. For that reason, the SMCA’s order of 10 January 2012 suspending the applicant from the first trial had been annulled. In the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court’s assessment, the applicant had consequently sustained pecuniary damage as a result of the SMCA’s decision to remove her from that trial.

29. Finally, the administrative court relied on the Supreme Court’s ruling of 13 November 2006 in civil case no. 3K-3-585/2006. In that ruling, the Supreme Court had held that plaintiffs were required to prove the amount of lost income claimed and that the amount had to be realistic. In determining whether income not received constituted pecuniary damage, it was necessary to consider whether the income had been anticipated, whether the plaintiff could reasonably have expected to obtain it, and whether its loss resulted from the defendant’s unlawful actions. Had the applicant not been suspended from conducting the first clinical trial in respect of the five remaining patients, she would have earned 6,128 euros (EUR). That amount had been fixed in advance in her contract with the pharmaceutical company, and she had failed to receive it because of the SMCA’s “unlawful actions” (neteisėti veiksmai). The court therefore awarded her EUR 6,128 in compensation for pecuniary damage.

30.
As to the second clinical trial, the court observed that, on 26 August 2011, the applicant had entered into a clinical-trial agreement with a pharmaceutical company under which she was to act as the principal researcher. She was subsequently suspended from conducting the trial by the decision of 12 January 2012 (see paragraph 10 above). However, as the applicant herself acknowledged at the hearing, she had declined to participate in the second trial, which consequently did not take place at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic. Although she maintained that she had withdrawn because of the psychological stress caused by the inspection of the first trial, no evidence supported that assertion. The court also considered it significant that the pharmaceutical company had notified the SMCA that no patients had participated in, or even been selected for, the second trial. Accordingly, the applicant’s claim for pecuniary damage relating to that trial had to be rejected.

31. Turning to non-pecuniary damage, the court noted the applicant’s complaint that her suspension from the first clinical trial had prevented her from carrying out research activities for almost two years, from 10 January 2012 to 6 December 2013 (see paragraphs 9 and 23 above). She further claimed that doubts cast on her professional competence had harmed her reputation, particularly because the SMCA had published on its website information concerning her suspension and critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules. The court reiterated that the decision of 10 January 2012 suspending her had been annulled as unlawful. Finding that exclusion from clinical trials for nearly two years could objectively have caused her a “negative experience” (neigiami išgyvenimai), it awarded her EUR 200 in compensation.

32. The applicant appealed, seeking compensation for pecuniary damage arising from the second clinical trial and challenging the failure to allow her non-pecuniary damage claim in full. The SMCA likewise appealed, contending that she had not substantiated her pecuniary-damage claim concerning the first clinical trial and was therefore not entitled to compensation under that head. It further argued that no monetary award should be made for non-pecuniary damage. In addition, the SMCA submitted that, in the second set of proceedings, the first-instance court had failed to examine the factual and legal aspects of the agency’s conduct that were relevant to determining the State’s liability in tort.
In the SMCA’s submission, the first-instance court had overlooked the fact that its head had ordered the applicant’s suspension on the basis of inspection findings identifying two critical violations: harm to a patient’s health and impairment of the integrity of the trial data. The SMCA further maintained that, in adopting the decisions to suspend the applicant, it had acted with the aim of protecting the health of the clinical-trial participants.

33. On 30 January 2017, following written proceedings, the Supreme Administrative Court granted the SMCA’s appeal, rejected the applicant’s civil claim for damages and dismissed her appeal.

34. The Supreme Administrative Court began by referring to its settled case-law on liability for damage resulting from unlawful acts by State institutions under Article 15 § 1 (3) of the Law on Administrative Proceedings (see paragraph 55 below). According to that case-law, the mere annulment of an administrative decision did not establish that the actions of a State institution had been unlawful or, consequently, that civil liability arose under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. The court also stated that the determination of a State institution’s civil liability was governed by Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, which constituted the “special provision” (specialioji norma), rather than by the general rule contained in the first paragraph of that Article (see paragraph 56 below).

35. The Supreme Administrative Court found that, under the principle of res judicata, factual and legal matters established by another judicial decision had to be accepted and could be relied on by the parties to the proceedings or by any other interested party. Nevertheless, that principle did not prevent a court hearing a damages case from examining allegedly unlawful conduct in the context of the State’s tortious liability. In the Supreme Administrative Court’s view, a legal assessment (teisinis vertinimas) of circumstances already established by a judicial decision did not negate that decision’s binding force or res judicata effect. Furthermore, administrative disputes concerning the annulment of administrative decisions were distinct from those relating to compensation for damage caused by unlawful acts of the State. In that connection, the Supreme Administrative Court cited its earlier ruling of 14 July 2011 in case no. A502-3034/2011, delivered by an enlarged chamber. Similarly, the “verification”
The court’s review (patikra) of allegedly unlawful conduct for the purposes of tort liability involved assessing the relevant factual and legal components under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. In proceedings seeking compensation for damage, that review could be carried out without calling into question the facts established, or their assessment, in earlier proceedings. In this regard, the Supreme Administrative Court referred both to the same judgment and to its judgment of 8 October 2015 in case no. A3155-624/2015, which had likewise been delivered by an enlarged chamber. It held that, when considering the applicant’s claim for damages (see paragraphs 25-31 above), the first-instance court had failed to take account of all the relevant case-law and had consequently issued an unlawful and inadequately reasoned decision.

36. The Supreme Administrative Court further stated that the question of the State’s civil liability in the present case had to be examined not only under domestic law, but also in the light of international and European Union law. It first invoked the principle that the interests and welfare of the individual take precedence over the sole interests of society or science. In that context, it also referred to the general rule that scientific research must be conducted freely while respecting legal provisions safeguarding human rights, as laid down respectively in Articles 2 and 15 of the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (see paragraph 48 below). According to the court, the principle contained in Article 2 of that Convention was also embodied in Article 5 § 1 of the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below) and point 2.3 of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below).

37. Secondly, the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 (“the Directive”; see paragraph 49 below) had been applicable and relevant at the material time. Lithuania had transposed the Directive through the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below), the Law on Pharmacy (see paragraph 52 below), and other pertinent legal instruments. Point 2 of the Directive’s preamble established the principle that individuals participating in clinical trials must be protected. The Directive also laid down “core provisions” (esminės nuostatos): once a clinical trial had begun, it had to be reviewed and supervised, and its conformity with Good Clinical Practice standards had to be monitored. Where objective evidence was identified, Member States were entitled to suspend or terminate the trial (point 18 of the preamble and Article 12 of the Directive; see paragraph 49 below). Finally, no clinical trial could begin without the approval of the ethics committee.
In Lithuania, responsibility for approving clinical trials lay with the SMCA and the Bioethics Committee under Article 18 § 4 of the Law on Pharmacy (see paragraph 52 below).

38. In the applicant’s case, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court had set aside the relevant part of the order relating to her. It found that the investigation’s conclusions concerning the applicant were insufficient to establish the two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules and that excessive weight had been attached to the subjective accounts provided by V.S.’s daughters (see paragraph 17 above). The Supreme Administrative Court considered it necessary to determine whether the authorities’ approvals for conducting the two clinical trials had complied with the law.

39. The Supreme Administrative Court found that the conclusions reached by the first-instance court in the initial administrative proceedings, which had resulted in the annulment of the decision of 10 January 2012, did “not in themselves constitute a basis” (savaime nėra pagrindas) for finding the SMCA’s conduct unlawful for the purposes of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. In order to determine whether the State could incur tortious liability under Article 6.271 § 4, a “broader legal assessment of the circumstances pertinent to the case and in a broader legal viewpoint” was required (turi būti atliktas platesnis bylai aktualių aplinkybių teisinis vertinimas platesniu teisiniu aspektu). When considering the damages claim, the court therefore had to establish whether both the SMCA’s decision to order the inspection and the manner in which the inspection had been conducted complied with the law. In particular, it had to assess whether the SMCA and its employees had acted lawfully, because any essential breach of the rules governing such inspections could justify a finding that the individual administrative decision based on the resulting conclusion amounted to unlawful conduct within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the court assessing the State’s tortious liability was also required to examine whether, in deciding to suspend the applicant, the SMCA had acted as legally required with respect to, first, protecting the individuals participating in the clinical trial and, second, verifying the reliability of the data obtained during that trial.

40. The Supreme Administrative Court then devoted several pages of its decision to a detailed examination of the SMCA’s conduct in light of the applicable legal framework, particularly the Good Clinical Practice Rules. It ultimately concluded that, for the purposes of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, the SMCA had acted within the scope of its authority and in the manner required by law.

41.
Against the background of the legal provisions cited above and the facts of the case, the Supreme Administrative Court endorsed the SMCA’s position. It found that, in applying to the applicant the measure provided for in point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure, on the basis of the inspectors’ findings, the agency had acted within its statutory powers and pursued legally prescribed aims: preventing infringements of individuals’ rights; safeguarding their safety and well-being; ensuring that the clinical trial was conducted in compliance with the Good Clinical Practice Rules and other legal instruments; and securing the reliability and quality of the data obtained from clinical trials. The Supreme Administrative Court saw no grounds for rejecting the SMCA’s arguments.

42. The Supreme Administrative Court further observed that the applicable legislation gave the head of the SMCA no discretion to “review” (revizuoti) the inspectors’ findings or to “amend them accordingly” (atitinkamai jas koreguoti). Nor, in carrying out his functions, was the head of the SMCA entitled to disregard those findings. Accordingly, the inspectors’ conclusions contained in the relevant report (see paragraph 8 above) constituted the factual basis for imposing measures on the clinical researcher. Their lawfulness and justification could be examined only “by a court” (tik teismine tvarka), through a challenge to the decision imposing measures on the researcher.

43. The Supreme Administrative Court also accepted the defendant’s argument that, once the inspectors’ findings adverse to the applicant had been received and had identified two critical (dangerous) violations committed by her, the head of the SMCA had no option other than to order her suspension. The fact that the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court subsequently annulled that suspension order did not, in itself, render the SMCA’s conduct in issuing it unlawful for the purposes of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. It was important to stress that, in the first set of judicial proceedings, the order of 10 January 2012 concerning the applicant had not been quashed because the court had found any of the absolute grounds for annulment listed in Article 89 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (see paragraph 55 below). Rather, it had been annulled because the court disagreed with the inspectors’ reasoning that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules. Consequently, the suspension order of 10 January 2012 had not been unlawful ab initio.

44. The Supreme Administrative Court also reconsidered the factual circumstances relating to the two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules that the inspection had attributed to the applicant.
As to the first critical violation, the Supreme Administrative Court reviewed the chain of events preceding S.V.’s death and the manner in which those events had been recorded in the inspection report. It held that none of the other material in the case file contradicted the findings made during the inspection. Those findings demonstrated that the applicant had failed to ensure that V.S. received appropriate medical care when side-effects arose on 11 April 2011. Nor had she taken effective steps to arrange the unscheduled medical consultations required under the Good Clinical Practice Rules.

45. The Supreme Administrative Court further relied on the addendum to the clinical-trial participation agreement, which V.S. and the applicant had signed on 6 April 2011. That document partially amended the original agreement of 9 November 2010 and warned that the medication being tested in the trial could entail a greater risk of serious, and at times fatal, infection. In the court’s view, the addendum placed an “increased duty of care” on the applicant in her capacity as a researcher (reikalavo iš tyrėjo padidinto budrumo), requiring her to safeguard the rights and well-being of the trial participants, including V.S. The court therefore found that the SMCA had remained within the scope of its authority when taking measures against the applicant.

46. Turning to the second critical (dangerous) breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, which related to the reporting of serious side-effects (see paragraph 8 above), the Supreme Administrative Court noted that “there were data in the case file” showing that the inspection had established the applicant’s failure to take steps to secure the “quality, completeness and reliability” of the clinical-trial documentation (dokumentų kokybę, pilnumą ir patikimumą). It also held that, pursuant to point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure, the first critical (dangerous) violation of the Good Clinical Practice Rules was in itself sufficient to justify the applicant’s suspension. The second critical violation identified during the inspection was, in essence, connected with the first and had not affected the decision to suspend her.

47. On the basis of those considerations, the Supreme Administrative Court concluded that, in adopting order no.
1A-29, for the purposes of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, had complied with Article 18 § 1 of the Law on Pharmacy and points 78, 79 and 79¹ of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below). Its actions had been aimed both at safeguarding the rights and welfare of persons participating in clinical trials and at ensuring the reliability and quality of the data obtained in those trials. Unlike the first-instance court (see paragraphs 25-31 above), the appellate court found no grounds for concluding that the SMCA had acted improperly. Consequently, the State could not incur civil liability under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code, because the SMCA had committed no unlawful act, which was an essential prerequisite for establishing such liability.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Council of Europe instruments and European Union law

48. The Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Dignity of the Human Being with regard to the Application of Biology and Medicine, also known as the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine, entered into force in respect of Lithuania on 1 February 2003. Its relevant provisions state:

Article 2 – Primacy of the human being

The interests and welfare of human beings must take precedence over the exclusive interests of society or science.

Article 15 – General rule

Scientific research in biology and medicine may be conducted freely, provided that it complies with this Convention and with other legal rules designed to protect human beings.

49. The relevant parts of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001, concerning the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States governing the application of good clinical practice when conducting clinical trials of medicinal products for human use, provide:

“Whereas:

...

(2) The recognised foundation for conducting clinical trials involving human beings is the protection of human rights and human dignity in connection with the application of biology and medicine ...

...

(18) Provision must also be made for monitoring adverse reactions arising during clinical trials ... so that any clinical trial presenting an unacceptable degree of risk can be stopped immediately ...”

Article 3

Protection of clinical-trial subjects

“1. This Directive does not affect national rules protecting clinical-trial subjects where those rules provide more extensive protection than the Directive ...

2. In particular, a clinical trial may be carried out only if:
(a) the reasonably foreseeable risks and burdens must be assessed in relation to the expected benefits for the individual trial participant and for other current and future patients. A clinical trial may begin only where the Ethics Committee and/or competent authority determines that the anticipated therapeutic and public-health benefits outweigh and justify those risks. The trial may continue only while ongoing monitoring confirms that this condition remains satisfied;

(b) before the trial, the participant ... must have been given an opportunity, during an interview with the investigator or a member of the research team, to understand the trial’s aims, risks and burdens, together with the conditions governing its conduct. The participant must also have been advised of the right to leave the trial at any time;

(c) safeguards must protect the participant’s right to physical ... integrity ...;

(d) after receiving information about the nature, importance, consequences and risks of the clinical trial, the participant ... must provide written consent ...;

... 3. An appropriately qualified doctor shall be responsible for the medical treatment provided to participants and for medical decisions taken on their behalf ... 4. Participants shall be given a point of contact through which they can request additional information.”

Article 12  
Suspension of a trial or breaches

“1. A Member State may suspend or prohibit a clinical trial if it has objective reasons to believe that the conditions stated in the application for authorisation ... are no longer fulfilled, or if it receives information casting doubt on the trial’s safety or scientific validity. The sponsor must be notified of that decision. ...

2. If a competent authority has objective grounds for concluding that the sponsor, investigator, or any other person participating in the conduct of the trial is no longer complying with the applicable obligations, it must immediately notify that person and specify the measures required to correct the situation. The competent authority must promptly inform the Ethics Committee, the other competent authorities and the Commission of the required course of action.”

Domestic law and practice

50. The Constitution provides:

Article 19

“The law shall protect every human being’s right to life.”
