“... No person may be subjected to scientific or medical experimentation without that person’s knowledge and freely given consent.”

Article 30

“Anyone whose constitutional rights or freedoms have been infringed is entitled to seek judicial redress. The law shall provide for compensation for material and moral [that is, non-pecuniary] harm caused to that person.”

Article 48

“Every person is free to choose an occupation or business and is entitled to appropriate, safe and healthy working conditions, fair remuneration, and social security in the event of unemployment.”

Article 53
“The State is responsible for safeguarding public health and must ensure that individuals receive medical assistance and services when they fall ill ...”

51. At the relevant time, the pertinent provisions of the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (Biomedicininių tyrimų etikos įstatymas) stated:

Article 5. Ethical standards governing biomedical research

“1. Biomedical research must be carried out in accordance with the principle that the interests of the individual take precedence over those of science and society ...”

The European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of the Second Section, was constituted as follows:

Jon Fridrik Kjølbro, President,  
Marko Bošnjak,  
Aleš Pejchal,  
Egidijus Kūris,  
Branko Lubarda,  
Pauliine Koskelo,

and Stanley Naismith, Section Registrar.

The Court took into account:

– application no. 53176/17, brought against the Republic of Lithuania under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Edita Gražulevičiūtė, a Lithuanian national (“the applicant”), and lodged with the Court on 21 July 2017;

– the decision to notify the Lithuanian Government (“the Government”) of the complaints relating to the right to a fair hearing, respect for private life, and an effective domestic remedy, while declaring the rest of the application inadmissible;

– the observations submitted by the parties.

Following private deliberations on 9 November 2021,

The Court delivers the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The applicant is both a doctor and a clinical researcher. She was suspended after one of her patients died. Relying on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the principle of res judicata, she complains that the final judicial ruling which exonerated her was subsequently set aside. She further alleges a violation of Article 8 because she received no compensation for the harm caused by her suspension.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1971, the applicant resides in Vilnius. She was represented by Ms L. Meškauskienė, a lawyer practising in Vilnius.

3. The Government’s representative was their Acting Agent, Ms L. Urbaitė.

4. The factual circumstances, as presented by the parties, may be outlined as follows.

5. The applicant is a rheumatologist and has practised in that professional capacity since 2004. A document supplied by her, apparently an extract from a tax declaration, indicates that she had worked as a clinical researcher (tyrėja) since 12 November 2004. A separate document issued by a private company, the Centre for Clinical and Basic Research, states that she was employed by that company as a “consulting doctor” between May 2007 and July 2011.

The applicant’s activities as a clinical researcher and her suspension
6. During 2011, the applicant worked as a clinical researcher alongside a team of other researchers and participated in several clinical trials. For part of that period, she was on maternity leave. One trial involved tocilizumab. On 14 April 2011, while that trial was under way, a patient identified as V.S. died. On 27 September 2011, V.S.’s daughters requested that the State Medicines Control Agency (Valstybinė vaistų kontrolės tarnyba, hereinafter “the SMCA”) examine whether the applicant had properly discharged her responsibilities in the clinical trial.

7. On 11 October 2011, the head of the SMCA directed that an unannounced good clinical practice inspection be conducted (hereinafter “the inspection”).

8. The inspection took place on 16 December 2011 and revealed a number of deficiencies. Two were classified as critical (dangerous) (kritiniai (pavojingi)) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraphs 53 and 54 below): the patient had not been accepted for an unscheduled appointment, and serious side-effects of the medicine under investigation had not been reported. The inspectors additionally recorded ten significant (reikšmingi) and six minor (nereikšmingi) violations of those rules. They also found that the researchers’ conduct might have harmed V.S.’s health and resulted in her death. In their view, V.S.’s welfare had not been safeguarded during the trial, in violation of her rights. The inspectors recommended applying to the principal researcher, A.V., and the applicant the measures specified in point 78 of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below).

9. By order (įsakymas) no. 1A-29, issued by the head of the SMCA on 10 January 2012, the applicant and A.V. were suspended (nušalinti) from the tocilizumab clinical trial conducted at the Santariškės Clinics of Vilnius University Hospital (hereinafter “the first clinical trial”). They were also barred from undertaking any new clinical trials. The order was to be published on the SMCA’s website.

10. In order (įsakymas) no. 1A-45 of 12 January 2012, the head of the SMCA suspended the applicant, in her capacity as principal researcher—a status granted to her by the SMCA on 25 July 2011—from the tocilizumab trial conducted at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic (Vilniaus rajono centrinė poliklinika, hereinafter “the second clinical trial”). On 29 May 2012, the head of the SMCA annulled that order himself.

11. On 27 August 2011, the authorities opened a pre-trial investigation into the circumstances surrounding V.S.’s death and commissioned a forensic examination. On 11 October 2012, the experts issued report no. DM 6 (76)/13 (01), concluding that V.S. had died from “sepsis which [had] developed as fast as lighting” (žaibiškai išsivystęs sepsis), rather than as a consequence of the applicant’s actions. The report further noted that sepsis could develop irrespective of whether tocilizumab was being taken.
It was further observed that, after learning that V.S.’s health had worsened, the applicant believed that the decline was not rheumatological in origin but stemmed from other medical problems or complications, including torn tendons or an infection, and recommended that V.S. consult a traumatology specialist. Administrative court proceedings concerning the applicant’s suspension from her position as a researcher
12. On an unspecified date, the applicant contested the suspension decisions referred to in paragraphs 9 and 10 above. She submitted, inter alia, that the SMCA inspectors had failed to assess all the available information properly before reaching their findings and that, consequently, the suspension decisions had been unlawful and without foundation. In relation to V.S.’s death, she maintained that the applicable legislation imposed no duty to arrange an unscheduled diagnostic appointment [at the patient’s house] where the patient refused to attend a medical institution. The applicant explained that, after being informed by telephone on 11 April 2011 that V.S.’s health had deteriorated, she had suspected complications. Following consultations with several other doctors, she had advised V.S. to go to the hospital immediately, but V.S. had not done so. This had made it impossible to examine her in good time and had ultimately led to her death.

13. In response to the applicant’s action, the SMCA maintained that the findings recorded in the inspection report were objective. It further stated that the orders suspending the applicant had been adopted “only because” the inspection had identified two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below). Accordingly, those two breaches alone were relevant to the judicial proceedings. The suspension orders had not been based on any other violations, whether significant or minor.

14. On 6 December 2013, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court allowed the applicant’s claim in full. It first explained that administrative courts adjudicate disputes concerning acts or decisions affecting a claimant’s rights or obligations. The inspection report itself, including the circumstances recorded in it (see paragraph 8 above), had produced no consequences for the applicant and therefore could not be challenged before a court. Her rights and obligations had been affected solely by the suspension orders, not by the inspection report. The court would therefore rule only on the circumstances identified in the report that had resulted in those orders. Since the applicant’s suspension and exclusion from clinical trials had rested on the two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 8 above), the court confined its examination to those matters.

15. With regard to the events preceding V.S.’s death, the court found that, before the clinical trial began, V.S. had signed an agreement to take part in it and had been told whom she should contact if complications arose. The agreement did not contain the applicant’s contact information; it listed only the details of doctor J.R. and of A.V., the principal researcher.
Although V.S.’s daughters had criticised the applicant’s conduct, they could not explain why V.S. had not contacted either of the other researchers, J.R. or A.V. The court further observed that V.S. had been required to notify the researchers of any deterioration in her health. Nevertheless, when her condition began to worsen on 9 April 2011, she instead consulted an outside doctor whom she “personally knew” (asmeniškai pažįstamo gydytojo), took medication prescribed by that doctor, and also used methadone. She did not contact the applicant until several days later.

16. The court considered the expert medical report produced during the criminal proceedings, which concluded that V.S. had died from acute sepsis rather than as a result of the applicant’s actions (see paragraph 11 above). It also heard evidence from J.R., a doctor who had participated in the same clinical trial and had been designated as one of the persons to contact if complications arose. J.R. confirmed that she had overheard the telephone conversation between V.S. and the applicant on 12 April 2011, during which the applicant “had insisted” (primygtinai liepė) that V.S. attend hospital and consult a traumatology specialist. According to J.R., when an ambulance eventually brought V.S. to hospital on 13 April 2011, she and the applicant examined V.S. together. They observed that V.S.’s leg was dark grey and that the complication had existed for at least four days. The court therefore determined that both J.R. and the applicant had examined V.S., rendering unfounded one of the inspection’s adverse conclusions against the applicant—namely, that she had not taken part in that examination.

17. The court additionally found that the inspectors had relied on statements made by V.S.’s daughters and had assumed that the applicant might have deliberately entered inaccurate information in the medical and other records to avoid trouble. That conclusion, however, had no factual foundation. It rested solely on the daughters’ subjective account, given after V.S.’s death, possibly to support their claims against the applicant.

18. In contrast to the assertions made by V.S.’s daughters, the applicant’s maternity leave (vaiko priežiūros atostogos) (see paragraph 6 above) was irrelevant, since she had not been the clinical trial’s sole researcher. J.R., another doctor, had also participated and had borne the same responsibilities as the applicant. The court expressly concluded that the applicant had not been an “irreplaceable person” in the trial and that her maternity leave, in itself, had neither complicated matters nor directly affected the conduct of the clinical trial.

19.
In view of the foregoing, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court found that the inspectors’ conclusion that the applicant had breached the Good Clinical Practice Rules by improperly organising unscheduled appointments was erroneous and inconsistent with the facts.

20. The court next examined the second critical (dangerous) breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules attributed to the applicant: her alleged failure to notify the clinical-trial sponsor (užsakovas), within twenty-four hours, of any “serious side-effects” (sunkus nepageidaujamas reiškinys) resulting in death, disability or other serious consequences. After reviewing the medical records and questioning a clinical-trials expert, the court determined that the applicant had not violated that reporting obligation. V.S. had initially suffered ankle pain, which did not constitute a serious side-effect of the medication under trial, and the applicant had immediately notified the sponsor once septic arthritis was suspected.

21. The court therefore held that the inspectors’ findings had rested on their subjective evaluation of the circumstances and that they had failed to explain why they had dismissed the applicant’s arguments. In the court’s view, there was no evidence permitting a categorical finding that those arguments were unfounded. It accordingly concluded that the applicant’s conduct in reporting adverse side-effects had been unjustifiably classified as a critical (dangerous) violation.

22. Having found that the inspectors had wrongly determined that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) violations, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court ruled that the restrictions imposed on her work as a researcher had been “unjust” (neteisingai). It therefore quashed the orders suspending her from the clinical trials and prohibiting her from participating in new trials (see paragraphs 9 and 10 above).

23. No appeal was lodged against that decision, which became final on 21 December 2013.

Administrative court proceedings concerning damage caused by the suspension
24. Subsequently, the applicant brought an action for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage against the State, represented by the SMCA, alleging that she had suffered such damage as a result of being suspended from the clinical trials. She stated, inter alia, that she had worked as a clinical researcher since 12 November 2004. In her view, the damage arose from the SMCA’s unlawful decisions to suspend her, which had been set aside by the court in the preceding proceedings (see paragraphs 12-23 above). She maintained that, but for the suspension, she would have earned income from both the first and the second trials. Emphasising the “particularly high requirements of care and professionalism” (ypač aukšti atidumo ir rūpestingumo reikalavimai) imposed on members of the medical profession, she argued that doubts concerning her competence had harmed her reputation and caused her considerable stress. She indicated that the first clinical trial had run from 11 October 2010 until 19 August 2013. In reply, the SMCA relied on the two critical violations identified by the inspectors: first, V.S. had not received mandatory medical assistance, contrary to the clinical-trial protocol and the applicable regulations; and, secondly, systemic shortcomings in the reporting of serious side-effects had compromised the integrity of the critical trial’s data. According to the SMCA, those two critical violations had justified its decision to suspend the applicant, and the measure had not been unlawful.

25. On 4 November 2015, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court granted the applicant’s claim in part. It first observed that she had sought, as pecuniary damage, the income she would have earned had the SMCA not issued the orders of 10 and 12 January 2012 suspending her from conducting the first and second clinical trials. The court further cited Article 6.249 § 1 of the Civil Code, which defined damage, as well as Articles 6.246 and 6.271 of that Code (see paragraph 56 below), under which unlawful conduct constituted one of the requisite conditions for civil liability.

26. The court additionally noted that Article 58 § 2 of the Law on Administrative Proceedings (see paragraph 55 below) dispensed with the need to prove again, in another administrative case involving the same parties, facts already established by a final judicial decision in an earlier administrative case. It then relied on the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court’s decision of 6 December 2013 in the dispute between the applicant and the SMCA. That decision had not been appealed and had become final (see paragraphs 14-23 above).
The court observed that “essentially the same parties [had been] taking part” in the present, second set of proceedings. It therefore considered it unnecessary to establish anew the conditions governing public liability (viešosios atsakomybės sąlygos) in relation to the applicant.

27. As regards the first clinical trial, the court found that an agreement had been signed on 17 August 2010 specifying the exact payment per participant for completion of the entire trial. The applicant had, in practice, conducted that trial until the SMCA suspended her by an order of 10 January 2012, which the administrative court subsequently annulled. Following the death of one patient, she had continued the trial with the other five. The material in the case file further demonstrated that the first trial had been completed and recorded in accordance with the plan. Nothing in the file suggested that the applicant’s conduct might have prevented the trial from taking place. Furthermore, despite the defendant’s submissions in those proceedings, the medical documentation confirmed that the applicant herself had conducted the clinical trials involving those five patients and that the trials had been completed in respect of each of them.

28. The court stressed that, as stated in the decision of 6 December 2013, the inspectors had wrongly concluded that the Good Clinical Practice Rules had been breached. Consequently, the SMCA’s order of 10 January 2012 suspending the applicant from the first trial had been annulled. In the opinion of the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court, the SMCA’s decision to remove her from that trial had therefore caused her pecuniary damage.

29. Finally, the administrative court relied on the Supreme Court’s ruling of 13 November 2006 in civil case no. 3K-3-585/2006. In that ruling, the Supreme Court had held that a plaintiff was required to prove the amount of lost income and that the claimed amount had to be realistic. In determining whether income not received constituted pecuniary damage, it was necessary to assess whether the income had been anticipated, whether the plaintiff could reasonably have expected to obtain it, and whether its loss resulted from the defendant’s unlawful conduct. In the present case, if the applicant had not been prevented from conducting the first clinical trial for the five remaining patients, she would have earned 6,128 euros (EUR). That amount had been calculated beforehand in her contract with the pharmaceutical company, and she had failed to receive it as a result of the SMCA’s “unlawful actions” (neteisėti veiksmai). The court accordingly awarded her EUR 6,128 in compensation for pecuniary damage.

30.
As to the second clinical trial, the court observed that on 26 August 2011 the applicant had entered into a clinical trial agreement with a pharmaceutical company, under which she was to act as the principal researcher. By a decision of 12 January 2012, she was subsequently suspended from conducting that trial (see paragraph 10 above). However, the court also took account of the applicant’s own confirmation at the hearing that she had declined to participate in the second trial, with the result that it had not been carried out at the Vilnius Region Central Polyclinic. Although she maintained during the hearing that she had withdrawn because of the psychological stress caused by the inspection of the first clinical trial, no evidence supported that assertion. The court further considered it significant that the pharmaceutical company had notified the SMCA that no patients had participated in, or even been selected for, the second trial. Accordingly, the applicant’s claim for pecuniary damage relating to the second clinical trial had to be rejected.

31. Turning finally to non-pecuniary damage, the court referred to the applicant’s complaint that her suspension from the first clinical trial had prevented her from carrying out research activities for almost two years, from 10 January 2012 until 6 December 2013 (see paragraphs 9 and 23 above). She had also argued that doubts concerning her professional competence as a doctor had harmed her reputation, particularly because information about her suspension and about critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules had been published on the SMCA’s website. The court reiterated that the suspension decision of 10 January 2012 had been annulled on the ground that it was unlawful. It found that being barred from clinical trials for nearly two years could objectively have caused the applicant a “negative experience” (neigiami išgyvenimai) and awarded her EUR 200 in compensation.

32. The applicant lodged an appeal, seeking compensation for pecuniary damage connected with the second clinical trial and challenging the failure to allow her non-pecuniary damage claim in full. The SMCA likewise appealed, contending that the applicant had not substantiated her claim for pecuniary damage arising from the first clinical trial and was therefore not entitled to compensation under that head. It further argued that she should receive no monetary compensation for non-pecuniary damage. In addition, the SMCA submitted that, in the second set of judicial proceedings, the first-instance court had failed to examine the factual and legal dimensions of the SMCA’s conduct that were pertinent to determining the State’s tortious liability.
According to the SMCA, the first-instance court had overlooked the fact that its head had ordered the applicant’s suspension on the strength of inspection findings identifying two critical infringements: harm to a patient’s health and impairment of the integrity of the trial data. The SMCA further submitted that, by deciding to suspend the applicant, it had intended to safeguard the health of the clinical-trial participants.

33. On 30 January 2017, following written proceedings, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the SMCA’s appeal, dismissed the applicant’s civil claim for damages and rejected her appeal.

34. As a preliminary point, the Supreme Administrative Court cited its settled case-law concerning liability for damage resulting from unlawful acts by State institutions under Article 15 § 1 (3) of the Law on Administrative Proceedings (see paragraph 55 below). Under that case-law, the mere annulment of an administrative decision did not establish that a State institution had acted unlawfully or, consequently, that civil liability arose under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. The court also stated that, in determining whether a State institution incurred civil liability, Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code had to be applied as the “special provision” (specialioji norma), rather than the general provision contained in the first paragraph of that Article (see paragraph 56 below).

35. The Supreme Administrative Court found that the principle of res judicata required factual and legal matters determined in another judicial decision to be accepted and permitted the parties to the proceedings, or any other interested party, to rely on them. Nevertheless, in damages proceedings, this did not prevent a court from examining allegedly unlawful conduct within the framework of the State’s tortious liability. In the Supreme Administrative Court’s view, a legal appraisal (teisinis vertinimas) of circumstances established by a judicial decision did not amount to rejecting that decision’s binding force or res judicata effect. It further observed that administrative disputes seeking the annulment of administrative decisions were distinct from disputes claiming compensation for damage caused by unlawful State action. In that connection, the Supreme Administrative Court referred to its previous ruling of 14 July 2011 in case no. A502-3034/2011, delivered by an enlarged formation. Similarly, the “examination”
The court’s review (patikra) of allegedly unlawful conduct for the purposes of tort liability involved assessing the relevant factual and legal elements under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. In proceedings concerning compensation for damage, that review could be conducted without calling into question either the facts established in an earlier case or the assessment of those facts. The Supreme Administrative Court referred both to the same judgment and to its judgment of 8 October 2015 in case no. A3155-624/2015, which had likewise been delivered by an enlarged chamber. It held that, when considering the applicant’s damages claim (see paragraphs 25-31 above), the first-instance court had not taken account of all that case-law and had therefore issued an unlawful and inadequately reasoned decision.

36. The Supreme Administrative Court further stated that the determination of the State’s civil liability in the present case required consideration not only of domestic legislation, but also of international and European Union law. It first invoked the principle that an individual’s welfare and interests take precedence over those of society and science. In that regard, it also cited the general rule that scientific research must be carried out freely while respecting legal provisions protecting human rights, as laid down, respectively, in Articles 2 and 15 of the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (see paragraph 48 below). The court observed that the principle contained in Article 2 of that Convention was also embodied in Article 5 § 1 of the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below) and in point 2.3 of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (see paragraph 53 below).

37. The provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 (“the Directive”; see paragraph 49 below) were also applicable and relevant at the material time. Lithuania had implemented the Directive through the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (see paragraph 51 below), the Law on Pharmacy (see paragraph 52 below), and other pertinent legal instruments. Point 2 of the Directive’s preamble established the principle that persons participating in clinical trials must be protected. The Directive also laid down “core provisions” (esminės nuostatos): after a clinical trial had begun, it had to be reviewed and supervised, and its conformity with Good Clinical Practice standards had to be monitored; where objective evidence was identified, Member States were entitled to suspend or terminate the trial (point 18 of the preamble and Article 12 of the Directive; see paragraph 49 below). Finally, no clinical trial could begin before receiving the ethics committee’s approval.
Under Article 18 § 4 of the Law on Pharmacy, the authorities responsible for authorising clinical trials in Lithuania were the SMCA and the Bioethics Committee (see paragraph 52 below).

38. In the applicant’s case, the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court had quashed the relevant part of the order concerning her. It found that the investigation’s conclusions regarding the applicant did not sufficiently establish the two serious (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules and that excessive weight had been attached to the subjective accounts provided by V.S.’s daughters (see paragraph 17 above). The Supreme Administrative Court considered it necessary to determine whether the authorities’ approvals for the conduct of the two clinical trials had been lawful.

39. The Supreme Administrative Court stated that the findings made by the first-instance court in the initial administrative proceedings, which had resulted in the decision of 10 January 2012 being annulled, did not “in themselves constitute a basis” (savaime nėra pagrindas) for concluding that the SMCA’s conduct had been unlawful for the purposes of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. Determining whether the State might incur tortious liability under Article 6.271 § 4 required a “broader legal assessment of the circumstances pertinent to the case and in a broader legal viewpoint” (turi būti atliktas platesnis bylai aktualių aplinkybių teisinis vertinimas platesniu teisiniu aspektu). In considering the damages claim, the court therefore had to establish whether both the SMCA’s decision to order the inspection and the manner in which the inspection was conducted had complied with the law. In particular, it had to determine whether the SMCA and its personnel had acted lawfully, because any fundamental breach of the rules governing such inspections could justify a finding that the individual administrative decision based on the inspection’s conclusion amounted to unlawful conduct within the meaning of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the court assessing the State’s tortious liability also had to consider whether, in deciding to suspend the applicant, the SMCA had fulfilled its legal duties concerning, first, the protection of persons participating in the clinical trial and, second, verification of the reliability of the data obtained during that trial.

40. The Supreme Administrative Court then devoted several pages of its decision to a detailed examination of the SMCA’s conduct in light of the applicable legal framework, particularly the Good Clinical Practice Rules. It ultimately concluded that, for the purposes of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, the SMCA had acted within the scope of its powers and in the manner required by law.

41.
Considering the legal provisions cited above together with the facts of the case, the Supreme Administrative Court endorsed the SMCA’s position. It found that, in applying to the applicant the measure provided for in point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure on the basis of the inspectors’ conclusion, the agency had acted within its statutory powers and pursued legally prescribed objectives: preventing violations of individuals’ rights; safeguarding their safety and well-being; ensuring that the clinical trial was conducted in compliance with the Good Clinical Practice Rules and other legislation; and securing the reliability and quality of the data obtained during clinical trials. The Supreme Administrative Court saw no basis for rejecting the SMCA’s arguments.

42. The Supreme Administrative Court further observed that the applicable legislation gave the head of the SMCA no discretion to “review” (revizuoti) or “amend accordingly” (atitinkamai jas koreguoti) the inspectors’ conclusions. Nor was the head of the SMCA entitled, in exercising his functions, to disregard those findings. Accordingly, the inspectors’ conclusions recorded in the relevant report (see paragraph 8 above) constituted the factual basis for imposing measures on the clinical researcher. Their legality and justification could be examined only “through court proceedings” (tik teismine tvarka), by contesting a decision that imposed measures on a researcher.

43. The Supreme Administrative Court also accepted the defendant’s contention that, once the inspectors’ findings adverse to the applicant had been received and had established that she had committed two critical (dangerous) violations, the head of the SMCA had no option other than to decide on her suspension. The subsequent annulment of the suspension order by the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court did not, in itself, establish that the SMCA had acted unlawfully when issuing that order for the purposes of Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. It was important that, in the first set of judicial proceedings, the order of 10 January 2012 concerning the applicant had not been annulled because the court had identified any of the absolute grounds for annulment listed in Article 89 of the Code of Administrative Procedure (see paragraph 55 below). Rather, it had been set aside because the court disagreed with the inspectors’ reasoning that the applicant had committed two critical (dangerous) breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules. Consequently, the order of 10 January 2012 suspending the applicant had not been unlawful ab initio.

44. The Supreme Administrative Court additionally reassessed the factual circumstances relating to the two critical (dangerous) violations of the Good Clinical Practice Rules that the inspection had imputed to the applicant.
As to the first critical violation, the Supreme Administrative Court reconstructed the events culminating in S.V.’s death and examined how they had been recorded in the inspection report. It held that none of the other material in the case file contradicted the findings made during the inspection. Those findings demonstrated that the applicant had failed to ensure that V.S. received appropriate medical care when side-effects arose on 11 April 2011. Moreover, contrary to her obligations under the Good Clinical Practice Rules, she had not adopted effective measures to secure unscheduled medical consultations.

45. The Supreme Administrative Court’s reasoning also relied on the addendum to the clinical-trial participation agreement, which V.S. and the applicant had both signed on 6 April 2011. That addendum partially modified the original clinical-trial participation agreement of 9 November 2010 and warned that the medication being tested in the trial could entail an increased risk of serious, and at times fatal, infection. In the Supreme Administrative Court’s view, the addendum placed an “increased duty of care” (reikalavo iš tyrėjo padidinto budrumo) on the applicant in her capacity as a researcher, requiring her to safeguard the rights and well-being of the trial participants, including V.S. It therefore found that the SMCA had remained within the scope of its authority when taking measures against the applicant.

46. With respect to the second critical (dangerous) breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, which concerned the reporting of serious side-effects (see paragraph 8 above), the Supreme Administrative Court further stated that “there were data in the case file” showing that the inspection had established the applicant’s failure to take steps ensuring the “quality, completeness and reliability” of the clinical-trial documentation (dokumentų kokybę, pilnumą ir patikimumą). It also held that, pursuant to point 78.1 of the Description of Control Procedure, the first critical (dangerous) violation of the Good Clinical Practice Rules had, by itself, provided sufficient grounds for the applicant’s suspension. The second critical violation identified during the inspection was essentially connected to the first and had not affected the decision to suspend her.

47. On the basis of the above considerations, the Supreme Administrative Court concluded that, in adopting order no.
In case 1A-29, the SMCA’s conduct, for the purposes of Article 6.271 § 4 of the Civil Code, complied with Article 18 § 1 of the Law on Pharmacy and points 78, 79 and 791 of the Description of Control Procedure (see paragraph 54 below). Its objectives were to safeguard the rights and welfare of persons participating in clinical trials and to ensure the reliability and quality of the data obtained from those trials. Thus, unlike the first-instance court’s conclusion (see paragraphs 25-31 above), there were no grounds for holding that the SMCA had acted improperly. Consequently, the State could not incur civil liability under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code, because the SMCA had committed no unlawful act, which was an essential prerequisite for such liability.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Council of Europe instruments and European Union law

48. The relevant provisions of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Dignity of the Human Being with regard to the Application of Biology and Medicine—the Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine, also known as the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine—which entered into force for Lithuania on 1 February 2003, provide as follows:

Article 2 – The primacy of the human being

The interests and welfare of human beings must take precedence over the exclusive interests of science or society.

Article 15 – General principle

Research in biology and medicine may be conducted freely, provided that it complies with this Convention and with all other legal rules intended to protect human beings.

49. The relevant parts of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001, concerning the approximation of the Member States’ laws, regulations and administrative provisions on applying good clinical practice when conducting clinical trials of medicinal products intended for human use, state:

“Recitals:

... (2) The recognised foundation for carrying out clinical trials involving human beings is the protection of human rights and human dignity in connection with the application of biology and medicine ...

... (18) Rules must also be established for monitoring adverse reactions arising during clinical trials ... so that any trial involving an unacceptable degree of risk can be stopped immediately ...”

Article 3

Protection of persons participating in clinical trials

“1. This Directive does not affect national rules protecting clinical-trial participants where those rules provide broader protection than the Directive ...

2. A clinical trial may be conducted only where, in particular:
(a) Before a clinical trial begins, the reasonably foreseeable risks and burdens must be balanced against the expected benefits for the individual trial participant and for other current and future patients. The trial may start only where the Ethics Committee and/or the competent authority determines that the expected therapeutic and public-health benefits warrant the risks. It may continue only while ongoing monitoring confirms that this condition remains satisfied;

(b) before participating, the trial subject ... must have been given an opportunity, during an interview with the investigator or a member of the investigative team, to understand the trial’s aims, risks and inconveniences, as well as the circumstances in which it will be carried out. The subject must also have been advised of the right to leave the trial at any time;

(c) safeguards must protect the subject’s rights to physical ... integrity ...;

(d) after receiving information about the nature, importance, consequences and risks of the clinical trial, the trial subject ... must have provided written consent ...;

... 3. Responsibility for the medical treatment provided to subjects, and for medical decisions taken on their behalf, shall rest with a suitably qualified doctor ... 4. Subjects shall be given a contact point through which they can request additional information.”

Article 12  
Trial suspension or breaches

“1. A Member State may suspend or prohibit a clinical trial if it has objective reasons to believe that the requirements set out in the application for authorisation ... are no longer fulfilled, or if it possesses information that creates doubts about the trial’s safety or scientific validity. The sponsor must be notified. ...

2. If a competent authority has objective grounds for concluding that the sponsor, investigator, or any other person participating in the conduct of the trial is no longer complying with the applicable obligations, it shall immediately notify that person and specify the steps required to correct the situation. The competent authority in question shall immediately inform the Ethics Committee, the other competent authorities and the Commission of the required course of action.”

Domestic law and practice

Constitutional and legal provisions concerning medical research and pharmacy

50. The Constitution provides:

Article 19

“The law shall protect every human being’s right to life.”

Article 21

“... A person may not be subjected to scientific or medical experimentation without that person’s knowledge and freely given consent.”

Article 30

“Any person whose constitutional rights or freedoms have been infringed shall be entitled to bring proceedings before a court. The law shall provide for compensation for material and moral [that is, non-pecuniary] damage caused to a person.”

Article 48

“Every person shall be free to choose an occupation or business and shall be entitled to appropriate, safe and healthy working conditions, fair remuneration for work, and social security in the event of unemployment.”

Article 53
“The State is responsible for safeguarding public health and must ensure that individuals receive medical assistance and services when they fall ill...”

51. At the relevant time, the pertinent provisions of the Law on Ethics of Biomedical Research (Biomedicininių tyrimų etikos įstatymas) stated:

Article 5. Ethical standards governing biomedical research

“1. Biomedical research must follow the principle that the interests of the individual take precedence over those of science and society ...”

52. The relevant provisions of the Law on Pharmacy (Farmacijos įstatymas), as applicable at the material time, provided:

Article 18. Conditions applicable to clinical trials of medicinal products

“1. Clinical trials of medicinal products shall be governed by the legal instruments of the Republic of Lithuania. The State Medicines Control Agency and other institutions authorised by law shall ensure compliance ... 2. A principal researcher must possess qualifications meeting the requirements laid down by the Minister of Health. 3. Every clinical trial of a medicinal product shall be planned, performed, registered and reported in conformity with the Good Clinical Practice [Rules] approved by the Minister of Health. 4. A clinical trial of a medicinal product may be carried out only after approval has been obtained from the Lithuanian Bioethics Committee and authorisation has been granted by the State Medicines Control Agency.

... 11. Where the State Medicines Control Agency or the Lithuanian Bioethics Committee ... possesses information that casts doubt on a clinical trial’s safety or scientific validity, it may decline to issue an authorisation for the trial of the medicinal product or a certificate of approval and must inform the sponsor accordingly.

... 14. Once a clinical trial of a medicinal product is under way, the State Medicines Control Agency may decide to suspend or terminate it within the country if there are reasonable grounds for finding that the authorisation conditions are not being complied with, or if concerns exist regarding the trial’s safety or scientific validity; the reasons for that decision must be specified ...”

53. The pertinent sections of the Good Clinical Practice Rules (Geros klinikinės praktikos taisyklės), adopted by Ministry of Health Order no. V-945 of 13 November 2006, provided:

“2.3. The rights, safety and health of a person participating in a clinical trial take priority over the interests of society and science.

...

3.1.1. The supervising institution’s commission/the independent ethics committee must ensure adequate protection of the rights, safety and well-being of individuals participating in the clinical experiment ...”
54. By Order No. V-692 of 18 July 2011, the Minister of Health adopted the Description of the Procedure for Granting Consent and Issuing Licences to Conduct Clinical Trials of Medicinal Products, and for the Performance and Supervision of Such Trials (Pritarimo atlikti klinikinį vaistinio preparato tyrimą liudijimų ir leidimų atlikti klinikinį vaistinio preparato tyrimą išdavimo, tyrimų atlikimo ir kontrolės tvarkos aprašas; hereinafter “the Description of Control Procedure”). At the relevant time, its pertinent provisions stated:

“77. Inspectors conducting a good clinical practice inspection shall prepare a report identifying the deficiencies discovered and any infringements of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, with particular emphasis on those capable of producing adverse consequences. Potential infringements shall be classified as follows:

77.1. dangerous (critical) infringements – circumstances, actions or procedures that violate patients’ rights or safety, harm their health, or compromise data quality or integrity; such infringements may involve substantial departures from Good Clinical Practice requirements, poor-quality data, or the lack of source documents; fraud also falls within this category;

77.2. significant infringements – circumstances, actions or procedures that may adversely affect patients’ rights, safety or health and/or the quality or integrity of the data; these constitute serious deficiencies directly contravening the requirements of the Good Clinical Practice Rules;

...

78. Where an inspection identifies dangerous and/or significant infringements of the Good Clinical Practice Rules attributable to the researcher, the SMCA shall apply one of the following measures:
78.1. where an inspection of a clinical trial in progress establishes at least one dangerous breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules, to remove (nušalinti) the researcher from conducting that trial, prohibit her or him from initiating any new clinical trials until the clinical trials already under way have ended, and publish on the SMCA’s website information concerning the prohibition, the researcher’s suspension, and the dangerous breach of the Good Clinical Practice Rules committed ...

79. After coordination with the Lithuanian Bioethics Committee, the SMCA shall implement the measures specified in point 78 of this Description. Those measures shall be imposed by an order issued by the head of the SMCA ...

791. A researcher against whom the measures set out in points 78.1 or 78.4 of this Description have been imposed because she or he committed critical breaches of the Good Clinical Practice Rules shall immediately be removed from every other clinical trial that she or he conducts as principal researcher. That suspension shall remain in effect until the SMCA, acting in accordance with the Rules for Inspection approved by the head of the SMCA, has performed an unscheduled inspection and evaluated whether all clinical trials conducted by that person as principal researcher comply with the requirements of the Good Clinical Practice Rules. ... The researcher’s suspension shall likewise be terminated if the SMCA fails to conduct the unscheduled inspections within the prescribed time-limit ...”

55. In so far as relevant, the Law on Administrative Proceedings (Administracinių bylų teisenos įstatymas), in the version applicable at the material time, provided:

...

3) claims for compensation in respect of damage caused by unlawful acts of [State or municipal] institutions in the sphere of public administration (Article 6.271 of the Civil Code) ...”

“1. No proof shall be required of circumstances that the court recognises as commonly known.

2. In other administrative proceedings involving the same persons, proof shall not be required of facts established by a final court decision in another administrative or civil case. ...”
