FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF ANATOLIY YEREMENKO v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 22287/08)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

15 September 2022

FINAL

15/12/2022

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström,
Lado Chanturia,
Arnfinn Bårdsen,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 22287/08) against Ukraine lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national, Mr Anatoliy Vasylyovych Yeremenko (“the applicant”), on 26 April 2008;

the decision to give notice to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint regarding the alleged violation of Article 10 of the Convention;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 31 August 2021 and 21 June 2022,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on the latter date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case concerns defamation proceedings brought against the applicant following the publication of an article he had written about alleged judicial corruption, as well as an injunction ordering the removal of the publication in question from the newspaper’s website pending examination of the defamation case. The applicant complains under Article 10 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant was born in 1949 and resides in Kyiv. He was represented by Ms L.L. Pankratova, a lawyer practising in that city.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

BACKGROUND TO THE CASE

The article of 12 March 2005

5. The applicant is a journalist. At the relevant time, he worked for the national weekly analytical newspaper Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, which had a circulation of around 57,000 copies.

6. On 12 March 2005, as part of a series of publications written by the applicant, an article entitled “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case” (“Чорна трійка: все інше справи не стосується”) appeared in that newspaper. On 18 March 2005, it was posted on the newspaper’s website.

7. In the article, the author referred to an earlier publication of his and observed that, in a certain case (no. 27/37), which had been pending before the courts for some time and had been remitted to the lower courts at least twice, a judgment had been issued on the basis of a forged copy of a document, the original of which formed part of the case-file materials in a particular set of criminal proceedings. Nevertheless, the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had delivered its judgment on the basis of the forged copy. The applicant continued by describing what he termed a “system for obtaining a required result”.
To obtain the result, a particular law firm had been contacted. The firm had been paid a substantial fee by the plaintiff but had then “surprisingly” taken no further part in the proceedings, in which the plaintiff (a State enterprise) had been represented by its own lawyers. As regards the courts, they had “carefully referred the case” to the Higher Commercial Court, which, in turn, had taken an excessively long time to deal with the proceedings before eventually remitting the case to a lower court “for the absence of a copy of the decision complained of”. In the meantime, the plaintiff had been liquidated, which, according to the applicant, had enabled numerous wrongdoings to be concealed.

8. The full text of the article is as follows:

“In May last year, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] (no. 21, 29 May 2004) published an article entitled ‘How the court validated the copy of the document while the original document was missing’ [“Як суд ‘легалізував’ ‘копію’ при відсутності оригіналу”]. It concerned an unprecedented legal incident in the history of Ukrainian justice that arose when, on the basis of a highly doubtful copy (in terms of the quality of the print and, even more so, its content) of a certain document [a guarantee letter], the court delivered a judgment that the respondent has now been challenging for four years. Incidentally, it was challenged at the same time as the presidential decree establishing appellate courts in Ukraine was issued, for one simple reason: according to the respondent, they had never issued a document bearing such a [registration] number to the plaintiff and had provided no guarantees. Nevertheless, since there are many different ways of making any conflict of interest palatable to Themis, the case has become a kind of symbol of dignity and a fetish of the deficiencies of the very structural judicial system borrowed from developed democracies, which was founded on a system tainted with ‘sovietness’ [совковостью] and the ‘telephone law’ formation of the principles of independence of the third branch of power in our State. [paragraph 1]

DT has repeatedly reported on the vicissitudes of the litigation and the parties’ mutual claims in the dispute. During the three years preceding the publication of the [above-mentioned] article, case no. 27/37 went through two rounds of court proceedings – from the court of first instance to the judgment of the Supreme Court of Ukraine. There was also a third round, based on newly discovered circumstances. In the course of criminal proceedings instituted against the limited liability company N., which stole from a State transport shipping enterprise, Intertrans, [something, it was not specified what] worth more than 8.2 million hryvnias (UAH) and then disappeared without a trace, the prosecutor’s office found the original of the disputed guarantee letter.
It turned out that the guarantee letter referred to by the plaintiff (Intertrans) had been provided by the defendant to an entirely different enterprise, as the party had stated from the outset at every court hearing. However, for some reason, this was never taken into account. The Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal could have set the record straight but instead, after establishing the existence of the guarantee letter in the criminal case file, issued a decision based on a ‘copy’ [of that letter]. Accordingly, this author naturally asked: ‘I wonder what the commercial justice system will come up with this time to protect the State enterprise/structure that caused substantial pecuniary damage to the State?’ [paragraph 2]

Reality has exceeded the boldest expectations. Further immersion into the twilight of this dark and shady subject—how commercial disputes in the Donetsk region are resolved—gives the impression that a system exists that is quite primitive in its scheme yet reliable in its effectiveness for obtaining the desired result in almost any case. At the same time, one gets the sense that the essence of the problem does not matter at all to those facilitating it. What matters is that the customer (usually the plaintiff) comes to the right place at the right time. [paragraph 3]

As a rule, this is a law firm to which large sums are legally transferred for ‘legal services’. Subsequently, it is difficult to determine what active role the law firm plays in the court proceedings. Instead, representatives appear, or, as in the case of Intertrans—which, for some unknown reason, paid a fee of UAH 400,000 to the mysterious I.—they are content with the participation of their own lawyers in the proceedings. Throughout the process, the case is considered by a host of servants of commercial justice in the Donetsk region, who carefully and attentively pass it along to the Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine. [paragraph 4]

Thus, when the original ‘copy’, followed by an additional document proving the forgery of that ‘copy’, was discovered, it became clear that it was no longer necessary to discuss the adversarial nature of the arguments, but rather falsification and intent, which are not the subject matter of commercial disputes but of criminal investigations. And again, just the facts. The Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine (HCCU) made its mark once more. Contrary to Part 3 of Article 114 of the Commercial Procedural Code of Ukraine, which provides a one-month period for examining a request to review a court decision due to newly discovered circumstances, the HCCU delayed its examination of the case for nine months. [paragraph 5]

First, the HCCU received all the necessary materials from the Donetsk Court of Appeal and scheduled the hearing date. But when the parties arrived at 6 Kopylenka St. in Kyiv, they found that nothing was going to happen. Apparently, the document was missing.
Accordingly, the HCCU immediately stated: ‘As can be seen from the content of the cassation appeal, the defendant challenged the ruling of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal of 30 June 2004. However, the case file does not contain the contested ruling or any reference thereto; therefore, case no. 27/37 must be remitted to the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court for proper registration in accordance with the requirements of the law in force.’ Thus, a new date was set and the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court was assigned a task, although it is clear that it was intended for the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. But these are different State institutions, are they not? Or perhaps they have long been a single structure, a fact that the judiciary of Ukraine’s largest commercial court of first instance still does not even suspect, but which is clear in Kyiv, and that is why they wrote it? [paragraph 6]

In short, no one has yet bothered to explain where the ruling was and how it suddenly appeared in the materials of case no. 27/37. They quietly sweep it under the carpet, although it was most likely no accident and they were pursuing a specific objective: to delay consideration of the case until 1 February 2005. Indeed, on that very day, pursuant to order no. 797 of 1 September 2004 of the Ministry of Transport, ‘in order to increase the efficiency of the use of State property’, the liquidation of Intertrans was completed and it was removed from the United State Register of Enterprises and Organisations of Ukraine. Everything went according to plan. The court hearing took place after the specified date, while the case file had still not been returned from Kyiv to Donetsk. Note that this is only part of the State problem inherited from the previous leadership of the Ministry of Transport. Informed sources claim that the liquidation of Intertrans made it possible to bury amounts far larger than the funds unjustly recovered from I.-Bank on the basis of the ‘copy’. However, this is another topic worthy of journalistic attention.” [paragraph 7]

9. The article concluded with the following paragraphs (the eighth and ninth paragraphs):

“Incidentally, [Ch.], the managing director of joint-stock company [D.], conducted an investigation and concluded that an organised group was operating in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. In a letter to the head of the parliamentary sub-committee on combating organised crime and corruption in law-enforcement bodies and courts, he listed the members of the group and described in detail how the entire scheme operated. As evidence, [Ch.] cited case no. 8/55, in which he had been a defendant in proceedings brought by the State enterprise Ugolnaya kompaniya ‘Krasnolimanskaya’ concerning the invalidation of a contract, as well as several other similar disputes that were subsequently quashed by the Supreme Court of Ukraine. The judges, well known from case no.
27/37, appear everywhere. [paragraph 8]The reason for my speech to the Verkhovna Rada – said [Ch.] – was case no. 8/55. While the case was proceeding through all the [judicial] instances, I felt the pressure of the system. Let us say an interested client comes knocking and seeks assistance with a case that is clearly bound to lose. They recommend that he approach law firm [L.]. A contract is then concluded with the client, the money is transferred, and the claim is prepared. Then, regardless of [any] existing procedure, the case is ‘allocated’ to the right judge. After that, the case is invariably decided in the client’s favour. If the other party files an appeal, there is a so-called ‘black triad’, which follows the principle [that] ‘nothing else matters in the case’. Most people who have gone through these two [judicial] instances give up. They lose faith in justice and do not pursue the matter elsewhere. They tell themselves, ‘they are all tarred with the same brush’.” [paragraph 9]Interim injunction proceedings10. On 7 April 2005, judges A., C., D., E., B., and F. applied to the Voroshylovsky District Court of Donetsk City (hereinafter the “District Court”) seeking the application of “preventive measures and securing of evidence” (заява про вжиття запобіжних заходів та про забезпечення доказів). They contended that the article of 12 March 2005, “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case”, contained a negative assessment of the activities of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal and was unsupported by any facts. The tone of the article was extremely negative. In particular, the claimants stated that the following assertions did not correspond to reality: “an organised group”, “the detailed mode of operation of the whole scheme”, “the pressure of the system”, “assistance with a case that will clearly lose”, “in spite of [any] existing procedure, the case is distributed to the right judge”, the existence of a “black triad”, and the principle that “nothing else matters in the case”. The applicant “had not verified the information in question” and had therefore failed to fulfil his professional duties. According to the claimants, the publication breached the honour, dignity, and professional reputation of the above-mentioned courts, their management, and the judges. In particular, it was noted that judges E., C., D., and F. had examined case no. 8/55, which was referred to in the publication, and that the article had therefore caused them non-pecuniary damage. Similar damage had been caused to A., the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who “was responsible for the organisational management of the court”, and B., the Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court, who “according to the distribution of duties, managed the structural unit that included the judges who had examined case no. 8/55”.11.
The claimants stated that they intended to bring a defamation claim for damages against the newspaper, the applicant and Ch. (which they eventually did on 18 April and 18 August 2005 (see paragraph 23 below)), as the article in question contained “elements of an interview, i.e. the last paragraph containing eventually the majority of the untrustful information”. Referring, inter alia, to Articles 277 and 278 of the Civil Code of Ukraine (“the CCU” – see paragraph 34 below), they submitted that their rights continued to be infringed while the article remained available online and requested its removal under Article 62-1 of the Code of Civil Procedure (“the CCP” – see paragraph 35 below).

12. The claimants requested an order requiring the newspaper’s editorial board to remove the article from its website. In addition, they sought the attachment of the property of the newspaper, the applicant and Ch. in order to secure their claims. Finally, they requested that the newspaper produce the documents used by its editorial board and the applicant to verify the information published in the article.

13. On 8 April 2005 the District Court ordered the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to remove the article from the newspaper’s website. In its one-and-a-half-page decision, the court simply reiterated the content of the claimants’ request. It then referred to Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, which listed the possible interim measures for securing a claim, and stated that the request should be granted in part, without providing any reasoning or assessment of the claimants’ position.

14. The applicant, the newspaper and Ch. appealed against that decision, noting, inter alia, that an interim injunction requiring an article to be removed from a website was not provided for under domestic law. Furthermore, they submitted that the court had relied on Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, which provided for interim measures after a claim had been lodged, rather than before. They also noted that the court had failed to give any reasons. In particular, they argued that the article had not identified a single judge and that the claimants had therefore failed to demonstrate that their rights had been infringed.

15. On 26 August 2005 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s decision. After reiterating the claimants’ request and quoting Article 278 § 2 of the CCU, the court stated as follows:

“The challenged article contains information disseminated on the Internet. Since such information is accessible to the general public and difficult to control, removing the article from the website (similar to attachment of property under paragraph 2 of Article 62-2 of the CCP) is the only measure capable of ensuring protection of the individual right pending examination of the merits of the case. [The first-instance] court relied on Article 152 of the CCP, which provides for securing a claim by prohibiting certain actions.”
Such a reference is erroneous, since no claim had been lodged by the time the ruling was delivered. However, this deficiency cannot constitute a ground for quashing the court’s ruling, as the request had been correctly examined on the merits”.

16. The applicant appealed in cassation, arguing that Article 62-2 of the CCP did not provide for any interim measure such as removing an article from a website. He also stated that the court had failed to give reasons for its decision and that the claimants had submitted no evidence in support of their contention that their rights had been infringed.

17. Approximately two and a half years later, on 15 January 2008, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, sitting as a cassation court, dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decisions of 8 April and 26 August 2005 for lack of evidence of any breach of the law.

18. The above judicial decisions were enforced, and the impugned article was removed from the newspaper’s website on an unspecified date, but no later than 18 August 2005.

Subsequent publication

19. On 28 March 2005, A., the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, and B., a former Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial[1] Court, sent a letter to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya demanding that the information published in the article of 12 March 2005 be retracted. They supplied a text for publication for that purpose. The letter was received at the newspaper’s office on 31 March 2005.

20. On 23 April 2005, following the interim injunction issued by the Voroshyloskyy District Court of Donetsk (see paragraphs 10-13 above), Dzerkalo Tyzhnya published an article entitled “Black triad: to be continued” (“Чорна трійка: далі буде”), identifying A. and B. as the authors of the letter requesting the retraction. The article, which appears to have summarised the text of their letter of 28 March 2005, reads as follows:

“Every court case is a complex tangle of the parties’ conflicting interests, and its resolution, regardless of [the outcome] ... will always leave one party dissatisfied. Even where a party understands that there are no grounds for appealing against the court’s decision, it is often only the obligation to pay court and legal fees that would deter it from lodging such an appeal. Most people naturally regard all decisions in their favour as lawful and fair, and vice versa. Anyone who has acted as a judge in a dispute knows that the losing party will most likely consider the decision unfair and biased.

On 12 March 2005, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] published an article by Anatoliy Yeremenko [entitled] ‘Black triad: nothing else matters in the case’. The article addressed highly important and relevant issues for contemporary Ukrainian society.
It recounts the story of the managing director of [joint-stock company D.], [Ch.], who allegedly uncovered unlawful activity [on the part] of judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal.

However, many were surprised by [Ch.’s] resentment towards the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. Indeed, considering the number of cases won by [joint-stock company D.] and the ‘strength’ of those cases, it would seem more likely that his opponents had reasons [to feel that way]. Take, for instance, the decision in case no. 38/251, under which the claimant, [joint-stock company D.], was awarded UAH 262,776.32 ...

However, another case – no. 8/55 – is also cited as an example in the article. For some unknown reason, [the newspaper article did not mention that] the request of [D.’s] managing director under Articles 4 to 6 of the Code of Commercial Procedure of Ukraine to [have] his case heard by a bench of judges was disregarded. For those who are not lawyers, we should explain that these Articles provide for cases to be examined by a bench of judges in a local commercial court where their category and complexity so require. However, [Ch.] based his request solely on the need to prevent the opposing party from exerting pressure on the court (which is not a ground for allowing the case to be examined by a bench of judges). Therefore, following the letter of the law, the court should have rejected [Ch.’s] request as unlawful. Nevertheless, having considered the category of the case and the large number of circumstances requiring examination, the court granted his request. It follows that the claimant either cannot understand the text of the law (yet takes the liberty of criticising court decisions), or deliberately provoked the court into rejecting the request so that he would later have an excuse to complain about the court’s bias.

Yet, despite the favourable decision regarding the composition of the court in case no. 8/55, [Ch.] asserts that ‘then, in spite of [any] existing procedure, the case is “distributed” to the right judge’. It is easy to see that this conclusion contradicts the facts, as do [the conclusions] that ‘the case is always decided in the client’s favour’ and that there is a so-called ‘black triad’ in the court of appeal. Even more offensive is his final conclusion that ‘they are all tarred with the same brush’.

The only lawful way to obtain a decision in your favour is to act within the law and present sufficient arguments and valid evidence. But some people (who could hardly be called law-abiding citizens) will stop at nothing. If the end justifies the means, why not try every one of them?
The easiest way, from a practical point of view—but, we emphasise, neither effective nor ethical—to persuade the court to adopt the ‘required’ decision is to issue a warning along the lines of: it is better not to mess with me. By manipulating public opinion, such people seek to influence the decisions of public servants, including judges. Indeed, hardly anyone would wish to be associated with the ‘black triad’.

Currently, the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court is examining a case in which [D.] is one of the parties. So, is the tragic farce of [Ch.] not an attempt to intimidate the court and influence its future judgment? It suggests [that] the ‘black triad’ article could be continued by adding the family names of all judges with firm beliefs, who could then be forced to prove their integrity publicly. It is well known that the higher a person’s social status, the more inclined society is to believe the most absurd gossip about them, leaving them to prove their innocence.

Therefore, the functioning of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal was negatively assessed without any basis. In particular, there is no reason to believe that an organised group engaged in unlawful activity operates in the above-mentioned courts. There is no practice in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court or the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal of helping interested clients [obtain] ‘positive decision[s]’ in ‘case[s] that will clearly lose’. Furthermore, employees of these courts never recommend specific law firms. It is also untrue that, notwithstanding the established procedure, cases are assigned to the ‘right judge’ to secure a decision in favour of the client. The court does not and cannot have ‘clients’, and decisions in the cases mentioned in the articles were made following an impartial examination of all the circumstances and the evidence submitted by the parties.

There are no grounds for concluding that most people who went through the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal gave up, lost faith in justice, and did not apply anywhere else.”

21. On 12 May 2005, the claimants sent another letter to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, demanding that the newspaper publish a retraction. They stressed that their previous request had not been adequately addressed, since the publication had appeared without the word “retraction” in its title and had included only summarised elements of their letter of 28 March 2005.

22. On 23 May 2005, the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya replied that the above demand was unfounded prior to the examination of the relevant claim by the courts and the delivery of the corresponding judgment.

Defamation proceedings

23. On 18 April and 18 August 2005, the same claimants (see paragraph 10 above) lodged defamation claims against the applicant, Ch.
and the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya. They alleged that the article in question had harmed their professional reputation, honour and dignity. In their view, the statements in the article had undermined the authority of the judiciary. In their amended claim, the judges asked the court to declare the following statements defamatory:

– “there was an organised group operating in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and in the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal”;

– that Ch. had uncovered “a detailed mode of operation of the whole scheme”;

– “the pressure of the system”;

– “an interested client comes knocking and asks for assistance with a case that will clearly lose. They recommend that he goes to law firm [L.]. Then the contract is concluded with the client, the money is transferred, and the claim is prepared. Then, despite [any] existing procedure, the case is ‘distributed’ to the right judge. After that, the case is always decided in the client’s favour”;

– “If another party lodges an appeal, a so-called ‘black triad’ exists, which embraces the principle [that] ‘nothing else matters in the case’”; and

– “they are all tarred with the same brush”.

They also asked the court to order the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to publish a retraction of those statements and to order the applicant and Ch. to pay each claimant 10,000 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

They acknowledged that the newspaper had partly restored their rights by allowing them to exercise their right of reply to the allegations made in the impugned article and by removing the article from its website.

24. In his reply to the claim, the applicant maintained that the statements at issue contained information of importance to the general public and that the sources of that information were Ch. and Ch.’s letter to the parliamentary sub-committee. He also noted that he had properly verified that the letter had indeed been submitted to Parliament and that it had formed the basis of a related inquiry by the law-enforcement authorities. At the same time, he stated that Ch.’s remarks were consistent with the findings of his own journalistic investigations into cases nos. 27/37 and 8/55, which had been based on the relevant case files. The applicant considered that, because he had obtained the information from “an official” of an organisation, he was exempt from liability for the published material under section 42(2) of the Press Act. Lastly, the applicant pointed out that the claimants had never been named in the article and that at least twelve other judges had examined the case at issue in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court but had not brought defamation proceedings. He also referred to his earlier article of 29 May 2004, in which A. and C. had been named but in respect of which they had never initiated defamation proceedings.
In support of his arguments, the applicant attached, among other things, Ch.’s letter to the parliamentary sub-committee, the files of several cases he had examined during his investigation, including case no. 27/37, and his earlier articles on the subject. 25. On an unspecified date, the applicant and Ch. also filed counterclaims. The applicant stated that, before bringing defamation proceedings and seeking the interim injunction, A., C., D., E., B., and F. had unlawfully obtained his personal information, including his name and contact details. He asked the court to declare those actions unlawful. Ch. asked the court to find that the information contained in the judges’ letter to the newspaper, published on 23 April 2005 (see paragraph 20 above), was untrue. 26. On 20 October 2005, the Petrovskyy Local Court considered the case on the merits. After analysing the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article in question, the court allowed the judges’ claim in part. It concluded that the statements in those paragraphs were defamatory (“had presented a distorted view of reality and were not based on actual facts”) and that their publication had caused non-pecuniary damage to all the claimants. 27. The relevant parts of the court’s judgment stated as follows:

“[T]he information contained in the relevant paragraphs of the article did not reflect reality and tarnished the honour, dignity and reputation of the claimants for the following reasons.

...

At the court hearing, the [applicant] confirmed that, in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article, he had used information provided by Ch., including the letter to the parliamentary sub-committee, together with [Ch.’s] succinct commentary, which contained elements of an interview.[2]

The respondent Ch. confirmed that the author had used the information supplied by him in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the impugned article.

An analysis of the ninth paragraph of the article establishes that it was published in the form of an interview.

Under section 13 of the Copyright and Related Rights Act, copyright in a recorded interview is considered co-authorship. The interviewee and the interviewer are co-authors of the interview.

The court finds that [the applicant] and Ch. are co-authors of the article ...

[In the letter addressed to the head of the parliamentary sub-commission on combating organised crime and corruption], Ch. stated that an organised criminal group was operating in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal which, on demand, issued judgments and rulings sought by clients. [He] identified the members of the group and explained how it operated.

...

Ch.
also sent this letter to the State Security Service and was informed that his allegations were under verification.... In response to an enquiry from the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, [on 22 April 2005] the Administration of the Security Service of Ukraine in the Donetsk Region reported that, following an examination [перевірки] of Ch.’s allegations, no evidence of the existence or activities of such an organised criminal group in the [above-mentioned courts] had been found. Therefore, [the relevant statements] published in the eighth paragraph of the article had not been substantiated and, accordingly, [they] were untrue.... The article referred to Ch.’s letter to ..., in which he explicitly mentioned a criminal organisation operating in the [above-mentioned] courts. Although the article did not reproduce the contents of that letter, the statements in the eighth and ninth paragraphs suggested to the reader that the existence of a ‘criminal group’ was under discussion.

In describing the procedure for distributing and examining cases, the co-authors of the article accused the [judges] of the above courts not only of breaching bylaws, but also of conduct that could be interpreted as abuse of office and a miscarriage of justice, both of which are criminal offences. ... The expression ‘organised group’ was used in the article in a criminal sense and was associated with a criminal offence committed by an organised group.

Under Article 62 of the Constitution of Ukraine, a person is presumed innocent of committing a crime until their guilt is proved in accordance with the law and established by a court verdict.

No such verdict has been delivered in respect of the claimants by any domestic court, and therefore [those statements] were defamatory.

At the same time, the court cannot take into account the defendants’ arguments that, at the court hearing, they had provided evidence supporting their statement concerning the existence of a special procedure for examining cases, for the following reasons.

As noted above, the statements concerning the existence of a special procedure for examining cases in the above-mentioned courts amount to an accusation that a crime has been committed, which ... must be proved by certain means.
In view of Article 62 of the Constitution concerning the presumption of innocence, the above statements can be established only by a court verdict, which does not exist in respect of the claimants....

Section 42 of the Press Act provides that a journalist is exempt from liability for publishing material that is untrue, defames the honour and dignity of citizens and organisations, infringes the rights and lawful interests of citizens, or constitutes an abuse of the freedom of the printed mass media and the rights of journalists if the information is contained in a reply to a request for access to official documents or to a request for written or oral information, provided in accordance with the Information Act.

Section 32 of the Information Act provides that a request for access to official documents is a request addressed to the relevant State authorities or their officials for the purpose of examining official documents.

Since joint-stock company D. was not a State body and its managing director, Ch., was not an official of a State authority, his letter could not be regarded as an official document within the meaning of section 42 of the Press Act and section 32 of the Information Act.

Under section 47-1 of the Information Act ... value judgments are not subject to retraction or proof of their veracity....

The information in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article, particularly the following statements, may be interpreted as containing factual information and therefore does not constitute value judgments: ‘Ch. came to the conclusion that there was an organised group operating in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal’; ‘an interested client comes knocking and asks for assistance with a case that will clearly lose. They recommend that he goes to the law firm [L.] Then a contract is concluded with the client, the money is transferred, and the statement of claim is prepared. Then, notwithstanding [any] existing procedure, the case is “distributed” to the right judge. After that, the case is invariably decided in the client’s favour’; ‘If another party lodges an appeal, there is a so-called “black triad”, which embraces the principle [that] “nothing else matters in the case”....

By virtue of Article 277 of the CCU, one of the elements of the offence is the dissemination of information about a person that would enable an observer to deduce that it concerns a specific identifiable individual or, at least, that the person belongs to a group of people to whom such information relates. Stating the person’s name is not obligatory: information may be considered to concern a specific person if he or she can be identified on the basis of other elements.

The claimants A., C., D. and E. are judges of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, while B. and F. are judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. In addition, A. is the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal and B.
used to be Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. In the article, the authors allege the existence of an organised group in the [above-mentioned] courts, which this court has found to be inaccurate/false. This fact alone tarnishes the dignity, honour and reputation of the managing officials of those courts, namely A. and B. As evidence of the existence of an organised group in the above-mentioned courts, the authors refer to case no. 8/55. Having examined the case file, the court established that B. had assigned F. to examine case no. 8/55; F. had been the presiding judge when the case was examined by the first-instance court; and E., C. and D. had subsequently examined the case in the court of appeal. Thus, as a result of the publication of false information, all the above-mentioned judges sustained non-pecuniary damage, including B., who at the relevant time was Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and managed the court division comprising the judges who had examined the case at first instance. A., the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who ... is responsible for the organisational management of the court in which the case at issue was examined on appeal, also sustained non-pecuniary damage. The court dismisses the respondents’ arguments that the claimants’ names had not been mentioned, since the co-authors of the article provided sufficient information to identify them. In addition, information concerning the judges examining domestic cases was not restricted, copies of the court decisions had been sent to the parties, and information about those judges could be known to an unlimited/unrestricted number of persons.”

28. When determining the compensation to be paid to the claimants by the applicant and Ch., the court noted that the applicant was guilty to a lesser degree, since it was Ch. who had provided him with the information. However, the applicant had failed to verify that information and had therefore failed to fulfil his professional duties as set out in section 26 of the Press Act.

29. The court ordered the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to publish a retraction of the statements contained in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article, and ordered the applicant to pay UAH 333 in respect of non-pecuniary damage to each claimant, together with their legal fees (UAH 333 per claimant) and court fees (UAH 100 per claimant). In total, the applicant was ordered to pay the equivalent of 331 euros (EUR) in respect of non-pecuniary damage and EUR 430.51 in legal and court fees. Ch. was ordered to pay UAH 1,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage to each claimant, together with legal and court fees.

Finally, the court dismissed the applicant’s and Ch.’s counterclaims as unsubstantiated.

30.
The applicant appealed against the judgment of 20 October 2005 of the Petrovskyy Local Court, relying on the following grounds: (i) the court had failed to establish the existence of non-pecuniary damage, as it had not provided concrete reasons concerning the effect of the article on the claimants and their psychological health; (ii) the court had failed to distinguish between facts and “value judgments”. In that regard, the applicant noted that the phrase “tarred with the same brush” was clearly a “value judgment”, yet it had not been examined separately by the court and had been found defamatory as part of the text as a whole; (iii) the material in the case files of case no. 8/55 and several other cases was sufficient to conclude that the statements published in the article were true; (iv) the court had failed to examine whether mens rea existed in respect of the applicant’s actions; (v) the court had gone beyond the scope of the complaints and had found the broader content of the statements published in the article defamatory; he referred to the fact that the court had relied on the full text of the eighth and ninth paragraphs rather than only the specific statements quoted by the claimants in their complaints (for example, the phrases “Ch. concluded ...” and “most of the people ...”); and (vi) the amount of court fees he had been ordered to pay to the claimants was excessive.

31. On 27 January 2006, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance court’s judgment on the merits and amended it as regards legal and court fees, reducing the court fees imposed on the applicant to the equivalent of EUR 244.08.

The relevant parts of the appellate court’s judgment read as follows:

“It follows from the content of the impugned article that the respondent Ch. had carried out his own investigation and concluded that there was an organised group in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, referring to the letter of the head of the sub-committee of the Verkhovna Rada ... which named the members of the group and described in detail how the entire scheme operated. References are made to cases nos. 8/55 and 27/37. The ninth paragraph contains direct speech and discusses, on behalf of Ch., case no. 8/55 ...

At the hearing, the respondents maintained that the published information concerning the existence of an organised group in the courts in question ... was true. They insisted that case no. 8/55, together with other cases, had been allocated by B. and A. to ‘their’ judges, in breach of the orders concerning the specialisation of the courts’ composition. They submitted the orders [allocating the cases], pointing to the breaches allegedly committed in the allocation of case no. 8/55 and other cases.

The court reasonably dismissed the respondents’ arguments.”
The allocation of cases in the courts concerned is an internal matter for the court, and such circumstances cannot indicate the existence of an organised group or the operation of a ‘scheme’ involving interested clients. At the time the article was published, the claimants had not been convicted or found liable for acts of corruption ...... It follows from the certificates in the case files that all the claimants serve as judges in the courts concerned. In the article, the claimants were accused of violating the law when examining commercial cases; however, such circumstances were not proved at the court hearing. In support of their arguments ... the respondents referred to the allocation of cases in breach of specialisation orders, but did not provide any factual data proving the information published in the article.”

32. In his cassation appeal, the applicant repeated his previous arguments and further noted that, after reading Ch.’s letter, he had conducted his own investigation and, relying on the materials in the case files, considered that he had verified the relevant information with due diligence.

33. By a final decision of 5 November 2007, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, sitting as a court of cassation, dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal against the decisions of 20 October 2005 and 27 January 2006. The court provided no reasoning apart from the standard conclusion that the applicant’s cassation appeal offered no grounds for finding that the lower courts had violated substantive or procedural law in their decisions.
