CASE OF ANATOLIY YEREMENKO v. UKRAINE

(Application no. 22287/08)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

15 September 2022

FINAL

15/12/2022

In accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment has become final. It may undergo editorial revision.

In the case of Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Síofra O’Leary, President,
Mārtiņš Mits,
Ganna Yudkivska,
Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström,
Lado Chanturia,
Arnfinn Bårdsen,
Mattias Guyomar, judges,

and Victor Soloveytchik, Section Registrar,

Having taken into account:

the application (no. 22287/08) brought against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Anatoliy Vasylyovych Yeremenko, a Ukrainian national (“the applicant”), on 26 April 2008;

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint alleging a violation of Article 10 of the Convention;

the observations submitted by the parties;

Having deliberated in private on 31 August 2021 and 21 June 2022,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on the latter date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case arises from defamation proceedings instituted against the applicant after the publication of an article he had written concerning alleged corruption within the judiciary. It also concerns an injunction requiring the article to be removed from the newspaper’s website while the defamation proceedings were pending. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complains about those measures.

THE FACTS

2. The applicant, who was born in 1949, resides in Kyiv. He was represented by Ms L.L. Pankratova, a lawyer practising in Kyiv.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, most recently Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. On the basis of the parties’ submissions, the relevant facts may be summarised as set out below.

BACKGROUND TO THE CASE

The article published on 12 March 2005

5. The applicant is a journalist. At the relevant time, he worked for Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, a nationwide analytical weekly newspaper with a circulation of approximately 57,000 copies.

6. As part of a series of pieces written by the applicant, the newspaper published his article entitled “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case” (“Чорна трійка: все інше справи не стосується”) on 12 March 2005. The article was subsequently posted on the newspaper’s website on 18 March 2005.

7. Referring to an earlier article he had written, the applicant stated that, in a particular case (no. 27/37) which had been before the courts for some time and had been remitted to the lower courts on at least two occasions, a judgment had been based on a forged copy of a document. The original document formed part of the case file in a separate set of criminal proceedings. Nonetheless, the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had rendered its judgment on the strength of the forged copy. The applicant then described what he characterised as a “system for securing the desired result”.
To obtain the desired outcome, a particular law firm was engaged. Although the plaintiff paid it a considerable fee, the firm then “unexpectedly” withdrew from any further involvement in the proceedings, leaving the plaintiff—a State-owned enterprise—to be represented by its in-house lawyers. The courts, meanwhile, had “carefully referred the case” to the Higher Commercial Court. That court took an excessively long time to consider the matter and ultimately returned it to a lower court “because no copy of the contested decision had been provided”. During this period, the plaintiff was liquidated, which, in the applicant’s view, made it possible to conceal numerous irregularities.

8. The article stated in full:

“In May of last year, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] (no. 21, 29 May 2004) published an article entitled ‘How the court validated a copy of a document when the original was missing’ [‘Як суд “легалізував” “копію” при відсутності оригіналу’]. It examined an incident unprecedented in the history of Ukrainian justice: relying on a highly questionable copy of a particular document [a guarantee letter]—questionable both as to the quality of the print and, even more so, as to its contents—the court issued a judgment that the respondent has now been challenging for four years. The challenge began at the same time as the presidential decree establishing appellate courts in Ukraine was promulgated, and for one straightforward reason: the respondent maintains that it never issued the plaintiff with a document bearing that [registration] number and never provided any guarantee. Yet, since there are various ways of making any conflict of interest acceptable to Themis, the case has come to symbolise dignity while also becoming a fetish representing the deficiencies of the very structure of the judicial system borrowed from developed democracies. That structure was imposed on a system corrupted by ‘sovietness’ [совковостью] and by the influence of ‘telephone law’ on the development of the principles governing the independence of the third branch of power in our State. [paragraph 1]

DT has repeatedly reported on the twists and turns of the litigation and on the parties’ competing claims. During the three years preceding publication of the [above-mentioned] article, case no. 27/37 passed through two complete cycles of judicial proceedings, from the first-instance court to a judgment of the Supreme Court of Ukraine. A third cycle also took place on the basis of newly discovered circumstances. In criminal proceedings brought against limited liability company N., which stole [an unspecified item or items] worth more than 8.2 million Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) from the State transport and shipping enterprise Intertrans before disappearing without a trace, the prosecutor’s office found the original of the disputed guarantee letter.”
The guarantee letter on which the plaintiff, Intertrans, relied had in fact been issued by the defendant to an entirely different enterprise. The defendant had raised this point from the outset and repeated it at every court hearing, yet, for reasons unknown, it was consistently disregarded. The Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had an opportunity to correct the record. Instead, after confirming that the guarantee letter existed in the criminal case file, it rendered its decision on the basis of a purported “copy” of that letter. The author therefore understandably asked: “I wonder what the commercial justice system will devise this time to protect the State enterprise/structure that inflicted substantial pecuniary damage on the State?” [paragraph 2]

Reality exceeded even the boldest expectations. Delving further into the murky and dubious practices surrounding the resolution of commercial disputes in the Donetsk region creates the impression of a system that is rudimentary in design but highly effective at securing the desired outcome in almost any case. Its facilitators seem wholly unconcerned with the substance of the dispute. What matters is that the customer—usually the plaintiff—approaches the right people at the right time. [paragraph 3]

Typically, the customer turns to a law firm and lawfully transfers substantial sums for “legal services.” It then becomes difficult to identify any meaningful part played by that firm in the ensuing proceedings. Representatives may appear; alternatively, as happened with Intertrans—which, for reasons that remain unclear, paid the mysterious I. a fee of UAH 400,000—the customer may simply rely on its own lawyers to conduct the litigation. From beginning to end, the case passes through the hands of numerous functionaries of commercial justice in the Donetsk region, who carefully and attentively shepherd it all the way to the Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine. [paragraph 4]

Once both the original of the supposed “copy” and an additional document demonstrating that the “copy” had been forged came to light, the issue could no longer be treated as a contest between opposing arguments. It had become a matter of falsification and intent—questions belonging not to commercial litigation but to a criminal investigation. Again, the facts speak for themselves. The Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine (HCCU) once more left its mark. Part 3 of Article 114 of the Commercial Procedural Code of Ukraine requires an application for review of a judicial decision on the basis of newly discovered circumstances to be examined within one month. Despite that requirement, the HCCU postponed consideration of the case for nine months. [paragraph 5]

Initially, the HCCU obtained all the required materials from the Donetsk Court of Appeal and scheduled a hearing. Yet when the parties arrived at 6 Kopylenka Street in Kyiv, they learned that no hearing would take place. Apparently, a document had gone missing.
Accordingly, the HCCU promptly stated: ‘The cassation appeal shows that the defendant challenged the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal’s ruling of 30 June 2004. Yet the case file contains neither the disputed ruling nor any reference to it. Case no. 27/37 must therefore be returned to the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court for proper registration in compliance with the legislation in force.’ Thus, another date was fixed and the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court was given an assignment, even though the assignment was clearly intended for the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. But these are separate State institutions, are they not? Or have they long formed a single structure—something apparently known in Kyiv, hence the wording used there, but still unsuspected by the judiciary of Ukraine’s largest first-instance commercial court? [paragraph 6]

In short, no one has yet troubled to explain where the ruling had been or how it suddenly appeared among the documents in case no. 27/37. The matter has been quietly brushed aside, although it was most likely no accident. Rather, a specific objective was being pursued: postponing examination of the case until 1 February 2005. On precisely that date, pursuant to Ministry of Transport order no. 797 of 1 September 2004, issued ‘in order to increase the efficiency of the use of State property’, Intertrans’s liquidation was completed and the company was removed from the United State Register of Enterprises and Organisations of Ukraine. Everything unfolded according to plan. The hearing was held only after that date, while the case file has still not been sent back from Kyiv to Donetsk. It should be stressed that this represents only one aspect of a broader State problem inherited from the Ministry of Transport’s former leadership. According to informed sources, Intertrans’s liquidation enabled the concealment of sums far exceeding the money unjustly recovered from I.-Bank on the strength of the ‘copy’. That, however, is another subject deserving journalistic scrutiny.” [paragraph 7]

9. The article concluded with the following two paragraphs, the eighth and ninth:

“Incidentally, [Ch.], managing director of joint-stock company [D.], carried out an investigation and concluded that an organised group was operating within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. In a letter addressed to the chair of the parliamentary subcommittee responsible for combating organised crime and corruption in law-enforcement agencies and the courts, he identified the group’s members and described in detail how the entire scheme functioned. In support of his allegations, [Ch.] referred to case no. 8/55, in which he had appeared as a defendant in proceedings brought against him by the State enterprise Ugolnaya kompaniya ‘Krasnolimanskaya’ concerning the invalidation of a contract. He also cited several comparable disputes, the decisions in which were later quashed by the Supreme Court of Ukraine. The judges, already well known from case no.
27/37, are found everywhere.

[paragraph 8] [Ch.] stated that case no. 8/55 had prompted his address to the Verkhovna Rada. As the proceedings moved through every [judicial] level, he experienced pressure from the system. He described a situation in which an interested client seeks help with a case that is plainly destined to fail and is advised to approach law firm [L.]. A contract is then signed, payment is made, and a claim is drafted. Regardless of [any] applicable procedure, the case is subsequently “allocated” to a suitable judge, who invariably rules for the client. Should the opposing party appeal, a so-called “black triad” applies the principle that “nothing else matters in the case”. Most people who pass through those two [judicial] levels abandon any further action. Having lost confidence in justice, they pursue no additional remedies and conclude that “they are all tarred with the same brush”.

[paragraph 9] Interim injunction proceedings

10. On 7 April 2005, judges A., C., D., E., B. and F. submitted an application to the Voroshylovsky District Court of Donetsk City (the “District Court”) seeking “preventive measures and the securing of evidence” (заява про вжиття запобіжних заходів та про забезпечення доказів). They maintained that the article published on 12 March 2005 under the title “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case” presented the work of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal in a negative light without any factual basis. They also characterised the article’s tone as extremely negative.

The claimants specifically disputed the accuracy of references to “an organised group”, “the detailed method by which the entire scheme operated”, “pressure from the system”, “help with a case that was clearly bound to fail”, the assertion that “regardless of [any] existing procedure, the case is assigned to the right judge”, and the alleged existence of a “black triad” guided by the principle that “nothing else matters in the case”. They contended that the applicant had failed to verify the information and had consequently neglected his professional obligations.

In their view, the publication infringed the honour, dignity and professional reputation of the courts concerned, their management and their judges. They noted in particular that judges E., C., D. and F. had adjudicated case no. 8/55, to which the article referred, and had therefore suffered non-pecuniary damage. They alleged that comparable harm had been sustained by A., Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who “was responsible for the court’s organisational management”, and by B., Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court, who “under the allocation of responsibilities, managed the structural unit comprising the judges who had examined case no. 8/55”.

11.
The claimants announced their intention to bring defamation proceedings for damages against the newspaper, the applicant and Ch.; they ultimately filed such claims on 18 April and 18 August 2005 (see paragraph 23 below). They maintained that the disputed article contained “elements of an interview, i.e. the last paragraph containing eventually the majority of the untrustful information”. Relying, among other provisions, on Articles 277 and 278 of the Civil Code of Ukraine (“the CCU” – see paragraph 34 below), they submitted that the continued online availability of the article infringed their rights and sought its removal under Article 62-1 of the Code of Civil Procedure (“the CCP” – see paragraph 35 below).

12. The claimants requested an order requiring the newspaper’s editorial board to delete the article from its website. To secure their claims, they also sought the attachment of property belonging to the newspaper, the applicant and Ch. Lastly, they asked the newspaper to disclose the documents used by its editorial board and the applicant to verify the information published in the article.

13. On 8 April 2005, the District Court directed the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to remove the article from the newspaper’s website. Its one-and-a-half-page ruling simply restated the substance of the claimants’ request. Without assessing their arguments or giving any reasons, the court then cited Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, which listed the available injunctive measures for securing a claim, and concluded that the request should be granted in part.

14. The applicant, the newspaper and Ch. appealed. They argued, among other things, that domestic law did not provide for an interim injunction requiring an article to be removed from a website. They further pointed out that Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, on which the court had relied, concerned interim measures imposed after a claim had been lodged, rather than beforehand. They also submitted that the court had given no reasons for its decision. In particular, because the article did not identify any judge by name, they contended that the claimants had failed to establish any infringement of their rights.

15. On 26 August 2005, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal affirmed the District Court’s decision. After restating the claimants’ request and citing Article 278 § 2 of the CCU, it held:

“The contested article contains information disseminated via the Internet. As that information is available to the general public and difficult to control, removing the article from the website—by analogy with attachment of property under paragraph 2 of Article 62-2 of the CCP—is the only measure capable of protecting the individual right pending determination of the case on the merits. The [first-instance] court relied on Article 152 of the CCP, which allows a claim to be secured by prohibiting certain actions.”
That reference was incorrect because, when the ruling was issued, no claim had yet been filed. Nevertheless, this defect does not justify setting aside the ruling, since the request was properly considered on its merits.”

16. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal, contending that Article 62-2 of the CCP did not provide for an interim measure requiring an article to be removed from a website. He also submitted that the court had given no reasons for its decision and that the claimants had produced no evidence substantiating their allegation that their rights had been violated.

17. Approximately two and a half years later, on 15 January 2008, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, acting as a cassation court, dismissed the applicant’s challenge to the decisions of 8 April and 26 August 2005, finding no evidence that the law had been breached.

18. Those judicial decisions were enforced. On an unspecified date, but no later than 18 August 2005, the contested article was taken down from the newspaper’s website.

Subsequent publication

19. On 28 March 2005, A., President of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, and B., a former Deputy President of the Donetsk Regional Commercial[1] Court, wrote to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, demanding that the information contained in the article of 12 March 2005 be retracted. They enclosed the text they wished to have published as the retraction. The newspaper’s office received the letter on 31 March 2005.

20. On 23 April 2005, in compliance with the interim injunction granted by the Voroshyloskyy District Court of Donetsk (see paragraphs 10-13 above), Dzerkalo Tyzhnya published an article entitled “Black triad: to be continued” (“Чорна трійка: далі буде”). It identified A. and B. as the authors of the letter seeking the retraction. The article, which appears to have summarised their letter of 28 March 2005, stated:

“Every judicial dispute involves a complex web of conflicting interests between the parties, and, whatever its outcome, its resolution ... will invariably leave one side dissatisfied. Even where a party recognises that there are no grounds for appealing against a court decision, it is often only the obligation to pay court costs and legal fees that dissuades it from doing so. People naturally tend to view decisions made in their favour as lawful and fair, and decisions against them in the opposite light. Anyone who has ever adjudicated a dispute knows that the losing party will most likely consider the decision unjust and biased.

On 12 March 2005, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] published an article by Anatoliy Yeremenko entitled ‘Black triad: nothing else matters in the case’. It addressed issues of great importance and immediate relevance to contemporary Ukrainian society.
The article recounts the case of [Ch.], managing director of [joint-stock company D.], who allegedly uncovered unlawful conduct by judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal.

Yet many found [Ch.’s] resentment toward those courts surprising. Considering both the number of cases won by [joint-stock company D.] and the apparent “strength” of its claims, one might have expected the opposing parties, rather than [Ch.], to feel aggrieved. In case no. 38/251, for instance, the claimant, [joint-stock company D.], was awarded UAH 262,776.32 ...

The article also refers to another matter, case no. 8/55. For reasons that remain unclear, however, it omitted the fact that [D.’s] managing director had requested, under Articles 4 to 6 of the Code of Commercial Procedure of Ukraine, that the case be heard by a panel of judges, and that this request was allegedly disregarded. For readers without legal training, those provisions permit a local commercial court to assign a case to a judicial panel when its category and complexity warrant such consideration. [Ch.], however, based his application solely on the need to prevent the opposing party from exerting pressure on the court—an argument that does not constitute legal grounds for a panel hearing. A strict application of the law would therefore have required the court to dismiss his request as unlawful. Nevertheless, after considering the nature of the dispute and the large number of circumstances requiring examination, the court granted it. This suggests either that the claimant cannot understand the statutory language, despite presuming to criticise judicial decisions, or that he deliberately sought to provoke a refusal so that he could later accuse the court of bias.

Notwithstanding the favourable ruling on the court’s composition in case no. 8/55, [Ch.] claims that “then, in spite of [any] existing procedure, the case is ‘distributed’ to the right judge.” That assertion plainly conflicts with the facts, as do his claims that “the case is always decided in the client’s favour” and that a so-called “black triad” operates within the court of appeal. More insulting still is his ultimate allegation that “they are all tarred with the same brush.”

The only lawful means of obtaining a favourable judgment is to comply with the law and present adequate arguments supported by valid evidence. Some people, however—hardly deserving to be called law-abiding citizens—will stop at nothing. If they believe the end justifies the means, why would they not try every possible method?
The simplest practical means of persuading a court to reach the “required” decision—although, we emphasise, neither effective nor ethically acceptable—is to issue a warning amounting to: “You had better not cross me.” By manipulating public opinion, individuals who resort to such methods seek to affect the decisions of public officials, judges included. After all, virtually no one would want to be linked to the “black triad”.

The Donetsk Regional Commercial Court is currently considering a case to which [D.] is a party. Could the tragic farce staged by [Ch.] therefore be an attempt to intimidate the court and influence its forthcoming judgment? The implication is that the article about the “black triad” might be expanded to include the surnames of every judge who firmly adheres to his or her convictions, leaving those judges to defend their integrity publicly. It is well known that the higher an individual’s social standing, the more readily society tends to believe even the most absurd rumours about that person, thereby forcing him or her to establish their innocence.

Accordingly, the work of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal was assessed negatively without any substantive basis. In particular, there are no grounds for alleging that an organised group engaged in unlawful activities operates within those courts. Nor is there any practice in either court of helping interested clients secure “positive decisions” in “cases that will clearly lose”. Moreover, employees of those courts never recommend specific law firms. The allegation that cases are assigned, irrespective of the applicable procedure, to the “right judge” so that a ruling favourable to the client may be delivered is likewise false. A court neither has nor can have “clients”. The decisions in the cases referred to in the articles were reached only after an impartial assessment of all relevant circumstances and of the evidence submitted by the parties.

There is also no basis for concluding that most individuals who appeared before the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal became discouraged, lost faith in justice, and consequently refrained from applying to any other authority.”

21. On 12 May 2005, the claimants sent a further letter to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, demanding that the newspaper publish a retraction. They emphasised that their earlier request had not been adequately addressed because the published material did not include the word “retraction” in its title and reproduced only a summary of parts of their letter of 28 March 2005.

22. On 23 May 2005, the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya responded that the demand was unfounded until the relevant claim had been examined by the courts and a judgment had been delivered.

Defamation proceedings

23. On 18 April and 18 August 2005, the same claimants referred to in paragraph 10 above brought defamation claims against the applicant, Ch.
and the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, alleging that the article had harmed their professional standing, honour and dignity. They maintained that its assertions had diminished public confidence in the judiciary. In an amended claim, the judges requested that the court declare the following statements defamatory:

– that “an organised group” was active within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal;

– that Ch. had uncovered “the detailed workings of the entire scheme”;

– the reference to “pressure from the system”;

– the allegation that “an interested client seeks help with a case that is certain to fail. The client is advised to approach law firm [L.], after which a contract is signed, payment is made and a claim is drawn up. Regardless of the applicable procedure, the case is then ‘assigned’ to the appropriate judge, who invariably rules in the client’s favour”;

– the assertion that, if the opposing party appealed, there was a so-called “black triad” guided by the principle that “nothing else in the case matters”; and

– the statement that “they are all tarred with the same brush”.

The judges also sought an order requiring the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to retract those statements publicly. In addition, they asked that the applicant and Ch. each be ordered to pay every claimant 10,000 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

They acknowledged that the newspaper had partially remedied the alleged infringement of their rights by giving them an opportunity to respond to the accusations made in the disputed article and by deleting the article from its website.

24. In his defence, the applicant argued that the statements conveyed information of public importance and that their sources were Ch. and the letter Ch. had sent to the parliamentary sub-committee. He added that he had properly confirmed both that the letter had been submitted to Parliament and that it had prompted a related investigation by the law-enforcement authorities. He further stated that Ch.’s comments were consistent with the findings of his own journalistic investigations into cases nos. 27/37 and 8/55, which had been based on the respective case files.

The applicant contended that, because the information had been obtained from “an official” of an organisation, section 42(2) of the Press Act exempted him from liability for its publication. Finally, he pointed out that none of the claimants had been identified by name in the article. He also observed that at least twelve other judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court had dealt with the case concerned but had not brought defamation proceedings. In addition, he referred to an earlier article of 29 May 2004 in which A. and C. had been expressly named, yet neither had instituted defamation proceedings in relation to it.
To substantiate his submissions, the applicant enclosed, among other documents, Ch.’s letter to the parliamentary sub-committee, the files of several cases reviewed during his investigation, including case no. 27/37, and articles he had previously written on the subject.

25. On an unspecified date, the applicant and Ch. also filed counterclaims. The applicant alleged that, before bringing the defamation proceedings and seeking the interim injunction, A., C., D., E., B. and F. had unlawfully acquired personal information about him, including his name and contact details. He requested that the court declare those actions unlawful. For his part, Ch. asked the court to find that the information in the judges’ letter published by the newspaper on 23 April 2005 (see paragraph 20 above) was false.

26. On 20 October 2005, the Petrovskyy Local Court considered the merits of the case. After examining the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article at issue, it upheld the judges’ claim in part. It found that the statements in those paragraphs were defamatory because they “had presented a distorted view of reality and were not based on actual facts”, and that their publication had caused non-pecuniary damage to each of the claimants.

27. The pertinent passages of the judgment stated:

“[T]he information in the relevant paragraphs of the article was inconsistent with reality and damaged the claimants’ honour, dignity and reputation for the following reasons....

During the hearing, the [applicant] acknowledged that, when writing the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article, he had relied on material supplied by Ch., including the letter sent to the parliamentary sub-committee, together with [Ch.’s] brief comments containing elements of an interview.[2]

The respondent, Ch., confirmed that the author had used the information he had provided in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the disputed article.

An examination of the article’s ninth paragraph shows that it was published in interview form.

Under section 13 of the Copyright and Related Rights Act, copyright in a recorded interview is held jointly. The interviewer and interviewee are therefore co-authors of the interview.

The court accordingly considers [the applicant] and Ch. to be co-authors of the article....

[In his letter to the head of the parliamentary sub-commission responsible for combating organised crime and corruption], Ch. alleged that an organised criminal group was active within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and that, upon request, it issued judgments and rulings sought by clients. [He] identified the group’s members and explained its method of operation....

Ch.
…had also forwarded the letter to the State Security Service and was informed that the allegations it contained were being verified.

…In reply to an enquiry from the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, the Administration of the Security Service of Ukraine in the Donetsk Region reported [on 22 April 2005] that its examination [перевірки] of Ch.’s allegations had uncovered no evidence that such an organised criminal group existed or operated within the [above-mentioned courts]. The relevant statements published in the eighth paragraph of the article were therefore unsubstantiated and, consequently, untrue.

…The article cited Ch.’s letter to …, in which he expressly referred to a criminal organisation operating in the [above-mentioned] courts. Although the article did not reproduce the letter’s contents, the wording of the eighth and ninth paragraphs conveyed to readers that the existence of a “criminal group” was under discussion.

By describing the manner in which cases were allocated and examined, the article’s co-authors accused the [judges] of those courts not merely of breaching bylaws, but also of conduct capable of being understood as abuse of office and a miscarriage of justice, both of which are criminal offences. … The term “organised group” was employed in its criminal-law sense and linked to an offence committed by an organised group.

Under Article 62 of the Constitution of Ukraine, everyone is presumed innocent of a criminal offence until their guilt has been proved in accordance with the law and confirmed by a court judgment.

Since no domestic court has delivered such a judgment against the claimants, the statements in question were defamatory.

The court is nevertheless unable to accept the defendants’ contention that, during the hearing, they submitted evidence supporting their assertion that a special procedure existed for the examination of cases, for the following reasons.

As stated above, alleging that such a special procedure operated in the courts concerned amounts to an accusation of criminal conduct and must therefore … be established through the prescribed means.
Given the presumption of innocence guaranteed by Article 62 of the Constitution, the foregoing allegations could be established only by a court judgment. No such judgment exists in relation to the claimants....

Section 42 of the Press Act releases a journalist from liability for publishing material that is false, damages the honour and dignity of individuals or organisations, violates citizens’ rights and lawful interests, or amounts to an abuse of the freedom of the printed mass media or journalists’ rights, where that information was supplied under the Information Act in response to a request for access to official documents or for written or oral information.

Under section 32 of the Information Act, a request for access to official documents means a request submitted to the relevant State authorities or their officials for the purpose of examining such documents.

Joint-stock company D. was not a State body, and its managing director, Ch., was not an official of any State authority. Consequently, his letter did not qualify as an official document for the purposes of section 42 of the Press Act and section 32 of the Information Act.

Section 47-1 of the Information Act provides that ... value judgments need neither be retracted nor proven true....

The material in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article—especially the statements quoted below—may be understood as assertions of fact and therefore cannot be classified as value judgments: “Ch. concluded that an organised group was operating within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal”; “an interested client approaches them and requests help with a case that is plainly bound to fail. The client is directed to the law firm [L.], after which a contract is signed, payment is made, and a statement of claim is drafted. The case is then ‘allocated’ to the appropriate judge, irrespective of [any] established procedure, and is invariably determined in the client’s favour”; and “where the opposing party appeals, there is a so-called ‘black triad’ which follows the principle that ‘nothing else in the case matters’”....

For the purposes of Article 277 of the CCU, an element of the offence is the dissemination of information about a person from which an observer can infer that it concerns a particular identifiable individual or, at minimum, a member of the group to which the information relates. The individual need not be named: information is regarded as concerning a specific person where other details make that person identifiable.

Claimants A., C., D. and E. serve as judges of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, while B. and F. are judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. Moreover, A. is the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, and B.
B. had previously served as Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. The authors alleged in the article that an organised group operated within the courts referred to above. The court found that allegation to be inaccurate and false. That statement alone damaged the dignity, honour and reputation of the officials responsible for managing those courts, namely A. and B.

To support their allegation that such an organised group existed in the courts concerned, the authors cited case no. 8/55. After reviewing that case file, the court established that B. had assigned case no. 8/55 to F.; that F. had presided over its examination by the first-instance court; and that E., C. and D. had subsequently considered the case on appeal.

Accordingly, the publication of false information caused non-pecuniary damage to all the judges named above. This included B., who, at the relevant time, was Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and managed the court division containing the judges who had heard the case at first instance. A., the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who ... was responsible for the organisational administration of the court that examined the case on appeal, likewise suffered non-pecuniary damage.

The court rejected the respondents’ argument that the claimants had not been named, finding that the article’s co-authors had included enough information for them to be identified. Moreover, information about the judges who considered domestic cases was not restricted; copies of the relevant judicial decisions had been sent to the parties, and the identities of those judges could therefore have become known to an unlimited number of people.”

28. In determining the compensation payable by the applicant and Ch. to the claimants, the court considered the applicant less culpable because Ch. had supplied the information. Nevertheless, the applicant had not checked its accuracy and had consequently failed to fulfil his professional obligations under section 26 of the Press Act.

29. The court directed the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to publish a retraction of the statements appearing in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article. It also ordered the applicant to pay each claimant UAH 333 for non-pecuniary damage, UAH 333 in legal costs and UAH 100 in court fees. In total, the sums imposed on the applicant were equivalent to EUR 331 for non-pecuniary damage and EUR 430.51 for legal costs and court fees. Ch. was required to pay each claimant UAH 1,000 for non-pecuniary damage, together with legal costs and court fees.

Lastly, the court dismissed the counterclaims lodged by the applicant and Ch. as unsubstantiated.

30.
The applicant challenged the Petrovskyy Local Court’s judgment of 20 October 2005 on the following grounds: (i) the court had not established that non-pecuniary damage had actually occurred, since it had provided no specific reasons explaining how the article had affected the claimants or their psychological health; (ii) it had failed to distinguish statements of fact from “value judgments”. In particular, the applicant argued that the expression “tarred with the same brush” was plainly a “value judgment”, but the court had not considered it separately and had instead found it defamatory as part of the text as a whole; (iii) the documents in the files of case no. 8/55 and several other cases provided a sufficient basis for concluding that the statements published in the article were true; (iv) the court had not considered whether the applicant had acted with mens rea; (v) it had exceeded the scope of the complaints by declaring a broader portion of the article defamatory. In that connection, he pointed out that the court had relied on the complete text of the eighth and ninth paragraphs rather than confining its examination to the specific statements cited by the claimants in their complaints, such as “Ch. concluded ...” and “most of the people ...”; and (vi) the court fees he had been ordered to pay to the claimants were excessive.

31. On 27 January 2006, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment as regards the merits, but amended the award of legal and court fees, reducing the court fees payable by the applicant to the equivalent of EUR 244.08.

The relevant passages of the appellate court’s judgment stated:

“The content of the contested article indicates that the respondent Ch. had carried out his own investigation and had concluded that an organised group was operating within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal. He referred to a letter from the head of a sub-committee of the Verkhovna Rada ..., which identified the group’s members and described in detail how the entire scheme functioned. The article also refers to cases nos. 8/55 and 27/37. The ninth paragraph contains a direct quotation in which case no. 8/55 is discussed on behalf of Ch. ...

At the hearing, the respondents asserted that the published information concerning the existence of an organised group in the courts concerned ... was accurate. They maintained that B. and A. had assigned case no. 8/55, together with other cases, to ‘their’ judges in breach of orders governing the specialisation of the courts’ composition. They produced the case-allocation orders and drew attention to the violations they alleged had occurred in the assignment of case no. 8/55 and other cases.

The court was justified in rejecting the respondents’ arguments.”
The distribution of cases among the courts concerned is an internal judicial matter and cannot, in itself, demonstrate either the existence of an organised group or the operation of a “scheme” involving interested clients. When the article appeared, none of the claimants had been convicted of, or held liable for, corrupt acts. ... The certificates contained in the case files establish that all the claimants are judges serving in the courts concerned. Although the article alleged that they had broken the law when examining commercial cases, those allegations were not substantiated during the court hearing. In support of their submissions ... the respondents relied on the assignment of cases contrary to specialisation orders, but failed to produce any factual evidence confirming the information published in the article.”

32. In his appeal on points of law, the applicant repeated his earlier arguments. He further stated that, after receiving and reading Ch.’s letter, he had carried out his own investigation and, on the basis of the material in the case files, believed that he had exercised due diligence in verifying the relevant information.

33. On 5 November 2007, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, sitting as a court of cassation, issued a final decision dismissing the applicant’s appeal against the decisions of 20 October 2005 and 27 January 2006. It gave no reasons beyond the standard finding that the appeal disclosed no basis for concluding that the lower courts had breached substantive or procedural law.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

THE 2003 CIVIL CODE

34. The relevant provisions of the Civil Code state:

Article 16  
Judicial protection of civil rights and interests

“Available remedies for the protection of civil rights and interests shall include:

...

3. bringing to an end the conduct that infringes the right;

...”

Article 23  
Compensation for non-pecuniary damage

“1. Where a person’s rights have been infringed, he or she shall be entitled to compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

2. Non-pecuniary damage shall include:

...

(4) humiliation of a natural person’s honour and dignity, and damage to the professional reputation of a natural or legal person ... [defamation] ...”

Article 277  
Correction of false information

“1. A natural person whose personality rights have been violated through the dissemination of false information about him or her shall be entitled both to respond and to have that information corrected.

...

3. Negative information circulated about a person shall be presumed false unless the person who disseminated it proves otherwise.

...

6. A person whose rights have been infringed ... shall be entitled to respond and to have the information corrected through the same mass-media outlet and in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law. ... The correction of false information shall not depend on whether the person who disseminated it was at fault.

7.
False information must be corrected by the same means through which it was circulated.”

Article 278 § 2  
Ban on disseminating information that violates personal non-property rights

“Where a personal non-property right has been infringed through a newspaper, book, film, television programme, or other work that has already been released, a court may prohibit or halt further dissemination until the infringement has been remedied ...”

Article 302  
Right to information

“... 2. Anyone who disseminates information must verify that it is authentic and accurate.
