INTRODUCTION

1. This case arises from defamation proceedings brought against the applicant after an article written by him about alleged corruption in the judiciary was published. It also concerns an injunction requiring the publication to be removed from the newspaper’s website while the defamation proceedings were pending. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complains about those measures.

THE FACTS

2. Born in 1949, the applicant resides in Kyiv. He was represented by Ms L.L. Pankratova, a lawyer practising in Kyiv.

3. The Government’s Agent was, most recently, Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. On the basis of the parties’ submissions, the relevant facts may be restated as follows.

BACKGROUND TO THE CASE

The article published on 12 March 2005

5. The applicant is a journalist. During the period at issue, he worked for Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, a nationwide analytical weekly newspaper with a circulation of about 57,000 copies.

6. As part of a series of pieces authored by the applicant, the newspaper published his article entitled “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case” (“Чорна трійка: все інше справи не стосується”) on 12 March 2005. The same article appeared on the newspaper’s website on 18 March 2005.

7. Referring to one of his earlier publications, the applicant wrote that, in a particular case (no. 27/37) which had remained before the courts for some time and had been returned to the lower courts on at least two occasions, a judgment had been based on a forged copy of a document. The original document formed part of the case-file materials in a certain set of criminal proceedings. Despite that, the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had given judgment using the forged copy. The applicant then described what he termed a “system for obtaining a required result”.
A certain law firm had been retained to secure the desired outcome. Although the plaintiff paid it a considerable fee, the firm then “unexpectedly” withdrew entirely from the proceedings, leaving the plaintiff—a State enterprise—to be represented by its in-house lawyers. The courts, meanwhile, had “meticulously passed the case” upward to the Higher Commercial Court. That court allowed the proceedings to drag on excessively before eventually returning the case to a lower court “because no copy of the contested decision had been provided”. During that period, the plaintiff was liquidated, which, in the applicant’s view, made it possible to conceal numerous irregularities.

8. The article’s complete text is reproduced below:

“In May of last year, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] (no. 21, 29 May 2004) ran an article under the headline ‘How the court validated a copy of a document when the original was missing’ [“Як суд ‘легалізував’ ‘копію’ при відсутності оригіналу”]. It examined a legal episode without precedent in the history of Ukrainian justice. Relying on an extremely questionable copy of a particular document [a guarantee letter]—questionable both because of the quality of the print and, even more so, because of its contents—the court gave a judgment that the respondent has now been challenging for four years. The challenge was initiated at the same time as the presidential decree establishing appellate courts in Ukraine, and for one straightforward reason: the respondent maintains that it never issued the plaintiff with any document bearing that [registration] number and never gave any guarantees. Yet, because there are numerous ways of making any conflict of interest acceptable to Themis, the case has come to represent both a kind of emblem of dignity and a fetish embodying the flaws of the judicial structure itself. That structure, borrowed from developed democracies, was superimposed on a system corrupted by ‘sovietness’ [совковостью] and by ‘telephone law’ in shaping the principles governing the independence of the third branch of power in our State. [paragraph 1]

DT has reported on multiple occasions about the twists and turns of the litigation and the opposing claims advanced by the parties to the dispute. During the three years preceding publication of the [above-mentioned] article, case no. 27/37 completed two full cycles of judicial proceedings, beginning in the court of first instance and ending with a judgment of the Supreme Court of Ukraine. A third cycle also took place, based on newly discovered circumstances. In criminal proceedings opened against limited liability company N., which stole [something—the item was not specified] valued at more than 8.2 million hryvnias (UAH) from Intertrans, a State transport shipping enterprise, and then disappeared without a trace, the prosecutor’s office located the original of the disputed guarantee letter.
From the outset, the defendant had maintained at every court hearing that the guarantee letter invoked by the plaintiff, Intertrans, had been issued to an entirely different enterprise. Yet, for reasons unknown, this fact was consistently disregarded. The Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had an opportunity to correct the record. Instead, after confirming that the guarantee letter existed in the criminal case file, it based its ruling on a “copy” of that letter. The author therefore understandably wondered: “What will the commercial justice system devise this time to shield the State enterprise/structure that inflicted substantial financial damage on the State?” [paragraph 2]

What actually followed exceeded even the boldest expectations. Delving further into the murky and dubious way commercial disputes are adjudicated in the Donetsk region creates the impression that there is a system whose method is fairly unsophisticated but whose effectiveness in securing the desired outcome in virtually any case is highly dependable. It also appears that those who facilitate the process are wholly indifferent to the substance of the dispute. The crucial point is simply that the customer—usually the plaintiff—must approach the correct place at the correct time. [paragraph 3]

Typically, that place is a law firm to which substantial sums are lawfully paid for “legal services.” It then becomes difficult to identify any active part played by that firm in the litigation. Representatives may appear; alternatively, as happened with Intertrans—which, for reasons that remain unclear, paid the mysterious I. a fee of UAH 400,000—the company may merely rely on its own lawyers to participate in the proceedings. From beginning to end, the case passes through the hands of numerous functionaries of commercial justice in the Donetsk region, who carefully and attentively move it onward until it reaches the Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine. [paragraph 4]

Once the original “copy” was found, followed by another document establishing that the “copy” had been forged, the issue could no longer be framed as an adversarial contest between competing arguments. It had become a matter of falsification and intent—questions belonging not in a commercial dispute but in a criminal investigation. Again, the facts speak for themselves. The Higher Commercial Court of Ukraine (HCCU) distinguished itself yet again. Part 3 of Article 114 of the Commercial Procedural Code of Ukraine requires a request to review a judicial decision on the basis of newly discovered circumstances to be examined within one month. Contrary to that requirement, the HCCU postponed consideration of the case for nine months. [paragraph 5]

Initially, the HCCU obtained all necessary materials from the Donetsk Court of Appeal and scheduled a hearing date. However, when the parties came to 6 Kopylenka St. in Kyiv, they learned that no hearing would take place. Apparently, a document had gone missing.
Accordingly, the HCCU promptly found: ‘The cassation appeal shows that the defendant contested the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal’s ruling of 30 June 2004. Yet neither that ruling nor any reference to it appears in the case file. Case no. 27/37 must therefore be sent back to the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court so that it can be properly registered in compliance with the legislation in force.’ Thus, another date was scheduled and the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court was given an assignment, even though the assignment was plainly intended for the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. But are these not separate State institutions? Or have they long formed a single structure—something that the judiciary of Ukraine’s largest first-instance commercial court still does not even realise, but that is apparently known in Kyiv, which would explain the wording? [paragraph 6]

In summary, no one has yet troubled to explain either where the ruling had been or how it suddenly appeared among the documents in case no. 27/37. The matter has been discreetly brushed aside, although it was most likely no accident and served a particular purpose: postponing the examination of the case until 1 February 2005. On precisely that date, pursuant to Ministry of Transport order no. 797 of 1 September 2004, issued ‘in order to increase the efficiency of the use of State property’, Intertrans’s liquidation was completed and the company was removed from the United State Register of Enterprises and Organisations of Ukraine. Everything proceeded according to plan. The hearing was held after that date, while the case file has still not been returned from Kyiv to Donetsk. It should be noted that this represents only one part of the State problem inherited from the former leadership of the Ministry of Transport. According to informed sources, liquidating Intertrans allowed sums far exceeding the money unjustly recovered from I.-Bank on the basis of the ‘copy’ to be buried. That, however, is another subject deserving journalistic scrutiny.” [paragraph 7]

9. The article concluded with the following two paragraphs, namely the eighth and ninth:

“Incidentally, [Ch.], the managing director of joint-stock company [D.], carried out an investigation and concluded that an organised group was active within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal. In a letter addressed to the head of the parliamentary sub-committee responsible for combating organised crime and corruption in law-enforcement bodies and courts, he identified the group’s members by name and described in detail how the entire scheme operated. In support of his allegations, [Ch.] referred to case no. 8/55, in which he had been a defendant in proceedings against the State enterprise Ugolnaya kompaniya ‘Krasnolimanskaya’ concerning the invalidation of a contract, along with several other comparable disputes that were later quashed by the Supreme Court of Ukraine. The judges, already well known from case no.
27/37, are found everywhere.

[paragraph 8] [Ch.] explained that case no. 8/55 had prompted his address to the Verkhovna Rada. As the case proceeded through every [judicial] level, he experienced pressure from the system. He described a scenario in which an interested client seeks help with a case that is plainly destined to fail and is advised to approach law firm [L.]. A contract is then signed, payment is made, and a statement of claim is drafted. Regardless of [any] applicable procedure, the case is subsequently “allocated” to the appropriate judge, after which it is invariably resolved in the client’s favour. Should the opposing party appeal, there is a so-called “black triad” operating according to the principle that “nothing else in the case is relevant”. The majority of people who pass through those two [judicial] levels abandon the matter: they lose confidence in justice, pursue no further remedies, and conclude that “they are all tarred with the same brush”.

[paragraph 9] Interim injunction proceedings

10. On 7 April 2005, judges A., B., C., D., E. and F. submitted an application to the Voroshylovsky District Court of Donetsk City (“the District Court”), seeking “preventive measures and the securing of evidence” (заява про вжиття запобіжних заходів та про забезпечення доказів). They maintained that the article published on 12 March 2005 under the title “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case” gave a negative assessment of the work of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal without relying on any facts. They also characterised the article’s tone as extremely negative.

More specifically, the claimants asserted that the following allegations were untrue: references to “an organised group”; a description of “the detailed manner in which the entire scheme operated”; claims concerning “pressure from the system” and “help with a case that is clearly bound to fail”; the assertion that, notwithstanding [any] established procedure, a case would be assigned to the desired judge; and statements about the existence of a “black triad” governed by the principle that “nothing else matters in the case”. They further argued that the applicant “had not checked the information concerned” and had consequently neglected his professional obligations.

In the claimants’ view, the publication infringed the honour, dignity and professional reputation of the two courts identified above, as well as those of their leadership and judges. They noted in particular that judges C., D., E. and F. had considered case no. 8/55, which the article mentioned, and had therefore sustained non-pecuniary damage as a result of its publication. Comparable damage had allegedly been suffered by A., Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who “was in charge of the court’s organisational management”, and by B., Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court, who, “under the allocation of responsibilities, managed the structural unit comprising the judges who had considered case no. 8/55”.

11.
The claimants announced their intention to bring defamation proceedings for damages against the newspaper, the applicant and Ch., which they subsequently did on 18 April and 18 August 2005 (see paragraph 23 below). They maintained that the article contained “elements of an interview, i.e. the last paragraph containing eventually the majority of the untrustful information”. Relying, among other provisions, on Articles 277 and 278 of the Civil Code of Ukraine (“the CCU” – see paragraph 34 below), they submitted that the continued online availability of the article infringed their rights and sought its removal under Article 62-1 of the Code of Civil Procedure (“the CCP” – see paragraph 35 below).

12. The claimants asked the court to direct the newspaper’s editorial board to delete the article from its website. To secure their claims, they also requested the attachment of property belonging to the newspaper, the applicant and Ch. Lastly, they sought an order requiring the newspaper to produce the documents on which its editorial board and the applicant had relied when verifying the information published in the article.

13. On 8 April 2005, the District Court directed the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to remove the article from the newspaper’s website. Its one-and-a-half-page ruling simply restated the substance of the claimants’ request. It then cited Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, which listed the interim measures available for securing a claim, and concluded, without evaluating the claimants’ arguments or giving reasons, that the request should be granted in part.

14. The applicant, the newspaper and Ch. challenged that ruling on appeal. They argued, among other things, that domestic law did not provide for an interim injunction requiring an article to be removed from a website. They further submitted that the court had relied on Article 152 § 2 of the CCP, although that provision concerned interim measures imposed after a claim had been lodged, rather than before. They also complained that the court had given no reasons for its decision. In particular, they pointed out that the article had not identified any judge and contended that the claimants had therefore failed to establish that their rights had been violated.

15. On 26 August 2005, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal affirmed the District Court’s ruling. After restating the claimants’ request and reproducing Article 278 § 2 of the CCU, it held:

“The disputed article contains information distributed via the Internet. Given that this information is available to the public at large and is difficult to control, removing the article from the website—analogous to attaching property under paragraph 2 of Article 62-2 of the CCP—is the only measure capable of safeguarding the individual right until the case is determined on its merits. [The first-instance] court relied on Article 152 of the CCP, which permits a claim to be secured by prohibiting specified actions.”
That reference was incorrect because no claim had been filed when the ruling was issued. Nevertheless, this defect could not justify setting the ruling aside, since the request had been properly considered on its merits.”

16. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal. He submitted that Article 62-2 of the CCP did not provide for an interim measure requiring an article to be taken down from a website. He also argued that the court had given no reasons for its decision and that the claimants had submitted no evidence demonstrating that their rights had been violated.

17. Approximately two and a half years later, on 15 January 2008, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, acting as a court of cassation, dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the decisions of 8 April and 26 August 2005, finding no evidence that the law had been breached.

18. Those judicial decisions were executed. The disputed article was removed from the newspaper’s website on an unspecified date, which was no later than 18 August 2005.

Subsequent publication

19. On 28 March 2005, A., Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, and B., a former Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial[1] Court, wrote to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, demanding that the information contained in the article published on 12 March 2005 be retracted. They enclosed the text they wished to have published as the retraction. The newspaper’s office received the letter on 31 March 2005.

20. On 23 April 2005, in compliance with the interim injunction ordered by the Voroshyloskyy District Court of Donetsk (see paragraphs 10-13 above), Dzerkalo Tyzhnya published an article entitled “Black triad: to be continued” (“Чорна трійка: далі буде”). It identified A. and B. as the authors of the letter seeking the retraction. The article, apparently summarising the contents of their letter of 28 March 2005, stated:

“Every judicial dispute consists of a complex web of conflicting interests between the parties. Whatever the result of its resolution ..., one party will invariably remain dissatisfied. Even where a party realises that there are no grounds for challenging a judicial decision, it is often deterred from appealing only by the obligation to pay court costs and legal fees. People naturally tend to view decisions made in their favour as lawful and just, while regarding decisions against them in the opposite way. Anyone who has ever adjudicated a dispute knows that the losing party will most likely see the outcome as unjust and biased.

On 12 March 2005, DT [Dzerkalo Tyzhnya] published an article by Anatoliy Yeremenko entitled ‘Black triad: nothing else matters in the case’. That article addressed issues of great importance and relevance to contemporary Ukrainian society.
The article recounts the allegations of [Ch.], managing director of [joint-stock company D.], who claimed to have uncovered illegal conduct by judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal.

Yet many found [Ch.’s] resentment toward those courts surprising. Considering both the number of cases won by [joint-stock company D.] and the apparent “strength” of its claims, the opposing parties would seemingly have had greater reason to feel aggrieved. In case no. 38/251, for instance, the claimant, [joint-stock company D.], was awarded UAH 262,776.32 ...

The article also refers to case no. 8/55, but, for reasons unknown, fails to mention that [D.’s] managing director submitted a request under Articles 4 to 6 of the Code of Commercial Procedure of Ukraine for the case to be heard by a panel of judges, and that this request was granted. For readers without legal training, those provisions permit a local commercial court to assign a case to a judicial panel when the case’s category and complexity warrant it.

[Ch.], however, supported his application solely by arguing that a panel was needed to prevent the opposing party from exerting pressure on the court. That argument does not constitute a legal basis for panel consideration. A strict application of the law would therefore have required the court to dismiss [Ch.’s] request as unlawful. Nevertheless, after considering the type of case and the large number of circumstances requiring examination, the court approved it.

This suggests either that the claimant cannot comprehend the wording of the law, despite presuming to criticise judicial decisions, or that he deliberately sought to provoke a refusal so that he could later accuse the court of partiality.

Although the court ruled in his favour regarding its composition in case no. 8/55, [Ch.] nevertheless alleges that, regardless of the established procedure, cases are subsequently assigned to a judge selected for the purpose. That assertion plainly conflicts with the facts. The same is true of his claims that cases are invariably resolved for the client and that the court of appeal contains a so-called “black triad.” More insulting still is his ultimate allegation that all of them are alike and equally culpable.

The sole lawful means of obtaining a favourable judgment is to comply with the law and present adequate reasoning supported by valid evidence. Some people, however—hardly deserving to be described as law-abiding citizens—will resort to anything. If they believe that the result excuses the methods used, why would they not attempt every available means?
From a practical perspective, the simplest—though, we emphasise, ineffective and least ethical—method of persuading a court to reach the “desired” ruling is to issue a warning to the effect that it would be unwise to cross the person concerned. By shaping public opinion, such individuals seek to affect the decisions of public officials, judges included. After all, almost no one would want to be linked to the “black triad”.

The Donetsk Regional Commercial Court is currently considering proceedings to which [D.] is a party. Could the tragic farce staged by [Ch.] therefore be an effort to intimidate the court and influence the judgment it will deliver? The implication is that the article about the “black triad” might be expanded to include the surnames of every judge who holds firm convictions, leaving those judges to demonstrate their integrity publicly afterward. It is common knowledge that the higher an individual’s social standing, the more readily society accepts even the most absurd rumours about that person, thus forcing them to establish their innocence.

Accordingly, the work of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal was assessed negatively without any substantive basis. In particular, there are no grounds for believing that an organised group engaged in unlawful activities operates within those courts. Neither the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court nor the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal has a practice of helping interested clients secure “positive decisions” in “cases that will clearly lose”. Moreover, staff members of those courts never recommend specific law firms. The allegation that cases are assigned, regardless of the applicable procedure, to the “right judge” so that a ruling favourable to the client can be issued is likewise false. A court neither has nor can have “clients”. The rulings in the cases referred to in the articles were adopted only after an impartial review of all relevant circumstances and of the evidence presented by the parties.

There is also no basis for concluding that most individuals whose cases passed through the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal surrendered, lost confidence in justice, and refrained from applying elsewhere.”

21. On 12 May 2005, the claimants addressed a further letter to the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, requesting that the newspaper publish a retraction. They emphasised that their earlier request had not been properly dealt with because the published item had not included the word “retraction” in its title and had reproduced only a summary of parts of their letter dated 28 March 2005.

22. On 23 May 2005, the chief editor of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya responded that the demand was unfounded until the courts had examined the relevant claim and delivered the corresponding judgment.

Defamation proceedings

23. On 18 April and 18 August 2005, the same claimants (see paragraph 10 above) brought defamation claims against the applicant, Ch.
and the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya, alleging that the impugned article had harmed their professional standing, honour and dignity. They maintained that the assertions published in it had diminished the authority of the judiciary. In an amended claim, the judges requested that the court declare the following statements defamatory:

– “there was an organised group operating in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and in the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal”;

– Ch. had uncovered “a detailed mode of operation of the whole scheme”;

– “the pressure of the system”;

– “an interested client comes knocking and asks for assistance with a case that will clearly lose. They recommend that he goes to law firm [L.]. Then the contract is concluded with the client, the money is transferred, and the claim is prepared. Then, despite [any] existing procedure, the case is ‘distributed’ to the right judge. After that, the case is always decided in the client’s favour”;

– “If another party lodges an appeal, a so-called ‘black triad’ exists, which embraces the principle [that] ‘nothing else matters in the case’”; and

– “they are all tarred with the same brush”.

The judges also sought an order requiring the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to retract those statements and directing the applicant and Ch. to pay each claimant 10,000 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) for non-pecuniary damage.

They acknowledged that the newspaper had partially restored their rights by giving them an opportunity to exercise their right of reply to the accusations made in the disputed article and by deleting the article from its website.

24. In his defence, the applicant maintained that the statements conveyed information of public importance and that their sources were Ch. and Ch.’s letter to the parliamentary sub-committee. He added that he had properly confirmed that the letter had in fact been submitted to Parliament and had prompted a related investigation by the law-enforcement authorities. He also stated that Ch.’s comments were consistent with the findings of his own journalistic investigations into cases nos. 27/37 and 8/55, which had been based on the files in those proceedings.

The applicant argued that, because the information had been provided by “an official” of an organisation, section 42(2) of the Press Act exempted him from liability for its publication. Finally, he pointed out that the claimants had not been identified by name in the article and that at least twelve other judges had considered the case at issue in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court without bringing defamation proceedings. He further referred to his earlier article of 29 May 2004, in which A. and C. had been named but in respect of which they had never instituted defamation proceedings.
To substantiate his arguments, the applicant submitted, among other materials, Ch.’s letter to the parliamentary sub-committee, files from several cases reviewed during his investigation—including case no. 27/37—and his earlier articles concerning the same subject.

25. On an unknown date, both the applicant and Ch. filed counterclaims. The applicant alleged that, before bringing the defamation proceedings and seeking the interim injunction, A., C., D., E., B., and F. had unlawfully acquired his personal information, including his name and contact details. He requested a judicial finding that their conduct had been illegal. Ch., in turn, asked the court to declare false the statements in the judges’ letter to the newspaper that had been published on 23 April 2005 (see paragraph 20 above).

26. On 20 October 2005, the Petrovskyy Local Court considered the merits of the case. After assessing the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article, it upheld the judges’ claim in part. It found the statements in those paragraphs defamatory because they “had presented a distorted view of reality and were not based on actual facts”, and concluded that their publication had caused non-pecuniary damage to each claimant.

27. The material portions of the judgment stated:

“[T]he information set out in the relevant paragraphs of the article was inconsistent with reality and damaged the claimants’ honour, dignity and reputation for the following reasons....

During the hearing, the [applicant] confirmed that, when writing the eighth and ninth paragraphs, he had relied on information supplied by Ch., including the letter sent to the parliamentary sub-committee, together with [Ch.’s] brief commentary containing elements of an interview.[2]

The respondent, Ch., confirmed that the author had used the information he provided in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the disputed article.

An examination of the article’s ninth paragraph establishes that it was published as an interview.

Under section 13 of the Copyright and Related Rights Act, copyright in a recorded interview constitutes co-authorship, with the interviewer and interviewee being joint authors.

The court therefore considers [the applicant] and Ch. to be co-authors of the article ...

[In his letter to the head of the parliamentary sub-commission responsible for combating organised crime and corruption], Ch. asserted that an organised criminal group was active within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal and, upon request, issued the judgments and rulings sought by its clients. [He] identified the group’s members and explained its methods of operation....

Ch.
This letter was also forwarded to the State Security Service, which informed him that his allegations were under verification....

In reply to an enquiry from the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, the Administration of the Security Service of Ukraine in the Donetsk Region stated [on 22 April 2005] that its examination [перевірки] of Ch.’s allegations had uncovered no evidence that such an organised criminal group existed or operated within the [above-mentioned courts]. Consequently, [the relevant statements] appearing in the article’s eighth paragraph had not been substantiated and were therefore untrue....

The article referred to Ch.’s letter to ..., in which he explicitly alleged that a criminal organisation existed in the [above-mentioned] courts. Although the article did not reproduce the letter’s contents, the wording of its eighth and ninth paragraphs conveyed to readers that the existence of a “criminal group” was at issue.

When describing how cases were allocated and examined, the article’s co-authors alleged that the [judges] of the courts concerned had not merely breached bylaws, but had also engaged in conduct capable of being understood as abuse of office and a miscarriage of justice, each of which constitutes a criminal offence. ... Within the article, the term “organised group” was used in its criminal-law sense and linked to a criminal offence perpetrated by an organised group.

Under Article 62 of the Constitution of Ukraine, everyone is presumed innocent of a criminal offence unless and until guilt has been proved according to law and confirmed by a court verdict.

As no domestic court has delivered such a verdict against the claimants, [those statements] were defamatory.

At the same time, the court cannot accept the defendants’ contention that, during the hearing, they submitted evidence supporting their assertion that a special procedure existed for examining cases, for the following reasons.

As stated above, alleging the existence of a special procedure for the examination of cases in the courts concerned amounts to an accusation that a criminal offence has been committed; such an accusation ... must be established by specific means.
Under Article 62 of the Constitution, which establishes the presumption of innocence, the statements set out above may be substantiated only by a court verdict, and no such verdict exists in relation to the claimants....

Section 42 of the Press Act releases a journalist from liability for publishing material that is false, damages the honour and dignity of individuals or organisations, violates citizens’ rights and lawful interests, or amounts to an abuse of freedom of the printed mass media or journalists’ rights, where that information was supplied under the Information Act in response to a request for access to official documents or to a request for information in written or oral form.

According to section 32 of the Information Act, a request for access to official documents means a request submitted to the appropriate State authorities or their officials for the purpose of examining such documents.

Joint-stock company D. was not a State authority, and its managing director, Ch., was not an official of any State authority. Consequently, his letter did not qualify as an official document for the purposes of section 42 of the Press Act and section 32 of the Information Act.

Section 47-1 of the Information Act provides that ... value judgments need neither be retracted nor proven true....

The material appearing in the eighth and ninth paragraphs of the article—especially the statements reproduced below—may be understood as assertions of fact and therefore does not constitute value judgments: Ch. had determined that an organised group was active within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal; an interested client would approach them seeking help with a case that was plainly destined to fail, and the client would be advised to contact law firm L.; a contract would then be signed, payment transferred, and a statement of claim drafted; regardless of any established procedure, the case would subsequently be “allocated” to the appropriate judge, after which judgment would invariably be given in the client’s favour; and, if the opposing party appealed, there was a so-called “black triad” guided by the principle that “nothing else in the case matters”....

Pursuant to Article 277 of the CCU, one constituent element of the offence is the dissemination of information about a person from which an observer could infer that it refers to a particular identifiable individual or, at minimum, that the individual belongs to the group of persons concerned by the information. It is unnecessary to state the person’s name: information may still be regarded as relating to a specific person when other details make that person identifiable.

Claimants A., C., D. and E. serve as judges of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, whereas B. and F. are judges of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. Furthermore, A. is the Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, and B.
He had previously served as Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court. The authors alleged in the article that an organised group operated within the [above-mentioned] courts; this court has determined that allegation to be inaccurate and false. That assertion alone damages the dignity, honour and reputation of the officials managing those courts, specifically A. and B.

To substantiate their allegation that an organised group existed in the above-mentioned courts, the authors relied on case no. 8/55. After reviewing the file in that case, the court found that B. had assigned case no. 8/55 to F.; that F. had presided over its examination by the first-instance court; and that E., C. and D. had subsequently considered it before the appellate court.

Accordingly, the publication of false information caused non-pecuniary damage to all the judges referred to above. This included B., who at the relevant time held the position of Deputy Head of the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and managed the court division containing the judges who had examined the case at first instance. A., Head of the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, who ... bears responsibility for the organisational management of the court that examined the case on appeal, likewise suffered non-pecuniary damage.

The court rejects the respondents’ argument that the claimants were not named, because the article’s co-authors included enough information for them to be identified. Moreover, information concerning judges who examined domestic cases was not restricted; copies of the relevant judicial decisions had been provided to the parties; and the judges’ identities could therefore have become known to an unlimited and unrestricted number of people.”

28. In determining the amount of compensation payable to the claimants by the applicant and Ch., the court observed that the applicant’s degree of fault was lower because Ch. had supplied the information. Nevertheless, the applicant had not verified that information and had therefore failed to discharge his professional obligations under section 26 of the Press Act.

29. The court directed the editorial board of Dzerkalo Tyzhnya to publish a retraction of the statements appearing in the article’s eighth and ninth paragraphs. It also ordered the applicant to pay each claimant UAH 333 for non-pecuniary damage, together with legal fees of UAH 333 per claimant and court fees of UAH 100 per claimant. Overall, the applicant was required to pay sums equivalent to 331 euros (EUR) for non-pecuniary damage and EUR 430.51 for legal and court fees. Ch. was ordered to pay each claimant UAH 1,000 in compensation for non-pecuniary damage, in addition to legal and court fees.

Lastly, the court rejected as unsubstantiated the counterclaims brought by the applicant and Ch.

30.
The applicant challenged the Petrovskyy Local Court’s judgment of 20 October 2005 on six grounds. First, he argued that the court had not established that non-pecuniary damage had occurred, since it had provided no specific explanation of how the article had affected the claimants or their psychological health. Second, he maintained that the court had failed to distinguish statements of fact from “value judgments”. In particular, he submitted that the expression “tarred with the same brush” was plainly a “value judgment”, but the court had neither considered it separately nor assessed it independently, instead finding it defamatory as part of the text as a whole. Third, he contended that the documents in the files of case no. 8/55 and several other cases provided sufficient grounds for concluding that the statements in the article were true. Fourth, he alleged that the court had not considered whether his actions involved mens rea. Fifth, he argued that the court had exceeded the scope of the complaints by declaring a broader portion of the published statements defamatory. In that connection, he pointed out that the court had relied on the complete wording of the eighth and ninth paragraphs rather than limiting itself to the specific statements cited by the claimants in their complaints, including, for example, the phrases “Ch. concluded ...” and “most of the people ...”. Sixth, he claimed that the court fees he had been ordered to pay to the claimants were excessive.

31. On 27 January 2006, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment as regards the merits but amended the decision concerning legal and court fees, reducing the court fees payable by the applicant to the equivalent of EUR 244.08.

The relevant passages of the appellate court’s judgment stated:

“The disputed article indicates that the respondent Ch. carried out his own investigation and reached the conclusion that an organised group existed within the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal. In doing so, he referred to a letter from the head of a sub-committee of the Verkhovna Rada ..., which identified the group’s members and described in detail how the entire scheme operated. The article also refers to cases nos. 8/55 and 27/37. The ninth paragraph contains direct speech and presents, on behalf of Ch., a discussion of case no. 8/55 ...

During the hearing, the respondents asserted that the published information concerning the existence of an organised group in the courts concerned ... was true. They maintained that B. and A. had assigned case no. 8/55, together with other cases, to ‘their’ judges, contrary to the orders governing the specialisation of the courts’ composition. They produced the case-allocation orders and identified the violations allegedly committed in assigning case no. 8/55 and the other cases.

The court was justified in dismissing the respondents’ arguments.”
The distribution of cases within the courts concerned is an internal judicial matter and cannot, in itself, demonstrate either the existence of an organised group or the operation of a “scheme” involving interested clients. When the article appeared, none of the claimants had been convicted of, or held liable for, corruption. ... Certificates contained in the case files show that every claimant serves as a judge in one of the courts concerned. Although the article alleged that the claimants had breached the law when adjudicating commercial cases, those allegations were not established during the court hearing. To substantiate their submissions, ... the respondents referred to cases having been allocated contrary to specialisation orders, but submitted no factual evidence confirming the information published in the article.”

32. In his cassation appeal, the applicant repeated his earlier submissions. He further stated that, after receiving Ch.’s letter, he had carried out his own investigation and, on the basis of the materials in the case files, believed that he had exercised due diligence in verifying the relevant information.

33. In a final decision delivered on 5 November 2007, the Kyiv Court of Appeal, sitting as a court of cassation, dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal concerning the decisions of 20 October 2005 and 27 January 2006. It gave no reasons beyond the standard finding that the cassation appeal disclosed no basis for concluding that the lower courts had breached substantive or procedural law in adopting their decisions.

The applicants were born in 1957 and 1953 respectively and were represented by Mr A. Bushchenko, at the relevant time a lawyer practising in Kyiv.3. In December 2004 it introduced amendments to the Constitution which, among other things, increased the parliamentary features of the political system and diminished the powers of the President of Ukraine. Possible irregularities as to the manner in which the constitutional amendments were introduced were a matter of public debate which was also a point of discussion in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), as reflected in its Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005 “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine” (see paragraph 43 below).7. On 4 August 2006 Parliament appointed the applicants as judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (“the Constitutional Court”).8. On 5 February 2008 the Constitutional Court, following an application by members of parliament, refused to open proceedings in relation to the constitutionality of the Act of Parliament by which the Constitution had been amended in December 2004. The court remarked that the provisions of an Act of Parliament amending the Constitution “had accomplished their function” once they had come into force. It then rejected the application for constitutional review on procedural grounds (for failure to indicate the full title and registration number of the impugned Act and the date of its enactment).10. On 26 June 2008 the Constitutional Court adopted a judgment declaring unconstitutional the provision of the Constitutional Court Act introduced in 2006 excluding from its jurisdiction Acts of Parliament on constitutional amendments (see paragraph 8 above). The court noted, in particular, that the Constitution established its power to examine the constitutionality of laws enacted by Parliament and made no exception as regards laws amending the Constitution.11. In February 2010 Mr V. Yanukovych was elected President of Ukraine.12. On 30 September 2010 the Constitutional Court, following an application by members of parliament lodged in July 2010, adopted a judgment declaring unconstitutional the 2004 amendments to the Constitution, finding that they had been enacted in breach of proper procedure. The court declared the amendments invalid with effect from the date of its judgment, and the applicability of the previous version of the Constitution was consequently restored. In its reasoning, the court referred, among other things, to PACE Resolution 1466 (2005) (see paragraphs 6 above and 49 below).Events of November 2013 to February 2014, change of power in Ukraine AND THE APPLICANTS’ REMOVAL13. In late November 2013 anti-government demonstrations commenced in Kyiv and then spread to other cities in Ukraine, turning into massive popular protests in the country, reportedly in response to the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision to suspend preparations for the signing of the Ukraine‑European Union Association Agreement. By late February 2014 the demonstrations had escalated into serious clashes between protesters and law‑enforcement authorities, causing numerous injuries and deaths (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others v. It also removed the Minister of the Interior from his post.15. On 22 February 2014 Parliament declared that Mr Yanukovych had unconstitutionally abandoned his duties as President. In that regard, Parliament referred to the reasoning of the Constitutional Court’s ruling of 5 February 2008 (see paragraph 9 above) that the Act amending the Constitution “accomplished its function”, having become a part of the Constitution. Parliament further stated that on 29 May 2013 the Constitutional Court had adopted a judgment which had effectively made it impossible to hold elections in the city of Kyiv and the Ternopil Regional Council until October 2015. Parliament considered that, with that judgment, the judges of the Constitutional Court had violated citizens’ rights to elections.19. Lastly, Parliament stated that on 25 January 2012 the Constitutional Court had adopted a judgment allowing the Cabinet of Ministers to “manually” regulate the level of social payments, despite having previously adopted contrary decisions on the same subject matter. In that regard, Parliament found that the judges of the Constitutional Court had violated citizens’ constitutional rights to social security and an adequate standard of living.20. Parliament concluded that the judges of the Constitutional Court who had adopted the above-mentioned judgments had failed in their obligation to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution and to protect the constitutional system and citizens’ constitutional rights in violation of Articles 3, 19 and 147 to 153 of the Constitution, and that those failings had not been compatible with the judicial oath and the honest and rigorous performance of duties by a judge of the Constitutional Court.21. In March 2014 the applicants submitted statements of resignation, wishing to terminate their duties on a voluntary basis rather than by way of sanction applied by Parliament. Simultaneously, they challenged the parliamentary resolution of 24 February 2014 on their dismissal for “breach of oath” in court (see below).22. In a separate development, the Office of the Prosecutor General initiated criminal proceedings for unconstitutional seizure of State power by President Yanukovych through the introduction of amendments to the Constitution as a result of the adoption of an illegal judgment by the Constitutional Court, abuse of power by the judges of the Constitutional Court and the rendering of a knowingly illegal judgment on 30 September 2010. On 4 May 2020 the Pecherskyi District Court issued an arrest warrant in absentia for Mr Yanukovych within those criminal proceedings and that order was upheld by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 25 March 2021. Moreover, Parliament had adopted the impugned decision by way of simplified procedure[1], which was not possible in the event of dismissal of judges of the Constitutional Court. In its decision, the HAC also referred to section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act establishing the principle that Constitutional Court judges would not be held legally liable for the results of their votes in that court. Judges, whether appointed or elected, shall have guaranteed tenure until a mandatory retirement age or the expiry of their term of office, where such exists....18. Judges shall be subject to suspension or removal only for reasons of incapacity or behaviour that renders them unfit to discharge their duties.19. All disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings shall be determined in accordance with established standards of judicial conduct.20. Decisions in disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings should be subject to an independent review. The Draft Universal Declaration on the Independence of Justice (“Singhvi Declaration”), prepared subsequently by the UN Special Rapporteur Mr. Singhvi, expands on the basic principles as follows:“Discipline and Removal26. (a)  A complaint against a judge shall be processed expeditiously and fairly under an appropriate practice and the judge shall have the opportunity to comment on the complaint at the initial stage. The examination of the complaint at its initial stage shall be kept confidential, unless otherwise requested by the judge.(b)  The proceedings for judicial removal or discipline when such are initiated shall be held before a Court or a Board predominantly composed of members of the judiciary. The power of removal may, however, be vested in the Legislature by impeachment or joint address, preferably upon a recommendation of such a Court or Board.27. All disciplinary action shall be based upon established standards of judicial conduct.28. The proceedings for discipline of judges shall ensure fairness to the judge and the opportunity of a full hearing.29. Judgments in disciplinary proceedings instituted against judges, whether held in camera or in public, shall be published.30. A judge shall not be subject to removal except on proved grounds of incapacity or misbehaviour rendering him unfit to continue in office.”In its Resolution 1989/32, the Commission on Human Rights invited governments to take into account the principles set forth in the declaration in implementing the United Nations’ Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary.53. In its General Comment no. 32 on Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Right to equality before courts and tribunals and to a fair trial) published on 23 August 2007, the UN Human Rights Committee stated as follows (footnotes omitted):“19. The requirement of competence, independence and impartiality of a tribunal in the sense of Article 14, paragraph 1, is an absolute right that is not subject to any exception. The requirement of independence refers, in particular, to the procedure and qualifications for the appointment of judges, and guarantees relating to their security of tenure until a mandatory retirement age or the expiry of their term of office, where such exist, the conditions governing promotion, transfer, suspension and cessation of their functions, and the actual independence of the judiciary from political interference by the executive branch and legislature. States should take specific measures guaranteeing the independence of the judiciary, protecting judges from any form of political influence in their decision-making through the constitution or adoption of laws establishing clear procedures and objective criteria for the appointment, remuneration, tenure, promotion, suspension and dismissal of the members of the judiciary and disciplinary sanctions taken against them. A situation where the functions and competencies of the judiciary and the executive are not clearly distinguishable or where the latter is able to control or direct the former is incompatible with the notion of an independent tribunal. In order to safeguard their independence, the status of judges, including their term of office, their independence, security, adequate remuneration, conditions of service, pensions and the age of retirement shall be adequately secured by law.20. The law applicable to judges may define, as far as possible in specific terms, conduct that may give rise to disciplinary sanctions as well as the procedures to be followed....15.5  All disciplinary proceedings should be determined by reference to established standards of judicial conduct, and in accordance with a procedure guaranteeing full rights of defence.Removal of Judges from Office16.1  A judge may be removed from office only for proved incapacity, conviction of a serious crime, gross incompetence, or conduct that is manifestly contrary to the independence, impartiality and integrity of the judiciary.16.2  Where the legislature is vested with the power of removal of a judge, such power should be exercised only after a recommendation to that effect of the independent authority vested with power to discipline judges.”55. In these circumstances, the Committee considers that the author’s dismissal from his position as a judge of the Constitutional Court, several years before the expiry of the term for which he had been appointed, constituted an attack on the independence of the judiciary and failed to respect the author’s right of access, on general terms of equality, to public service in his country.

FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF OVCHARENKO AND KOLOS v. UKRAINE

(Applications nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

12 January 2023

FINAL

12/04/2023

This judgment became final under Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Georges Ravarani, President,
Iulia Antoanella Motoc,
Mārtiņš Mits,
María Elósegui,
Mattias Guyomar,
Kateřina Šimáčková,
Mykola Gnatovskyy, judges,

and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the applications (nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15) against Ukraine submitted to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Vyacheslav Andriyovych Ovcharenko (“the first applicant”) and Mr Mykhaylo Ivanovych Kolos (“the second applicant”), on 20 May and 2 July 2015 respectively;

the decision to give notice of the applications to the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”);

the observations submitted by the parties;

Having deliberated in private on 29 November 2022,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case concerns the dismissal of two judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, allegedly in violation of Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. The applicants were born in 1957 and 1953 respectively and were represented by Mr A. Bushchenko, who at the relevant time was a lawyer practising in Kyiv.

3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The facts of the case can be summarised as follows.

Background facts

5. On 28 June 1996, the Parliament (Verkhovna Rada) of Ukraine adopted the Constitution of Ukraine.

6. In December 2004, it introduced amendments to the Constitution which, among other changes, strengthened the parliamentary features of the political system and reduced the powers of the President of Ukraine. Possible irregularities in the manner in which the constitutional amendments had been introduced were the subject of public debate and were also discussed in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), as reflected in its Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005, “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine” (see paragraph 43 below).

7. On 4 August 2006, Parliament appointed the applicants as judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (“the Constitutional Court”).

8. On the same date, Parliament amended the “Final and Transitional Provisions” of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine Act (“the Constitutional Court Act”), stipulating that the Constitutional Court was not authorised to review the constitutionality of Acts of Parliament concerning amendments to the Constitution.

9.
On 5 February 2008 the Constitutional Court, following an application by members of parliament, declined to open proceedings concerning the constitutionality of the Act of Parliament by which the Constitution had been amended in December 2004. The court observed that the provisions of an Act of Parliament amending the Constitution “had accomplished their function” once they had entered into force. It then rejected the application for constitutional review on procedural grounds (for failure to provide the full title and registration number of the impugned Act and the date of its enactment).

10. On 26 June 2008 the Constitutional Court delivered a judgment declaring unconstitutional the provision of the Constitutional Court Act introduced in 2006 that excluded Acts of Parliament on constitutional amendments from its jurisdiction (see paragraph 8 above). The court noted, in particular, that the Constitution established its power to review the constitutionality of laws enacted by Parliament and made no exception for laws amending the Constitution.

11. In February 2010 Mr V. Yanukovych was elected President of Ukraine.

12. On 30 September 2010 the Constitutional Court, following an application lodged by members of parliament in July 2010, delivered a judgment declaring the 2004 amendments to the Constitution unconstitutional, finding that they had been enacted in breach of the proper procedure. The court declared the amendments invalid from the date of its judgment, thereby restoring the applicability of the previous version of the Constitution. In its reasoning, the court referred, among other things, to PACE Resolution 1466 (2005) (see paragraphs 6 above and 49 below).

EVENTS OF NOVEMBER 2013 TO FEBRUARY 2014, CHANGE OF POWER IN UKRAINE AND THE APPLICANTS’ REMOVAL

13. In late November 2013 anti-government demonstrations began in Kyiv and subsequently spread to other cities in Ukraine, developing into massive popular protests across the country, reportedly in response to the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision to suspend preparations for signing the Ukraine-European Union Association Agreement. By late February 2014 the demonstrations had escalated into serious clashes between protesters and law-enforcement authorities, resulting in numerous injuries and deaths (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others v. Ukraine, nos. 15367/14 and 13 others, §§ 9-17, 21 January 2021).

14. On 21 February 2014 Parliament enacted the Revalidation of Certain Provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine Act (“the Revalidation Act”) to return to the 2004 Constitution with certain amendments. It also removed the Minister of the Interior from office.

15. On 22 February 2014 Parliament declared that Mr Yanukovych had unconstitutionally abandoned his duties as President.
On the same day and on 23 February 2014, Parliament dismissed the Prosecutor General and adopted a number of further decisions regarding the replacement of high-ranking State officials and the functioning of the executive branch (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others, cited above, §§ 44-45).

16. On 24 February 2014, Parliament adopted a resolution “On responding to the ‘breach of oath’ by judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine”. In that resolution, Parliament, relying on Article 126 of the Constitution, dismissed for “breach of oath” the judges of the Constitutional Court who had been appointed under Parliament’s quota, as stipulated in Article 148 of the Constitution (see paragraph 33 below), including the applicants. It then called on the acting President of Ukraine and the Congress of Judges to take steps to dismiss for “breach of oath” the other judges of the Constitutional Court (who had been appointed under the quotas of the President and the Congress of Judges, respectively). Finally, it requested that the Office of the Prosecutor General open a criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Constitutional Court’s adoption of its judgment of 30 September 2010 (see paragraph 12 above).

17. In explaining the reasons for adopting the above-mentioned resolution, Parliament stated that on 30 September 2010 the Constitutional Court had unconstitutionally amended the Constitution by usurping parliamentary powers, had violated the fundamental constitutional principles of democracy and separation of powers, and had altered the constitutional system. In that connection, Parliament referred to the reasoning in the Constitutional Court’s ruling of 5 February 2008 (see paragraph 9 above), according to which the Act amending the Constitution had “accomplished its function” by becoming part of the Constitution. Parliament also referred to the Venice Commission’s opinion of 20 December 2010 “On the constitutional situation in Ukraine” (see paragraph 50 below), stating that the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 had cast doubt on the legitimacy of the existing State institutions, as the President and Parliament had been elected under constitutional rules that were no longer recognised as valid; following that judgment, the President had enjoyed considerably greater powers than voters could have anticipated when electing him; and, since that judgment, the operation of the principal State bodies had been based on rules changed by a court rather than by Parliament as a democratically legitimate body.

18. Parliament also stated that on 29 May 2013 the Constitutional Court had delivered a judgment that had effectively made it impossible to hold elections in the city of Kyiv and to the Ternopil Regional Council before October 2015. Parliament considered that, through that judgment, the judges of the Constitutional Court had infringed citizens’ electoral rights.

19.
Lastly, Parliament stated that on 25 January 2012 the Constitutional Court had delivered a judgment allowing the Cabinet of Ministers to “manually” regulate the level of social payments, despite having previously issued contrary decisions on the same subject matter. In that regard, Parliament found that the judges of the Constitutional Court had violated citizens’ constitutional rights to social security and an adequate standard of living.

20. Parliament concluded that the Constitutional Court judges who had adopted the above-mentioned judgments had failed in their duty to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution and to protect the constitutional system and citizens’ constitutional rights, in violation of Articles 3, 19 and 147 to 153 of the Constitution, and that those failings had been incompatible with the judicial oath and the honest and rigorous discharge of the duties of a Constitutional Court judge.

21. In March 2014 the applicants submitted their resignations, wishing to terminate their duties voluntarily rather than by means of a sanction imposed by Parliament. At the same time, they challenged in court the parliamentary resolution of 24 February 2014 dismissing them for “breach of oath” (see below).

22. In a separate development, the Office of the Prosecutor General initiated criminal proceedings concerning the unconstitutional seizure of State power by President Yanukovych through the introduction of amendments to the Constitution following the adoption of an unlawful judgment by the Constitutional Court, abuse of power by the Constitutional Court judges, and the delivery of a knowingly unlawful judgment on 30 September 2010. On 4 May 2020 the Pecherskyi District Court issued an arrest warrant in absentia for Mr Yanukovych in those criminal proceedings, and that order was upheld by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 25 March 2021. The proceedings remain ongoing.

Proceedings brought by the first applicant

23. On 27 February 2014 the first applicant, relying on the Code of Administrative Justice, lodged a claim with the Higher Administrative Court (“the HAC”) challenging his dismissal.

24. On 18 June 2014 the HAC declared the parliamentary resolution of 24 February 2014 unlawful in so far as it concerned the first applicant’s dismissal. It found that Parliament had failed to comply with the procedure for dismissing a judge of the Constitutional Court. In particular, the Rules of the Constitutional Court established a procedure requiring preliminary consideration of the case by the Constitutional Court itself, but that procedure had not been followed. Furthermore, Parliament had adopted the impugned decision under a simplified procedure[1], which was not permissible in cases involving the dismissal of Constitutional Court judges.
In its decision, the HAC also referred to section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act, which established the principle that Constitutional Court judges could not be held legally liable for the results of their votes in that court. Lastly, the HAC mentioned international legal principles concerning judicial independence and concluded that Parliament had failed to respect those principles.25. Parliament asked the Supreme Court to review the case.26. On 2 December 2014, the Supreme Court quashed the HAC’s judgment and dismissed the first applicant’s claim as unfounded. It restated the facts of the case, the relevant provisions of domestic law and the parties’ positions, and further held:

“Having analysed the essence of the violations that formed the basis for the dismissal of V.A. Ovcharenko, the panel of judges of the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court considers it necessary to note the following.

As stated in the judgment [of 30 September 2010], the grounds for the Constitutional Court of Ukraine’s examination of the case were an assertion by 252 members of parliament that Law no. 2222-IV did not comply with the Constitution of Ukraine.

In deciding the issue raised in the constitutional complaint lodged by the above-mentioned members of parliament, the Constitutional Court noted, in the reasoning of the judgment [of 30 September 2010], that recognising Law no. 2222-IV as unconstitutional owing to a breach of the procedure for its examination and adoption entailed the restoration of the previous wording of the provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine that had been amended, supplemented or repealed by Law no. 2222-IV.

In item 3 of the operative part of that judgment, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine required the bodies of State power to execute the judgment immediately by bringing normative legal acts into conformity with the Constitution of Ukraine of 28 June 1996, as worded before the amendments introduced by Law no. 2222-IV.

This conclusion of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, as reflected in Resolution No. 775-VII, contradicts the procedure established by law for amending the Constitution of Ukraine, according to which the provisions of a law amending the Constitution, once they enter into force, become an integral part of the Basic Law – its individual provisions – while the law itself ceases to perform its function.

The Constitution of Ukraine does not confer on the Constitutional Court of Ukraine the power to recognise the invalidity (визнавати нечинність) of a constitutional provision, irrespective of the legal form in which it is expressed.

Under Article 85 § 1 (1) of the Constitution of Ukraine, the power to amend the Constitution of Ukraine is vested specifically in the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, within the limits and in the manner prescribed by Chapter XII of the Constitution.

The Constitutional Court, through its judgment [of 30 September 2010], in the adoption of which V.A.
Ovcharenko participated, failed to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution of Ukraine, effectively amended it, breached the fundamental constitutional principle of democracy (народовладдя), altered the constitutional order of Ukraine, and violated the constitutional principles of separation of powers and the legitimacy of the acting institutions of State power, which resulted in their activities being based on norms modified by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine rather than by the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine as the competent authority. The evident incompatibility of V.A. Ovcharenko’s actions in adopting the judgment [of 30 September 2010] with the oath he had taken, and the consequences of those actions, gave the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine grounds to regard his conduct as a breach of the oath of a judge of the Constitutional Court and to dismiss him from office.”

27. Regarding the Constitutional Court’s judgments of 25 January 2012 and 29 May 2013, which were also considered in the impugned parliamentary resolution, the Supreme Court found that those two judgments had been delivered by the Constitutional Court within the scope of its discretion and that the first applicant’s participation in their adoption did not amount to a “breach of oath”[2].

28. As to the procedure followed for the first applicant’s dismissal, the Supreme Court found that the HAC’s reference to the Rules of the Constitutional Court had been unfounded, since they were an internal document of the Constitutional Court and the latter had not been authorised by the Constitution or the Constitutional Court Act to regulate the procedure for dismissing its own members. By contrast, the first applicant had been dismissed through a procedure compatible with the Constitution and the Rules of Parliament.

Proceedings brought by the second applicant

29. On 5 March 2014 the second applicant, relying on the Code of Administrative Justice, filed a claim with the HAC challenging his dismissal.

30. On 26 January 2015 the HAC dismissed the claim, referring to the Supreme Court’s legal position set out in its decision of 2 December 2014 in the first applicant’s case.

31. The second applicant applied to the Supreme Court for a review of the case, arguing, among other things, that his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 could not constitute grounds for his dismissal, that Parliament had failed to ensure a fair and independent examination of the case, that the procedure prescribed by the Rules of the Constitutional Court had not been followed, and that he could not be held liable for a judgment for which he had voted as a member of the Constitutional Court.

32. On 28 April 2015 the Supreme Court upheld the decision of 26 January 2015, reiterating the reasoning given in the first applicant’s case.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Relevant domestic law

Constitution of 28 June 1996

33.
The relevant provisions of the Constitution, as in force at the material time (prior to 2 June 2016), read as follows:

Article 3

“The human being, his or her life and health, honour and dignity, inviolability and security, are recognised in Ukraine as the highest social value.

Human rights and freedoms and their guarantees define the essence and orientation of the State’s activity. The State is accountable to the individual for its activity.
To affirm and safeguard human rights and freedoms is the principal duty of the State.”

Article 19

“The legal order in Ukraine is based on the principle that no one shall be compelled to do what is not prescribed by law.

Bodies exercising State power and local self-government bodies, as well as their officials, are required to act only on the grounds, within the limits of their authority, and in the manner prescribed by the Constitution and the laws of Ukraine.”

Article 126

“The independence and immunity of judges are guaranteed by the Constitution and the laws of Ukraine.

Any influence on judges is prohibited.

A judge shall not be detained or arrested without the consent of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine until convicted by a court.

Judges hold office for an indefinite term, except for judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine and judges appointed to judicial office for the first time.

A judge shall be dismissed from office by the body that elected or appointed him or her in the event of:

(1) expiry of the term for which he or she was elected or appointed;

(2) the judge reaching the age of sixty-five;

(3) inability to continue performing his or her duties for health reasons;

(4) violation by the judge of incompatibility requirements;

(5) breach of the judicial oath;

(6) entry into legal force of a guilty verdict against him or her;

(7) termination of his or her citizenship;

(8) a declaration that he or she is missing or a pronouncement that he or she is dead;

Article 148

“The Constitutional Court of Ukraine consists of eighteen judges.

The President of Ukraine, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, and the Congress of Judges of Ukraine each appoint six judges to the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.

A citizen of Ukraine who has reached the age of forty by the date of appointment, has a higher legal education and at least ten years of professional experience, has lived in Ukraine for the preceding twenty years, and is proficient in the State language may serve as a judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.

A judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine is appointed for a nine-year term without the right to reappointment for an additional term.

The Chairman of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine is elected for a single three-year term by secret ballot at a special plenary meeting of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine from among its judges.”

Article 149

“Judges of the
Judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine are subject to guarantees of independence and immunity, the grounds for dismissal from office set forth in Article 126 of this Constitution, and the incompatibility requirements specified in paragraph two of Article 127 of this Constitution.”

Article 150

“The Constitutional Court of Ukraine has the authority to:

1) decide on the conformity with the Constitution of Ukraine (constitutionality) of:

acts of the President of Ukraine;

acts of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine;

legal acts of the Verkhovna Rada of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.

Such matters are considered upon application by: the President of Ukraine; no fewer than forty-five People’s Deputies of Ukraine [members of parliament]; the Supreme Court of Ukraine; the Authorised Human Rights Representative of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine; the Verkhovna Rada of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea;

2) provide the official interpretation of the Constitution of Ukraine and the laws of Ukraine.

Article 151

“Upon application by the President of Ukraine or the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine provides opinions on whether international treaties of Ukraine in force, or international treaties submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine for approval of their binding nature, conform to the Constitution of Ukraine.

“Laws and other legal acts, by decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, are deemed unconstitutional, in whole or in part, if such laws do not conform to the Constitution of Ukraine, or if the procedure established by the Constitution of Ukraine for their review, adoption, or entry into force was violated.

Article 153

“The procedure for the organisation and functioning of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, as well as the procedure for its review of cases, shall be determined by law.”

Chapter XIII

Introducing Amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine

Article 154

“A draft law on introducing amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine may be submitted to the Verkhovna
Rada of Ukraine by the President of Ukraine, or by no fewer than one-third of the constitutional composition of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.

Article 155

“A draft law on introducing amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine, except for Chapter I — “General Principles,” Chapter III — “Elections.
