“A draft law on introducing amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine shall be considered by the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine upon the availability of an opinion from the Constitutional Court of Ukraine regarding the draft law’s conformity with the requirements of Articles 157 and 158 of this Constitution.”

34.
On 2 June 2016 Parliament amended, inter alia, Article 149 of the Constitution to provide, in particular, that a Constitutional Court judge could not be subjected to legal liability for voting on judgments or opinions adopted by that court, except where the judge had committed a criminal or disciplinary offence.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (as in force at the material time)

35. Under Article 161 of the Code, when deciding a case, an administrative court had to determine, among other matters: (i) whether there were circumstances supporting the claim and objections and what evidence substantiated them; (ii) whether there was any other factual information relevant to the case and evidence supporting it; and (iii) which legal provision applied to the legal relations in dispute.

36. Article 162 of the Code stipulated that, where it found a claim substantiated, an administrative court could, among other things, declare the challenged decision, action or omission unlawful; overturn or annul the decision concerned; require the defendant to take or refrain from certain actions; or order the defendant to make payments. An administrative court could also adopt other decisions to ensure the protection of human and citizens’ rights, as well as the rights and interests of other subjects of public-law relationships.

37. Article 171-1 of the Code provided, among other things, that acts, actions or omissions of Parliament could be challenged before the HAC. Having examined the case, the HAC could: (i) declare an Act of Parliament unlawful in whole or in part; or (ii) declare Parliament’s actions or omission unlawful and require it to take certain actions. On 8 April 2014 Article 171-1 was amended to provide that, in cases of this kind, the HAC could also take additional measures as set out in Article 162 of the Code.

38. On 14 March 2014 Article 171-1 was further amended to provide that, in such cases, the HAC’s judgment entered into force only after review by the Supreme Court or after expiry of the time-limit for seeking such a review.

Criminal Code of 5 April 2001

39. Article 375 of the Code (as in force at the relevant time) provided:

“1. The adoption by a judge (or judges) of a knowingly wrongful conviction, judgment, decision or resolution shall be punishable by restriction of liberty for up to five years or imprisonment for a term of two to five years.

2. The same acts, where they resulted in serious consequences or were committed for financial gain or other personal benefit, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to eight years.”

Constitutional Court of Ukraine Act of 16 October 1996 (in force at the relevant time)

40. Section 3 of the Act provided:

“1. The organisation, competence and procedure governing the functioning of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall be determined by the Constitution and this Act.

2.
The Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall adopt acts [decisions] regulating the organisation of its internal operations in accordance with this Act.”

41. Section 28 of the Act provided:

“... Judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall not be held legally liable for the results of votes cast or statements made in the Constitutional Court of Ukraine and its chambers, except in cases of liability for insult or defamation expressed during the examination of cases, the adoption of judgments and the delivery of opinions by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.”

42. The new Constitutional Court Act was adopted on 13 July 2017. Section 24(3) reflects the revised wording of Article 149 of the Constitution (see paragraph 34 above) and provides that a Constitutional Court judge cannot have a measure of legal liability imposed on him or her for voting for judgments or opinions adopted by the Constitutional Court, except where the judge has committed a criminal or disciplinary offence.

The High Council of Justice Act of 15 January 1998 (“the HCJ Act 1998”), as worded at the relevant time

43. Section 32(2) of the Act defined a breach of oath by judges as follows:

“Breach of oath by a judge is:

(i)  the commission of actions which dishonour the judicial office and may cast doubt on his or her objectivity, impartiality and independence, as well as the fairness and incorruptibility of the judiciary;

(ii)  unlawful acquisition of wealth or expenditure by a judge exceeding his or her income and that of his or her family;

(iii)  deliberate delay in examining a case within the prescribed time-limits; [or]

(iv)  violation of the moral and ethical principles of the judicial code of conduct.”

44. The above provision was examined by the Constitutional Court in 2011 and found to be constitutional (see paragraph 47 below).

Judiciary and Status of Judges Act 2010 (“the 2010 Judiciary Act”)

45. Section 105 of the Act sets out the procedure for dismissing a judge from office in the event of a breach of oath:

“1. In accordance with paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Constitution of Ukraine, a judge shall be dismissed in the event of a breach of judicial oath.

2. Facts indicating a breach of oath by the judge shall be established by the High Qualifications Commission of Judges of Ukraine or the High Council of Justice.

3. Dismissal of a judge on the grounds of a breach of judicial oath shall be carried out upon a motion of the High Council of Justice after consideration of the matter at its meeting in accordance with [the HCJ Act].

4. On the basis of a motion by the High Council of Justice, the President of Ukraine shall issue a decree dismissing a judge.

5. On the basis of a motion by the High Council of Justice, the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine shall adopt a resolution dismissing a judge.”

Rules of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 5 March 1997, as subsequently amended (in force at the relevant time)

46.
In accordance with paragraph 63 of the Rules, where a body that had appointed a Constitutional Court judge raised the issue of a “breach of oath” by that judge, the Constitutional Court had to conduct an investigation and, following a conclusion by its Standing Committee on Rules and Ethics, decide whether grounds existed for the dismissal of the Constitutional Court judge. It had to notify the relevant body of that decision within three days.

Judgment of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 11 March 2011 on the constitutionality of certain provisions of the High Council of Justice Act

47. Following an application by fifty-three members of parliament, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine examined several provisions of the HCJ Act, including section 32(2). With regard to that provision, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine noted:

“The procedure for the appointment or election of a person to the position of judge and the grounds for dismissal from that position are governed by the Basic Law of Ukraine (Articles 126 [and] 128). Other matters concerning the legal status of judges are determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine (paragraph 14 of [Article 92 § 1] of the Constitution of Ukraine).

The legal status of a judge includes both constitutionally established guarantees of the independence and inviolability of judges in the administration of justice and legal liability for failure to discharge their duties. Under the Basic Law of Ukraine, a judge is dismissed by the body that elected or appointed him in the event, in particular, of a breach of oath by the judge; the submission of an application for the dismissal of judges falls within the powers of the High Council of Justice (paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 4], paragraph 1 of [Article 131 § 1]). The procedure and grounds for filing an application to dismiss judges for breaching their oath are set out in section 105 of the Judiciary Act and section 32 of [the HCJ Act]....

Observance of the oath is a judge’s duty under paragraph 4 of [section 54(4)] of the Judiciary Act and corresponds to paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Constitution of Ukraine. This provides grounds for considering a judge’s observance of the oath to be his constitutionally defined duty.
Thus, a judge’s oath has the legal nature of a unilateral, individual, public-law constitutional obligation. A judge’s proper performance of his or her duties is a necessary condition for public confidence in the judiciary and justice. A judge’s breach of oath is one of the grounds for dismissal under paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Basic Law of Ukraine. The legal regulation of a judge’s liability for failure to comply with the judicial oath, in the form of dismissal, is consistent with the 1998 European Charter on the Statute for Judges, which permits judges to be sanctioned for dereliction of one of the duties expressly defined by the statute (paragraph 5.1). Thus, the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, having legally established the criteria of liability for actions constituting a breach of oath by a judge, acted within its powers and in the manner prescribed by the Constitution and laws of Ukraine, and the provisions of section 32 of [the HCJ Act], which define acts amounting to a breach of oath by a judge, do not conflict with the Constitution of Ukraine.”

48. On these grounds, the Constitutional Court held the provision in question to be constitutional.

INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

Materials concerning the situation in Ukraine

49. In its Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005, “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine”, PACE stated as follows:

“14. The Assembly recalls its Resolutions 1346 (2003) and 1364 (2004), in which it emphasised that all provisions of the constitution in force should be fully respected ... . It deeply regrets that the constitutional amendments of 8 December 2004, adopted as part of a package deal to end the political turmoil, contained provisions that the Venice Commission has repeatedly found incompatible with the principles of democracy and the rule of law, particularly as regards the imperative mandate of people’s deputies and the powers of the Prokuratura. The Assembly is also concerned that the new constitutional changes were adopted without prior consultation with the Constitutional Court, as required by Article 159 of the Ukrainian Constitution and interpreted in the Constitutional Court of Ukraine’s 1998 decision. The Assembly therefore urges the Ukrainian authorities to address these matters as soon as possible in order to ensure the legitimacy of the constitutional amendments and their compliance with European standards.”

50. The relevant extract from Opinion no. 599/2010 of 20 December 2010, “On the constitutional situation in Ukraine”, adopted by the Venice Commission at its 85th Plenary Session (CDL-AD(2010)044), reads as follows:

“69. Ukraine’s recent constitutional history has involved continuing challenges and efforts to find the proper balance of powers between the President, the Cabinet and Parliament.
It soon became clear that the text of the 1996 Constitution did not, taking into account the realities in Ukraine, provide sufficient checks and balances and that there was a risk of an authoritarian presidential system. The Venice Commission therefore supported the efforts toward constitutional reform as early as 2003. These efforts resulted in the adoption of the 2004 constitutional amendments. The change introduced by these amendments was welcome in principle, but was neither coherent nor well thought out. The amendments therefore led to greater tension, particularly between the President and the Cabinet of Ministers.70. The reinstatement of the 1996 version of the Constitution by a judgment of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine raises questions about the legitimacy of past actions, since the institutions of Ukraine operated for several years on the basis of constitutional rules later declared unconstitutional. It also raises questions of legitimacy concerning the present state institutions, as the President and Parliament were elected under constitutional rules that are no longer recognised as valid. As a result of this judgment, the President of Ukraine enjoys far greater powers than voters could have foreseen when he was elected. The functioning of the main state organs is now based on rules changed by a court rather than on rules changed by the Verkhovna Rada as a democratically legitimate body.”

Materials concerning the independence of judges and their irremovability from office

The United Nations

51. The Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary were adopted by the Seventh United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, held in Milan in 1985. They were endorsed by UN General Assembly Resolutions 40/32 of 29 November 1985 and 40/146 of 13 December 1985. The relevant provisions read as follows:

“8. In accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, members of the judiciary, like other citizens, are entitled to freedom of expression, belief, association and assembly; provided, however, that in exercising such rights, judges shall always conduct themselves in a manner that preserves the dignity of their office and the impartiality and independence of the judiciary.

...

12. Judges, whether appointed or elected, shall have guaranteed tenure until a mandatory retirement age or the expiry of their term of office, where one exists.

...

18. Judges shall be subject to suspension or removal only for reasons of incapacity or conduct that renders them unfit to perform their duties.

19. All disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings shall be decided in accordance with established standards of judicial conduct.

20. Decisions in disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings should be subject to independent review. This principle may not apply to decisions of the highest court or those of the legislature in impeachment or similar proceedings.”

52.
The Draft Universal Declaration on the Independence of Justice (“Singhvi Declaration”), subsequently prepared by the UN Special Rapporteur, Mr. Singhvi, elaborates on the basic principles as follows:

“Discipline and Removal

26. (a) A complaint against a judge shall be dealt with expeditiously and fairly under an appropriate procedure, and the judge shall have the opportunity to respond to the complaint at the initial stage. The initial examination of the complaint shall remain confidential, unless the judge requests otherwise.

(b) Proceedings for judicial removal or discipline, once initiated, shall be conducted before a Court or a Board composed predominantly of members of the judiciary. The power of removal may, however, be vested in the Legislature through impeachment or joint address, preferably upon the recommendation of such a Court or Board.

27. All disciplinary action shall be founded on established standards of judicial conduct.

28. Disciplinary proceedings against judges shall ensure fairness to the judge and provide the opportunity for a full hearing.

29. Decisions in disciplinary proceedings brought against judges, whether conducted in camera or in public, shall be published.

30. A judge shall not be removed except on established grounds of incapacity or misconduct rendering him unfit to remain in office.”

In Resolution 1989/32, the Commission on Human Rights invited governments to take into consideration the principles set out in the declaration when implementing the United Nations’ Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary.

53. In its General Comment No. 32 on Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Right to equality before courts and tribunals and to a fair trial), published on 23 August 2007, the UN Human Rights Committee stated as follows (footnotes omitted):

“19. The requirement that a tribunal be competent, independent and impartial within the meaning of Article 14, paragraph 1, is an absolute right subject to no exception. The requirement of independence relates, in particular, to the procedure and qualifications for appointing judges; guarantees concerning their security of tenure until a mandatory retirement age or the expiry of their term of office, where applicable; the conditions governing promotion, transfer, suspension and termination of their functions; and the judiciary’s actual independence from political interference by the executive and legislative branches. States should adopt specific measures to guarantee judicial independence and protect judges from any form of political influence over their decision-making, through constitutional provisions or legislation establishing clear procedures and objective criteria for the appointment, remuneration, tenure, promotion, suspension and dismissal of members of the judiciary, as well as disciplinary sanctions imposed on them.”
A situation in which the functions and competencies of the judiciary and the executive are not clearly distinguishable, or in which the latter is able to control or direct the former, is incompatible with the notion of an independent tribunal. Judges must be protected against conflicts of interest and intimidation. To safeguard their independence, the status of judges, including their term of office, independence, security, adequate remuneration, conditions of service, pensions and retirement age, shall be adequately secured by law.

20. Judges may be dismissed only on serious grounds of misconduct or incompetence, in accordance with fair procedures ensuring objectivity and impartiality, as set out in the constitution or the law. The dismissal of judges by the executive, for example before the expiry of the term for which they were appointed, without specific reasons being provided and without effective judicial protection being available to challenge the dismissal, is incompatible with judicial independence. The same applies, for instance, to the dismissal by the executive of judges alleged to be corrupt without following any of the procedures prescribed by law.”

54. In 2006, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) adopted Resolution 2006/23, “Strengthening Basic Principles of Judicial Conduct”, by which it endorsed the Bangalore Principles. These were drafted by a group of chief justices and superior court judges from around the world (the Judicial Integrity Group) and were intended to establish standards of ethical conduct for judges. The “Measures for the Effective Implementation of the Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (the Implementation Measures)”, adopted by the Judicial Integrity Group in 2010, include the following sections on the discipline and removal of judges:

“Discipline of Judges

15.1  Disciplinary proceedings against a judge may be initiated only for serious misconduct. The law applicable to judges may define, as far as possible and in specific terms, conduct that may give rise to disciplinary sanctions, as well as the procedures to be followed.

...

15.5  All disciplinary proceedings should be decided by reference to established standards of judicial conduct and in accordance with a procedure guaranteeing full rights of defence.

Removal of Judges from Office

16.1  A judge may be removed from office only for proven incapacity, conviction of a serious crime, gross incompetence, or conduct that is manifestly contrary to the independence, impartiality and integrity of the judiciary.

16.2  Where the legislature is vested with the power to remove a judge, that power should be exercised only following a recommendation to that effect by the independent authority vested with the power to discipline judges.”

55. In 2013, the Human Rights Council, in its Resolution 35/12, “Independence and impartiality of the judiciary, jurors and assessors, and the independence of lawyers”
reaffirmed its earlier view and emphasized that: “3. ... the term of office of judges, their independence, security, adequate remuneration, conditions of service, pensions and retirement age should be adequately secured by law; that security of tenure for judges is an essential guarantee of judicial independence; that the grounds for their removal must be explicit and based on well-defined circumstances prescribed by law, involving incapacity or conduct rendering them unfit to discharge their functions; and that procedures governing the discipline, suspension or removal of a judge should comply with due process;”56. In its decision in Pastukhov v. Belarus, Communication No. 814/1998, UN Doc. CCPR/C/78/D/814/1998 (2003), the UN Human Rights Committee (CCPR) stated as follows: “7.3  The Committee notes the author’s claim that he could not be removed from the bench because, under the law in force at the time, he had been elected as a judge on 28 April 1994 for a term of 11 years. The Committee further notes that Presidential Decree No. 106 of 24 January 1997 was not based on the replacement of the Constitutional Court by a new court; rather, the decree referred to the author personally, and the sole reason given for his dismissal was the purported expiry of his term as a Constitutional Court judge, which was manifestly not the case. Moreover, no effective judicial remedies were available to the author to challenge his dismissal by the executive. In these circumstances, the Committee considers that the author’s dismissal from his position as a judge of the Constitutional Court, several years before the expiry of the term for which he had been appointed, constituted an attack on judicial independence and failed to respect the author’s right of access, on general terms of equality, to public service in his country.

CASE OF OVCHARENKO AND KOLOS v. UKRAINE

In the case of Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Chamber consisting of:

Georges Ravarani, President,  
Iulia Antoanella Motoc,  
Mārtiņš Mits,  
María Elósegui,  
Mattias Guyomar,  
Kateřina Šimáčková,  
Mykola Gnatovskyy, judges,

and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having taken into consideration:

the applications against Ukraine (nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15), submitted to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Vyacheslav Andriyovych Ovcharenko (“the first applicant”) and Mr Mykhaylo Ivanovych Kolos (“the second applicant”), on 20 May and 2 July 2015 respectively;

the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of the applications;

Having deliberated in private on 29 November 2022,

Delivers the following judgment, adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1. The case relates to the dismissal of two judges from the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, which was alleged to have violated Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. The first and second applicants were born in 1957 and 1953 respectively. They were represented by Mr A. Bushchenko, who was, at the relevant time, a lawyer practising in Kyiv.

3. The Government’s Agent was Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The relevant circumstances may be summarised as set out below.

Background

5. On 28 June 1996, the Ukrainian Parliament (Verkhovna Rada) adopted the Constitution of Ukraine.

6. Constitutional amendments were introduced in December 2004. Among other changes, they strengthened the parliamentary elements of Ukraine’s political system while reducing the powers vested in the President of Ukraine. Alleged procedural irregularities in the adoption of those amendments became the subject of public debate and were also discussed by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), as recorded in its Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005, entitled “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine” (see paragraph 43 below).

7. Parliament appointed both applicants as judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (“the Constitutional Court”) on 4 August 2006.

8. Also on 4 August 2006, Parliament amended the “Final and Transitional Provisions” of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine Act (“the Constitutional Court Act”). The amendment stated that the Constitutional Court had no authority to examine the constitutionality of Acts of Parliament amending the Constitution.

9.
On 5 February 2008, acting on an application lodged by members of parliament, the Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings concerning the constitutionality of the Act of Parliament through which the Constitution had been amended in December 2004. It observed that, once in force, the provisions of an Act amending the Constitution “had accomplished their function”. The application for constitutional review was then dismissed on procedural grounds because it failed to specify the impugned Act’s full title, registration number and date of enactment.

10. On 26 June 2008, the Constitutional Court delivered a judgment finding unconstitutional the provision added to the Constitutional Court Act in 2006 that excluded Acts of Parliament concerning constitutional amendments from its jurisdiction (see paragraph 8 above). In particular, the court observed that the Constitution empowered it to review the constitutionality of legislation enacted by Parliament, without creating any exception for laws amending the Constitution.

11. In February 2010, Mr V. Yanukovych was elected President of Ukraine.

12. On 30 September 2010, in response to an application submitted by members of parliament in July of that year, the Constitutional Court ruled that the 2004 constitutional amendments were unconstitutional because the proper procedure had not been followed when they were enacted. The court held that the amendments would cease to be valid from the date of its judgment, thereby restoring the applicability of the preceding version of the Constitution. Its reasoning referred, among other sources, to PACE Resolution 1466 (2005) (see paragraph 6 above and paragraph 49 below).

EVENTS BETWEEN NOVEMBER 2013 AND FEBRUARY 2014, THE CHANGE OF POWER IN UKRAINE AND THE APPLICANTS’ REMOVAL

13. Anti-government demonstrations began in Kyiv in late November 2013 before spreading to other Ukrainian cities and developing into mass protests nationwide. They were reportedly prompted by the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision to halt preparations for signing the Association Agreement between Ukraine and the European Union. By late February 2014, the protests had developed into serious confrontations between demonstrators and law-enforcement authorities, resulting in numerous deaths and injuries (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others v. Ukraine, nos. 15367/14 and 13 others, §§ 9-17, 21 January 2021).

14. On 21 February 2014, Parliament enacted the Revalidation of Certain Provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine Act (“the Revalidation Act”), restoring the 2004 Constitution subject to certain amendments. Parliament also dismissed the Minister of the Interior.

15. The following day, 22 February 2014, Parliament declared that Mr Yanukovych had abandoned his presidential duties in an unconstitutional manner.
On that day and on 23 February 2014, Parliament dismissed the Prosecutor General and adopted several additional decisions relating to the replacement of senior State officials and the operation of the executive branch (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others, cited above, §§ 44-45).

16. On 24 February 2014, Parliament passed a resolution entitled “On responding to the ‘breach of oath’ by judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine”. Relying on Article 126 of the Constitution, it dismissed for “breach of oath” the Constitutional Court judges appointed under Parliament’s quota pursuant to Article 148 of the Constitution (see paragraph 33 below), including the applicants. Parliament also called on the acting President of Ukraine and the Congress of Judges to take steps to dismiss, on the same ground, the remaining Constitutional Court judges, who had been appointed under the respective quotas of the President and the Congress of Judges. Finally, it requested that the Office of the Prosecutor General open a criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 (see paragraph 12 above).

17. In explaining that resolution, Parliament asserted that, on 30 September 2010, the Constitutional Court had unlawfully altered the Constitution by usurping Parliament’s powers, thereby violating the core constitutional principles of democracy and separation of powers and changing the constitutional system. In support of that position, Parliament cited the reasoning in the Constitutional Court’s ruling of 5 February 2008 (see paragraph 9 above), according to which the Act amending the Constitution had “accomplished its function” by becoming part of the Constitution. It also relied on the Venice Commission’s opinion of 20 December 2010, “On the constitutional situation in Ukraine” (see paragraph 50 below). That opinion stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 had cast doubt on the legitimacy of the existing State institutions because the President and Parliament had been elected under constitutional rules that were subsequently no longer regarded as valid. As a result of that judgment, the President had acquired substantially broader powers than voters could have anticipated when electing him, while the principal State bodies had thereafter operated under rules modified by a court rather than by Parliament, the democratically legitimate law-making body.

18. Parliament additionally stated that, in a judgment delivered on 29 May 2013, the Constitutional Court had effectively prevented elections from being held in the city of Kyiv and for the Ternopil Regional Council before October 2015. In Parliament’s view, by adopting that judgment, the Constitutional Court judges had infringed citizens’ electoral rights.

19.
Lastly, Parliament noted that on 25 January 2012 the Constitutional Court had delivered a judgment permitting the Cabinet of Ministers to determine the amount of social payments “manually”, notwithstanding its earlier rulings to the contrary on the same issue. Parliament considered that, in doing so, the Constitutional Court judges had infringed citizens’ constitutional rights to social security and to an adequate standard of living.

20. Parliament concluded that the Constitutional Court judges responsible for the judgments referred to above had failed to fulfil their duty to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution and safeguard the constitutional order and citizens’ constitutional rights, contrary to Articles 3, 19 and 147 to 153 of the Constitution. It further considered that those shortcomings were incompatible with the judicial oath and with the honest and rigorous discharge of the duties of a Constitutional Court judge.

21. In March 2014 the applicants tendered their resignations, seeking to end their service voluntarily rather than through a sanction imposed by Parliament. At the same time, they brought court proceedings challenging Parliament’s resolution of 24 February 2014 dismissing them for a “breach of oath” (see below).

22. Separately, the Office of the Prosecutor General opened criminal proceedings concerning the unconstitutional seizure of State power by President Yanukovych through amendments to the Constitution resulting from the Constitutional Court’s adoption of an unlawful judgment, the Constitutional Court judges’ abuse of power, and the delivery on 30 September 2010 of a judgment known to be unlawful. On 4 May 2020, in the context of those proceedings, the Pecherskyi District Court issued an arrest warrant for Mr Yanukovych in absentia. The Kyiv Court of Appeal upheld that order on 25 March 2021. The criminal proceedings remain pending.

Proceedings brought by the first applicant

23. On 27 February 2014, relying on the Code of Administrative Justice, the first applicant filed a claim before the Higher Administrative Court (“the HAC”) contesting his dismissal.

24. On 18 June 2014 the HAC held that Parliament’s resolution of 24 February 2014 was unlawful insofar as it concerned the first applicant’s dismissal. It found that Parliament had not complied with the procedure applicable to the removal of a Constitutional Court judge. More specifically, the Rules of the Constitutional Court required the matter first to be examined by the Constitutional Court itself, but no such examination had taken place. Furthermore, Parliament had adopted the contested decision under a simplified procedure[1], although that procedure could not be used to dismiss Constitutional Court judges.
In reaching its decision, the HAC also relied on section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act, which provided that judges of the Constitutional Court could not incur legal liability for the outcome of votes cast in that court. Finally, the HAC cited international legal standards on judicial independence and found that Parliament had failed to observe them.25.

Parliament sought review of the case by the Supreme Court.26. On 2 December 2014, the Supreme Court set aside the HAC’s judgment and rejected the first applicant’s claim as unfounded. After restating the circumstances of the case, the applicable provisions of domestic law and the parties’ positions, it continued:

“In examining the substance of the violations on which the dismissal of V.A. Ovcharenko was based, the panel of judges of the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court considers it necessary to make the following observations.

As indicated in the judgment [of 30 September 2010], the Constitutional Court of Ukraine examined the case following a submission by 252 members of parliament alleging that Law no. 2222-IV was incompatible with the Constitution of Ukraine.

When addressing the issue raised in the constitutional complaint lodged by those members of parliament, the Constitutional Court stated in the reasoning of its judgment [of 30 September 2010] that declaring Law no. 2222-IV unconstitutional because of breaches of the procedure governing its consideration and adoption entailed restoring the earlier wording of the provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine that had been amended, supplemented or repealed by that Law.

In point 3 of the operative part of the judgment, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine directed the State authorities to implement the judgment immediately by bringing normative legal acts into conformity with the Constitution of Ukraine of 28 June 1996, as it had stood before the amendments introduced by Law no. 2222-IV.

As stated in Resolution no. 775-VII, that conclusion of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine is inconsistent with the legally prescribed procedure for amending the Constitution of Ukraine. Under that procedure, once statutory provisions amending the Constitution enter into force, they become an integral part of the Basic Law as its individual provisions, while the amending law itself ceases to perform any function.

The Constitution of Ukraine does not confer on the Constitutional Court of Ukraine the authority to declare a constitutional provision invalid (визнавати нечинність), irrespective of the legal form in which that provision is expressed.

Pursuant to Article 85 § 1 (1) of the Constitution of Ukraine, the power to amend the Constitution is vested specifically in the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, subject to the limits and procedure laid down in Chapter XII of the Constitution.

Through its judgment [of 30 September 2010], in whose adoption V.A.
By participating in the adoption of that judgment, Ovcharenko failed to safeguard the supremacy of the Constitution of Ukraine and, in effect, amended it. He violated the fundamental constitutional principle of democracy (народовладдя), altered Ukraine’s constitutional order, and infringed the constitutional principles of the separation of powers and the legitimacy of the functioning institutions of State authority. As a result, those institutions operated on the basis of provisions modified by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine rather than by the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, the authority competent to make such changes. The manifest incompatibility between V.A. Ovcharenko’s conduct in adopting the [30 September 2010] judgment and the oath he had taken, together with the consequences of that conduct, provided the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine with grounds for treating his actions as a breach of the oath of a judge of the Constitutional Court and for removing him from office.”

27. Regarding the Constitutional Court’s judgments of 25 January 2012 and 29 May 2013, which were likewise considered in the contested parliamentary resolution, the Supreme Court concluded that both judgments fell within the Constitutional Court’s discretionary powers and that the first applicant’s involvement in their adoption did not amount to a “breach of oath”[2].

28. As to the procedure followed in dismissing the first applicant, the Supreme Court held that the HAC had wrongly relied on the Rules of the Constitutional Court. Those Rules were merely an internal instrument, and neither the Constitution nor the Constitutional Court Act authorised the Constitutional Court to regulate the procedure for removing its own members. The procedure by which the first applicant had been dismissed, on the other hand, was consistent with both the Constitution and the Rules of Parliament.

Proceedings brought by the second applicant

29. On 5 March 2014, relying on the Code of Administrative Justice, the second applicant filed a claim with the HAC contesting his dismissal.

30. The HAC rejected that claim on 26 January 2015, relying on the legal position established by the Supreme Court in its decision of 2 December 2014 concerning the first applicant.

31. The second applicant then asked the Supreme Court to review the case. He argued, among other points, that his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 could not justify his dismissal; that Parliament had failed to provide a fair and independent examination of the matter; that the procedure prescribed by the Rules of the Constitutional Court had not been observed; and that he could not incur liability for a judgment in favour of which he had voted as a member of that court.

32. On 28 April 2015, the Supreme Court upheld the decision of 26 January 2015, reiterating the reasoning it had adopted in the first applicant’s case.

Under paragraph 63 of the Rules, where the authority that had appointed a Constitutional Court judge raised an issue concerning that judge’s “breach of oath”, the Constitutional Court was required to investigate the matter. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 11 March 2011 concerning the constitutionality of certain provisions of the High Council of Justice Act47. Acting on an application lodged by fifty-three members of parliament, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine reviewed several provisions of the HCJ Act, among them section 32(2). In relation to that provision, the Court observed:

“The Basic Law of Ukraine governs the procedure for appointing or electing a person to judicial office, as well as the grounds for removing that person from office (Articles 126 and 128). All other matters relating to judges’ legal status are determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine (paragraph 14 of Article 92 § 1 of the Constitution of Ukraine).

A judge’s legal status encompasses both the constitutionally established guarantees of judicial independence and inviolability in the administration of justice and legal responsibility for failure to discharge judicial duties. The Basic Law of Ukraine provides that a judge is to be dismissed by the authority that elected or appointed him, including where the judge has breached his oath. The High Council of Justice is empowered to submit an application seeking a judge’s dismissal (paragraph 5 of Article 126 § 4 and paragraph 1 of Article 131 § 1). The procedure and grounds for submitting an application for dismissal on account of breach of oath are set out in section 105 of the Judiciary Act and section 32 of the HCJ Act.

Compliance with the oath constitutes a judicial duty under paragraph 4 of section 54(4) of the Judiciary Act and corresponds to paragraph 5 of Article 126 § 5 of the Constitution of Ukraine. Accordingly, observance of the oath must be regarded as a judge’s constitutionally prescribed obligation.”
Accordingly, a judge’s oath constitutes a unilateral and individual constitutional duty of a public-law nature. The proper performance by judges of their obligations is essential to maintaining public confidence in both the judiciary and the administration of justice. Under paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Basic Law of Ukraine, breach of the judicial oath is among the grounds on which a judge may be dismissed.

The statutory framework providing for a judge’s dismissal as a form of liability for failure to honour the judicial oath is consistent with the 1998 European Charter on the statute for judges. Paragraph 5.1 of that instrument permits sanctions against judges for neglecting duties expressly prescribed by statute.

Therefore, by establishing in law the criteria for liability in respect of conduct amounting to a breach of the judicial oath, the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine acted within its authority and followed the procedure laid down by the Constitution and the laws of Ukraine. Consequently, section 32 of [the HCJ Act], which specifies the conduct constituting a breach of a judge’s oath, is not incompatible with the Constitution of Ukraine.”

48. On the basis of that reasoning, the Constitutional Court held that the provision at issue was constitutional.

Materials relating to the situation in Ukraine

49. In Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005, entitled “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine”, PACE stated:

“14. The Assembly reiterates the position expressed in Resolutions 1346 (2003) and 1364 (2004), in which it stressed that every provision of the Constitution currently in force must be fully observed ... . “69. Ukraine’s recent constitutional history has been characterised by recurring challenges and continuing efforts to establish an appropriate balance of power among the President, the Cabinet and Parliament.
It quickly became clear that, in light of the situation in Ukraine, the 1996 Constitution did not establish adequate checks and balances and created a danger of an authoritarian presidential system. Consequently, as early as 2003, the Venice Commission supported initiatives aimed at constitutional reform. Those initiatives culminated in the adoption of the 2004 constitutional amendments. Although the shift introduced by the amendments was welcomed in principle, the changes lacked coherence and had not been sufficiently considered. As a result, they intensified tensions, particularly between the President and the Cabinet of Ministers.70

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine’s judgment restoring the 1996 version of the Constitution raises questions about the legitimacy of earlier actions because, for several years, Ukrainian institutions had operated under constitutional provisions that were subsequently declared unconstitutional. The ruling also calls into question the legitimacy of the existing State institutions, since both the President and Parliament were elected under constitutional rules that are no longer regarded as valid. Following the judgment, the President of Ukraine holds substantially broader powers than voters could have anticipated at the time of his election. The principal State institutions now function under rules altered by a court rather than by the Verkhovna Rada, the body possessing democratic legitimacy.

The United Nations

51. The Seventh United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, held in Milan in 1985, adopted the Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary. The UN General Assembly subsequently endorsed them through Resolutions 40/32 of 29 November 1985 and 40/146 of 13 December 1985. The relevant provisions state:

“8. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, judges, like all other citizens, enjoy freedom of expression, belief, association and assembly. In exercising those freedoms, however, they must always behave in a manner that safeguards the dignity of judicial office and preserves the judiciary’s impartiality and independence.

...

12. Whether selected by appointment or election, judges must be guaranteed tenure until they reach the compulsory retirement age or, where applicable, until their term of office expires.

...

18. A judge may be suspended or removed only on grounds of incapacity or conduct demonstrating that the judge is unfit to perform judicial duties.

19. Proceedings concerning discipline, suspension or removal must be decided in accordance with established standards governing judicial conduct.

20. Decisions made in disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings should be open to independent review. This requirement need not apply to rulings of the highest court or to legislative decisions in impeachment or comparable proceedings.”

52.
The Draft Universal Declaration on the Independence of Justice (“Singhvi Declaration”), subsequently prepared by the UN Special Rapporteur, Mr. Singhvi, further develops the basic principles in the following terms:

**Discipline and Removal**

**26.**  
**(a)** Any complaint made against a judge must be handled promptly and fairly in accordance with an appropriate procedure. At the preliminary stage, the judge must be given an opportunity to respond to the complaint. Unless the judge requests otherwise, the initial examination of the complaint must remain confidential.

**(b)** Once proceedings concerning the discipline or removal of a judge have begun, they must be conducted before a court or board whose membership consists predominantly of members of the judiciary. The authority to remove a judge may nevertheless be conferred on the legislature through impeachment or a joint address, preferably following a recommendation by such a court or board.

**27.** Every disciplinary measure must be founded on established standards governing judicial conduct.

**28.** Judicial disciplinary proceedings must be fair to the judge and must provide an opportunity for a full hearing.

**29.** Decisions issued in disciplinary proceedings against judges must be published, regardless of whether the proceedings took place in public or in camera.

**30.** A judge may be removed from office only where incapacity or misconduct has been proved and is of such a nature as to make the judge unfit to remain in office.

Through Resolution 1989/32, the Commission on Human Rights invited governments, when implementing the United Nations Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, to take account of the principles contained in the Singhvi Declaration.

**53.** In General Comment No. 32 concerning Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights—covering equality before courts and tribunals and the right to a fair trial—published on 23 August 2007, the UN Human Rights Committee stated the following, with footnotes omitted:

**19.** Under Article 14(1), the right to a competent, independent, and impartial tribunal is absolute and permits no exception. Judicial independence concerns, in particular, the procedures and qualifications applicable to judicial appointments; safeguards protecting judges’ security of tenure until any prescribed retirement age or until the end of a fixed term, where applicable; the rules governing promotion, transfer, suspension, and termination of judicial functions; and the judiciary’s practical freedom from political interference by the executive and legislative branches. States should adopt specific measures to secure judicial independence and protect judges from political influence over their decision-making. Such protection should be established through constitutional provisions or legislation setting out clear procedures and objective criteria for the appointment, remuneration, tenure, promotion, suspension, and dismissal of members of the judiciary, as well as for disciplinary sanctions imposed upon them.
An independent tribunal cannot exist where the respective roles and powers of the judiciary and the executive are blurred, or where the executive can direct or control the judiciary. Judges must be shielded from intimidation and conflicts of interest. To preserve judicial independence, the law must adequately guarantee judges’ status, including their tenure, independence, security, sufficient remuneration, working conditions, pensions, and retirement age.20. A judge may be removed from office only for serious misconduct or incompetence and solely through fair, objective, and impartial procedures established by the constitution or by law. Judicial independence is undermined when the executive dismisses judges—for example, before the end of their appointed terms—without providing specific reasons and without making effective judicial remedies available to challenge their removal. The same applies where the executive dismisses judges accused of corruption without observing any of the legally prescribed procedures.”

54. In 2006, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) adopted Resolution 2006/23, entitled “Strengthening Basic Principles of Judicial Conduct”, thereby endorsing the Bangalore Principles. Those Principles had been prepared by the Judicial Integrity Group, comprising chief justices and senior court judges from across the world, with the purpose of setting standards of ethical conduct for judges. The “Measures for the Effective Implementation of the Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (the Implementation Measures)”, adopted by the Judicial Integrity Group in 2010, include the following provisions concerning judicial discipline and removal:

“Discipline of Judges

15.1  Proceedings to discipline a judge may be initiated only in cases of serious misconduct. As far as possible, the law governing judges may specify the conduct capable of attracting disciplinary sanctions and the procedures that must be followed.

...

15.5  Every disciplinary case should be decided by applying established standards of judicial conduct and through a process that fully guarantees the rights of the defence.

Removal of Judges from Office

16.1  Removal from judicial office is permissible only where there is proven incapacity, conviction for a serious criminal offence, gross incompetence, or conduct plainly inconsistent with the judiciary’s independence, impartiality, and integrity.

16.2  If the legislature has authority to remove a judge, it should exercise that power only following a recommendation by the independent body responsible for judicial discipline.”

55. In 2013, the Human Rights Council adopted Resolution 35/12, “Independence and impartiality of the judiciary, jurors and assessors, and the independence of lawyers”
It reaffirmed its previous position, emphasizing that:

“3. ... the tenure of judges, as well as their independence, security, adequate remuneration, conditions of service, pensions, and retirement age, must be sufficiently protected by law; security of tenure is an indispensable safeguard of judicial independence; the grounds for removing judges must be expressly stated and defined by law, limited to incapacity or conduct rendering them unable to perform their duties; and any procedure governing the discipline, suspension, or removal of a judge must comply with due process.”56

In Pastukhov v. Belarus, Communication No. 814/1998, UN Doc. CCPR/C/78/D/814/1998 (2003), the UN Human Rights Committee (CCPR) held:

“7.3  The Committee notes the author’s contention that he could not lawfully be removed from judicial office because, under the law applicable at the time, he had been elected on 28 April 1994 to serve an 11-year term. It further observes that Presidential Decree No. 106 of 24 January 1997 did not arise from the replacement of the Constitutional Court by a new court. Instead, the decree identified the author personally and stated that the sole basis for his dismissal was the expiration of his term as a Constitutional Court judge, although his term had plainly not expired. Moreover, the author had no access to effective judicial remedies through which to challenge his removal by the executive. Given these circumstances, the Committee concludes that dismissing the author from his post as a Constitutional Court judge several years before the end of his appointed term undermined judicial independence and violated his right to equal access to public service in his country.”
