FIFTH SECTION

OVCHARENKO AND KOLOS v. UKRAINE

(Applications nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15)

JUDGMENT

STRASBOURG

12 January 2023

FINAL

12/04/2023

Pursuant to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, this judgment has become final. It remains subject to possible editorial revision.

In Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine,

the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Chamber of its Fifth Section, was composed of:

Georges Ravarani, President,
Iulia Antoanella Motoc,
Mārtiņš Mits,
María Elósegui,
Mattias Guyomar,
Kateřina Šimáčková,
Mykola Gnatovskyy, judges,

and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar.

The Court took into consideration:

– applications nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15, brought against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Ukrainian nationals, Mr Vyacheslav Andriyovych Ovcharenko (“the first applicant”) and Mr Mykhaylo Ivanovych Kolos (“the second applicant”), and lodged on 20 May and 2 July 2015 respectively;

– the decision to notify the Ukrainian Government (“the Government”) of those applications;

– the observations submitted by the parties.

Following private deliberations on 29 November 2022,

the Court gives the following judgment, adopted on the same date:

INTRODUCTION

1. This case relates to the removal from office of two judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, which was alleged to have violated Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2. The first and second applicants were born in 1957 and 1953 respectively. They were represented by Mr A. Bushchenko, who, at the relevant time, practised law in Kyiv.

3. The Government’s Agent was Mr I. Lishchyna.

4. The relevant circumstances may be outlined as set out below.

Background

5. On 28 June 1996, the Ukrainian Parliament (Verkhovna Rada) adopted the Constitution of Ukraine.

6. Constitutional amendments were introduced in December 2004. Among other changes, they strengthened the parliamentary elements of the political system and reduced the authority of the President of Ukraine. Alleged irregularities in the procedure by which those amendments had been adopted became the subject of public debate and were also discussed by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), as recorded in Resolution 1466 (2005) of 5 October 2005, entitled “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine” (see paragraph 43 below).

7. Parliament appointed the applicants as judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (“the Constitutional Court”) on 4 August 2006.

8. Also on 4 August 2006, Parliament amended the “Final and Transitional Provisions” of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine Act (“the Constitutional Court Act”) to provide that the Constitutional Court had no authority to examine the constitutionality of parliamentary Acts amending the Constitution.

9.
On 5 February 2008, in response to an application submitted by members of parliament, the Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings concerning the constitutionality of the parliamentary Act that had amended the Constitution in December 2004. It observed that, upon entering into force, the provisions of an Act of Parliament introducing constitutional amendments “had accomplished their function”. The court subsequently dismissed the constitutional-review application on procedural grounds because it did not specify the impugned Act’s full title, registration number or enactment date.

10. On 26 June 2008, the Constitutional Court delivered a judgment finding unconstitutional the provision added to the Constitutional Court Act in 2006 that excluded parliamentary Acts introducing constitutional amendments from the court’s jurisdiction (see paragraph 8 above). In particular, it pointed out that the Constitution empowered it to review the constitutionality of laws passed by Parliament without creating any exception for laws amending the Constitution.

11. In February 2010, Mr V. Yanukovych was elected President of Ukraine.

12. Acting on an application lodged by members of parliament in July 2010, the Constitutional Court issued a judgment on 30 September 2010 declaring the 2004 constitutional amendments unconstitutional because the proper procedure had not been followed when they were enacted. The court ruled that the amendments would cease to be valid from the date of that judgment, thereby restoring the applicability of the earlier version of the Constitution. Its reasoning referred, among other sources, to PACE Resolution 1466 (2005) (see paragraph 6 above and paragraph 49 below).

EVENTS FROM NOVEMBER 2013 TO FEBRUARY 2014, THE CHANGE OF POWER IN UKRAINE AND THE APPLICANTS’ REMOVAL

13. Anti-government demonstrations began in Kyiv in late November 2013 before spreading to other Ukrainian cities and developing into large-scale popular protests across the country. They were reportedly triggered by the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision to halt preparations for signing the Ukraine-European Union Association Agreement. By late February 2014, the demonstrations had developed into serious confrontations between protesters and law-enforcement authorities, resulting in numerous deaths and injuries (for additional details, see Shmorgunov and Others v. Ukraine, nos. 15367/14 and 13 others, §§ 9-17, 21 January 2021).

14. On 21 February 2014, Parliament enacted the Revalidation of Certain Provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine Act (“the Revalidation Act”), restoring the 2004 Constitution subject to certain amendments. Parliament also dismissed the Minister of the Interior.

15. On 22 February 2014, Parliament declared that Mr Yanukovych had abandoned his presidential duties in an unconstitutional manner.
On that date and on 23 February 2014, Parliament removed the Prosecutor General from office and adopted several additional decisions relating to the replacement of senior State officials and the operation of the executive branch (for further details, see Shmorgunov and Others, cited above, §§ 44-45).

16. On 24 February 2014, Parliament passed a resolution entitled “On responding to the ‘breach of oath’ by judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine”. Relying on Article 126 of the Constitution, it dismissed for “breach of oath” the Constitutional Court judges appointed under Parliament’s quota pursuant to Article 148 of the Constitution (see paragraph 33 below), including the applicants. Parliament also called on the acting President of Ukraine and the Congress of Judges to take steps to remove, on the same ground of “breach of oath”, the remaining Constitutional Court judges, who had been appointed under the respective quotas of the President and the Congress of Judges. Finally, it requested that the Office of the Prosecutor General open a criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 (see paragraph 12 above).

17. Explaining that resolution, Parliament asserted that, on 30 September 2010, the Constitutional Court had unlawfully altered the Constitution by usurping Parliament’s powers, thereby violating the basic constitutional principles of democracy and the separation of powers and modifying the constitutional system. In support of that position, Parliament cited the reasoning in the Constitutional Court’s ruling of 5 February 2008 (see paragraph 9 above), according to which the Act amending the Constitution had “accomplished its function” by becoming part of the Constitution. Parliament additionally relied on the Venice Commission’s opinion of 20 December 2010, “On the constitutional situation in Ukraine” (see paragraph 50 below). That opinion stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 had cast doubt on the legitimacy of the existing State institutions because the President and Parliament had been elected under constitutional provisions that were no longer regarded as valid. From the date of that judgment, the President had possessed substantially broader powers than voters could have anticipated when electing him, while the principal State bodies had thereafter operated under rules modified by a court rather than by Parliament, the democratically legitimate institution.

18. Parliament also noted that, on 29 May 2013, the Constitutional Court had delivered a judgment that had, in practical terms, prevented elections from being held in the city of Kyiv and for the Ternopil Regional Council before October 2015. Parliament concluded that, by issuing that judgment, the Constitutional Court judges had infringed citizens’ electoral rights.

19.
Lastly, Parliament noted that, on 25 January 2012, the Constitutional Court had delivered a judgment permitting the Cabinet of Ministers to determine the amount of social payments “manually”, notwithstanding that it had previously issued decisions reaching the opposite conclusion on the same matter. Parliament considered that, in doing so, the Constitutional Court judges had infringed citizens’ constitutional rights to social security and an adequate standard of living.

20. Parliament determined that the Constitutional Court judges responsible for the judgments referred to above had breached their duty to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution and safeguard the constitutional order and citizens’ constitutional rights, contrary to Articles 3, 19 and 147 to 153 of the Constitution. It further held that those shortcomings were incompatible with the judicial oath and with the honest and rigorous discharge of the duties of a Constitutional Court judge.

21. In March 2014, the applicants tendered their resignations, seeking to end their duties voluntarily instead of through a sanction imposed by Parliament. At the same time, they brought court proceedings contesting Parliament’s resolution of 24 February 2014 dismissing them for “breach of oath” (see below).

22. Separately, the Office of the Prosecutor General opened criminal proceedings concerning President Yanukovych’s unconstitutional seizure of State power by introducing amendments to the Constitution through the Constitutional Court’s adoption of an unlawful judgment, the Constitutional Court judges’ abuse of power, and the delivery of a knowingly unlawful judgment on 30 September 2010. In those proceedings, the Pecherskyi District Court issued a warrant on 4 May 2020 for Mr Yanukovych’s arrest in absentia. The Kyiv Court of Appeal upheld that order on 25 March 2021. The case remains pending.

Proceedings brought by the first applicant

23. On 27 February 2014, invoking the Code of Administrative Justice, the first applicant filed a claim before the Higher Administrative Court (“the HAC”) contesting his dismissal.

24. On 18 June 2014, the HAC ruled that Parliament’s resolution of 24 February 2014 was unlawful in so far as it concerned the first applicant’s dismissal. It held that Parliament had not complied with the prescribed procedure for removing a Constitutional Court judge. More specifically, the Rules of the Constitutional Court required the Constitutional Court itself to conduct a preliminary examination of the matter, but no such examination had taken place. In addition, Parliament had adopted the contested decision under a simplified procedure[1], although that procedure could not be used for the dismissal of Constitutional Court judges.
In reaching its decision, the HAC also cited section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act, which laid down the principle that judges of the Constitutional Court could not incur legal liability for the outcomes of their votes in that court. Finally, the HAC referred to international legal principles on judicial independence and found that Parliament had failed to observe them.

25. Parliament applied to the Supreme Court for review of the case.

26. On 2 December 2014, the Supreme Court set aside the HAC’s judgment and rejected the first applicant’s claim as unfounded. After restating the circumstances of the case, the applicable domestic-law provisions and the parties’ positions, it continued:

“When examining the substance of the violations on which the dismissal of V.A. Ovcharenko was based, the panel of judges of the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court considers it necessary to make the following observations.

According to the judgment [of 30 September 2010], the Constitutional Court of Ukraine examined the case following a submission by 252 members of parliament alleging that Law no. 2222-IV was incompatible with the Constitution of Ukraine.

When resolving the issue raised in the constitutional complaint lodged by those members of parliament, the Constitutional Court stated, in the reasoning of the judgment [of 30 September 2010], that declaring Law no. 2222-IV unconstitutional because the procedure for its consideration and adoption had been breached entailed restoring the previous wording of the provisions of the Constitution of Ukraine that Law no. 2222-IV had amended, supplemented or repealed.

In item 3 of the operative part of the judgment, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine required State authorities to implement the judgment immediately by bringing normative legal acts into conformity with the Constitution of Ukraine of 28 June 1996, in the version that had existed before the amendments introduced by Law no. 2222-IV.

As indicated in Resolution No. 775-VII, that conclusion of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine is inconsistent with the procedure prescribed by law for amending the Constitution of Ukraine. Under that procedure, once provisions of a law amending the Constitution enter into force, they become an integral part of the Basic Law—that is, its individual provisions—while the amending law itself ceases to perform its function.

The Constitution of Ukraine does not confer on the Constitutional Court of Ukraine the authority to declare a constitutional provision invalid (визнавати нечинність), irrespective of the legal form in which that provision is embodied.

Pursuant to Article 85 § 1 (1) of the Constitution of Ukraine, the authority to amend the Constitution of Ukraine belongs specifically to the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, subject to the limits and procedure set out in Chapter XII of the Constitution.

Through its judgment [of 30 September 2010], in whose adoption V.A.
Ovcharenko took part in the adoption of the judgment but failed to safeguard the supremacy of the Constitution of Ukraine and, in effect, altered it. He violated the fundamental constitutional principle of democracy (народовладдя), changed Ukraine’s constitutional order, and infringed both the constitutional principle of the separation of powers and the legitimacy of the functioning institutions of State authority. As a result, those institutions operated on the basis of provisions modified by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine rather than by the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine, the competent authority. The manifest inconsistency between V.A. Ovcharenko’s actions in adopting the judgment [of 30 September 2010] and the oath he had taken, together with the consequences of those actions, provided the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine with grounds for treating his conduct as a breach of the oath of a judge of the Constitutional Court and removing him from office.”

27. The impugned parliamentary resolution also addressed the Constitutional Court’s judgments of 25 January 2012 and 29 May 2013. In respect of those two judgments, the Supreme Court held that the Constitutional Court had acted within its discretionary powers and that the first applicant’s involvement in their adoption did not amount to a “breach of oath”[2].

28. Turning to the procedure used to dismiss the first applicant, the Supreme Court concluded that the HAC had wrongly relied on the Rules of the Constitutional Court. Those Rules were merely an internal document of that court, which had no authority under either the Constitution or the Constitutional Court Act to establish the procedure for removing its own members. The procedure through which the first applicant was dismissed, on the other hand, complied with the Constitution and the Rules of Parliament.

Proceedings brought by the second applicant

29. On 5 March 2014, invoking the Code of Administrative Justice, the second applicant filed a claim before the HAC contesting his dismissal.

30. On 26 January 2015, the HAC rejected that claim by reference to the legal position set out by the Supreme Court in its decision of 2 December 2014 concerning the first applicant.

31. The second applicant applied to the Supreme Court for review of the case. He submitted, among other arguments, that his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010 could not justify his dismissal; that Parliament had failed to provide a fair and independent examination of the matter; that the procedure prescribed by the Rules of the Constitutional Court had not been observed; and that he could not incur liability for a judgment in favour of which he had voted as a member of the Constitutional Court.

32. On 28 April 2015, the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of 26 January 2015, reiterating the reasoning it had used in the first applicant’s case.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK

Relevant domestic law

Constitution of 28 June 1996

33.
At the relevant time, before 2 June 2016, the applicable provisions of the Constitution were formulated as follows:

Article 3

“In Ukraine, the human being—including his or her life, health, honour, dignity, inviolability and security—is acknowledged as the highest social value.

The substance and direction of State activity are defined by human rights and freedoms and the guarantees afforded to them. The State is accountable to the individual for its actions.
The State’s primary obligation is to uphold and safeguard human rights and freedoms.”

Article 19

“Ukraine’s legal order rests on the principle that no person may be compelled to perform an act that is not required by law.

State authorities, local self-government bodies, and their officials must act solely on legal grounds, within the scope of their powers, and according to the procedures established by the Constitution and laws of Ukraine.”

Article 126

“The Constitution and laws of Ukraine guarantee the independence and immunity of judges.

Any form of influence upon judges is forbidden.

Unless and until a court convicts a judge, that judge may not be detained or arrested without the consent of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.

Judges serve for an indefinite period, with the exception of judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine and persons appointed as judges for the first time.

The body that elected or appointed a judge shall remove that judge from office in any of the following circumstances:

(1) expiration of the period for which the judge was elected or appointed;

(2) the judge reaches sixty-five years of age;

(3) the judge is unable to continue performing judicial duties because of health conditions;

(4) the judge violates incompatibility requirements;

(5) the judge breaches the judicial oath;

(6) a guilty verdict against the judge enters into legal force;

(7) the judge’s citizenship is terminated;

(8) the judge is declared missing or pronounced dead;

(9) the judge submits a resignation statement or requests voluntary dismissal from office.

A judge’s authority ends upon his or her death.

The State guarantees the personal safety of judges and members of their families.”

Article 147

“The Constitutional Court of Ukraine is Ukraine’s only body exercising constitutional jurisdiction.

It determines whether laws and other legal acts conform to the Constitution of Ukraine and issues official interpretations of both the Constitution and the laws of Ukraine.”

Article 148

“The Constitutional Court of Ukraine consists of eighteen judges.

Six judges each are appointed to the Constitutional Court of Ukraine by the President of Ukraine, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, and the Congress of Judges of Ukraine.

A person may serve as a judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine if, on the date of appointment, he or she is a Ukrainian citizen who is at least forty years old, possesses a higher legal education, has no fewer than ten years of professional experience, has lived in Ukraine throughout the preceding twenty years, and is proficient in the State language.

Each judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine is appointed for nine years and may not be reappointed for another term.

At a special plenary session, the judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine elect one of their members as Chairman by secret ballot for a single three-year term.”

Article 149

“The judges of the
Judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine are protected by guarantees of independence and immunity, may be removed from office only on the grounds specified in Article 126 of this Constitution, and must comply with the incompatibility requirements established by paragraph two of Article 127 of this Constitution.

Article 150

“The powers of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine include:

1) determining whether the following conform to the Constitution of Ukraine and are therefore constitutional:

laws and other legal instruments adopted by the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine;

acts issued by the President of Ukraine;

acts issued by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine;

legal instruments adopted by the Verkhovna Rada of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.

These matters may be brought before the Court by the President of Ukraine; at least forty-five People’s Deputies of Ukraine [members of parliament]; the Supreme Court of Ukraine; the Authorised Human Rights Representative of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine; or the Verkhovna Rada of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea;

2) issuing official interpretations of the Constitution of Ukraine and the laws of Ukraine.

Decisions rendered by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine on the matters provided for in this Article are final, cannot be appealed, and must be implemented throughout the entire territory of Ukraine.”

Article 151

“At the request of the President of Ukraine or the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine issues opinions on whether international treaties of Ukraine currently in force, or international treaties submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine for approval of their binding character, comply with the Constitution of Ukraine.

At the request of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine issues an opinion as to whether the constitutional procedure for investigating and considering a case concerning the removal of the President of Ukraine from office through impeachment has been followed.”

Article 152

“On the basis of a decision by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, laws and other legal instruments may be declared unconstitutional in whole or in part if they are inconsistent with the Constitution of Ukraine or if the constitutionally prescribed procedure for their consideration, adoption, or entry into force was violated.

Any law, other legal instrument, or individual provision declared unconstitutional ceases to have legal force on the date when the Constitutional Court of Ukraine adopts its decision finding it unconstitutional.

The State shall compensate natural and legal persons, in accordance with the procedure established by law, for material or moral damage caused by acts or actions declared unconstitutional.”

Article 153

“The law shall establish the procedures governing the organisation and activities of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, as well as the procedure by which it considers cases.”

Chapter XIII

Amending the Constitution of Ukraine

Article 154

“A draft law proposing amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine may be introduced to the Verkhovna
A proposal to amend the Constitution may be introduced in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine either by the President of Ukraine or by at least one-third of the National Deputies forming its constitutional composition.

Article 155

Except for amendments concerning Chapter I—“General Principles,” Chapter III—“Elections. Referendum,” or Chapter XIII—“Introducing Amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine,” a constitutional amendment bill that has already received the support of a majority of the Verkhovna Rada’s constitutional composition shall be regarded as adopted if, during the next regular session, at least two-thirds of that constitutional composition vote for it.

Article 156

A bill amending Chapter I—“General Principles,” Chapter III—“Elections. Referendum,” or Chapter XIII—“Introducing Amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine”—may be submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine by either the President of Ukraine or at least two-thirds of the Verkhovna Rada’s constitutional composition. It must then be passed by at least two-thirds of that constitutional composition and approved in an All-Ukrainian referendum called by the President of Ukraine.

A bill proposing amendments to Chapters I, III, or XIII on the same issue may be introduced again only before the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine of the next convocation.

Article 157

No amendment may be made to the Constitution of Ukraine if it provides for the elimination or limitation of human and citizens’ rights and freedoms, seeks to abolish Ukraine’s independence, or threatens the indivisibility of its territory.

The Constitution of Ukraine may not be amended while martial law or a state of emergency is in effect.

Article 158

If the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine has considered but rejected a constitutional amendment bill, that bill may not be resubmitted until at least one year has passed from the date on which the decision concerning it was adopted.

During a single term of its authority, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine may not amend the same constitutional provisions twice.

Article 159

The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine may consider a bill proposing amendments to the Constitution of Ukraine only after the Constitutional Court of Ukraine has issued an opinion confirming whether the bill complies with the requirements of Articles 157 and 158 of this Constitution.

34.
On 2 June 2016, Parliament amended Article 149 of the Constitution, among other provisions. The amendment stipulated, in particular, that no measure of legal liability could be imposed on a Constitutional Court judge for voting in favour of judgments or opinions adopted by that court, unless the judge’s conduct constituted a criminal or disciplinary offence.

Code of Administrative Justice of 6 July 2005 (wording applicable at the material time)

35. Under Article 161 of the Code, when determining a case, an administrative court was required to establish, among other matters: (i) whether circumstances supporting the claim and objections existed and what evidence substantiated them; (ii) whether any other factual information relevant to the case existed and what evidence supported it; and (iii) which legal provision governed the legal relations in dispute.

36. Article 162 stated that, where an administrative court considered a claim well-founded, it could, among other measures, find the contested decision, act or omission unlawful; set aside or annul the decision concerned; require the defendant to perform or refrain from performing specific actions; or direct the defendant to make payments. The court could also adopt other decisions necessary to safeguard human and citizens’ rights and the rights and interests of other parties to public-law relationships.

37. Article 171-1 provided, inter alia, that Acts, actions or omissions of Parliament could be contested before the HAC. Following its examination of the case, the HAC was empowered to: (i) find an Act of Parliament unlawful in whole or in part; or (ii) find Parliament’s actions or failure to act unlawful and require it to perform specified actions. On 8 April 2014, Article 171-1 was amended to permit the HAC, in cases of that kind, also to adopt additional measures provided for in Article 162 of the Code.

38. Article 171-1 was also amended on 14 March 2014 to stipulate that, in such cases, a judgment of the HAC would take effect only after review by the Supreme Court or once the time-limit for requesting such a review had expired.

Criminal Code of 5 April 2001

39. At the relevant time, Article 375 of the Code stated:

“1. Where a judge, or judges, knowingly adopt a wrongful conviction, judgment, decision or resolution, the offence shall be punishable by restriction of liberty for up to five years or by imprisonment for a term of two to five years.

2. Where the same acts result in serious consequences or are committed for financial gain or another personal benefit, they shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to eight years.”

Constitutional Court of Ukraine Act of 16 October 1996 (in force at the relevant time)

40. Section 3 of the Act stated:

“1. The organisation, powers and operating procedure of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall be governed by the Constitution and this Act.

2.
“The Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall adopt acts [decisions] governing the organisation of its internal activities in compliance with this Act.”

41. Section 28 of the Act stipulated:

“... Judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine shall incur no legal liability for votes cast or statements made in the Constitutional Court of Ukraine or its chambers, save where an insult or defamatory statement is made during the examination of cases, the adoption of judgments or the delivery of opinions by the Constitutional Court of Ukraine.”

42. A new Constitutional Court Act was enacted on 13 July 2017. Section 24(3), which reproduces the revised wording of Article 149 of the Constitution (see paragraph 34 above), provides that no measure of legal liability may be imposed on a Constitutional Court judge for voting in favour of judgments or opinions adopted by that court, unless the judge has committed a criminal or disciplinary offence.

The High Council of Justice Act of 15 January 1998 (“the HCJ Act 1998”), in the version applicable at the relevant time

43. Section 32(2) defined a judge’s breach of oath in the following terms:

“A judge breaches his or her oath by:

(i) carrying out acts that dishonour the judicial office and are capable of casting doubt on his or her objectivity, impartiality and independence, or on the fairness and incorruptibility of the judiciary;

(ii) unlawfully acquiring wealth, or incurring expenditure exceeding his or her income and that of his or her family;

(iii) intentionally delaying the examination of a case beyond the prescribed time-limits; [or]

(iv) failing to comply with the moral and ethical principles laid down in the judicial code of conduct.”

44. In 2011, the Constitutional Court reviewed the provision quoted above and held that it was compatible with the Constitution (see paragraph 47 below).

Judiciary and Status of Judges Act 2010 (“the 2010 Judiciary Act”)

45. Section 105 sets out the procedure for removing a judge from office for breach of oath:

“1. Pursuant to paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Constitution of Ukraine, a judge shall be removed from office if he or she breaches the judicial oath.

2. The High Qualifications Commission of Judges of Ukraine or the High Council of Justice shall establish the facts demonstrating that the judge breached the oath.

3. Following consideration of the matter at a meeting conducted in accordance with [the HCJ Act], the High Council of Justice shall submit a motion for the judge’s dismissal on the ground of breach of the judicial oath.

4. Acting on a motion from the High Council of Justice, the President of Ukraine shall issue a decree dismissing the judge.

5. Acting on a motion from the High Council of Justice, the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine shall pass a resolution dismissing the judge.”

Rules of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 5 March 1997, as subsequently amended and in force at the relevant time

46.
Under paragraph 63 of the Rules, where the authority that had appointed a Constitutional Court judge raised an issue concerning that judge’s “breach of oath”, the Constitutional Court was required to investigate. On the basis of a conclusion issued by its Standing Committee on Rules and Ethics, it then had to determine whether grounds existed for dismissing the judge and notify the authority concerned of its decision within three days.

Judgment of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 11 March 2011 concerning the constitutionality of certain provisions of the High Council of Justice Act47.

Acting on an application lodged by fifty-three members of parliament, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine reviewed several provisions of the HCJ Act, including section 32(2). Regarding that provision, it observed:

“Articles 126 and 128 of the Basic Law of Ukraine regulate the procedure for appointing or electing a person as a judge and the grounds for removing that person from judicial office. All other matters relating to judges’ legal status are governed exclusively by Ukrainian legislation (paragraph 14 of [Article 92 § 1] of the Constitution of Ukraine).

A judge’s legal status encompasses both the constitutionally established guarantees of judicial independence and inviolability in the administration of justice and legal responsibility for non-performance of judicial duties. The Basic Law of Ukraine provides that a judge is to be dismissed by the authority that elected or appointed him, including where the judge has breached his oath, and that the High Council of Justice has the power to submit an application seeking a judge’s dismissal (paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 4] and paragraph 1 of [Article 131 § 1]). The procedure and grounds for lodging an application for dismissal of a judge for breach of oath are laid down in section 105 of the Judiciary Act and section 32 of [the HCJ Act].

...

Paragraph 4 of [section 54(4)] of the Judiciary Act imposes on judges a duty to observe their oath, consistent with paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Constitution of Ukraine. Accordingly, observance of the oath must be regarded as a judge’s constitutionally prescribed duty.”
Accordingly, a judge’s oath constitutes a unilateral and individual constitutional duty of a public-law nature. Public confidence in the judiciary and the administration of justice depends on judges properly performing their duties. Under paragraph 5 of [Article 126 § 5] of the Basic Law of Ukraine, violation of the judicial oath is one of the grounds on which a judge may be dismissed. Providing for dismissal as a form of liability where a judge fails to honour the oath is consistent with the 1998 European Charter on the statute for judges, paragraph 5.1 of which permits sanctions against judges who neglect a duty expressly established by the statute. Therefore, by legally specifying the criteria for liability in respect of conduct amounting to a breach of the judicial oath, the [Verkhovna Rada] of Ukraine acted within its authority and followed the procedure laid down by the Constitution and the laws of Ukraine. Consequently, section 32 of [the HCJ Act], which identifies conduct constituting a breach of a judge’s oath, is not incompatible with the Constitution of Ukraine.”

48. Relying on those considerations, the Constitutional Court held that the provision at issue was constitutional.

INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

Materials relating to the situation in Ukraine

49. In Resolution 1466 (2005), entitled “Honouring of obligations and commitments by Ukraine” and adopted on 5 October 2005, PACE declared:

“14. The Assembly reiterates the position expressed in Resolutions 1346 (2003) and 1364 (2004), in which it stressed that every provision of the Constitution currently in force must be fully observed ... . It profoundly regrets that the constitutional amendments adopted on 8 December 2004 as part of a package agreement intended to end the political unrest included provisions that the Venice Commission had repeatedly considered inconsistent with democracy and the rule of law. This was particularly so in relation to the imperative mandate of people’s deputies and the powers vested in the Prokuratura. The Assembly is further concerned that the new constitutional changes were approved without prior consultation with the Constitutional Court, despite this being required by Article 159 of the Constitution of Ukraine, as interpreted in the Constitutional Court of Ukraine’s 1998 decision. It therefore calls on the Ukrainian authorities to resolve these matters at the earliest opportunity, with a view to ensuring both the legitimacy of the constitutional amendments and their conformity with European standards.”

50. The relevant passage of Opinion no. 599/2010, “On the constitutional situation in Ukraine”, dated 20 December 2010 and adopted by the Venice Commission during its 85th Plenary Session (CDL-AD(2010)044), states:

“69. Ukraine’s recent constitutional history has been marked by recurring challenges and continuing efforts to establish an appropriate distribution of powers among the President, the Cabinet and Parliament.
Given Ukraine’s actual circumstances, it quickly became clear that the 1996 Constitution lacked adequate checks and balances and created a danger that an authoritarian presidential system might emerge. For that reason, the Venice Commission had already endorsed attempts to reform the Constitution in 2003. Those initiatives culminated in the adoption of the 2004 constitutional amendments. Although the resulting change was welcomed in principle, it was neither coherent nor sufficiently considered. Consequently, the amendments intensified tensions, particularly between the President and the Cabinet of Ministers.70. By its judgment restoring the 1996 version of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine raised questions about the legitimacy of earlier actions, because Ukrainian institutions had operated for several years under constitutional provisions that were subsequently found to be unconstitutional. The ruling also casts doubt on the legitimacy of the current state institutions, since both the President and Parliament were elected pursuant to constitutional rules that are no longer regarded as valid. Following that judgment, the President of Ukraine possesses substantially broader powers than voters could have anticipated at the time of his election. The principal state bodies now function under rules altered by a court, rather than under provisions amended by the Verkhovna Rada in its capacity as a democratically legitimate institution.”

Materials relating to judicial independence and judges’ security of tenure

The United Nations

51. The Seventh United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, held in Milan in 1985, adopted the Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary. The UN General Assembly subsequently endorsed those Principles through Resolutions 40/32 of 29 November 1985 and 40/146 of 13 December 1985. The relevant provisions state:

“8. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, judges, like all other citizens, have the rights to freedom of expression, belief, association and assembly. However, when exercising those freedoms, they must always behave in a way that safeguards the dignity of judicial office and preserves the judiciary’s impartiality and independence.

...

12. Whether selected by appointment or election, judges must be guaranteed tenure until they reach the compulsory retirement age or, where a fixed term exists, until that term expires.

...

18. A judge may be suspended or removed only on grounds of incapacity or conduct that makes the judge unable or unsuitable to perform judicial duties.

19. Every disciplinary, suspension or removal procedure must be decided in accordance with established standards governing judicial conduct.

20. Rulings made in disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings should be open to independent review. This requirement need not extend to rulings of the highest court or to decisions made by the legislature in impeachment or comparable proceedings.”

52.
The Draft Universal Declaration on the Independence of Justice (“Singhvi Declaration”), later prepared by the UN Special Rapporteur, Mr. Singhvi, develops the basic principles further:

“Discipline and Removal

26. (a) Any complaint made against a judge must be handled promptly and fairly in accordance with an appropriate procedure. At the initial stage, the judge must be given an opportunity to respond to the complaint. Unless the judge requests otherwise, the initial examination of the complaint must remain confidential.

(b) Once proceedings concerning the discipline or removal of a judge have begun, they must be conducted before a Court or a Board composed predominantly of members of the judiciary. The Legislature may nevertheless be granted the authority to remove a judge through impeachment or joint address, preferably following a recommendation from such a Court or Board.

27. Every disciplinary measure must rest on established standards governing judicial conduct.

28. Disciplinary proceedings involving judges must guarantee fairness to the judge and provide an opportunity for a full hearing.

29. Decisions issued in disciplinary proceedings against judges must be published, regardless of whether the proceedings took place in camera or in public.

30. A judge may be removed only on proven grounds of incapacity or misbehaviour that make him unfit to remain in office.”

Through Resolution 1989/32, the Commission on Human Rights called upon governments, when implementing the United Nations’ Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, to take account of the principles contained in the declaration.

53. In General Comment no. 32 concerning Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Right to equality before courts and tribunals and to a fair trial), issued on 23 August 2007, the UN Human Rights Committee stated the following, with footnotes omitted:

“19. Under Article 14, paragraph 1, the entitlement to a competent, independent and impartial tribunal is absolute and permits no exception. Independence relates particularly to the procedures and qualifications applicable to judicial appointments; safeguards securing judges’ tenure until any prescribed retirement age or until the end of their term of office, where such arrangements exist; the rules governing promotion, transfer, suspension and termination of judicial functions; and the judiciary’s genuine freedom from political interference by the executive and legislative branches. States must adopt concrete measures to secure judicial independence and protect judges from every form of political influence over their decision-making. Such protection should be established through constitutional provisions or legislation setting out clear procedures and objective criteria concerning the appointment, remuneration, tenure, promotion, suspension and dismissal of members of the judiciary, as well as disciplinary sanctions imposed upon them.”
An independent tribunal cannot exist where the roles and powers of the judiciary and the executive cannot be clearly separated, or where the executive can direct or control the judiciary. Judges must be protected from intimidation and conflicts of interest. To preserve judicial independence, the law must adequately guarantee judges’ status, including their tenure, independence, security, sufficient remuneration, service conditions, pensions, and retirement age.20. A judge may be removed only for serious misconduct or incompetence, through fair, objective, and impartial procedures prescribed by the constitution or by law. Judicial independence is violated when the executive dismisses judges—for example, before their appointed terms expire—without providing specific reasons and without access to effective judicial protection through which they may challenge their removal. The same applies, for instance, when the executive dismisses judges accused of corruption without observing any legally established procedure.”

54. In 2006, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) adopted Resolution 2006/23, entitled “Strengthening Basic Principles of Judicial Conduct”, endorsing the Bangalore Principles. Those Principles were prepared by a worldwide group of chief justices and judges of superior courts—the Judicial Integrity Group—and were designed to set standards of ethical conduct for judges. In 2010, the Judicial Integrity Group adopted the “Measures for the Effective Implementation of the Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (the Implementation Measures)”, which include the following provisions concerning judicial discipline and removal:

“Discipline of Judges

15.1  Proceedings to discipline a judge may be initiated only in cases of serious misconduct. As far as possible, the law governing judges may specify the conduct capable of attracting disciplinary sanctions and the procedures that must be followed.

...

15.5  Every disciplinary proceeding should be decided by applying established standards of judicial conduct and through a process that fully guarantees the rights of the defence.

Removal of Judges from Office

16.1  Removal of a judge from office is permissible only where there is proven incapacity, a conviction for a serious crime, gross incompetence, or conduct plainly inconsistent with the judiciary’s independence, impartiality, and integrity.

16.2  If the legislature has authority to remove a judge, it should exercise that authority only upon a recommendation for removal made by the independent body empowered to discipline judges.”

55. In 2013, the Human Rights Council, in Resolution 35/12, “Independence and impartiality of the judiciary, jurors and assessors, and the independence of lawyers”
It reaffirmed its previous position, emphasizing:

“3. ... The law must adequately protect judges’ terms of office, independence, security, sufficient remuneration, service conditions, pensions, and retirement age. Security of tenure is a fundamental safeguard of judicial independence. The legal grounds for removing judges must be expressly stated and limited to clearly defined circumstances, such as incapacity or conduct that makes them unable to perform their duties. Any procedure concerning a judge’s discipline, suspension, or removal must satisfy due-process requirements.”56

In Pastukhov v. Belarus, Communication No. 814/1998, UN Doc. CCPR/C/78/D/814/1998 (2003), the UN Human Rights Committee (CCPR) held:

“7.3  The Committee notes the author’s contention that he was not lawfully removable from judicial office because, under the law applicable at the time, he had been elected as a judge on 28 April 1994 for an 11-year term. It further observes that Presidential Decree No. 106 of 24 January 1997 did not concern replacing the Constitutional Court with a newly established court. Instead, the decree identified the author personally, and the only reason it provided for dismissing him was the purported expiration of his tenure as a Constitutional Court judge, although his term had plainly not expired. Moreover, the author had no effective judicial remedy through which to challenge his dismissal by the executive. Given these circumstances, the Committee concludes that removing the author from his office as a Constitutional Court judge several years before the end of his appointed term undermined judicial independence and violated his right to access public service in his country on general conditions of equality.”
